3
Furthermore, auto-injectors vary markedly in their physical appearance . These differences stem
in part from the operation features (i .e., a single-dose pre-filled auto-injector looks considerably
different than one packaged as an un-filled auto-injector for use with two or more cartridges of
medication). Even auto-injectors that operate similarly can vary significantly in size, color, and
shape.
1 .2. Many Auto-Injectors are Designed to Treat Life-Threatening Conditions .
Drug and biologics manufacturers are increasingly relying on auto-injection technology because
many therapeutic agents, particularly biological agents, are not well-suited to oral administration .
In other cases, self-administration is critical . Auto-injectors offer physicians and their patients
opportunities for rapid and effective administration of therapeutic agents without intervention
from trained medical personnel. Many auto-injectors are thus developed to treat emergency, life-
threatening conditions such as anaphylaxis, where the time and difficulty of preparing and using
a familiar syringe (or even a pen injector requiring manual operation) could make a critical
difference in survival . 12 Other auto-injectors are designed to treat conditions where rapid relief
during a compromised state is essential, such as treatment of severe migraines or seizures that
affect individuals' ability to manage medication administration .13 Still others are being designed
as reliable methods to administer biological products . 14
Auto-injectors used to treat life-threatening conditions are typically designed for potentially
recurrent but irregular use. For instance, some individuals at risk of anaphylaxis may never have
to use an auto-injector if they avoid allergens, or may only use an auto-injector once every
several years. Nonetheless, such individuals must be prepared to use an auto-injector when the
need arises, even if at a moment far removed from an initial training in use of the auto-injector .
1.3. Release Mechanisms and Physical Characteristics of Auto-Injectors Play a
Crucial Role in Ensuring Effective Administration .
Because auto-injectors are typically used by patients or caregivers rather than trained medical
personnel, proper instruction in use of the auto-injector is critical to ensure that the drug products
are safe and effective in life-threatening or disabling situations . 1 5
Auto-injector manufacturers rely on clearly-distinguishing physical characteristics and
instructions with graphic illustrations to help ensure effective administration of the drug product
and to facilitate proper training in use of an auto-injector . (See Exhibits A to E for examples of
auto-injector operating instructions .) Most obviously, an auto-injector must be pointed in the
right direction. Unlike syringes, auto-injector needles are typically retracted and therefore not
visible prior to use of the auto-injector . Reversing the direction of an auto-injector would dela y
12 See, e.g., EpiPen Patient Package Inse rt; Twinject Patient Package Insert .
13 See, e.g., Imitrex STATdose System ® Patient Package Insert .
14 See, e,g., Serono One -ClicO Pen - Manufacturer's Insert.
15 FDA acknowledged the importance of effective training in a May 2004 video safety message regarding use of
epinephrine auto-injectors . . FDA noted that "patients may not always be well trained on how to use these devices, or
they may not remember what to do in an emergency ." FDA therefore offered a step -by-step review of how to use the
EpiPen® to deliver a single dose of epinephrine . See FDA, Teaching Patients to Use EPIPEN, available at
http://www.accessdata .fda .jzov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/psn/transcript .cfm?show=27 .
4
administration of drug product to the intended site of action or cause injury by triggering the
release of the syringe in an unintentional direction. To help distinguish the proper direction and
limit the potential for inappropriate administrations, auto-injector manufacturers typically rely on
one or more safety caps and color-coding .
For instance, the EpiPen® uses a spring-loaded auto-injector activated by applying pressure to
the front end of the unit .16 Therefore, to help avoid improper use, the EpiPeri label instructs
patients to grasp the auto-injector with the gray safety release cap toward the thumb while
pointing the black tip toward the thigh. Patients are instructed to "never put thumb, fingers, or
hand over black tip" because the needle comes out of the black tip and because accidental
injection may result in loss of blood flow.17 (The EpiPen Patient Package Insert is attached as
Exhibit A.)
In contrast, the Anapen auto-injector approved for use in the U .K., which delivers the same doses
of epinephrine in the same strengths for the same indication as the EpiPen® and EpiPen® Jr .
marketed in the U.S ., operates in an entirely different fashion . The Anapen is operated by a firing
button on the rear end of the auto-injector rather than applying pressure to the injection tip.
Whereas the EpiPeri instructions warn patients never to touch the black tip that houses the
needle, the Anapen requires that patients remove both a black needle cap as well as a black
safety cap that exposes a red firing button.18 While the EpiPen® requires that patients press the
auto-injector into the thigh to activate the injector, the Anapen requires that patients hold the
auto-injector in place against the thigh and then press a firing button . (Operating instructions for
the Anapen are attached as Exhibit D .)
1.4. Substitution of Auto-Injectors is Potentially Unsafe.
The potential for improper use of auto-injectors and the wide variety in operation and design of
auto-injectors raise significant safety concerns about the potential for substituting one auto-
injector drug product for another. Unless a patient is made fully aware of the differences between
two auto-injectors and is sufficiently trained in operation of a different auto-injector, patients
would be confused in a life-threatening or disabling situation . For instance, patients accustomed
to the EpiPeri pressure-triggered auto-injector and its warning never to touch the black tip
would be substantially confused if they were given a substitute auto-injector such as the Anapen,
which uses black caps on both ends and requires that patients press a firing button to activate the
unit. Similarly, significant differences in color-coding such as a reversal of the colors used for a
safety cap and a firing end of an auto-injector could inadvertently prompt a patient to hold an
auto-injector in the wrong direction, thereby rendering the auto-injector ineffective and
potentially causing harm if injected into a patient's fingers or thumb .
The potential for safety concerns is magnified by the public's education in the use of generic
drugs. Through an effective campaign promoting use of generic drugs, the public has been taught
that generic drugs are the same as branded drugs and that they work the same as branded drugs .19
16 EpiPen® Patient Package Insert .
►7 Id.
18 See operating instructions for Anapen auto-injector .
19 See, e.g., OGD, FDA, FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS ABOUT GENERIC DRUGS, available at
http://www.fda.gov/cder/consumerinfo/generics q&a .htm .
5
Consequently, patients who have begun a drug regimen either with a brand product or with a
particular generic product will not undertake any independent effort to read the labeling and
instructions for a substitute product but will instead assume they can continue to take their
medications in the same manner as the prior drug product with "total confidence . ,20
Similarly, patients obtaining re-fills of an auto-injector prescription will expect that a re-fill will
work in the same manner as the earlier drug product . Perhaps for this reason, FDA, to our
knowledge, has yet to approve an auto-injector under an ANDA or otherwise designate an auto-
injector drug product as therapeutically equivalent to another auto-injector product .
Consequently, each auto-injector product must be individually prescribed. Two auto-injector
products are not, and should not be, substitutable for one another.
1.5. Auto-Injectors are Different than Oral Drug Products and Other Combination
Products Because of the Way Differences Among Auto-Injectors Directly
Affect the Ability of Patients to Safely and Effectively Use Drug Products
Containing Auto-Injectors.
FDA has long approved copies of oral drug products and designated them therapeutically
equivalent to their brand or other generic counter-parts .21 More recently, FDA has approved, and
designated as therapeutically equivalent, copies of combination products such as transdermal
patches . However, substitution of drug products in these dosage forms does not present any
significant risk of confusion-induced safety and effectiveness problems ; differences in
appearance or release mechanisms are either invisible to the patient or irrelevant to proper
administration of the drug product .22
By contrast, as described above, differences in physical characteristics and release mechanisms
among auto-injectors will have a direct impact on safe and effective administration of the drug
product. Therefore, FDA should refuse to approve drug products containing an auto-injector
under an ANDA or otherwise make a therapeutic equivalence designation for such products,
unless FDA can ensure that the risks of problems in safety and effectiveness related to patient
confusion in a life-threatening or disabling situation are de minimis . Failure to provide this
assurance would result in an increase in ineffectual administration of drug products containing
auto-injectors as well as adverse events, which could thereby put patients' lives at risk .
20 "Generic Drugs: What You Need to Know," FDA Consumer Magazine, September-October 2002, available
at http://www.fda.gov/fdac/features/2002/502 generic.html (quoting Office of Generic Drugs Director Gary
Buehler) .
21 See OFFICE OF GENERIC DRUGS, FDA, APPROVED DRUGS WITH THERAPEUTIC EQUIVALENCE EVALUATIONS
iii (27"' ed. 2007) [hereinafter ORANGE BOOK] .
22 For instance, though differences related to release mechanisms in transdermal patches may be reflected in the
"Description" section of the label, these products can have identical patient instructions because the differences are
invisible to the patient and irrelevant to proper administration . Compare labeling for Duragesic0 (fentanyl) Patch,
Extended Release, available at http://dailvmed.nlm.nih. ov~ /dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?id=1436, with labeling for the
generic Fentanyl Transdermal System (fentanyl) Patch, available at
http://dailymed.nlm.nih. ovg /dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?id=3851 .
6
2. Drug Products Containing an Auto-Injector Should Not Be Approved
Under an ANDA or Designated Therapeutically Equivalent Unless the
proposed Auto-Injector is the "Same" as the Auto-Injector Contained
in the RLD.
There may be instances in which the ANDA approval pathway is suitable for some drug products
containing auto-injectors . To date, however, King is not aware of any auto-injector that has been
approved under an ANDA. Nor, to King's knowledge, has the Agency ever designated an y
product containing an auto-injector as therapeutically equivalent to another product .
There is no FDA guidance on how the ANDA approval pathway would apply to drug products
containing auto-injectors . While FDA does provide direction on the types of bioequivalence
studies required for certain non-oral dosage forms, such as "nasally administered drug products"
and "transdermal delivery systems," FDA does not provide any such direction for auto-
injectors .23 Similarly, FDA's May 2007 publication of Critical Path Opportunities for Generic
Drugs fails to make any mention of auto-injectors .24 The absence of such guidance may reflect
an internal conclusion by the Agency that the ANDA pathway is not suitable for products
containing auto-injectors ; or it may reflect that the Agency has not yet had an opportunity to
consider the unique regulatory issues posed by auto-injector products . In either event, this
Petition presents the Agency with an opportunity to publicly clarify the appropriate procedures to
be followed in the approval of auto-injector products .
Unlike 505(b)(2), which permits approval of a~roduct that is different than an RLD,25 the
guiding principle of an ANDA is "sameness."2 The FFDCA and FDA regulations27 require that

2.1. To Be Approved Under an ANDA or To Be Designated Therapeutically
Equivalent, a Proposed Drug Product Containing an Auto-Injector Should
Operate in Identical Fashion When Used by Patients and Caregivers and Meet
Identical Drug Delivery Performance Standards.
Consistent with general guidance for regulation of combination products,41 drug products
containing auto-injectors should be approved under an ANDA or considered to be therapeutically
equivalent only if the auto-injector operates identically and meets identical performance
specifications, as described below in relation to established regulatory criteria.
2.1.1. Same Active Ingredients
Regulations specify that the same active ingredients requirement for dosage forms such as
"prefilled syringes where residual volume may vary" means that such products must "deliver
identical amounts of the active drug ingredient over the identical dosing period."42 Auto-injector
design varies considerably regarding the quantity of solution used in the auto-injector and the
proportion that is dispensed upon activation . Consequently, an auto-injector should not be
approved as pharmaceutically equivalent to another auto-injector, and should not be approved
under an ANDA, unless the two auto-injectors are demonstrated to deliver identical amounts of
the active ingredients in an identical dispensing time based on comparative performance testing
of the auto-injectors .

2.1.2. Identical Dosage Form
Given the variety of auto-injectors, FDA's current dosage form classification for injectable
products does not comply with FDA's own standards of sufficiently distinguishing products with
real differences without being product-specific .43 Although FDA has classified oral and topical
dosage forms according to numerous fine distinctions, the Orange Book recognizes only three
injectable dosage forms: "injectable"; "injectable, lipid complex"; and "injectable, liposomal ."44
FDA states that a dosage form is based "on a drug product's physical appearance and the way the
drug is administered."45 Clearly, auto-injectors have a physical appearance distinguishable from
injectable drug products used with standard syringes, which are typically distributed in vials or
pouches. Auto-injectors are also administered differently than injectable products intended for
use with a traditional syringe because auto-injectors use various automated release mechanisms
activated by patients or caregivers rather than trained medical personnel . As described above
(and illustrated in Exhibits A to E), there is also considerable variation among auto-injectors .
FDA should establish new auto-injector dosage forms that distinguish among auto-injectors with
significant differences in administration and physical appearance as well as distinguish auto-
injectors from other injectable dosage forms. Injectable dosage forms could thereby achieve an
appropriate level of classification more consistent with the classification of oral and topical
products .
At a minimum, dosage forms for drug products containing auto-injectors should distinguish
pressure-activated auto-injectors from those that require use of a firing button, and pre-filled
fully-assembled auto-injectors from multiple-dose auto-injectors or auto-injectors equipped with
cartridges requiring assembly . These and similar distinctions among auto-injector dosage form s

changes in release mechanism or use of a new release mechanism.47 FDA does not need to have

approval of an ANDA .48 Rather, the Agency need only have a "reasonable basis to conclude that
one or more of the inactive ingredients of the proposed drug or its composition raises serious
questions of safety or efficacy ."49 As indicated above, differences in the way auto-injectors

make a difference in patient or caregiver administration of the drug product .

Be "the Same" Does Not Permit Differences in Operating Instructions or
Graphic Illustrations .
FDA regulations require that drug products approved under section 505(j) have "the same"
labelin9 as the RLD, which includes the container label as well as the package insert and patient

in route of administration, dosage form, strength, or use of a substituted active ingredient in a
combination drug may be permissible only if the FDA approved a suitability petition under 21
C.F.R. § 314.94. Additional differences in labeling may relate to expiration date, formulation,
bioavailability, requirements im~osed by FDA, or statements in the RLD labeling protected by
patent or accorded exclusivity .5

types of combination products could have a substantial adverse effect on proper administration
of an auto-injector and should therefore not be allowed . For instance, changes to the RLD's
labeling for a drug product containing an auto-injector with a different release mechanism and
different physical appearance should not be permissible as mere "minor aspects of labeling"54 if

2.3. A Drug Product Containing an Auto-Injector May Satisfy the Bioequivalence
Requirement By Demonstrating Identical Performance.
FDA regulations provide that bioequivalence may be self-evident for certain drug products
provided that "other data in the application" support such a finding and that the drug product
meets one of several sets of criteria, including "a parenteral solution intended solely for
administration by injection."57 The waiver of in vivo bioequivalence studies for injectable drug
products that use traditional syringes is therefore based not only on the nature of the parenteral
solution and its administration by injection but also the particular manner in which it is injected.
The bioequivalence of parenteral solutions in the form of vials or pouches is self-evident because
it is understood that the approved drug product will be properly administered by trained medical
personnel.
By contrast, the parenteral solution waiver should only apply to drug products containing auto-
injectors in the presence of "other data"58 in the form of comparative performance testing. Such
testing should show that the auto-injector used in a proposed drug product will (i) deliver the
same amount of drug (ii) to the same area (iii) in the same amount of time (iv) with the same
force (v) under similar conditions .

recommendations should be adopted only in accordance with FDA's recently-published process

3. Approval of an Auto-Injector under Section 505(b)(2) or through a
Suitability Petition Under Section 505(j) Should Require Clinical
Studies to Demonstrate the Safety and Effectiveness of a Proposed
Auto-Injector.
Differences among auto-injectors regarding release mechanisms and physical appearance can
significantly affect safe and effective use of an auto-injector and proper administration of a drug
product. If an auto-injector cannot be demonstrated to be the same as the auto-injector contained
in an RLD, and therefore eligible for review and approval under an ANDA, appropriate clinical
studies should be conducted to ensure that the proposed auto-injector will administer the drug
product as indicated in its labeling .
Existing regulations and guidance documents do not identify or explain the required clinical
studies for (i) a drug product containing an auto-injector that (ii) is submitted for approval under
Section 505(b)(2) or according to a suitability petition under Section 505(j), and that (iii)
references an existing auto-injector with the same active ingredients and for the same indication ;
but which (iv) does not contain the same auto-injector sufficient for approval under Section
505(j) without a suitability petition .
Generally, these types of drug products should be required to conduct a clinical study to assess
the safety and efficacy of an auto-injector when used by patients with live drug under the
conditions for which the auto-injector is intended . There may be circumstances in which this
type of clinical study is neither ethical nor feasible . However, because many auto-injectors are
intended for emergency use in life-threatening situations or for use in disabling states such as
severe migraines or onset of seizure, effective administration of the drug product cannot be
assured unless a particular auto-injector has been shown to be suitable and reliable for the
intended use .
FDA should therefore develop and disseminate guidance that describes the types of clinical
studies that may be necessary to obtain approval for a drug product containing an auto-injector as
well as the circumstances under which such studies are required .
4. Conclusion
Current regulations and guidance documents do not address the issues presented by drug
products containing auto-injectors . Designating these products- as therapeutically equivalent
raises serious safety concerns because differences in physical appearance and release
mechanisms among auto-injectors will have a significant impact on safe and effective use of an
auto-injector by patients and caregivers.
Consequently :
Drug products containing auto-injectors should neither be approved under Section 505(j)
nor designated therapeutically equivalent unless an auto-injector is shown to be the
"same" as the auto-injector contained in the RLD ;

B. Statement of Grounds
Background
MARINOL is approved in the United States for two separate indications : the treatment
of nausea and vomiting associated with cancer chemotherapy in patients who have failed to
respond adequately to conventional treatments (the CINV Indication) and the treatment of
appetite loss associated with weight loss in patients with A IDS (the AIDS Indication).
MARINOL is marketed by Unimed and has annual U .S. sales of approximately $145 million .
The active ingredient in MARINOL is dronabinol, a synthetic version of a naturally occurring
compound known as delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (delta-9-THC). Delta-9-THC is an
endogenous chemical component of the marijuana plant, Cannabis sativa L .
MARINOL was a product of the cooperation between Unimed and the National Cancer
Institute, which conducted clinical research on dronabinol for the treatment of nausea and
vomiting associated with cancer chemotherapy in patients who have failed to respond adequately
to conventional antiemetic treatments . FDA approved Unimed's new drug application (NDA) for
MARINOL for the CINV Indication in 1985 . This indication is no longer afforded any patent
protection or market exclusivity.
In 1991, dronabinol received orphan drug designation for appetite loss associated wit h
weight loss in patients with AIDS . Unimed received supplemental NDA approval for
MARINOL's AIDS Indication in December 1992 . The quantity of MARINOL dispensed for the
AIDS Indication represents the largest market segment, with A IDS patients being approximately
two-thirds of the MARINOL market in terms of prescriptions (based on IMS Health
Incorporated data - July 2006 to June 2007) .

1) Labeling For a Generic Version of MARINOL without the AIDS
Indication Will Be Misleading
As a threshold matter, Unimed does not challenge FDA's general authority to approve a
generic drug with "carved out" labeling and acknowledges that FDA's authority to do so has
been upheld generally by the courts . See Sigma-Tau Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v . Schwetz, 288 F.3d
141 (4th Cir. 2002); Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Shalala, 91 F.3d 1493 (D.C. Cir. 1996) .
Unimed also acknowledges that FDA "does not regulate . . .the possible substitution of a generic

(citations omitted)
Rather, as discussed herein, Unimed's contention is that, with regard to MARINOL, in
particular, FDA should require a generic version of MARINOL to contain the A IDS Indication
and important related safety information . To not require this would cause the product and patient
labeling to be misleading and in violation of sections 352(a) and 321(n) of the FD&C Act . This
argument is not foreclosed by the decisions in the Bristol-Myers Squibb and Sigma-Tau cases. In
both cases, the issue before the court was whether FDA's approval of a generic product wit h
exclusivity-protected labeling "carved out" was consistent with the ANDA approval provision s
of the FD&C Act in 21 U.S .C. § 355(j). In both cases, there was no discussion of false an d
misleading labeling or FD&C Act sections 352(a) and 321(n) .
FDA's authority to approve a generic product with "carved out" labeling must be read in
conjunction with the provisions of the FD&C Act, taken as a whole . In particular, it must be
read in conjunction with 21 U .S.C. § 352(a), which states that a drug is deemed misbranded if it s
labeling is "false or misleading in any particular ."
Regarding "misleading," the FD&C Act provides :
If an article is alleged to be misbranded because the
labeling or advertising is misleading, then in determining whether
the labeling or advertising is misleading there shall be taken into
account (among other things) not only representations made by or
suggested by statement, word, design, device, or any combination
thereof, but also the extent to which the labeling or advertising
fails to reveal facts material in light of such representations or
material with respect to consequences which may result from the
use of the article to which the labeling or advertising relates under
the conditions of use prescribed in the labeling or advertising

21 U.S .C. § 321(n) (emphasis added) .
The statutory language of section 321(n) is clear. If a product's labeling fails to reveal
material facts concerning the consequences that may result from use of the product under
customary or usual conditions of use, the product's labeling is misleading and thus the product i s
misbranded .
Due to the substantially different daily dose, timing of administration, duration o f
treatment, and likelihood of CNS adverse effects for the A IDS Indication as opposed to the
CINV Indication, MARINOL labeling with information concerning the AIDS Indication "carve d
out" would fail to reveal material facts concerning the consequences that may result from the us e
of MARINOL (hereinafter discussed).
Furthermore, there is no need to speculate about what the "customary or usual" use of a
generic version of MARINOL will be . As a matter of state formulary laws and despite th e
"carve out," it is certain that the generic drug will be dispensed for use as an appetite stimulant
for AIDS patients (as hereinafter discussed) . As noted above, this use of MARINOL account s
for two-thirds of the patients for whom MARINOL is prescribed and is properly considered the
drug's most "customary or usual" condition of use .
With regard to section 321(n), it is important to note that Congress used the word "or" t o
indicate that both the conditions of use prescribed in the labeling, as well as "such conditions o f
use as are customary or usual," must be examined separately. In addition, Regulation 21 C.F.R .
§ 201 .5(a) makes explicit that, in determining the adequacy of a drug's directions for use,

Indication .

a

CITIZEN PETITION
Warner Chilcott Inc. submits this petition in accordance with 21 C.F.R. § 10.20 and § 10 .30
regarding the acceptance for filing, review, and approval by the Commissioner of the Food
and Drug Administration (the "Commissioner") of abbreviated new drug applications
("ANDAs") for 0.4 mg Norethindrone (NE) and 35 µg Ethinyl Estradiol (EE) oral chewable
tablet products that list OVCON-35® Fe (now called Femcon® Fe) 28-day 0 .4 mg NE and 35
µg EE chewable tablets (NDA 21-490, referred to herein as the "Chewable Tablets") as the
reference listed drug. The petition requests that the Commissioner refrain from taking
administrative action regarding the approval of all such ANDAs in which bioequivalence has
not been established to the Ovcon-35 28-day oral tablet formulation (NDA 17-716, hereby
referred to as Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets) and to the Chewable Tablets, and that does not include
an oral irritation study showing equivalence to the Chewable Tablets .
As described in detail below, this action is requested to ensure that there is sufficient data
within the ANDA application to demonstrate that the generic formulation of 0 .4 mg NE and
35 µg EE chewable tablets is therapeutically equivalent to a marketed formulation, i .e.,
Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets, for which safety and efficacy have been previously determined
through clinical testing, as well as to the product for which it will be designated as being
substitutable, the Chewable Tablets .
A . Action Requested
By this petition the undersigned requests that the Commissioner stay final approval and/or
effective date of final approval of any 0.4 mg NE and 35 µg EE chewable tablet ANDAs
unless there is pharmaceutical equivalence and compliance with the applicable bioequivalence
regulations, specifically, 21 C.F.R. § 320, and, as amended Section 505(j)(8) of the Federal
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act ("FDCA") . Complete bioequivalence testing ensures the
generic version has the same clinical effect and is as safe as the innovator product . The new
drug application ("NDA") for the Chewable Tablets was approved based on data from a
bioequivalence study comparing the Chewable Tablets to Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets and an ora l

The requested actions for demonstration of bioequivalence for ANDAs of 0 .4 mg NE and 35
µg EE tablets, either oral or chewable, is based on the following :
I
The Chewable Tablets were approved on the basis of a bioequivalence study
comparing the chewable tablets (chewed) to Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets (swallowed), both
followed by 240 ml of water and a clinical study assessing the potential for irritation

I
The Chewable Tablets were approved as a new drug on the basis of information filed
in an NDA. However, no clinical efficacy and safety trials have been conducted for
this formulation; and
I
The Chewable Tablets were approved on the basis of bioequivalence data for both
chewed and swallowed methods of administration .
B. Statement of Grounds
1 . Regulatory History
Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets (NDA 17-716) were approved based on a new drug development
package of data including evidence of safety and efficacy . The Chewable Tablets, developed
as an alternative for potentially improved compliance, was approved on the basis of a
bioequivalence study comparing the Chewable Tablets to Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets, as well as a
targeted study assessing the potential for irritation of the oral mucosa by the chewable tablets .
As there had been no major safety or efficacy issues with Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets, FDA
reviewers agreed that it was reasonable to assume the same efficacy and safety profile for the
new, chewable formulation . FDA reviewers concluded that "a large clinical trial was not
needed since the Chewable Tablets is only a new formulation of norethindrone and ethinyl
estradiol that was shown to be bioequivalent to an approved combination hormonal
contraceptive product (Ovcon(& 35)"1 that had a long history of safe and effective use .
Because no Phase 3 clinical studies were done in support of the Chewable Tablets, this
formulation does not have an independently characterized efficacy and safety profile . Rather,
its safety and efficacy has been cross-referenced to the original formulation of Ovcon-35 Oral
Tablets through the demonstration of bioequivalence .

2. Demonstration of Bioequivalence
The Chewable Tablets can either be chewed and swallowed or swallowed whole . In the case
when the tablets are chewed, it is necessary to drink water or other fluids after chewing . This
ensures that chewed fragments of the Chewable Tablets reliably reach the stomach and are
absorbed. Accordingly, dosing for bioequivalence testing included immediately consuming 8
ounces of fluid after the tablets were chewed. Because bioequivalence testing was conducted
under these conditions, such instructions also are explicit in the Dosage and Administration
directions of the package insert .
The direct demonstration of bioequivalence of the Chewable Tablets (chewed) and Ovcon-35
Oral Tablets (swallowed) did not include a pharmacokinetic comparison of the two
formulations where both were swallowed, i .e., the Chewable Tablets swallowed intact was not
directly compared to Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets swallowed . Rather, formulation comparison and
in vitro dissolution data supported the proposed labeling for the Chewable Tablets, which may
be swallowed whole without chewing .
3 . Potential Importance of Bioequivalence Drift
Pharmacokinetic bioequivalence between an innovator drug and a generic formulation is a
necessary criterion for making a conclusion of therapeutic equivalence without proving such
equivalence with clinical determinations of efficacy and safety2 . Bioequivalence between
drug formulation B (generic) and drug formulation A (innovator) supports the assumption that
the therapeutic properties (efficacy and safety) of formulation B, though untested, are
equivalent to those previously demonstrated for formulation A . However, the assumed
therapeutic link between products demonstrated by bioequivalence testing is recognized to
suffer from the potential limitation of bioequivalence drift3 . According to the concept of
bioequivalence drift, sequential alterations in formulation, manufacturing process or other
variables may create a situation whereby consecutive formulations remain bioequivalent but
the latest vs. initial formulations may not prove bioequivalent . In such a situation, the
presumption of therapeutic equivalence between the latest and initial formulations, i .e., the
product that demonstrated safety and efficacy in well-controlled clinical trials in the patient
population may not be valid .
The Chewable Tablets represents a formulation change from Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets for
which the conclusion of therapeutic equivalence has been established through demonstration
of bioequivalence. However, a subsequent formulation change to a new version of chewable
tablets could potentially introduce sufficient bioequivalence drift to invalidate the implied
assumption of therapeutic equivalence with the initial swallowed drug formulation . Since
therapeutic efficacy of this product is all or none (pregnancy prevention or failure), it would
be imprudent to assume the link between pharmacokinetic and therapeutic equivalence to any

other reference product than Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets for which clinical properties have been
objectively determined.
4. Manufacturing Issue s
The Chewable Tablets is an immediate-release formulation . In the approval documents,
FDA's chemistry reviewer stressed the importance of "in process control or regulatory
specifications" to ensure lot uniformity, and further noted "important parameters" to
characterize the chewable formulation . Generic formulations of the Chewable Tablets could
potentially have unexpected properties of efficacy and/or safety if process control is not
sufficient to ensure lot uniformity.
5. Safety Considerations
The Chewable Tablets were investigated in an oral safety study to characterize the risk of
irritation to the oral soft tissues . Mimicking the daily oral dosing regimen for this drug, the
oral safety trial was a single cycle, 21-day multiple dose study . A detailed protocol, involving
scoring of irritation, inflammation, abrasions and infection at multiple oral sites, was
necessary to demonstrate the absence of product-related oral adverse reactions. Given the
chronic exposures necessary for successful oral contraception, equivalent tolerability of a
generic formulation of the Chewable Tablets could only be established by similar clinical
testing of irritation potential .
As with all safety studies, it can be difficult to assess causality of observed adverse effects . In
the case of the oral irritation study conducted for the Chewable Tablets, two aphthous ulcers
were concluded to be unlikely related to use of the tablets4 . Since the clinical investigator was
not able to discount the remote possibility that the tablets may have contributed to the ulcers,
it would be prudent for a generic formulation of the Chewable Tablets to evaluate this
potential risk, as well as others, with a cross-over comparative trial . In this way it would be
possible to conclude that oral irritation and other oral risks from the generic formulation were
not worse than with the original formulation .
6 . Overall Conclusions
The Chewable Tablets was approved as a new drug, yet clinical efficacy and safety trials were
not conducted for this formulation. Rather, its therapeutic characteristics were assumed by
reference to the non-chewable formulation, Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets . Any similar assumptions
of therapeutic properties of a generic formulation of the Chewable Tablets would only be
scientifically supportable if bioequivalence has been established with the reference listed drug
for which efficacy and safety are known, i.e. Ovcon-35 Oral Tablets, as well as with the
Chewable Tablets. Without such direct evidence of similarity, bioequivalence drift could

create the situation in which the generic chewable formulation was no longer therapeutically
equivalent to a reference listed drug of know clinical characteristics .
In bioequivalence testing of a generic formulation of the Chewable Tablets, which, by
regulation requires identical labeling (i.e., may be administered by chewing or swallowing
without chewing), it is scientifically justified to require swallowing with liquids after chewing
to ensure reliable dosing . It is also scientifically justified to require that evidence be
presented of bioequivalence of a generic of the Chewable Tablets when taken by swallowing
without chewing .
In oral safety testing of a generic formulation of the Chewable Tablets, irritation scores and
specific risks such as aphthous ulcers should be evaluated via cross-over oral irritation
studies, with the requirement that the generic formulation prove no worse than the innovator
product .
To further support the assumption of substitutability of a generic the Chewable Tablets, it is
furthermore justified to require that manufacturing process control and release specifications
match those of the Chewable Tablets.
C. Environmental Impact
An environmental assessment report on the action requested in this petition is not required
under 21 CFR §25 .3 1 .

economic indicators will be submitted only if requested by the Commissioner .

Biological Aspects 
Monosodium Glutamate is an amino acid readily utilized by glutamate receptors 
throughout the mammalian body. 
These glutamate receptors are present in the central 
nervous system as the major mediators of excitatory neurotransmission and excitotoxicity. 
Neural injury associated with trauma, stroke, epilepsy, and many neurodegenerative 
diseases such as Alzheimer's, Huntington's and Parkinson's diseases and amyotrophic 
lateral sclerosis may be mediated by excessive activation of the glutamate receptors . 
Neurotoxicity associated with excitatory amino acids encountered in food, such as 
monosodium glutamate, has also been linked to glutamate receptors . Glutamate receptors 
are found in the rat and monkey heart, the conducting system, nerve terminals and cardiac 
ganglia . They are also present in the kidney, liver, lung, spleen and testis . Therefore, food 
safety assessment should consider these tissues as potential target sites.

application ("NDA") for Lotrel* (amlodipine besylate ; benazepril hydrochloride), until 
after Pfizer's pediatric exclusivity for amlodipine has expired on September 25, 2007 .

The effective date of approval of any sNDAs for Lotrel* concerning the 
amlodipine ingredient in Lotrel8 should be deferred until after September 25, 2007,

Pfizer's amlodipine IND and NDA, effective midnight, March 25, 2007 . (Citizen

this revocation Novartis's Lotrelt NDA became an application under section 505(b)(2), 
subject to Pfizer's pediatric exclusivity for amlodipine . Moreover, any supplement to the 
Lotrel* NDA must also be considered as an NDA under section 505(b)(2) subject to 
pediatric exclusivity . 
Thus, as explained more fully in the Citizen Petition, FDA should defer the 
effective date of approval of any sNDA for LotrelS concerning the amlodipine ingredient 
in Lotrel* until after the expiration of the pediatric exclusivity period for amlodipine . 
Until now, Pfizer has been supplying amlodipine to Novartis for use in manufacturing

however, Pfizer is no longer supplying amlodipine to Novartis . Thus, Pfizer expects that 
Novartis may seek FDA approval for a manufacturing supplement in order to substitute 
an alternative amlodipine source .' FDA should defer the effective date of any such 
supplement until after September 25, 2007 . 
As set forth below, this Petition for Stay of Action satisfies the requirements for a 
mandatory grant of a stay under agency regulations . 21 CFR § 10.35(e) . 
The petitioner will otherwise suffer irreparable injury . Pfizer faces imminent, 
substantial and irreparable injury in the absence of a stay. Pfizer holds the NDA for

the monetary reward to which Pfizer is statutorily entitled after expending substantial 
efforts on studies of the safety and efficacy of its product in children .

have been "studied for their safety and effectiveness in treating serious or life-threatening
illnesses and that provide meaningful therapeutic benefit to patients over existing treatments ."lo

and the traditional FDA bioequivalence parameters (C max and AUC) are unlikely to predict the
pharmacodynamic impact of differences in plasma drug concentrations . While FDA's standard
of bioequivalence, requiring Cmax and AUC to show 90% confidence intervals within 80-125%
of the reference drug, is generally adequate to assure bioequivalence, in the case of extended-
release sedative hypnotics, which not only require early sleep induction and sleep maintenance ,

but alertness upon awakening, these parameters alone may not be adequate. FDA should rely
upon more specific pharmacokinetic parameters to assure generics to AMBIEN CR will b e

clinically equivalent. Sanofi-aventis suggests that generics demonstrate equivalence as a

awakening.
II. Brief Statement of Grounds
Pursuant to section 505(j)(2)(A)(iv) of the FDCA, any ANDA must contain, among other
things, information demonstrating that the generic drug is bioequivalent to the reference listed
drug ("RLD").' In most instances, FDA will statistically evaluate two pharmacokinetic
parameters -- area under the plasma concentration curve (AUC) and the peak drug concentration
(Cmax) -- to determine bioequivalence .2 According to the FDA, to establish bioequivalence, the
calculated 90% confidence interval for the ratios comparing the average AUC and Cmax values
between the generic applicant and the RLD should fall within the traditional bioequivalence limi t
~
of 80% to 125 %.3 In response to citizen petitions requesting that the agency impose additional
bioequivalence requirements, FDA has consistently defended its traditional bioequivalence
parameters, studies, and testing procedures. Although the agency has acknowledged the
importance of evaluating other pharmacokinetic parameters, such as Cn, ;n, Ct, Tmax, and Tlag, to
determine bioequivalence with respect to certain classes of drugs, FDA has not strayed so far
from its traditional evaluation methods as to require rigid statistical analysis for such parameters .
Due to the nature of AMBIEN CR's formulation, its sleep induction and maintenance
indications, and the specific safety concerns associated with hypnotic therapy, the current FDA
requirements that only CmaX and AUC need to be presented as a demonstration of bioequivalence
are insufficient to ensure that generic versions of AMBIEN CR are therapeutically equivalent to
AMBIEN CR. Based on the FDA requirements for bioequivalence, it is highly conceivable that
a generic formulation of AMBIEN CR with a different pharmacokinetic profile ("shape of the
curve") could be approved as a bioequivalent and substitutable generic product .

The AMBIEN CR formulation differs in important ways from most extended release
products. Generally, extended release preparations are developed with the primary goal of
reducing the number of daily doses needed to sustain an effect of a chronically administered drug
product that is rapidly cleared from the system. This fosters improved compliance and reduces
the incidence of adverse effects associated with peak plasma concentrations and periods of
inactivity associated with valleys in the plasma levels (reduction in peak to trough fluctuations) .
The major difference between the extended release zolpidem formulation, AMBIEN CR, and
typical extended release formulations is the combined need with AMBIEN CR for an
appropriately rapid onset of activity, maintenance of activity for a prolonged period, and reliable
cessation of drug activity. Reliable cessation of activity is not a common concern for most
extended release preparations. Residual effectiveness of a drug product as plasma levels decline
does not normally have the potential to interfere with the ability of a patient to function . For a
sleep medication, however, residual effects experienced in the morning after use have the
potential to negate any benefits accrued from achieving a full night of sleep. Thus, the entire
plasma profile defines the safety and effectiveness of AMBIEN CR from onset to cessation of
activity. Deviations from this profile have the potential to affect one or more key characteristics
of the clinical hypnotic profile of the product . These differences can lead to significant
consequences for patients . If extended-release zolpidem formulations have different
pharmacodynamic profiles, it would present a rather peculiar problem for physicians and
patients, because one would not know how the drug was going to perform, if at all effectively .
The differences in pharmacodynamic profiles may not be apparent based just on a
comparison of Cmax and AUC, and thus, generic formulations should be required to demonstrate
a greater concurrence of plasma concentration-time curves than are reflected in just
bioequivalent Cmax and AUC values . Because the total plasma concentration-time profile of
AMBIEN CR can be associated with three important qualities of sedative hypnotics -- time to
sleep onset, maintenance of sleep, and lack of residual effects -- Sanofi-aventis requests that
FDA take special consideration when reviewing any application for a generic version of
AMBIEN CR. Sanofi-aventis requests that the agency utilize specific bioequivalence
requirements that better assure clinical equivalence between generic zolpidem extended release
drug products and AMBIEN CR and require generic applicants seeking approval of a
therapeutically equivalent generic of AMBIEN CR to include immediate and extended-release
components in their tablets .

A. AMBIEN CR
AMBIEN CR contains either 6 .25 mg or 12.5 mg zolpidem tartrate, in a specific ratio of
immediate and extended-release formulation for oral administration . AMBIEN CR consists of a
coated two-layer tablet : one layer releases its drug content immediately and another layer allow s

for a slower release of zolpidem tartrate . AMBIEN CR is an extended release preparation
developed to meet the unique needs of individuals suffering from more than one symptom of

night. Importantly, the product was also developed with the goal of allowing individuals to
awaken in the morning without experiencing residual adverse drug effects on cognitive or
psychomotor functioning . The immediate release formulation of zolpidem (Ambien°) is rapidly
and nearly completely absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract with a limited first-pass effect .
This allows plasma levels to rise quickly and induce sleep. The immediate-release formulation is

further noted that formulations that varied from the Phase III formulation "did not fulfill
expected criteria in terms of increase in duration of activity without residual effect ."7

B. Statutory and Regulatory Background : Bioequivalence
Pursuant to section 505(j)(2)(A)(iv) of the FDCA, any ANDA must contain, among other
things, information demonstrating that the generic drug is bioequivalent to the reference listed

significant difference from the rate and extent of absorption
of the listed drug when administered at the same molar
dose of the therapeutic ingredient under similar
experimental conditions in either a single dose or multiple
doses .9
The statute defines "bioavailability" as "the rate and extent to which the active ingredient
or therapeutic ingredient is absorbed from the drug and becomes available at the site of drug
action."10 As a result, generic drugs often attempt to establish bioequivalence through what is
essentially a showing of equivalent bioavailability to the RLD . FDA's regulations appear to
sanction this approach stating :
Two drug products will be considered bioequivalent drug
products if they are pharmaceutical equivalents or
pharmaceutical alternatives whose rate and extent of
absorption do not show a significant difference when
administered at the same molar dose of the active moiety
under similar experimental perimental conditions, either single dose o r

In the March 2003 Guidance, FDA recommends two studies to demonstrate
bioequivalence for generic versions of modified-release products (which FDA has defined to
include both delayed-release and extended-release products) . The first study being a single-dose,
nonreplicate, fasting study comparing the highest strength of the test and reference listed drug
product and the second study being a food-effect, nonreplicate study comparing the highest

IV. Conclusions
As demonstrated above, evaluation of only CmaX and AUC parameters may fail to reveal
differences in pharmacodynamic characteristics and therapeutic equivalence . In order to provide
equivalent efficacy to marketed AMBIEN CR on sleep endpoints and minimal impairment of
cognitive function after 7-8 hours asleep, sanofi-aventis requests that generic formulations be
required to demonstrate a greater concurrence of plasma concentration-time curves than are
reflected in just bioequivalent CmaX and AUC values . Because the total plasma concentration-
time profile of AMBIEN CR can be associated with three important qualities of sedative
hypnotics -- time to sleep onset, maintenance of sleep, and lack of residual effects -- a generic of
AMBIEN CR should be required to include an immediate release and extended-release
component in the product to assure that the generic will have similar sleep induction and sleep
maintenance capabilities and a similar safety profile, particularly upon awakening . In addition to
the traditional FDA bioequivalence parameters (CmaX and AUC), FDA should require generics to
AMBIEN CR to demonstrate equivalence as a function of time such as AUCo-3h, AUC3-6n and
AUC6_- to assure clinical equivalence .

Pursuant to 21 C .F.R. § 10.33, the undersigned submit this Petition for 
Reconsideration of the March 24, 2008 decision of the Director of the Center for 
Drug Evaluation and Research in Docket No . 2007P-0399 . 
Decision Involved 
On March 24, 2008, the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research issued a 
decision denying the Citizen Petition and Petition for Stay of Action submitted in 
this docket by Purdue Pharma L.P . ("Purdue"), a manufacturer of approved new 
drug products containing oxycodone hydrochloride ("HCl"), and Rhodes 
Technologies ("Rhodes"), a manufacturer of oxycodone HC1 active ingredient 
("API"), which is an associated company of Purdue . The Citizen Petition 
requested that the Food and Drug Administration ("FDA") adopt, announce, and 
implement a consistent, CDER-wide standard for the acceptable level of 14-
hydroxycodeinone impurity in oxycodone HCl API approved by FDA for use in 
drug products . The accompanying Petition for Stay of Action requested that 
effective approval of NDAs or ANDAs for oxycodone HCl drug products 
manufactured using oxycodone HC1 API containing more than 10 ppm 14-
hydroxycodeinone impurity be stayed until the Agency adopts, announces, and 
Dockets Management Branch

implements a consistent, CDER-wide standard for the acceptable level of that 
impurity in API used in such products . 
Action Requested 
Purdue and Rhodes respectfully request that this Petition for Reconsideration 
be granted, and that the Commissioner withdraw CDER's March 24, 2008 
Decision, and grant Purdue and Rhodes' original Citizen Petition and Petition for 
Stay of Action. 
Statement of Grounds 
As detailed in the underlying Citizen Petition and Petition for Stay of Action 
("PSA"), when Petitioner Purdue sought approval in 2003 to use oxycodone HC1 
API manufactured by Rhodes to manufacture OxyContin® (oxycodone HCl 
controlled-release) Tablets, Purdue and Rhodes were unequivocally informed that 
approval of the Rhodes API would be contingent on successfully reducing the 
levels of 14-hydroxycodeinone, an a, (3-unsaturated ketone ("ABUK") impurity 
common to all commercial supplies of oxycodone HCl API . Specifically, in 
January 2004, Purdue and Rhodes were instructed by FDA either to provide 
extensive safety qualification data or to reduce the level of 14-hydroxycodeinone 
in the finished API to not more than ("NMT") 10 parts per million ("ppm") . 
Purdue and Rhodes proposed a very tight intermediate limit of 500 ppm on the 
impurity, and committed themselves to rapidly develop and implement process 
improvements to enable the consistent production of oxycodone HC1 API meeting 
a specification of NMT 10 ppm . Purdue and Rhodes successfully followed 
through on their commitment, qualifying and submitting a request on November 
12, 2004 for FDA approval to use Rhodes' low-ABUK (i. e., NMT 10 ppm) 
material . That supplemental application was approved by FDA on March 15, 
2005, and since that date Rhodes has consistently supplied Purdue with oxycodone 
HCl API containing NMT 10 ppm 14-hydroxycodeinone . 
Since that time, Purdue and Rhodes have sought and received assurance 
from the Agency that all other users and manufacturers of oxycodone HC1 API 
Dockets Management Branch 
March 31, 2008 
Page 3 of 19 
would be held to the same standard . However, upon confirming via testing that 
other oxycodone HC1-containing drug products, including recently approved 
products, contain far more than 10 ppm 14-hydroxycodeinone, Purdue and Rhodes 
petitioned the Agency to adopt, announce, and implement a consistent, CDER-
wide standard for the acceptable level of 14-hydroxycodeinone impurity in 
oxycodone HCl API approved by FDA for use in drug products and to refuse to 
approve pending NDAs or ANDAs for oxycodone HCl drug products 
manufactured using API that does not meet the standard imposed upon Purdue and 
Rhodes until such time as the Agency adopts, announces, and implements such a 
consistent, CDER-wide standard . 
The March 24, 2008 Decision ("Decision") denies Purdue and Rhodes' 
Petitions, but claims that CDER has nevertheless been "consistent" in its 
"approach" to 14-hydroxycodeinone impurity in oxycodone HCl API . As 
described below, the allegedly consistent "approach" described in the Decision is 
in fact inconsistent and seriously flawed in a number of critical respects, each of 
which requires reconsideration and withdrawal of the Decision . 
I. 
The Decision Acknowledges Unwarranted and Unjustified Disparate 
Treatment Among Individual Applicants and Groups of Applicants 
The Decision states that CDER has advised users and manufacturers of 
oxycodone HCl API of the same impurity limit goal (currently NMT 1 .5 mcg/day ; 
previously, NMT than 10 ppm) 1, but has imposed different consequences on 
' 
For NSAID or acetaminophen combination products, the Decision indicates that the 
original goal was NMT 100 ppm (p . 4) . Purdue and Rhodes have never previously been 
informed that the Agency had originally regarded 100 ppm to be an acceptable limit for 14-
hydroxycodeinone impurity . Similarly, it appears from the Comment submitted by Coastal 
Pharmaceuticals that Coastal (which indicates that it is developing a combination product) was 
not aware of this different goal either . See January 28, 2008 Letter to Dockets Management 
Branch from R. Moldin, President and Chief Executive Officer, Coastal Pharmaceuticals . In any 
event, Petitioners' tests in 2007, presented in the Citizen Petition, showed that none of the 
combination products tested had, even by that time, complied with this less stringent NMT 100 
ppm limit .

March 31, 2008

applicants unable or unwilling to meet the goal, depending on the type of 
submission pending before the Agency . The Decision further acknowledges that 
the consequences also differ depending on the nature of the particular applicants . 
At least three such distinctions are discernable from the Decision : new vs . 
supplemental approvals ; pioneer vs. generic approvals ; and companies using API 
from an affiliate vs . companies purchasing API from an independent company . As 
discussed in further detail below, there is no justification for any of these 
distinctions or for the corresponding disparate treatment among individual 
applicants and groups of applicants . 
New vs. supplemental approvals 
Citing the "medical importance," of approving new oxycodone HCl 
products, the Decision states that CDER has been and will continue to apply lower 
standards to new approvals than to supplemental approvals . Specifically, the 
Decision explains that CDER has delayed or denied approval of supplements to 
already approved applications due to the applicant's failure to meet CDER's target 
levels for 14-hydroxycodeinone, but has not delayed or denied approval of any 
new NDAs or ANDAs based on the applicant's failure to satisfy the standard . 
The Decision neither clearly defines the type(s) of supplements that have 
been impacted nor asserts that supplements seeking approval for the same type(s) 
of changes have been impacted in the same manner and/or to the same degree . 
Specifically, with respect to the impact on supplements, the Decision initially 
states that "we have held up approval of supplements to change API suppliers for 
failure to meet this standard" (p . 3) but later describes the impact as follows : 
"some supplements to NDAs may not have been approved based on the applicant's 
not meeting the requested specification and not providing an adequate plan for 
improving the quality of its drug substance" (p . 6) . In describing the experience of 
Purdue and Rhodes, the Decision acknowledges that approval of Purdue's 2003 
supplement to use oxycodone HC1 API manufactured by Rhodes to manufacture 
OxyContin® was indeed delayed by Purdue/Rhodes' inability to immediately meet 
the NMT 10 ppm standard communicated to them . 
Dockets Management Branch 
March 31, 2008 
Page 5 of 19 
CDER's general reference to the medical importance of new oxycodone HCl 
products in no way justifies the imposition of different consequences on applicants 
unable to immediately meet the 14-hydroxycodeinone target levels, depending on 
whether those applicants seek approval of a new product or a supplement to an 
already-approved application . As an initial matter, there is simply no medical 
significance to approving new ANDAs, which are, by definition, mere copies of 
already-approved products . Petitioners agree that there can be significant medical 
benefits to approving new pioneer products, and further agree that it may be 
appropriate, under certain circumstances, to require sponsors of NDAs for 
innovative products to address ABUK impurities as post-marketing commitments . 
However, to the best of Petitioners' knowledge, the only innovative oxycodone 
HCl product approved since 2002 was Combunox®, an ibuprofen/oxycodone 
combination product that was pending in 2002 and approved in 2004 through a 
505(b)(2) NDA.2 The only other products newly approved under this purported 
"medical significance" rationale since 2002 have been the subject of ANDAs . 
Pioneer vs . generic approvals 
The Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act ("FDCA"), as well as FDA's 
implementing regulations, impose the same safety and quality standards on pioneer 
and generic products, 3 and FDA has repeatedly assured the public that generic 
products are of the same safety and quality as the brand name product they copy . 
By way of example only, the website for the Office of Generic Drugs states : 
Health professionals and consumers can be assured that FDA approved 
generic drugs have met the same rigid standards as the innovator drug . To 
gain FDA approval, a generic drug must . .
. meet the same batch 
requirements for identity, strength, purity, and quality [and] be manufactured 
See the Summary Basis of Approval for Combunox (available at 
(http://www fda gov/cder/foi/nda/2004/-021378s000 CombunoxTOC .htm) . 
See, e.g., 21 C.F.R. §§ 314.50(d), 314.94(a)(9); 21 U.S.C . §§ 355(j)(4)(A), 355(d) . 
Dockets Management Branch 
March 31, 2008

under the same strict standards of FDA's good manufacturing practice 
regulations required for innovator products .4 
Despite the requirement that generic products be of the same safety and 
quality as the innovator product they copy, the Decision acknowledges that, 
although OxyContin® is manufactured using API containing less than 10 ppm 14-
hydroxycodeinone as a result of Agency demands, CDER has not and will not 
require new generic versions of the product to use API with 14-hydroxycodeinone 
levels as low as the pioneer, even though FDA demands for a reduction in ABUK 
levels are based on purported potential health concerns . This disparity is flatly 
inconsistent with the statute and FDA's implementing regulations . In this regard, 
CDER's "medical importance" rationale is, at least in the absence of a drug 
shortage, of no relevance because ANDA approvals by definition do not entail any 
medical advances . More importantly, although CDER also cites one policy 
underlying the Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act of 1984 
("Hatch-Waxman Act") - fostering the prompt approval of generic drug products -
it can cite no respect in which the Hatch-Waxman Act or any other provision of the 
FDCA sanctions the lowering of quality or safety standards so that inferior generic 
products can be approved more quickly . 
Finally, by permitting new ANDA applicants to use lower-quality API in 
order to get on the market more quickly, CDER has created a situation where the 
use of low-ABUK material will never become a standard . This is because, once 
higher-ABUK material is approved, API manufacturers other than Rhodes appear 
to find no incentive to meet their "robust accelerated timetables," and apparently 
suffer no negative consequences when they fail to do so.5 
4 
See "What are Generic Drugs?" available at : http://www.fda.gov/cder/olzd/#Introduction . 
The Decision cites the fact that Purdue still has approval to use oxycodone API from 
other suppliers, based on the fact that they were part of the original OxyContin® API approvals 
(p . 7) . However, but for CDER's own discriminatory policy, those other API suppliers would 
surely have responded as Rhodes did in 2004 - devoting significant resources to development of 
a process that could reliably produce low-ABUK API consistent with CDER's original demands . 
Thus, had CDER treated other suppliers of oxycodone HCl API the same way it treated Rhodes 
in 2004, Purdue could have used low-ABUK API from those suppliers when DEA failed in 2007

March 31, 2008

Controlled API suppliers vs. independent API suppliers 
As discussed in further detail below, the "flexible" approach described in the 
Decision has not been applied to Purdue and Rhodes . Instead, the 14-
hydroxycodeinone limits have been presented to Purdue and Rhodes as inflexible 
standards that must be satisfied, and there has been no suggestion that a four or 
more year delay would be satisfactory to the Agency . The Decision tacitly 
confirms6 that CDER presented its demands in this inflexible manner because 
Purdue and Rhodes are associated firms and Purdue was assumed to be able to 
control the resources Rhodes devoted to addressing the Agency's demands for 
reduced levels of 14-hydroxycodeinone . Petitioners are not aware of any legal 
basis to justify imposition of disparate standards upon applicants based on their 
affiliation or lack thereof with an API supplier . Certainly the safety and quality 
requirements imposed by the FDCA and FDA's regulations permit no such 
distinction . 
to provide Rhodes with permission to make enough oxycodone API to meet all of Purdue's 
needs . Instead, as a direct result of CDER's failure to require any API manufacturer other than 
Rhodes to produce API meeting low-ABUK standards, Purdue had no choice but to purchase and 
use higher-ABUK material from its backup suppliers in order to continue the supply of its 
product to patients . Had it not done so, all of Purdue's customers would have had to switch to 
the generic versions of the drug that were available at that time - all of which consistently and 
exclusively used high-ABUK material in the manufacture of their products . For these reasons, 
the Decision's citation to the ability of Purdue to use API from its original suppliers as a backup 
to Rhodes turns the actual consequences of CDER's inconsistent and incoherent policies on their 
head . 
The Decision states that reduction of 14-hydroxycodeinone levels requires changes in the 
API manufacturing process, and characterizes this as "a process typically outside of the 
sponsors' immediate control." (p . 4) . The unstated implication is that CDER has been more 
lenient with sponsors who are felt to have no control over the quality of oxycodone HCl API 
available to them . This dual-standard ignores the fact that dosage form manufacturers can exert 
significant influence over their API suppliers, particularly if FDA is insisting that they meet 
stringent quality standards . Moreover, as a practical matter, CDER's lenience simply 
perpetuates the manufacture of sub-standard API because it eliminates the competitive incentive 
for independent suppliers to seek to be first to meet the standard - or to meet the standard at all . 
Dockets Management Branch 
March 31, 2008

Of even greater significance, however, is CDER's failure to clearly state in 
the Decision that other applicants that are affiliated with API suppliers will also be 
subjected to the same rigid standards as were imposed upon Purdue and Rhodes . 
At a minimum, any sponsors affiliated with holders of DMFs for oxycodone HCl, 
such as Mallinckrodt,7 must be subjected to the same standards as Purdue and 
Rhodes . Testing presented in the Citizen Petition, however, suggests that CDER 
may not be treating all applicants affiliated with an API supplier (or otherwise 
jointly developing products with API suppliers) in the same manner as it treated 
Purdue and Rhodes . Specifically, the sample of Magnacetm (oxycodone HCl/ 
acetaminophen) tablets tested by Rhodes in 2007 contained 940 ppm 14-
hydroxycodeinone (per oxycodone HCl label claim) . This is far in excess of the 
NMT 10 ppm standard imposed upon Purdue and Rhodes, and even exceeds the 
100 ppm standard CDER states it set years ago for combination products .g The 
sponsor of the Magnacet application is Mikart, Inc ., but the product is distributed 
by Mallinckrodt Brand Pharmaceuticals, Inc . Whether CDER was unaware of this 
relationship or chose to overlook it in that case (or the parties delayed entering into 
their relationship until after the approval was granted), this example underscores 
how arbitrary the distinctions relied upon by CDER in the Decision are when 
applied, either retrospectively or prospectively, to the actual process of reviewing 
and approving drug products .
