Perrigo understands that FDA's Office of Generic Drugs ("OGD") has recently 
established, without public comment, an internal policy of permitting an ANDA sponsor who is 
seeking approval of a generic version of a drug that has switched from prescription to OTC 
status, to use the prescription version of the drug for purposes of demonstrating bioequivalence 
and obtain a waiver from demonstrating bioequivalence to the OTC drug provided two 
conditions are met: (1) the prescription and OTC versions do not differ in formulation with the 
exception of appearance (such as the existence of a belly band); and (2) the OTC version has 
been launched (hereinafter "FDA/OGD Policy"). 
B. 
Analysis 
1. 
The FDC Act and FDA's Implementing Regulations Require the Use 
of a Specific RLD for Bioequivalence Purposes 
Under the FDC Act and FDA's implementing regulations, an ANDA sponsor must cite a 
particular "listed drug" — a "reference listed drug" — and must demonstrate that its proposed 
product is bioequivalent to the RLD. The term "listed drug" is defined in FDA's regulations to 
mean:
a new drug product that has an effective approval under [FDC Act § 505(c)] for 
safety and effectiveness or under [FDC Act § 505(j)], which has not been 
withdrawn or suspended under [FDC Act §§ 505(e)(1) through (e)(5) or (j)(5)], and 
which has not been withdrawn from sale for what FDA has determined are reasons 
of safety or effectiveness. Listed drug status is evidenced by the drug product's 
identification as a drug with an effective approval in the current edition of FDA's 
[Orange Book] or any current supplement thereto, as a drug with an effective 
approval. A drug product is deemed to be a listed drug on the date of effective 
approval of the application or abbreviated application for that drug product. 
21 C.F.R. § 314.3(b). The term "reference listed drug" is defined in the same regulation to mean 
"the listed drug identified by FDA as the drug product upon which an applicant relies in seeking 
approval of its abbreviated application." Id. 
An applicant that meets the requirements under FDC Act § 505(j) for approval may 
reference FDA's finding of safety and effectiveness for the RLD, and need not repeat the 
extensive nonclinical and clinical investigations required for approval of a stand-alone NDA 
submitted under FDC Act § 505(b)(1). 
FDC Act § 505(j)(2)(A) governs the content of an ANDA and states in relevant part that 
an application must contain: 
(i) information to show that the conditions of use prescribed, recommended, or 
suggested in the labeling proposed for the new drug have been previously approved 
for a drug listed [in the Orange Book] (hereinafter in this subsection referred to as a 
"listed drug"); [and]
Division of Dockets Management 
November 17, 2011 
Page 4
(iv) information to show that the new drug is bioequivalent to the listed drug 
referred to in clause (i) . . . . 
FDC Act § 505(j)(2)(A)(i), (iv). 
Similarly, FDA's implementing regulations on the content and format of an ANDA state, 
in relevant part, that an ANDA "must refer to a listed drug," which ordinarily "will be the drug 
product selected by [FDA] as the reference standard for conducting bioequivalence testing," 21 
C.F.R. § 314.94(a)(3), and that the ANDA must contain "[t]he name of the [RLD], including its 
dosage form and strength," id. § 314.94(a)(3)(i), "[a] statement that the conditions of use 
prescribed, recommended, or suggested in the labeling proposed for the drug product have been 
previously approved for the [RLD]," id. § 314.94(a)(4)(i), and "[i]nformation that shows that the 
drug product is bioequivalent to the [RLD] upon which the applicant relies," 
§ 314.94(a)(7)(i). FDA's regulations at 21 C.F.R. §§ 320.21, 320.22, and 320.24 govern the 
requirements, methods, and procedures for a generic applicant to demonstrate bioequivalence for 
specific drug products, and state in pertinent part that an ANDA must contain "[e]vidence 
demonstrating that the drug product that is the subject of the [ANDA] is bioequivalent to the 
[RLD]." 21 C.F.R. § 320.21(b)(1). 
FDA may refuse to receive an ANDA if the "abbreviated application is incomplete 
because it does not on its face contain information required under [FDC Act § 505(j)] . .. or § 
314.94." 21 C.F.R. § 314.101(d)(3). And FDA may not approve an ANDA if "information 
submitted with the application is insufficient to show that each of the proposed conditions of use 
have been previously approved for the listed drug referred to in the application," FDC Act 
§ 505(j)(4)(B), and if "information submitted in the application is insufficient to show that the 
drug is bioequivalent to the listed drug referred to in the application" id. § 505(j)(4)(F). 
Similarly, FDA's regulations state that the Agency will refuse to approve an ANDA if 
"Nnformation submitted with the [ANDA] is insufficient to show that each of the proposed 
conditions of use has been previously approved for the listed drug referred to in the application," 
21 C.F.R. § 314.127(a)(2), or if "[i]nformation submitted in the [ANDA] is insufficient to show 
that the drug product is bioequivalent to the listed drug referred to in the [ANDA]," 
§ 314.127(a)(6)(i). 
2. 
The FDA/OGD Policy is Contrary to the Law and FDA Policy 
If FDA has, in fact, received an ANDA for a generic version of Prevacid®24HR 15 mg 
Capsules containing the results of bioequivalence testing in which the proposed new drug was 
compared to prescription Prevacid® Delayed-Release 15 mg Capsules as a result of the 
FDA/OGD Policy, then such receipt was improper. FDA must rescind receipt of such ANDA 
and require that it contain, upon ANDA submission, information demonstrating bioequivalence 
to the appropriate RLD Prevacidg24HR 15 mg Capsules approved under NDA No. 022327. 
What is clear from the statute and FDA's implementing regulations is that an RLD is a 
specific listed drug product. That is, an RLD is a drug product approved under a specific NDA,
Division of Dockets Management 
November 17, 2011 
Page 5 
on a specific date, and with specific conditions of use, even though another pharmaceutically 
equivalent, and potentially bioequivalent, drug that is otherwise the same drug (with the possible 
exception of some appearance differences) is approved under a different NDA. In this case, 
Prevacid® Delayed-Release 15 mg Capsules cannot serve as an RLD for bioequivalence testing 
purposes for a generic version of Prevacid®24HR 15 mg Capsules. The products, despite their 
similarities, are different RLDs (each identified separately in the Orange Book as such), 
approved under different applications (NDA No. 020406 and NDA No. 022327), on different 
dates (May 10, 1995 and May 18, 2009), and with different conditions of use (e.g., prescription 
or OTC use). 
Not only is the FDA/OGD Policy contrary to the plain text of the FDC Act and FDA's 
implementing regulations concerning the appropriate RLD, it is also contrary to FDC Act 
§ 505(j)(2)(D), which states that an ANDA sponsor "may not amend or supplement an 
application to seek approval of a thug referring to a different listed drug from the listed drug 
identified in the application as submitted to the Secretary." FDC Act § 505(j)(2)(D)(i). The 
FDA/OGD Policy allows an ANDA sponsor to violate this provision by permitting an ANDA 
sponsor to demonstrate bioequivalence to a prescription version of a drug to satisfy the 
requirements of an ANDA submission, and at the same time allows that application to request 
that FDA grant a biowaiver from demonstrating bioequivalence to a different listed drug — the 
launched OTC RLD. 
Permitting an ANDA sponsor to use Prevacid® Delayed-Release 15 mg Capsules for 
bioequivalence testing of a generic version of Prevacid®24HR 15 mg Capsules is also contrary 
to long-standing FDA policy. Many brand-name drug products marketed in the United States are 
marketed in foreign countries. ANDA sponsors have tried throughout the years to submit 
evidence to FDA that a drug product marketed in the United States and identified in the Orange 
Book as the RLD is the same drug product with the same specifications as a drug product 
marketed outside the United States, such that FDA could receive an ANDA containing 
bioequivalence testing data using the foreign drug product. FDA has flatly rejected such 
arguments and has maintained the position that an ANDA sponsor must demonstrate 
bioequivalence to the FDA approved RLD. FDA has defended this position by reason that the 
ANDA sponsor, which does not have visibility to certain chemistry, manufacturing and controls 
information in the RLD NDA, cannot certify without doubt that the United States and foreign 
marketed drug products are made at the same site, under the same process, with the same critical 
processing parameters, and with the same product specifications. Similar uncertainty exists with 
allowing an ANDA sponsor to rely on bioequivalence comparisons against the prescription 
version of a drug product that has switched to OTC status under a new NDA. Changes to any 
one of the parameters FDA has consistently used as a basis to reject requests to use a foreign 
marketed drug product in lieu of the FDA approved product could likewise affect the 
substantiation of bioequivalence. As such, FDA should not take any risk and should require 
ANDA sponsors to use the appropriate RLD — the approved OTC drug product — for 
bioequivalence testing purposes, and not a different drug — the approved prescription version of 
the switched drug. 
The criterion in the FDA/OGD Policy that requires the launch of the OTC RLD before 
FDA will permit the submission of an ANDA containing bioequivalence testing data and

November 17, 2011 
Page 6 
information to the prescription version of the drug product has no basis in law or regulation. 
There is simply no requirement that the date of ANDA submission must be pegged to the date of 
product launch. Instead, such an FDA-imposed requirement appears to be intended to shield the 
Agency from criticism from the OTC RLD NDA sponsor that FDA could accept an ANDA 
when there is no drug product on the market with which to demonstrate bioequivalence. 
Imposing a launch date requirement for ANDA submissions would unnecessarily place 
new burdens on sponsors to continuously monitor news about product launches (provided, of 
course, such information is made public, since product launches may not be a matter of public 
record). It is likely to lead to significant controversy requiring judicial resolution. 
As an initial matter, it is unclear what constitutes a product launch. If a small amount of 
product is released in one U.S. city but not nationwide, would that constitute a product launch for 
purposes of the FDA/OGD Policy? Moreover, FDA does not have a mechanism that requires a 
brand-name manufacturer to notify the Agency of a product launch, and it is unclear how FDA 
would validate a launch date against an ANDA submission date. Different ANDA sponsors may 
claim different launch dates supporting their submissions. 
Although it is not the case with Lansoprazole 15 mg Capsules, when such a situation 
involves a Paragraph IV certification and eligibility for 180-day exclusivity, one company may 
claim one date constituted the product launch/ANDA submission date and another company 
another date. To secure first applicant status, and because a product launch could occur at any 
time after NDA approval, ANDA sponsors will likely resort to serial ANDA submissions. Such 
serial ANDA submissions would not only unnecessarily waste scarce FDA resources, but could 
unnecessarily complicate the user fee assessment and waiver processes that would be established 
by the Generic Drug User Fee Act if it is enacted next year. 
Finally, a launch date criterion creates an uneven playing field for ANDA sponsors. Not 
all OTC product launches are nationwide, and therefore have the potential to advantage or 
disadvantage generic drug manufacturers based on the geographical outreach of individual 
companies.
3. 
FDA Must Amend its ANDA Regulations Through Notice-and-
Comment Rulemaking Before Receiving an ANDA Pursuant to the 
FDA/OGD Policy 
If FDA has received an ANDA for a generic version of Prevacid®24HR 15 mg Capsules 
pursuant to the FDA/OGD Policy as Perrigo suspects, then such ANDA was improperly received 
and such receipt should be rescinded, because FDA failed to employ notice-and-comment 
rulemaking prior to receiving such ANDA under a policy that effectively amended the rules 
governing generic drug submissions and approvals, and that treats similarly situated parties to 
divergent treatment in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act ("APA"). 
The APA requires notice of a proposed rule be published in the Federal Register and that 
such notice include the substance of and legal authority for the rule. $ee 5 U.S.C. § 553(b). In 
this case, FDA has not published any Federal Register notice of its intent to amend its
Division of Dockets Management 
November 17, 2011 
Page 7 
regulations to reflect the FDA/OGD Policy, let alone notice containing the substance of and legal 
authority for such a policy. 
Although FDA has discretion in establishing the appropriate methods for a generic drug 
applicant to demonstrate bioequivalence for specific drug products, the Agency does not have 
unbounded authority to waive the ordinary requirement that an ANDA sponsor demonstrate 
bioequivalence to the appropriate RLD — here, Prevacid®24HR 15 mg Capsules approved under 
NDA No. 022327. "An agency is not allowed to change a legislative rule retroactively through 
the process of disingenuous interpretation of the rule to mean something other than its original 
meaning." Caruso v. Blockbuster-Sony Music Entm't Ctr. at the Waterfront, 193 F.3d 730, 737 
(3d Cir. 1999) (internal quotations omitted); see also Shalala v. Guernsey Mem'l Hosp., 514 U.S. 
87, 100 (1995) ("APA rulemaking would still be required if [an interpretive rule] adopted a new 
position inconsistent with any of the Secretary's existing regulations."). Rather, without notice-
and-comment rulemaking, an agency may only issue an interpretation of a regulation that is 
"consistent with its language and original purpose." Nat'l Family Planning v Sullivan, 979 F. 
2d 227, 234 (D.C. Cir. 1992). When an "interpretation" of a rule "repudiates or is ineconcilable 
with [a prior legislative rule], the second rule must be an amendment of the first; and, of course, 
an amendment to a legislative rule must itself be legislative." Am. Mining Cong. v. Mine Safety 
& Health Admin., 995 F.2d 1106, 1109 (D.C. Cir. 1993). 
The FDA/OGD Policy is flatly inconsistent with, and thus constitutes an amendment of, 
FDA's bioequivalence regulations, which require a demonstration of bioequivalence to a specific 
RLD. Before adopting this policy, however, FDA failed to employ the notice-and-comment 
procedures that the APA mandates for regulatory amendments. Unless and until FDA's 
regulations are properly amended, the APA bars FDA from applying the policy the Agency has 
apparently adopted. 
FDA may not subject two similarly situated parties to divergent treatment; however, the 
FDA/OGD Policy does just that. The APA provides that a court may hold unlawful "agency 
action, findings, and conclusions found to be arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or 
otherwise not in accordance with law." 5 U.S.C. § 706(2). Under this "arbitrary and capricious" 
standard, courts have held that agency action that treats similarly situated parties in a different 
manner is a violation of the APA. See Federal Election Comm'n v. Rose, 806 F.2d 1081, 1089 
(D.C. Cir. 1986) ("[A]n agency's unjustifiably disparate treatment of two similarly situated 
parties works a violation of the arbitrary-and-capricious standard."); Bracco Diagnostics, Inc. v.  
Shalala, 963 F. Supp. 20, 28 (D.D.C.1997) ("What the FDA is not free to do, however, is to treat 
[similarly situated parties] dissimilarly and to permit two sets of similar products to run down 
two separate tracks, one more treacherous than the other."). The FDA/OGD Policy does not treat 
generic applicants uniformly. By arbitrarily setting the launch date as a criterion for ANDA 
submission, FDA creates an uneven playing field for some ANDA sponsors who because of their 
location may not learn of a product launch until well after the fact, thereby delaying a timely 
submission.

Successful management of current antimicrobials, and the continued development of new ones, 
is vital to protecting human and animal health against infectious microbial pathogens. 
Approximately two million people acquire bacterial infections in U.S. hospitals each year, and 
90,000 die as a result. About 70 percent of those infections are resistant to at least one drug. The 
trends toward increasing numbers of infection and increasing drug resistance show no sign of 
abating. Resistant pathogens lead to higher health care costs because they often require more 
expensive drugs and extended hospital stays. Resistant infections impact clinicians practicing in 
every field of medicine. The problem is not limited to hospitals. Community-acquired infections 
are also frequently resistant to multiple antibiotics, such as community-acquired methicillin-

Streptococcus pneumoniae, and gram-negative bacilli, which can infect humans through food. 
Armenpharm, Ltd. recently contracted with JMI Laboratories for determination of in vitro

difficil. In Attachment VIII, JMI Laboratories tested Chloramphenicol and comparator 
antimicrobial agents against Enterobacteriaceae strains carrying emerging resistance 
mechanisms. Chloramphenicol is not effective against enteric bacteria unless used in huge 
amounts. Other drugs were more effective at much smaller doses.

annentarium has been recognized by FDA and FDA has asked industry to do exactly what the

Iron sucrose Injection (NDA 021135) was approved by the agency on Nov 06, 2000 and 
currently it is marketed in the US as a Reference Listed Drug (RLD) under the trade name 
"Venofere". 
Venofer® (Iron Sucrose Injection, USP) is a brown, sterile, aqueous, complex of polynuclear 
iron (III)-hydroxide in sucrose for intravenous use. Iron sucrose injection has a molecular weight of 
approximately 34,000 — 60,000 daltons and a proposed structural formula: 
[Na2Fes08(OH) .3(H20)]n .In(C121122011) 
Where, n is the degree of iron polymerization and m is the number of sucrose molecules 
associated with the iron (III)-hydroxide. 
Each mL of injection contains 20 mg elemental iron as iron sucrose in water for injection. 
Venofer® is available in 5 mL single dose vials (100 mg elemental iron per 5 mL) and 10 mL single 
dose vials (200 mg elemental iron per 10 mL). The drug product contains approximately 30% 
sucrose w/v (300 mg/mL) and has a pH of 10.5- 11.1. The product contains no preservatives. The 
Osmolarity of the injection is 1250 mOsmol/L as provided in physician's inert labeling for Venofer® 
(Exhibit A).

Elemental Components in Venofer 
As described in the molecular formula of Iron sucrose complex printed in the Venofer®

RE: Annuloplasty Rings - Class II v. Class III and Death Report Analysis 
The undersigned submits this petition under the Medical Device Amendments to the 
Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act; the Code ofFederal Regulations, Title 21, Parts 
800-898; andlor any other statutory provision for which authority has been delegated to 
the Commissioner ofFood and Drugs under 21 CFR 5.10 to request the Commissioner of 
Food and Drugs investigate: 
1] The placement ofannuloplasty rings in Class II versus Class ill circa 2001, and 
2] The current number ofdeaths from annuloplasty rings for the most recent five year 
period compared to earlier time periods. 
These are the two ACTIONS REQUESTED in this petition. 
The STATEMENT OF GROUNDS for requesting the aforementioned investigations are 
as follows: 
ANNULOPLASTY RINGS, Class II versus III: 
According to a Chicago Tribune article ofMay 22, 2011, page 12, the FDA, CDRH in 
particular, used language originating from an industry petition as the basis to conclude 
that annuloplasty rings were safe and effective within the 51Ok approval scheme. This is 
a very limited basis to classify a serious device like an annuloplasty ring, destined for 
insertion in a human heart. This decision presumes that these rings can be classed with 
other Class II devices like dental cement and hearing aids. Whereas heart-lung bypass 
machines that support the patient's circulation and breathing, while an annuloplasty ring 
is inserted in their hearts, is a Class ill device. The heart-lung machine is withdrawn at 
the close ofthe operation; hence its ability to affect patient's outcomes is serious but brief 
when compared to an annuloplasty ring, which once implanted, is usually inside a 
patient's heart for their entire lifetime. The petition requests that the Commissioner 
investigate the basis for the Class II decision on annuloplasty rings and reclassify these 
rings to Class ill, PMA approval scheme. 
Cf  
Page 2, Annuloplasty Rings, Citizen's Petition, June 6,2011 
DEATH REPORTING ANALYSIS: 
Deaths in the last five years for annuloplasty rings have markedly increased, according to 
a Chicago Tribune article, dated May 22, 2011, page 13. Annuloplasty rings have had 
more deaths reported than other devices in Class II. Moreover, the rings have had only 
56 fewer reports than artificial heart valves, a Class III device, and the number ofdeaths 
associated with annuloplasty rings has increased markedly from the 465 events reported 
between 1991 and 1995. 
One solution to this dilemma is to reclassify annuloplasty rings to Class III devices 
requiring a PMA with clinical data. A second solution is to amend the device regulations 
and require that all ring manufacturers submit annual sales data for annulop)asty rings as 
part oftheir annual reports. A third solution is to retrospectively require ring 
manufacturers to submit annual sales data for prior years. These two last solutions would 
allow CDRH to assess the rise ofdeath reports over a multiple year period versus the 
increasing sales; the third solution is a 'best case' solution for the health and safety ofthe 
public. Annual unit sales are already required for prescription drugs-see 21 CFR 
314.81(b)(2)(ii). 
The petition requests that the Commissioner take action to assess the rising death reports 
with annuloplasty rings with the help ofmanufacturers' annual sales data and, 
subsequently reclassify annuloplasty rings to Class Ill. As may be necessary, the 
Commissioner should also communicate with those patients about to undergo 
annuloplasty ring heart valve surgery and the health care community doing such 
surgeries, and take any other actions permitted by law or regulation. 
ENVIRONMENTAL IMP ACT: A categorical exclusion is requested under 21 CFR 
25.34 for this petition.

I. 
Action Requested

Statutory and Regulatory Background 
Section 505 of the FDCA describes three types of new drug applications: (1) an 
application that contains full reports of investigations of safety and effectiveness (section 
505(b)(1), referred to as an NDA); (2) an application that contains full reports of 
investigations of safety and effectiveness but where at least some of the information 
required for approval comes from studies not conducted by or for the applicant and for 
which the applicant has not obtained a right of reference (section 505(b)(2), referred to as 
a 505(b)(2) application); and (3) an application that contains information to show that the 
proposed product is identical in active ingredient, dosage form, strength, route of 
administration, labeling, quality, performance characteristics, and intended use, among 
other things, to a previously approved product (section 505(j), referred to as an ANDA). 
1. 
Abbreviated New Drug Applications (ANDAs) 
Section 505(j) of the FDCA permits an ANDA applicant to rely on the safety and 
efficacy studies submitted for the RLD if the ANDA drug product has the same active 
ingredient, dosage form, strength, labeling, conditions of use, and route of administration 
as the RLD and is bioequivalent to the RLD. 19 The labeling of the ANDA drug product 
must be the same as the labeling for the RLD, except when the labeling differences are 
the result of a suitability petition or the generic drug is "produced or distributed by 
different manufacturers." 2° More specifically, FDA's regulations provide that the 
labeling for the RLD and ANDA drug product may have "differences in expiration date, 
formulation, bioavailability, or pharmacokinetics, labeling revisions made to comply with

Crestor 
As summarized in the Factual Background above, after reviewing and discussing 
JUPITER' s clinical trial results at the advisory committee meeting, FDA insisted in 
conjunction with approving the JUPITER primary prevention indication that AstraZeneca 
include protected diabetes related information in Crestor's labeling. Indeed, the 
JUPITER primary prevention indication and associated clinical trial data are protected by 
unexpired patent and/or marketing exclusivity periods. As a result, an ANDA and 
505(b)(2) applicant cannot include the protected JUPITER trial data associated with the 
diabetes related warning and adverse reaction information in any label until the 
associated marketing exclusivity period expires on February 8, 2013. In order to avoid 
the JUPITER related exclusivity periods, the ANDA and 505(b)(2) applicants would have 
to carve the JUPITER related diabetes warning and adverse reaction information out of 
their proposed labeling. If FDA were to permit a generic or 505(b)(2) drug product to 
omit such information from its labeling—after requiring its inclusion in the labeling for 
Crestor—the agency would run afoul of the Administrative Procedure Act's prohibition 
on arbitrary and capricious agency action.34

Statement of Grounds 
A. 
OxyContin (oxycodone HC1 controlled-release) Tablets — Purdue's 
Original Extended-Release Oral Formulation of Oxycodone 
The original formulation of OxyContin was approved in December 1995. In that 
original approval, OxyContin was indicated for the management of moderate to severe 
pain where use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate for more than a few days. 
Subsequently, the indication was modified to "the management of moderate to severe 
pain when a continous, around-the-clock analgesic is needed for an extended period of 
time." OxyContin was the first extended-release oxycodone product. Moreover, at the 
time of approval in 1995, FDA had not approved any other single-entity oxycodone 
products. 
Purdue's NDA for the original version of OxyContin (NDA # 20-553) provided 
for 10, 20 and 40 mg tablets. In 1996 and 2000, FDA approved two supplements 
providing for 80 and 160 mg tablets, respectively. Thereafter, in September 2006, FDA 
approved a supplement providing for three intermediate strength tablets: 15, 30, and 60 
rng.
Unlike immediate release oxycodone, OxyContin provides a controlled-release of 
oxycodone over twelve hours. The approved label for OxyContin thus provided for 
twice-a-day dosing when a continuous around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an 
extended period of time. In contrast, immediate release oxycodone products are 
administered four to six times a day.' 
1 
Immediate release single-entity solid-oral-dosage-form oxycodone products were first 
approved by FDA in August 2000, well after approval of the original version of OxyContin. All 
immediate release oxycodone products sold before that time had been sold without being 
covered by approved NDAs or ANDAs. It appears that the first approved immediate-release 
single-entity product, Roxicodone, relied in part upon FDA's previous findings of safety and 
efficacy for OxyContin. See, e.g., Review and Evaluation of Clinical Data for Roxicodone (NDA 
21-011) (August 26, 1999) at 6 (applicant acknowledging reliance on NDA 20-553 for 
OxyContin) and FDA's Review of Roxane's Response to the Approvable Letter (June 22, 2000) 
at 40 (citing particular OxyContin studies as supportive of safety), both available at: 
http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda docs/nda/2000/21-011 Roxicodone Medr Pl.pdf. 
2
Purdue Pharma L.P 
As the first extended-release oxycodone product, Purdue's NDA for OxyContin 
included substantial new clinical data. The NDA was supported with six controlled 
clinical studies, including five clinical studies that FDA considered essential to approval. 
In addition to establishing safety and efficacy, Purdue's studies provided the basis for 
establishing prescribing information regarding the dosing and administration of extended 
release oxycodone. For example, Purdue's studies established the basis for 
recommending conversion factors for use when switching patients from other opioids to 
oral oxycodone. They also provided information regarding appropriate dose titration for 
patients taking extended release oxycodone. Additionally, Purdue conducted 
pharmacokinetic studies in special patient populations, including patients with renal and 
hepatic impairment. FDA also required Purdue to conduct certain pre-clinical toxicology 
studies. The labeling for OxyContin reflects information from Purdue's extensive 
studies.
The labeling for OxyContin also reflects information from post-approval studies. 
Purdue has submitted numerous post-approval clinical study reports regarding extended 
release oxycodone. Based on post-approval study information, Purdue has revised the 
labeling for OxyContin to include information essential to the safe and effective use of 
extended release oxycodone. For example, Purdue changed the labeling for OxyContin 
to include enhanced safety information regarding post-operative use in light of 
information from a post-approval study involving post-surgical patients. Furthermore, 
based on post-approval experience with OxyContin, Purdue has also implemented a Risk 
Evaluation and Management Strategy ("REMS") to address the risks associated with 
extended release oxycodone. 2 Purdue's REMS for OxyContin includes a medication 
guide and elements to assure safe use, all of which are based, in large part, on 
information developed through the clinical testing and post-marketing surveillance and 
study of OxyContin. 
B. 
Purdue's New NDA for Extended-Release Oral Oxycodone 
Purdue has taken a number of steps, many in consultation with FDA, to address 
concerns of abuse and diversion of OxyContin, as well as inadvertent misuse by patients 
or their caregivers. For example, in response to reports of abuse, misuse, and diversion 
of the original formulation of OxyContin, Purdue began development work on a 
reformulation intended to help discourage misuse and abuse. Purdue evaluated several 
reformulation strategies, and ultimately pursued approval for a formulation with a

different inert excipient that changes the physiochemical properties of the tablets. An 
NDA for the reformulation was submitted in November 2007 (NDA # 22-272).3 
After review of the reformulation and data concerning its physiochemical 
attributes at two separate Advisory Committee meetings, the reformulation was approved 
in April 2010. NDA # 22-272 provides for 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 60, and 80 mg tablets.4 
Reformulated OxyContin, like the original, is indicated for management of moderate to 
severe pain when a continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an 
extended period of time, and is not for use on an as-needed basis or in the immediate

Data in NDA # 22-272 show that reformulated OxyContin is bioequivalent to the 
original formulation of OxyContin Tablets and has physical properties that provide 
resistance to certain methods which could defeat the controlled-release mechanism of the 
original OxyContin formulation. The reformulated tablets are hard, require time and 
effort to reduce their size, and create a viscous solution when hydrated. Due to these 
physiochemical properties, reformulated OxyContin is intended to be more difficult to 
prepare for abuse via multiple routes of administration and is less likely to be 
inadvertently crushed by patients or caregivers. Purdue is conducting several post-
marketing epidemiological studies designed to assess the effects of the reformulation on 
misuse and abuse of OxyContin and their potential consequences of addiction, overdose,

drug products to be pharmaceutical equivalents if they meet three criteria: (a) they 
contain the same active ingredient(s), (b) they have the same dosage form and route of 
administration, and (c) they are identical in strength or concentration. Pharmaceutically 
equivalent drug products may differ in characteristics such as shape, release mechanism, 
labeling (to some extent), scoring, and excipients (including colors, flavors, and 
preservatives).23 
When there is no listed drug that is a pharmaceutical equivalent to the drug 
product proposed in the 505(b)(2) application, FDA considers the relevant listed drug to 
be the one that is the most similar to the drug product that is the subject of the 505(b)(2) 
application, even if there is another drug that could serve as the basis for the application. 
See FDA Response to Citizen Petition, Docket No. 2004P-0386 (Nov. 30, 2004) at 9-10, 
available at: htt ://www.fda. • ov/ohrms/dockets/-dockets/04 0386/04 -0386- dn00001- 
vol 1 .pdf (Fenofibrate Decision). In the words of the agency: "[W]hen a section 
505(b)(2) application has been submitted and no pharmaceutically equivalent drug 
product has been previously approved, the 505(b)(2) applicant should choose the listed 
drug or drugs that are most similar to the drug for which approval is sought." 
Fenofibrate Decision at 9. 
In this case, Remoxy, a capsule product, is not pharmaceutically equivalent to 
OxyContin because tablets and capsules are technically considered different dosage 
forms. Nor is Remoxy pharmaceutically equivalent to the only approved oxycodone 
capsule products — a recently approved 5 mg immediate release product by Lehigh Valley 
(approved October 2010) and several immediate release combination capsule products 
containing oxycodone plus a non-opioid analgesic. Thus, Rernoxy is not 
pharmaceutically equivalent to any approved product and, so, the Rernoxy NDA must, 
instead, reference the approved product most similar to Remoxy. There can be no 
question that Remoxy is more similar to OxyContin than to any other approved 
oxycodone product listed in the Orange Book. The similarities between the products are

A. Action Requested 
By this petition, the Commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is hereby 
requested to declare that Fasprofen®, Orally Disintegrating Tablets, 100 mg. are suitable for 
submission as an AND A. The Reference-Listed Drug (RLD) product onwhich this petition is 
based is Motrin® (ibuprofen) 100 mg chewable tablets. Therefore, the petitioner requests a 
change from the RLD, McNeil Consumer's Motrin® chewable tablets, only in its dosage form 
(from chewable tablet to orally disintegrating tablet). 
B. Statement of Grounds 
The Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act provides for the submission of an ANDA for a drug 
product that differs in dosage form from that of the listed drug, provided the FDA has approved a 
petition that proposed filing such an application. The most recent internet listing of the 
"Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations" (Orange Book) lists the 
RLD ~Application Number N020601, approved Nov. 15, 1996 as OTC, McNeil Consumer, 
Motrin® Junior Strength chewable tablets. The proposed drug product is an otally disintegrating 
form of the tablet, in the same strength as the RLD. The proposed product contains the same 
active ingredient as the RLD and is intended to the same route of administration. Thus, the 
' 
1 
proposed product will be labeled with the same conditions of use as the listed drug and is 
expected to have the same therapeutic eftect when used as indicated in the labeling. 
The route of administration is the oral route, with disintegration of the tablet in the mouth and 
absorption in the mouth and GI tract. The RLD has absorption in the mouth during the act of 
chewing the tablet and also absorption of soluble ibuprofen in the GI tract. Swallowing of the 
soluble contents by either tablet has some absorption in the GI tract along with the mouth. 
Safety has been clearly established for low-dose 100 mg ibuprofen. Bioavailability ofFasprofen 
was shown to be 76% (J of Clinical Research Letters 2012;3(2):41-45). Most ofthe ibuprofen 
tablets are coated which opens in the small intestine presenting a concentrated bolus of ibuprofen 
creating an inflammatory reaction and leads to inflammatory bowel disease. These harmful 
effects to the intestinal mucosa have been demonstrated even in younger, healthier populations 
where small bowel injuries as well as reduced blood flow to the small intestine were observed 
within as little as 14 days (World J Gastroentero/2011:17(2):341-348). In a study comparing 
coated versus uncoated aspirin as an anti-coagulant, 65% of patients taking coated aspirin, 
irrespective of the strength. had no reduced clotting compared with 25% for those taking the 
uncoated formulation (Stroke 2004;35(1 ): 175-178). 
A copy of the RLD labeling is included in Attachment 1. The labeling of the proposed product is 
expected to be the same as that for the RLD, with the exception of the section denoting the 
manufacturer, and the change in dosage form, which will instruct the user to place the orally 
disintegrating tablet on the tongue, allowing it to dissolve and eventually swallowed,. A copy of 
the draft proposed package data is provided in Attachment 2.

point out that the Agency has previously approved ANDA suitability petitions allowing for a 
change in dosage form in many instances., A suitability petition was approved for the drug 
product Famotidine (Docket OOP-1422) to allow a change from a tablet to an orally disintegrating 
tablet. The petitioner is seeking the change in dosage form in an effort to make an alternate 
dosage form (rapidly disintegrating tablet) available for those individuals that may have 
difficulty swallowing an intact tablet or prefer the proposed dosage form.

314.55(c).

The information will be provided upon request by the Agency.

Dear Commissioner Hamburg: 
The subject of this petition is time-sensitive. A timely response from your

Pursuant to the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. §§ 551-559, 701-706

Regulations, Sections 10.30, 10.33, and 10.35, as related to the Federal

Petition To FDA: Resveratrol Partners LLC 
Page 4 
This petition is written in context of the FDA's position to promote 
innovation in medicine and to work in a timely manner regarding any 
irreversible threat to health that requires immediate agency action. 
This petition is being filed to request conditional approval of oral 
Longevinex® dietary supplement capsules for treatment of elderly patients 
with wet (neovascular) macular degeneration who have failed treatment 
with injectable anti-angiogenesis drugs bevacizumab (Avastin) and 
ranibizumab (Lucentis). 
This unusual petition is being submitted because all treatment options have 
been exhausted and these patients, most whom are in their eighth decade of 
life, face permanent vision loss unless timely and effective treatment is 
rendered. 
It is estimated that 1 in 6 patients treated with bevacizumab (Avastin) and 
ranibizumab (Lucentis) progress to registered blindness. As miraculous as 
'-' 
these drugs are, an estimated 30,000 elderly patients per year (8o-1oo 
patients per day) fail to be helped by injectable monoclonal antibody 
vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) blockers. 
While anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies have fundamentally altered the 
clinical management of choroidal neovascularization (wet macular 
degeneration), as these drugs were the first to reliably improve vision, even 
if only for 30-45 days between injections, a noted authority has stated that 
"anti-VEGF-A antibody therapy is not a panacea, as only one third of 
patients recover driving vision and one sixth progress to registered 
blindness. "1 
Preliminary cases treated with Longevinex® have rapidly responded to this 
oral medication with some dramatic unexpected remissions and measured 
restoration of functional vision. No side effects have been reported among 
these limited cases. Sixteen of the first seventeen cases treated responded 
1 Ambati, J. Age-Related Macular Degeneration and the Other Double Helix, Invest 
Ophthalmology Vis Sci. 2011; 52: 2166-2169 
Petition To FDA: Resveratrol Partners LLC 
Page 5 
positively to Longevinex (this was not a controlled trial, it was an 
accumulation of individual cases).2 Nor have serious side effects been 
reported among a broader group of thousands of adults who have taken this 
product over a period of 8 years for general health promotion. 
Resveratrol Partners LLC fully recognizes the conventional way to proceed 
with a nutriceutical intended to treat or cure any disease is to file an 
investigational new drug application and proceed with a double-blind 
placebo-controlled study of adequate duration. However, such a study will 
(a) delay timely treatment for thousands of patients and (b) would be 
unethical as it would force patients who are going blind to take an inactive 
placebo and (c) would be too costly for such a small patient population. (It 
is estimated a 1-year 1332-case study, similar to the study used to approve 
Lucentis, would cost over $4.5 million.) 
In the proposed trial, no placebos would be employed in agreement with 
the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki recommendations 
which stipulate that "In any medical study, every patient - including those 
of a control group, if any - should be assured of the best proven diagnostic 
and therapeutic methods."3 
Resveratrol Partners LLC maintains that bevacizumab (Avastin) and 
ranibizumab (Lucentis) should serve as the control group, which is a much 
more difficult comparison standard to demonstrate efficacy than 
comparison against placebo. 
The sponsor I applicant appeals to the FDA to accept this petition in place of 
a New Drug Application, which is beyond the capability of such a small 
2 Richer S, Stiles W, Ulanski L, First oral agent to quell invasive macular degeneration, 
restore lost vision. Poster Presentation: ARVO Meeting, Ft. Lauderdale, FL May 2012.

physicians in biomedical research involving human subjects. JAm Med Assn 1997;

business entity to fund. Furthermore, a NDA would delay approval and 
condemn many thousands to permanent loss of sight. 
Because of these unusual circumstances, Resveratrol Partners LLC 
petitions the Food & Drug Administration to allow it to proceed with use of 
its unique oral nutriceutical capsules for treatment of these cases as long as 
it can be shown with reasonable certainty that no patients will be harmed. 
Animal dosing and human and animal toxicity studies have been done and 
are presented in the appendix herein. 
Longevinex® is a dietary supplement manufactured in a GMP 
establishment in the U.S. It has been marketed in the U.S. since 2004 and 
sold to thousands of patients with no reported serious adverse reactions. 
Reported transient or minor adverse reactions associated with this 
nutriceutical are listed with commentary in this report. A printed product 
insert warns clinicians and consumers of potential drug interactions or 
other adverse effects. 
The sponsor/applicant makes the FDA aware that the ingredients in its 
product address the known reason why anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies 
fail. 
The study would recruit patients via publicity who fail to respond after six 
(6) Avastin/Lucentis treatments, who then would contact their eye 
physician to enroll them in the study. 
The treatment center would agree to comply with the study protocol and 
confirm it has the necessary equipment to perform required tests. 
Because the sponsor/applicant is a small business entity, it is not in a 
financial position to pay investigators a typical $3000 per patient fee to 
conduct tests and tabulate and submit data. Investigators would be 
participating voluntarily. 
Petition To FDA: Resveratrol Partners LLC 
Page 7 
The sponsor of the study applies to the FDA as a small business entity and 
applies for user fees to be waived. 
The number of subjects enrolled in the study would initially be limited to 
250 and expand as the sponsor is capable and FDA gives a go-ahead. 
The patients would qualify for the study if having undergone at least six (6) 
consecutive unsuccessful Avastin/Lucentis injections. 
Patients would be examined at baseline entry into the study, at 6 weeks, 
and 6 months. Because these patients face imminent permanent loss of 
vision, long-term data would not be deemed to be as important as 
intervention that would rapidly avert permanent vision loss. The length of 
the trial can be extended based upon 6-month data. 
Adverse reactions, serious or otherwise, would be reported on a 
standardized form and any serious adverse reactions would be immediately 
reported to the FDA. 
To repeat, public health is at grave risk. A timely response from your 
agency is necessary as it is estimated -7500 elderly patients will suffer 
permanent vision loss during the go-day response period.

2. Actions requested 
The applicant/petitioner pleads for the following: 
• Waiver of requirement to submit an application as an investigational 
new drug in light of its inherent delay in delivering a potential cure to 
otherwise hopeless patients who face permanent loss of vision. 
• Conditional approval to proceed with a human clinical trial based 
upon provision of toxicity and safety data, under the dictum "first do 
no harm." 
• Waiver of the traditional demand to compare its nutriceutical product 
against an inactive placebo. Placebo users would likely face 
permanent and inevitable loss of vision. A placebo-controlled trial 
would be unethical in these circumstances. The World Medical 
Association Declaration of Helsinki recommendations stipulate that 
"In any medical study, every patient - including those of a control 
group, if any - should be assured of the best proven diagnostic and 
therapeutic methods."4 
• Waiver of user fees and designation as a small business entity as the 
cost to perform a 1-year double-blind placebo-controlled study is

population, estimated at 30,000 per year who fail anti-VEGF 
treatment.

The undersigned submits this petition under Section 523 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C 
Act) to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to refrain from taking administrative action against lntertek 
by dismissing them as an Accredited Person for 51 O(k) Review under the FDA Modernization Act of 1997

A. Action requested 
lntertek, as an Accredited Person for 51 O(k) Review, was arbitrarily dismissed from providing a Primary 51 O(k) 
review as an Accredited Third Party without written notification or due process as provided for under Section 
523 of the FD&C Act. lntertek requests relief from this loss of their position as an Accreditl:ld Person and the 
resumption of their contracted responsibilities to BioPhotas, a Premarket Notification sponsor. 
B. Statement of grounds 
As the contracted Third Party Reviewer for the Premarket Notification (51 O(k)) sponsored by BioPhotas 
(K120036), lntertek submitted a 510(k) to CDRH in compliance with the requirements published in regulations 
(21 CFR part 807, subpart E) specifying 510(k) content and procedures. The packet was acknowledged by FDA 
on 05 Jan 2012.(Attachment 1). On 18 Jan 2012, an email containing an internal CDRH Memorandum, 
apparently referencing the same 51 O(k) submission, was received by lntertek (Attachment 2). The document 
was unsigned and undated and contained the recommendation: 
"The device is not eligible for third party review because it needs a self selection study, usability study and 
clinical data to demonstrate safety and effectiveness." 
The pronouncement of "not eligible for third party review" was based upon the reviewer's identification of the 
need for a "usability study" needed to "assess that perspective user's can correctly select this device for use and 
understand all parts of the user manual." The review also stated that the subject device was "not similar to the 
predicate device in energy output", which further necessitated clinical data. 
The details in this CDRH memorandum were inconsistent with the information submitted in the referenced 
51 O(k). No clinical data was either required or submitted for any of the three (3) predicate devices identified.

The undersigned submits this Citizen Petition to you to issue a regulation to allow the addition of fluoride 
to table salt or the fluoridation of edible salt. 
A. Action requested: A regulation to permit the addition of a micronutrient, potassium fluoride, KF, to 
iodized salt for the prevention of Iodine Deficiency Disease, IDD, and dental caries. 
B. Statement of grounds: Fluoridated salt has long been utilized by Switzerland for the prevention of 
dental caries as it has the same beneficial effect of reducing dental decay by 40 to 60 percent as water 
fluoridation. The World Health Organization, WHO, passed a resolution on oral health {WHA 60/17) at 
the World Health Assembly, in Geneva, Switzerland, in May, 2007, which declared that if water 
fluoridation for the prevention of dental caries was not feasible for any reason, then salt fluoridation 
should be implemented, as it is more economical and equally beneficial. This resolution followed 50 
years of experience in Switzerland and over 40 years following NICDR, formerly National Institutes of 
Health, supported a successful trial in Colombia. 
Millions of people in the Americas and worldwide use salt fluoridation when water fluoridation cannot 
be implemented for whatever reason. Many other countries in the European Union, including France, 
Germany and Hungary have reduced dental caries by 40 to 60 percent. 
Mexico presented the Pan American Organization {PAHO/WHO) Directing Council on the topic of salt 
fluoridation in the 1970's and recently announced total population coverage through water and salt 
fluoridation, including Mexico City that has water fluoridation. 
Here in the United States, a world leader in the prevention of disease, although we have implemented 
water fluoridation, after over 60 years, the penetration level has reached approximately 70 percent of 
our population due to cost, location, community size and/or well water. This leaves about 90 million 
Americans unable to benefit from the economical and effective prevention of dental decay by dietary 
sources. 
Just as consumers can choose to buy plain salt or iodized salt, this regulation, if passed and 
implemented by the salt manufacturers and distributors of the USA, will allow consumers, not living in 
water fluoridated areas, to enjoy the health benefits of IDD and dental decay reduction with the 
purchase of iodized and fluoridated table salt. These micronutrients have been shown to be safe and 
are perfectly compatible.

manufacturers can be directed to place a label restricting its usage for areas not having water 
fluoridation. However, even the combination of daily intake of both water and salt that has been 
fluoridated, it would not exceed 2 or 3 mg per day. This is well within a safe limit to prevent fluorosis, a 
cosmetic discoloration of the teeth. Fluorosis can occur when the intake of children during enamel 
formative years exceeds 5 or 6 mg per day. 
Organizations that promote water fluoridation, such as the American Dental Association and or the 
California Dental Association may object to salt fluoridation. These organizations may feel that anti-
fluoridationists will rise up and speak against water fluoridation if salt fluoridation becomes available. 
One person said that this product ~~muddies the waters for the promotion of water fluoridation." 
However, both can co-exist without any harm to consumers as in Mexico, Colombia, Costa Rica, other

Lorillard Tobacco Company ("Lorillard") submits this petition under sections 905(j) 
and 910 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act ("FDCA" or the "Act") (21 
U.S.C. §§ 387e(j) and 387(j) and 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 to request that the Commissioner of 
Food and Drugs exercise enforcement discretion with respect to section 910(a) of the 
FDCA and allow the marketing of products introduced after March 22, 2011, including 
two new Lorillard products (the "Products"), for which two reports have been filed with 
the Food and Drug Administration ("FDA") under section 905(j) and are currently 
under review, with the tracking numbers SE0003730 and SE0003731 (the "Reports"), 
for which substantial equivalence reports have been submitted, but are still under 
review by FDA. 
I. 
Action Requested 
Lorillard requests that FDA announce a policy of enforcement discretion with respect to 
the premarket approval requirements of section FDCA 910(a) with respect to new 
tobacco products first introduced into U.S. commerce after March 22, 2011, or modified 
in certain ways after that date, so long as the manufacturer has submitted a report under 
section 905(j) of the FDCA at least 90 days prior to introducing the new product (the 
"SE Report" or "905(j) Report"). On October 12, 2011, Lorillard has submitted the 
Reports to the FDA for review, and this enforcement discretion policy would apply to 
Lorillard's Reports. 
FDA's enforcement discretion would not apply to a new tobacco product if (i) FDA 
issued an order finding that the respective new tobacco product is not substantially 
equivalent to the predicate product, as defined by section 910(a)(3) of the FDCA; (ii) a 
new product, which is the subject product of a 905(j) report, is introduced into U.S. 
commerce on a date that is prior to 90 days following the submission of the respective 
Corporate Office: 
714 Green Valley Road 
Greensboro, NC 27408

report under section 905(j) of the FDCA; or (iii) the 905(j) Report pertaining to the 
respective new tobacco product does not contain the information required under section 
905(j) or 910(a)(3). 
II. 
Statement of Grounds 
A. 
Background 
1. 
Statutory and Regulatory Background 
President Obama signed the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act 
(Public Law No. 111-31) into law on June 22, 2009. The Act amended the Federal 
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. §§ 301-399d) to give the FDA the authority 
to regulate tobacco products. 
Among other authorities, the Act granted FDA the 
authority to require premarket review and approval of new tobacco products. 
The 
statute defined "new tobacco products" as products first marketed or modified in certain 
ways after February 15, 2007. 
In enacting the statute, Congress envisioned an efficient system allowing different 
levels of FDA review for different types of new tobacco products. As one option, 
manufacturers may submit a "new tobacco product application" under section 910 of 
the Act. 1 
This application requires an extensive amount of information and data, 
includin~ but not limited to clinical and non-clinical studies of the new tobacco 
product. 
Even for this complex new tobacco product application, however, the Act 
provides that FDA must act on these applications "[a]s promptly as possible, but in no 
event later than 180 days after the receipt of an application."3 
In contrast to a new tobacco product application under section 910 of the Act, Congress 
included a streamlined process under section 905(j) for expedited review of products 
that are "substantially equivalent" to a product that was on the market as of 
February 15, 2007 (or another product for which FDA has previously determined to be 
substantially equivalent to a product on the market as of February 15, 2007).4 
Substantial equivalence is defined to mean that the tobacco product at issue has the 
same characteristics of the predicate product, or has different characteristics, but the 
information submitted demonstrates that the product does not raise different questions 
of public health. 5 
The Act states that such substantial equivalence reports ("SE 
1 FDCA § 910, 21 U.S.C. § 387j. 
2 FDCA § 910(b), 21 U.S.C. § 387j(b). 
3 FDCA § 910(c), 21 U.S.C. § 387j(c). 
4 FDCA § 905(j), 21 U.S.C. § 387e(j). 
5 FDCA § 910(a)(3), 21 U.S.C. § 387j(a)(3). 
Page 2 of8 
Reports") must be submitted "at least 90 days prior to" introducing a product into 
. 
6 
mterstate commerce. 
In addition, the Act establishes two distinct timeframes for substantial equivalence 
reports. 
First, the statute creates one pathway for tobacco products that are first 
introduced to the market after March 22, 2011, or products that are changed in certain 
ways after March 22, 2011. 
These products are referred to as "non-provisional 
products." For non-provisional products, section 91 O(a)(2)(A) of the FDCA provides 
that an approval under a new tobacco product application is required unless a 
manufacturer obtains an order from FDA that the tobacco product is substantially 
equivalent to an appropriate predicate product and is in compliance with the Act.7 
Thus, FDA's position is that manufacturers need to have an affirmative FDA order 
finding the product to be substantially equivalent before the product can be introduced. 
In contrast, section 910(a)(2)(B) establishes a special rule for "provisional" products, 
defined as tobacco products that were first introduced to the market between February 
15, 2007 and March 22, 2011, or products that were changed in certain ways during the 
same time period. For products that meet those criteria, so long as the manufacturer 
submitted an SE Report to FDA before March 22, 2011, an affirmative order from FDA 
was not needed in order to market the respective product, unless FDA determined that 
the product was not substantially equivalent.8 
2. 
SE Reports Submitted to FDA 
The due date for submission of SE Reports for provisional products was March 22, 
2011. After March 22, 2011, Lorillard and other companies have submitted SE Reports 
to FDA for non-provisional products. According to information obtained pursuant to a 
Freedom of Information Act ("FOIA") request and the FDA website, FDA has stated 
that it received approximately 36 SE Reports between April and October 2011, for a 
total of approximately 118 from April 2011 to date.9 As stated above, FDA's position is 
that these non-provisional products may not be marketed until FDA affirmatively issues 
an order finding these products to be substantially equivalent, so manufacturers must 
wait for FDA action on these applications before the products may be commercialized. 
6 FDCA § 910(a)(3), 21 U.S.C. § 387j(a)(3). 
7 FDCA § 910(a)(2)(A), 21 U.S.C. § 387j(a)(2)(A). 
8 FDCA § 910(a)(2)(B), 21 U.S.C. § 387j(a)(2)(B). 
9 See FDA, Total Number of Product Submissions Received in the Month, 
http://www .accessdata.fda.gov /FDA Track/track?program=ctp&id=CTP -OS-total-
product -submissions-received. 
Page 3 of8 
3. 
FDA Action on SE Reports 
It is our understanding that FDA has not taken final action -- such as issuing an order 
finding a product to be either substantially equivalent or not substantially equivalent --
on any SE Report. As described above, many of these reports have been pending before 
the agency for more than a year. However, FDA's inaction on any SE Reports does not 
appear to be the result of the volume of reports that it has received. In an April 24, 
2012 webinar hosted by FDA's Center for Tobacco Products ("CTP"), officials stated 
that they have prioritized their review process to focus first on the few SE Reports 
submitted for non-provisional products. For provisional products, FDA appears to have 
made the decision to not review provisional SE Reports at this time. 10 
But even with FDA focusing only on non-provisional SE Reports, the agency has still 
not acted. As discussed above, on October 12, 2011, Lorillard submitted two 905(j) 
reports ("Reports") to the FDA for two new products Lorillard wished to introduce. 
Based upon a meeting with FDA officials on May 3, 2012, Lorillard's understanding is 
that FDA's review is only in its preliminary stages. Immediately following the meeting, 
Lorillard received a request from FDA to demonstrate that the predicate products were 
on the market as of February 15, 2007. Lorillard promptly provided the requested 
information on May 4, 2012. Lorillard's understanding is that FDA has not even begun 
the scientific review process for Lorillard's Reports. Lorillard learned that these reports 
had not even progressed to the second step in FDA's review process- which appears to 
be the review by the Office of Compliance -- despite that they had been pending for 
nearly seven months at the time. A review of any SE Reports at this time does not 
appear imminent, and it cannot be based on objective criteria, absent internal FDA firm 
criteria for SE Reports review. 
B. 
Argument 
1. 
FDA Should Review SE Reports within 90 Days of Receipt. 
Even though the Act refers to a 90-day review period, FDA has taken the position that it 
has no deadline for acting on any substantial equivalence reports. In its April 24, 2012 
webinar, a CTP official stated that FDA is "well aware" of the fact that the statute states 
that applicants must submit substantial reports at least 90 days before introducing the 
new product. 
11 However, the official stated that "there is no statutory mandate for when 
10 See FDA, Center for Tobacco Products, April24, 2012 Webinar on Substantial 
Equivalence Reports; available at 
http://www. fda.gov /TobaccoProducts/Resourcesfor Y ou!F or Industry/Retailer/ucm28865 
7.htm. 
II fd 
Page 4 of8 
an order must issue finding a tobacco product substantially equivalent or not 
substantially equivalent."
12 
FDA's assertion that there is no deadline associated with review of a substantial 
equivalence report renders the 90-day period stated in section 905G) meaningless. 13 
With no deadline on when a substantial equivalence report will be reviewed, it is 
impossible for any manufacturer to calculate a date that is 90 days before it will 
introduce a product into interstate commerce. FDA's position also would mean that 
Congress intended FDA to have greater discretion -- and a potentially infinite review 
period -- to review an SE Report than the 180 days it has for reviewing a new tobacco 
product application under Section 910 -which involves a more rigorous and lengthy 
process. 
This surely cannot be the intent of Congress, particularly when read in 
connection with the requirement in section 905G) that an SE Report be submitted 90 
days before introduction of the substantially equivalent product. 
Moreover, as a practical matter, FDA's position that it has no deadline whatsoever has 
led to the current situation, in which SE Reports are languishing before the agency, with 
no end in sight. This clearly was not what Congress intended. FDA should honor the 
statutory deadline imposed by Congress and review SE Reports within 90 days. 
2. 
FDA Should Exercise Eriforcement Discretion and Allow the 
Products to be Marketed While FDA Completes its Review 
Even putting aside whether FDA is required to review SE Reports within 90 days, it is 
undeniable that Congress intended the 905G) substantial equivalence process to be a 
more streamlined and efficient process than the section 91 0 new tobacco product 
application process. However, at this point, the agency appears to be unable to review 
SE Reports within an objectively reasonable timeframe, or against clear criteria and 
metrics. 
This inaction has created a situation in which the tobacco market is essentially frozen by 
a de facto embargo by FDA on new product introductions. 
This results in less 
competition and harms the ability of companies to engage in basic planning activities 
for the launch of new products. These problems are compounded by the agency's lack 
of transparency, which leaves companies in the dark on what they might expect from 
FDA's review process. 
12 !d. 
13 This position conflicts with well-established doctrines of statutory construction 
providing that statutes must be read to give effect to all provisions. Statutes should be 
construed "so as to avoid rendering superfluous" any statutory language. 
Astoria 
Federal Savings & Loan Ass 'n v. So/imino, 501 U.S. 104, 112 (1991); see also Bailey v. 
United States, 516 U.S. 137, 146 (1995) ("We assume that Congress used two terms 
because it intended each term to have a particular, nonsuperfluous meaning."). 
Page 5 of8 
Lorillard understands that the Center for Tobacco Products is a relatively new center 
within FDA. 
We also understand that the agency needs to develop the criteria, 
processes, and expertise to apply to the review of SE Reports. 
Nevertheless, this 
learning curve should not prevent the introduction of legitimate products. Furthermore, 
the Act authorized that CTP receive at least $944 million to date from tobacco 
manufacturers, and it therefore has more than adequate resources to service its users. 14 
If FDA needs more time to establish a reasonable and efficient regulatory system, 
Lorillard and the tobacco industry should not be punished. 
In light of these factors, it is appropriate for FDA to exercise enforcement discretion 
and allow Lorillard and other manufacturers to introduce non-provisional, substantially 
equivalent products to the market while the agency completes its review. FDA could 
then complete its review in a manner similar to provisional products. 
And like 
provisional products, should FDA conclude that the Products are not substantially 
equivalent, it could issue an order to that effect. 
Such a policy would treat provisional and non-provisional products in a consistent 
manner. The Act provided the date of March 22, 2011 for the end of the introduction of 
provisional products. This extended period of time, 21 months from the date the Act 
took effect, was clearly meant to recognize that FDA would need time to organize the 
Center for Tobacco Products in order to meet its obligations under the Act. 
Unfortunately, 21 months was insufficient for FDA to staff the CTP and establish a 
process to review the SE Reports within the 90 days that Congress intended. Industry 
should not be disadvantaged because FDA and CTP have been delayed through no fault 
of industry in fully meeting its obligations. 
3. 
FDA Has Clear Authority to Issue an Enforcement Discretion 
Policy. 
FDA's authority to exercise enforcement discretion under these circumstances is 
unquestioned. Federal agencies have wide latitude to decide when or how they will 
enforce provisions of federal law. 15 
FDA, moreover, has repeatedly exercised 
enforcement discretion over provisions of the FDCA, including premarket approval 
requirements. The examples of such enforcement discretion are numerous, and include 
the following: 
• 
Although the FDCA requires the submission and FDA approval of a new 
animal drug application for drugs for animals, FDA permits the introduction 
14 FDCA § 919, 21 U.S.C. § 387s. 
15 See, e.g., Heckler v. Chaney, 470 U.S. 821,831 (1985) (recognizing "that an agency's 
decision not to prosecute or enforce, whether through civil or criminal process, is a 
decision generally committed to an agency's absolute discretion"). 
Page 6 of8 
of drugs for non-food producing, mmor species under an enforcement 
discretion policy. 16 
• 
FDA takes the position that all compounded drugs for human use are "new 
drugs," subject to the approval requirements of Section 505 of the FDCA. 
Yet the agency has announced a policy of enforcement discretion for 
compounded medications produced in a manner consistent with the practice 
of pharmacy and FDA Compliance Policy Guide. 17 
• 
While FDA has taken the position that convenience kits -- copackaging 
various commercialized medical devices for the convenience of the health 
care provider -- are themselves medical devices, but announced that it would 
exercise enforcement discretion and not require a new device premarket 
notification of approval application for most convenience kits. 18 
• 
FDA announced a policy of enforcement discretion for hospitals that 
repackage drugs into unit-dose containers without conducting stability 
studies to support the expiration dates on those containers. 19 
Accordingly, FDA has ample authority to decide when to exercise enforcement 
discretion. 
Given the circumstances described above, a policy of enforcement 
discretion is appropriate. 
III. 
Conclusion 
Despite Congress including a streamlined process to allow companies to introduce new 
tobacco products that are substantially equivalent to existing products under section 
905G), FDA has not issued any orders permitting such products to enter the market --
despite having over 100 non-provisional submissions pending for more than a year. 
While we appreciate the difficulty of establishing a review process for SE Reports, this 
effective freeze on the market was not an outcome intended by Congress. 
In light of this situation, we respectfully request that FDA exercise enforcement 
discretion and allow Lorillard and other tobacco manufacturers to market non-
provisional products absent an order under section 910(a) until FDA is able to review 
16 See FDCA § 572, 21 U.S.C. § 360ccc-1; 21 C.F.R. § 516.111 (providing "standards 
and procedures to establish an index of legally marketed unapproved new animal 
drugs"). 
17 See FDA Compliance Policy Guide 460.200 (May 2002). 
18 See FDA, Center for Devices and Radiological Health, Convenience Kits Interim 
Regulatory Guidance (May 20, 1997). 
19 See FDA, Expiration Dating of Unit-Dose Repackaged Drugs: Compliance Policy 
Guide (May 2005). 
Page7of8 
the applications and issue such an order. 
This would allow such non-provisional 
products to be introduced and marketed in the same way as provisional products while 
FDA reviews its backlog of applications. 
IV. 
Required Material

Environmental Impact 
Lorillard incorporates the Environmental Impact Statements that were submitted with 
its pending substantial equivalence reports for the Products referenced in this Citizen 
Petition. 
B. 
Economic Impact 
An economic impact statement will be submitted at the request of the Commissioner. 
C. 
Certification 
The undersigned certifies that, to the best knowledge and belief of the undersigned, this 
petition includes all information and views on which the petition relies, and that it 
includes representative data and information known to the petitioner, which are 
unfavorable to the petition.

4. Justification for the proposed dosage form: 
a. Acceptance of the product: Since the product is a flavored paste which is directly

would be readily ingested by the dog. 
b. Accurate dosing of the product: Since the product will be dispensed using a

opposed to the need to break the tablet along a score or other division which is 
imprecise and could lead to incorrect dosing.

be utilized to administer different dosage strengths by the easy to use dial a dose 
syringe-plunger system. For example for a 25 mg dose, 1 gram of the paste can be 
administered, for 50 mg dose. 2 grams of the paste can be administered and for 75 
mg dose, 3 grams of the paste can be administered. This can be achieved by 
simply adjusting the dosing ring on the plunger of the syringe. 
d. Enhanced consumer compliance: This form of dosing would be more convenient 
for the pet owner than breaking a scored tablet to achieve different dosage
