Petition_Title: Citizen Petition from Spectrum Pharmaceuticals Inc
Petition_Text:
October 13, 2014 
 
Division of Dockets Management 
Food and Drug Administration 
5630 Fishers Lane, Room 1061 
Rockville, Maryland 20852  
 
CITIZEN PETITION 
 
Spectrum Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Spectrum or the Company) submits this Citizen Petition 
under 21 USC 355 and 21 CFR 10.30, among other provisions of law, to request that the 
Commissioner of Food and Drugs revise the approval date of Spectrum’s New Drug Application 
(NDA) for FUSILEV® (levoleucovorin) for injection (NDA 20-140).  Consistent with this, we 
also request an extension of the orphan drug exclusivity period for FUSILEV for use in rescue 
after high-dose methotrexate therapy in osteosarcoma, and for diminishing the toxicity and 
counteracting the effects of impaired methotrexate elimination and of inadvertent overdosage of 
folic acid antagonists (collectively, the Methotrexate Indications).   
 
The revision to the FUSILEV NDA approval date and the extension of the orphan 
exclusivity are necessary to account for the time immediately following the approval of the 
FUSILEV NDA, during which Spectrum was unable to launch the product because the Food and 
Drug Administration (FDA or the Agency) had not yet approved the FUSILEV proprietary 
name. 
 
We recognize that a substantial amount of time has elapsed since FUSILEV’s original 
approval.  We are submitting this request now because we only recently became aware of a 
similar situation involving the drug Razadyne® ER (galantamine hydrobromide) (NDA 21-615).1  
In that matter, FDA revised Razadyne ER’s approval date – and effectively granted an extension 
to the drug’s exclusivity period – because of the time it took for the NDA sponsor and the 
Agency to agree on the drug’s proprietary name. 
 
                                                      
1 See Citizen Petition Denial Response from FDA CDER to Eisai, Inc. and UCB, Inc. at 17-18, n.92, DOCKET NO. 
FDA-2013-P-0884 (April 30, 2014), http://www.regulations.gov/#!documentDetail;D=FDA-2013-P-0884-0006. 
Food and Drug Administration 
October 13, 2014

Due to the similarity in the underlying facts between Razadyne ER and FUSILEV, we 
hereby request that the listing for FUSILEV in the Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic 
Equivalence Evaluations (the Orange Book) be updated to state that the NDA for this product 
was approved on July 14, 2008.  Similarly, FDA should extend the expiration date of the orphan 
exclusivity for the FUSILEV Methotrexate Indications until July 14, 2015. 
 
ACTIONS REQUESTED 
 
For the reasons that follow, Spectrum requests that FDA revise the listing for FUSILEV 
in the Orange Book to state that the NDA for this product was approved on July 14, 2008.  
Spectrum also requests that FDA extend the expiration date of the orphan exclusivity for the 
FUSILEV Methotrexate Indications until July 14, 2015. 
 
STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
I. 
BACKGROUND 
 
A.   
Razadyne ER Regulatory History  
 
Johnson & Johnson (J&J) submitted an NDA for galantamine hydrobromide extended 
release capsules on February 25, 2003, and proposed a proprietary name of Reminyl ER.2  At 
that time, J&J had been marketing previously approved products with the same proprietary name 
(Reminyl), but with different formulations as the proposed new product, which was formulated 
as immediate release tablets and an oral solution.3   
 
On February 17, 2004, one year after submission, FDA notified J&J that “preliminarily 
[the proposed name] . . . appeared to be acceptable,” but noted that the final opinion of the 
Division of Medication Errors and Technical Support (DMETS) was pending.4  Despite this 
initial notification, on July 29, 2004, DMETS rejected “Reminyl ER” and also recommended that 
consideration be given to changing the proprietary name of the currently-marketed immediate-
release Reminyl products.  DMETS’ concerns were based on reports of post-marketing 
medication errors in which Reminyl had been confused with Amaryl (an oral hypoglycemic 
medication).5

During the Razadyne ER NDA review, the Agency also became aware of reports of two 
deaths related to patients receiving Amaryl instead of Reminyl.6  Upon learning of the second 
death, FDA engaged in discussions with J&J and ultimately “agreed with the sponsor that they 
must, and will, change the name of all Reminyl products.”7   
 
On December 22, 2004, FDA issued J&J an NDA Approval Letter, which only referred 
to the drug by its established name.  Although the letter stated that the application was 
“approved, effective on the date of this letter,” FDA recognized:   
 
We note your commitment to change the name of your Reminyl products, because 
of the recent medication errors associated with Reminyl and Amaryl.  We also 
note your commitment to adopt a new name for the controlled release formulation 
prior to its marketing, and to submit the new proposed proprietary names to the 
Agency for our review prior to implementation.  Because you have not yet 
submitted a new name for the controlled release formulation, it is being 
approved without a trade name.8 
 
 
On December 29, 2004, DMETS recommended against the use of several additional 
proposed names due to concerns relating to potential look-alike and/or sound-alike confusion 
with other names.9  
 
 
On January 24, 2005, FDA met with J&J to discuss a plan to implement a change in the 
proprietary name for both the recently approved Reminyl formulation, Reminyl ER, and the 
immediate release formulations.10  In that meeting, the Agency and J&J discussed several 
proprietary names, and FDA noted that its review of the names was ongoing.  To address the 
Agency’s concern that three different labels for the formulations would be available and 
potentially lead to medication errors, FDA and J&J decided that the following would be 
launched simultaneously: the newly approved extended-release formulation labeled with the new 
proprietary name, and the immediate-release products labeled both with the new proprietary 
name and a “formerly known as Reminyl” statement.11

On April 1, 2005 – 101 days after the original NDA Approval Letter – FDA notified J&J 
that it found the proposed trade name, Razadyne ER, to be acceptable.13  Soon thereafter, on May 
23, 2005, the sponsor began marketing Razadyne ER.14 
 
 
On November 11, 2005, J&J requested that FDA revise the NDA approval date from 
December 22, 2004 – the date of the original NDA Approval Letter – to April 1, 2005.  The basis 
of J&J’s request was that it was not until the later date that FDA and J&J agreed upon Razadyne 
as the proposed trade name for the product.15   
  
 
In response to J&J’s request, on June 13, 2006, FDA issued a letter to J&J, revising the 
approval date of the NDA to April 1, 2005, the date FDA issued the letter to J&J accepting the 
proposed trade name.16  The Agency provided the following rationale:

associated with the use of the trade name Reminyl for the approved galantamine 
hydrobromide immediate release product, J&J would not market the extended 
release product until a new trade name had been reviewed and approved by FDA.  
 
We have reviewed your letter and the NDA record, and concluded that the action 
letter of December 22, 2004, should be considered an approvable letter as 
described in 21 CFR 314.110.  In light of the concerns about medication errors 
expressed in that letter, it is reasonable to conclude that Razadyne ER was not 
approved until April 1, 2005, when the Agency completed its review of the 
proposed new trade name, found it acceptable, and conveyed this information to 
J&J.17

To reflect the new April 1, 2005 approval date, FDA amended its records and the

Importantly, in the passage quoted above, the Agency cited 21 CFR 314.110 in support of 
its decision that the December 22, 2004 NDA Approval Letter “should be considered an 
approvable letter.”  Before an amended version of 21 CFR 314.110 went into effect on August 
11, 2008, this regulation governed FDA’s practice of sending “Approvable Letters” to applicants 
when an NDA or abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) was “basically approvable 
providing certain issues are resolved.” 20  More specifically, the regulation stated: 
 
FDA will send the applicant an approvable letter if the application or abbreviated 
application substantially meets the requirements of this part and the agency 
believes that it can approve the application or abbreviated application if specific 
additional information or material is submitted or specific conditions (for 
example, certain changes in labeling) are agreed to by the applicant.  The 
approvable letter will describe the information or material FDA requires or the 
conditions the applicant is asked to meet.  As a practical matter, the approvable 
letter will serve in most instances as a mechanism for resolving outstanding issues 
on drugs that are about to be approved and marketed.21

version of 21 CFR 314.110 was in effect.22 
 
B.   
FUSILEV Regulatory History  
 
 
The regulatory history of FUSILEV is strikingly similar.  The original NDA for 
levoleucovorin was submitted to FDA on December 18, 1990.23  On July 10, 2007 – eight

As noted above, FDA expressed concerns with the similarity of “ISO-vorin,” the 
initially proposed trade name for levoleucovorin, with “leucovorin.”  As further background, 
leucovorin is a mixture of equal parts of the active levorotatory isomer of leucovorin that 
comprises levoleucovorin, along with the inactive dextrorotatory isomer.  As a result, leucovorin 
needs to be administered at twice the dose of levoleucovorin to provide the same dose of the 
active drug.   
 
Because of the similarity of their established names and approved indications, FDA has 
recognized that there is a potential for dosing errors between the two drugs.  With this risk in 
mind, the approved Package Insert for FUSILEV states, “Fusilev is dosed at one-half the usual 
dose of racemic d,l-leucovorin.”42  Additionally, FDA has acknowledged the “potential for 
dosing errors when interchanging leucovorin and levoleucovorin (Fusilev).”43  In fact, an 
instance was reported in the literature of a health care provider prescribing levoleucovorin, only 
to have the patient mistakenly be administered leucovorin due to an error by a pharmacy 
technician.44     
 
Thus, if a patient is prescribed leucovorin and mistakenly receives an equivalent 
amount of levoleucovorin, that patient would effectively be receiving twice the intended 
dose.  Given the potential for medication errors between these two drugs and the potential for 
overdoses, DMETS rejected ISO-vorin as a trade name for levoleucovorin:

II. 
ARGUMENT 
 
A.   
The Extensive Similarities Between the Approvals of Razadyne ER and 
FUSILEV Must Lead to Consistent Outcomes 
 
As can be seen above, the relevant underlying facts of the FUSILEV and Razadyne ER 
approvals are extremely similar.  It is well established that “an agency must treat similar cases in 
a similar manner unless it can provide a legitimate reason for failing to do so.” 48  In the present 
case, because of the clear parallels between the approvals of Razadyne ER and FUSILEV, we 
think it is both necessary and appropriate for the Agency to revise FUSILEV’s NDA approval

B. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS
I. 
Summary of Argument
The Alkermes NDA should not be accepted for filing because it does not satisfy the information
requirements of Section 505(b) and thus cannot be ultimately approved. Specifically, the
Alkermes NDA is deficient on its face because it cannot meet the statutory requirement for
demonstration of substantial evidence of effectiveness. First, FDA generally requires that NDAs
provide evidence of effectiveness based on at least two AWCTs of the proposed drug product to
ensure that the results are independently reproducible. However, the Alkermes NDA contains
full reports of only a single, new AWCT of axipiprazole lauroxil.
Second, the Alkermes NDA does not meet any of FDA's criteria for approving an NDA based on
only a single new AWCT. FDA has approved NDAs with reports of a single AWCT of a new use
of an already-approved drug. However, according to FDA's bright-line rule, aripiprazole lauroxil
is deemed to contain a new active moiety that has never been contained in a previously approved
drug product. Consequently, the single study of aripiprazole lauroxil is the only available study
of a drug with a new active moiety rather than a new use of an approved drug. In accordance
with the applicable FDA rule, having only a single study is not sufficient in this case to trigger
acceptance for substantive review.
FDA has also approved new drugs based on a single new AWCT of a drug with a new active
moiety. However, FDA has narrowly limited this exception to proposed drug products with a
single AWCT that have demonstrated certain types of effects (such as reduction in mortality)
where it would be unethical to require a second, confirmatory study. The Alkermes NDA,
according to Alkermes's public statements, does not meet these criteria.
A decision that a single AWCT is sufficient to support approval of the Alkermes NDA in this
instance would require an arbitrary and capricious break with prior precedent and a sharp
departure from FDA's well-established interpretations of relevant statutes and regulations. The
present application does not warrant commitment of agency resources for a substantive review
until the application is resubmitted with the legally necessary information as defined under the
Act. Furthermore, this petition presents a clear legal question that does not require substantive
scientific review for resolution. As described below, FDA can —and should —exercise its
discretion to refuse to accept for substantive review the Alkermes NDA because no amount of
substantive review can remedy the failure of the Alkermes NDA to meet applicable statutory and
regulatory requirements.
2
II. 
Legal Background
a. Standard for Refusing to Accept Application For Review
FDA may refuse to accept an NDA for review if, among other reasons, the application "is
incomplete because on its face it does not contain the information required under section
505(b)."5 According to FDA, 
this includes: "Failure to include evidence of effectiveness
compatible with statute and regulations."6 One such failure is: "Presentation of a single adequate
and well-controlled trial without adequate justification of why the single trial should be regarded
as fulfilling the statutory requirement for substantial evidence of effectiveness."~
According to FDA, "RTF [Refusal-to-file] is an important regulatory tool to help CDER avoid
unnecessary review of incomplete applications," because "[i]ncomplete applications can lead to
multiple-cycle reviews and inefficient use of CDER resources."g Moreover, "CDER also
believes an RTF action can allow an applicant to begin repair of critical deficiencies in the
application far sooner than if these were identified much later in a complete response action and
may lead to more rapid approval of safe and effective drug products."9 Consequently, substantive
review of a deficient application would be a waste of time and resources for both the agency and
the applicant.
b. Standard for Distinguishing New Active Moieties
FDA defines an NCE as "a drug that contains no active moiety that has been approved by FDA
in any other application submitted under section 505(b) of the act."10 An active moiety is
defined, in turn, as:
[T]he molecule or ion, excluding those appended portions of the molecule that
cause the drug to be an ester, salt (including a salt with hydrogen or coordination
bonds), or other non-covalent derivative (such as a complex, chelate, or clathrate)
of the molecule, responsible for the physiological or pharmacological action of
the drug substance. 1
According to this bright-line definition of active moiety, NCE status is determined exclusively
on the basis of chemical structure rather than on a case-by-case analysis of pharmacological
activity. Thus, "an ester, salt ... , or other noncovalent derivative ... of [a] molecule" is deemed
to be the same molecule (and thus same active moiety), whereas a molecule with anon-ester
covalent bond is deemed to be a different molecule (and thus a new active moiety) — "even if the

makes reference to "an application ... for a drug for which the investigations described in clause
(A) of such paragraph and relied upon by the applicant for approval of the application were not

Otsuka holds an NDA for Abilify (aripiprazole), an atypical antipsychotic initially approved in

(aripiprazole), along-acting, intra-muscular injection for the treatment of schizophrenia.36
Each of the approved formulations and dosage forms of Abilify, including Abilify Maintena, is

IV. 
Discussion
Alkermes seeks approval for an NCE supported by a single AWCT without adequate
justification for submitting results from a single AWCT. Because the Alkermes NDA does not —
and cannot —satisfy the information requirements of Section 505(b), the application should not
be accepted for substantive review.
a. The aripiprazole lauroxil NDA must contain reports from at least two AWCTs of
the proposed active moiety unless it meets established exceptions permitting only a
single new AWCT
Under FDA's bright-line rule, aripiprazole lauroxil and aripiprazole contain
different active moieties
FDA has established abright-line rule, based exclusively on chemical structure, for defining
whether the active moiety of a prodrug such as aripiprazole lauroxil is the whole molecule (i.e.
aripiprazole lauroxil) prior to the bioconversion process or the previously-approved molecule
ultimately released through a bioconversion process (i.e. aripiprazole). Under FDA's bright-line
rule, it is irrelevant that aripiprazole lauroxil "ultimately" "convert[s]"41 into aripiprazole when
determining whether the active moiety is aripiprazole lauroxil or aripiprazole. The deciding
factor is the chemical structure prior to bioconversion, and, specifically, whether there are
covalent structural modifications. The chemical structures of Abilify (aripiprazole) and
aripiprazole lauroxil, as depicted in Figures 1 and 2, respectively, are not identical. Aripiprazole
lauroxil consists of the aripiprazole moiety with a covalently bonded lauroxil group,42 which
makes aripiprazole lauroxil an NCE under FDA's bright-line rule.
Alkermes suggests that aripiprazole lauroxil is essentially the same drug as aripiprazole because
aripiprazole lauroxil undergoes a conversion process "that ultimately results in release of the
aripiprazole active moiety."43 However, Alkermes also acknowledges that the conversion process
includes "enzyme-mediated cleavage that generates an intermediate form (N-hydroxymethyl
aripiprazole), and dissociation of a covalently bonded hydroxymethyl group."44 These two
statements suggest that Alkermes is trying to benefit from both sides of FDA's bright-line rule.

The undersigned submits this petition under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA)
or the Public Health Service Act (PHS) or any other statutory provision for which authority has
been delegated to the Commissioner of Food and Drug under 21 Code of Federal Regulations
(C.F.R.) 10.30 to request the Commissioner of Food and Drug to issue guidance or amend
21 C.F.R. 101.12 to establish a new Reference Amount Customarily Consumed (RACC) per
eating occasion for nut cocoa based spreads such as Nutella®.
A. Action Requested
Nut cocoa based spreads such as Nutella® are currently not specifically listed in the regulation.
FDA concluded, in the preamble of the final rule, that the products belonged to the “Other
dessert toppings” category under “Dessert Toppings and Fillings” of 21 C.F.R. 101.12(b) with a
RACC of 2 tablespoon (tbsp). 1/ We are submitting this petition on behalf of our client, Ferrero
U.S.A., Inc. (“Ferrero”) and are requesting the Commissioner either (1) issue guidance
recognizing that nut cocoa based spreads should fall within the “Honey, jams, jellies, fruit butter,
molasses” category for the purpose of RACC determination or (2) amend 21 C.F.R. 101.12(b),
Table 2, to establish a new category for “Nut Cocoa Based Spreads” such as Nutella® with a
1 tbsp RACC. The regulation, 21 C.F.R. 101.12 (“Reference amounts customarily consumed per
eating occasion”), is attached as Appendix I of this petition.
B. Statement of Grounds
I. The Current Regulatory Mandate
The Nutrition Labeling and Education Act of 1990 established mandatory nutrition labeling for
packaged foods to enable consumers to make more informed food product choices by adding
Section 403(q) to the FFDCA. This section specifies, among other things, that the “serving size”

is “an amount customarily consumed and which is expressed in common household measure that
is appropriate to the food.” 2/ According to 21 C.F.R. 101.9 (“Nutrition labeling of food”), the
term “common household measure” means “cup, tablespoon, teaspoon … or other common
household equipment used to package food products.” 3/ The serving size is determined from the
RACC per eating occasion. 4/ FDA provides general principles and factors the agency will
consider in arriving at the RACC in 21 C.F.R. 101.12. Specifically, FDA calculated the
reference amounts for persons 4 years of age or older to reflect the amount of food customarily
consumed per eating occasion. 5/ RACC values are primarily based on the consumption data
derived from national consumption surveys. 6/ When survey data are insufficient, FDA takes
into consideration various other sources of information including: “(i) Serving sizes used in
dietary guidance recommendations or recommended by other authoritative systems or
organizations; (ii) Serving sizes recommended in comments; (iii) Serving sizes used by
manufacturers and grocers; and (iv) Serving sizes used by other countries.” 7/
For the RACC values currently listed in Table 2 of 21 C.F.R. 101.12(b), FDA primarily relied on
the 1977- 1978 and the 1987-1988 Nationwide Food Consumption Survey (NFCS) conducted by
U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). 8/ The agency reviewed food consumption data for
each product category and considered three statistical estimates, i.e., the mean (average), the
median (50th percentile), and the mode (most frequent value). 9/ Because Nutella® hazelnut
spread and other nut cocoa based spreads were not a commonly consumed food in U.S. in the
70s and 80s, they were not listed in the NFCS and their consumption data were unavailable when
the RACC values were established in 1993 and when Ferrero approached FDA in 1992. 10/ As
such, FDA relied on a consumer survey conducted by Ferrero in 1991 to determine the RACC
for Nutella®. 11/ The survey reported that 27% of the 157 primarily female grocery shoppers
surveyed in metropolitan areas including Chicago, Los Angeles, and Philadelphia preferred to
use Nutella® with ice cream whereas only 8% preferred to use Nutella® with bread. 12/ Based
on this consumer preference, FDA concluded that Nutella® resembled chocolate syrups used as
a dessert topping and belonged to the “Other dessert toppings” category with a RACC of

II. Nutella® Uses and Trends
Nutella® is a delicious sweetened and flavored nut cocoa based spread mainly made from the
combination of sugar, palm oil, roasted hazelnuts, skim milk, and cocoa. The origin of Nutella®
can be traced back to the food rationing days in Europe right after the World War II. As an
affordable nutritious spread to be used on a piece of bread, it gradually gained popularity in the
European continent. Since its launch in the U.S. market in the 1980s, Nutella has gained
immediate successes and a loyal following carrying it into the present day where it is used by its
growing consumer base as a spread on bread, bagels, English muffins and other baked goods
and as a substitute for jams and jellies. Recent market data show that breakfast accounts for
almost half of Nutella® consumption and is the most developed meal occasion.
Breakfast is the most important meal of the day. As a part of a healthful diet and lifestyle,
breakfast can positively impact children’s health and well-being. Ferrero’s most recent
advertising and promotion has advocated the consumption of a balanced breakfast with the
inclusion of Nutella® as a tasty, complementary spread to add on to nutrient-rich whole grain
breads, fruits, and dairy products. Nutella® is shown with bread (or other whole grain bakery
product), fruit, and milk in advertising to promote its use in a balanced breakfast in the same
manner with jams and jellies – for the purpose of making breakfast more tasteful and appealing
to children. Nutella® also can be used as a snack or as part of a meal for lunch or dinner.
To further understand the U.S. consumer use patterns of Nutella®, in 2012, Ferrero engaged a
marketing research firm to conduct a new consumer use survey. 15/ As summarized in the table

and fruits constitute another 5%.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced the availability of a 
draft guidance establishing bioequivalence recommendations for drug products containing

for oral lubiprostone capsules could establish bioequivalence to AMITIZA through a 
combination of:  (1) a comparative pharmacokinetic study of the 24 mcg dose; and (2) a 
clinical endpoint study of the 24 mcg dose in chronic idiopathic constipation.2  These 
criteria address neither the other approved dose, 8 mcg, nor the other two indications for 
which AMITIZA is approved, irritable bowel syndrome with constipation and opioid-
induced constipation.  The Draft Guidance states that studies of the second dose can be

waived upon a showing of:  bioequivalence at the 24 mcg dose, proportional similarity of

to pharmacokinetic data, are necessary to demonstrate bioequivalence of oral lubiprostone

into the systemic circulation, bioequivalence of a new product with AMITIZA 
(lubiprostone) capsules cannot be demonstrated with a pharmacokinetic study.  But the 
recommendations in the Draft Guidance are not sufficient to ensure that new products are 
safe and effective for all of AMITIZA’s approved indications.  A single study in patients with 
chronic idiopathic constipation is unlikely to predict effects in patients with irritable bowel 
syndrome with constipation or opioid-induced constipation.  In addition, the criteria 
described in the Draft Guidance would not adequately ensure that a generic lubiprostone 
product has the same safety profile as AMITIZA in those approved indications.   
 Sucampo therefore requests that, to establish bioequivalence for any ANDA 
that lists AMITIZA as the reference listed drug, FDA: 
• require a clinical endpoint study in patients for the treatment of irritable 
bowel syndrome with constipation; 
• require a clinical endpoint study in patients for the treatment of opioid-
induced constipation; 
• require clinical data demonstrating that the ANDA product has a safety 
profile equivalent to that of AMITIZA in all three populations (chronic 
idiopathic constipation, irritable bowel syndrome with constipation, and 
opioid-induced constipation); and  
• require the chronic idiopathic constipation clinical endpoint study described 
in the agency’s Draft Guidance to use frequency of spontaneous bowel 
movements as its endpoint. 
We further ask that the agency include these requirements in the final 
guidance.4 
3 Id., at 1. 
                                                        
 
II. 
Statement of Grounds 
A. 
Background 
1. 
AMITIZA (Lubiprostone) 
AMITIZA (lubiprostone) is a locally-acting chloride channel activator that 
promotes chloride-rich intestinal fluid secretion.  More specifically, lubiprostone enhances 
the secretion of fluid into the abdominal lumen through activation of chloride channels in 
the apical membrane of the epithelium, thereby increasing the passage of stool.  
Lubiprostone has low oral bioavailability and acts locally within the gastrointestinal tract.  
Indeed, lubiprostone is not detected in plasma, even after administration of a dose that is three-
fold higher than the highest dose currently approved.5  M3, an active metabolite of 
lubiprostone, is detectable in plasma.   
Sucampo holds NDA 21-908 for AMITIZA (lubiprostone) capsules for oral 
use.  AMITIZA was approved for the treatment of chronic idiopathic constipation (CIC) in 
adults (24 mcg twice daily) in January 2006.6  CIC is marked by infrequent bowel 
movements that are often difficult to evacuate and is thought to be a disorder of colonic 
motility.  In April 2008, FDA approved AMITIZA for the treatment of irritable bowel 
syndrome with constipation (IBS-C) in women over the age of 18 at a dose of 8 mcg twice 
daily.7  Irritable bowel syndrome is a chronic condition with clinical manifestations that include 
recurrent abdominal pain/discomfort and changes in bowel habits.  The underlying 
pathophysiology of irritable bowel syndrome is not well understood.8  In April 2013, FDA 
approved AMITIZA for the treatment of opioid-induced constipation (OIC) in adults with

355(q), due to pending ANDAs that list AMITIZA as the reference listed drug. Sucampo is simultaneously 
submitting these comments to the docket for the Draft Guidance, Docket No. FDA-2007-D-0369-0067.   
5 FDA, Clinical Pharmacology and Biopharmaceutics Review, NDA 21-908 (Jan. 2006), at 4. 
6 AMITIZA received new chemical entity exclusivity upon approval.  See FDA, Orange Book: Approved Drug 
Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations, Lubiprostone, Application No. 021908 (27th ed., 2007).  
7 AMITIZA received three-year exclusivity for this indication under 21 C.F.R. § 314.108(b)(4) upon approval.  
See FDA, Orange Book: Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations, Lubiprostone, 
Application No. 21908 (29th ed., 2009). 
8 See, e.g., FDA, Summary Review, NDA 21-908 Supplement 5 (Apr. 2008), at 3. 
                                                                                                                                                                                   
 
chronic, non-cancer pain (24 mcg twice daily).9  Constipation is a common adverse event 
with opioid treatment because opioid binding to peripheral opioid receptors in the 
gastrointestinal tract can result in decreased small intestine fluid as well as abnormal 
gastrointestinal motility.  Reflecting the significant differences in these three disease states, 
full and unique development programs were required to demonstrate safety and 
effectiveness and to support approval in each indication.10   
2. 
Legal and Regulatory Framework for Establishing Bioequivalence 
Pursuant to FDCA § 505(j)(2)(A)(iv), any ANDA must contain, among other things, 
information demonstrating that the generic drug is bioequivalent to the reference listed 
drug.11  The FDCA further states that bioequivalence of a generic drug is established if: 
the rate and extent of absorption of the drug do not show a 
significant difference from the rate and extent of absorption of 
the listed drug when administered at the same molar dose of 
the therapeutic ingredient under similar experimental 
conditions in either a single dose or multiple doses.12 
Most orally administered drugs are absorbed systemically, thus allowing the 
drug to be transported through the bloodstream to its site of action.  The statute presumes 
that measuring the rate and extent of absorption in the bloodstream will detect any 
meaningful differences in clinical activity of two products.  However, the FDCA recognizes 
that some drugs do not reach their site of action through absorption into the bloodstream 
but rather act locally (e.g., in the gastrointestinal tract) prior to absorption and detection in

See FDA, Orange Book: Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations, Lubiprostone, 
Application No. 21908 (33rd ed. Suppl. 11, 2013). 
10 Indeed, other innovators seeking approval of a drug for both CIC and IBS-C have likewise been required to 
conduct separate clinical development programs to support safety and effectiveness in each indication.  See, 
e.g. LINZESS® (linaclotide) Prescribing Information, at § 14; Zelnorm® (tegaserod maleate) Prescribing 
Information (Clinical Studies section). 
11 FDCA § 505(j)(2)(A)(iv), 21 U.S.C. § 355(j)(2)(A)(iv).  
12 FDCA § 505(j)(8)(B)(i), 21 U.S.C. § 355(j)(8)(B)(i); see also 21 C.F.R. § 320.23(b).  FDA’s regulations define 
bioequivalence, in pertinent part, as “the absence of a significant difference in the rate and extent to which the 
active ingredient or active moiety . . . becomes available at the site of drug action when administered at the 
same molar dose under similar conditions in an appropriately designed study.”  21 C.F.R. § 320.21(e). 
                                                        
 
the bloodstream.  For drugs that are not intended to be absorbed into the bloodstream, the 
FDCA permits FDA to “establish alternative, scientifically valid methods to show 
bioequivalence if the alternative methods are expected to detect a significant difference 
between the drug and the listed drug in safety and therapeutic effect.”13 
For two products whose primary mechanism of action depends on systemic 
absorption, FDA typically requires a comparison of drug and/or metabolite concentrations in 
blood, plasma, or urine.  The Agency has recognized, however, that this approach may not 
always be feasible, particularly where a drug has low bioavailability or is otherwise difficult to 
measure in vivo.  In such cases, FDA has stated that bioequivalence studies with clinical 
endpoints may be necessary to assure comparable safety and effectiveness:  “The use of 
bioequivalence studies with clinical endpoints can be appropriate to demonstrate BE 
[bioequivalence] for orally administered drug products when measurement of the active 
ingredients or active moieties in an accessible biological fluid (pharmacokinetic approach) or 
pharmacodynamic approach is infeasible.”14 
3. 
FDA’s Draft Guidance for Establishing Bioequivalence of Lubiprostone 
The Draft Guidance describes the criteria for establishing bioequivalence for 
oral lubiprostone capsules.15  It recommends a single-dose 48 mcg (2 x 24 mcg 
lubiprostone) in vivo bioequivalence study with pharmacokinetic endpoints.  Due to the 
low bioavailability of lubiprostone, it recommends that the pharmacokinetic study measure 
the plasma concentrations of a metabolite, M3.  But, as discussed above, lubiprostone acts 
locally in the gastrointestinal tract prior to absorption.  Differences in systemic M3 plasma 
levels may be due to differences in absorption, pre-systemic metabolism, or first-pass 
metabolism, each of which can be affected by the formulation used by the ANDA product.  
Therefore, the measurement of M3 concentrations systemically is not sufficient to ensure 
an equivalent rate and extent of exposure of lubiprostone at the site of action.  
Furthermore, the FDA recommended that Sucampo conduct a placebo-controlled clinical 
endpoint study to support a formulation change as a pharmacokinetic study would not be 
sufficient to support the new formulation.  A pharmacokinetic study alone cannot 
demonstrate bioequivalence of two lubiprostone products.  
13 FDCA § 505(j)(8)(C), 21 U.S.C. § 355(j)(8)(C). 
14 FDA, “Guidance for Industry: Bioavailability and Bioequivalence Studies for Orally Administered Drug 
Products—General Considerations”  (Mar. 2003), at 9-10, available at 
http://www.fda.gov/downloads/Drugs/.../Guidances/ucm070124.pdf. 
15 Draft Guidance, supra note 2. 
                                                        
 
Recognizing that pharmacokinetic data and in vitro dissolution testing are 
not sufficient to establish bioequivalence, the Draft Guidance also recommends a 
randomized, double-blind, parallel, placebo-controlled, clinical endpoint study of 24 mcg 
lubiprostone administered twice daily in patients with CIC.  But the Draft Guidance 
recommends waiver of in vivo testing of the 8 mcg dose based on “(i) acceptable 
bioequivalence studies on the 24 mcg strength, (ii) proportional similarity of the 
formulations across all strengths, and (iii) acceptable in vitro quantitative capsule rupture 
(dissolution) testing all strengths.”16  The Draft Guidance therefore recommends neither a 
pharmacokinetic nor a clinical endpoint study of the 8 mcg strength, which is the only 
strength labeled for the treatment of IBS-C.  Thus, use of a generic lubiprostone product in 
IBS-C would be based only on data of a different dose in a different indication.  In addition, 
the Draft Guidance does not recommend a clinical endpoint study in OIC.  In fact, the Draft 
Guidance does not address OIC in any manner, and therefore does not in any way account 
for differences in patient populations and disease states between CIC and OIC.    
B. 
Discussion 
1. 
FDA Should Require a Clinical Endpoint Study in the Treatment of 
Irritable Bowel Syndrome with Constipation 
To demonstrate bioequivalence of lubiprostone, the Draft Guidance 
recommends a clinical endpoint study only in CIC.  Although IBS-C is a different disease 
state and has a different effective dose, the Draft Guidance would permit ANDA applicants 
to waive a clinical endpoint study in this indication.  But there is no scientifically sound 
basis for extrapolating from bioequivalence at 24 mcg dose in CIC to bioequivalent safety 
and efficacy of the 8 mcg dose in IBS-C.  Rather, there may be significantly different efficacy 
or safety of a generic product in IBS-C even if bioequivalence in CIC is demonstrated.  
Therefore, FDA should require any ANDA seeking approval of a generic oral lubiprostone 
product to demonstrate bioequivalence through a clinical endpoint study in IBS-C. 
  Reflecting the unique pathophysiology of the different disease states, 
AMITIZA was approved for CIC and IBS-C on the basis of separate efficacy studies that used 
distinct endpoints.  Idiopathic constipation is defined principally by infrequent bowel 
movements.  As such, AMITIZA is approved for CIC on the basis of clinical data evaluating 
the frequency of spontaneous bowel movements (SBM).  In the two pivotal clinical studies, 
16 Id., at 1. 
                                                        
 
AMITIZA was shown to be superior to placebo on the primary efficacy endpoint of SBM 
frequency at one week.   
IBS-C is a chronic condition with clinical manifestations that include recurrent 
abdominal pain/discomfort as the predominant symptomatic complaint, as well as changes in 
bowel habits.  Although reduced SBM frequency may be a facet of the symptomatology of 
patients suffering from IBS-C, it is neither a requirement for an IBS-C diagnosis, nor is it 
typically the predominant symptomatic complaint.  Given the multiple clinical features of this 
functional bowel disorder, FDA required Sucampo to conduct studies that measured efficacy 
based on a patient’s own weekly global assessment of symptom relief as compared to baseline.17 
The primary efficacy endpoint in the pivotal studies evaluating IBS-C was the overall 
responder status based on a composite score of patient responses.  Subjects were 
considered an “overall responder” only if they were a “monthly responder” for at least two 
of the three months during double-blind treatment.  Subjects who were considered weekly 
responders were subjected to a set of criteria to determine the subject’s status as a 
“monthly responder.”  AMITIZA demonstrated statistically significant treatment differences 
in the percent of overall responders as compared to placebo.   
During the clinical development of lubiprostone for the treatment of IBS-C, 
SBM frequency rates were collected from patients.  Although mean increases in SBM 
frequency rates were greater in the lubiprostone group than in the placebo group, the 
differences between groups were not statistically significant.  These findings suggest that 
IBS-C patients respond differently to lubiprostone than CIC patients.  They also suggest that 
SBM frequency rate is not adequate to show a benefit in IBS-C patients, as improving SBM 
frequency may not be correlated with overall symptomatic relief, which is critical to 
effective treatment of IBS-C.  Moreover, an evaluation of efficacy in IBS-C requires at least 
three months of treatment (not simply one week, as with CIC) to demonstrate an 
appropriate risk/benefit profile. 
Further reflecting the differences between efficacy of lubiprostone in these 
two different disease states are the different doses at which lubiprostone is safe and 
effective.   For the treatment of CIC, AMITIZA was found to be safe and effective at 24 mcg 
twice daily.  A lower, 8 mcg strength was not efficacious in improving SBM frequency in this 
indication.18  On the other hand, in IBS-C patients, 8 mcg twice daily was demonstrated to 
17 FDA, Summary Review, NDA 21-908 Supplement 5 (Apr. 2008), at 5. 
18 See FDA, Clinical Review, NDA 21-908 (Dec. 2005), at 11. 
                                                        
 
be efficacious by improving global symptom relief and to have a better safety profile than 
16 and 24 mcg twice daily regimens.19 
The potential for unexpected findings in IBS-C versus CIC is illustrated by the 
experience with another product, LINZESS® (linaclotide).  LINZESS was approved in August 
2012 for both IBS-C and CIC, but at a lower dose for CIC (140 mcg once daily) and a higher 
dose for IBS-C (290 mcg once daily), the inverse of the situation for AMITIZA.20  The 
approvals for these two indications were based on clinical trials with different endpoints 
specific to the indication.21  Like AMITIZA, LINZESS is also locally acting and minimally 
systemically absorbed.22  That both AMITIZA and LINZESS were approved at different 
doses for CIC and IBS-C, yet with contrasting findings regarding the appropriate dose in 
each indication, is further evidence that the pathophysiology of the disease states and 
mechanism of action of the drugs is unique to each indication and that it is not appropriate 
to extrapolate between the two indications.   
Thus, AMITIZA’s pharmacodynamic responses and efficacy profiles differ 
across CIC and IBS-C, although the reasons for these differences are not fully understood.23  
Due to these differences, the efficacy and safety of oral lubiprostone in patients with IBS-C 
at 8 mcg cannot be predicted based on clinical response measurements in patients with CIC 
at 24 mcg.  As such, proportional similarity of a generic lubiprostone’s formulation to 
AMITIZA across both doses cannot guarantee proportional clinical response.  In addition, 
differences in the excipients in a generic lubiprostone product may affect the release of 
lubiprostone, which may in turn affect efficacy and/or safety in one but not another 
indication.  How and whether the efficacy and safety in IBS-C is affected by the formulation 
differences is impossible to predict without clinical testing in the IBS-C population, and 
cannot be predicted from testing in CIC.   
For these reasons, there is no scientifically sound basis for extrapolating 
bioequivalence from CIC to IBS-C.  FDA should therefore require that ANDA applicants 
conduct a clinical endpoint study in patients with IBS-C to demonstrate bioequivalence.     
19 See FDA, Clinical Review, NDA 21-908 Supplement 5 (Apr. 2008), at 11. 
20 Linzess Prescribing Information, at § 2.  
21 Linzess Prescribing Information, at § 12.1. 
22 Linzess Prescribing Information, at § 14. 
23 See Amitiza Prescribing Information, at § 12.2. 
                                                        
 
2. 
FDA Should Require a Clinical Endpoint Study in Opioid-Induced 
Constipation 
As noted above, the Draft Guidance currently recommends a clinical endpoint 
study only in CIC.24  Although the same 24 mcg twice daily dose is recommended for both 
CIC and OIC, safety and efficacy results from a clinical study in CIC cannot necessarily be 
extrapolated to show bioequivalence in OIC.  FDA should therefore require any ANDA 
seeking approval for use of an oral lubiprostone product to demonstrate bioequivalence 
through a clinical endpoint study in OIC.   
CIC and OIC have different etiologies, and FDA has historically viewed OIC as 
a separate condition and a different patient population than CIC.  The differences between 
the indications are reflected in the FDA requirement that Sucampo conduct a separate, full 
pivotal program to evaluate the product’s use in OIC, and further in FDA’s requirement for 
the use of different clinical endpoints to assess clinical efficacy of AMITIZA in the two 
populations.  The primary efficacy analysis for AMITIZA studies in CIC was SBM frequency 
at one week.  In OIC studies, the primary efficacy analysis was a comparison of the 
proportion of “overall responders” in each treatment arm (lubiprostone and placebo).  A 
patient was considered an “overall responder” if ≥1 SBM improvement over baseline were 
reported for all treatment weeks and ≥3 SBMs/week were reported for at least 9 of 12 
treatment weeks.   
Thus, the efficacy endpoints for CIC and OIC differ both in the clinical 
outcome measured and the duration of response measured.  The CIC study currently 
recommended by the Draft Guidance measures acute response at one week.  Unlike CIC, 
where early onset and response during the initial week of treatment would be predictive of 
overall treatment response, treatment response in OIC may be evident only after a longer 
period of product use.  FDA generally recommends chronic responder data, over twelve 
weeks, to assess efficacy in patients with OIC.25  The consistency and durability of response 
in these patients is critical to ensuring efficacy in this patient population, and extrapolating 
bioequivalence from acute response at one week to a durable twelve-week response is not 
24 Draft Guidance, supra note 2, at 1. 
25 See, e.g., AMITIZA Prescribing Information, at § 14.2; AstraZeneca, Press Release: New Drug Application for 
Naloxegol Accepted by United States Food and Drug Administration (Nov. 19, 2013) (noting that NDA for OIC 
is based on two pivotal twelve-week clinical studies), available at 
http://www.astrazeneca.com/Media/Press-releases/Article/20131119--new-drug-application-for-
naloxegol. 
                                                        
 
scientifically supportable.  In addition, although AMITIZA demonstrated statistically 
significant improvements in overall responders (i.e., improvements over baseline in SBM 
frequency at each week of treatment and at least three SBMs per week for at least nine of 
twelve weeks of treatment) in OIC, statistically significant differences in SBM frequency at 
isolated time-points were not consistently demonstrated.  Therefore, the efficacy of 
lubiprostone in OIC cannot be extrapolated from SBM frequency rates at one week in CIC 
patients.   
Another critical aspect of treatment of patients with OIC is the potential for 
drug therapy to interfere with opioid analgesia.  That is, patients receiving lubiprostone for 
their OIC should not report more pain or require higher doses of opioids with lubiprostone 
use.  Studies with AMITIZA in patients with OIC demonstrated that patients did not 
experience more pain or require higher doses of opioids with lubiprostone use.  Whether a 
generic lubiprostone product has the same effect on opioid analgesia cannot be assessed in 
a study of patients with CIC.   
Therefore, a clinical endpoint study in OIC patients is necessary to ensure 
that a generic lubiprostone product has the same safety and efficacy as AMITIZA in this 
patient population. 
3. 
FDA Should Require a Demonstration of Equivalent Safety 
The criteria proposed in the Draft Guidance for establishing bioequivalence 
would not require an ANDA applicant to demonstrate that the generic lubiprostone 
product has the same safety profile as AMITIZA, although safety data from the clinical 
endpoint studies should be collected.  As reflected in AMITIZA’s labeling, clinical use of 
AMITIZA may result in significant gastrointestinal adverse events, such as nausea, diarrhea, 
and vomiting.26  In general, the likelihood of experiencing gastrointestinal adverse events 
increases with increasing lubiprostone dose.27   
A generic lubiprostone product could demonstrate pharmacokinetic 
bioequivalence of a single-dose of 48 mcg, while having up to a 25% higher plasma 
concentration than AMITIZA.28  This higher effective dose could result in more adverse

available at http://www.fda.gov/downloads/Drugs/.../Guidances/ucm070244.pdf.

Section 5050) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) establishes af

CITIZEN PETITION 
 
The undersigned health care providers, specializing in the treatment of migraine, submit this petition 
pursuant to the Food and Drug Administration’s (“FDA’s”) regulations at 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 to request that the 
FDA require certain additional information to be included in the product labelling of drugs for the acute 
treatment of migraine.  We believe that this information may change physicians’ risk-benefit calculus regarding 
the use of particular therapies, and is necessary to ensure that patients receive optimal efficacy from their 
migraine therapies. 
I. 
ACTION REQUESTED 
This petition requests that manufacturers of acute treatments for migraine be required to include 2-hour 
pain free response rates in the prescribing information, in addition to the already available headache relief or 
partial response data. 
II. 
STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
A. Background Information  
Despite significant advances in the management of migraine in the past two decades, the condition 
continues to have a significant negative impact on the lives of those affected by it, and the level of 
dissatisfaction with acute treatment is widespread.  For example, in a survey of almost 30,000 migraine patients 
conducted by the National Headache Foundation, more than half of the responders reported missing family or 
social activities and decreased work, household or school productivity.1  In a separate study, 42% of migraine 
patients reported being dissatisfied with the degree of relief associated with their acute treatment, 37% were 
dissatisfied with the speed of onset, and 79% were willing to try another therapy.2  A likely reason for the sub-
optimal clinical outcomes in migraine is that health care practitioners over-rely on acute therapies with 
relatively low 2-hour pain free rates and because practitioners may be confusing “pain free response” and 
“headache relief.”  Most headache specialists and patients believe that the standard outcome measure of 2-hour 
pain free is more reflective of satisfaction with acute treatment and the ability to return to normal function.3,4 
B. Rationale and Supporting Information 
There currently exist a range of cost-effective, FDA-approved, US Headache Consortium-recommended 
acute migraine medications and treatment strategies available to effectively treat migraine symptoms including 
2 
 
headache.  Properly understood and utilized, these acute treatments may have additional benefits including 
reducing the progression of episodic to chronic migraine.5  However, these treatments and treatment strategies 
are under-utilized by people with migraine.6  We recommend that data regarding headache pain free responses 
within 2 hours of treatment (2-hour pain free response) be made available to healthcare professionals and the 
general public based on the following rationale:  
1. The International Headache Society's Clinical Trial Subcommittee recommends that the 
primary endpoint in acute migraine treatment research be the proportion of patients who 
are pain free within 2-hour post-medication administration.7 
In 2012, the International Headache Society (IHS) recommended that 2-hour pain free “be the primary 
measure of efficacy” in clinical trials.8  The IHS notes that, while “headache relief is statistically more powerful 
than the IHS-recommended criterion ..., the validity of the clinical argument has been challenged severely.”  
Furthermore, as noted in the most comprehensive analysis of acute treatments for migraine ever published, a 
significant advantage supporting the clinical relevance of pain free response relative to headache relief or partial 
response is that “pain free is intuitive, robust, less sensitive to placebo effect, and produces better dose-effect 
relationships.”9 
2. Data on 2-hour pain free rates are widely available. 
Two-hour pain free response data are available from randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trials for 
all migraine-specific acute therapies currently available in the U.S. market (Table 1).  Two-hour pain free 
response data for all oral triptans, with the exception of frovatriptan, were the subject of a meta-analysis by 
Ferrari et al.9  The 2-hour pain free rate for frovatriptan was reported in a subsequent study.10  Likewise, 2-hour 
pain free response data are available for non-oral triptans, such as sumatriptan nasal spray,11 zolmitriptan nasal 
spray12 and subcutaneous sumatriptan.13, 14 
3. Patients report that “pain free” is an attribute of treatment that they value and seek. 
In two separate studies, when asked to assess the level of satisfaction with their migraine treatment, 98% 
and 92% of patients who became pain free within 2 hours of treatment reported satisfaction with their treatment.  
Conversely, among patients who reported experiencing only “pain relief” – the primary end-point cited in the 
prescribing information of all migraine-specific therapies – only 67% and 57% of patients said they were 
satisfied.3 
In a subsequent study, patients were asked to select the most important attribute of their acute therapies 
for migraine.  In this assessment, 61% of patients selected pain free response, and only 15% selected headache 
relief.  In the same patient preference study, when physicians were asked what they believed patients wanted 
most out of their migraine treatment, 32% said pain free while 45% reported pain relief.4  These findings 
highlight the disconnect between what migraine patients value and what their healthcare professionals consider 
to be the important efficacy standard for acute migraine medications.  It is likely that healthcare professionals 
misunderstand this patient-desired outcome, at least in part, based on their awareness of, and reliance on, the 
efficacy information reported in package inserts. 
 
 
3 
 
 
4. Achieving pain free response within 2 hours may be associated with better long-term 
outcomes. 
Recent analyses from the American Migraine Prevalence and Prevention study suggest that not 
achieving pain free status within 2 hours may not only prolong individual attack-related disability, but also 
worsen the disease over time.  In particular, not experiencing pain free response within 2 hours of treatment has 
been linked to progression from episodic (<15 days/month with headache) to chronic migraine (≥15 days/month 
with headache).  In a recent study presented at the International Headache Congress and in the process of being 
published, the investigators concluded that patients with sub-optimal treatment were between 2.3 and 3.6 times 
more likely to transform or progress from episodic to chronic migraine than patients getting optimal response 
from their treatment, where pain free response was a key component of the treatment plan.5  This is a relevant 
clinical consideration, as chronic migraine is associated with greater attack-specific disability, overall disease 
burden and increased co-morbidity than episodic migraine.  
5. Getting patients to pain free within 2 hours may result in significant savings to the U.S. 
health care system. 
As acknowledged by a recent analysis, “migraine imposes a substantial burden on patients, families, 
employers and societies ... [and] ... emerging evidence suggests that [it] is a chronic and progressive disease.”  
On average, migraine patients miss about 10.7 days of work a year with a “presenteeism” rate of 20.5% 
(working with reduced functionality).  Overall direct costs total approximately $11 billion each year for 
prescription drugs and visits to physicians and emergency rooms. 15 
Progression of episodic to chronic migraine has been extensively associated with increased use of 
healthcare resources, disability to affected patients and other socio-demographic parameters, such as lower level 
of educational and professional achievement.  Specifically, treatment costs in terms of health care resources 
(including hospitalizations, visits to doctors and emergency rooms, treatments, etc.) were reported to cost 
$4,144/year in the U.S. for patients with chronic migraine compared to $1,533/year for patients with episodic 
migraine.16  Eliminating the headache and other migraine symptoms is essential to reducing the progression of 
episodic migraine to chronic migraine. 
C. Summary 
We urge the FDA to require manufacturers of acute treatments for migraine to state in the prescribing 
information the 2-hour headache pain free rate in addition to the already available headache relief or partial 
response data because it is the endpoint recommended by the International Headache Society, the data currently 
exist, it is valued by patients, and its dissemination and use may result in significantly improved clinical and 
financial outcomes.  This information may change physicians’ risk-benefit calculus regarding the use of 
particular therapies, and may impact physician and patient prescribing decisions.  Thank you for your 
consideration. 
 
 
4 
 
 
III. 
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT 
We claim a categorical exclusion from the requirement to submit an environmental assessment pursuant 
to 21 C.F.R. 25.30.

Citizen Petition 
Five leading nonprofit consumer, research and medical organizations identified 
below petition the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) pursuant to the Food, Drug, and 
Cosmetic Act 21 USC 352, 505(o)(4), and 21 CFR 10.30 to take action to improve the 
safety information included in the label for CHANTIX® (varenicline) tablets , a smoking 
cessation aid approved under NDA 021-928. 
The petitioners are the Institute for Safe Medication Practices, a nonprofit 
organization devoted entirely to medication error prevention and safe medication use; 
Consumer Reports, which serves consumers through unbiased product testing and ratings, 
research, public education and advocacy; National Center for Health Research, a 
nonprofit think tank that scrutinizes scientific and medical research with public health 
implications; National Physicians Alliance, a non-profit organization that promotes health 
and fosters physicians’ active engagement with their communities to achieve high quality 
affordable health care for all; and Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy organization with 
more than 350,000 members and supporters. 
 
A. Action Requested 
The petitioners request that FDA amend the Boxed Warning and Indications sections 
of the label for CHANTIX® (varenicline) Tablets [1] to reflect new scientific 
information that has become available since the agency required a Boxed Warning in July 
2009. We request specifically the following: 
 
 
Citizen Petition to strengthen Chantix warnings 
2 
 
1. Clarify and expand the scope of reported serious neuropsychiatric adverse 
effects in the Highlights and main Boxed Warning to include the full spectrum 
of events now known: suicidal behavior, aggression/violence, psychosis, and 
depression. 
 
2. Add language to the Boxed Warnings describing the risk of blackouts, 
convulsions, and impaired vision, adverse effects that could also endanger 
others in some settings such as operating aircraft, driving ambulances or large 
trucks. 
 
3. Add to the Indications section restrictions against use in persons in sensitive 
or hazardous occupations such as pilots, air traffic controllers, military missile 
crews, police, fire fighters, and emergency medical workers. Existing actions 
by the FAA, the Department of Transportation, and the Department of 
Defense should be expanded by a clear and uniform label restriction that 
would include non-federal workers. 
 
4. Remove inappropriate promotional material about CHANTIX benefits from 
paragraph 3 of the Highlights section Boxed Warning. A survey of Boxed 
Warnings for 10 classes of drugs showed no other Boxed Warning containing 
extraneous promotional statements about benefit.  
 
5. Delete recently-approved but misleading description of meta-analyses about 
the neuropsychiatric adverse effects of CHANTIX from the Warnings and 
Precautions section. 
B. Grounds 
Compelling Scientific Evidence 
The scientific evidence that CHANTIX (varenicline tartrate) increases the likelihood 
of suicidal thoughts and behavior, aggression/violence, psychosis, accidents, and 
depression is compelling and thoroughly documented. The adverse effects can be 
catastrophic, resulting in death, disability, and disruption of marriage, family 
relationships, and jobs. Severe symptoms can begin with the first doses even before 
stopping smoking, and many resolve soon after treatment is stopped. In some cases, 
symptoms reappear if treatment is resumed. The adverse effects of CHANTIX have been 
documented in three special studies by the FDA Office of Surveillance and Epidemiology 
(OSE),[2–4] by six studies in the peer reviewed literature,[5–10] and six reviews in 
QuarterWatch, a scientific publication about adverse drug events.[11–16] Psychiatric 
 
 
Citizen Petition to strengthen Chantix warnings 
3 
 
adverse effects of CHANTIX have also been observed worldwide and publicly reported 
in Canada,[17] France,[9] New Zealand,[5] and Australia.[18] The psychiatric adverse 
effects of CHANTIX have been reported to the FDA steadily and continuously over the 
eight years since the drug was approved, and have been roughly proportional to patient 
exposure.[14,16]  
Why Clear Warnings Are Essential  
Prominent warnings about the psychiatric and other adverse effects of CHANTIX 
provide important safety benefits to patients and the public. In many cases symptoms 
appear early, often in the first week, before stopping smoking. Effective patient and 
physician warnings to stop treatment immediately can prevent tragic events such as 
suicide and assault. In addition, two kinds of CHANTIX adverse effects—
aggression/violence and impaired consciousness/vision—can and have caused injury to 
others. The highest public health duty to warn involves emphasizing potential serious 
harm to innocent persons that can be prevented with early and appropriate action.  
An Estimated 2,500 CHANTIX Victims Compensated 
An exhaustive scientific evaluation of CHANTIX took place over four years in 
United States District Court, and involved thousands of cases of alleged injury caused by 
CHANTIX. Millions of pages of scientific data, analysis, and other records were 
available under seal to batteries of qualified scientific experts representing both the 
victims and the manufacturer. This mass of evidence was distilled into expert reports that 
were subject to rigorous legal criteria monitored by a federal judge to ensure that the 
judgments therein were reliable and met accepted scientific standards. The result of this 
exhaustive process was that Pfizer, the manufacturer, paid approximately $300 million in 
damages to an estimated 2,500 CHANTIX victims.[19] Thousands of other CHANTIX 
victims were not eligible for compensation because the judge barred payment if the 
injuries occurred after the July 2009 Boxed Warning. 
The Need to Update 2009 Warnings 
It is important for the FDA to revisit the Boxed Warnings because its 2008 
assessments, through no fault of the agency, substantially underestimated the psychiatric 
adverse effects and accident risks of CHANTIX. It was not until July 2010 that the FDA 
learned that Pfizer had failed to properly submit 26,000 adverse event reports, including 
589 serious cases, 150 completed suicides, 102 cases of hostility/aggression, and 56 cases 
of psychosis.[15] In addition, later peer reviewed studies provide important new insights 
into CHANTIX cases involving aggression/violence, as well as comparisons with other 
smoking cessation treatments. 
 
 
Citizen Petition to strengthen Chantix warnings 
4 
 
Information Adverse to Petition 
21 CFR 10.30 requires citizen petitioners to consider and report information adverse 
to the petition request. Safety concerns have contributed to a 73% decline in CHANTIX 
patient exposure since 2008, lessening its use in smoking cessation treatment.[16] Clearer 
warnings might further reduce smoking cessation treatment using CHANTIX. However, 
safer alternatives of approximately comparable long-term effectiveness are available. 
The two Pfizer-sponsored meta-analyses of its clinical trials that were recently added 
to the product label did not identify psychiatric adverse effects described in the current or 
proposed expanded Boxed Warning.[1] However, the clinical trials included in the meta 
analyses were inadequate in methodological design, including patient selection, adverse 
event ascertainment, and statistical power, to identify the infrequent but serious 
psychiatric adverse effects now known. 
 The FDA also conducted an observational study in electronic health records of the 
Departments of Defense and Veterans Affairs. It reported no difference in the rate of 
psychiatric hospitalization in the first 60 days after initiating treatment with CHANTIX 
or the nicotine patch.[20,21] However, those studies can not be considered conclusive 
because neither the underlying diagnosis codes nor the hospitalization endpoint was 
validated for regulatory purposes or previously used in a peer reviewed publication. In 
addition, the psychiatric hospitalization endpoint omits the 85% of reported psychiatric 
adverse events that do not result in hospitalization.[22] Additional studies and analysis on 
this topic appear in the Detailed scientific documentation section of this document.  
C. Environmental Impact  
Granting the actions requested in this petition would have no identifiable 
environmental impact.  
D. Economic impact 
The economic impact of this petition cannot be determined in absence of adequate 
data to assess the costs of reduced injuries resulting from more effective and accurate 
safety warnings.  
E. Certification 
Signature pages and certification appear at the end of this petition. 
 
 
 
 
Citizen Petition to strengthen Chantix warnings 
5 
 
F. Detailed Scientific Documentation 
Part 1: Four Psychiatric Adverse Effects of CHANTIX: the Evidence 
Part 2: Impairment in Sensitive/Hazardous Occupations 
Part 3: Inappropriate Promotional Material in Boxed Warning 
Part 4: Meta-Analysis and Observational Studies 
Part 5: References 
 
 
Section F: Detailed Scientific Documentation 
Part 1: Four Psychiatric Adverse Effects of CHANTIX: the Evidence 
The psychiatric adverse effects of CHANTIX fall into these four psychiatric 
diagnostic categories: suicidal behavior, aggression/violence, psychosis, and depression. 
The primary scientific evidence in this section is shown in Table 1. 
 
Many CHANTIX psychiatric episodes share distinctive features and overlap these 
four analytical categories: An episode of paranoia may lead to or involve violence. 
Aggression and rage are rechanneled and result in self-harm. Depression may lead to 
suicidal behavior. Sleep disturbances may border on exceptionally vivid dreams that 
resemble psychotic hallucinations. Sleep disruptions have erupted in violence.  
This analysis focuses on the most clearly researched common features that include 
early onset, often before stopping smoking; remission on discontinuation; a senseless act 
in patients with no previous psychiatric history; and rechallenge, the reappearance of 
symptoms if the medication is restarted. There is less published scientific information

6 
 
available for two additional subsets of psychiatric cases: a) Cases that begin on 
discontinuation; b) Cases where the adverse effects are persistent. These cases require 
further research. 
Suicidal Behaviors 
Suicidal and self-injurious thoughts and acts are a prominent and established side 
effect of many therapeutic drugs, with at least 58 drugs currently carrying some form of 
warning on the product labels.[10] For CHANTIX, suicidal ideation, attempted suicide, 
and completed suicide carry the most prominent label warning language and have been 
documented through multiple sources. The 2008 FDA OSE Suicidal Behavior Study of 
adverse event data [3] had only limited cases available but concluded: 
 “The AERS data suggest a possible association between suicidal events 
and use of varenicline and bupropion, given that there were postmarketing cases 
of positive dechallenge/rechallenge, close temporal relationship between the 
event and drug use, and the occurrence of suicidal events in patients without any 
psychiatric history.”  
 This report was a primary source in the FDA decision to mandate a boxed warning 
in 2009. 
A peer-reviewed survey of British adverse event data found a disproportionate 
number of cases of suicidal behaviors for CHANTIX, notably fewer cases for bupropion, 
and few or none for nicotine replacement products. For completed suicides, for example, 
there were 22 reported for CHANTIX, 6 reported for bupropion, and none for nicotine 
products. For suicidal ideation, there were 377 cases reported for CHANTIX, 131 for 
bupropion for all indications, and 2 for nicotine.[8] Exposure to nicotine replacement 
products was 7 times larger than varenicline, but bupropion exposure for smoking 
cessation could not be assessed because of its multiple indications.  
A larger and more formal disproportionality analysis reported similar results in a 
peer-reviewed study.[10] When CHANTIX was compared to nicotine replacement 
products for suicidal/self injury, the odds ratio (OR) was 8.4, (95% CI 6.8-10.4). For 
CHANTIX compared to bupropion the results were: OR = 2.9 (95% CI 2.3-3.7). The 
large number of CHANTIX reported cases also adds scientific weight to the findings. In 
the Suicidality/Depression in Smoking Cessation study, CHANTIX accounted for 1,818 
reported cases of suicidal thoughts or behavior compared to just 50 for nicotine products, 
even though patient exposure to nicotine replacement products was much greater and 
measured over a longer period of time. [10] 
 
 
Citizen Petition to strengthen Chantix warnings 
7 
 
Suicidal behaviors were also prominently featured in regulatory agency reports of 
adverse events in Canada [23] and Australia,[18]  and in the New Zealand patient 
monitoring study.[5] 
Aggression/Violence 
Thoughts and acts of aggression/violence associated with drugs are quite familiar 
(such as domestic violence associated with alcohol intoxication), but the association with 
correctly administered therapeutic drugs (involuntary intoxication) has not been well 
studied in systematic scientific research.  
CHANTIX, however, has proved a valuable research topic because adverse event 
reports were so numerous, and they occurred in a diverse smoking cessation population 
(most often women of middle years) where fewer alternative causes of violence were 
likely confounding variables. 
The FDA’s OSE studied five report terms describing aggression and violence using a 
Bayesian statistical technique applied to a small early subset of CHANTIX adverse event 
data.[4] The primary measure–Empirical Bayes Geometric Mean (EBGM)–returned a 
relative risk equivalent compared to all other drugs that ranged from 17.1 for homicidal 
ideation to 5.4 for hostility. In comparison, bupropion had an EBGM of 4.4 for homicidal 
ideation and no reported cases of hostility. 
A peer-reviewed study of

This Aggression/Violence PRR study identified 31 drugs associated with thoughts 
and acts of violence and ranked them by PRR (a relative risk concept). The study 
compared the proportion of aggression/violence events for each drug, to the proportion 
for all other drugs, thereby adjusting for differences in the total number of reports. 
CHANTIX accounted for more thoughts/acts of violence than any other therapeutic drug 
by all measures in the study.

8 
 
Table 2 shows that CHANTIX accounted for 18 times as many reports of violent 
thoughts and acts as would be expected given the total number of reports for that drug 
(PRR = 18), and compares it to two other smoking 
cessation treatments. CHANTIX accounted for 
408 cases in total, more than any other therapeutic

the 23 calendar quarters in the study. Bupropion 
also indicated increased risk but to a lesser degree. 
A French pharmacovigilance research team 
performed a related case/non-case study in the 
French PharmacoVigilance Database.[9] Although 
the French data universe was substantially 
smaller, the Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) for 
CHANTIX was 29.2 (95% CI 10.8-78.9). Note 
that the CHANTIX PRR of 18 in the U.S. study overlaps the broad confidence intervals 
in the French study. 
An additional study in QuarterWatch examined all reports of homicidal thoughts for 
all drugs, but focused on all the adverse event data from 2007 through the third quarter of 
2013, essentially capturing the entire period CHANTIX was marketed. An unadjusted 
ranking is shown in Table 3.[16] 
These data show that CHANTIX accounted for more reports of homicidal ideation 
than any other therapeutic drug over a 75-month period. The number of cases was 5-
times larger than second-ranked quetiapine, and 12-times larger than pregabalin. In 2013 
Q3 all the other drugs on the list of 10 most frequently reported drugs had greater patient 
exposure than CHANTIX, except for interferon beta, where exposure was unknown and 
the patient population is smaller. 
Psychosis 
Psychosis may involve auditory or visual hallucinations, paranoia, delusions, or 
disorganized speech. These may involve acts of violence related to the delusions or 
paranoia. These are not typical symptoms of smoking cessation. 
Psychotic behaviors have been identified in CHANTIX patients in clinical studies 
[24], the Pfizer-Tonstad meta-analysis [25], an FDA OSE report[4], and in QuarterWatch 
assessments [11]. 
The 2008 FDA OSE report identified 98 cases of psychosis for CHANTIX with 3.5 
times as many cases as bupropion, adjusted for prescription volume. The OSE 
disproportionality analysis compared CHANTIX to all other drugs and showed an
