the BPCIA process balances the interests of biosimilar applicants, the reference product 
sponsor and the public:  increased choice in biological medicines and the need to 
protect the intellectual property rights and innovation of the reference product sponsor.  
Its purpose is to increase availability of biological products by establishing an 
abbreviated pathway that permits approval based on the biosimilar applicant’s  
demonstration of a high degree of similarity of the biosimilar product to a previously 
approved reference product, instead of the full complement of data, including a de novo 
demonstration of safety and effectiveness of the biosimilar product.  At the same time, 
the BPCIA seeks to protect the intellectual property rights of reference product sponsors 
and provides significant periods of data exclusivity for the innovator. 
Both objectives are equally important.  On the one hand, the streamlined 
approval process for biosimilar products in subsection (k), which relies on the safety and 
efficacy data previously developed by the reference product sponsor, facilitates delivery 
of potentially lower cost versions of approved biological products to the market.  On the 
other, the patent provisions in subsection (l) ensure in part that the necessary incentives 
to invest in research and development of new life-saving biological products will 
continue to exist.  Both objectives—fostering competition and preserving the incentive to 
innovate—advance the public health. 
The new statutory pathway thus provided a substantial benefit to a diverse group 
of stakeholders, including developers of biosimilars, by creating an abbreviated 
approval framework for FDA approval of biological products that are “biosimilar” to a 
previously licensed originator product (i.e., the “reference product”) at a substantially 
reduced cost and effort.  In providing this benefit for sponsors of biosimilar products, 
however, the BPCIA also imposes attendant obligations and limitations.  More 
specifically, in exchange for allowing biosimilar applicants to rely on the prior licensure 
of a reference product, a license secured at significant expense and effort of another 
company, Congress mandated that biosimilar applicants make specific disclosures, 
participate in a specific sequence of exchanges of information, participate in 
negotiations, and provide certain notices in accord with specific timelines.   
This process, laid out in explicitly mandatory language in § 351(l) of the PHSA, 
was designed to run concurrently with FDA’s review of a biosimilar application under 
§ 351(k).  Timely identification of patent disputes implicated by the biosimilar product 
and its processes of manufacture is a central purpose of the Act—the BPCIA patent 
provisions were included to enable patent disputes to be identified at the beginning of 
FDA’s review of biosimilar application under § 351(k) and to be resolved before the 
biosimilar product is approved by FDA or put before the courts before the first 
commercialization of the approved biosimilar product.

reference product sponsor designed to identify patent disputes, if any, to be resolved

processes of manufacture are critical to orderly operation of the statutory scheme.  The 
disclosure mandated by § 351(l)(2)(A) serves two purposes. It enables the reference

been accepted for review by the FDA. It also provides the reference product sponsor 
with information to identify patents implicated by the biosimilar product, its intended use, 
or its processes of manufacture:  information that is known to the biosimilar applicant at 
the filing date of the application, but unlikely to be otherwise available to the reference 
product sponsor.  The process of identifying and listing of patents, in turn, allows the 
parties to articulate their positions on each patent, and to then work together to identify 
which of the disputed patents may be licensed or require immediate litigation.

biosimilar product and its manufacture are to have been made by this point pursuant to 
subsection (l)(2)(A), the subsection (l) process may proceed without disturbing FDA’s 
review of the biosimilar application under subsection (k).

B. Statement of Grounds 
I. 
Factual Background 
A. 
Advanced Parkinson's disease 
Parkinson's disease is a debilitating and progressive disorder. 
Patients with 
Parkinson's disease often have impaired manual dexterity and poor coordination such that they 
have difficulty with common manual and bi-manual tasks (e.g., eating, fastening buttons, etc.).1 
With advancing disease, the fluency, coordination, efficiency, and speed of composite and fine 
motor movements are increasingly affected, further impairing patients' ability to grasp and 
manipulate objects? In addition, patients with advanced Parkinson's disease frequently have 
reduced muscle strength, which can further impair their ability to handle objects.3 Parkinson's 
disease patients may also experience cognitive changes, such as difficulty making decisions, 
poor concentration, difficulty maintaining a train of thought, and difficulty recalling timefrarnes 
or sequences of events. 4 
Among the most frustrating and challenging complications faced by advanced 
Parkinson's disease patients are so-called "off-episodes," or motor fluctuations. 
As 
occupational therapy guidelines explain, "[t]he terms 'on' and 'off' are used to describe the

Off-

Care nurse. This training is most effective, and recommended to take place, when the patient is 
in an "on" state, in order to ensure maximum retention of the information. Completing this 
training is essential to patients' (and care partners') safe and effective use of apomorphine that is 
administered through a medical device such as the Apokyn® auto-injector. Similarly robust 
training requirements are planned for the ambulatory pump, which is being developed to 
administer apomorphine as a continuous, subcutaneous infusion. 
2. 
Apokyn® Human Factors Studies 
Through human factors testing, US WorldMeds has gained critical insights into 
the administration of apomorphine, including: (a) the necessity of appropriately training 
Apokyn® users (and their care partners) on the drug-delivery device before first use, and (b) the 
importance of designing an apomorphine drug-device combination product to meet the specific 
needs of the advanced Parkinson's disease population. 
In connection with the human factors/usability engineering program for the 
development of a new Apokyn® pen, US WorldMeds conducted a comparative study of the 
original Apokyn® pen and the new Apokyn® pen to ensure that the new device had at least 
comparable usability for all intended users, including patients, care partners, and healthcare 
professionals. US WorldMeds' first human factors study comparing the two pens was a 
combined user-preference and formative usability study that provided a side-by-side comparison 
of the two devices. Patients in this study "self-taught" about the use of the drug-delivery device, 
utilizing only the product's instructions for use (IFUs), and without any supportive training. 
10 "Initiation, is defined as the first instance in which a patient is administered Apokyn® under 
the supervision of a healthcare professional. 
4 
Participants then engaged in a simulated use evaluation with each pen, during which observers 
recorded use errors, difficulties, or actions (such as incorrect dose selection per the simulated 
requirements or poor needle handling practices) that could lead to safety concerns. US 
WorldMeds observed several use errors in this study with respect to both pens. However, these 
errors were considered atypical of observed events seen with commercial Apokyn® patients 
because of the absence of training comparable to that provided by the Circle of Care nurse 
services, through which US WorldMeds offers prescribing-office education/training, in-home 
initiation assistance, and pre-initiation patient (and care partner) education on the product, in 
order to facilitate the safe and effective use of Apokyn ® pens by patients, care partners, and 
healthcare professionals. This first study highlighted the potential risk of patients (or care 
partners) relying on self-teaching as a primary method for learning about and understanding the 
apomorphine drug-delivery device's functionality and important safety information. The 
unexpected outcomes of this initial study caused US WorldMeds to consider incorporating the 
training services offered by its Circle of Care nurses when planning a second formative human 
factors study. 
Informed by the results of the first study, US WorldMeds conducted a second 
human factors study, again comparing the two versions of the Apokyn® pen. However, along 
with minor changes in the IFUs, the second study also included a 30-minute, one-on-one training 
session with a qualified nurse trainer for all participants prior to participating in the simulated 
use evaluation for both pens. Introducing the one-on-one training component allowed the second 
study to more closely model, and therefore more accurately reflect, the commercial distribution 
of Apokyn ®. The second study showed a pronounced reduction in overall use errors with both 
pens. Figures 1 and 2 below show the reduction in error rates by primary operating function 
under Study 1 (untrained) versus Study 2 (trained) conditions across all participant groups 
(patients, care partners, and healthcare professionals combined), for Pen A and Pen B, 
respectively.

Taken together, these two studies demonstrate the critical role that proper training plays in use of 
the Apokyn® pen by advanced Parkinson's disease patients (defined within the study as those 
with Parkinson's disease complicated by motor fluctuations not satisfactorily managed with 
conventional treatments), as well as their care partners and healthcare professionals. The major 
design variable between the two studies was the self-training methodology employed in Study I 
versus the one-on-one training methodology delivered by a qualified nurse trainer in Study 2. 
The data show that the introduction of one-on-one training with a qualified nurse trainer can 
have a significant impact on the use error: profile of auto-injectors intended for use with 
apomorphine: the total number of Pen A use errors was reduced from 20 (Study I with n=20 
participants) to 3 (Study 2 with n=22 participants) with proper training, and the total number of 
Pen B use errors was reduced from 20 (Study 1 with n=20 participants) to 6 (Study 2 with n=22 
participants) with proper training. The key conclusion drawn from these two human factors 
studies is that a one-on-one device training program is highly effective in trying to mitigate the 
risk of apomorphine auto-injector pen use errors in an advanced Parkinson's population, 
regardless of the specific pen design. It was also noted that some use errors were not completely 
eliminated in Study 2, which may be a test artifact associated with the artificial 30-minute time 
limitation imposed on the study training session. 
Thus, training programs should include 
allowances for variable duration and content reinforcement specific to the user's comprehension 
level, in order to maximize effectiveness and ensure optimal safety of the drug-delivery device 
when operated by the end user (i.e., the patient or care partner). 
The conclusions from the human factors studies of the two Apokyn® pens were 
reinforced by the results of the human factors studies conducted during the device development 
program for the ambulatory pump being developed for continuous, subcutaneous infusion of 
apomorphine. As part of this development program, US WorldMeds used a "controP' patient 
user group, which was asked to complete the simulated use assessment without any prior training 
on the use of the device. Patients (or patient-care partner pairs) in this group "self-taught" about 
the use of the drug-delivery device, utilizing only the product's written instructions for use 
(IFUs) and instructional video, and without any supportive training. Use of this control group 
allowed a direct comparison of use error rates between the trained and untrained patient cohorts. 
Patients were further characterized as "dependent'' or "independent", based on their responses to 
a screening questionnaire, which established the degree of assistance they each routinely require 
with their medications and other personal care activities. Patients classified as "independent" 
participated in the simulated use session without being accompanied by a care partner. Patients 
classified as "dependent" were accompanied by his or her care partner. For the trained group of 
dependent patients, training was provided to both the patient and the care partner simultaneously, 
in order to most closely replicate the commercial training that would occur in that scenario. The 
results of this study showed that there is a marked decrease in use error rates when one-on-one 
training is offered by an experienced and qualified nurse trainer in advance of initial (simulated) 
use of the drug -delivery system, as shown in Figure 3 below. 11 The total number of Pump use

groups for both independent and dependent patients, this study also supports that, for patients 
who often rely on a care partner for medication assistance, the patient-care partner pair will also 
benefit significantly from one-on-one training for the apomorphine drug-delivery device before

In summary, the human factors studies of the apomorphine drug-delivery auto-
injector pen and ambulatory pump systems demonstrate that device-use training is a critical step 
in helping to ensure proper use of the drug and optimization of the drug's benefits and risks. 
Further, despite substantial reduction in use errors following appropriate training, it was 
observed that training under the study conditions did not fully eliminate use errors, and so 
perhaps a more narrowly-tailored and/or variably-timed training session, such as those offered in 
the commercial training envirorunent by the Circle of Care Nurse Network, would further reduce 
safety issues and increase usability by catering to the specific learning requirements of individual 
patients and their care partners.

3. 
Commercial Training Experience 
The Circle of Care Nurse Network is a highly sophisticated and comprehensive 
educational program that provides training support for Apokyn®. This support is focused on the 
patient (and his or her care partner, when applicable), but also includes peer-to-peer training for 
qualified healthcare professionals. The education and training for the patient (and care partner) 
is provided in a one-on-one setting and includes pre-initiation education, initiation training, and 
post-initiation support for the use of Apokyn®. 
The peer-to-peer, healthcare professional-
focused training ensures the prescribing physician and his or her staff are adequately trained to 
educate the patient and care partner using the same standard of training employed by Circle of 
Care nurses during training sessions with patients and care partners directly. Thus, the two 
"arms" of the Circle of Care training program create multiple ways for Apokyn® patients and 
their care partners to receive adequate education and training on the product prior to first use, 
either through direct contact with a Circle of Care nurse or through office visits to their 
prescriber, whose staff has also received Circle of Care nurse training. The extensive education 
and training sessions cover the following key topics: 
• 
Why the physician has prescribed Apokyn ® for the patient; 
• 
Important Safety Information; 
• 
Key elements concerning the proper use of Apokyn ® and proper administration via the 
auto-injector pen; and 
• 
Care, disposal, and storage of Apokyn® and Apokyn® ancillary supplies. 
The nurse professionals are highly trained and have direct knowledge and experience with 
Apokyn® and patients with advanced Parkinson's disease. 
The nurses' comprehensive 
knowledge allows for use of good clinical judgment when assessing a patient's (or care 
partner's) understanding of important safety information and his or her comfort level with the 
device prior to first use. 
On average, 90% of a Circle of Care nurse's time is focused on educating and/or 
training the patients and their care partners on Apokyn® therapy, while the remaining 10% is 
dedicated to the first initiation visit. The educational/training visits are conducted prior to 
initiation and again after initiation, if warranted, as part of ongoing follow-up support. For 
example, additional education and training may be indicated post-initiation if the patient 
experiences a change in health; changes care partner; expresses difficulties or concerns with 
handling the product, which indicates a loss of skills or knowledge gained during the initial 
training visit; or directly requests such a visit, based on his or her individual needs and 
preferences. The number of educational visits and/or follow-up phone calls per patient varies 
widely from 1 to 6 per month; this highlights the variability of needs of individual users, as well 
as the importance of having a program that can be tailored to meet those needs by maintaining 
consistent, standardized, and validated training content and methodology that is utilized by all 
nurse trainers. 
Historical research on commercial Apokyn® patients indicates that 89% of all 
Circle of Care pre-initiation education/training visits and initiation visits are conducted with both 
the patient and care partner present. Further, approximately 50% of all Apokyn® injections are 
provided by a care partner, consistent with the varying levels of dependence on medication 
8 
administration assistance within the advanced Parkinson's population, as studied in the human 
factors programs described above. Thus, again, it is critical that training programs employ 
approaches that involve both patients and care partners, particularly when a patient is likely to 
rely on his or her care partner for apomorphine administration assistance. 
In summary, the Circle of Care Nurse Network program is a support program 
specifically designed with the needs of the advanced Parkinson's patient in mind, and is an 
effective and comprehensive tool used to ensure that users of US WorldMeds' apomorphine 
drug-device combination product, Apokyn®, have ample access to robust product education and 
device training, which together have been proven to be exceptionally important factors for 
minimizing device safety issues and usability concerns. 
4. 
Training Program Conclusions 
The ambulatory pump and auto-injector development programs, together with US 
WorldMeds' commercial training experience in treating and providing educational services to 
the advanced Parkinson's population, support the following considerations for apomorphine 
drug-delivery device development and commercial support for these patients: 
• 
Parkinson's disease patients are faced with challenging, disease-related, physical and 
cognitive limitations or impairments that prevent a "one-size-fits-all" training 
program from being optimally effective. Therefore, training programs should offer 
standardized content to make sure that all important use and safety information is 
communicated. 
However, the individual sessions must be customized for each 
patient in terms of duration, hands-on practice, and reinforcement of important points, 
guided by the patient's unique needs and comprehension level. Further, due to the 
progressive nature of the disease, follow-up visits are useful to ensure that the training 
resulted in long-term safe use of the product and to reinforce product education as 
necessary; 
• 
Training is most effective in a "one-on-one" setting, conducted by healthcare 
professional educators experienced with both the drug-device combination product 
and Parkinson's disease patients, due to the judgment required to assess a patient's 
comprehension of critical information. Reliance on only printed instructions for use 
or instructional videos leaves the patient to his or her own judgment and does not 
provide the important assessment and feedback component that a proper training 
session offers, rendering a self-guided approach to training far less effective than a 
professionally-guided training program that is offered on a one-on-one, hands-on 
basis; 
• 
Training is most effective when conducted in the "on" state. No comparative data 
were generated on use error profiles from simulated use when trained in the "off' and 
"on" states due to the practicalities and ethical considerations in requesting usability 
study participants to attend a long study session while intentionally impaired. 
However, the challenges that the "off' state presents to patients are well-documented. 
In a drug-device training situation, an "off' episode will affect a patient's ability to 
manipulate the combination product constituents, gain hands-on experience with the 
9 
touch and feel of device operations, or recall a substantial volume of important use 
information as relayed by a healthcare professional trainer. Therefore, US 
WorldMeds' commercial experience and the study data support the conclusion that 
training is most effective when conducted in the "on" state; and 
• 
Patients who rely on a care partner for medication assistance due to either physical or 
cognitive limitations also benefit from training when that training is provided to the 
patient-care partner pair. Because of the progressive nature of Parkinson's disease, 
ongoing follow-up and educational visits provide an opportunity for continual 
reassessment of training needs. 
C. 
Device Design Considerations for Advanced Parkinson's Disease Patients 
In addition to providing a training program to enhance safety and usability of 
apomorphine drug-delivery devices, the devices themselves should be designed with the specific 
needs of the patient in mind to ensure optimal performance and ease of use. The following 
points should drive device-engineering considerations for drug-delivery systems intended for use 
in the advanced Parkinson's population: 
• 
Compromised dexterity in a Parkinson's patient should be considered, with efforts 
made to minimize the number of manual operations associated with the drug-delivery 
device. For example, the requirement to disassemble and reassemble a reusable auto-
injector pen in order to load and reload cartridges could present a potential challenge 
for patients. Reducing the number of manual tasks required for a successful drug 
administration could enhance usability; 
• 
The strength limitations of a Parkinson's patient should be considered, with efforts 
made to minimize the force required by a patient to manage the device or deliver an 
apomorphine dose. For example, an auto-injector with a manual driven injection 
mechanism could present a potential challenge for patients. In the event a patient is 
unable to depress fully a manually-operated injector, only a partial dose may be 
delivered. 
Manually-actuated drug-delivery devices are likely to offer adequate 
safety profiles, but introduction of a force-assisted (electronic, mechanical, etc.) 
actuation mechanism may enhance usability by addressing the disease-induced 
strength limitations of the intended user; and 
• 
The cognitive impairment of a Parkinson's patient should be considered, with efforts 
made to create intuitive steps and optimize the ability of a Parkinson's patient to 
deliver the appropriate dosage. Apomorphine is a drug that is titrated to optimal 
effectiveness for each individual, given that tolerability and doses required for 
efficacy can vary widely from patient to patient. Thus, device design should enable 
easy selection of doses across an appropriate range while minimizing the potential for 
dosing error to the extent possible. 
For example, an easy-to-understand dose-
correction button on an auto-injector may enhance usability by ensuring that 
unintentional over-dialing on a variable-dose pen can be easily adjusted to the correct 
dose.

Petition_Title: Citizen Petition From Dr  Richard Sherman
Petition_Text:
Citizen Petition 
Date: March 17, 2015 
 
The undersigned submits this petition under 21 CFR Section 10.20, and 10.30  of the Federal Food, Drug, 
and Cosmetic Act to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to require that  drug manufacturers 
report the phosphorus content of their products and, when equal to 10 mg or more, note this in the 
Warning/Precaution and Special Population sections of the product's package insert. 
 
A. Action Requested 
 
The Commissioner shall require that manufacturers producing drugs containing phosphorus measure its 
quantity in their products and include this information in the package insert. If the quantity is 10 mg per 
dose or more, this should be noted in the Warning/Precaution and Special Population sections of the 
package insert noting that the phosphorus in the drug may, in patients treated with chronic dialysis, 
exacerbate hyperphosphatemia and/or increase the dose of phosphorus binder medication required. 
 
B. Statement of Grounds 
 
Dietary phosphate has historically been considered to originate largely in dairy or protein based food 
products.  Investigations in recent years have highlighted additional sources of phosphate, particularly 
additives to food products and beverages (including wine and beer, as well as soda).1-3  Medications 
have been reported to contain phosphate as an excipient ingredient but the extent of the problem and 
the quantities of phosphate involved have not been reported.4 While a drug’s package insert indicates 
whether the medication contains phosphate these reports do not quantify the amounts nor, for generic 
manufacturers, are the reports uniformly available. We have investigated this issue by a review of 
package inserts and , where indicated,performed a chemical analysis of drugs identified as potentially 
containing phosphate.  
 
We acknowledge that our report is relatively superficial and incomplete. This was inevitable because of 
the overwhelming number of potential analyses that would be needed for a more definitive 
presentation.  For example, amlodipine is manufactured by 137 different companies 
(www.medinia.net/drug-price/amlodipine.htm, accessed 12/29/2014).  The investigation is intended to 
provide some limited information on whether the phosphate content of drugs may be more than trivial 
(it is), how it varies among different drug manufacturers (quite a bit) and how it varies among different 
doses of a given drug (unpredictably). 
 
Dialysis Clinic, Inc. supplied a list of commonly prescribed medications for patients at their dialysis 
centers.  The package inserts for the branded formulations of these drugs were reviewed and those 
containing phosphate were identified. Samples of these drugs, in both generic and branded form, were 
then purchased at local pharmacies.   
 
Ten to 30 doses of each drug (minimum 3 gm) were packaged, coded and then transported to the 
laboratory for analysis (New Jersey Feed Laboratory, Inc., Trenton, NJ).  Laboratory technicians were 
blinded to drug information.  All samples were ground prior to analysis.  Sample weights were obtained 
with a Sartorius Model CPA224S balance (Sartorius Corp., Edgewood, NY).  Phosphorus was measured 
using the Association of Analytical Communities official method 984.27; the assay is an inductively 
coupled plasma atomic spectroscopy procedure.  All instruments were calibrated according to 
manufacturers’ specifications.  Samples from the laboratory were routinely analyzed for accuracy by the 
American Association of Feed Control Officials and the American Oil Chemists Society.   
 
Since the excipients used by drug manufacturers vary, we also investigated whether phosphate may be 
found in generic forms of drugs when the corresponding branded formulations are phosphate free.  We 
therefore reviewed the available package inserts for 16 generic drug manufacturers (all those producing 
at least one drug on our phosphate containing drug list) for the commonly prescribed medications 
previously identified.  
 
The review of the package labels for branded prescription drugs found that phosphate was listed as an 
excipient ingredient in the following drugs:  amlodipine (Norvasc, Pfizer), clonidine (Catapres, 
Boehringer Ingelheim), lisinopril (both Prinivil, Merck and Zestril, Astra Zeneca), sertraline (Zoloft, Pfizer) 
azithromycin (Zithromax, Pfizer), paroxetine (Paxil, GlaxoSmithKline), sitagliptin (Januvia, Merck), 
rapaglinide (Prandin, NovoNordisk), bisoprolol (Zebeta, Duramed), rosuvastatin (Crestor, AstraZeneca), 
glyburide (Diabeta, Sanofi), megestrol (Megace, Bristol Myers Squibb). 
 
The phosphate content of a selection of branded and generic forms of these drugs is shown in the 
accompanying  table. We found generic forms of branded, phosphate containing drugs most often (but 
not always) also contain phosphate but in differing amounts indicating substantial differences among 
manufacturers in the composition of the excipient fraction of the drug. 
 
Our investigation of whether generic formulations of non phosphate containing branded products might 
contain phosphate was only partially successful.  We sought to review the package inserts for the 
products of 16 generic drug manufacturers but found that only eight companies made this information 
available on their website.  Of the 91 drugs reviewed, we found only one drug (pravachol, Eon) that 
contained phosphate when the branded form of the drug did not. 
 
When phosphate is found in drugs, it is almost always part of its excipient fraction. There are 34 
phosphate containing chemicals used in FDA approved drug products in the U.S. 
(www.accesssdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/iig/getiigweb.cfm, accessed 12/29/2014). Excipients are often 
referred to as inert ingredients suggesting a lack of pharmacologic or other effects.  However, this is 
inaccurate.  Over 100 people died from acute kidney injury in the US in 1937 from a presumed inert 
ingredient (diethylene glycol) in an elixir of sulfanilamide5.  This event led to the US Food and Drug 
Administration’s current regulatory authority over drugs.  Allergies to certain excipients are also well 
described. 
 
We provide evidence here that phosphate containing excipients in drugs are also not inert in that they 
can significantly add to dietary phosphate intake, a particular problem in end stage renal disease (ESRD) 
patients.  The amounts of phosphate in question are generally a small portion of the typical target 
phosphate intake of about 1000 mg/d but can be clinically important when the issue is considered more 
closely. 
 
The phosphate removed by hemodialysis is limited (about 1000 mg/treatment or an average of 400 
mg/d for thrice weekly dialysis) and phosphate binders are required to compensate.  A 10% increase in a 
dietary phosphate intake of 1000 mg/day (to 1100 mg/day) increases the daily extra-dialytic phosphate 
burden (600 mg: 1000 - 400 mg) by about 17% (100 mg divided by 600 mg).  However, inorganic 
phosphate, such as that in food additives and excipients, is potentially fully absorbed unlike the organic 
phosphate in foods where a 60% absorption rate is often cited 6. That 10% increase in phosphate intake 
may therefore be as much as 28% of the absorbable, extra-dialytic phosphate burden [100 mg divided 
by (0.6 x 600 mg)]. 
 
This problem is further magnified by the relative ineffectiveness of phosphate binders.  The most widely 
used agents bind quite small amounts of phosphate – 3.2 mg and 4.3 mg per 100 mg of sevelamer and 
calcium acetate, respectively 7.  Thus, the drug we found to have the highest phosphate content 
(paroxetine, 40 mg, GlaxoSmithKline) would require 4.4 doses of sevelamer (800 mg each) to 
counterbalance its phosphate content of 111.5 mg. 
 
As things currently stand, minimizing phosphate intake from medications will be problematic.  We found 
the phosphate content of a 10mg amlodipine tablet varies from absent to clinically important: 0 to 40.1 
mg for the five different manufacturer’s products we tested.  The values for the 132 other drug 
companies that produce amlodipine are unknown.  This variability in phosphate content for drugs made 
by different pharmaceutical companies highlights the unpredictable nature of the problem.  We did find 
a high likelihood that the presence of phosphate in a branded drug predicted its presence in the generic 
forms but this was not uniform and certainly not predictive in a quantitative sense.  More predictable 
was the finding that the absence of phosphate in a branded drug indicated its likely absence in generic 
forms of the drug.  Again, this was not uniform (pravachol) with an additional large caveat that only a 
very small sample of the large number of generic drug manufacturers and their products was examined. 
However, pharmaceutical companies frequently change vendors for excipients with the new vendor 
supplying a chemically different product (personal communication, Barton Cobert, BL CMD Associates, 
Chapel Hill, NC). 
 
 
The absence of reliable information on the phosphate content of medications creates much uncertainty 
in managing hyperphosphatemia in dialysis patients.  Questions arise: is the patient who is prescribed 
lisinopril (10 mg twice daily) and amlodipine (10 mg daily) receiving products that add 105 mg to dietary 
phosphate or only 15 mg (a difference accounting for a change of about four calcium acetate or 
sevelamer doses)? Did the patient’s pharmacy change its supplier of these medications accounting for 
an otherwise unexplained change in phosphate binder dose requirement?  
 
 
If alternative agents of similar safety, effectiveness and cost are available, they could be substituted for 
high phosphate medications.  Such a strategy might be appropriate for many “high risk” drugs such as 
lisinopril, bisoprolol and amlodipine.  However there is no assurance that a generic form of a phosphate 
free branded drug is formulated using a similar phosphate free methodology.   
We have recently pointed out that greater transparency by drug manufacturers in reporting the 
phosphate content of their products should be required as well the need for improved accessibility to 
these data by the public8. The nephrology community needs to know when medications given to dialysis 
patients have clinically important levels of phosphate.  How to achieve this goal should be addressed. As 
a start, we believe that the US Food and Drug Administration require that pharmaceutical companies 
measure and report the phosphate content of their products. When clinically significant, appropriate 
cautions should be added to the package label. 
 
 
References   
 
1.  Sherman RA, Mehta O: Dietary phosphorus restriction in dialysis patients: potential impact of 
processed meat, poultry, and fish products as protein sources. Am J Kidney Dis  54: 18-23, 2009 
2. Sherman, RA, Mehta, O: Phosphorus and potassium content of enhanced meat and poultry products: 
implications for patients who receive dialysis. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol, 4: 1370-1373, 2009. 
3. Lindley, E, Costelloe, S, Bosomworth, M, Fouque, D, Freeman, J, Keane, D, Thompson, D: Use of a 
Standard Urine Assay for Measuring the Phosphate Content of Beverages. J Renal Nutr, 24: 353-
356, 2014. 
4. Calvo, MS, Uribarri, J: Contributions to total phosphorus intake: all sources considered. Semin Dial, 26: 
54-61, 2013. 
 5. Ballentine C. Taste of raspberries, taste of death: The 1937 Elixir Sulfanilamide Incident. Available at: 
http://www.fda.gov/aboutfda/whatwedo/history/productregulation/sulfanilamidedisaster/defa
ult.htm.  Accessed February 3, 2015 
 
6. Ramirez, JA, Emmett, M, White, MG, Fathi, N, Santa Ana, CA, Morawski, SG, Fordtran, JS: The 
absorption of dietary phosphorus and calcium in hemodialysis patients. Kidney Int, 30: 753-759, 
1986. 
7. Daugirdas, JT, Finn, WF, Emmett, M, Chertow, GM, Frequent Hemodialysis Network Trial, G: The 
phosphate binder equivalent dose. Semin Dial, 24: 41-49, 2011. 
8. Sherman, RA, Ravella S, Kapoian T: A dearth of date - The problem of phosphorus in prescription   
medications. Kidney Int (in press)

Supriya Ravella, M.D. 
Toros Kapoian, M.D. 
 
 
 
C. Environmental Impact 
 
Petitioner claims a categorical exclusion under § 25.30 of this chapter. 
 
D. Economic Impact 
 
The Petitioner will submit an economic impact statement at the request of the Commissioner. 
 
E. Certification 
 
The undersigned certifies, that, to the best knowledge and belief of the undersigned, this petition 
includes all information and views on which the petition relies, and that it includes representative data 
and information known to the petitioner which are unfavorable to the petition.

2 
 
The undersigned submits this petition under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, 21 
U.S.C. § 348, to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to amend a recent Notice and 
Declaratory Order determining that partially hydrogenated oils, the primary dietary source of 
industrially-produced trans fatty acids, are no longer generally recognized as safe for any use in 
human food. In lay terms, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is now banning partially 
hydrogenated oils from human food.  
 
On behalf of its more than 150,000 members, the Physicians Committee for Responsible 
Medicine requests that the Commissioner extend this determination and ban to all trans fatty 
acids, including those that occur naturally in dairy and meat products, because all trans fatty 
acids are harmful, regardless of their origin. 
 
A. Action Requested 
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) published the Notice and Declaratory Order in the 
Federal Register on June 17, 2015. Final Determination Regarding Partially Hydrogenated Oils, 
80 Fed. Reg. 34,650 (June 17, 2015), available at http://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/FR-2015-06-
17/pdf/2015-14883.pdf. The Physicians Committee requests that the Commissioner, consistent 
with FDA regulations, amend the language of the Notice and Declaratory Order to: 
 
• determine that there is no consensus among qualified experts that trans fatty acids of any 
type are generally recognized as safe for any use in human food; and 
 
• eliminate any language creating exemptions for naturally occurring trans fatty acids, fully 
hydrogenated oils, or edible oils that contain industrially produced trans fatty acids as an 
impurity, see e.g., 80 Fed. Reg. at 34,652, 34,653. 
 
B. Statement of Grounds 
On June 17, 2015, FDA issued a Notice and Declaratory Order pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 554(e) 
determining—with no exceptions based on low threshold amounts—that partially hydrogenated 
oils, the primary dietary source of industrially-produced trans fatty acids, are not generally 
recognized as safe for human consumption. 80 Fed. Reg. at 34,650, 34,664, 34,666. 
 
As explained by FDA, current scientific evidence highlights the health risks associated with 
consumption of trans fats, including coronary heart disease, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular 
disease, and stroke. 80 Fed. Reg. at 34,660. For example, recent expert panels recognize the 
progressive linear relationship between LDL-C (increase) and HDL-C (decrease) and trans fat 
intake, concluding that trans fats are not essential nutrients in the diet and that consumption 
should be kept as low as possible. Id.  
 
A 2013 National Institutes of Health, National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute expert panel 
conducted a systematic evidence review and concluded with moderate confidence that for every 
one percent of energy from trans fatty acid replaced by mono- or polyunsaturated fatty acids, 
LDL-C decreases by an estimated 1.5 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL) and 2.0 mg/dL, 
respectively. 80 Fed. Reg. at 34,665. The panel also concluded that replacement of trans fatty 
acid with saturated fatty acids, monounsaturated fatty acids, or polyunsaturated fatty acids 
increases HDL-C by an estimated 0.5, 0.4, and 0.5 mg/dL respectively. Id. The panel’s 
3 
 
conclusions were not limited to a specific trans fatty acid dose range and did not indicate any 
threshold trans fatty acid intake. Id. 
 
On these and similar other scientific grounds, FDA “conclude[d] that there is no currently 
identifiable threshold below which there is general recognition that [partially hydrogenated 
oils] may be safely used in human food.” 80 Fed. Reg. at 34,664 (emphasis added). Oddly, 
FDA came to the opposite conclusion with respect to naturally occurring fatty acids. 
Specifically, FDA stated that the “order does not apply to ingredients that contain only naturally 
occurring trans fat, such as those ingredients derived from ruminant sources,” 80 Fed. Reg. at 
34,652, the most common of which are “the fat component of dairy and meat products,” 80 Fed. 
Reg. at 34,653. 
 
The past five years saw several reviews comparing cardiovascular death risk factors of 
industrially produced trans fatty acids created by partial hydrogenation and naturally occurring 
trans fats produced in the guts of ruminant animals and present in animal products and by-
products. Brouwer et al (2010)1 was the first published quantitative review to look at the effect of 
both types of trans fatty acids on human blood lipoproteins. The review examined 39 
intervention studies that reported the effects of both types of trans fatty acids on lipid profiles. 
The researchers recalculated the effects of trans fatty acids for each study to determine effects on 
lipid profiles if all studies had included a control treatment that isocalorically replaced trans fatty 
acids with cis monounsaturated fatty acids. Results showed that all trans fatty acids raise the 
LDL to HDL ratio, with no significant differences between naturally occurring trans fats 
and industrially produced trans fatty acids. 
 
In light of the health detriments present in all trans fatty acids, and in keeping with FDA’s zero 
tolerance for partially hydrogenated oils, FDA should determine that no trans fatty acids are 
generally recognized as safe for any use in human food. To impose an absolute ban on trans 
fatty acids that are industrially-produced but no limit on trans fatty acids that occur naturally in 
dairy and meat products is arbitrary and capricious, in violation of the standards applied to 
agency action under the Administrative Procedure Act. See 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A). 
 
C. Environmental Impact 
We believe that this petition does not require an environmental impact statement pursuant to 21 
C.F.R. § 25.32. This information will be provided if requested by the Commissioner. 
 
D. Economic Impact 
This information will be provided if requested by the Commissioner.

and LDL cholesterol levels in humans–a quantitative review. PloS one, 5(3). Please see attachment. 
4

The undersigned certifies, that, to the best knowledge and belief of the undersigned, this petition 
includes all information and views on which the petition relies, and that it includes representative 
data and information known to the petitioner that are unfavorable to the petition.

Dear Sir or Madam: 
Physical Pharmaceutica LLC (''Physical Pharmaceutica") respectfully submits this citizen 
petition in accordance with Food and Drug Administration ("FDA") regulations set forth in 21 
CFR§ 1 0.30. This citizen petition concerns the approval of any Abbreviated New Drug 
Application ("AND A'') that references RESTASIS as the reference listed drug ("RLD") based on 
the biowaiver provisions put forth by the Draft Guidance on Cyclosporine of June 2013 ("FDA-
Cyclosporine-2013"). Physical Pharmaceutica requests that FDA take the actions described 
below with respect to any ANDA submitted to FDA and listing RESTASIS 0.05% ophthalmic 
emulsion as the RLD. 
In FDA-Cyclosporine-2013, FDA indicates that ANDA's can establish bioequivalence with the 
RLD by being Q1/Q2 equivalent, displaying acceptable physicochemical characterizations via 
six "parameters to measure" (the globule size distribution, viscosity, pH, zeta potential, 
osmolality, surface tension), and display comparable results from "acceptable comparative in vitro 
drug release rate tests of cyclosporine from the test and RLD formulations". Collectively, these 
1 
would serve as sufficient surrogates for appropriate in vivo bioequivalence studies .. FDA-
Cyclosporine-2013 does not give details regarding any comparative in vitro drug release rate test, 
but indicates that such tests will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis as part of each AND A. 
In disagreement with FDA-Cyclosporine-2013, Allergan, the maker ofRESTASIS, submitted 
several citizen petitions regarding ANDA's referencing RESTASIS. Of relevance to this 
document are the citizen petitions filed by Allergan on February 28, 2014 ("Allergan-Feb-2014", 
public docket FDA-2014-P-0304) and December 23, 2014 ("Allergan-Dec-2014", public docket 
FDA-2015-P-0065). Allergan also filed a supplemental document to public docket FDA-2014-P-
0304 on May 29,2014 ("Allergan-May-2014") in support of its arguments presented in 
Allergan-Feb-2014. FDA responded to Allergan-Feb-2014 on November 20, 2014 ("FDA-Nov-
2014"). The subsequent citizen petition Allergan-Dec-2014 is essentially a restatement of 
Allergan-Feb-2014 and response to FDA's position put forth in FDA-Nov-2014. Physical 
Pharmaceutica submitted two comments on Allergan-Dec-2014 to public docket FDA-2015-P-
0065. The second comment, dated March 18, 2015 ("PhysPharm-March-2015"), differed from 
the first (dated March 11, 2015) only by the inclusion of the required Verification section. 
In Allergan-Feb-2014, Allergan petitioned that FDA require in vivo (clinical) bioequivalence 
studies for ANDA submissions for cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsion. In addition, Allergan 
petitioned that FDA refuse to approve and refuse to accept as complete any ANDA submission 
that seeks to establish bioequivalence based on in vitro data alone, even if the data satisfy the 
guidance criteria set forth in FDA-Cyclosporine-2013. Further, Allergan-Feb-2014 asserts that 
the comparative in vitro release studies were problematic because no known in vitro testing 
methods were appropriate for cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsions. 
In Allergan-May-2014, Allergan noted that the rate and extent of cyclosporine absorption at the 
ocular surface is formulation dependent, and cited its research presented as a poster at the ARVO 
(Association for Research in Vision and Ophthalmology) Annual Meeting held May 4-8,2014 1• 
1 Attar M., Graham R., Borbridge L., Neervannan S. The Rate and Extent of Cyclosporine 
Absorption is Formulation and Tissue Dependent following Topical Ophthalmic 
Administration. Poster D0076, 2014 ARVO Annual Meeting. Abstract at 
http://www.arvo.org/webs/am2014/abstract/sessions/376.pdf.

Allergan-May-2014 also reiterated the position of Allergan that there is currently no "validated 
test methodology for RESTASIS specifically or cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsion generally". 
In the response FDA-Nov-2014, FDA disagreed with Allergan with regard to requiring clinical 
studies to establish bioequivalence. FDA also maintained its position that comparative in vitro 
release studies should be required to establish bioequivalence, but did acknowledge that none of 
the currently known comparative in vitro release rate tests are appropriate. 
Consistent with that position, FDA has performed internal studies and funded external grants to 
study the problem of establishing in vivo equivalence from in vitro data for ophthalmic emulsion 
formulations, but as yet has not identified a suitable comparative release. For instance, FDA 
scientists published a manuscript in the peer reviewed journal Molecular Pharmaceutics in 2014

equivalent characterization within an in vitro test suite would imply equivalent drug delivery in 
VIVO.

bioequivalence for products referencing RESTASIS is by in vitro methods. In addition, clinical 
studies should not be accepted unless they provide direct quantitative evidence ofbioequivalence

release rate tests.

adequate guidance as to what data or information such a comparative in vitro release rate test 
should provide to be used for the purpose of establishing in vitro bioequivalence. Specifically, a 
comparative in vitro release rate test should be considered as relevant or appropriate only if it 
provides data that quantitatively distinguishes between inequivalent formulations in the first 5-l 0 
minutes of the release test, which corresponds to the timeframe during which the formulation 
would release the drug to the ocular tissues. If a test takes significantly longer than that to 
establish any release behavior, it will not be able to differentiate between formulations in a 
timeframe of a few minutes, and thus cannot be considered as an acceptable comparative in vitro 
release rate test for the purpose of establishing bioequivalence for cyclosporine ophthalmic 
emulsion. In addition, any such test must include release data obtained at multiple times, starting

cumulative amount released after only one time, such as the amount of drug released after five

5.

shown by clinical endpoint studies). 
DISCUSSION 
The following points are fundamental to our position and the actions requested. 
When used for dry eye disease, cyclosporine works topically and does not penetrate tissues or 
membranes that represent significant diffusional barriers to reach the site of action. Thus, 
penetration of the tissues is not the rate limiting step for delivery of the drug to the site of action 
in the ocular tissues, but rather it is the rate at which the drug becomes available from the 
formulation that controls the delivery to the site of action. 
In Allergan-Feb-2014 and Allergan-Dec-2014, Allergan has vigorously argued that clinical 
studies are the only appropriate route to establish bioequivalence for cyclosporine ophthalmic 
8 
emulsion. However, this premise is flawed. Quantitative determination of the rate and extent of 
drug delivery to ocular tissues is not feasible in clinical studies. Since the total dose of 
cyclosporine that would be absorbed systemically is extremely small, blood levels would not be 
able to determine bioequivalence between two formulations. The alternative would be sampling 
ocular tissues, but that is not permissible in human studies. 
If clinical studies are used to establish bioequivalence, the alternative to quantitatively 
determining tissue or blood levels is to perform studies with clinical endpoint measurements. 
However, while these may be appropriate for establishing efficacy, they do not quantitatively 
establish bioequivalence. Tests such as the Schirmer Tear Test, which measure tear prodl!ction 
and evaluate effectiveness through increased tear production, do not quantitatively measure the 
quantity of drug delivered to the ocular tissues, nor the rate of delivery. 
In addition, clinical endpoint studies relevant to cyclosporine ophthalmic emulsion, including the 
Schirmer Tear Test, can be highly variable. In fact, concerns have been expressed about all 
clinical endpoint tests that measure tear production, especially with regard to their accuracy and 
reproducibility even for diagnosis of dry eye disease. "Clinically, it appears clear that no single 
test is capable of repeatedly differentiating dry-eyed from non-dry-eyed individuals."10 Basing 
the determination of bioequivalence on clinical endpoint studies that are highly variably and 
provide at best indirect evidence, is scientifically unsound and not defensible. 
Considering the above points, including the fact that cyclosporine does not cross complex 
barriers to reach the site of action, it is clear that the most valid and reliable approach to establish 
bioequivalence would be through in vitro characterizations. This would require establishing a set 
of parameters or tests that would be sufficient to imply equivalent release of the drug in vivo if 
the ANDA product and RLD were equivalent with respect to those parameters and tests in vitro. 
Although ophthalmic emulsions are more complex than solutions, for which biowaivers are not 
disputed, it is possible to identify a set of parameters and tests that, if two formulations showed 
equivalent data, would be necessary and sufficient to imply bioequivalence.

establish bioequivalence. Dissolution, which is required for drug delivery from a suspension, is a 
complex set of processes that depends on factors such as the drug solubility, particle size and 
surface area, wetting, diffusion through complex media, etc. Factors such as dilution with tears 
and surface morphology of the suspended particles can also bring about major differences in the

hand, release from emulsions requires only diffusion of the dissolved molecules between media, 
and is a much simpler process than dissolution from the standpoint of drug transport. In addition, 
for ophthalmic suspensions, the required residence time of the drop in the eye may be longer 
than what is required for ophthalmic emulsions because dissolution can be slower than 
redistribution.

The undersigned respectfully submits this citizen petition on behalf of Mylan Specialty, 
L.P. (Mylan Specialty) under 21 USC 355 and 21 CFR 10.30, among other provisions of law, to 
request that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs (the Commissioner) take certain actions with 
respect to abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) 90-589, submitted by Teva

Specialty’s EpiPen® (epinephrine injection) as the reference listed drug (RLD).  Among other 
things, Mylan Specialty asks that the Commissioner refrain from approving the Teva ANDA 
unless, after conducting an appropriately rigorous review under the established standards for 
proposed generic emergency use auto-injectors, the agency concludes that the proposed product 
is the “same as” the EpiPen® auto-injector.  This includes that patients, caregivers, and other

differences in design and operating principles, EpiPen®-trained users will not be able to safely

auto-injector instructions for use. 
 
Epinephrine auto-injectors are used for the emergency treatment of allergic reactions, 
including potentially fatal anaphylaxis, which can progress from exposure to cardiorespiratory 
arrest in as little as five minutes.  These products are used primarily by patients, including 
children, and caregivers (not medical professionals) under highly stressful, time-sensitive 
conditions where they must recognize the signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis and execute a 
successful injection.  Thus, it is imperative that the users understand how to quickly and properly 
administer the product in an emergency.  In that regard, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA 
or the agency) has concluded that proposed generic epinephrine auto-injectors pose unique issues 
of sameness that are essential to safety and effectiveness, and that involve both the drug and 
device components of this combination product.1

III. LEGAL STANDARDS 
A. 
ANDA Approval Standards 
Under Section 505(j) of the FDCA, an ANDA applicant must demonstrate, among other 
things, that its proposed product is the same as the RLD with regard to active ingredient, dosage 
form, route of administration, strength, labeling, and conditions of use, and that it is 
bioequivalent, as well.23  A product that meets these standards may be approved and receive an 
“A” rating in the Orange Book, connoting therapeutic equivalence.  The agency has explained 
that “[a]n ‘A’ rating reflects FDA’s judgment that the products generally may be substituted for 
each other without physician intervention with the expectation that the substituted product will 
produce the same clinical effect and safety profile as the RLD when used for the labeled uses.”24   
Generally, a proposed generic product that is pharmaceutically equivalent25 and 
bioequivalent to, and has the same labeling as, the RLD will be approved under an ANDA and 
receive an “A” rating.26  There are circumstances, however, where a proposed product, even 
though bioequivalent and pharmaceutically equivalent, differs from the RLD in therapeutically 
significant ways that preclude approval via an ANDA.   
In some instances, product differences may require changes in labeling that go beyond 
the permitted exceptions to the “same labeling” requirement for generic products.  Generally, 
exceptions are permitted if they are required because of minor product differences approved in a 
suitability petition (e.g., change in dosage strength) or because the proposed generic and 
reference listed drugs are produced or distributed by different manufacturers.27  Permitted 
differences include minor labeling variations, such as in expiration date, formulation, 
bioavailability, or pharmacokinetics; labeling revisions to comply with FDA guidance, and

ribaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, etc.) contraindicated for patients with non-valvular 
atrial fibrillation (NVAF).  
Specifics of the action requested 
 
The exact wordings of the product labels for FDA approved anticoagulants are as follows:

Prophylaxis and treatment of thromboembolic complications associated with atrial 
fibrillation and/or cardiac valve replacement (1)

3. Ribaroxaban (Xarelto):

4. Pradaxa (dabigatran): 
PRADAXA is a direct thrombin inhibitor indicated: To reduce the risk of stroke and systemic

With these drugs and any other anticoagulants, this petition requests that FDA approval for the 
indications for prophylaxis and treatment of non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) be 
withdrawn and that each of these drugs should be designated “contraindicated” for prophylaxis 
or treatment for patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation. 
Statement of grounds 
 
This section will be presented in the form of an adaptation of my systematic review of 
randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies regarding anticoagulants as stroke 
and embolus prophylaxis for people with NVAF. This review shows the lack of proven efficacy 
and safety of anticoagulants for NVAF, and it presents evidence for harm from major bleeding 
and rebound-hypercoagulation related thromboses—spikes in thrombotic events after 
discontinuing warfarin.  
 
 
Abstract 
 
Objectives To critically reanalyse the randomized controlled trials (RCTs) for non-valvular 
atrial fibrillation (NVAF) patients that compared warfarin with placebo as prophylaxis against 
ischemic stroke and systemic embolus and put the findings in the context of recent observational 
studies  
 
Design Systematic review of RCTs and observational studies 
 
Data sources Citations for RCTs comparing warfarin versus placebo for NVAF came from 
previous meta-analyses supplemented by searches of Medline and bibliographies of retrieved 
articles. For relevant observational studies, I searched in Medline and citations in bibliographies. 
 
Study eligibility criteria All warfarin versus placebo or no treatment RCTs for NVAF patients 
were eligible. Eligible observational studies included those regarding the demographics, 
3 
 
epidemiology, natural history, of atrial fibrillation (AF) and those relating warfarin prophylaxis 
to incidences of thromboembolic events and major bleeding.  
 
Data extraction and synthesis I extracted applicable data from RCTs onto Excel sheets and 
subsequently tables. Major heterogeneity in the RCTs precluded performing a meta-analysis.  
 
Main outcome measures Primary outcomes comprised rates of ischemic strokes and systemic 
emboli. Secondary outcomes included rates of major, fatal and intracranial bleeding, vascular 
disease deaths, other thrombotic events, and total mortality.  
 
Results The 6 warfarin versus placebo for NVAF RCTs (n=2854) had follow-up periods 
averaging only 1.6 years. "Rebound-hypercoagulation" related strokes and other thrombotic 
events—spikes in thrombotic events after discontinuing warfarin—were not counted after 
patients dropped out of the RCTs and discontinued warfarin. Observational studies documented 
that the overall mean rate of ischemic stroke in AF patients in the USA is 1.5% / year rather than 
the widely quoted 4% - 5% / year. In about 1.9 million people with AF in the USA, 
anticoagulants account for about 45,000 excess incidents of thromboembolic events and deaths. 
Based on averages of observational study data, major, intracranial, and fatal bleeding due to 
warfarin and novel oral anticoagulants occur in about 130,000, 26,000, and 22,000 AF patients 
per year in the USA, respectively.  
 
Conclusion Flaws in the original 6 warfarin versus placebo RCTs together with recent 
observational study data suggest that warfarin causes net harm for patients with NVAF. Clinical 
practice guidelines calling for anticoagulant drug prophylaxis for NVAF patients and Food and 
Drug Administration approval for anticoagulants for NVAF should be retracted. 
 
Introduction 
 
Non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) refers to the 95% of atrial fibrillation (AF) cases that are 
in people who do not have mitral valve disease or artificial heart valves in place. As a 
consequence of NVAF, blood may stagnate in parts of the left atrium, sometimes leading to the 
formation of thrombi. A left atrial thrombus may break loose and travel to the brain, causing an 
embolic stroke. These embolic strokes can be ischemic or unclassified. Since strokes in people 
with AF that are determined to be ischemic or unclassified have the same presumed 
cardioembolic etiology, I will consider “unclassified strokes” ischemic strokes as is often done 
for simplicity. A thrombus originating in the heart may also embolize and travel to other organs 
(e.g., kidney, liver, arm, etc.) and cause ischemia and necrosis from lack of blood flow. 
 
NVAF may be paroxysmal (terminating spontaneously), recurrent persistent (e.g., terminating 
with cardioversion or drugs), or permanent. The incidence of NVAF increases with age, with the 
average age about 75-years-old.[1]  
 
Researchers have standardized the measurement of cardiovascular risk in patients with NVAF 
with various risk stratification schemes. The most commonly used schemes are (1) “CHADS2 
(revised)” (an acronym for congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75, diabetes mellitus, and 
prior stroke or transient ischemic attack (doubled)) and (2) “CHA2DS2-VASc” (an acronym for 
4 
 
congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 (doubled), diabetes mellitus, and prior stroke or 
transient ischemic attack (doubled), vascular disease, age 65 – 74 years, female sex). CHADS2 
(revised) and CHA2DS2-VASc, scores of 0, 1, and ≥2 translate into low-risk, moderate risk, and 
high-risk, respectively.[2] The percentages of NVAF patients with CHADS2=0, 1, and ≥2 are 
about 2%, 31%, and 67%, respectively. The percentages of NVAF patients with CHA2DS2-
VASc=0, 1, and ≥2 are about 0%, 6%, and 94%, respectively.[3]  
 
Six randomized placebo-controlled trials (RCTs) published in the late 1980s and early 1990s 
established the efficacy of warfarin to prevent strokes and systemic emboli in people with 
NVAF. [4-9] Consequently, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) permitted warfarin to be 
labeled as indicated to prevent strokes and systemic emboli in people with NVAF. RCTs 
comparing warfarin with dabigatran,[10] rivaroxaban,[11] apixaban,[12] and edoxaban[13] 
subsequently showed that these drugs are not inferior to warfarin in efficacy and safety and were, 
therefore, also approved by the FDA for prophylaxis against stroke and systemic embolus in 
NVAF patients.  
 
Guidelines recommending that warfarin or novel oral anticoagulant drugs should be used for 
stroke prophylaxis in NVAF patients have been published by the American Heart Association / 
American Stroke Association (AHA / ASA)[2] and the American College of Chest Physicians 
(ACCP).[14]  
 
 
Methods 
 
I performed this systematic review in accordance with the guidelines for preferred reporting 
items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA).[15]  
 
Data sources, searches, and study selection 
 
Since RCTs of warfarin versus placebo for NVAF has been previously reviewed, [16-21] I began 
with the data sources of those reviews. I searched Medline and bibliographies for more warfarin 
versus placebo RCTs for NVAF patients.  
 
I also searched for observational studies relevant to the demographics and epidemiology of AF 
patients. NVAF cases are not distinguished from all AF cases in most population-based and 
many clinical observational studies. In addition, observation studies relevant to the efficacy and 
safety of warfarin prophylaxis against stroke, systemic embolus, other thrombosis (e.g., 
myocardial infarction, heart failure, and venous thromboembolism), and death were included. A 
full electronic observational study search strategy for Medline looked for relevant articles: 
(atrial fibrillation[Title]) AND (observational[Title] OR demographic[Title] OR 
epidemiologic[Title] OR population-based[Title] AND ("1990"[Date - Publication] : 
"3000"[Date - Publication])) I added articles from citations, bibliographies, and targeted Medline 
searches to those observational studies retrieved from the above Medline search strategy. I 
selected observational articles according to their relevance to the prevalence of AF, the incidence 
of ischemic stroke, and to the efficacy and safety of warfarin prophylaxis of AF patients.  
 
5 
 
 
Data extraction for RCTs 
 
For all 6 warfarin versus placebo RCTs, I extracted the following:  
 
1. the risk stratification levels of participants if available (i.e., low, moderate, and high-
risk—CHADS2, CHA2DS2-VASc and other more precise classification systems did not 
appear until after 2001), 
2. to what degree patients with low and moderate risk were entered into the RCTs, 
3. the mean ages of the patients, 
4. the INR target range,

outcomes,

Data extraction for observational studies 
 
As a check on the validity of the efficacy and safety findings from the 6 RCTs, I extracted data 
from observational studies regarding anticoagulants for AF (most observational studies did not 
distinguish all people with AF from those with NVAF). These studies included ones that were 
demographic, epidemiological, and population-based. They also embraced clinical and 
population-based studies involving warfarin treatment. The questions relevant to the efficacy 
and safety of warfarin for AF included the following:

2. the projected prevalence of AF in the USA in 2015 
3. the trend of the incidence of ischemic stroke in the USA over the past 50 years

5. the trend concerning the use of warfarin and novel oral anticoagulant drugs in the USA as 
stroke prophylaxis for AF over the past 40 years 
6. the estimated portion of the AF population in the USA that will receive an anticoagulant 
drug at some time for stroke prophylaxis over the course of their lives

Assessment of risk of bias in included RCTs 
 
Potential biases analysed included:  
(1) extrapolating warfarin treatment outcomes from low and moderate risk NVAF patients to 
high risk patients, 
(2) extrapolating warfarin related efficacy and safety outcomes in younger NVAF patients to 
older patients (the average age patient with NVAF = 75 years old) 
(3)  including warfarin related outcomes in NVAF patients treated with INR target ranges 
extending into what is now considered subtherapeutic (INR < 2.0) with those treated to 
currently considered therapeutic target ranges (i.e. INR from 2.0 – 3.0),  
(4) allowing patients already taking warfarin to enter the RCTs and to then be randomized to 
continue or discontinue the warfarin, subjecting those discontinuing warfarin to rebound-
hypercoagulation related strokes and other thromboses,  
(5) terminating RCTs early, 
(6)  not complying with intention-to-treat principles (e.g., not counting primary events 
occurring after the discontinuation of warfarin in the analysis),  
(7) assessing the rates of withdrawal of NVAF patients from RCTs, and 
(8) comparing the average duration of the RCTs with the average survival of NVAF patients 
to see if the duration of the RCTs was long enough to be meaningful (i.e., short on-study 
time of RCTs bias).

Statistical Methods 
 
I intended to do a meta-analysis, using dichotomous variables that reflected each outcome 
measured in the RCTs (e.g., ischemic stroke versus no ischemic stroke). Using χ2 tests, I 
intended to calculate the risk ratios (RRs), 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and P values to 
estimate treatment effects of anticoagulation versus no anticoagulation. I intended to use SAS 9.2 
for these analyses. However, because of the heterogeneity between RCTs (e.g., intent-to-treat 
principles utilised, primary versus secondary prophylaxis, INR target range, risk levels of NVAF 
patients, inclusion of patients already taking warfarin, etc.), these statistical methods were not 
appropriate.

Using the Medline electronic search strategy detailed in the methods, 201 articles fit the search 
criteria. Of those articles, 30 were relevant to the objectives of this review and were included. An 
additional 22 observational studies came from bibliographies, citations, or targeted searches.  
 
Trends in prevalence and incidence of AF and incidence of embolic stroke  
 
Prior to about 2000, the medical literature indicated that the prevalence of AF was about 0.9% of 
the USA population.[22-24] This consisted primarily of “permanent” or “chronic” AF. 
Investigators usually did not count patients with AF that was paroxysmal or intermittently 
persistent. More recently, paroxysmal and intermittently persistent AF have been counted in 
studies of prevalence of AF, in part accounting for an increased prevalence of AF. For example, 
investigators with the Framingham Heart Study looked at trends in incidence, prevalence, and 
risk factors for AF and its association with stroke and mortality between 1958 and 2007.[25] In 
men, AF increased in prevalence 4.7 fold from 2.0% in 1958 – 67 to 9.6% in 1998 – 2007. In 
women, the prevalence of AF increased 3.6 fold from 1.4% in 1958 – 67 to 4.9% in 1998 – 2007.  
 
According to the most recent prevalence and incidence projections that include paroxysmal and 
intermittently persistent AF, about 6.9 million people in the USA are projected to have AF in 
2015 (2.3% of the overall population). About 1.5 million Americans will be newly diagnosed 
with AF in 2015, rising to about 2.2 million by 2024.[26]  
 
African Americans have a lower prevalence of AF than Caucasians in the USA possibly because 
of under-diagnosis of AF in African Americans.[27] A population-based study from Olmstead 
County Minnesota, a largely Caucasian region, reported a AF prevalence of 2.8%.[28] An area in 
northern Sweden, likewise predominantly Caucasian, found a similar prevalence of AF of 2.5% 
of the population.[29] A study from Spain reported a somewhat lower prevalence of AF (1.5% / 
year).[30] 
 
According to the AHA/ASA 2015 statistical update, about 795,000 people in the USA 
experience new or recurrent strokes each year, of which 87% are ischemic. The AHA/ASA 
estimates that about 15% of ischemic strokes are associated with AF.[31] Given these data, about 
104,000 ischemic strokes each year are associated with AF (795,000 strokes x 0.87 (87% 
ischemic) x 0.15 (15% of ischemic strokes related to AF) ≈ 104,000). In accordance with this 
calculation, Sridhar and Lakkireddy independently estimated the number of ischemic strokes per 
year in the USA associated with AF in 2010 to be 101,000.[32]  
 
In international studies of people with ischemic stroke, estimates of the prevalence of AF have 
ranged widely: 15%,[31] 15%,[32] 31.7%,[33] 24.6%,[34] 38%,[35] and 18.7%.[36] Most of 
these estimates do not distinguish between stroke victims with previously known AF and stroke 
patients in which AF was found for the first time after the stroke. It may be that the prevalence of 
previously known AF in patients with ischemic strokes has risen modestly from the current 
AHA/ASA estimate of 15% but this has not been definitively documented.

AbbVie Inc. (AbbVie) respectfully submits this citizen petition (Petition) to the Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA) under 21 C.F.R. §§ 10.25 and 10.30, sections 201(n) and 502(a) of the Federal 
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA), section 351 of the Public Health Service Act (PHSA), as amended 
by the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act of 2009 (BPCIA), and sections 4(e) and 10 of the 
Administrative Procedure Act (APA). 
I. 
ACTION REQUESTED 
This Petition requests that FDA require that the approved prescription drug labeling for 
biological products licensed under section 351(k) of the PHSA contain: 
(a) 
A clear statement that the product is a biosimilar, that the biosimilar is licensed for 
fewer than all the reference product’s conditions of use (if applicable), and that the 
biosimilar’s licensed conditions of use were based on extrapolation (if applicable); 
(b) 
A clear statement that FDA has not determined that the biosimilar product is 
interchangeable with the reference product (if applicable); and 
(c) 
A concise description of the pertinent data developed to support licensure of the 
biosimilar, along with information adequate to enable prescribers to distinguish data 
derived from studies of the biosimilar from data derived from studies of the reference 
product. 
Biosimilars are not generic drugs and should not be labeled like generic drugs.  Including the 
above information in biosimilar labeling is necessary to enable rational and informed prescribing 
decisions regarding these complex products, to avoid potentially unsafe substitution of biosimilars and 
reference products, and to combat widespread misconceptions among prescribers about biosimilars and 
their relationship to reference products.  Without this information, biosimilar labeling will not reflect the 
unique licensure provisions established by the BPCIA and will be materially misleading in violation of the 
FDCA and FDA regulations.  Moreover, FDA proposed in 2012 to include similar information in biosimilar 
labeling, but recently reversed its position without providing any explanation.  The Agency’s unexplained 
about-face on this important public health issue is a violation of the APA.

II. 
BACKGROUND 
The BPCIA amended section 351 of the PHSA to create a two-tiered abbreviated licensure 
pathway for follow-on biological products.  A biological product can be licensed under the BPCIA if it is 
“biosimilar” to a “reference product” as set out in section 351(i)(2).  Separately, a biosimilar can be 
deemed “interchangeable” with the reference product if certain heightened showings required by 
section 351(k)(4) have been made. 
To date, FDA’s efforts to implement the BPCIA generally have focused on issuing guidance 
regarding the new statutory standards.  FDA began releasing draft guidance documents for public 
comment in February 2012.  In the draft entitled “Scientific Considerations in Demonstrating 
Biosimilarity to a Reference Product” (Draft Scientific Guidance), FDA stated that biosimilar labeling 
should disclose that the product is a biosimilar, the scope of its approval, and whether it has been found 
to be interchangeable.  According to the Draft Scientific Guidance, including this information in labeling 
is “necessary” to enable informed prescribing and adequate postmarket safety monitoring.1  When the 
guidance was finalized at the end of April 2015 (Final Scientific Guidance), however, it made no mention 
of biosimilar labeling or the need for biosimilar labeling to provide this information.2 
On March 6, 2015, while the Draft Scientific Guidance was pending, FDA approved the first 
biosimilar product in the United States.  Zarxio® (filgrastim-sndz), developed by Sandoz Inc., is biosimilar 
to the reference biological product Neupogen® (filgrastim), which was developed by Amgen, Inc.3  Zarxio 
has not been found interchangeable with Neupogen, and the approved labeling for Zarxio does not 
include the information that FDA had identified as “necessary” in the Draft Scientific Guidance.  Instead, 
the labeling for Zarxio mimics the approved labeling for Neupogen, which suggests that FDA has decided 
to apply the “same labeling” requirement found in FDCA section 505(j) for small-molecule generic drugs 
to biosimilars licensed under section 351(k) of the PHSA. 
Publicly available materials from FDA’s review of Zarxio confirm that FDA followed a “same 
labeling” approach.  According to the action package for Zarxio, in November 2013, Sandoz proposed 
and FDA agreed that the biosimilar and reference product labeling “should be essentially the same.”4  In 
February 2015, FDA provided the labeling for Neupogen to Sandoz for use “as a template” in developing 
the labeling for Zarxio, and instructed Sandoz to track any changes made to the Neupogen labeling and 
provide annotations to explain and justify any such changes.5  That is essentially what FDA regulations

It would be legally unsound for FDA to adopt a “same labeling” approach to biosimilars, as the 
Agency has done with respect to Zarxio.  First, a “same labeling” approach is flatly inconsistent with the 
BPCIA, which—unlike the Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) provisions in section 505(j)—
includes no “same labeling” requirement and recognizes that biosimilars are different from their 
reference products (infra § III.A).  Second, a “same labeling” approach to biosimilars would result in 
labeling that omits material information necessary for safe and informed prescribing, and would 
exacerbate, rather than dispel, misconceptions among prescribers regarding biosimilars (infra § III.B).  
Finally, FDA has not provided the reasoned explanation required by the APA for its decision to abandon 
the approach taken in the Draft Scientific Guidance, which stated that the labeling of a biosimilar 
product should disclose that the product is a biosimilar, the scope of its approval, and whether it has 
been found to be interchangeable, on the ground that this information is “necessary” for informed 
prescribing (infra § III.C).  For all of these reasons, as discussed below, FDA should take the actions

STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
A. 
The “Same Labeling” Requirement That Applies To Generic Drugs Does Not Exist In, 
And Is Contrary To, The BPCIA. 
 
FDA’s apparent decision to apply a “same labeling” requirement to biosimilars is inconsistent 
with the BPCIA.  Congress established a distinct approval pathway for biosimilars, and that pathway 
includes no analogue to the same labeling requirement that exists for small-molecule generic drugs 
under the ANDA provisions of the FDCA. 
Under section 505(j), an ANDA must contain information to show, among other things, that a 
proposed generic drug’s active ingredient is “the same as” that of the reference listed drug (RLD).8   The 
ANDA also must contain information to show, subject to a few exceptions not relevant here, that the 
proposed labeling for the generic drug is “the same as” the labeling for the RLD.9  FDA cannot approve
