FDA has acknowledged that the 505(j) pathway “is predicated on a finding of the ‘same’ active 
ingredient” and, therefore, “will not ordinarily be available” for biological products.12  As the current 
Director of CDER told Congress during consideration of the BPCIA, “there is general recognition that the 
idea of sameness, as the term is used in the generic drug approval process . . . and applied to small 
molecules, will not usually be appropriate for more structurally complex molecules of the type generally 
licensed as biological products.”13  Consequently, it is “impossible to demonstrate that [a follow-on 
biological product] is identical to” a previously approved product.14  The BPCIA pathway therefore does 
not require a showing that biosimilars are the same as their referents.  Instead, biosimilars may be 
licensed if they are shown to be “sufficiently similar to products already on the market.”15 
Significant public health considerations flow from the fact that biosimilars are not the same as 
their reference products.  In particular, increased risks of immunogenicity can arise if patients are 
sequentially or repeatedly exposed to similar, but not identical, biological products.  Immunogenic

such as anaphylaxis, rash, fever and kidney problems,” as well as potential cross-reactions with 
endogenous proteins.16  Immunogenic responses also can have a significant impact on effectiveness, 
“including the potential to decrease or block the clinical effect.”17  For these reasons, an accurate 
“assessment of immunogenicity” is “critical” when evaluating all biological products, including 
biosimilars.18  At FDA’s urging, Congress addressed these risks by requiring more from biosimilar

decision not to borrow the same labeling requirement makes clear that FDA cannot follow that 
approach to biosimilar labeling.  Under the BPCIA, a biosimilar applicant must seek approval for 
“conditions of use” that were “previously approved for the reference product,” and must show that the 
“route of administration, the dosage form, and the strength” of the biosimilar are “the same as those of

BPCIA does not, however, contain anything comparable to the 505(j) same labeling requirement.23 
In other words, Congress chose to include in the BPCIA some provisions from section 505(j) and 
to exclude other ANDA requirements.  Under settled rules of statutory construction, Congress is 
presumed to have acted “‘intentionally and purposely in the disparate inclusion or exclusion.’”24  
Indeed, FDA previously concluded that Congress acted intentionally when it omitted the same labeling

Another crucial distinction between the BPCIA and 505(j) pertains to therapeutic equivalence.  
The same labeling requirement reflects the fact that ANDA drugs generally are therapeutically 
equivalent to, and substitutable for, their respective RLDs.27  Even when FDA exempts an ANDA drug 
from the same labeling requirement, FDA usually specifies that the drug is substitutable for the RLD.28  
As FDA has explained, the concept of therapeutic equivalence applies “to drug products containing the 
same active ingredients,” but does not encompass “different therapeutic agents.”29 
A non-interchangeable biosimilar is a “different therapeutic agent” from its reference product as 
a matter of law.  Congress, as part of the BPCIA, amended section 505A of the FDCA, the Pediatric 
Research Equity Act (PREA), to state that a non-interchangeable biosimilar is “a new active ingredient” 
for purposes of pediatric research, but an interchangeable product is not.30  The sponsor of a non-
interchangeable biosimilar therefore must conduct pediatric assessments unless that requirement is 
deferred or waived by FDA.31  Congress’s decision to subject biosimilars to the PREA—which does not 
apply at all to ANDA drugs32—underscores that Congress was aware that biosimilars differ from their 
reference products, unlike generic drugs in the ANDA context. 
In sum, the characterizing feature of the BPCIA pathway is that it deems biosimilars to be 
different from their referents, which distinguishes the BPCIA from the FDCA’s ANDA provisions.  
Applying the same labeling requirement for ANDA products to biosimilars would conflict with the novel 
licensing scheme established by the BPCIA.  The same labeling approach in this context is therefore 
legally unsound, and FDA should not use this approach in reviewing the labeling for products submitted 
for review under the BPCIA.

B. 
Applying A “Same Labeling” Requirement To Biosimilars Leads to Labeling That Is 
Misleading In Violation Of The FDCA And FDA Regulations. 
 
In addition to conflicting with the BPCIA, a “same labeling” approach to biosimilars would create 
serious misbranding issues under the FDCA and FDA regulations.  Under section 502(a) of the FDCA, a 
drug is misbranded if its labeling is false or misleading in any particular.33  Under section 201(n), labeling 
is misleading if it omits material facts as described in that provision.34  FDA regulations governing 
physician labeling likewise prohibit material omissions.35  As detailed below, a “same labeling” approach 
to biosimilar labeling violates these basic statutory and regulatory requirements in several respects. 
1. 
Biosimilar Labeling Must Include Information Necessary To Enable Informed 
Prescribing And To Dispel Common Misconceptions. 
 
The labeling statements requested in this Petition are necessary to enable informed prescribing 
decisions and to dispel common and widespread misconceptions among prescribers about biosimilars 
and their relationship to their respective reference products.  FDA has long recognized that physician 
labeling is “the primary source of information about a product” for prescribers.36  Consistent with 
section 201(n) of the statute, FDA regulations provide that labeling “shall be deemed to be misleading if 
it fails to reveal facts that are . . . [m]aterial in light of other representations made or suggested by 
statement, word, design, device or any combination thereof.”37  Whether an omission is material “is 
determined by the degree to which [the] information is objectively important, relevant, or substantial to 
the target audience.”38  In other words, a material fact is one that reasonably would influence “the 
intended audience.”39 
The intended audience for physician labeling is the health care professional prescribing the 
drug.40  FDA has recognized that “[t]he relevant properties of a product” are core material facts that 
must be disclosed.41  A recent survey of 400 U.S. board-certified physicians shows definitively that the

product. As defined in the FDA's draft guidance MDI and DPI Drug Products - Chemist1y,

the actuator. This may result in an overdose, inadequate dose or no dose, all of which present a 
serious patient safety risk given the use of these products as symptomatic rescue medications. 
With patents expiring on the original albuterol sulfate MDI products, generic products are

Pursuant to 21 CFR I 0.30 and other provisions of law, Hogan Lovells US LLP (Hogan 
Lovells) submits this petition regarding parenteral 1 drug manufacturing standards on behalf of a 
parenteral drug manufacturer. The United States Pharmacopeia (USP) has long provided that 
parenteral drug products must be "essentially free" of visible particulates2 But regulators and 
industry have struggled to consistently interpret this term. Recently, on August I, 2014, in an 
effort to clarify what "essentially free" of visible particulates means, the USP issued General 
Chapter 790, Visible Particulates in Injections (USP <790> ). USP <790> provides that the 
'·essentially free" standard is achieved when parenteral drugs are inspected and no more than a 
specified number of units are observed to contain visible particulates. More specifically, for 
parenteral drugs subject to I 00% inspection, the "essentially fi·ee" standard is met when a batch 
meets an acceptable quality level (AQL) of0.65% or lower. And if it becomes necessary to 
evaluate product that has been shipped to customers (e.g., because of a complaint or regulatory 
concern), a firm can sample and inspect 20 units. If no pmiicles are observed in the sample, the 
batch is considered "essentially free" of visible particulates. 
In other words, "essentially free" does not mean "completely free of' or "zero" visible 
particulates for the simple reason that such a standard would be unattainable. Although zero 
particulates can be the goal for the manufacture of all batches of parenteral drug products, it is 
not a practical limit or specification, and USP has officially recognized this fact.

2 See USP General Requirements <I>, fnject;ons. 
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) current Good Manufacturing Practice

and the associated regulations dictate that FDA accept the compendia! methods as sut1icient for

recall parenteral drug products even though the products are "essentially free" of visible particles

STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
I. 
Parenteral Drug Products and Visible Particulates 
Every year, billions of parenteral drug products are administered worldwide3 These 
include vaccines, anesthetics, antivirals, antibiotics, and therapies to treat a wide variety of 
diseases. Manufacturing these products presents ce1iain challenges. In particular, parenteral 
drug products inevitably contain a small number of randomly sourced particulates~"extraneous 
mobile undissolved particles, other than gas bubbles, unintentionally present in solutions."4 To 
minimize the possible introduction of particulates, parenteral drug manufacturing must be done

in conformance with cGMP, including using appropriate production and process controls 
designed to minimize the potential for particulate matter in the finished product. Even with the 
strictest adherence to eGMP, however, it is impossible in most contexts to produce parenteral 
drug products that are completely free of particulates. 
Particles are generally classified as intrinsic or extrinsic, depending on the source. 
Intrinsic particles are associated with the package, formulation ingredients, or assembly process, 
and can include numerous types of substances, such as glass, stainless steel, rubber from 
stoppers, and gasket material.5 By contrast, extrinsic particles are inherent in the manufacturing 
process but not part of the product formulation; they may include fibers, cellulosic matter, 
clothing fragments, metal, or plastic6 
Although product inspection strategies are devised to prevent and identify the presence of 
visible particulate in product, even the best strategies remain probability-based, and therefore 
cannot guarantee the total absence of particulates in the finished product 7 Accordingly, the USP 
recommends an "essentially free" standard for visible particulates in parenteral drugs, as opposed 
to a "zero tolerance" standard. 
Factors affecting the risk posed by particulates include product sterility, intended route of 
administration, and patient-related factors such as underlying health status8 A recent review 
article published by the Parenteral Drug Association (PDA) comprehensively explores these very 
considerations and potential areas of clinical risk. For example, the PDA article states that 
particles in injections administered intramuscularly and subcutaneously generally have little 
clinical impact, while the intravenous infusion of particles presents a greater risk ofharm9 
There are limited clinical data in humans regarding the impact of particles, and studies of the 
effect are often small, highly experimental, use excessive quantities of particulates, or derive 
from high-risk situations like that of intravenous drug use.

caused by the underlying physical ailment. For example, it is believed that particles that are inert 
and primarily obstructive in nature, such as cellulose and metal, have little clinical impact.

sterile raise little risk of harm.

II. 
The USP's "Essentially Free" Standard for Visible Particulates 
USP <I> has long provided that parenteral drug products must be "essentially free" of 
visible particulates. The term, however, is not selt~evidenl. On August 1, 2014, USP <790> 
became of1icial and for the first time clarified the meaning of"essentially fl·ee" of visible 
particulates. 
Specifically, USP <790> provides that the "essentially free" standard is achieved when 
parenteral drugs are inspected and no more than a specified number of units are observed to 
contain visible particulates. For parenteral drugs subject to 100% inspection, the "essentially 
free" standard is met when a batch meets an AQL of 0.65% or lower. If it becomes necessary to 
evaluate product that has been shipped to customers (e.g., because of a complaint or regulatory 
concern), a firm can sample and inspect 20 units. If no particles are observed in the sample, the 
batch is considered "essentially free" of visible particulates. The USP "essentially Jl·ee" 
standard, then, recognizes that due diligence in manufacturing, strict compliance with cGMP, 
and rigorous inspection procedures cannot serve as a warranty for the absolute absence of 
particles. Thus, the USP has rejected a "zero tolerance" standard. 
The capabilities and limitations of visual inspection illustrate the rationale for this 
principle. Neither human manual inspection nor fully automated inspection systems can provide 
assurance of particulate-free products. "Visual inspection is a probabilistic process, with 
detection probabilities less than 100%, especially for particles less than 200 ,tm in diameter."
15 
Visible particle testing is influenced by multiple, highly variable factors such as drug and 
container clarity, lighting, particle size, optical density, refractive index, color, contrast, and 
operator or automated inspection sensitivity and reliabilityi 6 
Again, because of the limitations of current manufacturing technology, the variability 
inherent in inspection processes, and the inevitability of some amount of particulate matter being 
present in the product, the USP's "essentially free", risk-based approach to the control of visible 
pm1iculates is necessary. And the most intensive prevention and inspection strategies should be 
targeted at the processes that control attributes most likely to affect patient safety. Industry 
recognizes the imperative to monitor the presence of particulate matter in injectable products, 
and to reduce the number of pm1iculates through all reasonable means. Nonetheless, sporadic 
reports of particulate matter in marketed products are not unexpected.

The USP's "Essentially Free" Standard is cGMP 
Manufacturing in conformance with cGMP assures that a drug is safe and has the 
characteristics of identity, strength, quality and purity that it purports or is represented to possess, 
by rigorously controlling the manner of froduction. 17 If manufacturing processes do not comply 
with cGMP, the product is adulterated_~ The goal ofcGMP is to assure that manufacturing

phases of drug product manufacturing, including particulate control. They are intended to be 
flexible and can be tailored to pm1icular products and manufacturing processes. This flexibility 
allows manufacturer to establish cGMP controls and systems that are appropriate for the 
particular product and manufacturing process at issue. At the same time, however, the 
regulations' general approach can result in a lack of clarity and specific standards.

regulatory bodies worldwide-incorporate the USP into their respective regulatory schemes 
because the methods published in the USP general chapters are developed by experts through a 
rigorous public process. Proposed standards are reviewed and tested by USP's scientific staff 
and other relevant experts, published for public review and comment, and approved by a USP 
Expert Committee of scientists, academicians, and practitioners.20 In fact, USP <790> was 
developed by the Visual Inspection Expert Committee, which included a representative member 
of FDA.

IV. 
FDA Guidance Must Incorporate the USP Standard 
Although the USP's "essentially free" standard is considered cGMP and represents the 
touchstone for the regulation of visible particulates in parenteral drug products, FDA has never

as a "zero tolerance threshold."27 Should FDA embrace a zero tolerance standard moving 
forward, we could only expect product recalls to continue to increase because of the unattainable 
nature of the standard. Such a policy is inconsistent with the legal standard governing 
particulates-the USP's "essentially free" standard,-creates considerable uncertainty in 
industry, and risks instilling potentially unnecessary fear among consumers. Moreover, in such 
an environment, shortages of critical drug products are inevitable, whether caused by regulatory 
pressure, recalls, or industry-initiated compliance attempts. When regulatory policy results in 
such consequences, a change in course is due. 
The necessity of rigorous standards for these products is the reason the "essentially free" 
standard depends on a robust quality management system with a I 00% inspection process, 
particle identification processes, and good investigation and monitoring practices designed to

impractical, unnecessary, and in contravention of the USP and cGMP. Any product-specific 
risks related to visible particulates should be addressed to the extent possible in the regulatory 
review process of New Drug Applications, Biological License Applications, and product labeling 
and in the health hazard evaluation conducted under FDA's recall guidance. And, FDA 
investigators and recall coordinators should apply USP <790> when reviewing industry 
compliance with these standards. 
V. 
CONCLUSION 
The USP standard, requiring that parenteral drugs be "essentially free" from visible 
particulates, is the result of a broad consensus of researchers, clinicians, academicians, and 
regulatory parties, both nationally and internationally. FDA and Congress have recognized 
USP's technical expertise and experience in developing such methods and standards, and they 
have been legally adopted as cGMP. The USP's public, cooperative development process and 
the unambiguous standards that result provide predictability and clear expectations for 
industry-which is essential to investment and innovation.

STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
A. 
The First Acura Petition Raised Legitimate Issues Concerning 
 
 
505(b)(2) NDAs for Abuse-Deterrent Drugs That Need to be Addressed. 
 
The Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (“FDCA”) allows the submission of a 505(b)(2) 
NDA for a drug product that copies most, but not all, of the characteristics of a previously-
approved listed drug. To take advantage of this regulatory shortcut, however, the applicant must 
“reference” the previously-approved listed drug or drugs that share relevant characteristics with 
the proposed drug product.5   The critically important basis for that requirement is to protect the 
intellectual property rights of innovative companies whose patents might be infringed by the 
proposed competing product. As FDA has long recognized and acknowledged, the 505(b)(2) 
NDA “listed drug” reference requirements are meant to “ensure that the 505(b)(2) applicant does 
not use the 505(b)(2) process to end-run patent protections that would have applied had an 
ANDA been permitted.” 6 As the Agency has also explained, referencing the proper listed drug is 
necessary “to prevent applicants from using the 505(b)(2) pathway to avoid patent protections 
that would have applied had the application been submitted under section 505(j).”7

Purdue’s own admission, pharmaceutically equivalent to OXAYDO, Acura reasonably expects 
that FDA will fully consider the merits of its First Citizens Petition with regard to protecting

DEAR SIRS: 
The undersigned signatory, Food & Water Watch,1 (“Petitioner”), submits the attached 
document, which, along with the attached attachments, constitutes a citizen petition and all 
required supplemental information with respect to AquaBounty Technologies’ (“ABT”) 
genetically engineered (“GE” or “transgenic” or “genetically modified”) AquAdvantage salmon,2 
pursuant to the Food, Drug and Cosmetic, Act § 409(b)(1) (21 U.S.C. § 348(b)(1)) (the “Act”) 
and the Food and Drug Administration’s (the “Agency”) regulations, 1 C.F.R. §§ 10.20; 10.30; 
170.30(f), (f)(2); 170.38; 171.1; 171.130; and 189.1(c). 
	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  
1 Food & Water Watch is a national non-profit consumer orgnization that advocates to ensure that food, water and 
fish is safe, accessible and sustainably produced. 
2 More technically, ABT’s seeks approval for a triploid female Atlantic salmon bearing a single copy of the stably 
integrated α-form of opAFP-GHc2 at the α-locus in the EO-1α line. 
 
 
 
	  
2 
This petition respectfully requests that the Office of Food Additive Safety (“OFAS”) take 
all of the following actions:  
• Review ABT’s New Animal Drug Application (“NADA”) for AquAdvantage salmon 
under the Act’s food additive provisions and deem the AquAdvantage salmon a food 
additive.  Atlantic salmon is a substance traditionally regarded as safe.  ABT’s GE 
process significantly alters the salmon’s composition, however, in a way that is 
reasonably expected to alter its nutritive value or concentration of constituents, and the 
new substance raises safety concerns.  Under the Agency’s regulations and guidelines, 
such a substance must be treated as a food additive and the Agency must make a closer 
inquiry into the safety of its consumption, including, but not limited to, subjecting it to 
extensive pre-market safety testing.  
• Review the AquAdvantage salmon’s components, including its gene expression product 
(the “GEP”) of the recombinant DNA (“rDNA”) construct, and deem them food additives 
under the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, § 201(s) (21 U.S.C. § 321). 
• Render the GEP of the AquAdvantage salmon an added substance under the Act’s 
adulteration provisions.  
• Make a finding that neither the AquAdvantage salmon, nor the GEP used to create it, is 
generally recognized as safe (“GRAS”) for human consumption.  Food additives are 
presumed to be unsafe, and the processor carries the burden to prove that a food additive 
is GRAS.  The data supplied by ABT to the Agency’s Center for Veterinary Medicine 
(“CVM”), which are the only known data on the food safety of ABT’s transgenic salmon, 
are incomplete and biased and cannot be relied upon to show that AquAdvantage salmon 
is safe to consume.  
 
 
 
	  
3 
If the Agency were to permit the first GE animal to enter the food supply without review as a 
food additive as sought in this petition, neither AquAdvantage salmon nor its component GEP 
will have been subjected to the appropriate safety assessments, rendering such a decision  
contrary to the law and otherwise arbitrary and capricious.  
A. ACTION REQUESTED 
 
Based on the fact that the AquAdvantage salmon and all of its components meet the Act’s 
definition of food additives and are not GRAS, Petitioner proposes the following food additive 
regulations in order to establish that there are no conditions under which such additives are 
considered safe. 
To be inserted after 21 C.F.R. § 170.60: 
 
§ 170.70 Atlantic salmon bearing a single copy of the stably integrated α-form of opAFP-GHc2 at 
 the α-locus in the EO-1α line (the AquAdvantage salmon) and all of its components.  
 
(a) Atlantic salmon, regardless of ploidy, bearing a single copy of the stably integrated α-
form of opAFP-GHc2 at the α-locus in the EO-1α line, and all of the components within such 
salmon, including but not limited to the growth expression product resulting from genetic 
manipulation, are food additives.  There are no conditions under which such additives may be 
safely used without the establishment of an authorizing food additive regulation.  A food 
additive petition, submitted with supporting data pursuant to §§ 171.1 and 171.100 of this 
chapter, is required to demonstrate that such food additives are safe.  
To be inserted after 21 C.F.R. § 189.191: 
 
 
§ 189.192 Atlantic salmon bearing a single copy of the stably integrated α-form of 
 
opAFP-GHc2 at the α-locus in the EO-1α line (the AquAdvantage salmon) and 
 
all of its components.  
 
(a) Atlantic salmon, which bears a single copy of the stably integrated α-form of opAFP-
GHc2 at the α-locus in the EO-1α line, along with all of its components, commonly known as 
 
 
 
	  
4 
the AquAdvantage salmon, have been created by inserting an rDNA construct comprised of 
sequences from an Ocean Pout fish gene, a Chinook Salmon gene, and synthetic linkers into 
a female triploid Atlantic Salmon. 
 
(b) Atlantic salmon, regardless of ploidy, bearing a single copy of the stably integrated α-
form of opAFP-GHc2 at the α-locus in the EO-1α line, along with all of the components 
within such salmon are deemed adulterated in violation of the act. 
B. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
I. Background (corresponding to FDA Form 3503 Parts I, II, and III) 
The AquAdvantage salmon that is the subject of this food additive petition would be the 
first GE animal intended for human consumption.  ABT genetically engineers the salmon by 
inserting an rDNA construct into diploid Atlantic salmon.  Additional steps in the process 
attempt to create all-female triploid salmon (containing three sets of chromosomes).3  The rDNA 
construct inserted into the salmon is made up of two components: a Chinook salmon growth-
hormone gene and a gene sequence from an ocean pout fish intended to promote the regulation 
of the growth hormone.  Synthetic linkers are also added to help assemble the two inserts.  Both 
the ocean pout protein and the synthetic linkers act as the backbone of the rDNA construct.4  The 
Chinook salmon growth hormone is the primary GEP of the rDNA construct, which actively 
attempts to spur an increased growth rate with the aim that the AquAdvantage salmon reach 
market size in half the time as Atlantic salmon.5  
	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  
3 Rearranging the chromosomes is supposed to ensure that the female salmon are infertile. 
4 FDA CVM.  Veterinary Medicine Advisory Committee, Briefing Packet: AquAdvantage Salmon, at 10-11, 
(September 20, 2010 (pre-released September 3, 2010)) (hereinafter, “Briefing Packet”).  (Attached as Exhibit A.) 
5 ABT Technologies, http://www.aquabounty.com/products/aquadvantage-295.aspx 
(last visited September 8, 2011).  (Attached as Exhibit B.) 
 
 
 
	  
5 
ABT has now submitted its new animal drug application (“NADA”) to CVM for review, 
and, as part of this process, the Agency is to take into consideration the evaluation of the 
Veterinary Medicine Advisory Committee (“VMAC”).  To make its evaluation, VMAC has 
ostensibly reviewed the Agency’s briefing packet and ABT’s research, contained in a draft 
Environmental Assessment.6  Utilizing VMAC’s recommendations, CVM will make its decision 
on whether or not to approve ABT’s AquAdvantage salmon.   
The primary responsibility of CVM is to evaluate the safety of new animal drugs and 
animal feed.  To do so, CVM applies what is essentially a “substantial equivalence” test, 
comparing the characteristics and composition of the GE animal and non-GE comparators.7  
Substances that are subject to a food additive review, on the other hand, are required to undergo 
comprehensive toxicological studies from producers to ensure that foods entering the market are 
safe to consume and are properly labeled.   
Because the AquAdvantage salmon is the first GE animal meant for human consumption, 
any unintended consequences of the genetic modification on food composition will be directly 
passed from animals to humans.  And while some of the possible unintended consequences are 
better understood, such as elevated levels of hormones or increased allergenicity, many still may 
be unknown.  
As discussed in detail in this petition, not only is it critical that AquAdvantage salmon be 
subject to OFAS’ more in-depth toxicological review of food additives in order to more fully 
understand the consequences of humans ingesting the GE animal and to determine whether it is 
truly safe for humans, the Agency’s regulations, guidelines, and organic statute require it. 
	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  
6 Briefing Packet at 17. 
7 See, e.g., id. at 5 (“The food and feed safety step of the hierarchical review process addresses the issue of whether 
food or feed from the GE animal poses any risk to humans or animals consuming edible products from GE animals 
compared with the appropriate non-transgenic comparators.”) (emphasis added). 
 
 
 
	  
6 
II. Petition (corresponding to FDA Form 3503 Parts IV.A, V, and VI) 
A. In accordance with Agency regulations, OFAS must review AquAdvantage salmon as 
a food additive. 
 
As outlined in this section, under the Agency’s regulations, OFAS must deem and 
review AquAdvantage salmon and all of its components as food additives and subject them to 
closer inquiry, such as extensive pre-market safety testing.  The Agency’s general classification 
of rDNA constructs as new animal drugs does not displace or override the Agency’s regulations 
and guidelines, and nothing precludes the Agency from also regulating the GE salmon and its 
components as food additives.  A contrary determination would be contrary to the law, arbitrary 
and capricious, and in contravention of these regulations and guidelines.8  
According to the Agency’s regulations at 21 C.F.R. § 170.30(f)(2) (2014), “[a]ny 
substance of natural biological origin that has been widely consumed for its nutrient properties in 
the United States prior to January 1, 1958, without known detrimental effect, for which no health 
hazard is known, that has had significant alteration of composition by breeding[9] or selection[10] 
after January 1, 1958, where the change may be reasonably expected to alter the nutritive value 
or the concentration of constituents” will be “reviewed as and affirmed as GRAS or determined 
to be a food additive . . . .”11  Food substances that are not GRAS will be categorized as food 
	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  	  
8 See, e.g., Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983).  See also 21 C.F.R. § 
10.115(d)(3) (“FDA employees may depart from guidance documents only with appropriate justification and 
supervisory concurrence.”)  (Attached as Exhibit C.) 
9 “Breeding” means to “[t]o raise animals or plants, often to produce new or improved types.”  The American 
Heritage Science Dictionary, 2002, Houghton Mifflin. 
10 “Selection” means “a natural or artificial process that results or tends to result in the survival and propagation of 
some individuals or organisms but not of others with the result that the inherited traits of the survivors are 
perpetuated.  Merriam-Webster's Medical Dictionary, 2007, Merriam-Webster, Inc. 
11 (Attached as Exhibit D.) 
 
 
 
	  
7 
additives, and the Agency will issue a notice in the Federal Register providing for the use of the 
additive in food or require the discontinuation of the additive.12  
 
Likewise, 21 C.F.R. § 189.1(a), (c), which is the product of a 1974 Agency listing of food 
ingredients that were prohibited in food by previous actions of the agency, see 39 Fed. Reg. 
34,172 (Sept. 23, 1974), provides for the addition of substances from the list by a petition where 
“they present a potential risk to the public health or have not been shown by adequate scientific 
data to be safe for use in human food.”  § 189.1(a), (c); accord 21 C.F.R § 121.106 (1974).   
In the case of the present petition, Atlantic salmon and all of its components (which 
obviously have been widely consumed for their nutrient and generally non-adverse properties 
before January 1, 1958 and to the present) have undergone significant alteration due to breeding 
or selection through genetic engineering to create the AquAdvantage salmon, and this change is 
reasonably expected to alter the nutritive value or the concentration of the Atlantic salmon’s 
constituents, as detailed below.  Therefore, under § 170.30(f)(2) (2014), the Agency is obligated 
to review the substance to determine whether it is GRAS or an unsafe food additive.  Since the 
Agency cannot find AquAdvantage salmon to be GRAS, as also demonstrated below, the 
Agency must find AquAdvantage to be an unsafe food additive.13    
Likewise, as demonstrated below, the evidence demonstrates that AquAdvantage 
salmon’s GEP presents a public health risk and it has not been shown by adequate scientific data 
to be safe for use in human food.  Thus, under § 189.1(a)-(b), the AquAdvantage’s GEP should 
be prohibited as an ingredient in food. 
 
Finding that the AquAdvantage salmon should be prohibited as an unsafe food additive 
aligns with the agency’s current guidelines. bioengineered foods in 1992, the Agency has said that genetically engineered foods would fall 
under its food additive provisions.  The Guidance to Industry for Foods Derived from New Plant 
Varieties (“1992 Guidance”), which VMAC’s briefing packet cites for support,14 reiterates § 
170.30(f) and says that foods or substances of natural biological origin that have historically 
been regarded as safe, but that have been significantly altered by modification, “fall within the 
scope of the FDA’s food additive authority.”15  The same guidance indicates that “specifically, 
consistent with the statutory definition of ‘food additive’ and the overall design of FDA’s current

CITIZEN PETITION 
 
The Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI), representing 800,000 members and 
supporters, petitions the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to ban the retail distribution of 
pure and highly concentrated caffeine as a dietary supplement.  The recent commencement of 
pure or highly concentrated caffeine marketing has been associated with ill effects in consumers, 
including deaths.  CSPI thus requests that FDA limit the form in which caffeine is sold to prevent 
unreasonable risks to adolescents and others from overdoses of caffeine. 
FDA should find that pure caffeine marketed as a dietary supplement presents “a 
significant or unreasonable risk of illness or injury under conditions of use suggested or 
recommended in the labeling,” or, in the absence of such labeling, “under ordinary conditions of 
use.”1  Alternatively, the Secretary of Health and Human Services should declare that caffeine 
sold in pure or highly concentrated form “pose[s] an imminent hazard to public health or safety,” 
and institute an immediate ban to that effect.2  Under either standard, highly concentrated 
caffeine must be deemed adulterated and removed from the market under the Federal Food, 
Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) and the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act 
(DSHEA). 
I. 
Actions Requested 
CSPI calls on the FDA and/or HHS to: 
1. Ban the retail distribution of highly concentrated caffeine marketed as a dietary 
supplement because it presents a “significant or unreasonable risk of illness or injury” 
or an “imminent hazard to public health.”3 
 
2. Specify limits on the form in which caffeine is sold, including its labeling, serving 
sizes, and potency, to minimize the risk of accidental overdose by all potential users, 
including younger consumers.

II. 
Statement of Grounds 
This petition relates to pure or highly concentrated caffeine, which is currently sold in 
bulk online in a powder form by retailers of dietary supplements.4  This petition does not address 
caffeine sold in energy drinks, energy shots, or other novel retail products, although we applaud 
the FDA’s efforts to understand the potential hazards of these products.5  While we recognize 
that substantial data and analysis will be necessary to forge new policies to ensure the safe use of 
energy drinks and other caffeinated products, CSPI believes that highly concentrated caffeine 
presents a unique, self-evident danger to consumers that justifies an immediate ban and 
corresponding adjustments to FDA’s regulations.   
Pure or highly concentrated caffeine is dangerous due to the possibility of consuming 
unintentionally large quantities.  Just one teaspoon of powder caffeine, which amounts to 
approximately 3 grams, is equivalent to drinking 25 cups of coffee.6  It is so concentrated, in 
fact, that its suggested serving size – generally between 1/32 and 1/16 of a teaspoon – is beyond 
the measurement capabilities of a typical consumer and would require specialized equipment not 
found in a typical kitchen.  Because consumers do not have the ability to measure out a safe 
dose, the risk of unintentional overdose is significant.  We can also envision some youths 
experimenting to see how much caffeine they could consume without realizing the substantial 
risks.  Symptoms of caffeine overdose can include rapid or dangerously erratic heartbeat, 
seizures, and even death.  The dangers of pure, powdered caffeine were tragically illustrated 
earlier this year when an Ohio high school student, Logan Stiner, died after consuming caffeine 
powder that he obtained from a friend who purchased it on the Internet.7  Another young man, a 
24-year-old in Georgia, James Wade Sweatt, also tragically died last summer after ingesting 
caffeine powder and suffering cardiac arrest at his home.  Statements from the parents of Logan 
Stiner and Wade Sweatt are attached to this Petition as Exhibit B. 
FDA specifically acknowledged the danger of pure, powdered caffeine by issuing a 
consumer advisory in 2014.8  While the advisory was a useful first step, we urge FDA to take

a. Description of Product 
Caffeine, or 1,3,7-trimethylxanthine, is a mild central nervous stimulant that occurs 
naturally in coffee beans, cocoa beans, tea leaves, and certain other botanical sources.12  Caffeine 
(whether derived by decaffeination or manufactured synthetically) is also added to many 
beverages, such as energy drinks and colas, and to candies, chewing gum, and other non-
beverage food items.13  In addition to caffeinated foods and beverages, caffeine is also produced, 
sold, and consumed in forms more akin to a dietary supplement.14  For example, “energy shots” 
are a specialized form of energy drink sold in 2-oz. containers as a dietary supplement.15  
Caffeine is also marketed in tablet form as an over-the-counter drug or dietary supplement to 
alleviate fatigue and drowsiness.16   
 
Recently, thanks to the Internet, caffeine in pure or highly concentrated form has become 
more widely available to consumers, allowing consumers to ingest massive quantities nearly 
instantaneously.  Pure or highly concentrated caffeine powder has become popular as a dietary 
supplement, particularly among athletes, to whom it is marketed as performance enhancing.17

b. Caffeine’s Effects on Health 
Caffeine is consumed daily by a majority of Americans.  In the United States, the average 
daily consumption per adult is 300 mg, or roughly the equivalent of three cups of coffee.19  At 
that exposure level, caffeine is generally assumed to be compatible with health; in fact, moderate 
consumption of caffeine (generally defined as under 400 mg per day) may even be beneficial for 
healthy, non-pregnant adults.20  However, FDA has articulated concerns about the considerable 
increase in caffeine exposure over the past half-century.21  Today, many individuals consume 
much more than the 400 mg per day cited as a safe amount for most adults.22  Moreover, the 
nature of caffeine-containing products is changing and the impacts that might have on public 
health are incompletely understood.23  High daily caffeine intake, especially over 500 mg per 
day, is considered a significant health risk, and is linked to anxiety, cardiovascular symptoms, 
and gastrointestinal complaints.24  Caffeine, of course, also causes insomnia.25   
While the full implications of high daily caffeine consumption remain unknown, it is 
undisputed that caffeine is toxic when consumed in large doses.  Overdose may result in 
hypertension, hypotension, tachycardia, vomiting, fever, delusions, hallucinations, seizures, 
arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, coma, and death.26  In children, caffeine toxicity is manifested by 
severe vomiting, tachycardia, and central nervous system agitation.27  Serious adverse effects are

FDA has the authority to regulate dietary supplements under the Dietary Supplement 
Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA).  DSHEA defines “dietary supplement” as a 
“product . . . intended to supplement the diet” that contains a vitamin, mineral, herb, amino acid, 
or dietary substance but is not intended “for use as a conventional food.”37  Under DSHEA and 
the FDCA, FDA may restrict use of a dietary ingredient in a dietary supplement if it is 
determined to be adulterated.38   
Under the law, FDA may invoke two separate grounds for finding pure powder caffeine 
adulterated under DSHEA.  First, FDA may find a product to be adulterated if it can demonstrate 
that the ingredient presents an unreasonable risk of illness or injury under the conditions of use 
recommended in the labeling of the supplement.39  This requires FDA to show that a dietary 
supplement, when taken as recommended, presents a significant or unreasonable risk to 
consumers.40  Second, DSHEA provides authority for the Secretary of Health and Human 
Services to declare any old or new dietary supplement or dietary ingredient to be an illegal 
imminent hazard to public health or safety, and immediately remove the product from the 
market.41  We submit that pure or highly concentrated caffeine powder may be banned under 
either standard.

use and is therefore an adulterated substance under 21 U.S.C. § 
342(f)(1)(A). 
Pure or highly concentrated caffeine powder presents an unreasonable risk of illness or 
injury under the conditions of use recommended in the labeling of the supplement.  DSHEA 
requires evidence of a “significant or unreasonable risk” of illness or injury,42 but the law does

for use in the product’s labeling or, if the labeling is silent, under ordinary conditions of use.44  It 
further found that, “[i]n the absence of a sufficient benefit, the presence of even a relatively small

The standard for “unreasonable risk” is easily met with regard to pure or highly 
concentrated caffeine powder.  It is well established that caffeine in large doses is highly toxic to 
adults and in smaller amounts when it comes to young children.  The inherent problem with 
caffeine powder is that its highly concentrated form makes it extraordinarily difficult for 
consumers to differentiate between a safe dose and a potentially lethal dose – if they are even 
aware that large amounts can be toxic.  Caffeine powder thus presents an “unreasonable risk” 
when used as directed for the simple reason that it is essentially impossible to use as directed: 
just one teaspoon of pure caffeine powder contains the amount of caffeine in 30 cups of coffee.  
The dose of caffeine powder recommended by the labeling of some products is 1/32 to 1/16 of a 
teaspoon – an amount that the typical consumer is not capable of measuring using implements 
available in a typical kitchen.  Because the recommended dose of caffeine powder is difficult to 
administer, this particular form of caffeine substantially heightens the risk of unintentional 
overconsumption and overdose.  In 2014, there were at least two deaths that were apparently 
caused by accidental overdoses of pure caffeine.46  News reports indicate that there have been as 
many as 30 cases of pure caffeine overdoses reported to poison control centers nationally during 
the first nine months of this year.47  How many other overdoses occurred, but were not reported, 
is unknown. 
This risk of unintentional overdose far outweighs any putative benefits of pure or highly 
concentrated caffeine.  Even if moderate caffeine consumption can be beneficial, its benefits are 
easily obtained via safer means, such as coffee or tea.  As a result, the benefits offered by 
caffeine marketed in powder form do not justify its risks.  As FDA has noted, “[i]n the absence 
of a sufficient benefit, the presence of even a relatively small risk of an important adverse health 
effect to a user may be unreasonable.”48  FDA should thus find that powder caffeine’s significant 
risks, when balanced with its minimal benefits, render the product an “unreasonable risk” under 
DSHEA.    
This conclusion is supported by, and is in fact far simpler than, FDA’s one previous 
finding of “unreasonable risk” under the statute, when it concluded that dietary supplements 
containing ephedrine alkaloids were adulterated.49  In that case, FDA banned the use of 
ephedrine alkaloids in all dietary supplements; as a result, any purported benefits of ephedrine 
would not be readily available from other sources.  That required FDA to make a much higher 
showing of ephedrine’s risks in order to demonstrate that they outweighed its benefits.50  By 
contrast, here, CSPI merely proposes that one especially dangerous and totally unnecessary form 
of caffeine be declared adulterated and removed from the market.  We do not argue that caffeine 
should be banned in all forms, nor that it is unsafe when used in moderation by healthy, non-

Because the risks and harms of caffeine powder far outweigh any potential benefits, FDA has the

While it is axiomatic that the dose makes the poison, when caffeine is sold in pure or 
highly concentrated form, the consumer has a very limited ability to administer a safe dose.  That 
renders the substance unavoidably poisonous.  Thus, FDA should find that caffeine powder, due 
to its form and bulk packaging, inherently poses an unreasonable risk to consumers, even if low 
doses of caffeine are safe.  Pure or highly concentrated caffeine should therefore be declared an 
adulterated substance and banned under 21 U.S.C. § 342(f)(1)(A) for posing a significant and

ii. The Secretary of Health and Human Services should declare that pure 
or highly concentrated caffeine poses an imminent hazard to public 
health or safety and is therefore an adulterated substance under 21 
U.S.C. § 342(f)(1)(C). 
DSHEA also permits the Secretary of Health and Human Services to declare pure or 
highly concentrated caffeine to be an illegal imminent hazard to public health or safety.52  
According to FDA regulations, an “imminent hazard” exists where the evidence is “sufficient to 
show that a product or practice, posing a significant threat of danger to health, creates a public 
health situation (1) that should be corrected immediately to prevent injury and (2) that should not 
be permitted to continue while a hearing or other formal proceeding is being held.”53  Once the 
Secretary declares a supplement to be an imminent hazard, the substance is immediately banned, 
and administrative proceedings are automatically instituted to determine whether to affirm or 
withdraw the ban.   
While this provision of DSHEA has not been exercised to date, we believe that pure or 
highly concentrated caffeine powder presents an appropriate instance for HHS to employ this 
statutory authority.  The danger of caffeine powder, as a result of caffeine’s toxicity and the 
inherent danger of the concentrated form, is clear.  That is reflected by reports of adverse events 
that have occurred as pure caffeine has become more readily available to consumers.  However, 
the data on the dangers of pure or highly concentrated caffeine are (fortunately) limited because 
the product has only been marketed and monitored recently.  To assess the safety of dietary 
supplements, FDA typically reviews adverse event reports that are submitted in accordance with

III. 
Conclusion and Requested Actions 
 
Because pure or highly concentrated caffeine has only recently become widely available 
to consumers, the full extent of its dangers have yet to be discovered.  FDA has the opportunity 
to get in front of a problem that has the potential to grow exponentially, and to address its risks 
before they can be fully realized.  FDA should act now to ban direct sales of caffeine powder 
because even when used as directed, it presents an unreasonable risk to consumers, and the

this product, on the grounds that  the manufacturer has not demonstrated reasonable assurance 
that the device is safe and effective under its current conditions of use, and there is a reasonable

I. 
Actions Requested 
 
We request that the FDA Commissioner, pursuant to Sections 515 and 518 of the Federal Food, 
Drug, and Cosmetic Act and 21 C.F.R. Parts 810 and 814: 
 
(1) Withdraw the premarket approval of Seprafilm (P950034); and 
  
(2) Initiate a mandatory recall of all remaining unused Seprafilm devices.

II. 
Statement of Grounds 
 
a. Background on the Device and Regulatory Actions 
 
Seprafilm is an anti-adhesion barrier device used in abdominal and pelvic surgical procedures to 
prevent the formation of postoperative adhesions (fibrous bands that form between tissues and 
organs). The device is a bioresorbable membrane composed of sodium hyaluronate and 
carboxymethylcellulose, which adheres to tissue surfaces and hydrates to form a viscous gel 
coating in one to two days.1 Seprafilm is typically resorbed from the application site within seven 
days and cleared from the body within 28 days.2 It has been postulated that Seprafilm is able to 
reduce postoperative adhesions by acting as a physical/mechanical barrier, separating adjacent 
serosal tissues during the critical stages of wound repair.3,4 However, its precise mechanism of 
action remains unclear.5,6  
The FDA approved the Seprafilm premarket approval (PMA) application on August 12, 1996. 
The device is indicated for use in patients undergoing abdominal or pelvic laparotomy as an 
adjunct intended to reduce the incidence, extent, and severity of postoperative adhesions between 
the abdominal wall and the underlying viscera, and between the uterus and surrounding 
structures.7 At the time of approval, the FDA ordered the product’s sponsor, Genzyme, to 
conduct a postmarket safety study, later dubbed SF97-0601 (Study 601), to address the agency’s 
concerns with a large number of serious adverse events detected in the Seprafilm group during 
one of the two pivotal efficacy studies that Genzyme submitted in support of the PMA 
application. 
Genzyme conducted Study 601 and subsequently filed two PMA supplements, Supplement 26 
(August 2003)8 and Supplement 27 (December 2004),9 requesting updates to the Seprafilm 
package insert regarding the product’s safety and effectiveness. As part of those updates, 
Genzyme asked that the label be updated to indicate that Seprafilm was effective at reducing the 
incidence of small bowel obstruction requiring re-operation.10,11 The FDA reviewers raised 
concerns about the requested efficacy claim, which the company subsequently withdrew.12 But

b. FDA Regulatory Authority 
 
The FDA may issue an order withdrawing a PMA if the agency determines that any of the 
grounds under Section 515(e)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act applies.13 One of 
these grounds is a conclusion, 
on the basis of new information before [the FDA] with respect to [a] device, evaluated 
together with the evidence available to [the FDA] when the application was approved, 
that there is a lack of a showing of reasonable assurance that the device is safe or 
effective under the conditions of use prescribed, recommended, or suggested in the 
labeling thereof.14 
The FDA may also issue a mandatory recall under Section 518(e) of the FDCA, upon finding “a 
reasonable probability that a device intended for human use would cause serious, adverse health 
consequences or death.”15
c. Three Major Efficacy Studies Failed to Show Clinically Meaningful 
Benefits and Raised Serious Safety Concerns 
 
Genzyme submitted to the FDA data from three randomized, controlled clinical trials — 
including two that were conducted prior to approval of the original PMA application — to 
support the efficacy claims in the Seprafilm label. Despite elaborate attempts by the company to 
present the data from these studies in a favorable light, the studies failed to demonstrate 
effectiveness at achieving a clinically meaningful endpoint and, instead, raised serious safety 
concerns. 
The first two efficacy trials were submitted as part of the original Seprafilm PMA application: 
HF92-0901 (Study 901), a randomized, controlled trial assessing the safety and effectiveness of 
Seprafilm for preventing postoperative adhesion formation following abdominal surgery in 183 
subjects, and HF92-0902 (Study 902), a randomized, controlled trial assessing the safety and 
effectiveness of Seprafilm for preventing postoperative adhesion formation following uterine 
myomectomy in 127 subjects.16 These studies were published in medical journals by Becker et 
al. (1996) and Diamond (1996), respectively.17,18

The third trial was the mandatory postmarket study ordered by the FDA at the time of approval,

These studies all were plagued by a host of serious issues, including major protocol violations at 
one of the key trial sites in Study 901 and several highly questionable re-analyses of the data 
from Study 601. Most importantly, none of these three studies submitted in support of the 
Seprafilm PMA application established the product’s efficacy in improving any important 
clinically meaningful outcomes, and two of the studies raised serious safety concerns that have 
not been adequately addressed by the product’s sponsor. 
i. Studies 902 and 901 
Studies 902 and 901, the two pivotal clinical trials submitted to support effectiveness in the 
original Seprafilm PMA application, were not designed to assess Seprafilm’s effectiveness at 
improving important clinically meaningful outcomes such as bowel obstruction, pain, 
complications during re-operation, or infertility. Instead, the two trials assessed the incidence, 
extent, and severity of postoperative adhesions, based on the hypothesis that improvements in 
these surrogate endpoints could, theoretically, have positive clinical implications.  
Study 902 was a randomized, controlled trial enrolling 127 subjects undergoing gynecologic 
surgery.21 The study showed that rate and severity of adhesion, evaluated during second-look 
laparoscopy, were lower in the Seprafilm-treated group, with comparable rates of adverse events 
between groups.22 However, the study did not assess clinically meaningful outcomes. 
Study 901 was a randomized, control trial enrolling 183 subjects undergoing abdominal 
surgery.23 In Study 901, while the overall rates of adverse events were similar in Seprafilm- and 
control-group subjects (90% versus 94%, respectively), subjects assigned to the Seprafilm group 
experienced a higher rate of serious adverse events than control subjects, a difference which 
approached statistical significance (42% versus 24%, respectively; p = 0.074).24 Of note, rates of 
abscesses and pulmonary emboli were higher among Seprafilm-treated subjects compared to 
control subjects. Seven of 91 subjects (8%) in the Seprafilm group and two of 92 subjects (2%) 
in the control group developed abscesses (p = 0.10), and four subjects (4%) in the Seprafilm

Rather than accept these results — which were potentially disastrous with respect to the

d. Additional Data From Prospective Randomized Clinical Trials 
Data from additional prospective, randomized, controlled trials evaluating the safety and efficacy 
of Seprafilm do not change the overall risk-benefit profile of the device or establish reasonable 
assurance that the device is safe and effective.  
We note at the outset that publication bias could have strongly influenced the results of these 
studies in favor of showing a benefit from Seprafilm. For example, we identified one 
unpublished prospective study of 1,885 patients indicating that the use of Seprafilm was 
associated with “a higher incidence of pelvic sepsis and wound infection.”48 This study was 
presented as an abstract at an annual conference of the American Society of Colon and Rectal 
Surgeons, but never published in a peer-reviewed journal.  
A Cochrane analysis published in 2009 found too few studies of Seprafilm to develop a funnel 
plot assessing publication bias.49 Additional unpublished studies showing negative results similar 
to the study described above may be missing from the literature.

CITIZEN PETITION 
 
This citizen petition is submitted on behalf of Supernus Pharmaceuticals, Inc. 
(“Supernus”) pursuant to Section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (“FDCA”), 
21 U.S.C. § 355, and 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 to request that the Food and Drug Administration 
(“FDA”) require specific bioequivalence parameters to govern the review and approval of any 
product that is the subject of an abbreviated new drug application (“ANDA”) under Section 
505(j) of the FDCA, 21 U.S.C. § 355(j), where the reference listed drug (“RLD”) is OXTELLAR 
XR® (oxcarbazepine).    
 
Supernus is the New Drug Application (“NDA”) holder for OXTELLAR XR, a novel 
once-daily extended-release antiepileptic drug approved for use as an adjunctive therapy in the 
treatment of partial seizures in adults and children six years of age and older.  In July 2014, FDA 
issued draft guidance containing recommendations for a study to evaluate the bioequivalence of 
oxcarbazepine extended-release tablets where OXTELLAR XR is the RLD for that study 
(hereinafter “Draft Guidance”).1  As described more fully herein, the traditional bioequivalence 
parameters recommended by the Draft Guidance are inadequate to assure the safety and 
effectiveness of any generic version of OXTELLAR XR.  Indeed, reliance solely on these 
metrics may not detect potentially significant and clinically meaningful differences between the 
pharmacokinetic (“PK”) profiles of OXTELLAR XR and proposed generic products.  This 
would be especially problematic if OXTELLAR XR and generic products with different release 
properties are switched, resulting in patients undergoing periods with inadequate oxcarbazepine 
release that could result in decreased efficacy and breakthrough seizures, and periods of 
increased oxcarbazepine release that could result in dose-limiting adverse events. 
                                                 
1  See FDA, Draft Guidance on Oxcarbazepine (July 2014) [hereinafter “Oxcarbazepine Draft Guidance”], available 
at http://www.fda.gov/downloads/Drugs/GuidanceComplianceRegulatoryInformation/Guidances/UCM406335.pdf.   
 
 
-2- 
 
 
I. 
ACTIONS REQUESTED 
 
Supernus requests that FDA include the following criteria as part of the bioequivalence 
demonstration that is required for any generic extended-release oxcarbazepine product for which 
OXTELLAR XR is the RLD: 
 
1. Applicants should measure partial area under the curve (“pAUC”) at 0-Tmax and Tmax-t, in 
addition to the traditional bioequivalence metrics of AUC0-t, AUC0-∞, and Cmax. 
2. Applicants should meet acceptance criteria for the 90% confidence interval for Cmax, 
AUC, and pAUC measures of 90%-125%.   
II. 
STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
A. 
Background 
1. 
Epilepsy 
Epilepsy is a chronic neurological condition affecting the nervous system and causing 
seizures.2  According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, approximately 5.1 
million people in the United States have had a diagnosis of epilepsy or seizure disorder in the 
past, with roughly 2.9 million currently active cases.3  The total indirect and direct cost of 
epilepsy in the United States is estimated to be as high as $15.5 billion annually.4 
The clinical presentation of epilepsy is different from person to person, and seizures may 
vary in duration, frequency, and type.5  While many people with epilepsy can lead full, active 
lives, for many patients with epilepsy, the impact on their lives is significant.  The occurrence of 
seizures is unpredictable and often dangerous, with a high risk of injury, hospitalization, and 
mortality.6  On top of the devastating physical consequences of seizures, for many people with 
epilepsy their condition results in unemployment, underemployment, or an inability to live 
alone.7  In addition, many states will not issue a driver’s license to an individual with epilepsy 
unless the person can document that they have been seizure-free for a specific amount of time, 
where the waiting period can vary from several months to several years.8 
                                                 
2 Nat’l Inst. of Health (NIH), The Epilepsies and Seizures: Hope Through Research, 
http://www.ninds.nih.gov/disorders/epilepsy/detail_epilepsy.htm (last visited June 29, 2015) (Exh. 1). 
3 Ctrs. for Disease Control & Prevention (CDC), Epilepsy Fast Facts, http://www.cdc.gov/epilepsy/basics/fast-
facts.htm (last visited June 29, 2015) (Exh. 2). 
4 Id. 
5 NIH, supra note 2.  
6 See M. P. Kerr, The Impact of Epilepsy on Patients’ Lives, 194 Acta Neurol. Scand. Suppl. 1, 1–2 (2012) (Exh. 3). 
7 Inst. of Med. (IOM), Epilepsy Across the Spectrum: Promoting Health and Understanding 1–2 (Mary Jane 
England et al. eds., 2012) (Exh. 4).  
8 NIH, supra note 2. 
 
 
-3- 
 
Fortunately, epilepsy can often be controlled with medication. Antiepileptic drugs 
(“AEDs”) are effective for more than half of the people diagnosed with epilepsy.9  The goal of 
treatment with AEDs is to achieve freedom from seizures with minimal side effects.  The 
threshold serum concentration of AEDs at which seizure control is achieved, however, varies 
from patient to patient.10  In order to reach an effective serum concentration for each patient, 
clinicians must carefully titrate patients’ doses of AEDs until they pass this threshold and 
achieve seizure control.11 
Once a patient has been titrated to an effective dose, it is crucial that they maintain a 
sufficient serum AED concentration to remain seizure free.  Even a small reduction in serum 
concentration may result in a “breakthrough” seizure with devastating consequences.12  In some 
patients, even a single breakthrough seizure can result in status epilepticus, a condition of 
prolonged seizure with a mortality rate estimated to be as high as 20%.13  In addition, the relative 
risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (“SUDEP”), a term used to describe the sudden and 
unexplained death of someone with epilepsy who was otherwise healthy, is increased as much as 
23 times once seizure control is lost and a patient experiences even a single breakthrough 
seizure.14  Further, if a breakthrough seizure occurs unexpectedly while a patient is driving, this 
could easily result in death or injury to the patient or bystanders.  Even in cases where the 
consequences of breakthrough seizures are less dire, breakthrough seizures may still result in 
physical injury or significant reduction in quality of life, such as loss of driver’s license, loss of 
employment, depression, and social stigmatization.15 
                                                 
9 CDC, Epilepsy Frequently Asked Questions, http://www.cdc.gov/epilepsy/basics/faq.htm (last visited June 29, 
2015) (Exh. 5). 
10See Erik K. St. Louis, Minimizing AED Adverse Effects: Improving Quality of Life in the Interictal State in 
Epilepsy Care, 7 Current Neuropharmacology 106, 111 (2009) (“AED dosing must be individualized to achieve 
optimal results. The usual strategy is to titrate the AED toward a target dose that has proven effective for most 
individuals in pivotal clinical studies and in subsequent clinical experience. Dose adjustment can then be made in 
the event of adverse drug reactions or recurrent seizures.”) (Exh. 6); see also Citizen Petition of UCB, Inc., Docket 
No. FDA-2006-P-0405, 5–7 (Oct. 3, 2006), available at http://www.regulations.gov/#!documentDetail;D=FDA-
2006-P-0461-0011 (Exh. 7).

http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2012/202810s000lbl.pdf (describing the process by which

(Exh. 10).

http://www.epilepsy.com/learn/impact/seizure-emergencies (Exh. 11); NIH, supra note 2. 
14 See Torbjörn Tomson et al., Sudden Unexpected Death in Epilepsy: A Review of Incidence and Risk Factors, 46 
(Suppl. 11) Epilepsia 54, 58 (2005) (reporting results of a study demonstrating a twenty-three times higher rate of 
SUDEP in epilepsy patients who experienced at least one seizure during the year of observation compared to 
patients who remained seizure free) (Exh. 12); Cyndi Wright et al., Epilepsy Foundation, SUDEP, (Aug. 2013), 
http://www.epilepsy.com/learn/impact/mortality/sudep (“If seizures are uncontrolled the risk of SUDEP increases to 
more than 1 out of 150.”) (Exh. 13). 
15 See Kerr, supra note 6, at 1–2; IOM, supra note 7, at 1–2; NIH, supra note 2; Citizen Petition of UCB, Inc., supra 
note 10, at 5–7.   
 
 
-4- 
 
2. 
OXTELLAR XR 
On October 19, 2012, FDA approved an NDA authorizing Supernus to market 
OXTELLAR XR as an adjunctive therapy in the treatment of partial seizures in patients six years 
of age and older.  OXTELLAR XR is a novel once-daily extended-release formulation of the 
AED oxcarbazepine.  Prior to the approval of OXTELLAR XR, oxcarbazepine had only been 
approved in the United States as an immediate-release formulation, requiring twice-daily 
administration.16   
While immediate-release formulations of oxcarbazepine are effective in reducing 
seizures, the higher daily doses of these products necessary for seizure control in some patients 
often result in significant, treatment-limiting side effects.  As noted in the FDA-approved 
labeling for immediate-release oxcarbazepine (TRILEPTAL), “daily doses above 1200 mg/day 
show somewhat greater effectiveness in controlled trials, but most patients were not able to 
tolerate the 2400 mg/ day dose, primarily because of CNS effects.”17  Indeed, in the clinical trial 
of that drug, over 65% of patients assigned to the 2400 mg per day arm discontinued due to 
adverse events.18  
 
Therefore, in addition to seeking improved adherence through once-daily dosing, part of 
the goal in developing OXTELLAR XR as an extended-release formulation of oxcarbazepine 
was to yield a “flatter” PK profile for improved tolerability at the 2400 mg dose required for 
efficacy in some patients.19  OXTELLAR XR ultimately proved successful in this regard.  In 
fact, FDA acknowledged this success in its review of the OXTELLAR XR NDA, stating, “[I]t is 
clear that, in general, the incidence of common adverse events is substantially lower with the ER 
as compared to the IR formulation.”20  This improved tolerability with OXTELLAR XR is born 
out in a significantly lower discontinuation rate among patients receiving 2400 mg daily doses in 
the OXTELLAR XR clinical study (30% as compared to 65% in the clinical trial of immediate-
release oxcarbazepine).21   
                                                 
16 Novartis Pharm. Corp., TRILEPTAL U.S. Prescribing Information § 2 (2014), available at 
http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2014/021014s033,021285s027lbl.pdf (Exh. 14). 
17 Id. at § 2.1. 
18 Id. at § 14.2. 
19 FDA, Application Number: 202810Orig1s000: Clinical Pharmacology and Biopharmaceutics Review(s), 7 (Feb. 
16, 2012) [hereinafter “OXTELLAR XR Clinical Pharmacology Review”], available at 
http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2012/202810Orig1s000ClinPharmR.pdf (“The rationale for the 
development of OXC-ER included targeting an improved treatment adherence to a once daily regimen. Moreover,

profile with OXTELLAR XR is characterized by 10-monohydroxy metabolite (“MHD”) exposures (AUC and 
Cmax) about nineteen percent lower than with TRILEPTAL and MHD trough concentrations (Cmin) about sixteen 
percent lower than TRILEPTAL. MHD is the active metabolite responsible for the clinical effects of oxcarbazepine. 
OXTELLAR XR U.S. Prescribing Information, supra note 11, at § 12.3. 
20 FDA, Application Number: 202810Orig1s000: Summary Review, 7 (Oct. 13, 2012), available at 
http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2012/202810Orig1s000SumR.pdf (Exh. 16). 
21 FDA, Application Number: 202810Orig1s000: Medical Review(s), 47 (Feb. 24, 2012) [hereinafter “OXTELLAR 
XR Medical Review”], http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2012/202810Orig1s000MedR.pdf (Exh. 
17); TRILEPTAL U.S. Prescribing Information, supra note 16, at §14.2. 
 
 
-5- 
 
 
OXTELLAR XR is available in dosage strengths of 150 mg, 300 mg, and 600 mg 
extended-release tablets, allowing for careful dose titration.  The recommended daily dose for 
adults is 1200 mg to 2400 mg, given once per day.  Adults are instructed to initiate with a dose of 
600 mg once per day, where 600 mg per day dose increases can be made at weekly intervals to 
achieve the recommended daily dose.22  
B. 
Statutory And Regulatory Framework Governing Approval Of Generic 
Drugs 
Under Section 505(j) of the FDCA, a generic applicant need not conduct human trials to 
demonstrate that its proposed product is safe and effective.  Rather, through the filing of an 
ANDA, the manufacturer may rely on FDA’s findings of safety and effectiveness for the RLD.  
To rely on those findings, however, the generic drug manufacturer must demonstrate that its 
proposed product is both pharmaceutically equivalent and bioequivalent to the RLD.23  Indeed, if 
the proposed product cannot make this showing (or otherwise qualify for a suitability petition), 
then there would be no way to ensure that FDA’s findings of safety and efficacy for the RLD are 
applicable to the generic drug product. 
Strict compliance with the requirements for bioequivalence and pharmaceutical 
equivalence is critical because, upon approval of an ANDA, FDA designates the generic product 
as “therapeutically equivalent” to the RLD and assigns an “A” rating to that product in its 
publication, Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations (the “Orange 
Book”).24  FDA, physicians, and pharmacists interpret an “A” rating to mean that a generic drug 
is fully substitutable for the RLD.  By operation of certain state laws and numerous health 
insurance programs, FDA’s designation of an “A” rating often results in substitution of the 
generic drug for the RLD without the knowledge or consent of either the prescribing physician or 
patient.25 
 
Before FDA may approve an ANDA and assign an “A” rating to a proposed generic 
product, FDA must determine that, among other things, the product is bioequivalent to the RLD.   
Under the FDCA, a generic drug is considered bioequivalent to the listed drug if “the rate and 
extent of absorption of the drug do not show a significant difference from the rate and extent of 
the listed drug when administered at the same molar dose of the therapeutic ingredient under

“Orange Book”], available at 
http://www.fda.gov/downloads/Drugs/DevelopmentApprovalProcess/UCM071436.pdf.  
25 One review found that thirty-one states, along with the District of Columbia, require reference to the Orange Book 
for the selection of generic drugs that may be legally substituted for brand-name products. Those states are Alabama, 
Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indian, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, 
Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, 
Pennsylvania, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Wisconsin, Wyoming, and West Virginia.

http://pharmacistsletter.therapeuticresearch.com/pl/ArticleDD.aspx?nidchk=1&cs=&s=PL&pt=2&segment=1186&d
d=220901 (Exh. 18). 
 
 
-6- 
 
similar experimental conditions in either a single dose or multiple doses.”26  In its regulations 
implementing these statutory provisions, FDA directs all ANDA applicants to “conduct 
bioavailability and bioequivalence testing using the most accurate, sensitive, and reproducible 
approach available” among certain methodologies set forth in the regulations.27 
 
To establish bioequivalence of systemically absorbed drugs, FDA generally recommends 
that applicants conduct single dose, crossover or parallel group PK studies, measuring 
concentrations of the generic and reference drugs in the blood or plasma as a function of time.28  
These data are plotted on a curve where time is represented on the x-axis and concentration on 
the y-axis.  Applicants then rely upon certain parameters to compare the drug concentration vs. 
time “curve” or PK profile.  For most products, these parameters typically include the maximum 
concentration (Cmax) and the area under the curve (AUC), both from dosing until the last 
measured time point (AUC0-t) and extrapolated to infinity (AUC0-∞).  Cmax is believed to reflect 
the rate of the drug’s absorption into the systemic circulation, while AUC0-t and AUC0-∞ are 
believed to reflect the extent of the drug’s absorption.29   
In most cases, FDA requires the generic applicant to report 90% confidence intervals for 
the ratios of the test and reference products (i.e., the proposed generic and the RLD, respectively) 
for Cmax, AUC0-t, and AUC0-∞.  To be considered bioequivalent to the RLD, the 90% confidence 
interval for the proposed generic must fall entirely within the boundaries of 80% and 125% of 
the reference drug.30 
 
C. 
Cmax And AUC Are Insufficient To Capture Potentially Significant 
Differences In The PK Profiles Of Generic Extended-Release Oxcarbazepine 
Products 
1. 
OXTELLAR XR Is Characterized By Complex Chemical And 
Pharmacokinetic Properties 
OXTELLAR XR is characterized by low water solubility and low intra-subject variability 
in PK parameters, qualities that increase the likelihood that formulation differences in generic 
products will result in therapeutic differences in the clinical context even if they are considered 
bioequivalent according to FDA’s traditional bioequivalence metrics.31   
                                                 
26 See 21 U.S.C. § 355(j)(8)(B)(i). The FDA has indicated that two drug products will be considered bioequivalent if 
they “display comparable bioavailability when studied under similar experimental conditions.” Orange Book, supra 
note 24, at viii.  Bioavailability is, in turn, defined as “the rate and extent to which the active drug ingredient or 
therapeutic ingredient is absorbed from a drug product and becomes available at the site of the drug action.”  21 
U.S.C. § 355(j)(8)(A).  
27 21 C.F.R. § 320.24(a).  
28 21 C.F.R. § 320.24(b)(1)(i).  
29 See 21 C.F.R. § 320.26(c); FDA, Draft Guidance for Industry: Bioavailability and Bioequivalence Studies 
Submitted in NDAs or INDs—General Considerations (Mar. 2014), available at 
http://www.fda.gov/downloads/drugs/guidancecomplianceregulatoryinformation/guidances/ucm389370.pdf.  
30 Orange Book, supra note 24, at ix. 
31 See P. Crawford et al., Are There Potential Problems with Generic Substitution of Antiepileptic Drugs? A Review 
of Issues, 15 Seizure 165, 167–68, 170 (2006) (describing problems with generic substitution of drugs with low 
water solubility) (Exh. 19); Statement of Dr. Lawrence Yu, Deputy Dir. for Sci. & Chemistry, Office of Generic 
 
 
-7- 
 
 
As described in the FDA-approved labeling for OXTELLAR XR, oxcarbazepine is 
characterized by low water solubility.  Specifically, the label provides that “[i]n aqueous media 
over pH range 1 to 8, oxcarbazepine is practically insoluble and its solubility is 40 mg/L (0.04 
g/L) at pH 7.0, 25°C.”32   
 
OXTELLAR XR also exhibits low within subject variability in PK.  In clinical PK study 
804P104, the intra-subject coefficients of variation (“CV”) for OXTELLAR XR’s active 
metabolite, 10-monohydroxy derivative (“MHD”), were 11.01 for Cmax, 11.72 for AUC0-t, and 
12.06 for AUC0-∞.33 
 
2. 
OXTELLAR XR Exhibits A Strong Concentration-Response 
Relationship And Dose-Dependent Adverse Events 
Coupled with these chemical and pharmacokinetic properties that increase the likelihood 
that generic extended-release oxcarbazepine products may have different PK profiles from 
OXTELLAR XR, even if they meet FDA’s traditional bioequivalence criteria, oxcarbazepine is 
also characterized by a strong concentration-response relationship and dose-dependent adverse 
events.  An MHD concentration that is too low may lead to inadequate seizure control and 
breakthrough seizures, and an MHD concentration that is too high may lead to dose-limiting 
adverse events.  As a result, differences in the PK profile of a generic version of OXTELLAR 
XR may have a significant clinical impact. 
 
FDA recognized this strong concentration-response relationship in its review of the 
OXTELLAR NDA, stating, “A concentration-response relationship was observed with 
percentage reduction in seizure frequency as a function of MHD Cmin concentrations.”34  FDA 
further concluded that to achieve clinical response, “‘optimal’ trough plasma concentrations 
[should be] above 14 mg/L.”35  
 
In addition, adverse events with OXTELLAR XR are linked to dose, peak plasma 
concentration, and rate of absorption.  Common adverse events experienced with OXTELLAR 
XR include dizziness, somnolence, headache, balance disorder, tremor, vomiting, diplopia, 
asthenia, and fatigue.36  These adverse events are linked to the dose, peak plasma concentration,

increases in the presence of sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS).”).

34 Id. at 2. 
35 Id. at 58.
