and live customer and technical support.  This package of products and services is called 
INOMAX Total Care®.13  
 
Since 2000 INOMAX Total Care® has been refined to further enhance patient safety.  
These changes reflect the company’s and its customers’ experiences with INOMAX Total Care® 
as well as medical advancements in the care of neonates with hypoxic respiratory failure.  For 
example, it is now well understood that abrupt discontinuation or interruption of nitric oxide 
therapy can lead to worsening oxygenation and increasing pulmonary artery pressure, i.e., 
rebound pulmonary hypertension syndrome, which can be fatal.  Accordingly, several elements 
of INOMAX Total Care® are intended to reduce the risk of abrupt discontinuation or interruption 
of therapy.

the following elements necessary to assure the safe and effective use of INOMAX:   
 
• INOMAX (nitric oxide) for inhalation; 
• An integrated NODS, the INOmax DSIR Plus, for the safe and effective delivery of 
INOMAX, which has been carefully validated as compatible for use with all ventilation 
modalities, as well as all patient ranges (neonate, pediatric, or adult) available on sixty-

• Additional NODS.  All customers, even the smallest hospitals, are provided with at least 
two INOmax DSIR Plus units to assure an available primary system backup; 
• Emergency delivery of INOMAX, NODS, and support components, typically available 
within four to six hours; 
• Comprehensive periodic training on the safe and effective use of the delivery system 
provided by a team of expert clinicians/technicians, including web-based training and 
live, in-hospital in-service training for all shifts of healthcare professionals that will use 
INOMAX and the NODS;    
• Multi-lingual customer support for technical and general customer matters, operating 24 
hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year; 
• An INOblender®, a state of the art transport delivery system;

The undersigned, on behalf of Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals (“Mallinckrodt”), submits 
this Citizen Petition pursuant to 21 C.F.R. Parts 3, 10, 314, 800, and 807 and Sections 210, 503, 
505, and 510 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (“FDCA”), 21 U.S.C. §§ 321, 353, 
355, 360.  Mallinckrodt’s affiliate, Mallinckrodt Hospital Products IP Limited, is the holder of 
NDA 20845 for INOMAX® (nitric oxide) 800 ppm for inhalation, as well as 510(k) clearances 
for the specialized delivery system required to administer INOMAX to patients, called the 
INOmax DSIR® Plus. 
 
The undersigned previously submitted a Citizen Petition dated June 30, 2016, Docket No. 
FDA-2016-P-1955, which addressed similar issues and requested similar actions as the present 
petition.  Mallinckrodt’s June 30th petition (“Previous Petition”) was the subject of a non-
substantive denial on November 23, 2016, because no generic applications were otherwise ready 
for approval at the time the Agency’s response to the petition was due pursuant to the deadlines 
imposed in Section 505(q) of the FDCA, 21 U.S.C. § 355(q).  The Agency’s November 23, 2016 
response explains that the Agency is “denying without comment [Mallinckrodt’s] requests on the 
requirements for approval, accepting for review, or appropriate Orange Book listing for any 
505(b)(2) NDA or ANDA referencing INOMAX.”1  Because FDA has not yet taken a 
substantive position on the merits of Mallinckrodt’s requests, Mallinckrodt submits the present 
petition to assure those requests remain pending before the Agency as it considers the first 
application to market a generic version of INOMAX.  The current Petition also updates the

See FDA Response, Docket No. FDA-2016-P-1955 (Nov. 23, 2016), available at:

record with Mallinckrodt’s responses to comments submitted on the Previous Petition on behalf

Introduction 
 
INOMAX is approved for use in the treatment of newborn children (neonates) greater 
than 34 weeks gestational age suffering from hypoxic respiratory failure.  Newborns with this 
form of respiratory failure do not transfer enough oxygen into their blood, are unable to breathe 
on their own, and have high blood pressure in the blood vessels of their lungs, i.e., pulmonary 
hypertension.  These patients are critically ill, almost universally requiring ventilatory support 
and other life sustaining therapies.  INOMAX is a vasodilator that, when inhaled, specifically 
relaxes the blood vessels surrounding the alveoli in the lungs of the newborn, which improves 
blood flow to the lungs, allowing more oxygen to enter the blood stream, and reduces the need 
for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.  
 
The safe and effective use of inhaled nitric oxide is inextricably linked to the device 
through which it is administered to patients.  As described in further detail below, administration 
of INOMAX involves a complex and multi-faceted interaction among the drug product 
INOMAX, a specialized, highly sophisticated 510(k)-cleared delivery system called the INOmax 
DSIR Plus, and a breathing or ventilation system.  Successful inhaled nitric oxide therapy requires 
seamless interaction of these three modalities within the neonatal intensive care (“NICU”) 
environment.  In 2010 the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development convened 
a panel of experts to discuss the general topic of NICU-related errors.  The article summarizing 
the workshop succinctly explains the setting in which INOMAX is used and the unique 
challenges presented by that setting:   
 
Patients in the NICU are very small and fragile, many with immature organ 
systems, and superimposed serious illness. Such infants are likely to receive 
complex care, including a large number of medications, and/or invasive 
procedures for diagnosis and treatment over an extended hospitalization. . . . . 
These increase the potential for errors and add additional demands for a higher 
threshold for device safety and efficacy, exemplifying the need for error-free 
devices and instruments. Given the narrow margin of safety, the patients are also 
more likely to suffer from harmful consequences of errors sooner. Because of 
their unique vulnerability, even minor errors can lead to devastating short and 
long-term consequences. In large general hospitals, patient safety efforts are likely 
to be targeted toward adult patients or treatment units, with little appreciation for 
the unique needs of the NICUs and their patients.3

1955-0007 (“Praxair Comment”) and the submission on behalf of Air Liquide/Airgas is available at: 
https://www.regulations.gov/document?D=FDA-2016-P-1955-0008 (“Air Liquide/Airgas Comment”). 
 
3

Educational Opportunities, Pediatr Res. 2011 July; 70(1): 109–115. doi:10.1038/pr.2011.334, at p. 5,

Since approval of INOMAX and the associated delivery system in December 1999, and 
January 2000, respectively, Mallinckrodt has worked closely with its hospital customers to refine 
and optimize the safe and effective use of INOMAX to treat these fragile NICU patients.  This 
feedback has enabled Mallinckrodt to respond to the significant changes in the means and 
methods of safely delivering nitric oxide, as well as the overall practice of medicine in the NICU.  
Mallinckrodt has sought to translate the experience of is customers, and the information learned 
through pharmacovigilance activities, into delivery device improvements to enhance the safe and 
effective administration of nitric oxide.  The INOmax DSIR Plus platform is the latest generation 
nitric oxide delivery system designed from user feedback and quality considerations to best 
enhance patient safety. 
 
Mallinckrodt submits this Petition to assure that follow-on drug products citing 
INOMAX as the reference listed drug incorporate the features necessary for the safe and 
effective administration of inhaled nitric oxide.  This necessitates not only the customary Agency 
review of the quality of the proposed drug product, but also careful evaluation of the design and 
operation of the associated delivery system to assure it is equivalent to the INOmax DSIR Plus 
delivery system used for INOMAX, and includes the same critical safety features.     
 
INOMAX is stored as a gas mixture of nitric oxide and nitrogen in an aluminum cylinder.  
In order for the gas to be administered to patients, the cylinder is attached to a high pressure 
regulator, which is then attached to the INOmax DSIR Plus.  In turn, the INOmax DSIR Plus is 
attached to the ventilator via an injector module placed between the ventilator inspiratory outlet 
and the humidifier.  To ensure safety, upon the initiation of therapy, the INOmax DSIR Plus first 
communicates wirelessly with the INOMAX cylinder to confirm that the attached cylinder is the 
correct concentration, a cylinder of INOMAX and not another gas cylinder, and that the drug is 
within expiration date.  Based on the ventilator flow, the INOMAX cylinder concentration, and 
the INOMAX dose set by the user, the INOmax DSIR Plus delivers INOMAX into the ventilator 
circuit via the injector module where it mixes with the breathing circuit gas flow to achieve the 
set dose. When used with one of the sixty-four ventilators and breathing systems that 
Mallinckrodt has carefully validated as compatible with the INOmax DSIR Plus, the delivery 
system operates to deliver a constant dose of INOMAX to the patient, as set by the user, 
regardless of the ventilator flow pattern or breath rate.  Certain breathing systems and ventilators 
are not compatible with the INOmax DSIR Plus and these systems are not appropriate for use on 
patients receiving INOMAX therapy, due to the risk of under- or over-dosing. 
 
A number of steps must be undertaken to assure the safe delivery of INOMAX therapy.  
Prior to initiating INOMAX therapy, the user must properly establish the connections between 
drug, delivery device, and ventilator/breathing system; the latter of which differs depending on 
the specific ventilator/breathing system in use on the patient.  The INOmax DSIR Plus must 
undergo a pre-use checkout process in order to verify the accuracy of the electronic controls and 
monitors, the function of the backup switch, the performance of the backup system, and the 
physical integrity of the delivery circuit.  The delivery system must also be purged to remove 
unwanted nitrogen dioxide from the system prior to initiating patient therapy.  In addition, the 
user must set and/or verify alarm thresholds appropriate to the current patient conditions.  Initial 
calibration, as well as regular periodic calibration during therapy, is also necessary to assure the 
-4- 
 
nitric oxide, oxygen, and nitrogen dioxide gas sensors are functioning properly and providing 
accurate readings. 
 
During therapy, the INOmax DSIR Plus monitors inspired nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide, 
and oxygen using a second channel, separate from the channel used for INOMAX delivery.  
Because the delivery system and monitoring measurements are independent, the two subsystems 
cross-check one another and notify the user of any discrepancy between monitored values and 
user established parameters (e.g., dose of nitric oxide).  Within the monitoring subsystem, the 
sample gas is withdrawn from the breathing circuit immediately prior to drug delivery to the 
patient and passes through a series of components to electrochemical gas monitoring sensors.  
The sensors provide an electronic signal proportional to the concentration of the gas, triggering 
alarms if monitored values are outside of those parameters set by the user.  Additional alarms are 
triggered in other circumstances unrelated to monitored values, e.g., failure of any INOmax DSIR 
Plus component, low cylinder pressure, cylinder valve closed, low battery, etc. 
 
Abrupt discontinuation or interruption of nitric oxide therapy can lead to worsening 
oxygenation and increasing pulmonary artery pressure, i.e., rebound pulmonary hypertension 
syndrome, which can be fatal.  To minimize this risk, the INOmax DSIR Plus includes two 
backup systems.  The first is an integrated pneumatic backup system that may be used in the 
event the main system is not functioning, and it is medically appropriate for the patient to remain 
on the ventilator.  This system delivers a fixed flow of INOMAX into the injector module, 
designed to provide 20 ppm of nitric oxide when added to a continuous ventilator gas flow of 10 
L/min.  The INOmax DSIR Plus also includes the INOblender®, which also functions as a backup 
for use when the patient is temporarily removed from the ventilator.  The INOblender connects 
to both an oxygen supply and a cylinder of INOMAX, and allows clinicians to select a 
concentration of nitric oxide to be mixed into a user-established flow of oxygen, which is then 
delivered to the patient.  Both backup systems can be operated without main or battery power, 
though the INOmax DSIR Plus also has a six-hour battery backup to further reduce the risk of 
abrupt discontinuation or interruption of therapy. 
 
To safely administer INOMAX therapy, the user must be trained and knowledgeable 
about all aspects of the INOmax DSIR Plus and its backup systems.  The user must be able to set 
up the INOmax DSIR Plus with a compatible, validated ventilator, program it for individual 
patient therapy, monitor that therapy, rapidly respond to any alarms or other problems that arise 
during INOMAX delivery, and engage one or both backup systems as needed.  Due to the 
complexities of administering nitric oxide therapy, the INOMAX prescribing information 
requires that the manufacturer provide comprehensive, periodic training for all potential users of 
the delivery device to ensure the safe and effective administration of INOMAX.  In addition, to 
further reduce the incidence of user errors, and minimize the consequences of any user errors, 
mechanical failures, or other problems encountered during therapy, the drug labeling requires the 
manufacturer to provide live technical support on an around-the-clock basis, 365 days a year.   
 
Each of the safety features of the INOmax DSIR Plus, as well as Mallinckrodt’s robust 
user training program and live technical support, contribute materially and directly to the safety 
of INOMAX.  For a follow-on nitric oxide product to be as safe and effective as INOMAX, as 
legally required, it must be delivered using a system that duplicates all the safety features of the 
-5- 
 
INOmax DSIR Plus, and is supported by equivalent training and access to live 24/7 technical 
expertise.  Mallinckrodt appreciates that the Agency approves only those follow-on drug 
products that are shown to be as safe and effective as their reference listed drugs, with the same 
risk-benefit profile.  In the case of inhaled nitric oxide, this determination necessitates careful 
Agency review of data and information on the device through which the proposed follow-on 
product will be administered, to confirm the device (a) has the same performance characteristics, 
operating principles, and critical design attributes as the INOmax DSIR Plus, (b) does not 
introduce any new or heightened risks, compared to the INOmax DSIR Plus, and (c) is supported 
by a validated infrastructure capable of providing a national, comprehensive training program, 
and 24 hour/365 days per year technical support equivalent to the training and technical support 
provided by Mallinckrodt.

The undersigned submits this Petition under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and 21 
C.F.R. 10.30 to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to (i) require proposed generic 
versions of Intranasal (IN) naloxone products to provide specific pharmacokinetic (PK), device, 
stability and Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC) data, as set-out herein, within the 
ANDA, to support the interchangeability of generic IN naloxone and the IN naloxone Reference 
Listed Drug (RLD); (ii) not to approve any generic IN naloxone applications until the FDA 
opines on these data requests and issues a formal guidance with requirements for approval of 
such a generic application; and (iii) the generic application meets such requirements. 
Adapt Pharma Operations Limited (“Petitioner”) believes these requirements are critical to 
ensuring the public health and, as such, FDA should address this petition before approving a 
generic IN naloxone product, as provided under 505(q) of the Act.   
IN naloxone products intended for community use are deployed in life-threatening 
circumstances, and often by people who are not medically trained.  They are used to counteract 
opioid overdoses that can be fatal or result in irreversible brain damage, and are often 
administered by a friend or relative who is treating an unconscious person.  There is a narrow 
timeframe for treatment of an opioid overdose and consequently, rapid administration of 
naloxone and onset of action are critical.  Accordingly, the ‘sameness’ required of a generic IN 
naloxone must go beyond the standard parameters and should be rigorously applied.   
Importantly the requested PK requirements for generic IN naloxone are consistent with briefing 
materials presented by FDA to the Joint Meeting of the Anesthetic and Analgesic Drug Products 
Advisory Committee and the Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee on 
October 5, 2016 (the “ADCOM”).  Certain of these requirements are consistent with 
requirements for the approval of the Narcan® Nasal Spray (“Narcan”) New Drug Application, the 
first IN naloxone containing product approved for this indication, and with what we understand 
has been required of other similar products (e.g., Evzio – naloxone auto-injector).  Narcan is the 
IN naloxone RLD (4 mg).

A. Actions Requested 
The undersigned submits this petition under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and 
21 C.F.R. 10.30 to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to: 
a. Not approve a generic application for an IN naloxone product intended for 
community use prior to the Agency establishing a Guidance for a Product Specific 
Bioequivalence Recommendation that addresses the following: 
1. The product must meet bioequivalence standards necessary to ensure safe 
and effective use of intranasal naloxone in the emergency treatment for 
opioid overdose intended for community use, specifically, (i) bioequivalence of 
partial AUC at 10 minutes (AUC0-10); (ii) bioequivalence of mean naloxone 
plasma concentration at 10 minutes (C10min); (iii) detectable naloxone plasma 
concentrations in all subjects from the earliest time point (within 2-3 minutes of 
administration); (iv) bioequivalence at 2 hours post administration (C120min). 
2. The device is comparable to the RLD device and can be safely and effectively 
used interchangeably with the RLD using the RLD label and instructions for 
use without a requirement for training or the intervention of a learned 
intermediary.  Additionally, the device should deliver a non-titratable fixed 
volume of spray and should demonstrate it is as reliable as the RLD. 
b. Ensure that the stability of the generic product should be established in three 
storage positions - horizontal, upright, and inverted at cold temperature and 
accelerated storage conditions for 24 months or over the shelf life period, together 
with specific CMC requirements set-out in this petition. 
c. Not approve ANDA No. 209522 Naloxone Hydrochloride Nasal Spray, 4 mg/spray, 
until all the requested actions listed above have been evaluated and implemented by 
FDA and met by the ANDA Sponsor.

23 November 2016

B. Statement of Grounds 
This Citizen’s Petition is being submitted since there are special PK, device, stability and CMC 
considerations for any product purporting to be interchangeable with IN naloxone RLD.  This 
Citizen’s Petition requests FDA not to approve any generic applications for IN naloxone until the 
FDA opines on these requests, issues a formal guidance with requirements for approval of a 
generic IN naloxone application, and the generic applicant meets such requirements. 
These special requirements reflect (i) naloxone’s use as an emergency treatment for reversal of 
respiratory depression induced by opioid overdose, where every minute of delay in achieving 
effective treatment may be associated with significant morbidity or mortality; (ii) the expansion 
of naloxone access to non-medically trained witnesses in community settings, often family 
members or friends dealing with a highly emotive and stressful medical emergency; and (iii) the 
recent dramatic increase in rapid onset and highly potent opioids (such as fentanyl) implicated in 
overdose fatalities, as identified by Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).  These 
rapid onset and highly potent opioids may further narrow the window for successful emergency 
treatment with naloxone.   
The success of the public policy initiative of expanded naloxone access in the community 
depends, in part, on non-medically trained individuals, who may not have recourse to additional 
naloxone or other medical interventions, rapidly, easily, reliably and safely administering an 
appropriate naloxone dose to achieve a consistently adequate exposure of this potentially life-
saving medication. 
The consequences of a purportedly substitutable product that does not achieve comparable onset, 
exposure and duration of effect, or which does not replicate the ease-of-use, reliability or 
physical characteristics of the IN naloxone RLD (collectively ‘sameness’), could be life-
threatening.  
1. 
Key Strategy Considerations for Petition 
a. The Opioid Overdose Epidemic in United States 
Opioid overdose is a major public health problem in the United States (US) and other countries.  
In the US, opioid overdose contributes to a significant number of accidental deaths among 
persons that either misuse or abuse illicit and prescription opioids.  It was estimated by the 
National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) and CDC that in 2014 there were nearly 29,000 drug 
overdose deaths from opioid analgesics and heroin and this number has increased significantly 
over time with increased use of opioid products to treat pain.  Each day, according to statistics, 
78 persons die from opioid overdose in the US and the vast majority of such deaths happen in 
non-medical facilities, most frequently in the decedent’s home, according to data from CDC 
WONDER database. 
 
 
Adapt Pharma Operations Ltd 
Citizen Petition 
 
23 November 2016 
 
 
 
 
Page 5 of 20 
Opioids include illegal drugs such as heroin and non-pharmaceutical fentanyl and carfentanil as 
well as prescription medications (legal or illegal) to treat pain such as morphine, codeine, 
methadone, oxycodone, hydrocodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl and buprenorphine.  These 
products are often used to treat pain or other indications, but are also used illegally being sourced 
from prescription medications, compounding pharmacies or illegal sources.  During the past 
decade, prescription opioid use became more prevalent in the US and the death rate due to 
overdose of opioid analgesics increased considerably.  The vast majority of opioid overdose 
cases, including pediatric cases (children 18 or younger), were a result of accidental overdose 
and unintentional. 
While proper opioid use is an effective method of treating pain, accidental overdose is a life-
threatening situation in which severe respiratory depression can result in respiratory and cardiac 
arrest.  This is even more significant in situations where persons combine opioids with alcohol or 
other medication use that increases the risk of respiratory depression, slowed heart rate and other 
CNS functions. 
Those most at risk of opioid overdose are typically chronic users of opioids for chronic pain or 
those persons who use illicit drugs such as heroin and fentanyl.  Risk increases when being 
treated with rotating opioid medication regimens, which may not allow for complete tolerance to 
develop to any one opioid.  The risk of opioid overdose is also increased with persons discharged 
from emergency medical care after opioid intoxication or poisoning, and with persons who 
combine legitimate use of opioids with illicit use.  There is also documented increased risk of 
opioid overdose in opioid dependent persons who complete opioid detoxification programs or are 
incarcerated, but later initiate opioid use again, presumably due to reduced opioid tolerance. 
Thus, opioid overdose from prescription and illicit opioids is a significant life-threatening public 
health issue in the US.   
There are several strategies being employed to reduce opioid overdose deaths.  First is 
prevention by changing opioid prescribing practice and education of patients, opioid users and 
caregivers about the risk of opioid overdose.  Next is expanding access to treatment for opioid 
dependent persons.  Finally, NIDA, amongst many others, strongly recommend expanded access 
to naloxone to enable witnesses to administer an emergency treatment for opioid overdose in the 
community setting, as a bridge to the arrival of professional medical care.   
b. Naloxone in the Treatment of Opioid Overdose 
As a narcotic antagonist, naloxone displaces opioids from receptor sites in the brain and can 
reverse respiratory depression that is usually the cause of overdose deaths (1, 2).  Naloxone is an 
essentially pure opioid antagonist, i.e., it does not possess the “agonistic” or morphine-like 
properties characteristic of other opioid antagonists.  When administered in usual doses and in 
the absence of opioids or agonistic effects of other opioid antagonists, it exhibits essentially no 
pharmacologic activity.  Naloxone has not been shown to produce tolerance or cause physical or 
psychological dependence.  In the presence of opioid dependence, opioid withdrawal symptoms 
 
 
Adapt Pharma Operations Ltd 
Citizen Petition 
 
23 November 2016 
 
 
 
 
Page 6 of 20 
may appear within minutes of naloxone administration and typically subside in about 2 hours.  
The severity and duration of the withdrawal syndrome is complex but relates to the dose of 
naloxone and to the degree and type of opioid dependence. 
While the mechanism of action of naloxone is not fully understood, in vitro evidence suggests 
that naloxone antagonizes opioid effects by competing for the mu, kappa, and sigma opioid 
receptor sites in the central nervous system (CNS), with the greatest affinity for the mu receptor.  
When naloxone hydrochloride is administered by the intravenous route (IV), the onset of action 
is generally apparent within 2 minutes; the onset of action is slightly less rapid when it is 
administered by subcutaneous injection (SC) or intramuscular injection (IM).  The duration of 
action is dependent upon the dose and route of administration of naloxone hydrochloride.  IM 
administration produces a more prolonged effect than IV administration.   
Since the duration of action of naloxone may be shorter than that of some opioids, the effects of 
the opioid may return as the effects of naloxone dissipate.  The requirement for repeat doses of 
naloxone, however, will also be dependent upon the amount, type, and route of administration of 
the opioid being antagonized. 
Naloxone hydrochloride injection has been approved by FDA and used for more than 40 years 
by EMS personnel or hospital emergency rooms to reverse opioid overdose and resuscitate 
persons who may have otherwise died (3).  However, not all EMS personnel or other first 
responders are trained to care for overdose and may not be allowed to stock injectable forms of 
naloxone.  In some states, first responders are not protected by laws to prevent prosecution of 
caregivers trying to save a person from death if they make a mistake in treatment or 
administration of rescue medication.  Finally, since many opioid overdose victims are using 
drugs illegally they may be at heightened risk for blood borne diseases.  Thus, untrained 
caregivers or other first responders may inadvertently infect themselves in accident situations or 
be reluctant to intervene in overdose situations.  As such, the access to naloxone injectable 
products for rescue medications is more limited and as such there is a significant gap in the 
public health system and ability to care for overdose victims.   
There is significant evidence in the community that opioid overdose is not well managed (2, 4-
6).  Typical recommendations from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) are to administer a 
dose of naloxone up to 2 mg by the IM or IV route for any person that is suspected to be 
experiencing an opioid overdose (2, 4, 6).  The safety of this dose is considered to be well 
established and the duration of effect is expected to be 30 to 90 minutes.  It is also possible that 
additional doses may be needed to properly treat an opioid overdose situation and as such more 
than one administration of Naloxone is sometimes required.  An adequate dose of naloxone to 
effectuate reversal of opioid overdose symptoms is specific to each event and depends on patient 
factors as well as other factors such as the type of opioid consumed, other substances taken (e.g., 
benzodiazepines) etc.  Naloxone is typically given every 2 to 3 minutes until the patient 
responds.

23 November 2016

The IN route of administration is an important option to ensure patients can be properly treated 
in emergency situations, especially in the out of hospital setting by non-medical professionals, 
including friends and family.  The use of a less invasive and lower needle-stick risk approach to 
administration, such as IN administration, has also allowed caregivers and first responder 
personnel to safely administer rescue medication to persons in an opioid overdose situation.   
c. Expanding Access to Naloxone for Emergency Opioid Overdose 
Expanding access to naloxone is a key element of the public policy response to the opioid 
overdose epidemic.  This is because most opioid overdose deaths happen outside medical 
facilities, and the majority happen at the decedent’s home, according to data from the CDC 
WONDER database.   
Recently, FDA approved an IN form of naloxone, Narcan, which delivers a 4 mg naloxone dose 
in a single administration.  The product is the RLD for IN naloxone (4 mg) and is supplied as a 
carton including two devices, each delivering 4 mg in a 0.1ml spray (for a total of 8 mg per 
carton).  Narcan allows for broader naloxone access in an easy to use delivery system.  To be 
sure that appropriate intervention and dosing in opioid overdose situations is possible without 
needing multiple administrations of lower doses IN naloxone which may not be available in the 
community, Narcan was formulated to rapidly achieve naloxone exposure approximately five 
times greater than 0.4 mg by IM injection, with a single IN administration. 
Potential opioid overdose witnesses equipped with an appropriate naloxone product intended for 
community use may be solely reliant on that product as an initial emergency treatment to bridge 
to the arrival of medical help.  The witness may not have access to medical training or equipment, 
alternative resuscitative techniques, or additional doses of naloxone.   
It is therefore critical that naloxone products intended for community use demonstrate that they 
rapidly, easily, reliably and safely achieve consistently adequate naloxone exposure as an initial 
treatment for a known or suspected opioid overdose.  
d. The Importance of Time  
Over the last two years, non-pharmaceutical fentanyl, a synthetic opioid estimated to be 30 to 50 
times more potent than heroin, has emerged as a significant factor driving the rapid increase in 
opioid overdose fatalities.  CDC issued fentanyl reports in June 2013 and August 2013, and a 
Health Alert in October 2015 (7).  In March 2015, the Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) issued 
a nationwide alert on fentanyl as a threat to health and public safety.  DEA Administrator 
Michele Leonhart commented, “Drug incidents and overdoses related to fentanyl are occurring at 
an alarming rate throughout the United States and represent a significant threat to public health 
and safety” (8).   
Published data from 13 states representing almost one third of all opioid overdose deaths, 
indicate almost one in every four opioid overdose deaths involved fentanyl in 2014, 
 
 
Adapt Pharma Operations Ltd 
Citizen Petition 
 
23 November 2016 
 
 
 
 
Page 8 of 20 
approximately double the rate in the prior year.  State level data for 2016 point to yet further 
increases, with Massachusetts and New York City reporting that fentanyl was implicated in 66% 
and 47% of opioid overdose deaths, respectively in the first 6 months of 2016 (9, 10).  
While overdoses from fentanyl can be reversed with naloxone, because of its potency, rapid 
onset and long lasting respiratory depressive effects, the window of intervention may be 
narrower and a higher dose of naloxone may be needed.  Prescription fentanyl’s respiratory 
depressive effects peak in 5-15 minutes and, depending on dose, these effects may last for many 
hours (11). 
In addition, the FDA convened a Joint Meeting of the Anesthetic and Analgesic Drug Products 
Advisory Committee and the Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee on 
October 5, 2016 (the “ADCOM”).  In its briefing materials, FDA states “in the community, there 
is a five (5) to ten (10) minute window before hypoxic injury is irreversible and adequate 
ventilatory support is often not available” (12).   
In the context of new users, new administration settings (in the community) and more potent 
opioids implicated in opioid overdose fatalities, we believe both device attributes that support 
rapid, reliable and easy administration, and PK characteristics that support the rapid attainment 
of significant naloxone exposure especially in the critical early time period, are essential for 
patient recovery and safety. 
2. 
Analysis 
Key Pharmacokinetic Issues and Bioequivalence Implications for IN Naloxone Generics 
During an opioid overdose situation the most critical adverse effects are respiratory depression 
and cardiac arrest.  Many opioid overdose victims die from respiratory and cardiac arrest, or if 
they survive, may have brain damage from lack of oxygen due to respiratory depression.  Thus, 
the time it takes to administer a rescue medication and for that medication to take effect is 
critical in avoiding death or serious co-morbidities from an incident of opioid overdose.  In 
addition, the duration of effect of many opioids may be longer than that of naloxone, and persons 
that are initially recovered from opioid overdose may relapse into respiratory depression before 
medical helps arrives, as naloxone’s effects wear off.  This risk may be particularly acute in rural 
areas due to longer EMS response times.  Thus, the duration of effect of the naloxone 
administered is critical. 
The importance of these PK parameters was raised by FDA which stated, in its briefing 
document to the recently convened ADCOM on dosing for community use naloxone products, 
“in the community, there is a five (5) to ten (10) minute window before hypoxic injury is 
irreversible and adequate ventilatory support is often not available” (12).  Additionally, the 
importance of the entire PK profile was emphasized in a slide presented by FDA to the ADCOM 
(13).   
 
 
Adapt Pharma Operations Ltd 
Citizen Petition 
 
23 November 2016 
 
 
 
 
Page 9 of 20 
Thus, the standard FDA bioequivalence criteria for AUC and Cmax would not alone be adequate 
to cover the time period of the onset of action and duration of effect.  Therefore, the FDA should 
require IN naloxone generic applicants to demonstrate bioequivalence based on criteria that 
appropriately address these two critical point, in addition to standard requirements to 
demonstrate bioequivalence for IN generic products.  Different formulations of nasal naloxone 
products may exhibit different PK profiles.  These concerns are consistent with FDAs actions in 
reviewing applications for other nasal naloxone products submitted under the 505B(2) route.  
FDA issued a complete response letter to Indivior plc, in respect of its application for nasal 
naloxone.  Indivior, plc, reported “the FDA’s response was principally focused on clinical 
pharmacology that found the early stage uptake of naloxone nasal spray did not fully meet the 
FDA’s threshold as determined by the reference product (0.4 mg naloxone by intramuscular 
injection).” 
Bioequivalence of partial AUC at 10 minutes (AUC0-10) and mean naloxone plasma 
concentration at 10 minutes (C10min) 
 The rate of absorption and the time to reach plasma concentrations that correlate with 
effectiveness, in this case, the reversal of respiratory depression are critical.  As 
naloxone’s initial effect of reversal of respiratory depression is within minutes, the initial 
naloxone plasma levels are as important as maximum concentration.  FDA's traditional 
PK parameters (Cmax, AUC0-t, and AUC0-∞) should be maintained but alone are NOT 
sufficient to account for the early clinical exposure needed to achieve effectiveness with 
naloxone containing products intended to treat opioid overdose.  FDA should require 
applicants to demonstrate bioequivalence using statistical evaluation of an additional PK 
parameter, partial AUC at 10 minutes (AUC0-10) along with Concentration at 10 minutes 
(C10min).  These PK parameters, which are required in addition to the standard PK 
parameters, are necessary to assure the therapeutic equivalence of a generic to the IN 
naloxone RLD at the clinically relevant early exposure period.  
The plasma concentrations of naloxone after administration of the IN naloxone RLD 
show a lag-time of approximately 2 minutes; therefore, a partial AUC value at 10 minutes 
would be the most appropriate and robust parameter.  In addition, when preparing a study 
design for bioequivalence for this parameter, at a minimum the PK time points of 0 hour 
(baseline), 2.5 minutes, 5 minutes and 10 minutes, should be mandatory to insure the 
proper correlations can be conducted. 
The standard bioequivalence criteria can be used for the additional PK parameter; log-
transformed exposure measure (AUC0-10min and C10min) falls completely within the range 
80-125%. 
In the case of the IN naloxone RLD, the rate of absorption was faster when compared to 
0.4 mg naloxone by IM injection.  The IN naloxone RLD labeling emphasizes the rapid 
absorption of both a single and two-dose administration as compared to the widely used 
0.4 mg IM naloxone products (see Figure 1).   In the pivotal PK study, a single dose of 
 
 
Adapt Pharma Operations Ltd 
Citizen Petition 
 
23 November 2016 
 
 
 
 
Page 10 of 20 
the IN naloxone RLD achieved 3.5 fold (at 2.5 minutes), 4.8 fold (at 5 minutes) and 5.6 
fold (at 10 minutes) the mean naloxone plasma concentration, compared to 0.4 mg 
naloxone administered by IM.  
Detectable naloxone plasma concentrations in all subjects from the earliest time point  
 Because of the mortality and morbidity risks associated with delayed onset, any proposed 
generic formulation of IN naloxone RLD must demonstrate detectable plasma 
concentrations of naloxone in each subjects for its formulation in its bioequivalent studies 
from the earliest measured blood sample time point, which should be taken in the first 2-3 
minutes.  This is a critical time period for effectiveness, and necessary to properly 
characterize the early PK profile.  This is also critical to ensure that an adequate naloxone 
exposure is consistently achieved in all persons, rapidly enough, to have an effect in an 
opioid overdose emergency where respiratory depression or arrest can cause death or 
serious co-morbidities. 
This requirement is consistent with the profile of the IN naloxone RLD.  In the pivotal 
PK study, each subject that received a single dose of the IN naloxone RLD had detectable 
naloxone plasma levels at each of the early time points (2.5, 5 and 10 minutes). 
This approach to early onset parameters mirrors the approach FDA has adopted to 
support approval of community use naloxone products submitted under 505B(2).  FDA 
states in a memorandum to the ADCOM Re: Clinical Pharmacology Background, 
October 5, 2016 AADPAC/DSaRM Meeting to Naloxone Products dated September 2, 
2016 from Dr. Yun Xu Ph.D. “Because overdose may lead to apnea, onset of naloxone 
action is critical if the brain is to be spared permanent hypoxic injury.  The current FDA 
guidance on bioavailability and bioequivalence studies recommends the use of partial 
AUC to assess the onset of therapeutic effect” (12).   
Bioequivalence at 2 hours post administration (C120min) 
 The overall absorption and duration of effect is critical because naloxone’s duration of 
effect may be shorter than that of the opioid, causing the victim to potentially relapse into 
respiratory depression before medical help arrives.  The generic application should 
address duration of effect by requiring bioequivalent concentration at 2 hours (C120min).    
The duration of exposure is critical to ensure comparable blood levels are maintained for 
at least 2 hours to allow for subjects to start to recover from the opioid overdose and for 
additional medical assistance to be accessed.  This may be particularly important in rural 
settings, where many overdoses occur, because emergency response times may be longer 
and responders are more likely to have EMT – basic training only.  Most state scope of 
practice models preclude naloxone administration by such EMT – basic responders (14).

cohort) that would lead to trials of precision therapies, among other things. The Working 
Group’s recommendations were adopted by the Director. The cohort is expected to have over 
one million participants within four years, according to the NIH News Release issued that same 
day. 
To support the progress of the Precision Medicine Initiative, the FDA adopted its 
“precisionFDA” program that consists of a research and development portal that would allow 
community members to test, pilot, and validate existing and new bioinformatics approaches for 
processing the vast amount of genomic data that is collected using Next Generation Sequencing 
technology. See: www.precision.fda.gov. 
As with other new drug initiatives, Precision Medicine Initiatives require FDA approval before 
they can be marketed to the public. The FDA utilizes the Center for Drug Evaluation and 
Research (CDER) to fulfill its responsibilities in this regard.  
The FDA’s CDER procedures are such that new drugs have typically taken 12-15 years to be 
approved at an average cost per approved drug of over $1 billion.  The FDA approves about 25 
new drugs a year on average.  See, e.g., www.FDAReview.org, The Drug Development and 
Approval Process (2016). 
Without modifications of the CDER’s procedures for application to Precision Medicine 
Initiatives, it is likely that tangible results from the President’s program will take more than 15 
years to reach the public – and will do so only if the precision initiatives targeted to small 
groups of people can withstand the cost burden of FDA regulations on a per-person basis 
(which is unlikely). 
Accordingly, this Petition requests the FDA to issue an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking 
to address what modifications, if any, are appropriate to the FDA’s approval process for new 
drugs and treatments emanating from Precision Medicine Initiatives. 
3 
 
The issues raised by this Petition include: 
a) Can any therapies emanating from the Precision Medicine Initiative be introduced into 
interstate commerce without FDA approval?  Does the existing legislation provide the FDA with 
flexibility to tailor its regulations to fit the circumstances of precision therapies or to create 
partial or full exemptions of the regulations for certain precision medicines? 
b) If the FDA were to adopt a separate classification for Precision Medicine Initiatives, what 
should the inclusion criteria be for this class? 
c) Can and should the FDA regulate PMI treatments emanating from the NIH cohort differently 
than those emanating from non-governmental run cohorts? 
d) Can the typical Precision Medicine treatment sustain the high costs and resultant high per-
person prices that would result from the application of the existing FDA regulations to a 
therapy with a very small target market? 
e) What regulatory alternatives exist to the current drug approval process that would provide 
increased incentive for private capital formation to fund R&D for Precision Medicine Initiatives 
without compromising consumer safety?   
f) What are the risks and rewards of different regulatory approaches for Precision Medicine 
Initiatives?   
g) Should the FDA develop, maintain and publish a scorecard that keeps track and provides 
annual updates of the progress of all Precision Medicine Initiatives (both private and public)? 
The national cohort under NIH will take several years to build before it will begin to show signs 
of progress.  Nevertheless, the time for action on this Petition is now because there are many 
more private precision medicine research initiatives that would proceed with the certainty of a 
well-functioning regulatory framework.

I. Action Requested 
 
On February 11, 2016, I wrote to the FDA to ascertain whether it had started or planned any 
rulemakings addressing Precision Medicine Initiatives. I did not receive a response. 
This Petition requests the FDA to issue a comprehensive Advance Notice of Proposed 
Rulemaking seeking legal, economic and scientific input on how best to analyze and approve, as 
appropriate, new Precision Medicine Initiatives. 
This action is warranted now because much greater efforts would be put in place for Precision 
Medicine Initiatives in private sector with the proper regulatory procedures in place. 
The Petition seeks to have the FDA lay out in fine detail the entirety of its drug approval process 
so that commenters can provide estimates for the impact of the various FDA procedures on the 
cost, risk and delay of new therapies as well as the benefits flowing to the public from the 
regulations. 
The Petition also sets out alternative regulatory procedures for Precision Medicine Initiatives so 
that the FDA can seek informed comment on various approaches as the research community 
seeks to pivot from R&D focused on blockbuster drugs to therapies focused on personalized 
care. 
II. Statement of Factual Grounds for the Requested Action 
 
Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations confers upon the FDA the responsibility to ensure 
that drugs are safe and effective before being marketed to the public. 
This responsibility confers huge benefits and costs upon society.   
The costs can be identified as direct and indirect.  Direct costs would address the out-of-pocket 
costs to gain regulatory approval.  
For example, economist Joe Dimasi of the Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development 
estimates the out-of-pocket costs to get FDA approval to be approximately $1.4 billion per 
drug.   This estimate is roughly consistent with the total spending for drug research divided by 
the number of approved drugs over a specified number of years. See, e.g., “The High Cost of 
Inventing New Drugs – and of Not Inventing Them”, The Institute for Policy Innovation (April 16, 
2015). 
Indirect costs would include the loss of benefits to patients from unnecessary regulatory delay.  
6 
 
The amount of time needed to advance varies widely by initiative, but it typically takes 1-6 
years for preclinical research, 6-11 years for clinical trials and up to 2 years for review and 
approval.  The typical cycle involves 12-15 years of development before approval. 
Another form of indirect costs includes the loss of efficacious discoveries that never make it 
through the process.  Researchers refer to this syndrome as the “Valley of Death” because the 
risk, cost and delay of the FDA drug approval process makes it impossible for them to raise 
private capital to pursue the research. 
On the other side of the ledger, the benefits of FDA regulatory procedures include the cessation 
of death and prevention of other significant adverse events in clinical trials and subsequently in 
the public market.  Similarly, if inefficacious drugs can be kept off of the market, this represents 
a direct benefit to the public in terms of cost avoidance. 
The two most widely quoted examples that demonstrate these benefits relate to Sulfanilamide 
and Thalidomide. 
In 1937, a Massengill, a Tennessee drug company, began to market a liquid drug called Elixir 
Sulfanilamide.  The solvent in this drug was a highly toxic variant of antifreeze; as a result, over 
100 people died from taking this drug. 
In the 1960’s, Thalidomide, a sedative that was marketed to combat the symptoms associated 
with morning sickness in pregnant women, caused birth deformities in thousands of babies 
throughout Europe. 
The value of human life is a delicate matter, but for purposes of public policy, the FDA has used 
a figure of $7.9 million in cases related to cigarette smoking.  For purposes of the analysis raised 
by this Petition, the FDA should also establish monetary values for: 1) avoiding significant 
adverse effects (other than death) on a per-person basis, and 2) the delay of cures on a per-
person basis. The FDA could use benchmark values of $1 to $4 million for these events, 
depending on the circumstances. 
For example, the FDA has approved MRI-guided focused ultrasound for treating cancer.  
Therefore, for purposes of using the same technology to treat tremors, the FDA’s focuses on 
efficacy rather than safety.  For purposes of illustration, if the FDA were to add a rigorous safety 
component to the clinical trials that use this technology for tremors, the net benefit of that 
component could be estimated to be: 
Net gain/loss = (($6.9M x number of lives saved) + ($4M x the number of significant adverse 
effects avoided)) minus ($Y x probability of approval x number of likely recipients), where Y is 
7 
 
set based on the expected length of the delay.  For example, Y might be set at $1M if the added 
delay was projected to be two years. 
Similar formulae can be used to determine the net gain or loss for every variable in the FDA 
drug approval process identified in Section III as well as the alternative approaches identified in 
Section V. 
By using such a framework, the FDA will be able to identify the optimal drug approval 
procedures for Precision Medicine Initiatives.                                 
III. The FDA Should Detail the Parameters, Activities and Results of its 
Drug Approval Process as Part of the Advance Notice of Proposed 
Rulemaking 
 
The Precision Medicines Initiative is made possible by the emergence of “Big Data”.  Big Data 
allows the collection, storage and computation of massive amounts of information on an 
economic basis. As such, it fundamentally changes the approach to experimental design. Today, 
researchers can afford to collect virtually unlimited amounts of data and search for significant 
patterns in the data. 
The same principle applies to regulatory procedures.  With detailed specifications of CDER’s 
activities on a relatively large sample of drug initiatives along with the associated results, 
researchers and the FDA will be able to better isolate and discern how each process produces 
benefits and costs to the public. 
The FDA has a variety of classifications along with different procedures that it uses for new 
drugs including Fast-Track, Breakthrough, Priority Review and Accelerated Approval.  It also 
tracks whether the drugs are First-In-Class and/or targeted to fewer than 200,000 recipients 
(i.e., so-called Orphan Drugs). 
Its principal tools are issuing guidelines for good laboratory practices, conducting quality 
assurance oversight of pre-clinical research and thorough examination of all data submitted for 
each phase of the clinical trials.  It also uses a series of Advisory Committees to help in its 
deliberations and relies heavily on the recommendations of Institutional Review Boards for final 
decisions. 
The FDA implements its mandate by examining the outputs of research affecting toxicology 
(pre-clinical), safety (Phases I-III), dosing (Phase II), efficacy (Phase II-III) and side effects (Phase 
III).   
8 
 
The FDA procedures also vary depending upon whether a drug was approved for another 
application.  In these cases, the FDA’s focus is efficacy with a diminished focus on safety. 
The FDA’s procedures have also varied over time, principally as a result of new legislation. 
For example, the length of time for the FDA approvals began increasing after the 1962 
legislative amendments; from about 1 year to 3 years by the end of the decade and then up to 
10 years in the 1970’s. 
Similarly, the cost of research and development per approved drug has increased from $100m 
in 1975 to $300 million in 1987 to over $1 billion more recently.  
The various procedures employed by the FDA over time have produced different results.  The 
results of greatest import include: 1) the probability of proceeding from each stage of research, 
2) the time required for each phase, 3) the out-of-pocket expenses for each step in the process 
and 4) whether the new drug was safe and effective in the market. 
Taken together, the FDA has thousands of data points of inputs and outputs to its drug approval 
process that, if made available to the public, would enable researchers and the FDA itself to 
systematically evaluate the various procedures it employs today and that it has employed over 
time to determine the benefits and costs of each of the tools and procedures that it has used. 
For example, the data might show that complex, novel discoveries attract more FDA attention 
in pre-clinical research and when that occurs the probability of success in clinical research goes 
up (or down) by an average of x%.  Conversely, the data might show that when a therapy has 
been approved for other applications, the time to market decreases by Y years (thereby 
isolating one of the costs of the safety component of the FDA’s review). 
Armed with information to correlate regulatory actions and the associated outcomes, the FDA 
will be in a position to determine the optimal procedures for addressing the approval process 
for Precision Medicine Initiatives. 
Accordingly, this Petition requests that the FDA include in the requested Advance Notice of 
Proposed Rulemaking detailed information in tabular form providing the classification(s), the 
various tools employed, and the outputs for those classifications and tools for a wide variety of 
individual discoveries and drugs. 
In particular, the FDA should specify this information for such wide-ranging research as 
polio/virus vaccines to treat cancer, stem cells to treat Parkinson’s disease, and various 
research initiatives for metastatic cancer and Alzheimer’s disease, among others, including 
discoveries (and failures) in earlier times. 
9 
 
IV. The FDA Should Solicit Comments on the Key Issues Raised by the 
Emergence of Precision Medicine Initiatives 
 
The FDA should seek comment on the following issues: 
A. Definition of Precision Medicine Initiatives 
The FDA should define the drugs and discoveries that fall into the classification of Precision 
Medicine Therapies.  For example, the FDA uses the classification “Orphan Drugs” for therapies 
with a population target of less than 200,000. 
In kicking off the PMI, President Obama noted that Precision Medicine Initiatives will be 
developed on an individualized basis based on a person’s genome sequence, metabolomics, 
microbiome and other specific data about the patient. 
Therefore, one definition of PMI could be any research initiative that utilizes genetic 
information in combination with other personal data to treat health conditions.  Under this 
approach, research for diseases such the cancer resulting from a BRCA mutation would be 
considered a PMI. 
Alternatively, the PMI definition could follow the approach of the “Orphan Drugs” classification 
and include all research with a target population of less than a specific number of patients 
(presumably less than 200,000). 
Thirdly, the FDA could combine the two approaches to create the definition of Precision 
Medicine Initiatives based on target size and the inclusion of genetic information. 
Finally, the FDA could use one (or more) of its existing classifications for Precision Medicine 
Initiatives. 
To provide an example of the definitional challenge for PMIs, thirteen gene mutations 
associated with Parkinson’s disease (PD) have been identified. In some cases, the genetic 
mutations are rare such as with the alpha-synuclein gene.  In other cases, a mutation might 
lead to PD and additional disorders such as Lewy body dementia.  To compound the complexity, 
the first disorder may affect a population above the target threshold and the second disorder 
may be below the target threshold. Moreover, as more genetic and personal data are gathered, 
the size of the target population for specific treatments will get smaller over time.  For example, 
going back to the BRCA mutation example above, today BRCA mutations are categorized as 
Triple Negative. However, on-going research is likely to show that BRCA-related Triple Negative 
cancer behaves very differently than non-BRCA Triple Negative cancer and therefore deserves a 
separate categorization.  
10 
 
B. Legal Issues  
The FDA should seek comment on whether any therapies emanating from the Precision 
Medicine Initiative can be introduced into interstate commerce without FDA approval. 
The emergence of “Big Data” capabilities has brought a class of new pioneers to healthcare, 
namely those from Silicon Valley.  These new entrants have no experience with regulatory 
procedures.  In many instances, these entrants have the attitude of the lead actor in the movie 
“Dallas Buyer’s Club” (2013), namely that they will find a cure and the FDA will not be able to 
stop them once the cure takes hold in the market.  Such a confrontation can be avoided with 
the proactive approach requested by this Petition and the “market” will operate more 
efficiently. 
Another legal issue that the FDA should seek comment relates whether the existing legislation 
provides the FDA with flexibility to tailor its regulations to fit the circumstances of precision 
therapies and/or to create partial or full exemptions of the regulations for certain precision 
medicines. 
The FDA should also seek comment as to whether it can (and should) regulate treatments 
emanating from the NIH cohort differently than those emanating from non-governmental 
research cohorts. 
C. The Economics of Precision Medicine Initiatives 
The FDA should seek comment on whether the typical Precision Medicine treatment can 
sustain the high costs and resultant high per-person prices that would result from the 
application of the existing FDA regulations to a therapy with a very small target market. 
In the same vein, the FDA should seek comment as to whether the current drug approval 
process has inadvertently devolved into a system that accommodates mostly expensive, 
blockbuster drugs, while keeping low-cost, targeted, competitive alternatives such as PMIs from 
entering the market. 
D. Reporting 
Management science tells us that when improvement is desired, leaders must focus on the 
relevant item(s) that needs improvement, develop a strategic plan to address these items, 
organize the resources necessary to execute the plan, track progress against the plan’s 
objectives and make adjustments to the plan when needed.

US Food and Drug Administration

5630 Fishers Lane, Room 1061 
Rockville, MD 02852 
 
Citizen Petition 
 
Date: May 12, 2016 
 
The undersigned submits this petition under 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 of the Federal Food, Drug, and 
Cosmetic Act to request that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs amend the package labeling 
for low-dose vaginal estrogen products and the Guidance for Industry: Noncontraceptive 
Estrogen Drug Products for the Treatment of Vasomotor Symptoms and Vulvar and Vaginal 
Atrophy Symptoms—Recommended Prescribing Information for Health Care Providers and 
Patient Labeling (Guidance) as specified below (Action Requested).  
 
A. ACTION REQUESTED 
 
The North American Menopause Society (NAMS) and the Working Group on Women’s Health 
and Well-Being in Menopause request that the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) modify 
the label for low-dose vaginal estrogen products approved for treating symptoms of 
vulvovaginal atrophy (VVA) and the Guidance as follows. This would apply to low-dose vaginal 
estrogen products approved for symptoms of VVA, with pharmacokinetic data showing that the 
systemic absorption of estrogen maintains blood levels within or below the postmenopausal 
range. This request does not apply to estrogen products approved for treatment of VVA (hot 
flashes). Low-dose vaginal estrogen products approved for treatment of VVA should have a 
different product label than systemic (higher-dose) oral or transdermal estrogen products. 
 
The label should be modified to accurately reflect the relevant evidence-based information for 
low-dose vaginal estrogen products. 
 
The “Warnings and Precautions” section of the labeling should highlight (bold) the information 
related to the following medical concerns for those using low-dose vaginal products for VVA: 
 
a. Genital bleeding is a concern because bleeding may be a sign of endometrial 
cancer. 
b. Women with estrogen-sensitive breast cancer should consult with their 
oncologists before use of the product. 
2 
 
The warnings identified in the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) trials of oral systemic (higher-
dose) hormone therapy (HT) should remain in the label (“Warnings and Precautions”) in regular 
text and font, but the boxed warning should be removed. The warnings related to high-dose 
oral estrogen and progestin products may not be applicable in women using low-dose vaginal 
estrogens, and hence, not generally using progestins. 
 
The Patient Labeling should reflect these changes (specific wording suggestions for the 
modified label are provided in the Menopause editorial, “Why the Product Labeling for Low-
Dose Vaginal Estrogen Should Be Changed,”1 attached). 
 
B. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
1. BACKGROUND 
 
Overview 
The Working Group on Women’s Health and Well-Being in Menopause, affiliated with a number 
of medical societies, including NAMS, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, 
The Endocrine Society, the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, the International 
Society for the Study of Women’s Sexual Health, and other professional and women’s 
organizations, is requesting FDA to modify the product labeling of low-dose vaginal estrogen 
products approved for treatment of symptoms of VVA. The working group was convened at 
the request of a Town Hall Meeting held at the NAMS 2014 Annual Meeting. The findings of the 
Working Group were published in the September 2014 issue of the journal Menopause (see 
attached editorial) and presented at a workshop convened by FDA on low-dose estrogen on 
November 10, 2015, with many materials and written testimonials submitted online in advance 
of the workshop. 
 
Background 
Vulvovaginal atrophy (also known as genitourinary syndrome of menopause) is a common and 
progressive condition that adversely affects the health and quality of life of many 
postmenopausal women.2 
 
Vulvovaginal atrophy is a medical condition estimated to affect approximately 32 million 
women in the United States; however, it is estimated that less than 7% (2.3 million) of affected 
women use FDA-approved prescription therapy.3 Symptoms of VVA are often overlapping and 
include vaginal dryness, itching and burning, vulvar irritation, and painful intercourse 
(dyspareunia) and may be associated with a higher risk of vaginal infections or recurrent 
bladder infections. A recent survey of women’s knowledge of VVA, the REVIVE survey, reported 
that the most commonly occurring VVA symptoms included vaginal dryness (55% of 
participants), dyspareunia (44%), and irritation (37%), with negative effects on enjoyment of 
sex (59%).3 Also reported were interference with sleep, diminished general enjoyment of life, 
and temperament reported by 24%, 23%, and 23% of participants, respectively. In addition to 
adversely affecting women and their partners’ quality of life, there is an increase in medical 
3 
 
healthcare costs because of increases in office visits, need for treatment of infections, and 
potential hospitalization for sepsis caused by bladder infections in older women.4 
The most efficacious treatment of VVA includes products containing estrogen. Currently 
available estrogen-containing treatments include oral, transdermal, and vaginal products. Low-
dose vaginal estrogen therapy has low systemic exposure, with blood levels similar to 
endogenous estrogen levels normally found in postmenopausal women.5-7 
 
However, the product labeling of all these products, regardless of the mode of delivery or dose, 
carry the same warnings and do not provide distinction among oral products, which undergo 
hepatic first-pass metabolism, systemic transdermal doses, and low-dose to very-low-dose 
vaginal products. Concerns about the safety of VVA because of the current boxed warning has 
been reported as preventing the use of FDA-approved low-dose vaginal therapy.1 
 
FDA Background and Label for Hormone Therapy 
 
FDA approves drugs for use in HT for menopause symptoms and advises women who choose to 
use hormones to use them, in consultation with their healthcare providers, for the shortest 
time necessary at the lowest effective dose. The product label includes the risks of HT, including 
that, for some women, HT may increase their chance of getting blood clots, heart attacks, 
strokes, breast cancer, and gallbladder disease. For a woman with a uterus, estrogen increases 
the chance of getting endometrial cancer (cancer of the uterine lining). Adding a progestin or 
progesterone has been shown to lower this risk. 
 
The National Institutes of Health’s Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) conducted several large, 
randomized, clinical studies, including a large study to determine the effects of conjugated 
equine estrogens (CEE) 0.625 mg daily combined continuously with the progestin 
medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) 2.5 mg on the prevention of heart disease. The 
participants in the study were not taking the medication for an FDA-approved use. The estrogen 
plus progestin study was halted in 2002 because the health risks appeared to outweigh the 
benefits for participants taking estrogen with progestin for chronic disease prevention. Results 
from this study reported that the enrolled population taking oral CEE with MPA had an 
increased risk of early cardiovascular disease, stroke, breast cancer, and blood clots. The initial 
publication of the study findings reported that the absolute excess risks per 10,000 woman-
years in the group treated with the combination estrogen-progestin product were seven more 
heart attacks, eight more strokes, 18 more blood clots, and eight more invasive breast cancers 
than in the placebo control group. Conversely, the absolute risk reductions per 10,000 woman-
years for the estrogen-progestin group were six fewer colorectal cancers and five fewer hip 
fractures than in the placebo group. 
 
As a result of the WHI hormone studies, FDA requested changes to the existing boxed warning 
in FDA-approved labeling for estrogen-alone drugs and requested that a boxed warning be 
added to FDA-approved labeling for combination estrogen-progestin drugs. In addition, FDA 
requested that a boxed warning be added to FDA-approved labeling for progestin-alone drugs 
approved for use in combination with estrogen because the progestin-alone drugs are 
4 
 
frequently used concomitantly with estrogen-alone drugs and would therefore share the same 
or similar risks as fixed-dose combination estrogen-progestin drugs. In general, the warnings 
highlight that the WHI study reported increased risks of heart attack, stroke, breast cancer, and 
blood clots, and because of these risks, estrogens with or without progestins should be 
prescribed at the lowest effective doses and for the shortest duration consistent with 
treatment goals and risks for the individual woman. 
 
2. ARGUMENT 
 
The current boxed warning on the package label for low-dose vaginal estrogen products used 
for VVA indications is not evidence based or appropriate to the risks identified with low-dose 
vaginal estrogens used for VVA. The boxed warning, which reflects current oral estrogen class 
labeling, states: WARNING: ENDOMETRIAL CANCER, CARDIOVASCULAR DISORDERS, BREAST 
CANCER, and PROBABLE DEMENTIA. This warning is based on extrapolations of data from 
randomized, clinical trials of systemic HT, primarily the WHI, which involved substantially higher 
oral doses leading to increased systemic levels of estrogen and do not apply to low-dose vaginal 
estrogen products used for the treatment of symptoms of VVA that do not undergo first-pass 
hepatic metabolism and are without evidence of systemic exposure.  
 
The American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists released a Committee Opinion in 
March 2016 (no. 659) on the use of vaginal estrogen in breast cancer survivors8: “Among 
women with a history of estrogen-dependent breast cancer who are experiencing urogenital 
symptoms, vaginal estrogen should be reserved for those patients who are unresponsive to 
non-hormonal remedies. The decision to use vaginal estrogen may be made in coordination 
with a woman’s oncologist. Additionally, it should be preceded by an informed decision-making 
and consent process in which the woman has the information and resources to consider the 
benefits and potential risks of low-dose vaginal estrogen. Data do not show an increased risk of 
cancer recurrence among women currently undergoing treatment for breast cancer or those 
with a personal history of breast cancer who use vaginal estrogen to relieve urogenital 
symptoms.” 
 
This petition by NAMS and the Working Group on Women’s Health and Well-Being in 
Menopause is based in part on the following issues: 
 
a. 
The dramatic differences in blood hormone levels achieved by low-dose vaginal 
estrogen (eg, Vagifem tablets [estradiol 10 µg], Estring [releasing estradiol 
7.5 µg/d], or comparable low-dose vaginal estrogen cream formulations) versus 
standard systemic estrogen therapy (whether oral, transdermal, or vaginal ring). 
b. 
Differences in metabolism of oral and local low-dose vaginal products. 
c. 
Absence of randomized trial evidence or consistent observational evidence linking 
low-dose vaginal estrogen to cancer, cardiovascular disease, dementia, or other 
conditions highlighted in the boxed warning. 
d. 
Absence of evidence that changes in blood hormone levels of the small magnitude 
achieved with these products increased the risk of any of these conditions. 
5 
 
e. 
As a result of the boxed warning, a large number of older women with symptomatic 
VVA and genitourinary symptoms are being undertreated or turn to unapproved, 
unlabeled compounded products and do not receive the substantial health and 
quality-of-life benefits that the low-dose vaginal estrogen products approved for 
VVA could provide. 
f. 
The boxed warning on the package label for low-dose vaginal estrogen discourages 
clinicians from prescribing the product and women from taking it even after 
purchase. 
g. 
The inclusion of boxed warnings for estrogen plus progestin, although progestin is 
not generally needed with low-dose vaginal estrogen products. 
1. 
This labeling is confusing to healthcare providers, indicating that perhaps 
they should be prescribing a progestin. One of the benefits of low-dose 
vaginal products is the lack of a need for concomitant progestins. 
 
Specific products that meet the definition of low-dose vaginal products having blood levels 
within the physiologic hormone postmenopausal range when dosed appropriately include 
Pfizer—7.5 µg vaginal estradiol ring (Estring) 
Pfizer—Low-dose vaginal CEE cream dosed 0.5 mg every 21 of 28 days or twice weekly 
(Premarin) 
Novo Nordisk—Vaginal estradiol 10 µg tablets twice weekly (Vagifem) 
Generic Vagifem—Vaginal estradiol 10 µg tablets twice weekly 
 
Other products currently in development include low-dose vaginal gel by TherapeuticsMD and a 
low-dose vaginal estradiol (Estrace) cream by Actavis. 
 
On November 10, 2015, FDA convened a workshop on the topic of the labeling for lower-dose 
estrogen products delivered vaginally, intended to treat moderate to severe symptoms of VVA 
caused by menopause. Prominent experts in the menopause field, including leaders from 
NAMS, testified in support of the label change. 
 
Efforts by NAMS to change the product label have been supported by the Endocrine Society, 
the American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the American Medical Women’s 
Association, the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, the Academy of Women’s Health, 
the International Society for the Study of Women’s Sexual Health, the American Association of 
Nurse Practitioners in Women’s Health, the American Association of Nurse Practitioners, the 
South Atlantic Association of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Society for Women’s 
Health Research, among others. Consumer organizations include the National Women’s Health 
Network, the National Organization for Women, the RedHot Mamas, ellendolgen.com, 
blogher.com, vibrantnation.com, and speakingofwomenshealth.com, among others. The 
Citizen’s Petition launched by NAMS received 430 signatures when submitted to FDA for the 
workshop on November 10, 2015, and currently has 620 signatures.  
 
 
6 
 
C. 
CONCLUSION 
 
NAMS and the Working Group on Women’s Health and Well-Being in Menopause recommend a 
modification to the current label for low-dose vaginal estrogen products approved for VVA in 
order to clarify and better inform postmenopausal women and their healthcare providers. We 
understand that changing the label and boxed warnings for HT products is complex. The 
modified label would more closely reflect the safety profile of low-dose vaginal estrogen 
products, which would ENHANCE patient safety by emphasizing the key information that 
women and clinicians need to know about the products. 
 
Modification of the product label for low-dose vaginal estrogen products reflects additional 
knowledge and safety that has arisen from safety surveillance of increased use of low-dose 
vaginal estrogens over the past approximately 14 years since the class labeling reflecting the 
WHI: this will also demonstrate FDA’s commitment to ensuring that consumers 
(postmenopausal women) and healthcare providers are updated and well informed about the 
appropriate and relevant risks. 
 
Information for the Public  
 
Educational efforts by FDA could include a public awareness campaign about the use of low-
dose vaginal estrogen products for VVA that would highlight the low systemic blood levels 
comparable to those of normal postmenopausal women and FDA approved products that 
currently meet that standard and could include warnings about the unique risks of 
compounding for those choosing to use compounded non-FDA-approved vaginal estrogen 
therapies. 
 
D. 
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT 
 
The actions requested in this petition are not within any of the categories for which an 
environmental assessment is required, pursuant to 21 CFR 25.22. 
 
E. 
ECONOMIC IMPACT 
 
Information on the economic impact of this proposal will be submitted if requested by the
