Citizen Petition 
 
 
Date: December 21, 2016 
 
On behalf of Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy organization with more than 400,000 
members and supporters nationwide, the undersigned submits this petition under Section 352 the 
Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and under Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 
regulations at 21 C.F.R. §§ 10.30 and 201.56 to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to 
immediately require that: 
(1) The label of repaglinide-containing medications (PRANDIN, PRANDIMET) include 
information on a serious drug-drug interaction with clopidogrel (PLAVIX) that could 
result in severe hypoglycemia; and  
(2) The labels of both repaglinide-containing medications and clopidogrel include a 
contraindication to the use of the two drugs together due to this interaction. 
A. ACTION REQUESTED 
Immediately require that: 
(1) The label of repaglinide-containing medications (PRANDIN, PRANDIMET) include 
information on a serious drug-drug interaction with clopidogrel (PLAVIX) that could 
result in severe hypoglycemia; and  
(2) The labels of both repaglinide-containing medications and clopidogrel include a 
contraindication to the use of the two drugs together due to this interaction. 
B. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
1. Background: Repaglinide and clopidogrel 
 
Repaglinide is marketed, both on its own (PRANDIN) and in combination with the diabetes 
medication metformin (PRANDIMET), for the treatment of Type 2 diabetes.1 It is a member of 
the family of diabetes drugs known as meglitinides, which stimulate the release of insulin from 
cells in the pancreas.2  
 
                                                           
1 In the remainder of this petition, repaglinide-containing medications will be referred to collectively as 
“repaglinide.” 
2 Carilion Materials Management. Label: PRANDIN (repaglinide) tablets. August 2016. 
https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=e2a07020-a596-4282-bb7c-
c9ebe6edcd61&audience=consumer. Accessed December 20, 2016. 
 
Public Citizen 
Petition to the FDA on Repaglinide-Clopidogrel Interaction 
December 21, 2016 
2 
 
Clopidogrel (PLAVIX) is a widely used drug that decreases blood clot formation by interfering 
with platelet activation and aggregation.3 It was approved by the FDA to reduce the long-term 
risk of a new heart attack or stroke in patients who have suffered a recent heart attack or stroke 
or have established peripheral vascular disease (for example, evidence of narrowed or blocked 
arteries in the legs or neck). The drug also is approved for the immediate treatment of acute 
coronary syndrome to reduce the chance of subsequent heart attack or stroke.  
 
2. Studies showing risk of dangerous drug interaction 
 
In October 2014, a study (Tornio et al.) demonstrating a significant interaction between 
clopidogrel and repaglinide was published in the journal Clinical Pharmacology & 
Therapeutics.4 Researchers in Finland studied 9 healthy subjects who were given repaglinide 
with and without clopidogrel over separate three-day periods, using a crossover design. 
Repaglinide at a 0.25 milligram (mg) dose was given to subjects one hour after either a placebo 
or clopidogrel on the first and third days of each study period. During the clopidogrel 
administration period, a dose of 300 mg of clopidogrel was given on the first day of treatment, 
with 75 mg given on the second and third days. The researchers then measured blood levels of 
both repaglinide and glucose at 5 minutes before and 15, 30, 45, 60, 80, and 100 minutes after 
and at 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5, 7, and 9 hours after the administration of repaglinide.  
 
Clopidogrel increased the geometric mean area under the concentration-time curve of repaglinide 
by 5.1-fold on day 1 of clopidogrel administration (300 mg dose), and by 3.9-fold on day 3 of 
administration (75 mg dose), compared to levels of repaglinide when given alone (P < 0.001). 
The elimination half-life of repaglinide was lengthened by 42% after the 300 mg dose of 
clopidogrel on the first day and by 22% after a 75 mg dose on the third day (P < 0.005). 
 
The increased blood levels of repaglinide resulted in a significant drop in blood glucose levels 
when subjects were given clopidogrel concomitantly, as seen in the following table:

The combination of repaglinide and a 300 mg dose of clopidogrel caused the minimum glucose 
concentration to decrease by a clinically significant average of 39% from baseline by day 1 (the 
decrease was statistically significant compared with placebo).  
 
Based on an in vitro study, the authors identified the metabolite clopidogrel acyl-β-D-
glucuronide as the likely culprit acting as a strong inhibitor of the CYP2C8 hepatic enzyme 
responsible for the metabolic clearance of repaglinide. 
 
A 2016 Japanese study confirmed both the degree of and the probable mechanism behind the 
clopidogrel-repaglinide interaction.5 The researchers tested various drug interactions, including 
clopidogrel and repaglinide, in 24 healthy male volunteers. In the initial phase, subjects received 
0.1 mg of repaglinide, followed by water; in the second, drug interaction phase, subjects received 
0.1 mg of repaglinide, along with 300 mg of clopidogrel. Blood samples were taken at 0.25, 0.5, 
1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 24 hours after dosing. 
 
The concentration of repaglinide, as measured by the area under the curve up to 8 hours after 
dosing, increased by 3.1-fold when co-administered with clopidogrel, compared to repaglinide 
given alone (P < 0.05). Similar to the 2014 study, the researchers’ tests concluded that 
clopidogrel acyl-β-D-glucuronide, inhibiting CYP2C8, was most likely responsible for the 
interaction with repaglinide. 
 
3. Health Canada and FDA actions thus far 
 
On July 31, 2015, Health Canada issued an alert to health care professionals warning about the 
risk of dangerously low blood sugar levels when repaglinide and clopidogrel are taken together.6 
Health Canada also required that the Canadian product labels for both drugs be updated to reflect 
information about this dangerous drug interaction and to include a contraindication that warns 
against taking the two drugs together under any circumstances. The Canadian warning for 
patients explains, “Severe hypoglycemia [low blood sugar] can cause loss of consciousness, 
seizure, brain damage and even death.”7 
 
The FDA has not taken similar actions. Regarding the U.S. product labels, only the label for 
clopidogrel includes information on the interaction with repaglinide, within the Drug Interactions 
section.8 Inexplicably, the FDA has not required the same information to be inserted into the

label for repaglinide.9 Moreover, there is no contraindication to the use of the two drugs together 
in either label,10,11 as was put in place in Canada. 
 
4. Reasons to include a contraindication, in both labels, in addition to information in the 
Drug Interactions section 
 
In addition to adding information on the clopidogrel-repaglinide interaction to the repaglinide 
label, there are several compelling reasons to add a contraindication to both labels. 
 
First, the degree of hypoglycemia seen in the 2014 study (Tornio et al.) that served as the basis 
for the 2015 Health Canada risk communication was clinically significant (see Table) and poses 
a substantial danger for certain diabetic patients who are already at risk for hypoglycemic 
episodes. Second, clopidogrel is very widely used, including in the diabetes population (which 
has a higher rate of cardiovascular disease than the general population) for whom repaglinide is 
indicated. And third, because there are many alternatives to repaglinide for diabetes treatment, 
the risks of using these two drugs concomitantly outweigh any benefits. 
 
C. ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT  
 
We claim categorical exclusion under 21 C.F.R. § 25.31(a) from the environmental assessment 
requirement. An assessment is not required because the requested action would not increase the 
use of the active moiety that is the subject of this petition.

Citizen Petition to FDA Commissioner 
Revoke FDA Clearance of The Pneumoliner Containment Device for Power Morcellators 
Date: 4115116 
The undersigned submits this petition under Statute 10.30 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic 
Act or the Public Health Service Act to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to revoke the 
recent clearance, by CDRH, of the uPneumoliner'' Containment System for use with Power 
Moree/la tors. 
A. Action Requested 
Revoke CDRH clearance of the Pneumoliner Containment System manufactured by Advanced 
Surgical Concepts of Bray, Ireland. This clearance was announced in a FDA press release dated 
4f7/16 by CDRH chief scientist, Dr. William Maisel. 
The present citizen petition is respectfully requesting that the commissioner immediately revoke FDA 
clearance of this medical device on the basis of inadequate oncological safety information and testing. 
Options moving forward are to: 1) ban the device or 2) reclassify it to a class Ill device and require 
PMA assessment. We also request that the commissioner seek active guidance from the FDA's Center 
for Hematology and Oncology Products for expert assessment of the CDRH's action regarding both 
the "power morcellator" and "Pneumoliner" devices. 
B. Statement of Grounds 
This Citizen Petition is focused on the recent CDRH clearance of a containment device, termed 
"Pneumoliner" manufactured by Advanced Surgical Concepts based in Bray, Ireland. This device is 
designed for use in gynecological surgery in association with a medical device known as a "power 
morcellator". 
On April 7, 2016 CDRH, via Dr. Maisel, released the following press-release announcing the CDRH 
clearance of the "Pneumoliner device": 
http://www.fda.gov/NewsEvents/Newsroom/PressAnnouncements/ucm494650.htm 
As background, following a year long public health campaign and careful analysis by the FDA's public 
health experts starting in November 2013, the CDRH released an liE black-box warning against the 
use of power morcellator devices in the vast majority of women. This decision in November 2014 has 
virtually eliminated power morcellation as a routine practice. The decision was made given the 
inordinately high, and previously unreported, risk of iatrogenic cancer upstaging in women with occult 
uterine cancers. In November 2014, it was clarified that up to one in 350 unsuspecting women across 
the United States and abroad, with symptomatic uterine fibroids are placed in potentially deadly harm's 
way by gynecological morcellation. 
It was a striking fact for medical history that, despite being unable to definitively diagnose occult 
uterine cancers preoperatively, a vast majority of gynecological surgeons were willing to morcellate 
uterine fibroid tumors and risk mechanically upstaging potentially deadly malignancies. 
Even more surprising was the CDRH leadership failed to ban the power morcellator device from 
market - this, despite having identified the high oncological risk of morcellation and having recognized 
that hundreds, if not thousands, of unsuspecting women had been harmed and killed by iatrogenic 
cancer upstaging using these FDA cleared power morcellators for nearly 2 decades. 
The CDRH action on "power morcellator devices" can be found here: 
http://www.fda.gov/downloads/MedicaiDevices/DeviceRegulationandGuidance/GuidanceDocuments/U 
CM424123.pdf 
We find it of significant interest that the designer and manufacturer of the Pneumoliner device were 
present at the FDA hearing of July 10-11 , 2014, apparently, by invitation to present their novel 
technology. 
The Pneumoliner device was subsequently cleared by the CDRH for marketing in the United States in 
April2016, without any clinical trials to demonstrate its oncological safety. 
It is astonishing to have heard the CDRH's chief scientist state that: "We want to be clear that, 
although the device [i.e., the pneumoliner] has been shown to successfully contain morcellated tissue, 
it has not been proven to reduce the risk of cancer spread during surgery." From an ethical and public 
health perspective, this is an astonishing statement and demonstrates the magnitude of the logical 
(and ethical) error committed by the CDRH leadership in releasing this device into the US 
marketplace. 
The present critique and citizen petition centers on the fact that the CDRH leadership understands the 
unacceptable and high risk of iatrogenic cancer upstaging using power morcellation. The CDRH also 
recognizes (and was advised by their expert panel in July 2014) that the practice of morcellating 
tumors with malignant potential inside a patient's body cavity is considered an serious technical error 
by every surgical specialty, except gynecology. Yet, in a shockingly illogical action, the CDRH 
leadership cleared the Pneumoliner device for use in women- this, without requiring any appropriate 
clinical trial to demonstrate that this device is. in fact, oncologically safe. 
Indeed, the only published peer-review study of a containment device (not the Pneumoliner itself ) 
used with power morcellators demonstrated a near 10% "leak" rate - even in the absence of the bag 
breaking. Here is a link to that study: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26348384 
Based on the unacceptably high AVOIDABLE mortality risk posed by iatrogenic cancer upstaging 
using morcellation, the present Citizen Petition is submitted to request the following actions of the FDA 
commissioner: 1) immediate reclassification of the Pneumoliner device to a Class Ill status and 
requirement of Pre-Market Approval (PMA) standards, 2) Immediate requirement that the manufacturer 
perform well powered pre-clinical and clinical safety and efficacy trials, subjected to objective cross-
disciplinary peer review, to specifically demonstrate oncological safety. 3) consider whether a clinical 
trial to demonstrate oncological safety of the Pneumoliner device is even ethically feasible (that is, who 
will the subjects be? can subject patients with suspected uterine cancer be subjected to power 
morcellation using the Pneumoliner device to determine if their cancers spread? Can a broad subset of 
patients consisting of patients with occult and unidentifiable malignancies be subjected to power 
morcellation in a trial?), 4) Actively seek guidance from the FDA's Office of Hematology and Oncology 
Products to formally weigh whether it is acceptable to retain the Pneumoliner device and power 
morcellators on the market- given their high and indeterminate oncological risk, respectively. 
This Citizen Petition is prompted by the CDRH leadership's unacceptable and unsafe clearance of 
the Pneumoliner device, while admitting that its oncological risk is fully unknown. We hope the FDA 
commissioner will take a close look at this inappropriate regulatory behavior and correct this potentially 
deadly regulatory action. 
The FDA commissioner must consider carefully that with the availability of this potentially unsafe 
device to gynecological surgeons. under the guise of being a safety device. could resurrect the use of 
power morcellators in unsuspecting women. 
A Fundament fact is that, the oncological safety of this new device is, as the CDRH's chief scientist 
stated, "not proven". When the use of the power morcellator itself was restrained because of the 
unacceptable oncological risk, how can the CDRH logically (or ethically) justify releasing a 
compendium module for this device whose cancer risk was not definitively assessed and ruled out? 
Please note, that to date many gynecological surgeons continue to believe the oncological hazard of 
power morcellation to be overblown and the FDA, and others', studies to over-estimate the risk of 
occult or missed uterine cancers. 
We ask that the commissioner move immediately to act on the present petition to secure women's 
health from this indeterminate and potentially deadly hazard.

Petition_Text:
1 
 
ELECTRONIC SUBMISSION 
Dockets Management Branch, HF A‐305 
US Food and Drug Administration 
Division of Dockets Management 
US Food and Drug Administration 
Department of Health and Human Services 
5630 Fishers Lane, Room 1061 
Rockville, MD 02852 
 
Citizen Petition 
 
Date: May 12, 2016 
 
The undersigned submits this petition under 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 of the Federal Food, Drug, and 
Cosmetic Act to request that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs amend the package labeling 
for low‐dose vaginal estrogen products and the Guidance for Industry: Noncontraceptive 
Estrogen Drug Products for the Treatment of Vasomotor Symptoms and Vulvar and Vaginal 
Atrophy Symptoms—Recommended Prescribing Information for Health Care Providers and 
Patient Labeling (Guidance) as specified below (Action Requested).  
 
A.  ACTION REQUESTED 
 
The North American Menopause Society (NAMS) and the Working Group on Women’s Health 
and Well‐Being in Menopause request that the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) modify 
the label for low‐dose vaginal estrogen products approved for treating symptoms of 
vulvovaginal atrophy (VVA) and the Guidance as follows. This would apply to low‐dose vaginal 
estrogen products approved for symptoms of VVA, with pharmacokinetic data showing that the 
systemic absorption of estrogen maintains blood levels within or below the postmenopausal 
range. This request does not apply to estrogen products approved for treatment of vasomotor 
symptoms (hot flashes). Low‐dose vaginal estrogen products approved for treatment of VVA 
should have a different product label than systemic (higher‐dose) oral or transdermal estrogen 
products. 
 
The label should be modified to accurately reflect the relevant evidence‐based information for 
low‐dose vaginal estrogen products. 
 
The “Warnings and Precautions” section of the labeling should highlight (bold) the information 
related to the following medical concerns for those using low‐dose vaginal products for VVA: 
 
a. Genital bleeding is a concern because bleeding may be a sign of endometrial 
cancer. 
b. Women with estrogen‐sensitive breast cancer should consult with their 
oncologists before use of the product. 
2 
 
The warnings identified in the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) trials of oral systemic (higher‐
dose) hormone therapy (HT) should remain in the label (“Warnings and Precautions”) in regular 
text and font, but the boxed warning should be removed. The warnings related to high‐dose 
oral estrogen and progestin products may not be applicable in women using low‐dose vaginal 
estrogens, and hence, not generally using progestins. 
 
The Patient Labeling should reflect these changes (specific wording suggestions for the 
modified label are provided in the Menopause editorial, “Why the Product Labeling for Low‐
Dose Vaginal Estrogen Should Be Changed,”1 attached). 
 
B.  STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
1. BACKGROUND 
 
Overview 
The Working Group on Women’s Health and Well‐Being in Menopause, affiliated with a number 
of medical societies, including NAMS, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, 
The Endocrine Society, the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, the International 
Society for the Study of Women’s Sexual Health, and other professional and women’s 
organizations, is requesting FDA to modify the product labeling of low‐dose vaginal estrogen 
products approved for treatment of symptoms of VVA. The working group was convened at 
the request of a Town Hall Meeting held at the NAMS 2014 Annual Meeting. The findings of the 
Working Group were published in the September 2014 issue of the journal Menopause (see 
attached editorial) and presented at a workshop convened by FDA on low‐dose estrogen on 
November 10, 2015, with many materials and written testimonials submitted online in advance 
of the workshop. 
 
Background 
Vulvovaginal atrophy (also known as genitourinary syndrome of menopause) is a common and 
progressive condition that adversely affects the health and quality of life of many 
postmenopausal women.2 
 
Vulvovaginal atrophy is a medical condition estimated to affect approximately 32 million 
women in the United States; however, it is estimated that less than 7% (2.3 million) of affected 
women use FDA‐approved prescription therapy.3 Symptoms of VVA are often overlapping and 
include vaginal dryness, itching and burning, vulvar irritation, and painful intercourse 
(dyspareunia) and may be associated with a higher risk of vaginal infections or recurrent 
bladder infections. A recent survey of women’s knowledge of VVA, the REVIVE survey, reported 
that the most commonly occurring VVA symptoms included vaginal dryness (55% of 
participants), dyspareunia (44%), and irritation (37%), with negative effects on enjoyment of 
sex (59%).3 Also reported were interference with sleep, diminished general enjoyment of life, 
and temperament reported by 24%, 23%, and 23% of participants, respectively. In addition to 
adversely affecting women and their partners’ quality of life, there is an increase in medical 
3 
 
healthcare costs because of increases in office visits, need for treatment of infections, and 
potential hospitalization for sepsis caused by bladder infections in older women.4 
The most efficacious treatment of VVA includes products containing estrogen. Currently 
available estrogen‐containing treatments include oral, transdermal, and vaginal products. Low‐
dose vaginal estrogen therapy has low systemic exposure, with blood levels similar to 
endogenous estrogen levels normally found in postmenopausal women.5‐7 
 
However, the product labeling of all these products, regardless of the mode of delivery or dose, 
carry the same warnings and do not provide distinction among oral products, which undergo 
hepatic first‐pass metabolism, systemic transdermal doses, and low‐dose to very‐low‐dose 
vaginal products. Concerns about the safety of VVA because of the current boxed warning has 
been reported as preventing the use of FDA‐approved low‐dose vaginal therapy.1 
 
FDA Background and Label for Hormone Therapy 
 
FDA approves drugs for use in HT for menopause symptoms and advises women who choose to 
use hormones to use them, in consultation with their healthcare providers, for the shortest 
time necessary at the lowest effective dose. The product label includes the risks of HT, including 
that, for some women, HT may increase their chance of getting blood clots, heart attacks, 
strokes, breast cancer, and gallbladder disease. For a woman with a uterus, estrogen increases 
the chance of getting endometrial cancer (cancer of the uterine lining). Adding a progestin or 
progesterone has been shown to lower this risk. 
 
The National Institutes of Health’s Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) conducted several large, 
randomized, clinical studies, including a large study to determine the effects of conjugated 
equine estrogens (CEE) 0.625 mg daily combined continuously with the progestin 
medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) 2.5 mg on the prevention of heart disease. The 
participants in the study were not taking the medication for an FDA‐approved use. The estrogen 
plus progestin study was halted in 2002 because the health risks appeared to outweigh the 
benefits for participants taking estrogen with progestin for chronic disease prevention. Results 
from this study reported that the enrolled population taking oral CEE with MPA had an 
increased risk of early cardiovascular disease, stroke, breast cancer, and blood clots. The initial 
publication of the study findings reported that the absolute excess risks per 10,000 woman‐
years in the group treated with the combination estrogen‐progestin product were seven more 
heart attacks, eight more strokes, 18 more blood clots, and eight more invasive breast cancers 
than in the placebo control group. Conversely, the absolute risk reductions per 10,000 woman‐
years for the estrogen‐progestin group were six fewer colorectal cancers and five fewer hip 
fractures than in the placebo group. 
 
As a result of the WHI hormone studies, FDA requested changes to the existing boxed warning 
in FDA‐approved labeling for estrogen‐alone drugs and requested that a boxed warning be 
added to FDA‐approved labeling for combination estrogen‐progestin drugs. In addition, FDA 
requested that a boxed warning be added to FDA‐approved labeling for progestin‐alone drugs 
approved for use in combination with estrogen because the progestin‐alone drugs are 
4 
 
frequently used concomitantly with estrogen‐alone drugs and would therefore share the same 
or similar risks as fixed‐dose combination estrogen‐progestin drugs. In general, the warnings 
highlight that the WHI study reported increased risks of heart attack, stroke, breast cancer, and 
blood clots, and because of these risks, estrogens with or without progestins should be 
prescribed at the lowest effective doses and for the shortest duration consistent with 
treatment goals and risks for the individual woman. 
 
2. ARGUMENT 
 
The current boxed warning on the package label for low‐dose vaginal estrogen products used 
for VVA indications is not evidence based or appropriate to the risks identified with low‐dose 
vaginal estrogens used for VVA. The boxed warning, which reflects current oral estrogen class 
labeling, states: WARNING: ENDOMETRIAL CANCER, CARDIOVASCULAR DISORDERS, BREAST 
CANCER, and PROBABLE DEMENTIA. This warning is based on extrapolations of data from 
randomized, clinical trials of systemic HT, primarily the WHI, which involved substantially higher 
oral doses leading to increased systemic levels of estrogen and do not apply to low‐dose vaginal 
estrogen products used for the treatment of symptoms of VVA that do not undergo first‐pass 
hepatic metabolism and are without evidence of systemic exposure.  
 
The American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists released a Committee Opinion in 
March 2016 (no. 659) on the use of vaginal estrogen in breast cancer survivors8: “Among 
women with a history of estrogen‐dependent breast cancer who are experiencing urogenital 
symptoms, vaginal estrogen should be reserved for those patients who are unresponsive to 
non‐hormonal remedies. The decision to use vaginal estrogen may be made in coordination 
with a woman’s oncologist. Additionally, it should be preceded by an informed decision‐making 
and consent process in which the woman has the information and resources to consider the 
benefits and potential risks of low‐dose vaginal estrogen. Data do not show an increased risk of 
cancer recurrence among women currently undergoing treatment for breast cancer or those 
with a personal history of breast cancer who use vaginal estrogen to relieve urogenital 
symptoms.” 
 
This petition by NAMS and the Working Group on Women’s Health and Well‐Being in 
Menopause is based in part on the following issues: 
 
a. 
The dramatic differences in blood hormone levels achieved by low‐dose vaginal 
estrogen (eg, Vagifem tablets [estradiol 10 µg], Estring [releasing estradiol 
7.5 µg/d], or comparable low‐dose vaginal estrogen cream formulations) versus 
standard systemic estrogen therapy (whether oral, transdermal, or vaginal ring). 
b. 
Differences in metabolism of oral and local low‐dose vaginal products. 
c. 
Absence of randomized trial evidence or consistent observational evidence linking 
low‐dose vaginal estrogen to cancer, cardiovascular disease, dementia, or other 
conditions highlighted in the boxed warning. 
d. 
Absence of evidence that changes in blood hormone levels of the small magnitude 
achieved with these products increased the risk of any of these conditions. 
5 
 
e. 
As a result of the boxed warning, a large number of older women with symptomatic 
VVA and genitourinary symptoms are being undertreated or turn to unapproved, 
unlabeled compounded products and do not receive the substantial health and 
quality‐of‐life benefits that the low‐dose vaginal estrogen products approved for 
VVA could provide. 
f. 
The boxed warning on the package label for low‐dose vaginal estrogen discourages 
clinicians from prescribing the product and women from taking it even after 
purchase. 
g. 
The inclusion of boxed warnings for estrogen plus progestin, although progestin is 
not generally needed with low‐dose vaginal estrogen products. 
1. 
This labeling is confusing to healthcare providers, indicating that perhaps 
they should be prescribing a progestin. One of the benefits of low‐dose 
vaginal products is the lack of a need for concomitant progestins. 
 
Specific products that meet the definition of low‐dose vaginal products having blood levels 
within the physiologic hormone postmenopausal range when dosed appropriately include 
Pfizer—7.5 µg vaginal estradiol ring (Estring) 
Pfizer—Low‐dose vaginal CEE cream dosed 0.5 g (0.5 g = 0.625 mg) is administered 
intravaginally in a twice‐weekly regimen or in a cyclic regimen of 21 days of therapy 
followed by 7 days off therapy (Premarin) 
Novo Nordisk—Vaginal estradiol 10 µg tablets twice weekly (Vagifem) 
Generic Vagifem—Vaginal estradiol 10 µg tablets twice weekly 
 
Other products currently in development include low‐dose vaginal gel by TherapeuticsMD and a 
low‐dose vaginal estradiol (Estrace) cream by Actavis. 
 
On November 10, 2015, FDA convened a workshop on the topic of the labeling for lower‐dose 
estrogen products delivered vaginally, intended to treat moderate to severe symptoms of VVA 
caused by menopause. Prominent experts in the menopause field, including leaders from 
NAMS, testified in support of the label change. 
 
Efforts by NAMS to change the product label have been supported by the Endocrine Society, 
the American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the American Medical Women’s 
Association, the American Society for Reproductive Medicine, the Academy of Women’s Health, 
the International Society for the Study of Women’s Sexual Health, the American Association of 
Nurse Practitioners in Women’s Health, the American Association of Nurse Practitioners, the 
South Atlantic Association of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Society for Women’s 
Health Research, among others. Consumer organizations include the National Women’s Health 
Network, the National Organization for Women, the RedHot Mamas, ellendolgen.com, 
blogher.com, vibrantnation.com, and speakingofwomenshealth.com, among others. The 
Citizen’s Petition launched by NAMS received 430 signatures when submitted to FDA for the 
workshop on November 10, 2015, and currently has 620 signatures.  
 
 
6 
 
C. 
CONCLUSION 
 
NAMS and the Working Group on Women’s Health and Well‐Being in Menopause recommend a 
modification to the current label for low‐dose vaginal estrogen products approved for VVA in 
order to clarify and better inform postmenopausal women and their healthcare providers. We 
understand that changing the label and boxed warnings for HT products is complex. The 
modified label would more closely reflect the safety profile of low‐dose vaginal estrogen 
products, which would ENHANCE patient safety by emphasizing the key information that 
women and clinicians need to know about the products. 
 
Modification of the product label for low‐dose vaginal estrogen products reflects additional 
knowledge and safety that has arisen from safety surveillance of increased use of low‐dose 
vaginal estrogens over the past approximately 14 years since the class labeling reflecting the 
WHI: this will also demonstrate FDA’s commitment to ensuring that consumers 
(postmenopausal women) and healthcare providers are updated and well informed about the 
appropriate and relevant risks. 
 
Information for the Public  
 
Educational efforts by FDA could include a public awareness campaign about the use of low‐
dose vaginal estrogen products for VVA that would highlight the low systemic blood levels 
comparable to those of normal postmenopausal women and FDA approved products that 
currently meet that standard and could include warnings about the unique risks of 
compounding for those choosing to use compounded non‐FDA‐approved vaginal estrogen 
therapies. 
 
D. 
ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT 
 
The actions requested in this petition are not within any of the categories for which an 
environmental assessment is required, pursuant to 21 CFR 25.22. 
 
E. 
ECONOMIC IMPACT 
 
Information on the economic impact of this proposal will be submitted if requested by the 
Commissioner. 
 
F. 
CERTIFICATION  
 
The undersigned certifies, that, to the best knowledge and belief of the undersigned, this 
petition includes all information and views on which the petition relies, and that it includes 
representative data and information known to the petitioner which is unfavorable to the 
petition.

The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), Earthjustice, Food Animal Concerns 
Trust, Public Citizen, U.S. Public Interest Research Group, and California Public Interest 
Research Group submit this Supplement to their September 13, 2016 Petition (docket 
FDA-2016-P-2737) to withdraw approval of the use of medically important antibiotics in 
livestock and poultry for disease-prevention purposes.1 
FDA has not ruled on the Petition or referred it to hearing. Accordingly, the petitioners

resubmission. 21 C.F.R. § 10.30(g).  
Since the Petition was filed, evidence supporting withdrawal of disease-prevention uses

disease-prevention purposes is not safe.

Metabolic Therapy Inc.  recognizes that the administrative record of a final monograph 
may be reopened to consider new data and information, see 2 1 CFR 330.10 (a)( 12)(i), and that 
the Commissioner may publish a proposed amendment if the Commissioner finds general 
recognition of safety, effectiveness and labeling under 21 CFR 330.10 (a)(4).  Metabolic Therapy 
Inc. submits this petition under section 10.30 of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act to 
request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to amend the OTC Acne Drug Products 
monograph for active ingredient to indicate that chromium is safe and effective for acne 
treatment.  
 
I. 
Action Requested 
 
Pursuant to 21 C.F.R. § 10.30, Metabolic Therapy asks the Commissioner of the Food 
and Drug Administration (FDA) to amend the OTC Acne Drug Products monograph to address 
chromium herein as an active ingredient for purposes of the Acne Drug Products monograph, 
instructing that topical acne products containing chromium are covered under the monograph 
2 
 
instead of "new drugs" for which manufacturers must complete a New Drug Application (NDA) 
in accordance with 21 U.S.C. section 355.  
  
II. 
Statement of Grounds 
 
Insulin and blood sugar abnormalities have been identified to be involved in the 
promotion of acne. The acne vulgaris is a chronic disorder of pilosebaceous units on the face, 
chest and back. Acne lesions are caused by a combination of bacteria normally found on the skin, 
including Propionibacterium acnes (P. acnes) and coagulase-negative staphylococci and 
micrococci. P. acnes produce a lipase enzyme that hydrolyzes triglycerides of the sebaceous 
gland into free fatty acids. The therapeutic value of tolbutamide and other oral sulphonylureas in 
acne has resulted in some scientists referring to acne as diabetes of the skin [1]. When glucose 
levels and insulin levels rise, the liver responds to the higher insulin levels by converting the 
higher glucose levels into higher levels of systemic triglycerides in the blood. Also, insulin may 
promote acne by its peripheral effect on cellular carbohydrate metabolism [2]. While human 
sebum also consists of squalene, esters of glycerol, wax and cholesterol, as well as free 
cholesterol and fatty acids, triglycerides and fatty acids, taken together, account for the 
predominant proportion (57.5%), followed by wax esters (26%) and squalene (12%) [3]. When 
there are higher triglycerides available in the blood, the skin cells will convert the increasing 
levels of triglycerides to increase the sebum production. Increased sebum secretion is considered, 
among all features, the major one involved in the pathophysiology of acne [4] as the higher 
peroxidation of sebum production, the better environment favorable for bacteria to develop acne.  
 
Epidemiological studies suggest that traditional diets with a low glycemic load are 
protective against acne [5] and one open label trial showed that 400 mcg of chromium improves 
acne [6]. Further, there is significant scientific agreement among experts qualified by scientific 
training and experience to evaluate such claims that chromium reduces insulin resistance and 
aids carbohydrate metabolism. Chromium supplements are widely used as an alternative remedy 
for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). Vitro study findings show that chromium may improve 
insulin sensitivity by enhancing intracellular insulin receptor. (September 
2007,http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17697867).  
3 
 
 
Chromium supplement alone additionally improve triglycerides and HDL-C levels, and 
usual doses of chromium supplementation does not increase the risk of adverse events compared 
with placebo (June 2014, http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24635480). It is also suggested 
that the amelioration of acne vulgaris by insulin may depend more on its effect on the cellular 
intermediary metabolism of glucose than on its effect on blood sugar levels. Studies that 
chromium as a nutritional enhancement to glucose metabolism can be traced back to the 1950s, 
when it was suggested that brewer’s yeast contained a glucose tolerance factor (GTF) that 
prevented diabetes in experimental animals [7]. Further, interest regarding chromium 
administration in patients with diabetes was kindled by the observation in the 1970s that it truly 
was an essential nutrient required for normal carbohydrate metabolism. 
 
Chromium supplementation is safe for long-term use. Recent reviews of the safety of 
chromium by the Institute of Medicine [8] and by Berner et al. [9] have concluded that 
chromium is safe. Results from controlled clinical trials have shown that treatment with 
chromium at doses up to 1,000 μg/day and for periods as long as 64 months does not result in 
any toxic effects [10]. There have been isolated reports of serious adverse events, including 
kidney failure, associated with chromium treatment, but no evidence suggests that chromium 
increases the damages and the relationship of chromium to these events is not clear.  
 
Details of the literature review and analysis are included as part of this submission for 
convenience.

CITIZEN PETITION 
Sandoz Inc. (“Sandoz”) hereby submits this citizen petition pursuant to 21 C.F.R. 
§§ 10.25, 10.30 and Sections 505(j) and 505(q) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act 
(“FDCA”), 21 U.S.C. §§ 355(j), (q).  For the scientific reasons discussed herein, Sandoz 
respectfully requests that the Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) refrain from approving any 
abbreviated new drug application (“ANDA”) that references Advair Diskus 100/50 (fluticasone 
propionate 100 mcg and salmeterol 50 mcg inhalation powder) as the reference listed drug 
(“RLD”) unless it contains the results of a pharmacokinetic (“PK”) bioequivalence study that 
meets the necessary study design parameters described below in order to ensure the safety and 
efficacy of all ANDA products referencing this RLD. 
I. 
ACTIONS REQUESTED 
Sandoz is one of the largest generic pharmaceutical manufacturers in the United States.  
In 2010, Sandoz acquired Oriel Therapeutics, Inc., gaining additional technology and experience 
in the development of generic orally inhaled drug products (“OIDPs”), including ongoing 
research and development of a fluticasone propionate/salmeterol combination product.  Based on 
its extensive in-house research, Sandoz has a highly informed perspective on the development of 
generic versions of Advair Diskus. 
GlaxoSmithKline (“GSK”) is the developer and manufacturer of Advair Diskus.  
Although the final patent listed for Advair Diskus in FDA’s Approved Drug Products with 
Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations (“Orange Book”) expired on August 23, 2016 (with six-
month pediatric exclusivity), there are still no FDA-approved generics.  This is largely due to the 
fact that, until relatively recently in 2013, FDA had not articulated the type and quantum of data 
it would require for approval of generic OIDPs.  Among other issues, the PK batch-to-batch 
Page 2 of 20 
 
variability of OIDPs has been a consistent concern for both regulators and industry in the context 
of generic development for several years.1 
In September 2013, FDA released its bioequivalence recommendations for generic 
versions of Advair Diskus.2  FDA’s recommendations provide specific guidance on the design of 
bioequivalence studies that the agency expects to see in ANDAs referencing Advair Diskus as 
the RLD.  However, as discussed below, FDA’s draft guidance lacks the study design 
requirements that are necessary to address certain drug-specific characteristics of the Advair 
Diskus 100/50 RLD—namely, the degree of PK batch-to-batch variability and the rapid onset of 
peak plasma concentration for both active ingredients.  As a result of these RLD characteristics, 
targeted study design requirements are needed to accurately demonstrate PK bioequivalence for 
generic versions of Advair Diskus 100/50.      
Sandoz is aware that FDA has accepted for review ANDAs that reference Advair Diskus 
as the RLD.  However, to the extent that these ANDA applicants relied solely on FDA’s draft 
guidance in conducting their PK bioequivalence studies, Sandoz is concerned that the 
applications may fail to contain accurate and generalizable evidence of PK bioequivalence for 
their low-strength (100/50) products.  Accordingly, Sandoz requests that FDA refrain from 
approving any ANDA for a generic version of Advair Diskus 100/50 unless the agency ensures 
that: 
(1) Type I error rate is adequately controlled in PK bioequivalence testing, including 
accounting for Type I error rate inflation caused by batch-to-batch variability of 
the RLD; 
(2) the dose used in PK bioequivalence testing retains the necessary sensitivity to 
product differences existing at the marketed single inhalation dose of the RLD; 
and 
(3) the sampling schedule used in PK bioequivalence testing is robust and centered 
around the actual time to maximum plasma concentration of both active 
ingredients at the marketed dose of the RLD.  
As discussed below, Sandoz’s research confirms that the above PK bioequivalence study 
design requirements are essential to ensuring: (i) an accurate and generalizable bioequivalence 
conclusion with adequate Type I error rate control in light of the inherent RLD batch-to-batch 
variability, and (ii) an adequate capture, and thereby accurate comparison, of maximum plasma 
concentrations in light of the rapid absorption of the RLD product.  These requirements are

II. 
STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
A. 
The Advair Diskus RLD 
Advair Diskus is a combination product containing fluticasone propionate (a 
corticosteroid) and salmeterol (a long-acting beta2-adrenergic agonist (“LABA”)) in a powder 
formulation for oral inhalation.  The product is indicated for long-term, twice-daily use for 
treatment of asthma in patients ages 4 years and older and for maintenance treatment of airflow 
obstruction and reducing exacerbations in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 
(“COPD”).  GSK first obtained approval for Advair Diskus on August 24, 2000 and currently 
markets three strengths of the product:  low-strength (100/50 mcg), mid-strength (250/50 mcg), 
and high-strength (500/50 mcg).3    
In July 2012, Congress passed the Generic Drug User Fee Amendments of 2012 
(“GDUFA”) as part of the Food and Drug Administration Safety and Innovation Act 
(“FDASIA”).  In its GDUFA Performance Goals letter, FDA agreed to begin work on several 
specific regulatory science initiatives.4  These initiatives addressed, as the first item, the 
bioequivalence of locally acting OIDPs, which currently lack generic competition.  FDA 
promised to continue to develop “new and improved” study designs or establish “alternative 
approaches” to ensure the bioequivalence of locally delivered OIDPs in order to facilitate more 
efficient development of generic products in this sector.5  FDA held a public meeting on its 
initiatives a year later in June 2013, where representatives of both industry and academia 
emphasized the need for reliable, high-quality generic versions of respiratory drug-device 
combination products.6   
FDA’s regulatory science initiatives played a key role in its published recommendations 
for demonstrating the bioequivalence of generic OIDPs.  In September 2013, FDA released its 
draft guidance on bioequivalence recommendations for generic versions of Advair Diskus, which 
represented only FDA’s second such guidance in this space.7  The resulting fluticasone 
propionate/salmeterol draft guidance provides specific recommendations on bioequivalence

B. 
The Bioequivalence Standard 
Under Section 505(j) of the FDCA, an ANDA must contain “information to show that the 
new drug is bioequivalent to the [RLD],” and FDA may refuse to approve an ANDA if, among 
other things, “information submitted in the application is insufficient to show that the drug is 
bioequivalent to the [RLD].”8  A generic drug is considered to be bioequivalent to an RLD if 
“the rate and extent of absorption of the drug do not show a significant difference from the rate 
and extent of absorption of the [RLD] when administered at the same molar dose of the 
therapeutic ingredient under similar experimental conditions in either a single dose or multiple 
doses.”9  Notably, FDA’s regulations make clear that this bioequivalence standard may only be 
met “in an appropriately designed study.”10   
As part of the requirement that there not be a “significant difference” in the rate and 
extent of absorption (i.e., the bioavailability11) of a generic drug when compared to that of the 
RLD, FDA has generally adopted an 80-125% limit of acceptance for bioequivalence testing 
results.  Specifically, FDA guidance provides that, in order to establish bioequivalence, “the 
calculated confidence interval should fall within a [bioequivalence] limit,” and this limit is 
“usually 80-125%… based on a clinical judgment that a test product with [bioavailability] 
measures outside this range should be denied market access.”12  Nonetheless, it is critical that 
any study obtaining bioequivalence results to be judged within the 80-125% limit be 
appropriately designed to provide a valid comparison. 
In addition, Type I error rate control is fundamental to bioequivalence testing, as it is the 
standard for statistical hypothesis tests that form the basis of FDA drug approval decisions.  In 
the bioequivalence context, the Type I error rate is defined as the probability of concluding that 
the Test and Reference product averages are equivalent when, in fact, they differ enough to be 
considered non-equivalent.13  In most situations, a two one-sided tests procedure controls the 
Type I error rate at the nominal significance level of 5%, a fact that substantially contributed to 
FDA’s acceptance of the two one-sided tests procedure for most bioequivalence testing.14  Prior

Within this framework, FDA routinely releases recommendations on the design of 
bioequivalence studies for specific products that meet the agency’s bioequivalence standards for 
generic drug approval.  However, as with all FDA guidance documents, product-specific 
bioequivalence recommendations represent only the agency’s current thinking on the topic, and 
guidance revisions are common.  Indeed, FDA has stated that its published bioequivalence 
recommendations “will be revised as appropriate to ensure that the most up-to-date 
[bioequivalence] information is available to the public.”16  Moreover, FDA has made clear that it 
is not bound to its published recommendations in assessing whether an ANDA contains adequate 
evidence of bioequivalence.  Rather, in its review of proposed generic products, FDA considers 
all available relevant information, “which may include information submitted by the public to 
dockets for citizen petitions.”17 
 
Under the statute, once a generic product is approved, it is listed in the Orange Book with 
a therapeutic equivalence code.18  An “AB” code signifies that the generic drug is therapeutically 
equivalent to the RLD and, as such, “can be substituted [for the RLD] with the full expectation 
that the substituted product will produce the same clinical effect and safety profile as the 
[RLD].”19  This substitutability is based on the guarantee that a “therapeutically equivalent” drug 
“can be expected to have the same clinical effect and safety profile [as the RLD] when 
administered to patients under the conditions specified in the labeling.”20  The substitutability of 
AB-rated generic drugs underscores the public health importance of ensuring accurate 
bioequivalence evaluations for purposes of product approval.  In the case of ANDAs referencing 
Advair Diskus 100/50, reliable approval decisions require PK comparisons with a firm basis in 
the actual performance characteristics of the RLD, including the demonstrated and substantial 
batch-to-batch PK variability and rapid onset of peak plasma concentration observed for both 
active ingredients in Advair Diskus 100/50.

Potassium chloride is a drug that is used to treat patients suffering from potassium 
deficiency, i.e., hypokalemia.1 Potassium is a vital mineral for the human body and participates 
“in a number of essential physiological processes including the maintenance of intracellular 
tonicity; the transmission of nerve impulses; the contraction of cardiac, skeletal, and smooth 
muscle; and the maintenance of normal renal function.”2 For most humans, potassium obtained 
through the diet is sufficient to support all necessary bodily functions. Nevertheless, in certain 
situations patients require external supplemental potassium in order to prevent hypokalemia. 
Hypokalemia can be life-threatening and increases “the risks of morbidity and mortality in 
patients with cardiovascular disease. »3

often sold without approval from FDA because many potassium chloride products predated the

A.
Description of Inulin-Type Fructans Extracted from Chicory Root
ITF are non-digestible carbohydrates naturally occurring as an energy reserve in a
variety of plants, including chicory root. ITF are polysaccharides composed primarily of
fructose units joined by f3 (2-1) glycosidic linkages, usually connected to a single terminal
glucose molecule. The degree of polymerization (“DP”) (i.e., the number of
monosaccharide units in one molecule) of ITF naturally ranges from three to greater than
60.
ITF are extracted from chicory root by hot water. The DP of ITF varies due to a
number of factors, including the time of harvest, and the duration and conditions of post-
harvest storage. Additional separation techniques are used to isolate shorter or longer
chain lengths.1 All ITF are non-digestible carbohydrate using the Official Methods of
Analysis of AOAC International (“AOAC Methods”). Chain length influences
technological characteristics, e.g. shorter chains taste slightly sweet while longer chains
give a creamy taste, but as further described below, they all have the same physiological
health benefits which are associated with the f3 (2-1) binding of the fructans chains.
As defined in this Petition, the term ITF refers to a group of inulin-type fructans
derived from chicory root and includes, g1. inulin, long-chain inulin, oligofructose, and
various combinations of these ingredients.
•
Inulin: A polysaccharide extracted from chicory roots consisting of a
mixture of polymers of (2-1) linked fructose units mostly linked to a
terminal glucose unit. The DP ranges from 3 —60. See Food Chemical
Codex (2016). Oligofructose and long chain inulin are components of
inulin.
•
Long-chain inulin: is manufactured by isolating ITF with a DP of 10 or
more.
This Petition does not address short-chain Fmctooligosaccharides (sc-FOS). This
commercial product is not derived from inulin from chicory, but is synthesized
from sucrose. Chemically, it is a fructans compound typically with more than
85% of the molecules having a DP of three or four, and only negligible occurrence
of DP>5.

Oligofructose (synonym: fructooligosaccharide or FOS): A large portion of
the molecules in inulin have a DP of 10 or less, which are referred to as
Oligofructose. This shorter-chain fraction in inulin increases with harvest
time, due to enzyme activities in the root. In the production process,
enzymes may also be added to inulin to split longer chains into shorter
chains. This product can be described as a fructans compound with DP<10,

ITF share common physiological characteristics and mechanisms underlying their
physiological effects beneficial to health, irrespective of their DP. ITF are
physiologically characterized as non-digestible carbohydrates and filly fermentable
dietary fibers.
Due to the (2-l) glycosidic bonds, ITF resist hydrolysis and absorption in the
human small intestine. This non-digestibility of ITF has been demonstrated in humans
using an ileostomy model and the breath hydrogen determination method. These studies
show that ITF of any DP are not hydrolysed and absorbed in the human small intestine,
and that they reach the large intestine essentially complete (Ellegárd, et al., 1997,
Rumessen & Gudmand-Høyer, 1998; Teuri, et al., 1999). In the large intestine, ITF are

lactate (Roberfroid & Slavin, 2000; Cummings & Macfarlane, 2002; Roberfroid, 1999).

The purpose of this citizen petition is to highlight the potential risk of loperamide abuse, its lethal effect and 
therefore make an amendment for OTC availability of loperamide to a prescription drug. Loperamide is an 
opioid agonist, in 1969, loperamide (4(4-chorophenyl)-4-hydroxy-N-dimethyl-alpha, alpha diphenyl-1-
piperidine-butanamide hydrochloride), a phenylpiperidine derivative was manufactured. In 1976, the US FDA 
approved loperamide up to 16 milligrams daily for the treatment of acute and chronic diarrhea.1  
Loperamide has low potential for abuse due to low permeability through the blood brain barrier (BBB). Recently 
published research suggests that an average dose of 70-800 milligrams of loperamide daily was abused by 
people with opioid use disorder (OUD) to treat opioid withdrawal symptoms.2 There are several death reports 
since early 1990s due to loperamide toxicity and this is due to intestinal distension, respiratory depression and 
cardiac arrhythmia. Loperamide metabolized by the cytochrome P450 (CYP) system and is a substrate for the 
CYP3A4 isoenzyme. Concurrent administration with CYP3A4 inhibitors may elevate loperamide 
concentrations. Loperamide inhibits intestinal peristalsis through mu-opioid receptor agonist, calcium channel 
blockade, calmodulin inhibition, and reducing paracellular permeability.1 Loperamide is a peripheral mu-opioid 
receptor agonist that is excluded from the BBB by p-glycoprotein at therapeutic doses. High dose of 
loperamide penetrate the central nervous system leading to abuse.  At high doses, loperamide crosses the 
BBB and reaches central opioid receptors in the brain, leading to central opiate effects including euphoria and 
respiratory depression. Loperamide is often abused by people with OUD and cause arrhythmogenic effect on 
the heart.3  
Because of easy availability and being inexpensive, loperamide is known as poor man’s methadone.4 Abuse of 
OTC drugs often gets overlooked by health care providers.

A. Action Requested 
The petitioner requests that the Commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration: (1) 
determine whether the original formulation of Apothecon's Kenalog-40 (triamcinolone 
acetonide) Injectable Suspension was discontinued for reasons related to safety or effectiveness 
and (2) accept abbreviated new drug applications for Triamcinolone Acetonide Injectable

B. Statement of Grounds 
The FDA regulations require that generic parenteral drug products generally contain the same 
inactive ingredients, and in the same concentration, as the inactive ingredients contained in the 
Reference Listed Drug (RLD). 
(See 21 CFR § 314.94(a)(9)(iii).) The only differences in 
excipients that are routinely permitted are differences in a preservative, buffer, or antioxidant. 
(21 CFR § 314.94(a)(9)(iii)). 
When an ANDA applicant seeks approval for a parenteral formulation that is the same as that 
previously marketed by the innovator, the FDA may determine that a waiver of the requirement 
to contain the same inactive ingredients (except for preservative, buffer, or antioxidant) is 
appropriate. In which case, the FDA may rely upon 21 CFR § 314.99(b) to grant a waiver ofthe 
inactive ingredient regulatory requirements under 21 CFR § 314.94(a)(9)(iii), so long as the 
statutory safety requirements are met. These statutory safety requirements are met if the inactive

While the quantitative changes relative to sodium chloride and carboxymethylcellulose sodium

Citizen Petition to Test Polyethylene Glycol 3350 Products for Selenium Content 
and Recall 
The undersigned submits this petition under Title 21, Food and Drugs Chapter I, Department of Health and 
Human Services Subchapter A, General, Section 10.30 Citizen Petition to request the Commissioner of Food 
and Drugs to conduct a thorough test of all polyethylene glycol 3350 (PEG 3350) laxative products, both over-
the-counter and prescription, for the presence of selenium and issue a recall if selenium is found.  
We petition the Commissioner to take the following actions due to the finding of selenium in PEG 3350 
products tested by Empire State Consumer Project and the widespread (off-label) prescribing of PEG 3350 to 
children for long term use. Selenium also interacts with a number of medications and should not be used by 
people with certain medical conditions. 
A.  Action Requested 
  
This petition requests that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs take administrative action in the form of: 
 
1. 
Testing all brands of PEG 3350 products sold in the U.S. and sold by U.S. companies overseas, 
both over-the-counter and prescription, for the presence of selenium. 
 
2. 
Determining the source of selenium (multiple brands may be manufactured by the same company). 
 
3. 
Issuing a recall of PEG 3350 products containing selenium. 
 
4. 
Establishing a safe selenium limit on pharmaceuticals prescribed to children for long term use, 
including off-label prescribing. 
B.  Statement of Grounds 
In 2012, due to thousands of adverse event reports filed with the FDA, Empire State Consumer Project 
petitioned the FDA to investigate the safety of polyethylene glycol 3350 (PEG 3350) laxatives for use in 
children (http://www.regulations.gov/#!searchResults;rpp=25;po=0;s=fda-2012-P-0566;fp=true;ns=true). 
The petition was granted with a study at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, which, according to the hospital’s 
website, has not yet begun recruiting participants.  
 
As we stated in our petition, PEG 3350 laxatives are not approved for use in children, and are only approved 
for 7 days use in adults, but are prescribed routinely for children by doctors in adult doses for daily use for 
months and years at a time. Infants, who should not receive supplements of selenium are also prescribed PEG  
3350. Adverse events reported in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System that include at least one PEG 
3350 product are now over 13,000. 
 
B.  Statement of Grounds, Continued 
 
This month, Empire State Consumer Project tested three PEG 3350 laxative products and found selenium in 
all samples tested. Selenium is an essential, yet highly toxic trace mineral, which is found in soil, water, and 
some foods. Selenium can also be used as a catalyst in the pharmaceutical manufacturing process. Exceeding 
the Tolerable Upper Intake Levels (ULs) can lead to selenosis, selenium poisoning.  
 
We are requesting that the FDA conduct a thorough study of PEG 3350 laxative products (both over-the-
counter and prescription) for the presence of selenium and, given the high doses of PEG children are 
prescribed and the conditions under which selenium should not be taken, issue a product recall if selenium is 
found. We are also requesting that the FDA use these findings to establish a safe selenium limit for any 
pharmaceutical prescribed to children for long term use, including off-label prescribing.  
 
 
Selenium Toxicity  
 
From the National Institutes of Health (NIH) website: 
 
“Chronically high intake levels of the organic and inorganic forms of selenium have similar effects. Early 
indicators of excess intake are a garlic odor in the breath and a metallic taste in the mouth. The most common 
clinical signs of chronically high intakes, or selenosis, are hair and nail loss or brittleness. Other symptoms 
include lesions of the skin and nervous system, nausea, diarrhea, skin rashes, mottled teeth, fatigue, irritability, 
and nervous system abnormalities. 
 
Acute selenium toxicity can cause severe gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms, acute respiratory 
distress syndrome, myocardial infarction, hair loss, muscle tenderness, tremors, lightheadedness, facial 
flushing, kidney failure, cardiac failure, and, in rare cases, death.” 
 
The finding of selenium in our testing adds another level of concern for children’s safety, as many of the 
symptoms parents report are similar to those of ethylene glycol (EG) and diethylene glycol (DEG) toxicity (EG 
and DEG were both found in FDA’s testing) and some symptoms are also similar to those of excess selenium 
intake. 
 
https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Selenium-HealthProfessional/ 
 
 
Medication Interactions 
 
Excerpted from the University of Maryland Medical Center website: 
 
Selenium interacts with a number of medications: 
 
Anticoagulants and Antiplatelet Drugs (blood thinners) 
 
When taken with these drugs, selenium may increase the risk of bleeding: 
 
Clopidogrel (Plavix) 
Warfarin (Coumadin) 
Heparin 
Aspirin 
 
 
 
 
B.  Statement of Grounds, Continued 
Medication Interactions, Continued 
 
 
Barbiturates 
 
In animal testing, selenium seems to make the sedative effects of these drugs last longer: 
 
Butabarbital (Butisol) 
Mephabarbital (Mebaral) 
Phenobarbital (Nembutal) 
Secobarbital (Seconal) 
 
 
Chemotherapy 
 
Although selenium may help reduce side effects from drugs such as cisplatin, doxorubicin, and belomycin, it 
may also interfere with their cancer-fighting ability. 
 
 
Cholesterol-lowering Medications 
 
Simvastatin (Zocor) and niacin have been shown to lower LDL cholesterol and raise HDL cholesterol. Taking 
certain antioxidant supplements together, including selenium, along with these drugs may make them less 
effective. In theory, selenium may also reduce the effectiveness of: 
 
atorvastatin (Lipitor) 
fluvastatin (Lescol) 
lovastatin (Mevacor) 
prevastatin (Pravachol) 
 
 
Birth Control Pills 
 
Some studies show that women taking birth control pills have higher selenium levels in their blood. Adding 
additional selenium should be done under the advice of a medical professional.  
 
 
Medical Conditions 
 
Selenium should not be taken without talking to a doctor if a person has the following conditions: 
 
Hypothyroidism 
Skin cancer 
At risk of skin cancer 
High selenium intake may increase the risk of diabetes and high cholesterol. 
 
http://umm.edu/health/medical/altmed/supplement/selenium 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
B.  Statement of Grounds, Continued 
 
Selenium Exposure 
 
It should be noted that some children’s supplements also contain selenium. According to the NIH, the average 
daily intake of selenium in Americans aged 2 years and older from foods is 108.5 mcg, almost double the RDA 
for adults, and from both foods and supplements is 120.8 mcg. Both of these levels are already well above the 
Tolerable Upper Intake Levels (ULs) for children 3 and under.  
 
Permitted Daily Exposure (PDE) to selenium allowed by the FDA in its Guidance on Elemental Impurities for 
Pharmaceuticals is 150 mcg daily, also well over the Tolerable Upper Intake Levels (ULs) for children 3 years 
and under and at the Tolerable Upper Intake Level for children 4-8 years old.  
 
http://www.fda.gov/downloads/drugs/guidancecomplianceregulatoryinformation/guidances/ucm371025.pdf

North American Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (NASPGHAN) 
Guidelines 
 
The North American Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (NSAPGHAN) has 
created guidelines for off-label prescribing of PEG 3350 laxatives to children. Parents report that many doctors 
are prescribing even higher doses. Children are often given multiple adult doses daily for months and years at 
a time. 
 
Based on NASPGHAN dosing, one gram of PEG 3350 per kg of body weight would be 10 grams of PEG for a 
22 lb. child, which, in the sample tested, would contain 14 mcg of selenium. 1.5 grams of PEG per kg of body 
weight would total 21 mcg of selenium in the sample tested. This amount is in addition to the 108.5 mcg 
average daily intake of selenium for Americans over 2 years of age.

A. FDA’s Historical Interpretation of the 5-Year Exclusivity Provisions 
 
Under the FDCA, 5-year exclusivity is available to new drugs in the following 
circumstances:

no active ingredient (including any ester or salt of the active ingredient) of 
which has been approved in any other application under subsection (b) of

was submitted before the expiration of five years from the date of the 
approval of the application under subsection (b) of this section . . . 11 
 
Thus, the statute includes clauses describing eligibility criteria for 5-year exclusivity (the 
eligibility clause) and the parameters of such exclusivity once it attaches (the bar clause).  The 
term “drug” as used in this provision is not defined in section 505 of the FDCA.  Historically,

the eligibility clause, “drug” means “drug product”; in the bar clause, “drug” means “drug

exclusivity.  However, if the single-entity product were approved first and the FDC drug product

Under Section 505U) of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act ("FDCA"), an 
applicant may file an abbreviated new drug application ("ANDA") for approval of a 
generic copy of an already-approved innovator drug product. An ANDA is not supported 
by clinical studies establishing safety and efficacy of the proposed generic drug product. 
Instead, the applicant references FDA's findings of safety and effectiveness for a

molar dose of the therapeutic ingredient under similar experimental conditions in either a 
single-dose or multiple doses."3 To aid generic applicants in designing bioequivalence

recommendations. 4
