Nucynta ER®, and anything less will overlap the new use code and infringe the patent.  
Therefore, ANDA applicants with section viii statements must amend their applications to 
address the new use code as required by FDA regulations.   
 
                                                 
13 The litigations involve Orange Book patents in addition to the ‘130 patent.  
14 See 21 C.F.R. §§ 314.107(c); 314.127(a)(7). 
 
 
 
5 
 
 
1. An amended use code that completely overlaps both indications cannot be 
carved out of a generic label under a section viii statement; a patent 
certification is required. 
 
Because the amended ‘130 patent use code overlaps both Nucynta ER® indications, a 
section viii statement and label carve out is no longer appropriate or permissible.  In the past, 
when a use code has been amended such that a pending section viii statement carve out is no 
longer permissible, FDA has required the ANDA applicant to withdraw its section viii 
statement and file a patent certification.   
 
In May 2009, FDA addressed an almost identical situation involving the Novo Nordisk 
drug Prandin (repaglinide).15  In that case, Prandin had been approved for glycemic control in 
adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus under three conditions of use: as a monotherapy and in two 
different combination therapies.  Initially, Novo Nordisk listed a method patent in the Orange 
Book with a use code that covered only one of the combination uses.  Subsequently, FDA 
required all diabetes drug manufacturers to revise their labels to contain only a single “diabetes” 
indication.  Novo Nordisk thereupon amended its use code to cover the treatment of diabetes, 
the sole indication on the label.  In light of the now complete overlap by the new use code, 
FDA determined that it could no longer be carved out and directed the then-pending ANDA 
applicant to withdraw its section viii statement and file a patent certification.  Significantly, 
FDA required the filing of a patent certification despite the fact that the use code was amended 
years after the patent was first listed.16   
 
The situation here is virtually identical to what FDA faced in the Prandin matter.  Where 
an amended use code completely overlaps all of the indications on the brand label, it cannot be 
carved out under a section viii statement.  Thus, based on precedent established in Prandin, 
FDA must direct ANDA applicants referencing Nucynta ER® to amend or withdraw their 
section viii statements for the ‘130 patent and file an appropriate patent certification before 
final approval can be granted.    
 
FDA’s policy on use code amendments was also addressed recently in a case involving 
the Hospira drug Precedex.17  There, the brand manufacturer amended a use code that fully 
protected one indication so that it would partially overlap a second indication to prevent a 
section viii carve out by ANDA applicants.  FDA asked for public comment on the use code 
amendment tactic (including the question of whether an amended use code should be 
considered a “late submission” of patent information) and ultimately determined that its rules 
would allow a use code to partially overlap a labeled indication provided all references to the 
carved out use were removed from the label.18  In so ruling, FDA distinguished its earlier ruling 
                                                 
15 See generally, Docket Nos. FDA-2008-P-0343 and FDA-2008-P-0411. 
16 In subsequent Paragraph IV litigation that eventually reached the Supreme Court, Novo Nordisk’s amended 
use code was found to be impermissibly overbroad because it prevented the marketing of a generic drug for an 
approved use (e.g. the monotherapy) that was not claimed by the patent.  Caraco Pharm. Labs., v. Novo Nordisk 
A/S, 566 U.S. __, 132 S. Ct. 1670 (2012).  However, FDA’s decision to require the pending ANDA applicant to 
withdraw its section viii statement and file a patent certification in response to the amended use code was never 
challenged.   
17 See Dear Applicant Letter from FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research re Dexmedetomidine 
Hydrochloride Injection NDA/ANDA Applicant, Docket No. FDA-2014-N-0087 (Jan. 15, 2014). 
18 Hospira Inc. v. Burwell, No. 14-02662-GJH, 2014 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 123972 (D. Md. Sept. 5, 2014). 
 
 
 
6 
 
 
in Prandin on the basis that the overlap in Prandin was complete and, therefore, could not be 
allowed under the rules.19    
 
Like the use code overlap in Prandin and unlike the use code overlap in Precedex, the 
amended ‘130 use code completely overlaps all of the labeled indications for Nucynta ER®.  
As noted, Nucynta ER® is currently approved for two indications: (1) the management of pain 
severe enough to require daily, around-the-clock, long-term opioid treatment and for which 
alternative treatment options are inadequate; and (2) the management of neuropathic pain 
associated with diabetic peripheral neuropathy (“DPN”) in adults severe enough to require 
daily, around-the-clock, long-term opioid treatment and for which alternative treatment options 
are inadequate.  The ‘130 use code reads “Management of pain severe enough to require daily, 
around-the-clock, long-term opioid treatment, including neuropathic pain associated with 
Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathy.”  Both indications fall squarely within this use code, and the 
use code overlaps both indications completely; thus, neither indication can be carved out under 
a section viii statement by an ANDA applicant.20   
 
2. FDA rules require a pending ANDA with a section viii statement to be 
withdrawn or amended and an appropriate certification filed for the ‘130 
patent. 
An examination of FDA rules clearly shows that a pending ANDA is required to be 
amended if a section viii carve out statement is impacted by a use code change.21  Section 
314.94(a)(12)(i)(A) requires an ANDA applicant to file “a certification with respect to each 
patent” listed in the Orange Book, making clear that certifications are to be submitted on a 
patent by patent basis.  In addition, section 314.94(a)(12)(viii)(C) requires an ANDA applicant 
to amend “a submitted certification” if it learns that it is no longer accurate; however, an 
amendment is not required if the inaccuracy is due to the “late submission of patent 
information.”22  FDA rules define “late submission of patent information” as follows:  
Late submission of patent information.  If a patent on the listed 
drug is issued and the holder of the approved application for the 
listed drug does not submit the required information on the 
patent within 30 days of issuance of the patent, [an ANDA 
applicant] . . . is not required to submit an amended certification.  
                                                 
19 See Dear Applicant Letter from FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research re Dexmedetomidine 
Hydrochloride Injection NDA/ANDA Applicant at 10, Docket No. FDA-2014-N-0087 (Aug. 18, 2014) where 
FDA summarized its holding in Prandin: “in light of the explicit and complete overlap of the new use code and 
the only approved indication for repaglinide, FDA determined that it could no longer approve any ANDAs with 
carved out labeling because ANDAs could not carve out the only approved indication that was claimed to be 
protected by the ‘358 patent (as described in the use code).” 
20 Where a patented use is a subset of a broad indication that is not protected by a patent, the brand has no option 
other than to file a use code that reads on the broad indication; otherwise there is no way of identifying the 
labeled use that will infringe the patent.  Form FDA 3542 Section 4.2b recognizes this as the correct procedure 
by instructing the filer to “submit the description of the approved indication or method of use” that is on the 
label for FDA to include as the use code.  
21 See Abbreviated New Drug Applications and 505(b)(2) Applications; Proposed Rule, 80 Fed. Reg. 6802, 
6833 (Feb. 6, 2015). 
22 In the Precedex case, FDA asked for comments on whether a use code amendment outside the 30 day filing 
window should be considered a late submission of patent information but declined to reach a decision. See Dear 
Applicant Letter from FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research re Dexmedetomidine Hydrochloride 
Injection NDA/ANDA Applicant at 15, Docket No. FDA-2014-N-0087 (Aug. 18, 2014).     
 
 
 
7 
 
 
An applicant whose abbreviated new drug application is 
submitted after a late submission of patent information, or whose 
pending abbreviated application was previously submitted but 
did not contain an appropriate patent certification at the time of 
the patent submission, shall submit a certification . . . .23  
Based on the unambiguous meaning of the first sentence in this regulation, the 
exemption from filing a certification amendment applies only to ANDA applicants who had 
already submitted a patent certification.  In other words, the exemption does not apply to an 
applicant who filed a section viii statement in lieu of a patent certification because, as to such 
an applicant, there is no certification for that applicant to amend.     
The second sentence in the regulation, therefore, is the operative provision and controls 
in this instance.  As this sentence clearly states, an applicant whose pending ANDA did not 
contain “an appropriate patent certification” at the time of patent submission is required to 
submit “a certification” based on the submission of the new patent information (e.g. the new 
use code).  An ANDA that contains a section viii statement in lieu of a patent certification for 
the listed patent will not have an “appropriate patent certification” at the time of patent 
information (i.e. use code) submission.  Thus, for these section viii applicants, the rule requires 
that they submit “a certification” and not an “amended certification” – which further indicates 
that the rule set forth in the second sentence is directed to first time certification submitters, 
including section viii statement filers who must now submit a patent certification for the first 
time.24  In addition, if the ANDA applicant files a Paragraph IV certification challenging the 
patent, it is required to provide notice pursuant to 21 C.F.R. § 314.95(d).25 26 
3. Staying final approval of any ANDA until the applicant has fully complied 
with FDA’s patent certification rules is necessary to protect public health.  
 
A delay in approval in this instance is “necessary to protect the public health” as 
required by section 505(q).  ANDA applicants that have not filed patent certifications based on 
the new use code submitted for the ‘130 patent are in violation of the FDCA and FDA 
regulations.  Such violations undermine the core fabric of the Hatch-Waxman Act, which is 
designed to respect patent rights to encourage new innovations in medicine.  Failure to enforce 
                                                 
23 21 C.F.R. § 314.94(a)(12)(vi) (emphasis added).  As noted, the patent itself was submitted for listing in the 
Orange Book within 30 days of issuance.  The use code change is the only potentially “late filed” aspect of the 
patent.   
24 The foregoing rule construction of the “late submission” rule makes perfect sense because it ensures labeling 
sameness between brand and generic drugs, a core tenet of Hatch-Waxman.  If a pending ANDA applicant with 
a section viii statement were permitted to ignore a “late-filed” use code amendment, it could result in a generic 
label that would be in violation of Section 314.127(a)(7) and potentially expose the ANDA applicant to charges 
of drug misbranding.   
25 In its February 2015 proposed rule implementing the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and 
Modernization Act of 2003 (“MMA”), FDA clearly explained that the MMA requires ANDA applicants to give 
notice to the NDA holder if a Paragraph IV certification is included in an amendment.  This notice must be 
submitted at the time the applicant submits the amendment.  Abbreviated New Drug Applications and 505(b)(2) 
Applications; Proposed Rule, 80 Fed. Reg. 6802, 6804, 6833 (Feb. 6, 2015).  See also 21 C.F.R. § 314.95(d).  
Depomed has not received notice of any Paragraph IV certifications arising from such an amendment.   
26 It should be noted that the rule does not necessarily require a pending ANDA applicant to withdraw a valid 
section viii statement.  It only requires the applicant to file an “appropriate” certification or section viii 
statement in response to the new patent information.  A section viii statement may still be appropriate for certain 
in a patent whereas a certification might be required for other claims.  This type of “split” certification has long 
been permissible under FDA rules. 
 
 
 
8 
 
 
this statutory scheme and preserve the patent rights of brand manufacturers is inherently 
harmful to the public health.   
 
Deficient enforcement of FDA requirements raises significant policy considerations 
that also implicate public health.  FDA’s regulations are designed to fulfill the agency’s 
responsibility to protect the public; however, these regulations can protect the safety and 
efficacy of the drug supply only if they are adequately applied and enforced.  FDA itself has 
noted that “without effective FDA regulatory oversight and enforcement, some regulated 
entities will disregard even the clearest regulations or will not be adequately vigilant to ensure 
compliance with the law, potentially harming the public.”27  Furthermore, effective 
enforcement ensures corporate responsibility and compliance vigilance and “that those who do 
comply with the law are not unfairly disadvantaged.”28 
 
The actions requested in this petition are plainly necessary to protect the public health, 
which requires drug labels to be clear, unambiguous, safe, and effective.  Patients and 
physicians must not be confused or misled as to a drug’s approved indications and related side 
effects.  But that is exactly what will happen if ANDAs are approved with section viii carve 
outs under the old ‘130 patent use code because these carved out labels will be omitting safety 
and efficacy information required on the brand label for the remaining non-protected use of 
Nucynta ER®.     
 
When Nucynta ER® was initially approved in August 2011, clinical data from the first 
trial involving “neuropathic pain associated with DPN” was a required labeling element 
because it conveyed safety and efficacy information relevant to the broad pain indication, the 
sole indication approved for the drug.  In other words, neuropathic pain associated with DPN 
was intended to be included within the broad pain indication, and the proof of this was the DPN 
clinical data that appeared prominently on the approved label.  In 2012, a second DPN clinical 
trial was completed, additional data was added to the label, and FDA approved the highlighting 
of DPN as a separate indication.  But this was not done because DPN was considered to be 
outside the scope of the broad pain indication; rather, it was simply to call attention to DPN as 
an approved sub-indication for the drug.  No steps were ever taken to remove DPN from the 
broad pain indication, which has never been amended.29  
In 2013, when the ‘130 patent was issued, J&J filed a use code specific to the now 
newly highlighted DPN indication.  An ANDA applicant that wanted to file section viii 
statement to avoid the ‘130 patent use code would have been required to carve out the DPN 
indication along with all other information related to this indication appearing on the label.  
Under FDA rules, however, a carved out generic label cannot omit information that would 
render the generic less safe or effective than the brand for all remaining non-protected 
conditions of use.  For Nucynta ER®, this would mean that a section viii carve out could not 
involve the removal of DPN information from the first clinical trial that FDA determined, in 
August 2011, was required for safe and effective use for the broad pain indication.30  Thus, an 
ANDA applicant seeking to file a section viii statement under the old ‘130 use code faced an 
insurmountable problem: it would be required to remove all labeling references to DPN, yet it

http://www.fda.gov/downloads/ICECI/EnforcementActions/UCM225183.pdf.   
28 Id. (emphasis added). 
29 FDA could have elected to amended the broad pain indication to make clear that it did not apply (or no longer 
applied) to DPN either by stating as much, or perhaps, by enumerating all the pain treatments covered by the 
first indication without mentioning DPN.   
30 See 21 C.F.R. §314.127(a)(7).

could not omit the DPN clinical information that FDA determined was necessary for the safe 
or effective use of the drug for the remaining, broad pain indication.  The end result is that a 
section viii statement under the original ‘130 use code would not be permissible due to safety 
and efficacy concerns that are necessary to protect the public health.   
 
Regardless of which use code is applied, FDA rules clearly preclude the use of a section 
viii statement in place of a patent certification for the ‘130 patent.  Any pending ANDA that 
contains a section viii statement must be withdrawn and, in its place, an appropriate 
certification must be filed along with the other relief requested herein.   
 
D.  
505(q) petition

statute, therefore, FDA must provide a response within 150 days.  As noted in Guidance, FDA 
interprets 505(q) to apply to petitions that are submitted to FDA after September 27, 2007; 
submitted in writing pursuant to 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 or 10.35; relevant to a pending application 
at time of petition submission; and requesting an action that could delay approval of a pending 
application.31  This petition meets all of these qualifications.32   
 
Furthermore, this petition does not fall within any of the exceptions described in section 
505(q)(4).  This petition does not relate solely to the timing of an approval pursuant to the 180 
day exclusivity provision of the FDCA and is not from the sponsor of the abbreviated 
application.  Depomed therefore requests a response to this petition within 150 days.

Environmental Impact 
 
This petition is categorically exempt from the requirement for an environmental

I. INTRODUCTION 
 
On January 13, 2016, the FDA issued a Warning Letter to Kirkman Industries, Inc. 
(“Kirkman”) in which the Agency called on Kirkman to “discontinue marketing all of the 
unapproved prescription drugs manufactured at [the] facility immediately.” The 
unapproved prescription drugs at issue in this letter were sodium fluoride-containing 
drops and tablets sold for the labeled purpose of preventing dental caries.  
 
In the Warning Letter, FDA stated that sodium fluoride-containing drops and tablets used 
for caries prevention purposes (i.e., “fluoride supplements”) are “drugs” under 21 U.S.C. 
§ 321(g), “new drugs” under 21 U.S.C. § 321(p)(1), and “unapproved new drugs” under 
21 U.S.C § 355.  Accordingly, because the Food Drug & Cosmetic Act (FDCA) prohibits 
the introduction of unapproved new drugs into interstate commerce, FDA informed 
Kirkman that the “marketing of these drugs . . . without an approved application 
constitutes a violation of the Act.”  
 
FDA’s decision to take enforcement action against Kirkman for its marketing of fluoride 
supplements is a commendable step in the right direction, because a large body of 
scientific and medical evidence demonstrates that fluoride supplements are neither safe 
nor effective.   
 
The FDA, however, should not limit its enforcement action against fluoride supplements 
to only Kirkman, as there are other, larger companies (e.g., Libertas Pharma, Inc.; 
Sancilo & Company, Inc.; and Qualitest) that are manufacturing and distributing identical 
fluoride supplements, which are being sold throughout the country by the nation’s four 
largest pharmacies (Walgreens, CVS, Rite Aid, and Walmart).  Each and every one of 
the issues that FDA identified with Kirkman’s fluoride supplements applies with equal 
force to the fluoride supplements being manufactured and sold by these other 
Citizen Petition to FDA Re: Fluoride Drops, Tablets, & Lozenges 
 
3 
companies.  The widespread sale of fluoride supplements in the U.S. thus constitutes a 
systematic violation of the Food Drug & Cosmetic Act.  
 
Petitioners write today not just because manufacturers, distributors, and sellers of 
fluoride supplements are violating the law, but because their unlawful actions are 
unnecessarily placing millions of children in harm’s way.    
 
Fluoride supplements were launched in the 1940s/50s on the universally discredited 
premise that fluoride needs to be ingested during early childhood to provide a 
meaningful role in cavity prevention.  The overwhelming body of evidence today shows 
that fluoride’s predominant effect on cavities comes from topical application, not 
ingestion.  Further, the decades-old studies purporting to demonstrate benefits from 
fluoride supplements have been universally critiqued for their low quality, highly biased 
study designs.  Today, leading experts in the fields of dental research and health care 
interventions, including the prestigious Cochrane Collaboration, have concluded that 
fluoride supplements are neither necessary nor effective, particularly in the current 
context of widespread exposures to fluoride toothpaste and topical fluorides.  In short, 
fluoride supplements have become a useless relic of a discredited paradigm. 
 
Fluoride supplements are not just ineffective, they are dangerous.  A large body of 
science demonstrates that fluoride is a developmental neurotoxin and endocrine 
disrupting agent, whose ingestion during childhood poses serious potential risks to brain 
development and thyroid health, as well as other harm, including dental fluorosis, bone 
fragility, osteosarcoma, and impaired glucose metabolism. 
 
The problem today is not under-exposure to fluoride, but over-exposure.  Recent 
national survey data collected by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control shows that 
between 41% and 64% of adolescents now have dental fluorosis, with 4% to 29% of 
adolescents having advanced forms of this condition.  Dental fluorosis is a visible 
mineralization defect of tooth enamel caused by excessive fluoride intake, which can be 
disfiguring when present on a child’s front teeth.  
 
Fluoride supplements remain a significant cause of the over-exposure problem in the 
U.S.  Studies have repeatedly demonstrated that inappropriate prescription of fluoride 
supplements is a widespread and persistent problem in the U.S., with many children 
being prescribed these drugs despite having high background exposure to other sources 
of fluoride, including fluoridated water and fluoride toothpaste.  Such poorly monitored, 
highly variable exposures to a neurotoxic, endocrine disrupting agent, is a recipe for 
long-term disaster that demands decisive action now.  
 
Rather than continuing to supplement children’s intake of fluoride, the urgent need now 
is to find ways to reduce fluoride exposure.  Eliminating unapproved fluoride drugs from 
the market is the most obvious place for FDA to start.  The dangers posed by these 
drugs, coupled with their ineffectiveness, deceptive marketing practices, misbranding 
violations, and undermining effect on FDA’s OTC Monograph on fluoride, make fluoride 
supplements a high priority drug for FDA enforcement actions per the considerations set 
forth in the Agency’s Compliance Policy Guide for Marketed Unapproved Drugs.

II. ACTION REQUESTED 
 
Petitioners request that the Commissioner issue a notice of the FDA’s intent to take 
enforcement actions (including seizures, injunctions, civil penalties, and/or criminal 
sanctions) against any and all companies that manufacture, distribute, and/or otherwise 
introduce into interstate commerce unapproved sodium fluoride-containing drops, tablets, 
and lozenges that are sold for the intended purpose of caries prevention (i.e., “fluoride 
supplements”). 
 
III. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
A. FLUORIDE “SUPPLEMENTS” ARE UNAPPROVED NEW DRUGS 
 
In its Warning Letter to Kirkman, the FDA confirmed that fluoride supplements are “drugs” 
under 21 U.S.C. § 321(g), “new drugs” under 21 U.S.C. § 321(p)(1), and have never 
been approved as safe and effective under 21 U.S.C. § 355.1  Introducing fluoride 
supplements into interstate commerce, therefore, violates the Food Drug & Cosmetic Act 
(FDCA), as the FDCA plainly prohibits the sale of unapproved new drugs.  21 U.S.C § 
331(d); 21 U.S.C. § 355(a).  
 
Kirkman has challenged FDA’s conclusion that fluoride supplements are “new drugs” 
under 21 U.S.C. § 321(p)(1), based on Kirkman’s contention that fluoride supplements 
are “generally recognized as safe and effective.”2  Kirkman’s argument, however, is at 
odds with both law and science.  As set forth herein, FDA’s conclusion that fluoride 
supplements are “new drugs” is factually, legally, logically, and scientifically unassailable. 
 
1. Fluoride Is a “Drug” When Used for Caries Prevention  
 
The FDA has consistently classified fluoride as a “drug” when used to treat or prevent 
disease, including the disease of tooth decay (“caries”).3  FDA’s classification of fluoride 
as a drug is in clear harmony with the FDCA, which defines drugs, inter alia, as articles 
“intended for use in the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease in 
man or other animals.”  21 U.S.C. § 321(g).  
 
2. Fluoride Supplements Are “New Drugs” When Sold for Caries Prevention 
 
As set forth in 21 U.S.C. § 331(d), the FDCA prohibits the sale of “new drugs” that have 
not been approved as safe and effective by FDA per the rigorous requirements of 21 
U.S.C. § 355.  A “new drug” is “any drug,” except those that meet the following two “very 
narrow”4 exceptions: (1) It was on the market prior to June 25, 1938 with the same 
“labeling” and “representations concerning the conditions of its use,” and/or (2) it is 
“generally recognized, among experts qualified by scientific training and experience to 
evaluate the safety and effectiveness of drugs, as safe and effective under the 
conditions prescribed, recommended, or suggested in the labeling.”  21 U.S.C. § 
321(p)(1).   
 
For the following reasons, fluoride supplements do not meet either of these “very narrow” 
exceptions.

a. Fluoride Supplements Were Not on the Market Prior to June 1938 
 
Sodium fluoride was never used prior to June 1938 as a caries preventive agent, let 
alone with the same labeling and recommended conditions for use as sodium fluoride 
drugs that are now on the market.  Prior to 1938, sodium fluoride was commonly used as 
a roach and rodent poison, but its use in American medicine was virtually unknown, with 
the exception of a rare use as an externally applied antiseptic and antiperiodic. 5  
Importantly, sodium fluoride had no use in dentistry, let alone as an agent to be 
swallowed by children for caries prevention. This is confirmed by the 1940 edition of the 
Merck Index, which is attached as Exhibit 5, as well as the 1938 and 1940 editions of the 
United States Pharmacopeia, which are attached as Exhibits 7 and 8.  This fact is further 
confirmed by scientific reviews of the fluoride supplement literature, which unanimously 
state that fluoride supplements were introduced no earlier than the mid-1940s, and were 
not widely used until the late 1950s or early 1960s.6  
 
b. Fluoride Supplements Are Not Generally Recognized as Safe & Effective 
(GRASE) 
 
In its January 13, 2016 Warning Letter to Kirkman Industries, Inc. (“Kirkman”), FDA 
stated its position that Kirkman’s fluoride supplements “are not generally recognized as 
safe and effective under the conditions prescribed, recommended, or suggested in their 
labeling.”  Importantly, the only labeling information from Kirkman’s fluoride supplements 
that FDA identified in its Warning Letter is the claim that these supplements are an “aid 
in the prevention of dental caries.” Accordingly, FDA’s conclusion that Kirkman’s 
supplements are not generally recognized as safe and effective (GRASE) applies 
equally to all fluoride supplements with labeling that makes caries prevention claims.7  
 
FDA’s conclusion that fluoride supplements are not GRASE for caries prevention is 
abundantly supported by both (A) the case law defining GRASE, and (b) the scientific 
literature on fluoride supplements.  We begin first with a summary of the case law, 
before proceeding to a discussion of the science.    
 
i. 
The Legal Standard for Determining GRASE 
 
The U.S. Supreme Court has made clear that the standard for proving GRASE is a 
"rigorous one," which is equally as stringent as the standard FDA uses for assessing a 
New Drug Application (NDA) under 21 U.S.C. § 355.  Weinberger v. Hynson, Westcott & 
Dunning, Inc., 412 U.S. 609, 629-30 (1973). Under both the GRASE and NDA inquiries, 
there must be "substantial evidence" of safety and effectiveness, which includes 
“adequate tests by all methods reasonably applicable” to demonstrate safety, and 
"adequate and well-controlled investigations" to demonstrate effectiveness.  21 U.S.C. § 
355(d); 21 C.F.R. § 314.126; Weinberger v. Bentex Pharms., Inc., 412 U.S. 645, 653 
(1973) ("[T]he reach of scientific inquiry under both [21 U.S.C. § 355] and [21 U.S.C. § 
321(p)] is precisely the same.").  Accordingly, "to qualify as GRASE, a drug must meet 
the same elaborate, technical, scientific testing requirements that it would have to meet 
to win approval as a 'new drug.'"  United States v. 50 Boxes, 909 F.2d 24, 26 (1st Cir. 
1990).   
Under the rigorous GRASE standard, it is immaterial if physicians "believe" that a drug 
works, or if poorly-conducted studies indicate a benefit, because the "clinical 
impressions of practicing physicians and poorly controlled experiments do not constitute

6 
an adequate basis for establishing efficacy."  Weinberger, 412 U.S. at 630.  Even when 
there is an “expert consensus” that a drug is safe and effective, the consensus does not 
constitute GRASE if it is not based on adequate and well controlled studies that 
independently satisfy the requirements of 21 U.S.C. § 355.  See id. at 632 (“[A] drug can 
be 'generally recognized' by experts as effective for intended use within the meaning of 
the Act only when that expert consensus is founded upon 'substantial evidence' as 
defined in [21 U.S.C. 355].” (emphasis added)).8 
Whereas expert consensus is not sufficient, without more, to establish a drug’s status as 
GRASE, a dispute among experts is sufficient, without more, to preclude a drug’s 
classification as GRASE.  Premo Pharm. Labs., Inc. v. United States, 629 F.2d 795, 803 
(2d Cir. 1980) ("[A] genuine dispute among qualified experts regarding a drug product’s 
safety and effectiveness preclude[s] its qualifying for exclusion as 'generally 
recognized.'"); accord United States v. Articles of Drug for Veterinary Use, 50 F.3d 497, 
501 (8th Cir. 1995); Tri-Bio Labs., Inc. v. United States, 836 F.2d 135, 141 (3d Cir. 
1987).  
 
Based on the “very narrow”9 grounds on which drugs can qualify as GRASE, the FDA 
has stated that, although “theoretically possible,” “it is not likely that any currently 
marketed prescription drug” satisfies the GRASE exception.10  
 
ii. 
The Science on Fluoride Supplements  
 
It is quickly apparent upon reviewing the scientific literature on fluoride supplements that 
these drugs are not generally recognized as safe and effective by experts in the field, 
particularly under modern conditions where the vast majority of children are receiving 
fluoride from many other sources besides water, such as toothpaste and processed 
beverages made with fluoridated water.   
 
The existing state of scientific research on fluoride supplements permits the following 
conclusions, each of which undermines the claim that fluoride supplements qualify as 
GRASE: 
 
a) There Are No Studies Demonstrating the Safety of Fluoride Supplement Use 
 
In order to qualify as GRASE, there must be “adequate tests by all methods reasonably 
applicable to show whether or not such drug is safe for use under the conditions 
prescribed, recommended, or suggested in the proposed labeling.”  21 U.S.C. § 
355(d)(1).  In the case of fluoride supplements, such studies do not exist. 
 
In a recent systematic review of randomized and quasi-randomized trials on fluoride 
supplements, the Cochrane Collaboration was unable to locate a single qualifying study 
that investigated adverse effects other than dental fluorosis, and even with fluorosis, the 
Cochrane Collaboration could only locate a single study.11 According to the Cochrane 
Collaboration review, "No data were available concerning adverse effects related to 
fluoride supplementation in children aged less than 6 years. The ratio benefit/risk of 
fluoride supplementation was thus unknown for young children.”12 
 
Fluoride has recently been classified as a developmental neurotoxin that can harm 
cognitive abilities like learning and memory;13 an endocrine disruptor that can impair 
thyroid and insulin function;14 and is widely recognized as a bone-seeking element that

7 
can weaken bone15 and plausibly induce osteosarcoma.16  As discussed below, there is 
compelling reason to believe that fluoride supplements may cause some or all of these 
harms.17  Yet, as the Cochrane review has revealed, not a single one of these risks, or 
any other non-dental risk associated with fluoride ingestion, has ever been investigated 
in a randomized or quasi-randomized trial of fluoride supplements.  On this basis alone, 
fluoride supplements lack the substantial evidence of safety that is necessary for 
establishing GRASE, per 21 U.S.C. § 355(d)(1). 
 
b) Fluoride Supplements Cause Dental Fluorosis 
 
A drug cannot be classified as GRASE if adequate tests “show that the drug is unsafe 
for use” under the recommended conditions of use.  21 U.S.C. § 355(d)(2).  As noted 
above, there have been no randomized trials investigating the non-dental effects of 
fluoride supplements, but there has been a randomized trial, as well as many cross-
sectional and case-control studies, investigating the relationship between fluoride 
supplement use and dental fluorosis.  These studies have consistently indicated that 
supplement use causes fluorosis, including in its “mild to moderate” forms.18  As noted in 
one review, “Supplement use by children younger than 5 years entails a risk of fluorosis 
which, at the community level, becomes a certainty.”19  
 
Fluorosis is a mineralization defect of tooth enamel that is likely caused by fluoride’s 
interference with tooth-forming cells.20  It is evident, therefore, that fluoride supplements 
induce physiological changes in the body that go beyond cavity prevention,21 and it is 
biologically plausible that cells in other tissues, including the pinealocytes in the pineal 
gland, can be affected at the same doses that impair enamel-forming cells.22  In fact, 
among the very few (non-randomized) studies to consider the non-dental effects of 
fluoride supplements, a range of systemic effects have been observed, including 
headaches, listlessness, gastric distress, weakness, skin rashes, wheezing, and 
reductions in alkaline phosphatase activity.23  
 
Further, the CDC has recognized24—and research has repeatedly demonstrated25—that 
the tooth staining caused by both “mild” and “moderate” fluorosis are “esthetically 
objectionable” conditions when present on the front teeth. Although this staining is 
sometimes dismissed as a mere “cosmetic effect,” research has found that esthetically 
objectionable staining on the front teeth, including the white splotches and streaks 
produced by fluorosis, can cause significant embarrassment and social anxiety for 
growing adolescents,26 which can have damaging consequences for self-esteem and 
mental well-being.27  In fact, after reviewing photographs of dental fluorosis, a National 
Institute of Mental Health panel concluded that “individuals who have suffered impaired 
dental appearance as the result of moderate to severe (dental) fluorosis are probably at 
increased risk for psychological and behavioral problems or difficulties.”28  
 
Since studies clearly show that fluoride supplements cause dental fluorosis when used 
under the recommended conditions, the results of existing supplement studies—even 
though profoundly limited in scope—negate the status of supplements as GRASE under 
21 U.S.C. § 355(d)(2).

c) Effectiveness of Supplements Is “Marginal at Best” and Based on Weak, 
Outdated, and Inconsistent Science 
 
Fluoride supplements were introduced in the 1940/50s on the now universally 
discredited premise that fluoride’s predominant benefit to teeth comes from ingesting an 
“optimal” dose of fluoride during the preeruptive stage of tooth development.29  As 
explained in the Journal of the American Dental Association, “fluoride incorporated 
during tooth development is insufficient to play a significant role in cavity protection.”30  
Both the Centers for Disease Control and National Research Council have confirmed 
this, declaring, respectively, that “fluoride’s predominant effect is posteruptive and 
topical,”31 and “the major anticaries benefit of fluoride is topical and not systemic.”32  In 
other words, fluoride works when it is applied directly to the outside of erupted teeth (i.e. 
topical), not when swallowed (i.e. systemic).  This paradigmatic shift 33  in our 
understanding of fluoride’s cariostatic mechanism largely eviscerates the basis for 
fluoride supplements (i.e., ingesting an “optimal” dose of fluoride). As noted in one 
expert review: 
 
There was a time when ingestion of fluoride in the range of 
0.05 to 0.07 mg F/kg body weight/day was considered 
‘optimal’ for preeruptive caries prevention. In light of 
present knowledge that preeruptive fluoride has little 
preventive effect, this range has better application as an 
estimate of the maximum amount to be ingested by young 
children if fluorosis is to be kept at its lowest level.34  
 
The Cochrane Collaboration has seconded this assessment, noting: 
 
Now the common view is that it is through the posteruptive 
(topical) effect that fluorides have caries preventative 
action. In this context, ingestion of the supplements is not 
necessary nor needed to obtain a preventive effect as the 
topical application of fluoride compounds is all that is 
required to provide preventive effect on dental caries.35 
 
Further, it bears emphasizing that most of the studies purporting to demonstrate the 
effectiveness of fluoride supplements are methodologically flawed studies36 that were 
conducted at a time when fluoride toothpastes, and other topical fluorides, were not 
widely used.37  Modern reviews of the supplement literature have questioned, therefore, 
whether supplements will have any demonstrable benefits if investigated with 
methodologically sound study designs in the current context of widespread background 
exposure to topical fluoride products and other fluoride sources.38   
 
This expert skepticism about the effectiveness of fluoride supplements gains empirical 
support from a series of studies published since 1990 which have failed to find any 
caries preventative benefit at all. 39  The evidence of effectiveness has thus been 
characterized as “very thin,”40 “weak,”41 “low,”42 and “inconsistent.”43  The evidence of 
effectiveness of supplements is particularly weak for infants and toddlers. 44  And, 
although the American Dental Association now only recommends fluoride supplements 
for children with “high caries-risk,”45 the effectiveness of supplements for high caries-risk

children is “unknown.”46  In fact, several recent studies, including a two-year double blind 
trial, have failed to find any benefit of supplements in high caries-risk populations.47   
 
The following are some observations from the scientific literature on the effectiveness of 
supplements that address the aforementioned issues.  We begin first with comments on 
the methodological flaws in most of the supplement studies: 
 
“Like most recent dental or medical systematic reviews, 
our review also demonstrated that the majority of the 
studies were highly biased.”48  
 
“The basis for the widespread acceptance of fluoride 
supplements in caries prevention is a large number of 
mostly small clinical trials in the late 1950’s and 1960’s. 
The early studies have been reviewed again recently in a 
series of publications and they have again been criticized. 
The criticisms are serious and virtually none of the early 
fluoride supplement studies would be published today, 
because of methodological and other shortcomings."49 
 
“There are always aspects of study design and methods in 
clinical trials that can be criticized. Sometimes, the flaws 
do not compromise the validity of the findings, but it would 
appear that the way many early clinical trials of fluoride 
supplements were performed undermines their conclusions. 
In mitigation, it can be conceded that epidemiology was 
not so well developed as a science in the 1960s and 1970s, 
analytical methods were similarly poorly understood, and 
today’s easy access to computers did not exist. These 
explanations may excuse the fact that the early studies 
were done, but they do not excuse us today if we base 
policy on these studies.”50 
 
“The design of these early studies did not follow the now 
accepted protocol calling for random allocation, blind 
examinations, and use of standard criteria for diagnosis of 
caries. They also included a small number of children and 
the majority of their findings could be used to provide 
support for the topical effect of fluoride supplements as 
well as systemic effects. Overall, these early findings can 
only be treated as ‘indications for further investigation.’”51  
 
“The quality of the trials included in this review was 
generally low and many reports lacked important data or 
methodological information. This is probably due to the fact 
that most of the studies were relatively old.”52 
 
“Few studies with good quality were identified in general. 
Only 3 out of 779 studies were acceptable.”53

It bears emphasizing that the Cochrane Collaboration is the one of the world’s most pre-
eminent research bodies for investigating the effectiveness of health care interventions.  
It’s conclusion, therefore, that there is a “lack of evidence” to make “actual good 
recommendations” about the effectiveness of supplements in caries prevention today is 
fatal to the notion that supplements are generally recognized as effective “among 
experts qualified by scientific training and experience to evaluate the safety and 
effectiveness of drugs.”  21 U.S.C. § 321(p)(1).  
 
d) Many Experts Disagree that Fluoride Supplements Are Safe and Effective  
 
As noted earlier, federal courts have held that “a genuine dispute among qualified 
experts regarding a drug product's safety and effectiveness preclude[s] its qualifying for 
exclusion as 'generally recognized.”  Premo Pharm., 629 F.2d at 803 (emphases added); 
accord Articles of Drug for Veterinary Use, 50 F.3d at 501;Tri-Bio Labs., 836 F.2d at 141.  
This rule of law is again fatal to a determination of fluoride supplements as GRASE, for 
as indicated above, and as further explained herein, many experts have rejected the 
premise that fluoride supplements are safe and effective, particularly under modern 
conditions of high background exposures to fluoride.  
 
While some expert reviewers continue to recommend the use of fluoride supplements,57 
others have called for their complete elimination.58  This split in expert opinion was 
recognized in a recent publication, which noted that: “Lack of consensus exists among 
researchers: some support the retention of the existing fluoride schedule, while others 
feel strongly about reducing or completely eliminating the fluoride supplement as a 
caries prevention agent.”59

"Procedures for Class 113 Device Exemptions from Premarket Notification, Guidance 
for Industry and CDRH Staff' issued Feb. 19, 19984, is presented as part of this 
petition. 
A. Description of Device and Principle 
A "Method, Metallic Reduction, Glucose (Urinary, Non-Quantitative)" is a 
device intended to non-quantitatively or semiquantitatively detect I measure 
reducing sugars such as glucose in urine. Measurements obtained by this 
device are used in the diagnosis, monitoring and treatment of metabolic 
disorder such as diabetes mellitus. 
Relying on the definition of "generic type of device" found in the medical 
classification procedures, a generic device means a grouping of devices that 
do not differ significantly in purpose, design, materials, energy source, 
function, or any other feature related to the safety and effectiveness, and for 
which similar regulatory controls are sufficient to provide reasonable 
assurance of safety and effectiveness. In the case of urinary, non-quantitative 
glucose by metallic reduction method devices, the generic type of devices 
include devices which measure glucose and other reducing sugars such as 
galactose, fructose and lactose etc. by classic Benedict's solution5 or in a 
tablet format where the tablet , such as Clinitest Reagent Tablet by BA YER6, 
readily dissolves to form the solution. The principle of Benedict's test is that 
when reducing sugars are heated in the presence of an alkali, they get 
converted to powerful reducing compounds known as enediols. Enediols 
reduce the cupric ions (Cu2+) present in the Benedict's reagent to cuprous ions 
(Cu +)which get precipitated as insoluble red copper (I) oxide(Cu20). 
The current urinalysis dipsticks are only specific for the detection of increased 
levels of glucose and will not detect increased levels of other reducing 
substances (galactose9•10, fructose, lactose, and pentose). A copper reduction 
test, in a solution or tablet format, detects some hereditary disorders due to its 
ability to non-specifically detect reducing sugars such as galactose, which 
may be present in pediatric patients8. 
3 
B. Device History, formulation and mode of action 
The Benedict's test, in solution or tablet format ( Clinitest Reagent Tablets by 
BAYER, now discontinued), 
has been used for over 70 years to detect 
reducing sugars in urine5. In tablet format, it was developed by Alfred and 
Helen free ( Miles Laboratories, Elkhart, IN) in 1940s7. The tablet contained 
Copper Sulfate (anhydrous), Citric Acid, Sodium carbonate and Sodium 
Hydroxide. To perform the test, two drops of a urine specimen are added to a 
glass test tube. An additional 10 drops of water are added followed by 
dropping the reagent tablet into test tube6. When a reducing sugar is present, 
the copper sulfate is converted to Cuprous Oxide in the presence of alkaline 
pH due to the heat generated by Sodium Hydroxide present in the tablet (no 
external source for heating is needed). The tablet is readily dissolved or fizzles 
due to Citric acid reaction with Sodium Carbonate. The carbon dioxide 
produced in the reaction keeps the Copper Sulfate from reacting with the 
atmospheric oxygen. The resultant color change, depending on the amount of 
reducing sugar present, from light olive green to reddish brown is compared 
against a color chart to determine the amount of sugar present in the urine. 
This method is capable of semi-quantitatively measuring a reducing sugar, 
including glucose, from a trace (about 0.25 g I dl ) to 5 g/dl 12 in a specimen 
and it takes about 30 seconds to perform the test. The test, due to its 
simplicity, can be readily performed as a "point of care" test or in a clinic, 
hospital or laboratory. 
C. Detection of Safety and Effectiveness Changes 
As most other in vitro diagnostic devices, Metallic /Copper Reduction, 
Glucose (Urinary, Non-Quantitative)" require routine testing of control 
material. Routine testing of control materials (available commercially) is an 
acceptable means for a user to readily detect changes in the device that could 
affect safety and effectiveness. In accordance with in vitro diagnostic labeling 
requirements, "details of kinds of quality control procedures and materials 
required" will be included as part of the "Copper Reduction, Glucose 
(Urinary, Non-Quantitative)" device labeling and included in the product 
insert brochure. In addition, state and Clinical Laboratory Improvement 
Ammendments of 1988 (CLIA)
11 requirements direct laboratories with 
specific instructions in regards to quality control procedures. Furthermore, 
4 
copper reduction test is often a screening and complementary test to other 
more specific tests which detect glucose and other reducing sugars in urine. 
A search of Medical Device Reports (MDR) on Manufacturer and User 
Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) at FDA website13 for the last 10 years 
from 2006 to 2015 did not tum up any filing of a case of patient or user injury 
for the tablet format (Bayer's Clinitest of the Copper Reduction, Glucose 
(Urinary, Non-Quantitative) device. 
D. CLIA Waiver 
Furthermore, the tablet format of the Copper Reduction, Glucose (Urinary, 
Non-Quantitative) device, in a tablet format, has a "Waived" status by 
Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) 14 owing to its non-
complexity and safety of performance by a user. 
E. Device Classification 
Metallic /Copper Reduction, Glucose (Urinary, Non-Quantitative) devices, in 
a tablet format, are classified as class II devices 15. As described previously, 
these devices have been in use for over 70 years and their use is well 
established without any reports of patient or user injury within the last 10 
years. 
F. Conclusion 
For the reasons cited within this petition the device "Copper Reduction, 
Glucose (Urinary, Non-Quantitative)" in a tablet format satisfies the 
requirements for exemption from the premarket notification requirement.

STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
I. 
BACKGROUND 
 
A. 
Statutory And Regulatory Background 
 
1. Approval of new drugs under section 505(b) and 505(j) of the FDCA 
 
To obtain approval to market an innovative drug, a manufacturer must submit an NDA 
under section 505(b) of the FDCA.  The NDA must contain scientific data and other information 
demonstrating that the drug is safe and effective.8  Specifically, the NDA must show that the 
“drug is safe for use,” and “will have the effect it purports or is represented to have under the 
conditions of use prescribed, recommended, or suggested in the proposed labeling.”9  FDA must 
then weigh the evidence submitted by the applicant, along with other relevant scientific 
information, to determine whether the proposed labeling is accurate, truthful, not misleading, 
and adequate.10   
 
All 505(b) NDAs must contain “full reports of investigations of safety and effectiveness,” 
i.e., clinical data demonstrating that the product is safe and effective for the proposed use.11  To 
be approved under section 505(b)(1), the applicant must include in its NDA data that it has itself 
developed and owns, or has a right of reference to.12  A 505(b)(2) NDA is, on the other hand, an 
NDA for which some or all of the clinical studies relied on for approval “were not conducted by 
or for the applicant and for which the applicant has not obtained a right of reference or use from 
the person by or for whom the investigations were conducted.”13  More specifically, a 505(b)(2) 
NDA may rely on reports in scientific literature regarding another drug, or on the Agency’s 
finding of safety or effectiveness of a previously approved drug.14   
 
Products approved under section 505(b)(2) of the FDCA may be significantly different 
from their reference products, including in their labeling and conditions of use, and yet may still 
be approved on the basis of FDA’s prior approval of a listed drug or multiple listed drugs, and/or

In contrast, section 505(j) of the FDCA establishes an abbreviated approval pathway for a

demonstrate the safety and effectiveness of its proposed drug.18   
 
To rely in this way on FDA’s previous findings for the RLD, an ANDA must include 
information to show that the conditions of use prescribed, recommended, or suggested in the 
labeling proposed for the new drug have been previously approved for the RLD.  A generic 
applicant must also demonstrate that the proposed generic drug product is “the same as” the RLD

and (with narrowly permitted exceptions) labeling – and that it is bioequivalent to the RLD.19 
 
In most cases, generic products are not required to be exactly the same as their reference 
products in characteristics other than those specified in the statute, including in their formulation, 
method of manufacture, container closure systems, or package configurations.  Nevertheless, 
even where a generic may differ from its RLD, FDA seeks to ensure that the two products are 
not so dissimilar that the generic manufacturer would need to make significant changes to its 
labeling or conduct new clinical studies to show that the product, despite its differences, is 
equivalent to the RLD.  Substantially different labeling and the review of new clinical data 
beyond what is required to show bioequivalence are both prohibited in the context of ANDAs.

STATEMENT OF GROUNDS
A.
Factual Background
1.
Abase ofExtended-Release Opioid Products
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (“CDC”) estimates that, from
2001 to 2014, the number of opioid overdose deaths increased over three-fold, from
approximately 6,000 to 19,000 deaths per year (National Institute on Drug Abuse, 2015).
Approximately 1.9 million people in the United States are dependent on or abuse pain
relievers (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2014).
Opioid medications are often manipulated for purposes of abuse. A common
method for opioid abuse is transforming ER opioids into an Immediate-release (“IR”)
form for oral. Intranasal (IN”). or Intravenous (“IV”) administration. In an effort to
combat such forms of abuse, opioid formulations have been developed which include
physical and chemical characteristics to decrease effectiveness of tampering. However,
even with formulation advancements, people continue to abuse ER opioids by crushing
and chewing, injecting, and insufflating (also known as snorting).
In 2010, Purdue Pharma, L.P. (“Purdue”) introduced reformulated OxyContin
controlled-release (OxyContin ADF; approved under NDA 022272), a hard tablet with
gelling properties on exposure to water. The introduction of OxyContin ADF decreased
abuse compared with the original formulation, but currently available data demonstrate
that relatively simple manipulations such as simply chewing the tablets or crushing with
common household tools defeat the extended-release mechanism, in effect, creating an IR
oxycodone (Gudin et al., Pain Medicine, 2015). OxyContin ADF, therefore, retains
warnings that “crushing, chewing, or dissolving OXYCONTIN tablets can cause rapid
release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of oxycodone.” OxyContin Prescribing
Information, Warnings (Aug. 2015).
An analysis recently presented at the 2016 American Pain Society meeting
examined the prevalence of manipulation before oral administration for OxyContin ADF
and two other available products
— Opana® ER (oxymorphone HCI) extended-release
tablets, and Nucynta® ER (tapentadol) extended-release tablets
— designed as hard-to-
crush tablets that use a similar delivery teclmology. The analysis examined the
prevalence of various administration routes used in the last 30 days among over 18,000
abusers entering substance abuse treatment. Approximately 40% of oral abusers reported
manipulating the tablets before swallowing; chewing was the most prevalent

manipulation method (approximately 35%) (Butler S, et al., 2016). These data highlight
the need for continued advances in abuse-deterrent formulation technology for ER
opioids, particularly the development of technologies that prevent dose dumping upon
simple manipulations such as crushing, chewing or dissolving. These simple methods of
manipulations have been shown to be the precursor for all routes of abuse whether it be
oral, injection or snorting. Preventing “dose dumping” by these methods would be a
significant advancement in abuse-deterrent technology and set a new standard for the
approval of new formulations claiming abuse-deterrence.

Xtampza ER
FDA approved Xtampza ER (NDA 208090) on April 26. 2016. A comprehensive
evaluation of the abuse-deterrent properties of Xtarnpza ER was conducted in accordance
with the FDA’s Abuse-Deterrent Guidance. Per FDA’s Abuse-Deterrent Guidance, pre
marketing studies are referred to as Category 1 (laboratory-based in vitro manipulation
and extraction studies). Category 2 (pharmacokinetic studies), and Category 3 (clinical
abuse potential studies). OxyContin ADF (NDA 022272) was used as the comparator in
many of the studies throughout the development program including a head-to-head,
cross-over study that compared the effects of physical manipulation on the
pharmacokinetic profile of Xtampza ER and OxyContin ADF.
These studies resulted in FDA approved labeling that includes Category
1 (in

appearing in the labeling of OxyContin ADF: “Instruct patients to swallow fProductJ
tablets whole; crushing, chewing, or dissolving fProductJ tablets can cause rapid
release and absorption ofa potentiallyfatal dose ofoaycodone.”

provides a significant safety advantage for those patients that may inadvertently misuse
their product in order to facilitate swallowing as well as providing significant barriers to
an abuser seeking to use simple methods of manipulation to facilitate rapid drug release.

Oral Administration of Manipulated Xtampza ER (Study -17):’ Oral PK Study I
(as defined in the approved label) was an open-label, randomized, active-controlled,
naltrexone-blocked, single-dose, 7-period, crossover comparison study of 42 healthy
subjects. The study was designed to assess the effect of crushing or chewing on the PK
profile of Xtampza ER. Treatment arms in the study evaluated 36 mg of Xtampza ER
(equivalent to 40 mg of oxycodone HCI) dosed as either intact capsules, or as crushed or
chewed capsule contents in both fed and fasted states. Oxycodone IR solution (40 mg) in
the fasted state was used as the comparator.
Figure 4 (page 11) displays the mean Cmax values for the Xtampza ER treatment
arms (fed), comparing manipulated Xtampza ER with intact Xtampza ER and IR
oxycodone. Crushing or chewing Xtampza ER did not increase the mean Cna, relative to
intact Xtampza ER capsules (i.e., the dosage form intended to produce a therapeutic PK
profile). Under fasted conditions, the Cmax for all Xtampza ER treatment groups (intact,
crushed, and chewed) fell below the Cmax for intact, fed administration of Xtampza ER.
These data illustrate very little difference between manipulated Xtampza ER treatments
and intact Xtarnpza ER, showing that the product retains its ER characteristics upon
physical manipulation.
This study is listed as “Oral PK Study 1” in the Xtampza ER Prescribing Information.

CITIZEN PETITION 
 
 
The undersigned submits this Petition pursuant to Sections 501, 502, 510 and 513 of the 
Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the "Act") and 21 CFR § 10.30 to request that the 
Commissioner of Food and Drugs (the "Commissioner") take action to protect patient safety by 
detaining the product manufactured or sold by 
 
 
Magnacoustics, Inc. 
Product Offerings:   
• MagnaTouch MRI Music System 
• Genesis Ultra MRI Music System 
• MagnaAlarm  
 
which are accessories under the product type classified as "System, Nuclear Magnetic 
Resonance Imaging" under 21 CFR § 892.1000 and are not cleared nor approved and thus 
misbranded within the meaning of Section 502(o) of the Act. These devices do not 
 
(i) conform to the general controls of the Act, including the establishment registration 
and device listing requirements described in 21 CFR §  807, Subpart B and the 
premarket notification requirements described in 21 CFR § 807, Subpart E;

controls which, when combined with the general controls of the Act, shall be 
sufficient to provide reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness of such 
devices in light of the specific risks to health associated with such devices; and 
 
(iii) did not obtain a substantial equivalence determination from the FDA prior to 
marketing such devices. 
 
If any such determination by the Commissioner are made in the affirmative, the Petitioner 
respectfully requests that the Commissioner under its authority seize all existing models of the 
MagnaTouch MRI Music System, Genesis Ultra MRI Music System and MagnAlarm products  
presently on the market, enjoin the parties presently manufacturing or selling such products from 
continuing to market such unapproved and misbranded devices, and/or enter other appropriate 
relief.

been provided to FDA as required by such Section 502(o) or Section 510(k) of the Act.

Legal Framework

The Act defines a "device" to be:

Expanding access to naloxone is a key element of the public policy response to the opioid 
overdose epidemic.  While naloxone hydrochloride, administered by injection, has been 
approved by FDA and used for more than 40 years to treat opioid overdose symptoms, its use has 
historically been intended for clinicians and other medically trained personnel, such as EMS.   
Naloxone Properties 
Naloxone is an essentially pure opioid antagonist, i.e., it does not possess the “agonistic” or 
morphine-like properties characteristic of other opioid antagonists.  When administered in usual 
doses and in the absence of opioids or agonistic effects of other opioid antagonists, it exhibits 
essentially no pharmacologic activity.  Naloxone has not been shown to produce tolerance or 
cause physical or psychological dependence.  In the presence of physical dependence on opioids, 
naloxone will produce withdrawal symptoms, which may appear within minutes of 
administration and subside in about 2 hours.  The severity and duration of the withdrawal 
syndrome are related to the dose of naloxone and to the degree and type of opioid dependence.  
While the mechanism of action of naloxone is not fully understood, in vitro evidence suggests 
that naloxone antagonizes opioid effects by competing for the mu, kappa, and sigma opiate 
receptor sites in the Central Nervous System (CNS), with the greatest affinity for the mu 
receptor. When naloxone hydrochloride is administered by intravenous injection (IV), the onset 
of action is generally apparent within 2 minutes; the onset of action is slightly less rapid when it 
is administered by subcutaneous injection (SC) or intramuscular injection (IM).   
Naloxone Dosing Instructions 
Injectable formulations of naloxone have been FDA approved for the treatment of opioid 
overdose symptoms for many years at initial doses of 0.4mg to 2mg naloxone by the IM or IV
