Petition for Reconsideration (FDA-2017-P-3196) 
Dear Sir or Madam, 
The undersigned submits this petition for reconsideration of the decision of the Commissioner of 
Food and Drugs in Docket No. FDA-2017-P-3196. 
A. Decision Involved 
We are requesting that FDA reconsider its denial of our citizen petition submitted to the agency 
on May 18, 2017 (the May 18 petition). That petition requested FDA to withdraw the fish 
consumption advice it issuedjointly with the EPA on January 18, 2017 (the 2017 advice) and 
issue new advice designed to achieve FDA' s frequently stated purpose of obtaining the most 
possible benefits to neurodevelopment that fish can provide while minimizing risk from 
methylmercury. The new advice would be tested through randomized, controlled, experimental 
studies with consumers in advance of issuance to ensure that it is likely to succeed. If FDA 
declined to do these things, the May 18 petition requested that the agency respond to a series of 
questions that would enable the public health and scientific communities, as well the public at 
large, to understand and evaluate FDA's reasoning. 
On October 13, 2017, FDA denied the May 18 petition primarily on the grounds that the advice 
is likely to succeed in encouraging fish consumption by pregnant women and nursing women, 
women who might become pregnant, and parents of young children by enabling them to make 
informed choices regarding fish that are healthy and safe to eat. FDA refused to answer the 
specific questions on the grounds that it is not obligated to do so when responding to a citizen 
petition. The agency claimed that its decision not to test the 2017 advice with consumers was 
not a significant deficiency, that it had other funding priorities, and that it was under no 
obligation to test. 
B. Action Requested 
We request that FDA reconsider its denial (FDA's denial) as delineated below. 1 Our request is 
made in accordance with the standards for reconsideration in 21 C.F.R. 10.33, including that 
1 The denial partially granted our request that fish consumption advice be located on FDA' s web site other than on 
the "Food Illness and Contaminants Page" in order to better encourage fish consumption by a highly risk averse 
target population. 
1 
"relevant information and views contained in the administrative record were not previously or 
adequately considered" by FDA (10.33(d)(l)). 
C. Statement of Grounds 
C(l). Summary 
Areas of Agreement: 
As we read it, FDA agrees with us that: 
• 
For the most part, pregnant women2 do not eat enough fish (FDA denial p. 2). 
• 
Consumption advice can play an important role in encouraging pregnant women to eat more 
fish (FDA denial p. 2). 
• 
Pregnant women should eat 8-12 ounces of a variety offish per week during pregnancy to 
nutritionally benefit the developing fetus while minimizing risk from methylmercury (FDA 
denial p. 2). 
• 
In order to effectively encourage pregnant women to eat 8-12 ounces offish per week, the 
advice should: 
• 
Credibly articulate the benefits and risks of fish consumption (FDA denial p. 5). 
• 
Provide "detailed, targeted advice" (FDA denial p. 4) that enables adoption of the 
recommendations contained within through "informed choice" (FDA denial p. 2). 
Areas of Disagreement: 
The core disagreement is whether the 2017 advice is likely to succeed or fail to motivate 
pregnant women to eat 8-12 ounces/week. The advice states that fish convey no special benefits 
to their offspring other than to "growth and development" in a general sense, similar to other 
"protein-rich" foods. It then provides that pregnant women should take care in selecting types 
and amounts of fish in order to avoid an implied significant risk to their offspring from 
methylmercury at levels of consumption germane to the advice. We contend that the 2017 
advice is likely to fail because it does not credibly articulate the benefits or risks of fish 
consumption making informed choice impossible, nor does it provide detailed, targeted advice 
that pregnant women want. 
FDA's denial reveals that: 
• 
FDA longer accepts that fish consumption during pregnancy is likely to benefit fetal 
neurodevelopment, notwithstanding the weight of evidence in support of this special and 
apparently unique benefit. 3 The evidence for this benefit has accumulated over decades and 
a mainstream scientific consensus has coalesced around it. The agency offers little in the 
way of explanation of how it came to this conclusion or how it could have come to it based 
on the totality of the evidence in the administrative record. 
2 As the term is used here, "pregnant women" refers to women who are pregnant or may become pregnant and to 
nursing mothers. 
3 FDA originally initiated the development of new fish consumption advice in order to encourage and enable 
pregnant women to maximize benefits to neurodevelopment for their children. 
2 
• 
FDA has concluded that the fish consumption studies that consistently show the beneficial 
relationships between eating fish during pregnancy and fetal neurodevelopment actually only 
show beneficial relationships to "growth and development" in a general sense. The agency 
offers little in the way of explanation of how it came to this conclusion or how it could have 
come to it based on the totality of the evidence in the administrative record. 
• 
FDA is willing to imply to pregnant women that de minimus shifts in exposure to 
methylmercury trigger significant shifts in risk, i.e., likelihood and severity of harm, at 
relatively low levels of fish consumption. without any scientific evidence in support of this 
implication and apparently without due consideration of the science to the contrary as 
contained in the administrative record. 
• 
FDA placed no significant priority on determining in advance whether the 2017 advice could 
possibly increase fish consumption to 8-12 ounces/week- a four to six-fold increase for 
many women- or even increase fish consumption at all from its current low level. FDA 
chose not to test the advice with consumers or show it to peer reviewers. Instead, the agency 
relied on published studies with messages containing significant differences to the 2017 
advice while ignoring studies in the administrative record, including its own focus group 
studies in 2014, that should have raised significant doubts. 
C(2). Whether the 2017 Advice Credibly Articulates the Benefits and Risks of 
Fish Consumption 
This question addresses whether the target audience is being given the information it needs to 
make truly informed decisions about whether to eat 8-12 ounces/week or close to it. 
"Benefits and risks" refers to the likelihood of specific health effects on: (1) offspring from a 
mother's consumption offish during pregnancy and while nursing; and (2) young children from 
their own consumption of fish. "Fish consumption" refers to eating commercially available 
types offish (fish in "interstate commerce" under the regulatory jurisdiction of FDA) but not to 
freshwater fish caught for recreation or subsistence. 
C(2)(a). The Articulation of the Benefits 
C(2)(a)(i). The Characterization of the Fish Studies 
Questions and Answers (Q & A) accompanying the 2017 advice say "Studies with pregnant 
women have found that the nutritional benefits offish, like other protein-rich foods [emphasis 
added], are important for their children's growth and development [emphasis added] during 
pregnancy and childhood" (section IV, Q & A #1). As addressed throughout the 
administrative record, the "studies with pregnant women" have overwhelmingly found 
associational relationships between eating fish during pregnancy and enhancements to their 
children's neurodevelopment. As documented in the administrative record, major national 
and international public health authorities have concluded that that the weight of the evidence 
for benefits from fish consumption during pregnancy involves neurodevelopment. The 2017 
advice makes no mention of it. 
Nothing in FDA's denial disputes the facts regarding the fish studies. Nonetheless, for 
reasons the agency does not explain, FDA is willing to rely on these studies as showing 
benefits to health in general ("growth and development") but is unwilling to point in the 
advice to the benefits to neurodevelopment that are the consistent focus of these studies. 
3 
The May 18 petition pointed out that the characterization of the fish studies in the 2017 advice 
does not square with their results. The May 18 petition took the position that if fish 
consumption advice is to succeed, it is imperative that the advice make the connection 
between fish consumption during pregnancy and enhancements to fetal neurodevelopment. It 
pointed to focus group results from FDA's own testing in 2014 and from testing conducted 
outside of FDA that pregnant women are motivated by details that show how fish may be 
unique in terms of the benefits they can convey. FDA did not acknowledge or respond to this 
evidence about motivation, and does not appear to have adequately considered it. 
The totality of FDA's denial regarding neurodevelopment was that the 2015-2020 Dietary 
Guidelines for Americans (DGA) "indicates consumption offish by women who are pregnant 
or breastfeeding is associated with improved infant health outcomes but not specifically 
neurodevelopment'' (FDA denial p.5). But a close reading of the 2015-2020 DGA on fish 
consumption reveals that it is essentially a summary of the position taken in the 2010-2015 
DGA, which represented a major development on this subject. In recommending that people 
eat more fish than they typically do, the 2010-2015 DGA stated that fish consumption during 
pregnancy is associated with "improved infant health outcomes, such as visual and cognitive 
development." The 2015-2020 DGA reiterated this point but did not include the examples of 
''visual and cognitive development." 
FDA is now relying on the absence of the "such as" clause in the 2015-2020 DGA to claim 
that the studies show only benefits to growth and development in some general sense that does 
not include fetal neurodevelopment. But what the studies overwhelmingly examined and 
reported on -- neurodevelopment -- is a fact that does not tum on the presence or absence of 
the "such as" clause in the 2015-2020 DGA. FDA does not appear to have adequately 
considered the actual findings from these studies or the analyses and conclusions of major 
international public health entities based on them. FDA does not appear to have adequately 
considered how misrepresenting those facts (primarily by omission) fails to provide the 
detailed advice that women want about specific benefits, undermines informed decision 
making, and raises questions about why pregnant women should eat fish at all if the same 
benefits can be obtained from other high protein foods that do not contain methylmercury. 
We therefore request that FDA reconsider its denial of our request that the advice connect the 
benefits from the fish studies to fetal neurodevelopment show. 
C(2(a)(ii). 8-12 Ounces ofFish Per Week 
FDA's decision to treat all the studies as showing benefit to "growth and development" but 
not to neurodevelopment has consequences that ripple through the 2017 advice. One 
consequence is that it leaves FDA unable to explain why it is important that pregnant women 
eat 8-12 ounces/week as opposed to some other amount or what the specific gains to their 
children are likely to be. The 2017 advice is silent on these matters. Moreover, as the May 18 
petition pointed out, Q & A accompanying the advice ask what would happen if a pregnant 
woman were to eat more or less than 8-12 ounces in a week but do not actually answer these 
questions (section II, Q & A # 3 and 4). FDA's denial does not claim that they do or even 
acknowledge the point. 
4 
Most pregnant women will have to commit to significant increases in fish consumption over 
an extended period of time to reach or even approach 8-12 ounces/week.4 By FDA's own 
reckoning, such a commitment would likely require detailed, targeted information enabling 
informed decision making. For that reason, the May 18 petition requested that the advice 
explain that 8-12 ounces per week falls within a range of optimum amounts that can provide 
the most benefits to neurodevelopment5 and that the advice provide coherent, scientifically 
valid answers to questions about eating more or less than 8-12 ounces/week over time. Few 
women in the United States eat more than 8-12 ounces/week but most women eat 
considerably less, as noted above. For many of these women, reaching 8-12 for a protracted 
period oftime will be challenging at best, as FDA's 2014 focus group results revealed. The 
May 18 petition requested that new advice inform pregnant women that significant benefits 
are obtainable even if they cannot consistently reach 8-12 ounces/week.6 
The May 18 petition argued that providing all this information would credibly articulate the 
benefits, be highly motivational, and would promote informed decision making. FDA's 
denial did not address or acknowledge any of this. We understand that if FDA continues to 
insist that fish consumption during pregnancy does not benefit fetal neurodevelopment, its 
advice cannot claim that 8-12 ounces/week represents an optimum for fetal 
neurodevelopment. But 8-12 ounces/week has to represent something. The advice has to 
have a rational underpinning that is scientifically defensible as a matter of responsible public 
health policy, otherwise it is simply arbitrary and capricious. 
As pointed out in the May 18 petition, the draft of the 2017 advice (which was issued for 
public comment in 2014) recommended 8-12 ounces/week because the 2010-2015 DGA 
recommended 8-12 ounces/week. That draft advice reflected a compromise by FDA and EPA 
in order to break a deadlock between the two agencies over what the advice should 
recommend. But 8-12 ounces per week in the 2010-2015 DGA came from an analysis by its 
Advisory Committee that took into account the results of studies that showed beneficial 
relationships between fish consumption and fetal neurodevelopment. It is not clear how FDA 
can continue to recommend 8-12 ounces/week while denying the existence of data that led to 
this recommendation. 
All of this is contained in the administrative record, which does not appear to have been 
adequately considered. We therefore request that FDA reconsider its denial on these matters. 
C(2)(a)(iii). Omega-3 fatty acids 
The ripple effects from FDA's denial of benefits to neurodevelopment extend to a dismissal in 
the 2017 advice of that omega-3 fatty acids in fish are important contributors to those benefits. 
That dismissal is contrary to the mainstream scientific viewpoint on omega-3 fatty acids, 
including that of the European Food Safety Authority, the Food and Agriculture Organization 
of the United Nations (FAO), the World Health Organization (WHO) and the 2015-2020 
4 An FDA survey cited in the petition and acknowledged in FDA's denial showed a median consumption of 1.8 
ounces per week among pregnant study participants. 
5 As made clear in the administrative record, the existence of optimum amounts that can provide the most possible 
benefits was revealed by the FDA and FAO/WHO assessments of net effects. 
6 The FDA and F AO/WHO assessments of net effects reveal that benefits are still obtainable when consumption is 
below optimum amounts. 
5 
DGA. (See the May 18 petition, pp. 47-8.) There is no certainty, however, whether omega-3 
fatty acids in fish are the sole source of those benefits or whether they contribute to them in 
conjunction with the other nutrients in fish. Nonetheless, given the strong possibility that 
omega-3 fatty acids are important one way or the other, the 2015-2020 DGA, which FDA 
cites for its belief that the fish studies do not show benefits to fetal neurodevelopment, 
recommends that consumers eat at least some fish that are higher in omega-3 fatty acids. 
That recommendation is lacking in the 2017 advice. The May 18 petition requested that it be 
added. In support rejecting it, FDA cites a recent review of evidence relating to dietary 
supplements containing omega-3 fatty acids by the Agency for Health Research and Quality 
(AHRQ). That review concluded that controlled trials involving dietary supplements indicate 
no clear benefit to neurodevelopment. FDA pointed out that "This type of evidence can be 
used to determine if associations observed for food exposures can be attributed to specific 
nutrients found in those foods" (FDA denial p. 7). 
The May 18 petition provided several reasons why the dietary supplement results are unlikely 
to be germane to whether omega-3 fatty acids in fish contribute to the beneficial effects on 
fetal neurodevelopment, or to whether there are benefits to neurodevelopment from fish in the 
first place. (See the May 18 petition, pp. 48-49.) These reasons were not acknowledged or 
addressed in FDA's denial. 
Equivocal results from dietary supplements is not a new development. The recent AHRQ 
review is an update to a 2004 AHRQ review that reported essentially the same thing. The 
2004 review issued well before the European Food Safety Agency, the Food and Agricultural 
Organization of the United Nations together with the World Health Organization, the Institute 
of Medicine, and the both the 2010-2015 and the 2015-2020 DGA concluded that omega-3 
fatty acids in fish are key contributors to neurodevelopmental benefits. 
FDA only considered one review of evidence relating to dietary supplements without 
considering the totality of evidence linking omega-3 fatty acids to brain development or the 
analyses and conclusions of important scientific organizations on this subject. We therefore 
request that FDA reconsider its refusal to include in new advice the recommendation in the 
2015-2020 Dietary Guidelines for Americans that pregnant women eat at least some fish that 
are higher in omega-3 fatty acids. 
C(2)(a)(iv). The FDA and FAOIWHO assessments of net effects 
In support of its positions on neurodevelopment and omega-3 fatty acids, FDA's denial 
denigrates its own assessment of net effects in ways that do not fully or accurately reflect the 
contents or history of that assessment as revealed by the administrative record. The FDA 
assessment of net effects, which issued in 2014, combined data from beneficial associations 
with fetal neurodevelopment with data from adverse associations with methylmercury to 
calculate the overall effects, i.e., the "net effects" on fetal neurodevelopment from eating fish 
during pregnancy. An assessment by the F AO together with the WHO used the same basic 
approach. The results from the two assessments are fundamentally consistent with each other. 
Both assessments calculated that the net effects on fetal neurodevelopment are 
overwhelmingly beneficial at and beyond U.S. levels of fish consumption. They further 
revealed that there are optimum amounts of weekly fish consumption over time at which these 
6 
beneficial net effects are likely to be at their greatest. From 2011 through 2014, the 
Department of Health and Human Services, FDA, and FDA in conjunction with the 
Department of Justice informed the Congress, the public, its own Advisory Committee on 
Risk Communication, and the courts that FDA's assessment of net effects enables the 
development of fish consumption advice for the specific purpose of maximizing 
neurodevelopmental benefits while minimizing risk. The May 18 petition reminded FDA of 
this history. 
FDA's denial revealed that FDA now views the benefits calculations in its assessment of net 
effects as having no practical utility. As a consequence, the objective of fish consumption 
advice is no longer to encourage eating an optimum amount of fish for fetal 
neurodevelopment. 
FDA offers two reasons for this newly stated view of its own assessment. First, "the modeling 
of benefits was based on only one study [Hibbeln et al. (2007)] rather than using a totality of 
the evidence approach to modeling benefits" (FDA denial p. 6). Secondly, the dietary 
supplement results as reported in the AHRQ evidence review undermine the validity of one of 
the models in the assessment that assumed the benefits to fetal neurodevelopment are solely 
from the omega-3 fatty acids in fish.7 
With regard to the claim that FDA only used data from Hibbeln et al. (2007), FDA is wrong 
on two counts. First, the agency also used data that were used by Daniels et al. (2004 ). 
Second, the agency gave due consideration to the strength of those data both separately and in 
total. The data came from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children in the United 
Kingdom. 8 They included results from 7,421 mother/infant pairs on the effects offish 
consumption on early age verbal development and from 9,000 mother/infant pairs on IQ and 
later age verbal development. These are very large cohorts, both individually and collectively. 
FDA performed its own analysis of those data and did not rely solely on the analyses by 
Hibbeln et al. and Daniels et al. 
FDA also ignores that totality of the evidence for modeling purposes can only reasonably 
mean the totality of evidence that meets certain criteria; the phrase cannot mean any evidence 
7 Since the exact contribution of each nutrient in fish to fetal neurodevelopment, either alone or in combination with 
other nutrients is not fully understood, the FDA assessment modeled the beneficial effects twice. One model 
assumed that fish are identical "packages" of nutrients that convey the beneficial effect. The other assumed that the 
omega-3 fatty acids in fish are the sole source of the benefits. As with all risk assessment assumptions, these have 
their strengths and weaknesses, as FDA acknowledged in the assessment. The view within FDA at the time was that 
the results from the two models provide a range of beneficial values in which actual values are likely to fall. 
8 The Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children, operated by the University of Bristol in England, is 
tracking nearly 14,000 children from birth in 1991- 1992 through adulthood to obtain information on mental and 
physical health, educational achievement, and general well-being. 
7 
published anywhere. 9 FDA's modeling criteria for this assessment10 were subject to rigorous 
scientific review, both within FDA and by peer reviewers outside of FDA. Based on those 
criteria, FDA did not model data from studies conducted the United States, Denmark, and 
elsewhere even though they appeared to have been well conducted and indicated benefits to 
neurodevelopment. FDA still reviewed those studies for purposes of context, i.e., to determine 
whether its modeling results were consistent with the totality of the evidence from all the fish 
studies. FDA would not have proceeded to publish its assessment as it did, on the same day in 
2014 that it published draft fish consumption advice with EPA, if the modeling results had not 
fit the totality of the evidence involving fish consumption.11 
C(2)(b). The Risks 
"Risk," as we use it here and in the May 18 petition, means likelihood and severity ofharm. The 
May 18 petition contended that the 20 17 fish consumption advice implies a greater risk from 
methylmercury than the science indicates actually exists at levels of consumption germane to the 
advice. In so doing, it undermines the possibility that that a highly risk averse population will 
increase fish consumption to optimum or near optimum amounts 
The advice divides individual fish into categories. It implies that it would be unsafe to eat any 
more than one serving of a "good" fish in a week (or eat any other fish if a "good" fish is eaten 
that week) or three servings of "best" fish in a week (so long as no "good" fish are also eaten). 
These conswnption recommendations imply that any "good" fish is three times riskier than any 
"best" fish. They also imply that the upper limit of 12 ounces per week (in the recommendation 
to eat 8-12 ounces of fish per week unless a "good" fish is eaten that week) is a dividing line 
between safe and unsafe, i.e., between no likelihood of harm and significant likelihood of harm. 
The May 18 petition argued that these implications are not scientifically defensible on the basis 
of actual risk. For example, one one-hundredth of a part per million (ppm) of methylmercury 
separates the "good" and "best" categories. Fish containing 0.15 ppm or less are "best" while 
fish containing 0.16 ppm or more are "good." The clear implication that this de minimis 
difference in exposure results in a three-fold difference in actual risk cannot be justified by 
anything in the administrative record or anything we know of in the greater scientific record. 
9 Thus, for example, when considering the non-cancer health effects of arsenic during pregnancy (effects on fetus), 
infancy, and early childhood, FDA excluded a variety of data, including data from review articles and data from 
studies that were not in peer reviewed journals. U.S. Food and Drug Administration. 2016. Arsenic in Rice and Rice 
Products Risk Assessment Report, pp.25-26. Available at

10 FDA Quantitative Assessment of the Net Effects on Fetal Neurodevelopment from Eating Commercial Fish (As 
Measured by IQ and also by Early Age Verbal Development in Children, Section IV( d)(!), Preferences for Selecting 
Research Results for Input into the Dose-Response Modeling. 
11 FDA's criticism regarding totality of evidence may actually be referring to the studies involving dietary 
supplements. FDA did not model data from those studies or take them into account. The agency' s selection criteria 
for modeling ruled out data that did not come from fish consumption. The dietary supplement data not involving 
fish contained so much uncertainty about their relevance to fish consumption that they could not be considered truly 
evidentiary in the context of the assessment. The reasons FDA provided in its assessment of net effects were 
essentially the same as those offered to FDA in 2016 correspondence from former agency food officials and 
scientists that FDA never acknowledged and in the petition ofMay 18. It does not appear that FDA has adequately 
considered the administrative record on these matters. 
8 
Likewise, the recommendation to limit "good" fish to only once per week based on an implied 
significant actual risk at two servings per week also has no such basis. The same holds true for 
the implication that eating any amount of "best" fish beyond three servings per week 
immediately generates a significant increase in actual risk. Both the administrative and greater 
scientific records indicate the opposite is true in each of these cases. 
FDA's denial did not claim that these implications do not exist or were not intended in the 2017 
advice, nor did it contest that they misrepresent actual risk or that significant risk of harm 
requires consumption well in excess of the recommended limits. FDA broadly claimed that "as a 
matter of public health policy it is appropriate to provide consumption advice that will help 
ensure that the target population limits exposure to methylmercury" (FDA denial p. 5). We 
agree, but contend that as a matter of public health policy it is appropriate to limit exposure by 
limiting actual risk while optimizing the benefits. That objective can be achieved through advice 
that does not imply that actual risk is greater than it is. 
FDA essentially contended that it took risk into account by designing consumption categories 
that would keep exposures to mercury from exceeding the EPA Reference Dose for 
methylmercury (the RID). Risk was accounted for because the RID represents a level of 
exposure to methylmercury likely to be without appreciable risk over time (FDA denial p.5). 
The RID, like all "safety assessment" levels, contains a significant exposure cushion that makes 
it likely to be without appreciable risk and likely to be below higher exposures to methylmercury 
that are also without appreciable risk. In this respect the RID can be a useful in showing risk 
managers how much of a safety cushion the advice is providing in terms of overall exposure. 
But a safety assessment level such as the RID is not a bright line between no risk and 
appreciable or significant risk. We are not aware of any responsible scientific or public health 
agency that contends otherwise. Care must be taken to ensure that consumption 
recommendations do not reflexively treat very small differences in exposure as if they were 
significant differences in actual risk in order to keep overall exposure below the RID. There is 
simply no good evidence in the administrative or greater scientific records to justify equating 
exposure with actual risk in this way. Measurements of actual risk involve classic 
methodologies as are employed in quantitative risk and dose-response assessments. Both the 
FDA and F AO/WHO assessments of net effects utilized these methodologies and also took into 
account how the benefits to fetal neurodevelopment affect that risk. 
FDA does not appear to have considered the totality of the administrative record on the question 
of risk. For that reason, we request that FDA reconsider its denial with regard to the 
consumption categories. 
C(J). Insight into Whether the 2017 Advice is Likely to Succeed or Fail 
The 2017 advice is unique relative to previous advice in that it recommends to pregnant women 
- a highly risk averse population - that they increase their fish consumption to four to six times 
more than they typically eat. By contrast, previous advice focused on limiting consumption to 
avoid risk and appears to have been influential in that regard. Significantly increasing 
consumption requires pioneering messaging unlike anything issued before. 
FDA cannot know whether the 2017 advice will succeed in increasing fish consumption four to 
six-fold because the agency has not conducted randomized, controlled, experimental studies of it, 
9 
and has not even provided documentation of consultations with experts on the likelihood of the 
advice's success (compare with the updated nutrition facts final rule, where FDA cited expert 
opinion on likely consumer understanding of "includes" in the context of added sugars (81 Fed. 
Reg 33741, 33827; May 27, 2016). 
FDA states that it is not obligated to conduct such studies, that they are resource intensive and 
time consuming to complete, and that in any case the 2017 advice "was based on the input of a 
wide segment of the public, ranging from the individuals who commented on the draft June 2014 
advice, to the experts on FDA's Risk Communications Advisory Committee (RCAC), to the 
external peer reviewers" of the advice. (FDA denial p.8.) We address each of these points in 
tum. 
Nothing in the citizen petition regulations suggests, much less requires, that a petitioner 
demonstrate that FDA is required to proceed as requested. Here, the question is not whether the 
law requires FDA to conduct randomized, controlled, experimental studies, but, rather, whether 
it should have done so in the interest of public health. Given FDA's agreement with us on the 
points set out above, conducting such a study was plainly in the interest of the public health. 
FDA's foods budget in recent years has approached a billion dollars, with more than 25 per cent 
of that amount allocated to FDA's Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition. If our 
memories are serving us well, a randomized, controlled, experimental study of the advice should 
run about $250,000, a miniscule fraction of the funds available to the foods program. And even 
if the study took a year or two from conception to execution, that would not be time consuming 
in relation to the 13 years between the 2017 advice and the previous advice issued in 2004, or the 
11 years between the 2017 advice and the decision to undertake an assessment of the net effects 
of eating fish during pregnancy for purposes of informing that advice. 
Relying on comments from individuals, no matter how well intended or schooled, amounts to 
reliance on anecdote, which has long been, and must remain, an anathema to a science-based 
agency. The experts on the RCAC did not review the 2017 advice nor did the external peer 
reviewers who, on the eve of issuance, were not even asked whether the 20 17 advice was likely 
to succeed. 
FDA's denial indicates that it was influenced by three published studies. It is not clear, however, 
how these studies could have provided FDA with confidence that its 2017 advice would increase 
fish consumption well beyond anything that has previously occurred. Oken et al. (2013), a small 
pilot study, showed increases in fish consumption, but the advice that apparently motivated the 
gains emphasized eating fish high in omega-3 fatty acids, which FDA discounts, in addition to 
fish that are lower in methylmercury. In addition, the group with the greatest gains received a 
gift card as well as the advice and a research assistant reviewed the advice with each participant 
during an in-person visit. The Burger et al. (2008) study of risk communication failure pointed 
to the lack of detailed information about benefits as well as risks from seafood consumption. 
The agency's denial ignores the fact that Burger et. al. concluded that effective advice should 
include details about the benefits. By contrast, FDA's 2017 advice is highly generalized 
regarding benefits in addition to being highly questionable from a scientific standpoint. And 
tellingly, FDA's denial fails to disclose that "The Maine Family Fish Guide: Advice from the 
Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention" studied by Teisl et. al. (2011) lists "Best 
Choices" as "Seafood High in Omega 3 Oils and Low in Mercury," and "Next Best Choices" as 
"Other Seafood Low in Mercury but Not as High" in such oils. The Maine advice characterizes

Emergency Citizens’ Petition for Five Year

In order to implement the legal requirements for vaccine safety and the applicable International 
Humanitarian Law principle of Informed Consent, on behalf of the signatory organizations and 
individuals and others who communicate their inclusion in this Petition to the Agency (herein, 
the Petitioners) the undersigned hereby Petition the Food and Drug Administration and the 
Centers for Disease Control (the Agency) to exercise regulatory discretion and issue Regulations 
to implement a Five Year Moratorium on all Childhood Vaccinations (the Moratorium), even 
during any declared local, national or international Health Emergency.  
We, the undersigned, on our own behalf and for all the Petitioners herein or hereafter, hereby 
Petition the Agency, under the First Amendment Right to Petition for Redress, under the 
Administrative Procedures Act (APA) and 21CFR10.30, for an emergency ruling to promulgate 
Regulations on an emergency basis, implementing the Moratorium, in the form attached hereto 
as Exhibit A (page 17), entitled “Vaccine Moratorium Regulation” and made a part hereof, as 
though fully set forth herein (hereinafter, the Regulation).  
The proponents of this formal Petition under the APA have also filed a Petition at 
WhiteHouse.gov in support of the Vaccine Moratorium, https://petitions.whitehouse.gov/petition/five-
year-moratorium-childhood-vaccines.  The information web page for this APA Petition is: 
http://tinyurl.com/vaccinemoratorium. 
[A] Actions Requested 
(1) Exercise of regulatory discretion to immediately promulgate the requested Regulation 
as an emergency ruling to protect the public health, and especially the health of children.   
(2) Hold hearing(s), permit public comments, issue permanent regulations, consistent 
with our expressive association rights and humanitarian law, implementing the 
emergency discretion and emergency Regulation on a regular basis.

Reservation of Rights: Petitioners reserve all rights, including violation of First 
Amendment by rules that censor speech about health; unclean hands by restraint of trade; 
ultra vires Congressional grant of authority; nothing herein shall be construed to be an 
admission of Agency authority to approve, recommend or mandate vaccines.  
(4) The science is settled. Vaccinated children are less healthy than unvaccinated 
children.

[B] Statement of Grounds 
[1] Statement of Facts 
1. The undersigned Petitioners are private individuals (including vaccine-injured or other 
children by their parents or guardians) and members of private associations aggrieved by the 
uninsurable risks of "unavoidably unsafe" vaccines which thereby violation Informed Consent.  
2. The undersigned communicants engage in constitutionally protected expressive association 
communications regarding the risks of vaccination, especially to children.   
3. The communicant associates seek guidance regarding the exercise of their fundamental 
expressive association right to Informed Consent with regard to any and all medical

interventions, including vaccinations or other health-related strategies and procedures 
recommended or mandated by governmental authority. 
4. The undersigned communicate to the public with regard to the legal requirements that 
vaccines be safe and effective.  
5. The undersigned advise the communicants regarding the exercise of their Right to Informed 
Consent to refuse Childhood Vaccines without regard to State or Federal vaccine mandates, but, 
in the absence of a clear Regulation, is unsure of the best practices with regard to exercising 
Informed Consent consistent with vaccine safety.  
6. The communicants and undersigned are thereby prevented from fully exercising the Right of

Humanitarian Law; this unlawfully restricts the Petitioners’ exercise of their First Amendment

7. The Centers for Disease Control, under the aegis of the Food and Drug Administration, have 
failed the Public Trust and have lost public confidence.[1] The agency, like so many other 
Federal agencies, is viewed by the public as serving the interest of politically connected “crony” 
corporations, but not the safety and privacy interests of the public. Under such circumstances, the 
urgency of the redress for which this Petition is submitted should be compelling. The Public will 
not trust the Federal Public Health Authorities without a clear Regulation faithfully 
implementing Informed Consent as the sine qua non of Public Health interventions such as 
Childhood Vaccination and the requirements of law that same be safe and effective.  
8. The Public Interest can only be met by imposing on the regulated drug companies the 
requested Moratorium and requiring them to place on their vaccine labeling, "Not for Childhood 
Vaccination." 
 
 
 
http://www.vaclib.org/sites/debate/Vaccines.html

[2] Legal Authority 
1. The Legal Basis for this Petition is the First Amendment to the Constitution of the United 
States: “Congress shall make no law… abridging the… the right of the people… to petition the 
Government for a redress of grievances.” This Citizens’ Petition is submitted pursuant to 
21CFR10.30 and a copy of it is being submitted through http://www.regulations.gov at Generic 
Docket No. FDA 2013-S-0610-0001 [2]. In so far as this Petition seeks the addition of certain 
information regarding Informed Consent to vaccine package inserts, it is grounded on the 
statutory authority of the FDA to specify the contents of drug packaging.[3]  
2. The Legal Basis for the Proposed Regulatory Discretion is [A] the aforesaid Constitutional

underpin Informed Consent, and Section 3512 of Title 19 and specifically, 19 USC 3512(a)(1) 
and (a)(2) and [B] the drug safety laws, as hereinafter described, including but not limited to 21

211, 211.1, Part 601, 601.2(a), 601.4(a) and 610.15(a), as applied to the protection of human life, 
mandated, in the instance of vaccination, by the United States Supreme Court in the case of 
Jacobson vs Commonwealth of Massachusetts. [4]  
[A] Informed Consent 
Federal Regulation acknowledges Informed Consent for formal Institutional Review Board 
(IRB) overseen experimentation. [5]  
The recognition of the application of Informed Consent during the less formal “final stage” of 
experimentation on drugs (including vaccines) released to the public is not adequately 
implemented by law or regulation,  
“…Phase 4 trials are conducted after a product is already approved and on the market to 
find out more about the treatment's long-term risks…” [6]  
Where there is unavoidable risk, as there is with Childhood Vaccination, the right to Informed 
Consent must be respected, but the Federal Government practice of recommending now over 50 
Childhood Vaccines without effective implementation of the vaccine safety laws eviscerates the 
right to Informed Consent. 
With regard to all communications about health care decisions, the members of the public have 
the right to make Informed Consent decisions, even if a decision may be considered a “bad” 
decision by the Government. The Supreme Court indicated, in Thompson v Western States, 535 
U.S. 357 (2002): [7] 
"We have previously rejected the notion that the Government has an interest in 
preventing the dissemination of truthful commercial information in order to prevent 
members of the public from making bad decisions with the information."

CITIZEN PETITION  
The undersigned, on behalf of Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Research Services, Inc. (“PMRS”) 
submits this petition pursuant to 21 C.F.R. §§ 10.30 and 10.31, and Section 505(q) and other 
provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (“FD&C Act”).  This petition requests 
the Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) to refrain from approving NDA 209653, submitted 
by Intellipharmaceutics Corp. (“NDA 209653” or the “Intellipharmaceutics product”), with the 
proposed indication or any other labeling that suggests that the product is appropriate for chronic 
use.  This petition further requests that FDA refrain from approving any other pending or future 
marketing application for such use.  
A. 
ACTION REQUESTED 
To protect the public health interest in ensuring the responsible prescribing and use of opioid 
drug products, PMRS respectfully requests that the FDA take the following action: 
 Refrain from approving pending NDA 209653 with the proposed indication of 
“management of moderate-to-severe pain when a continuous around-the-clock 
analgesic is needed for an extended period of time.” 
 Refrain from approving all other pending or future applications for opioids indicated 
for chronic use, including use over “an extended period of time,” use for “long-term 
opioid treatment,” or any other labeling for chronic use.

B. 
STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
If NDA 209653 is approved with the proposed indication of “management of moderate-to-severe 
pain when a continuous around-the-clock analgesic is needed for an extended period of time,” it 
would be misbranded and its presence on the market would negatively affect the public health, 
potentially further fueling the current epidemic of opioid addiction. 
For the reasons discussed herein, the proposed indication is false and misleading, and lacks 
“substantial evidence consisting of adequate and well-controlled investigations” as required by 
the FD&C Act. 
I. 
Indication of opioids for the treatment of chronic pain lacks substantial evidence 
According to its guidance document on analgesic indications, the FDA defines chronic pain as 
“either pain persisting for longer than 1 month beyond resolution of the underlying insult, or pain 
persisting beyond 3 months.”1  However, as PMRS has articulated in a previously-filed Citizen 
Petition (FDA-2017-P-1359), beginning with the approval of original OXYCONTIN in 1995, the 
Agency has unlawfully allowed extended-release opioids to be marketed with chronic-use 
labeling, despite a lack of evidence to support the chronic-use indication.2  Even today, there 
remains a lack of evidence that prescription opioids are effective or safe therapeutics in the 
chronic pain setting.3 
Indeed, the lack of evidence to support the efficacy of prescription opioids in the treatment of 
chronic pain has been recognized by the CDC.  In its March 2016 Guideline for Prescribing 
Opioids for Chronic Pain, the CDC acknowledged that: “[T]he guideline uses the best available 
scientific data to provide information and recommendations to support patients and clinicians in 
balancing the risks of addiction and overdose with the limited evidence of benefits of opioids for 
the treatment of chronic pain.” 4  The CDC Guideline is the culmination of almost three years of

II. Public Impact – Opioid Morbidity and Mortality 
As pain experts have explained, “[a]ddiction develops slowly, usually only after month of

typically not remit with opioid discontinuation and will carry a high risk of relapse for years 
without proper treatment.” 10 As such, abuse-deterrent opioids were originally approved and 
marketed to correct what is now known to be a flawed premise: that addiction was a consequence 
of abuse and misuse.11  However, it is not the abuse of opioids that creates addicts; addiction 
causes abuse of opioids.  
The United States is experiencing an iatrogenic opioid epidemic that continues to rage out of 
control.  According to the CDC, “[s]ince 1999, the amount of prescription opioids sold in the 
U.S. nearly quadrupled, yet there has not been an overall change in the amount of pain that 
Americans report.” 12  And, in 2015, “there were over 33,000 deaths involving opioids,

III. CONCLUSION 
The root cause of the United States opioid epidemic is the FDA’s approval of opioid drug 
products for the treatment of chronic pain absent substantial evidence of efficacy. Exacerbating 
the problem, the FDA-approved labeling provided the medical community with false reassurance 
that opioids are safe and effective in the treatment of chronic pain despite a lack of evidence to 
support such an indication.  This led the medical community to change its long-held beliefs and 
practices about prescribing low-dose opiates only for acute injury and only for short durations 
due to severe risk of addiction and a lack of empirical data of efficacy for chronic pain. 
Ultimately, the FDA’s action to approve prescription opioids for chronic pain is in violation of 
the FD&C Act requirement that FDA have “substantial evidence consisting of adequate and 
well-controlled investigations.” Since being wrongfully approved for treatment of chronic pain, 
it is estimated that opioids have killed over 200,000 people. 22  By approving opioids indicated 
for the treatment of chronic pain without substantial evidence of their efficacy for this indication, 
the FDA has helped to facilitate the launch of the U.S. opioid epidemic—an escalating public 
health crisis unprecedented in our country. 
To address these concerns, PMRS requests that the FDA refrain from approving pending NDA 
209653 with the proposed indication of “management of moderate-to-severe pain when a 
continuous around-the-clock analgesic is needed for an extended period of time,” or any other 
labeling that suggests that the product is appropriate for chronic use.  PMRS further requests that 
FDA refrain from approving any other pending or future marketing application for such use.

PMRS submitted a New Drug Application (NDA) on January 16, 2017 under Section 505(b)(2)

treatments are inadequate.  This proposed indication is specifically for the management of acute 
pain, and not for chronic use.  In addition, the dosage guidance for this NDA adheres to the 
CDC’s recommendations for MME maximum dose and duration.

CITIZEN PETITION 
 
The undersigned respectfully submits this citizen petition on behalf of Mylan Inc. 
(“Mylan”) under 21 U.S.C. § 355 and 21 C.F.R. § 10.30, among other provisions of law, to 
request that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs (the “Commissioner”) take the actions 
described below with respect to any abbreviated new drug application (“ANDA”) for fluticasone 
propionate and salmeterol xinafoate inhalation powder (“FP/SX”) that relies on Advair Diskus® 
as the Reference Listed Drug (“RLD”).  Specifically, Mylan asks the Agency to refrain from 
approving any ANDA that relies on multiple-batch pharmacokinetic (“PK”) bioequivalence 
(“BE”) study designs unless, after conducting an appropriately rigorous review under the 
established standards for establishing BE, generally, and for this product specifically, FDA 
concludes that such a study design is valid and will ensure patients receive a robust and reliable 
therapeutically equivalent product.   
 
Based on our work developing a FP/SX product, we know that a sponsor need not turn to 
unvalidated alternative methods as it is possible, with an adequate understanding of the RLD and 
a well-designed proposed generic, to demonstrate BE using straightforward and established 
single-batch BE studies designed in accordance with FDA’s guidance, experience, and 
precedent. FDA’s September 2013 Draft Guidance on Fluticasone Propionate and Salmeterol 
Xinafoate (the “Guidance”), which was developed over multiple years and reflects FDA 
research, discussion with industry, academia, and other stakeholders, and current scientific 
standards, represents a well-balanced, workable, and best approach to satisfying the ANDA 
approval standard in terms of in vitro BE, in vivo BE (PK and clinical), and overall equivalent 
device performance.  
I. 
ACTIONS REQUESTED 
 
Mylan is the world’s third largest generic and specialty pharmaceutical company and the 
largest global generics company headquartered in the United States.  Today, one out of every 11 
prescriptions dispensed in the United States, brand or generic, is a Mylan product.  Over the 
course of its 50-year history, Mylan has demonstrated an unwavering commitment to enhancing 
patient access to high-quality, affordable generics, which are as safe and efficacious as their 
brand counterparts.  As part of that commitment, Mylan has submitted an FP/SX ANDA that 
relies on Advair Diskus as the RLD.  We therefore have a strong interest in providing patients in 
the near future with a robust, reliable, and more affordable therapeutically equivalent and fully 
substitutable version of this important medication.  
Division of Dockets Management 
December 5, 2017  
Page 2 
 
 
 
 
We are aware of a recent abstract and podium presentation exploring a multiple-batch PK 
BE study with a very large number of test and reference product batches as a way of 
demonstrating PK BE between a proposed generic and the Advair Diskus.1  This unprecedented 
multiple-batch design is proposed in order to take account of high batch-to-batch variability 
occurring within the RLD.  It clearly contrasts with the straightforward, well-established 
approach outlined in the Guidance, which provides for a single-batch PK BE study based on the 
comparison of one batch of test and reference product. These batches must be representative of 
the products based on careful in vitro analysis of product characteristics, particularly those that 
are shown to be critical determinants of product performance in vivo. 
 
We are concerned that applicants may be attempting to rely on novel, unprecedented PK 
BE study designs to support bioequivalence of a proposed product to the RLD because they have 
not adequately performed the necessary development work to understand the RLD product and 
the proposed generic and, as a result, are unable to demonstrate PK BE using accepted methods 
as provided by the Guidance.  Such an unprecedented design has not been demonstrated to 
constitute valid, reliable data that could support ANDA approval, and sponsors who have failed 
to show BE using more straightforward and well-established methods should not be permitted to 
take failed studies and attempt to instill them with meaning using an atypical multiple-batch 
study design – especially when the more straightforward, well-understood design provided for in 
the Guidance is sufficient to establish BE.  This is, of course, true for any departure from the 
approach articulated in the Guidance, particularly a proposed departure based on a failed study. 
 
Accordingly, Mylan requests that FDA refrain from approving any ANDA unless it 
contains the results of a PK BE study that reflects sound development work and clearly 
demonstrates equivalent rigor to the well-established single-batch test versus reference study 
design outlined in the Guidance and used broadly by FDA.  The multiple-batch approach 
described in the recent abstract and presentation raises critical questions under this standard and, 
as discussed in more detail below, is ultimately unnecessary as PK BE can be demonstrated 
using the straightforward method described in the Guidance.  
 
 
II. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
1. Product and Legal Background  
 
Advair Diskus is a dry powder inhaler that combines a corticosteroid, fluticasone 
propionate, and a long-acting beta2-adrenergic agonist, salmeterol xinafoate, used for the 
treatment of asthma in patients ages 4 years and older and for maintenance treatment of airflow 
obstruction and reducing exacerbations in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 
                                                      
1 Elise Burmeister Getz, Kevin J. Carroll, Abstract, Pharmacokinetic Bioequivalence of Two Fluticasone 
Propionate/Salmeterol Dry Powder Inhalers, OT329 Solis, and Advair Diskus, Chest (Oct. 2017), Vol. 152:4 
Supp. at A768 (Exhibit A); Elise Burmeister Getz, Kevin J. Carroll, Pharmacokinetic Bioequivalence of Two 
Fluticasone Propionate/Salmeterol Dry Powder Inhalers, OT329 Solis® and Advair Diskus®, Presentation at 
Annual Meeting of Am. College of Chest Physicians, Toronto, Canada (Oct. 31, 2017) (Exhibit B). 
Division of Dockets Management 
December 5, 2017  
Page 3 
 
 
 
(COPD).  It is currently available in three strengths, with a low strength of 100mcg/50mcg of 
fluticasone propionate/salmeterol xinafoate, a middle strength of 250/50, and a high strength of 
500/50. 
 
Under section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (“FDCA”), an ANDA 
applicant must demonstrate, among other things, that its proposed product is the same as the 
RLD with regard to active ingredient, dosage form, route of administration, strength, labeling, 
and conditions of use, and is bioequivalent.2  A generic drug is considered BE to the RLD if “the 
rate and extent of absorption of the [generic] drug do not show a significant difference from the 
rate and extent of absorption of the [RLD] when administered at the same molar dose of the 
therapeutic ingredient under similar experimental conditions . . . .”3   
FDA requires that the data generated to establish BE is sound in terms of design and 
statistical measures under the regulations: “Applicants shall conduct bioavailability and [BE] 
testing using the most accurate, sensitive, and reproducible approach available . . . .”4  BE is 
critical to ensuring a generic drug will provide the same clinical effect and safety profile as the 
RLD, and notably, FDA may refuse to approve an ANDA if, among other things, the data is 
insufficient to show BE.5 
2. Consistent with FDA’s guidance, experience, and precedent, sponsors can 
demonstrate generic FP/SX product BE with a single-batch PK BE study so long 
as the applicant develops a robust understanding of the performance 
characteristics of the RLD and uses it to design an ANDA that will match RLD 
performance 
 
FDA’s Office of Generic Drugs (“OGD”) issued the Guidance in September 2013 to 
inform generic applicants’ approaches to evaluating BE of FP/SX drugs in comparison to Advair 
Diskus.6  Issuance of the Guidance culminated a multi-year effort to determine appropriate 
measures of BE for oral inhalation products in general and FP/SX drugs in particular.  
Developing BE measures for orally inhaled drug products has been a topic of much discussion 
both at FDA and in various scientific fora in which FDA, academic experts, and industry have all 
participated.  Mylan engaged in this debate from the early stages, welcomed the Guidance, and 
has designed its development program to conform to it.   
 
                                                      
2 FDCA § 505(j)(2)(A)(i)-(v); see also 21 C.F.R. § 314.94(a)(4)-(8). 
3 FDCA § 505(j)(8)(B)(i). 
4 21 C.F.R. § 320.24(a). 
5 FDCA § 505(j)(2)(A)(iv); see also 21 C.F.R.  § 314.94(a)(7)(i); 21 C.F.R.  § 314.127(a)(6)(i). 
6 Subsequent to the Guidance, many other product-specific orally inhaled product guidances have been issued 
which adopt the same key tenets of in vitro equivalence, PK BE in a single-dose 2-way crossover design across 
all strengths, and a Clinical Endpoint study.  See, e.g., Draft Guidance on Budesonide; Formoterol fumarate 
dihydrate (June 2015); Draft Guidance on Fluticasone Propionate (Oct. 2017); Draft Guidance on Tiotropium 
Bromide (Oct. 2017).

The Guidance sets out recommendations for both in vitro and in vivo studies and 
similarity in device performance in terms of mode and mechanism of use compared to the RLD 
to ensure that any approved ANDA delivers a robust, reliable therapeutically equivalent version 
of Advair Diskus to patients.  To establish BE of a proposed generic FP/SX product to the RLD, 
the Guidance outlines three key elements:   
1) In vitro testing to evaluate single actuation content (SAC) and aerodynamic particle size 
distribution (APSD);  
2) A PK BE study for each proposed product strength; and 
3) A clinical endpoint study for the lowest strength. 
All three elements are critical to meeting the standard of approval and, based on our experience, 
developing a robust and complete understanding of the performance characteristics of the RLD 
and proposed generic product through in vitro testing is critically important to developing a 
therapeutically equivalent generic to the RLD.  This is, in part, due to the well-known batch-to-
batch variability present in all strengths of the RLD.   
 
For instance, the USP monograph for Advair Diskus makes clear that the APSD 
performance, a measure describing the lung deposited fraction of the orally inhaled dose, is 
permitted to vary up to 2-fold.7  This is a far wider range than what would typically be permitted 
for the geometric mean ratio of exposures (0.9-1.11-fold) which would be expected, in a standard 
well-powered PK BE comparison, to yield 90% confidence intervals within the 80-125% limits 
established for BE.  
 
It is therefore necessary to understand this and any other variability present with the 
RLD, as well as the effect of that variability on PK BE and the overall product properties that 
make one batch of the RLD BE to another in order to effectively develop a generic version of the 
product that is equivalent to the RLD. Of course, as part of this development, a sponsor must also 
reach a corresponding understanding of its proposed generic, allowing control of any 
characteristics of that product which may contribute to difference from the RLD performance. 
 
Our experience indicates that with careful and thorough examination of the in vitro and in 
vivo (i.e., PK) characteristics of the RLD (and generic products), clear relationships can be 
established between the two, allowing critical in vitro determinants of in vivo product 
performance to be established.  These critical in vitro determinants are conserved across all 
product strengths and explain the vast majority of between-batch variability observed for the 
RLD (and generic) product such that batch-to batch-variability within the RLD is shown not to 
be randomly occurring.  Establishing an in vitro in vivo relationship (IVIVR) is the key to 
understanding the RLD and proposed generic products and a workable development program.8  
                                                      
7 Fluticasone Propionate and Salmeterol Inhalation Powder, U.S. Pharmacopeia National Formulary, USP40-
NF35 at 4303 (current through Apr. 30, 2018) (Exhibit C). 
8 Because PK BE is not assessed for every commercial batch, this IVIVR not only plays an important role in 
developing a robust generic equivalent of such a complex RLD as Advair Diskus, but is also key in

With sound development work, the Guidance provides that the sponsor demonstrate in 
vitro equivalence of the products with studies using a minimum of three batches of the RLD as 
compared to a minimum of three batches of the proposed generic for SAC and APSD using a 
Population BE statistical test.  This test supports equivalence for the RLD and generic product 
batch populations, and we maintain, consistent with the Guidance, is the appropriate place for 
population BE, including batch-to-batch variability, to be established.   
 
The Guidance also provides that the sponsor follow a straightforward approach, 
examining all strengths of the RLD and proposed generic, typically based on a two-period 
crossover study comparing one batch of test product with one batch of RLD product.  The 
sponsor’s in vitro work analyzing the properties and performance of the products should be the 
foundational work for the PK BE comparison.  Once a sponsor understands and characterizes the 
variability of the products and establishes an IVIVR, it can design and execute an appropriately 
robust PK study that relies upon a single batch of the RLD compared to a single batch of the 
proposed generic, which is the study design described in the  Guidance.9  In other words, if an 
IVIVR is established by the sponsor, a PK study can be conducted using test and RLD batches 
representative of the product populations with a high degree of certainty to demonstrate PK BE, 
and in this case, a sponsor should be able to develop a model for the RLD and its proposed 
generic products that can be shown to predict relative in vivo exposure based on in vitro 
parameters alone. 
 
Simply put, with sound scientific analysis to develop a thorough understanding of the 
product characteristics and the impact of any variability in these characteristics on PK, an 
applicant can demonstrate BE against all three strengths of Advair Diskus using the standard 
well-understood and reliable PK BE study design described in the Guidance. This is the 
paradigm which we, and we presume other sponsors, have followed to demonstrate PK BE 
between all three strengths of our proposed generic product and the corresponding strength of the 
Advair Diskus product.  
 
This work to develop a thorough understanding of the characteristics and performance of 
the RLD and the proposed generic toward establishing an IVIVR is not only the foundation of 
the PK BE studies, but also supports the clinical BE studies and development of data related to 
device performance required by the Guidance to ensure equivalent exposure at the local site of 
action and similarity of device performance.  As with the PK BE studies, a sponsor with a sound 
understanding of the products and a well-designed proposed generic should be able to meet the 
                                                      
establishing biorelevant in vitro commercial specifications, which can be used to ensure a reliable generic 
equivalent is being produced time after time. 
9 Note that randomness appears to be a key rationale for a multiple-batch proposal, as suggested in Dennis 
Sandell et al., PK Bioequivalence testing when between-batch variability is high: A multiple-batch proposal, 
Inhalation at 13 (Dec. 2017) (Exhibit D).  However, the single batches envisioned in the Guidance are not 
random and must be justified as representative.  When viewed in this context, the multiple-batch proposal is 
offering a solution to a problem that does not exist.

equivalence requirements of the Guidance and will not need to rely on alternative models or 
methods. 
 
3. Use of an unvalidated multiple-batch approach to demonstrating PK BE may 
indicate an issue with the sponsor’s proposed generic product or the sponsor’s 
overall inability to understand the product well enough to design the single-
batch PK BE study envisioned by FDA 
 
Based on the recent presentation and abstract, at least one sponsor, Sandoz Inc. 
(“Sandoz”), appears to be having difficulty establishing BE of its proposed product and the RLD, 
at least at the lowest 100/50 strength, and appears to be considering a multiple-batch approach to 
demonstrating BE, presumably for this strength alone.10  Sandoz’s approach describes both the 
pooling of multiple (5 in this case) studies which presumably have followed the Guidance but 
which have each failed to demonstrate PK BE, and a prospective multiple-batch PK BE study.11  
 
The use of multiple batches, however, is unnecessary and, in our view, FDA should 
exercise caution with regard to accepting any new BE methodology in circumstances in which 
the sponsor was apparently unable to achieve acceptable BE results with the recommended 
methodology, presumably either because there is an issue with the product or there is limited 
understanding of the test and/or reference product to design the BE study envisioned by FDA.  
This is especially true when the proposed methodology is new, relatively untested, and carries 
with it a number of design risks. 
 
With respect to the pooling of multiple failed PK BE studies in order to demonstrate 
equivalence, which is also included in the Sandoz publication, such a method is clearly 
retrospective and, at best, hypothesis generating not hypothesis testing.  Following up these 
failed PK BE studies with a prospective PK BE assessment using multiple batches does not 
improve matters.  Any multiple-batch BE study must use study designs, statistical models, and 
acceptance criteria that are clearly understandable, valid, and free of significant confounding 
factors to be sure that the evaluation of BE is not obscured by chance or testing to compliance. 
Only by doing so can such studies demonstrate that the confidence in true BE obtained from the 
study is at least as high as that obtained from standard studies, after taking into account 
additional confounding factors that would arise from these complex, non-traditional BE study 
designs.  
 
                                                      
10 Getz and Carroll, Presentation, supra n. 1; Getz and Carroll, Abstract, supra n. 1. 
11 Id.  The study was a prospective multiple-batch pivotal PK BE assessment which was conducted in 96 
healthy adult subjects across 16 batches per product (products being the Sandoz generic and Advair Diskus; 
both 100/50 strength).  A single inhalation was administered in a randomized crossover design. PK blood 
samples were collected pre-dose and 32-56 hours after inhalation.  Treatment difference estimates were 
obtained by analysis of variance of log-transformed PK metrics.

This is not a simple matter.  Taking the recent publication as an example of such a study, 
the rationale for a study design containing multiple batches (in this case, 16) each of test and 
reference products must include 
• A statistically justified explanation for the use of multiple batches and the number of 
batches being used (e.g., 16).  The explanation should include data to demonstrate the 
nature of the inter-batch variation requiring the use of such a large number of batches to 
provide a representative set for test and reference product. The explanation should also 
justify that there is no suitable means to represent the product variability identified with a 
smaller number of batches, by an alternative study design, improved test product 
characterization, or more suitable statistical analysis. 
• A statistically justified explanation for the study design including the number of subjects, 
number of cohorts, number of batches within cohorts, the number of periods, and the 
randomization strategy for batches across subjects and periods, in particular how were 
test and RLD batches assigned for dosing individual subjects.  
• Method and rationale for inclusion of each batch, spanning the respective batch 
distribution of each product, in addition to any prospective batch parameters used to infer 
the type of batch distribution used and whether these overlaid each other for test and 
RLD. 
• Assurance that the commercial population distribution of RLD was fully sampled based 
on characteristics implied for PK and that such sampling was adequately weighted to be 
representative of the distribution population. 
• Evidence that the number of subjects receiving each batch is statistically sufficient to 
fully understand the variability of subjects within each batch, and also the inter-batch 
variability within each product.  
• A statistical analysis plan including a justification of the treatment of “batch” and 
“cohort” and any interaction effects in the statistical model to ensure that these sources of 
variability are fully accounted for in the study analysis. 
• If batch is included as a random effect, a justification of the method of calculating the 
90% confidence intervals with respect to demonstration of BE and whether the standard 
BE limits are appropriate.  
• The study design for all strengths of the product (100/50, 250/50, 500/50) should be the 
same to ensure that equivalent rigor is applied to the demonstration of BE on all product 
strengths. 
• Finally, the requisite PK studies should include batches that are representative of the 
batch size and process proposed for commercial scale manufacturing. 
 
There may be additional considerations relevant to validating this study design, or other 
forms of multiple-batch PK BE studies, which underscores the complexity and uncertainty with 
such an approach.  We are not aware that FDA has relied on multiple-batch studies as part of any 
Division of Dockets Management 
December 5, 2017  
Page 8 
 
 
 
prior generic approval.12  FDA must ensure such an approach is scientifically sound and does not 
mask potential differences between products.  FDA will also want to consider the broader 
implications to other product-specific orally inhaled product guidances and whether using a large 
number of batches for determination of PK BE represents a reasonable, generalizable BE 
standard for these generics, particularly in light of the Agency’s prior work developing the 
Guidance into a workable, best approach for potential generic applicants.   
 
The effort on behalf of FDA, industry, academia, and other stakeholders that went into 
creating the clear, well-balanced, data-driven Guidance to set out a workable standard for BE 
should not be cavalierly discounted, especially in the face of failures to meet any element of it, 
whether it be PK BE, clinical BE, or device performance.  Our experience supports the adequacy 
of the Guidance, especially with regard to accommodating the batch-to-batch variability of the 
RLD.  In terms of PK BE, the single-batch approach in the Guidance represents the most 
straightforward, well-established approach to demonstrate equivalence.  Any consideration of 
whether to depart from the Guidance, in terms of PK BE, clinical BE, or otherwise, should 
involve the same level of engagement and discussion with industry, academia, and other 
stakeholders that led to the current Guidance. 
 
III. CONCLUSION 
Mylan appreciates FDA’s careful and ongoing work to make a more affordable generic 
version of Advair Diskus available to patients.  For the reasons stated above, Mylan requests that 
FDA refrain from approving any ANDA unless it contains the results of a PK BE study that 
reflects sound development work and clearly demonstrates equivalent rigor to the well-
established single-batch test versus reference study design outlined in the Guidance and used 
broadly by FDA.  In our view, FDA should exercise caution toward any approach, like the 
multiple-batch approach described in the recent abstract and presentation, that proposes a new 
BE methodology in circumstances in which the sponsor was apparently unable to achieve 
acceptable BE results with the recommended methodology, presumably either because there is 
                                                      
12 There is one class of products (highly variable drug products (“HVDPs”)) where, after multiple years of 
analysis, discussion, and verification, FDA did start permitting an alternative approach to the typical PK BE 
model.  See, Haidar et al., Bioequivalence Approaches for Highly Variable Drugs and Drug Products, Phar. 
Res. (Jan. 2008), Vol. 25(1) at 237-241 (Exhibit E); see also Draft Guidance on Progesterone (Feb. 
2011).  HVDPs are characterized by high intra-subject variability (“ISV”) (over 30%), and that variability is 
used to adapt BE criteria, which is referred to as Scaled Average Bioequivalence (“SABE”).  ISV represents a 
source of variability for which PK is dependent on the subject receiving the drug product on a dose-to-dose 
basis with same batch and is applicable when receiving either test or RLD.  ISV is an inherent source of 
variability that cannot be controlled or manipulated.  The variability of Advair Diskus, however, does not 
qualify as an HVPD because ISV is reported to be less than 30%.  See, Getz and Carroll, Abstract, supra 
n.1.  As far as we are aware, none of the type of careful, collaborative work that was done to justify the use of 
SABE to widen BE criteria, in relationship to higher degrees of RLD ISV, has been done to validate a 
multiple-batch approach to demonstrating PK BE.  Any approach that attempts to average out any potential 
differences between RLD batches has the potential to mask underlying BE differences between the test and 
RLD batches and, more importantly, is entirely unnecessary given that a thorough understanding of critical 
characteristics of the test and RLD would allow a well-developed generic product to demonstrate BE using as 
standard straight-forward BE study, based on one test batch compared to one RLD batch.

an issue with the product or because it does not understand its product sufficiently well to design 
the single batch BE study.  This is true for any proposed departure from the current Guidance

number of design risks, and may mask meaningful product differences.

The undersigned submits this petition under 10.20 and 10.30 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act 
or the Public Health Service Act or any other statutory provision for which authority has been delegated to 
the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to issue regulations.  
 
A. 
Action Requested 
 
Because the FDA currently mandates minimal medical testing of sperm and egg donors (no other 
regulation exists), we request that the commissioner of the FDA look into the state of affairs 
surrounding the sperm donation industry, and then develop the appropriate and much needed
