DISCUSSION 
 
 
Although the Food and Drug Administration has vowed to support drug competition in a 
manner that is “efficient, predictable, and science‐based,”4 Agency actions continue to fall short 
of these policy goals and applicable legal requirements with respect to potential cyclosporine 
ophthalmic emulsion generic products.   
 
 
Dry eye disease is a serious disorder of the tear film that, if not treated properly, can 
progress from creating ocular discomfort, to visual fatigue, sensitivity to light, blurred vision, 
corneal infection, scarring, and vision loss.5  RESTASIS® is a complex, emulsion dosage form6 
that has been proven (through clinical trials) to be safe and effective in the treatment of dry eye 
disease.    The  record  includes  extensive  information  about  the  significance  of  the  RESTASIS® 
emulsion  formulation  and  its  ability  to  deliver  its  safe  and  effective  levels  of  hydrophobic 
cyclosporine  to  multiple  ocular  tissues,  notwithstanding  the  uniquely  complex  ocular 
environment that (i) is filled with water, (ii) is constructed to actively and rapidly exclude and 
remove  foreign  substances,  (iii)  has  dynamic  characteristics  as  it  exercises  its  protective 
functions, creating a changing environment (physical and chemical) that a drug product must 
overcome;  and  (iv)  includes  multiple  tissues  at  the  target  surface  in  the  eye  with  differing 
absorption  properties,  and  where  the  specific  physical  interactions  essential  to  RESTASIS®’ 
safety and effectiveness have not been well defined.7

FDA cannot reasonably review or approve any ANDA that relies on in vitro‐only testing 
before the Agency has developed a thorough understanding of the relevant science

standards in compliance with applicable legal requirements. 
 
 
There is no dispute that the demonstration of bioequivalence provides the fundamental 
guarantee  that  a  generic  drug  will  be  safe  and  effective  for  use  by  patients  and  may 
appropriately be interchanged with a clinically‐proven innovator drug.  Once a generic drug is 
approved and marketed, consumers generally have little to no choice about which drug they 
will  receive.    Scientifically  valid  bioequivalence  determinations  are  the  only  protection  that 
consumers have that the generic drugs they receive will be therapeutically the same as clinically 
proven, established brand name drugs.

Citizen Petition 
 
INRange Systems, Inc. (the “Petitioner”) submits this petition pursuant to Sections 501, 
502, 510 and 513 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the “Act”) and 21 CFR §10.30.   
 
Petitioner requests that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs (the “Commissioner”) 
take action to protect patient safety by detaining the product manufactured or sold by; 
 
 PharmRight Corporation under the product name “Livi” 
 
which is of the generic type classified as “Remote Medication Management Systems” under 21 
CFR Section 880.6315 and it is not cleared nor approved and is misbranded within the meaning 
of Section 502(o) of the Act.  This device does not; 
 
(i) conform to the general controls of the Act, including the establishment registration 
and device listing requirements described in 21 CFR §807 Subpart B and the premarket 
notification requirements described in 21 CFR §807 Subpart E;  
 
(ii) address, as determined by the Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”), the special 
controls which, when combined with the general controls of the Act, shall be sufficient to 
provide reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness of such devices in light of the 
specific risks to health associated with such devices; and  
 
(iii) did not obtain a substantial equivalence determination from FDA prior to marketing 
such devices.   
 
If any such determination by the Commissioner are made in the affirmative, the 
Petitioner respectfully requests that the Commissioner under its authority seize all existing 
models of “Livi” Remote Medication Management Systems presently on the market, enjoin the 
parties presently manufacturing or selling such products from continuing to market such 
unapproved and misbranded devices, and/or enter other appropriate relief. 
 
A. 
Action Requested 
 
The Petitioner respectfully requests:

of the Act, as (i) the “Livi” device is a class II device as it is within the generic type 
of devices classified as “Remote Medication Management Systems” and subject to 
21 CFR Section 880.6315, (ii) neither the device nor the establishment 
manufacturing or selling it having been listed with the FDA, and (iii) no notice or 
other information respecting the device has been provided to FDA as required by 
such Section 502(o) or Section 510(k) of the Act: 
 
B. 
Statement of Grounds 
 
1. Legal Framework 
 
a. 
FDA Classification and Regulation of Devices  
 
The Act defines a “device” to be: 
 
“. . . an instrument, apparatus, implement, machine, contrivance, implant, in 
vitro reagent, or other similar related article . . .intended for use in the diagnosis 
of disease or other conditions, or in the cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention 
of disease . . . or intended to affect the structure or any function of the body . . . 
and which does not achieve any of its primary intended purposes through 
chemical action within or on the body . . . and which is not dependent upon being 
metabolized for the achievement of any of its primary intended purposes.”1 
 
FDA has identified a broad range of products which are “devices” within the meaning 
of the Act, and which it has further determined shall be classified as class I, class II or class III, 
                                            
1 21 USC §321(h) 
 
 
 
 
Page - 3 - 
according to the relative predictability of their safety and effectiveness when used for their 
intended purposes.  For example and relevant to this Petition, FDA has identified “daily activity 
assist devices” for use with a patient’s medications as “devices” within the meaning of the Act, 
and has classified certain generic types of such devices as class I devices.2 
 
 
b. 
FDA Classification and Regulation of Devices Intended for Use as Medication 
Dispensers or Reminders 
 
21 CFR §890.5050 defines “daily activity assist devices” to include  
 
“ . . . a modified adaptor or utensil (e.g., a dressing, grooming, recreational 
activity, transfer, eating, or homemaking aid) that is intended for medical 
purposes to assist a patient to perform a specific function.”3 
 
FDA has further identified two generic types of devices within this category of “daily 
activity assist devices” which are intended to assist a patient with his or her medications:  
 
1). “Solid Medication Dispenser” (Product Code – NXB), which is intended “ . 
. . to issue solid (pills) medication” and which “ . . . can function independently, with 
components or within a system”4; 
 
and  
 
2). “Medication Reminder” (Product Code – NXQ), which is intended “ . . . to 
provide alerts to patients or healthcare providers for pre-determined medication dosing 
schedules . . . ” and which “ . . . may incorporate wireless communication”.5 
 
A review of the devices listed with FDA with reference to these Product Codes 
establishes that the devices classified as “Solid Medication Dispensers” are typically traditional 
pill boxes or other simple containers which may be components of “Medication Reminders” 
providing visible or audible alerts when the patient should take the medications the patient had 
previously loaded into the Dispenser.6   
 
Other devices which have not been listed with FDA clearly fall into this generic category 
of a simple “assist” device, such as the plastic pill box or pill organizer (pictured below).

Dispenser. 
 
 
These devices are typically filled by the patient or a caregiver based upon the pharmacy 
labels on the prescription bottle.  They contain compartments which show the time of day and 
the day of the week when the pills are to be taken.  Pills to be taken by the patient are placed 
into their respective compartment. 
 
A more current adaptation of these Solid Medication Dispensers are Medication 
Reminders which incorporate medication storage and alerts (shown below).

These devices are variations of the Dispenser shown in Figure #1, but they also include 
alarm clocks which remind the patient when to take a medication and which compartment holds 
that medication.   
 
Significantly, these generic types of “daily assist” devices do not select and deliver 
individual medications for the patient.  The patient or caregiver must manually load each 
compartment with the proper medications, so that these devices are merely organizers and 
reminders. 
 
This revolution in patient medication management from pill box (with or without an 
alarm clock) to Remote Medication Management Systems was marked by FDA on October 19, 
2007, when the Agency announced in the Federal Register a final rule classifying “Remote 
 
 
 
 
Page - 5 - 
Medication Management Systems” as class II (special controls) devices “in order to provide a 
reasonable assurance of safety and effectiveness of these devices”.7   
 
 
c. 
FDA Classification and Regulation of Remote Medication Management Systems 
 
On September 20, 2006, FDA issued an order automatically classifying a remote 
medication management system manufactured by INRange Systems, Inc. (referred to hereafter 
as the “INRange Device”) in class III   
 
“ . . . because [the INRange Device] was not within the type of device which 
was introduced or delivered for introduction into interstate commerce for 
commercial distribution before May 28, 1976, or a device that was subsequently 
reclassified into class I or class II.”8 
 
On September 25, 2006, INRange petitioned FDA to reclassify the INRange Device, 
recommending that the Device be classified into class II9.  On June 13, 2007, FDA issued an 
order to INRange classifying the INRange Device into class II.10 
 
By order announced October 17, 2007, FDA announced that it was classifying devices 
of the generic type represented by the INRange Device into class II (special Controls).11  At the 
same time, FDA amended 21 CFR Part 880 by the addition of new Section 880.6315 (“Remote 
Medication Management System”), and it announced the availability of a guidance document 
entitled, “Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff; Class II Special 
Controls Guidance Document: Remote Medication Management System” (referred to hereafter 
as the “Medication Management System Guidance”).12   
 
In announcing this regulatory action, FDA identified the following risks to health 
associated with a Remote Medication Management System to explain the need for Special 
Controls to provide reasonable assurance of safety and efficacy: 
 
 
Improper dosage delivered to patient; 
 
Cross-contamination of medications; 
 
Compromised information security; 
 
Failure of the device;  
 
Electromagnetic interference; and

Electrical and mechanical hazards.13 
 
FDA further defined a Remote Medication Management System of the type included 
within the meaning of Section 880.6315 and subject to the Medication Management System 
Guidance to be:  
 
“ . . . composed of clinical and communications software, a medication delivery 
unit, and medication packaging[;]”14 
 
and to be intended: 
 
“ . . . [1] to store the patient's prescribed medications in a delivery unit, [2] to 
permit a health care professional to remotely schedule the patient's prescribed 
medications, [3] to notify the patient when the prescribed medications are due 
to be taken, [4] to release the prescribed medications to a tray of the delivery 
unit accessible to the patient on the patient's command, and [5] to record a 
history of the event for the health care professional.”15  
 
FDA further identified that such a System “is intended for use as an aid to health care 
professionals in managing therapeutic regimens for patients in the home or clinic.”16 
 
Significantly, FDA did not find that the general controls of the Act of the type applicable 
to “daily assist devices” within the scope of 21CFR Section 890.5050, such as Solid Medication 
Dispensers or Medication Reminders, were sufficient to address the safety issues presented by 
devices within the generic type of devices it had classified as Remote Medication Management 
Systems.  FDA had identified these risks in announcing its order establishing this classification; 
it elaborated on these risks in the Medication Management System Guidance as follows17:

to miss necessary medication, or receive an incorrect dose of a 
drug or the wrong drug, which could lead to serious injury or

Medications 
“Cross-contamination between different medications, either 
through contact within the medication delivery unit or through 
medication residues in the medication delivery unit creates a 
potential for adverse reactions, especially if a medication is no 
longer used by the patient because an allergy to that medication 
developed or was discovered.”19 
 
 
The Medication Management System Guidance emphasizes FDA’s concern over the 
ability of the Remote Medication Management System to correctly identify, select and deliver 
the medication prescribed for the patient.  In particular, FDA has observed that  
 
“[o]ne source of medication error is the inability of the patients to properly 
identify their medications.  The medication delivery unit of the remote 
medication management system should identify the medication without relying 
upon the patient to accomplish this task[;]  
 
and 
[b]ecause patients may rely on the device to properly deliver their medications, 
the electromechanical systems of the medication delivery unit should reliably 
discharge a medication at the prescribed time and in the prescribed dose.”20 
 
These risks were identified because the indications for use include the treatment of 
patients who require detailed medication management in their home or domicile similar to that 
provided in an acute care environment.  The patients relying on the device to properly 
administer their medications are often without immediate access to the pharmacist instructions 
(usually located on the prescription label located on the front of the amber bottle).  Therefore, 
the patient relies solely on the device to properly deliver the medications.  The risks associated 
with the device improperly delivering the medications include hospitalization and even death.  
 
 
2. The “Livi” device is a Remote Medication Management System within the scope 
of 21 CFR 880.6315 and is Misbranded and is an Adulterated Devices 
 
The “Livi” system is pictured below (additional product information attached hereto as 
Exhibit A).

Its operation is described in the available product marketing information as; 
 
 “All medication orders are entered using our cloud-based application from mobile 
devices or web browsers. Once the med order is entered, Livi’s container can easily and 
quickly be configured to handle the specific pill size and shape. After that, simply pour 
the contents of a pill bottle into one of Livi’s containers and follow the set-up prompts 
on the display. Repeat for up to 15 different meds or supplements. Livi will then begin 
dispensing the right medication at the right time, in the right quantity with the right 
instructions.” 
 
By its intended function and intended use, the “Livi” System is clearly a Remote 
Medication Management System within the meaning of 21 CFR §880.6315.  Consequently, in 
the absence of device and establishment registration and pre-market notification as required 
under the Act, the “Livi” System is a misbranded device. 
 
C.   Conclusion 
 
The FDA Ruled that in-home medication management devices that can be remotely 
controlled are class II medication devices subject to 21 CFR Section 880.6315.  If action is not 
taken by FDA to require manufacturers of such devices to conform to the general controls of 
the Act, including the establishment registration and device listing requirements described in 
21 CFR §807 Subpart B and the premarket notification requirements described in 21 CFR §807 
Subpart E, as required under 21 CFR Section 880.6315, a potential major and growing risk to 
patient health will remain unaddressed. 
 
The “Livi” device is an unapproved and misbranded device, as it has the same intended 
functions and intended use as generic devices of the type classified as “Remote Medication 
 
 
 
 
Page - 9 - 
Management Systems” and subject to requirements for establishment registration, device listing 
and premarket notification as set forth in 21 CFR Section 880.6315.   
 
As such, the potential risks to patient safety resulting from this device require that 
immediate action be taken to require PharmRight Corporation to conform to the general 
controls of the Act, including the establishment registration and device listing requirements 
described in 21 CFR §807 Subpart B and the premarket notification requirements described in 
21 CFR §807 Subpart E.   
 
A. Environmental Impact 
 
The action requested is subject to a categorical exemption from environmental 
assessment under 21 C.F.R. § 25.34.

Introduction 
 
INOMAX is approved for use in the treatment of newborn children (neonates) greater 
than 34 weeks gestational age suffering from hypoxic respiratory failure.  Newborns with this 
form of respiratory failure do not transfer enough oxygen into their blood, are unable to breathe 
on their own, and have high blood pressure in the blood vessels of their lungs, i.e., pulmonary 
hypertension.  These patients are critically ill, almost universally requiring ventilatory support 
and other life sustaining therapies.  INOMAX is a vasodilator that, when inhaled, specifically 
relaxes the blood vessels surrounding the alveoli in the lungs of the newborn, which improves 
blood flow to the lungs, allowing more oxygen to enter the blood stream, and reduces the need 
for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.  
 
The safe and effective use of inhaled nitric oxide is inextricably linked to the device 
through which it is administered to patients.  As described in further detail below, administration 
of INOMAX involves a complex and multi-faceted interaction among the drug product 
INOMAX, a specialized, highly sophisticated 510(k)-cleared delivery system called the INOmax 
DSIR, and a breathing or ventilation system.  Successful inhaled nitric oxide therapy requires 
seamless interaction of these three modalities within the neonatal intensive care (“NICU”) 
environment.  In 2010 the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development convened 
a panel of experts to discuss the general topic of NICU-related errors.  The article summarizing 
the workshop succinctly explains the setting in which INOMAX is used and the unique 
challenges presented by that setting:   
 
Patients in the NICU are very small and fragile, many with immature organ 
systems, and superimposed serious illness. Such infants are likely to receive 
complex care, including a large number of medications, and/or invasive 
procedures for diagnosis and treatment over an extended hospitalization. . . . . 
These increase the potential for errors and add additional demands for a higher 
threshold for device safety and efficacy, exemplifying the need for error-free 
devices and instruments. Given the narrow margin of safety, the patients are also 
more likely to suffer from harmful consequences of errors sooner. Because of 
their unique vulnerability, even minor errors can lead to devastating short and 
long-term consequences. In large general hospitals, patient safety efforts are likely

Since approval of INOMAX and the associated delivery system in December 1999, and 
January 2000, respectively, Mallinckrodt has worked closely with its hospital customers to refine 
and optimize the safe and effective use of INOMAX to treat these fragile NICU patients.  This 
feedback has enabled Mallinckrodt to respond to the significant changes in the means and 
methods of safely delivering nitric oxide, as well as the overall practice of medicine in the NICU.  
Mallinckrodt has sought to translate the experience of is customers, and the information learned 
through pharmacovigilance activities, into delivery device improvements to enhance the safe and 
effective administration of nitric oxide.  The INOmax DSIR platform is the latest generation nitric 
oxide delivery system designed from user feedback and quality considerations to best enhance 
patient safety. 
 
Mallinckrodt submits this Petition to assure that follow-on drug products citing 
INOMAX as the reference listed drug incorporate the features necessary for the safe and 
effective administration of inhaled nitric oxide.  This necessitates not only the customary Agency 
review of the quality of the proposed drug product, but also careful evaluation of the design and 
operation of the associated delivery system to assure it is equivalent to the INOmax DSIR 
delivery system used for INOMAX, and includes the same critical safety features.     
 
INOMAX is stored as a gas mixture of nitric oxide and nitrogen in an aluminum cylinder.  
In order for the gas to be administered to patients, the cylinder is attached to a high pressure 
regulator, which is then attached to the INOmax DSIR.  In turn, the INOmax DSIR is attached to 
the ventilator via an injector module placed between the ventilator inspiratory outlet and the 
humidifier.  To ensure safety, upon the initiation of therapy, the INOmax DSIR first 
communicates wirelessly with the INOMAX cylinder to confirm that the attached cylinder is the 
correct concentration, a cylinder of INOMAX and not another gas cylinder, and that the drug is 
within expiration date.  Based on the ventilator flow, the INOMAX cylinder concentration, and 
the INOMAX dose set by the user, the INOmax DSIR delivers INOMAX into the ventilator 
circuit via the injector module where it mixes with the breathing circuit gas flow to achieve the 
set dose. When used with one of the sixty-four ventilators and breathing systems that 
Mallinckrodt has carefully validated as compatible with the INOmax DSIR, the delivery system 
operates to deliver a constant dose of INOMAX to the patient, as set by the user, regardless of 
the ventilator flow pattern or breath rate.  Certain breathing systems and ventilators are not 
compatible with the INOmax DSIR and these systems are not appropriate for use on patients 
receiving INOMAX therapy, due to the risk of under- or over-dosing. 
 
A number of steps must be undertaken to assure the safe delivery of INOMAX therapy.  
Prior to initiating INOMAX therapy, the user must properly establish the connections between 
drug, delivery device, and ventilator/breathing system; the latter of which differs depending on 
the specific ventilator/breathing system in use on the patient.  The INOmax DSIR must undergo a

During therapy, the INOmax DSIR monitors inspired nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide, and 
oxygen using a second channel, separate from the channel used for INOMAX delivery.  Because 
the delivery system and monitoring measurements are independent, the two subsystems cross-
check one another and notify the user of any discrepancy between monitored values and user 
established parameters (e.g., dose of nitric oxide).  Within the monitoring subsystem, the sample 
gas is withdrawn from the breathing circuit immediately prior to drug delivery to the patient and 
passes through a series of components to electrochemical gas monitoring sensors.  The sensors 
provide an electronic signal proportional to the concentration of the gas, triggering alarms if 
monitored values are outside of those parameters set by the user.  Additional alarms are triggered 
in other circumstances unrelated to monitored values, e.g., failure of any INOmax DSIR 
component, low cylinder pressure, cylinder valve closed, low battery, etc. 
 
Abrupt discontinuation or interruption of nitric oxide therapy can lead to worsening 
oxygenation and increasing pulmonary artery pressure, i.e., rebound pulmonary hypertension 
syndrome, which can be fatal.  To minimize this risk, the INOmax DSIR includes two backup 
systems.  The first is an integrated pneumatic backup system that may be used in the event the 
main system is not functioning, and it is medically appropriate for the patient to remain on the 
ventilator.  This system delivers a fixed flow of INOMAX into the injector module, designed to 
provide 20 ppm of nitric oxide when added to a continuous ventilator gas flow of 10 L/min.  The 
INOmax DSIR also includes the INOblender®, which also functions as a backup for use when the 
patient is temporarily removed from the ventilator.  The INOblender connects to both an oxygen 
supply and a cylinder of INOMAX, and allows clinicians to select a concentration of nitric oxide 
to be mixed into a user-established flow of oxygen, which is then delivered to the patient.  Both 
backup systems can be operated without main or battery power, though the INOmax DSIR also 
has a six-hour battery backup to further reduce the risk of abrupt discontinuation or interruption 
of therapy. 
 
To safely administer INOMAX therapy, the user must be trained and knowledgeable 
about all aspects of the INOmax DSIR and its backup systems.  The user must be able to set up 
the INOmax DSIR with a compatible, validated ventilator, program it for individual patient 
therapy, monitor that therapy, rapidly respond to any alarms or other problems that arise during 
INOMAX delivery, and engage one or both backup systems as needed.  Due to the complexities 
of administering nitric oxide therapy, the INOMAX prescribing information requires that the 
manufacturer provide comprehensive, periodic training for all potential users of the delivery 
device to ensure the safe and effective administration of INOMAX.  In addition, to further 
reduce the incidence of user errors, and minimize the consequences of any user errors,

Mallinckrodt.

NDA 20845 for INOMAX (nitric oxide) for inhalation was approved on December 23, 
1999.  INOMAX is approved for treatment of Hypoxic Respiratory Failure (“HRF”) in newborns 
greater than 34 weeks gestational age.4  Because newborns with this form of respiratory failure 
are extremely ill, receiving ventilatory support and other life sustaining therapies, INOMAX 
therapy is provided in the critical care unit of the hospital.   
  
INOMAX must be administered to patients using a specialized and highly sophisticated 
delivery system.  The delivery system, called a Nitric Oxide Delivery System, or NODS, 
interfaces with a mechanical breathing system (e.g., ventilator, anesthesia, or respiratory care 
device, such as Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (“CPAP”)) to deliver the user-established 
dose of nitric oxide directly to the gases breathed by the patient.   
 
In the years prior to submission of the NDA for INOMAX, FDA repeatedly advised that 
the associated NODS could be cleared through the 510(k) premarket notification process, with 
clearance issuing upon or shortly after approval of the NDA for the drug product.  In accordance 
with this instruction, the company5 submitted a 510(k) seeking clearance to market a version of 
the delivery system used in two of the INOMAX clinical trials, the INOvent® delivery system.  
FDA’s Center for Devices and Radiological Health (“CDRH”) determined that the INOvent 
delivery system was not substantially equivalent to devices marketed in interstate commerce

FDA denied the Petition? With respect to the second prong of Par's request, FDA stated in 
pertinent part that a generic product (i) need not have impurity specifications identical to those of 
the reference listed drug ("RLD"), as variables such as differences in manufacturing processes or 
ingredient sources may affect levels of impurities and appropriate test and acceptance criteria; 
(ii) that the potential safety or efficacy impacts of any differences in impurity profiles would be 
assessed on a case-by-case basis, as would FDA's determination of what additional information 
might be needed from an ANDA applicant to address any safety or efficacy concerns; (iii) that 
Par had agreed to conduct its postmarket testing, and had not been required to do so by FDA; and 
(iv) that principles of fairness and equity did not obligate FDA to reject ANDAs for generic 
products that do not have the same or lower levels of impurities as reformulated Adrenalin® as 
demonstrated through testing commensurate with Par's postmarket testing. 
Par believes that certain conclusions reached by FDA in its response to the Petition were 
improper, as they were based on erroneous assumptions and/or a misunderstanding of the 
chemistry of the products at issue and therefore of the basis for the requests set forth in the 
Petition. In particular, FDA's rote adherence to the general policy that all ANDAs require a 
case-by-case review to determine acceptable impurity levels belies the scientific realities with 
respect to Adrenalin®. As detailed below, any differences in the impurity profiles of 
reformulated Adrenalin® and generic products with respect to the particular impurities that were 
the subject of Par's postmarket studies, and that are the focus of this petition, would result solely 
from differences in the degradation or reaction of the active ingredient. Therefore, while 
differences in manufacturing processes or ingredient sources might conceivably affect the levels 
of those impurities (to the extent that these differences impact the degradation or reaction of the 
active ingredient), these differences should not impact whether the levels of those impurities are 
deemed to be acceptable, contrary to FDA's conclusion in response to the Petition. Moreover, 
differences in the levels of those specific impurities would undoubtedly affect the efficacy of the 
proposed products, inasmuch as any increase in their levels has a commensurate. decrease in the 
amount of active ingredient. As FDA's regulations permit generic parenteral products to contain 
inactive ingredients that differ from the RLD only if, among other things, these differences do 
not impact safety or efficacy, any proposed generic epinephrine injection 1 mg/mL product in a 1 
mL vial, ampule, pre-filled syringe or similar parenteral administration modality that has higher 
levels of these impurities than reformulated Adrenalin® would not in any case meet FDA's 
requirements for approval.

Dear Madam or Sir: 
Pursuant to 21 C.F.R. § l 0.33 ("Administrative reconsideration of action"), the undersigned 
officer of Drug Watch International, Inc., hereby petitions the Commissioner of the Food and 
Drug Administration (FDA) to reconsider the action taken by Janet Woodcock, MD, Director,

A. Decision Involved: 
By letter, dated July 2, 2018, Dr. Janet Woodcock, Director, FDA Center for Drug Evaluation 
and Research (CDER), denied in full a Citizen Petition, assigned Docket No. FDA-20 l 7-P-6692, 
submitted to the FDA by DrugWatch International and requesting that a negative monograph be 
established for marijuana (aka marihuana) and tetrabydrocannabinols (THC) and codified at 21 
C.F.R., Part 310. 
B. Action Requested: 
Drug Watch International, Inc. hereby requests the Commissioner of the FDA to reconsider the 
action taken by Dr. Woodcock of the CDER to deny the request contained in the Citizen Petition 
1 
submitted to the FDA by DrugWatch International, Inc. By this petition for reconsideration of 
this action DrugWatch International, Inc. renews its request that the FDA establish by its 
rulemaking authority a negative monograph for marijuana and THC at 21 C.F.R., Part 310. 
C. Statement of Grounds: 
In the Citizen Petition dated November 21, 2017, submitted by DrugWatch International, Inc., a 
discussion of current negative monographs is presented. An example of one of about two dozen 
negative monographs mentioned in the petition is reproduced here to prepare our argument for 
reconsideration: 
§ 310.519 Drug products marketed as over-the-counter (OTC) daytime sedatives. 
(a) Antihistamines, bromides, and scopolamine compounds, either singly or in combinations, 
have been marketed as ingredients in over-the-counter (OTC) drug products for use as daytime 
sedatives. The following claims have been made for daytime sedative products: "occasional 
simple nervous tension," "nervous irritability," "nervous tension headache," "simple nervousness 
due to common every day overwork and fatigue," "a relaxed feeling," "calming down and 
relaxing," "gently soothe away the tension," "calmative," "resolving that irritability that ruins 
your day," "helps you relax," "restlessness," "when you're under occasional stress ... helps you 
work relaxed." Based on evidence presently available, there are no ingredients that can be 
generally recognized as safe and effective for use as OTC daytime sedatives. 
(b) Any OTC drug product that is labeled, represented, or promoted as an OTC daytime sedative 
(or any similar or related indication) is regarded as a new drug within the meaning of section 
20l(p) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act for which an approved new drug application 
under section 505 of the act and part 3 14 of this chapter is required for marketing. 
(c) Clinical investigations designed to obtain evidence that any drug product labeled, represented, 
or promoted as an OTC daytime sedative (or any similar or related indication) is safe and 
effective for the purpose intended must comply with the requirements and procedures governing 
the use of investigational new drugs set forth in part 312 of this chapter. 
(d) Any OTC daytime sedative drug product introduced into interstate commerce after December 
24, 1979, that is not in compliance with this section is subject to regulatory action. [44 FR 36380, 
June 22, 1979; 45 FR47422, July 15, 1980, as amended at 55 FR 11579, Mar. 29, 1990] 
As the clear language text of the above provision of Title 21, Part 310.519 of the Code of Federal 
Regulations shows, a negative monograph can be a general statement involving categories and 
classes of drugs (e.g., "Antihistamjnes, bromides, and scopolamine compounds .... ") as well as 
vague claims of therapeutic benefits attributed to these drugs in single entity or compounded 
forms (e.g., "nervous irritability," "nervous tension headache," "simple nervousness due to 
common every day overwork and fatigue," "a relaxed feeling," "calming down and relaxing," 
"gently soothe away the tension," "calmative," "resolving that irritability that ruins your day," 
"helps you relax," "restlessness," "when you're under occasional stress ... helps you work 
relaxed."). 
The false medical claims cited in the above regulation for daytime sedatives are similar to the 
false medical claims made by purveyors of marijuana for medical use. In November 2017, the 
2 
FDA Office of Regulatory Affairs acknowledged this when it issued warning letters to four 
companies for illegally selling CBD (cannabidiol) products online that claimed to prevent, 
diagnose, treat, or cure cancer "without evidence to support these outcomes."' 
The FDA letters included the following warning: 
The claims on your website establish that the products are drugs under section 20l(g)(l)(B) of the 
Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the Act) [21 U.S.C. 32l(g)(I)(B)] because they are 
intended for use in the diagnosis, cme, mitigation, treatment, or prevention of disease. As 
explained ... introducing or delivering these products for introduction into interstate commerce 
for such uses violates the Act.2 
The unlawful acts of the four companies that were cited are not uncommon but, instead, quite 
typical of many, if not most, commercial medical marijuana dealers. That the FDA decided to 
warn four companies, while somewhat commendable, speaks to the inability of the agency to 
address the thousands of other companies engaged in similar activities 
DrugWatch International, Inc., believes that false medical claims being made by the burgeoning 
medical marijuana industry pose a far more pernicious danger to the public health than, for 
example, any false medical claims that may have been made on behalf of drugs and conditions 
referenced in the list of negative monographs found at 21 CFR § 310. 
Dr. Woodcock's denial of the Drug Watch petition appears to rest on the basic premise that a 
negative monograph is unnecessary for taking regulatory action against an unapproved drug 
("(I)n the case of an illegally marketed, unapproved new drug, FDA regulatory action or 
enforcement against such a product does not depend on the presence or absence of a negative 
monograph."). This, we presume, is not the case when it comes to daytime sedatives for which a 
negative monograph was deemed necessary to codify. This, of course, begs the question of why a 
decision was made by the agency that daytime sedatives required the added sanction of a 
negative monograph but medical marijuana does not merit the same treatment? 
In terms of public health risks, there is no reasonable comparison between the health risks posed 
by daytime sedatives and those posed by marijuana. 
With respect to marijuana, the President's Commission on Combatting Drug Addiction and the 
Opioid Crisis issued a report last November that stated: 
The Commission acknowledges that there is an active movement to promote the use of marijuana 
as an alternative medication for chronic pain and as a treatment for opioid addiction. Recent 
research out of the NIH's National Institute on Drug Abuse found that marijuana use led to a 2 Yi 
times greater chance that the marijuana user would become an opioid user and abuser. The 
Commission found this very disturbing. There is a lack of sophisticated outcome data on dose, 
potency, drug-drug interactions, effectiveness, and long-term consequences of marijuana used for 
medical purposes. This minors the lack of data in the l 990's and early 2000's when opioid 
prescribing multiplied across health ca.re settings and led to the current epidemic of abuse, misuse 
1 See: https://www.fda.gov/NewsEvents/Newsroom/PressAnnouncements/ucm583295.htm 
2 Ibid. 
3 
and addiction. The Commission urges that the same mistake is not made with the uninformed 
rush to put another drug legally on the market in the midst of an overdose epidemic.3 
This brief statement from the Commission refutes the reasoning given by Dr. Woodcock in her 
denial of the Drug Watch International, Inc. petition. Efforts thus far by the FDA to curb the use 
of marijuana for medical purposes have been as ineffective as efforts put forth by the FDA to 
mitigate and minimize the risks associated with the excessive use of prescription opioids.4 We 
agree with the Commission's statement that another mistake should not be made with the rush to 
put another drug - marijuana - legally on the market in the midst of an overdose epidemic. 
The FDA decision not to establish a negative monograph for cannabis-based medicines can only 
be interpreted as helping to keep unapproved drug products on the market. Indeed, the public 
disclosure of the FD A's denial of the Drug Watch petition was heralded by supporters of the 
commercial marijuana industry as a victory or, as one reporter for the industry headlined the 
denial in an online blog, "FDA rejects move to further restrict cannabis (Newsletter: July 6, 
2018)."5 
We accept Dr. Woodcock' s reasoning that a negative monograph is not necessary to establish a 
basis for regulatory or enforcement action against unapproved drugs (including "unapproved 
new OTC marijuana and THC products [that] are not GRAS/E"). It was not, and is not, our 
intention to suggest that a negative monograph would be the only grounds to establish a 
regulatory basis to take enforcement action against an unapproved drug. But the fact that the 
FDA bas sought negative monographs in almost two dozen cases of other drugs suggests that the 
approach is suitable for products - like marijuana - marketed OTC under state laws for 
generalized medical indications unsupported by evidence of safety and efficacy. 
Since passage of the Pure Food and Drug Act in 1906 and, more specifically, the 1962 Kefauver-
Harris Amendments, the imprimatur of government approval bas protected the health and well-
being of consumers and patients. When it comes to non-prescription drug products sold OTC, 
FDA's oversight is critical, inasmuch as OTC products can be purchased by children and adults 
at retail outlets and used without medical supervision. 
To protect the public health, in 1972 the FDA adopted a monograph system for approving OTC 
drugs. Perhaps the best way to describe the structure and importance of the monograph system is 
to provide the FDA's own description of it:

Over-the-Counter (OTC) Drug Review 
Although OTC drugs were originally included in DESI, FDA eventually concluded that this was 
not an efficient use of resomces. The Agency also was faced with resource challenges because it 
was receiving many applications for different OTC drugs for the same indications. Therefore, in 
1972, the Agency implemented a process of reviewing OTC drugs through rulemaking by 
therapeutic classes (e.g., antacids, antiperspirants, cold remedies). This process involves 
convening an advisory panel for each therapeutic class to review data relating to claims and 
active ingredients. These panel reports are then published in the Federal Register, and after 
FDA review, tentative final monographs for the classes of drugs are published. The final step is 
the publication of a final monograph for each class, which sets forth the allowable claims, 
labeling, and active ingredients for OTC drugs in each class (see, e.g., 21 CFR part 333). Drugs 
marketed in accordance with a final monograph are considered to be generally recognized as safe 
and effective (GRAS/GRAE) and do not require FDA approval of a marketing application. 
Final monographs have been published for the majority of OTC drugs. Tentative fmal 
monographs are in place for virtually all categories of OTC drugs. FDA has also finalized a 
number of negative monographs that list therapeutic categories (e.g., OTC daytime sedatives, 21 
CFR 310.519) in which no OTC drugs can be marketed without approval. Fina!Jy, the Agency has 
promulgated a list of active ingredients that cannot be used in OTC drugs without approved 
applications because there are inadequate data to establish that they are GRAS/GRAE (e.g., 
phenolphthalein in stimulant laxative products, 21CFR310.545(a)(l2)(iv)(B)). 
OTC drugs covered by ongoing OTC drug monograph proceedings may remain on the market as 
provided in current enforcement policies (see, e.g., CPG sections 450.200 and 450.300, and 21 
CFR part 330). This document does not affect the current enforcement policies for such drugs. 
OTC drugs that need approval, either because their ingredients or claims are not within the scope 
of the OTC drug review or because they are not allowed under a final monograph or another final 
rule, are illegally marketed. For example, this group would include a product containing an 
ingredient determined to be ineffective for a particular indication or one that exceeds the dosage 
limit established in the monograph. Such products are new drugs that must be approved by FDA 
to be legally marketed. 6 
As this excerpt from an FDA guidance document attests, the monograph system is an essential 
component of how the FDA protects the public health in the marketing and availability of OTC 
drugs that are not subjected to the more stringent requirements of the IND/ND A (Investigational 
New Drug/New Drug Application) process required for marketing prescription drugs used under 
medical supervision. 
While the FD A's vigilance with respect to the safety of OTC drugs may be considered adequate 
in most instances, the agency falls short when it comes to the marketing of cannabis products 
sold OTC under state laws and promoted as medicine or food. A Google search of the query 
"Buy Medical Marijuana" returned 172 million responses in less than a half second. According 
to industry sources, as of January 2018, there were 9,397 active licenses for marijuana businesses

Guidances/ucm070290.pdf 
5 
in the U.S. Included among these licensees are cultivators, manufacturers, retailers, dispensaries, 
distributors, deliverers and testing labs. 7 
The commercial marijuana industry generated $9 billion in sales in 2017 and estimates are that 
this will more than double to $21 billion by 2021 . Thirty states and the District of Colwnbia 
permit medical marijuana, nine states permit medical and non-medical (recreational) marijuana, 
and 16 states permit lawful commerce in cannabidiol (CBD), a non-psychoactive cannabinoid 
sold as medicine for humans and animals. 8 
By any measure, the government should take more aggressive action to control a burgeoning 
marijuana industry posing serious risks to the public health. In November 2017, as previously 
noted, the FDA sent warrung letters to four online distributors of CBD being unlawfully 
marketed to treat cancer. Yet, thousands, perhaps tens of thousands, of other online and brick-
and-mortar distributors of unapproved cannabinoid medicines are simply ignored by the agency 
on a daily basis. 
Dr. Woodcock's denial of the Drug Watch petition cites regulations pertaining to FDA guidance 
on the development ofbotarucal drugs. But this, like Dr. Woodcock's claim that present laws 
negate the need for a negative monograph, simply states more provisions in the agency's 
rulebook without noting that they are not being enforced to halt the unlawful marketing of 
unapproved cannabinoid medicines. 
The issue is not - and never has been - whether FDA has the legal authority to halt the 
marketing of unapproved drugs. The issue is, simply, that when it comes to baiting the promotion 
and sale of unapproved cannabis-based drugs by enforcing its legal authorities, the FDA falls far 
short. 
According to the FDA, in 2017, the agency's Office of Regulatory Affairs issued a total of 
15,318 warning letters of which 97 percent ( 14,875 letters) were issued pursuant to the Family 
Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act.9 This Act regulates warnings on tobacco products 
and in their advertising with the goal of discouraging minors and young adults from smoking. 10 
In the same year, 2017, the FDA sent four warning letters - that is, four letters out of a total of 
15,318 - to online CBD vendors accused of marketing unapproved cannabis-based drug products 
that they falsely claimed could be used to treat and cure cancer. 11 
This appears to speak clearly to the fact that when it comes to enforcing its laws, the FDA is 
willing to take regulatory action against tobacco industry while overlooking the vast majority of 
commercial cannabis licensees and others marketing cannabis-based products as medicinal.

cy/ORA/UCM556104.pdf

DrugWatch International, Inc. understands that a negative monograph for cannabis-based 
medications will not change the FDA's attitude toward enforcing the law but it may provide 
additional information for the public to understand the health risks in using unapproved 
cannabinoid drugs marketed for medicinal purposes. Moreover, as more and more users of 
cannabis drugs realize that they have been harmed by these unlawful products, the fact of having 
a negative monograph with the force of regulatory law may assist victims in their pursuit of tort 
claims against the marketeers of these unlawful nostrums. 
In sum and substance, Dr. Woodcock's denial of the DrugWatch petition is based mostly, if not 
entirely, on the grounds that a negative monograph is unnecessary because marijuana already is a 
regulated drug under the Controlled Substances Act and, therefore, cannot be lawfully prescribed 
or marketed for medical treatment in the U.S. This reasoning would be acceptable - or, at least, 
w1derstandable - if the FDA actually was enforcing the law to prevent the marketing and 
promotion of unapproved cannabinoid drugs. This, however, is not the case. 
In regulating the medical marijuana industry, the FDA disregards its own enforcement priorities 
as described in a 2011 guidance document setting forth the enforcement priorities of the agency: 
For unapproved drugs commercial.ly used or sold as of September 19, 2011, FDA's 
enforcement priorities are described below. 
A. Enforcement Priorities 
Consistent with our risk-based approach to the regulation of pharmaceuticals, FDA intends 
to continue its current policy of giving higher priority to enforcement actions involving 
unapproved drug products in the following categories: 
Drugs with potential safety risks. Removing potentially unsafe drugs protects the public from 
direct and indirect heal th threats. 
Drugs that lack evidence of effectiveness. Removing ineffective drugs protects the public 
from using these products in lieu of effective treatments. Depending on the indication, 
some ineffective products would, of course, pose safety risks as well. 
Health fraud drugs. FDA defines health fraud as "[t]he deceptive promotion, advertisement, 
distribution or sale of articles ... that are represented as being effective to diagnose, prevent, 
cure, treat, or mitigate disease (or other conditions), or provide a beneficial effect on health, but 
which have not been scientifically proven safe and effective for such purposes. Such practices 
may be deliberate or done without adequate knowledge or understanding of the article" (CPG 
[ed., Compliance Policy Guide] Sec. 120.500). Of highest priority in this area are drugs that 
present a direct risk to health. Indirect health hazards exist if, as a result ofreliance on the 
product, the consumer is I ikely to delay or discontinue appropriate medical treatment. Indirect 
health hazards will be evaluated for enforcement action based on section 120.500, Health Fraud -
Factors in Considering Regulatory Action (CPG Sec. 120.500). FD A's health fraud CPG outlines 
priorities for evaluating regulatory actions against indirect health hazard products, such as 
whether the therapeutic claims are significant, whether there are any scientific data to support the 
7 
safety and effectiveness of the product, and the degree of vulnerability of the prospective user 
group (CPG Sec. 120.500). 
Drugs that present direct challenges to the new drug approval and OTC drug monograph 
systems. The drug approval and OTC drug monograph systems are designed to avoid the risks 
associated with potentially unsafe, ineffective, and fraudulent drugs. The drugs described in the 
preceding three categories present direct challenges to these systems, as do unapproved drugs that 
directly compete with an approved drug, such as when a company obtains approval of a new drug 
application (NDA) for a product that other companies are marketing without approval (see 
section III.C, Special Circumstances - Newly Approved Product). Also included are drugs 
marketed in violation of a final and effective OTC drug monograph. Targeting drugs that 
challenge the drug approval or OTC drug monograph systems buttresses the integrity of these 
systems and makes it more likely that firms will comply with the new dmg approval and 
monograph requirements, which benefits the public health. 
Unapproved new drugs that are also violative of the Act in other ways. The Agency also 
intends, in circumstances that it considers appropriate, to continue its policy of enforcing the 
preapproval requirements of the FD&C Act against a drng or firm that also violates another 
provision of the FD&C Act, even if there are other unapproved versions of the drug made by 
other firms on the market. For instance, if a firm that sells an unapproved new drug also violates 
current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) regulations, the Agency is not inclined to limit an 
enforcement action in that instance to the CGMP violations. Rather, the Agency may initiate a 
regulatory action that targets both the CGMP violation and the violation of section 505 of the 
FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 355). This policy efficiently preserves scarce Agency resources by 
allowing the Agency to pursue all applicable charges against a drng and/or a firm and avoiding 
duplicative action. See United States v. Sage Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 210 F.3d 475, 479-80 (5th 
Cir. 2000). 
Drugs that are reformulated to evade an FDA enforcement action. The Agency is also aware of 
instances in which companies that anticipate an FDA enforcement action against a specific type 
or formulation of an unapproved product have made formulation changes to evade that action, but 
have not brought the product into compliance with the law. Companies should be aware that the 
Agency is not inclined to exercise its enforcement discretion with regard to such products. 
Factors that the Agency may consider in determining whether to bring action against the 
reformulated products include, but are not limited to, the timing of the change, the addition of an 
ingredient without adequate scientific justification (see, for example, 21 CFR 300.50 and 
330. I O(a)( 4)(iv)), the creation of a new combination that has not previously been marketed, and 
the claims made for the new product. 12 
As noted below, marijuana is considered by the FDA to pose serious potential safety risks. 
Therefore, it would appear to warrant high priority in the FDA's enforcement program - yet, we 
find that just the opposite is true, i.e., only four online dealers of CBD drugs were sent Warning 
Letters by the FDA last year while 14,875 FDA Warning Letters were sent to tobacco industry 
entities. We are not minimizing the importance of enforcing the Family Smoking Prevention and 
Tobacco Control Act and commend the FDA for taking aggressive action to protect the public

8 
health against the risks posed by tobacco products, but the contrast between the two drugs in how 
they are regulated by the agency is striking. 
We cite this comparison to illustrate the insouciance of the agency's leaders to address the 
unlawful marketing of unapproved cannabinoid drugs. It is incontrovertible that, despite Dr. 
Woodcock's impressive recitation of the authorities for regulating the commercial medicine 
industry, when it comes to enforcing the laws pertaining to cannabinoid drugs, the agency -
according to its own Office of Regulatory Affairs - does very little 
In the list of enforcement priorities noted above, the FDA considers drug safety its highest 
priority for enforcing the law. We question whether this is so when it comes to marijuana. In 
2016, at the request of the Drug Enforcement Administration, the FDA provided a medical and 
scientific evaluation of marijuana. Of the eight factors required by law to be assessed when 
considering the scheduling or rescheduling of a drug, Factor #6 is specific to the public health 
risks of the drug in question, which, in this case, was marijuana: 
6. WHAT, if Any, Risk There Is to the Public Health 
Under the sixth factor, the Secretary [ed. , of the Department of Health and Human 
Services] must consider the risks posed to the public health by marijuana. Factors 1, 4, and 5 
include a. discussion of the risk to the public health as measured by emergency room episodes 
and drug treatment admissions. Additionally, Factor 2 includes a discussion of marijuana's 
central nervous system, cognitive, cardiovascular, autonomic, respiratory, and immune system 
effects. Factor 6 focuses on the health risks to the individual user in terms of the risks from acute 
and chronic use of marijuana, as well as the "gateway hypothesis." 
Risks From Acute Use of Marijuana 
Acute use of marijuana impairs psycbomotor performance, including complex task 
performance, which makes operating motor vehicles or heavy equipment after using marijuana 
inadvisable (Ramaekers et al., 2004; Ramaekers et al., 2006a). A meta-analysis conducted by Li 
et al. (2011) showed an association between marijuana use by the driver and a significantly 
increased risk of involvement in a car accident. Additionally, in a minority of individuals who use 
marijuana, some potential responses include dysphoria and psychological distress, including 
prolonged anxiety reactions (Haney et al., 1999). 
Risks From Chronic Use of Marijuana 
A distinctive marijuana withdrawal syndrome following long term or chronic use has 
been identified. The withdrawal syndrome indicates that marijuana produces physical dependence 
that is mild, short-lived, and comparable to tobacco withdrawal (Budney et al., 2008). Marijuana 
withdrawal syndrome is described in detail below under Factor 7. The following states how the 
DSM-V (2013) of the American Psychiatric Association describes the consequences of Cannabis 
25 abuse: Individuals with cannabis use disorder may use cannabis throughout the day over a 
period of months or years, and thus may spend many hours a day under the influence. Others may 
use less frequently, but their use causes recurrent problems related to family, school, work, or 
other important activities (e.g. , repeated absences at work; neglect of family obligations). Periodic 
cannabis use and intoxication can negatively affect behavioral and cognitive functioning and thus 
interfere with optimal performance at work or school or place the individual at increased physical 
risk when performing activities that could be physically hazardous (e.g., driving a car; playing 
certain sports; performing manual work activities, including operating machinery). Arguments 
9 
with spouses or parents over the use of cannabis in the home, or its use in the presence of 
children, can adversely impact family functioning and are common features of those with 
cannabis use disorder. Last, individuals with cannabis use disorder may continue using marijuana 
despite knowledge of physical problems (e.g., chronic cough related to smoking) or psychological 
problems (e.g., excessive sedation or exacerbation of other mental health problems) associated 
with its use. 
Marijuana as a "Gateway Drug" 
Kandel (1975) proposed nearly 40 years ago the hypothesis that marijuana is a "gateway 
drug' ' that leads to the use or abuse of other illicit drugs. Since that time, epidemiological 
research explored this premise. Overall, research does not support a direct causal relationship 
between regular marijuana use and other illicit drug use. The studies examining the gateway 
hypothesis are limited. First, in general, studies recruit individuals influenced by a myriad of 
social, biological, and economic factors that contribute to extensive drug abuse (Hall & Lynskey, 
2005). Second, most studies that test the hypothesis that marijuana use causes abuse of illicit 
drngs use the determinative measure any use of an illicit drug, rather than DSM- 5 criteria for 
drug abuse or dependence on an illicit drug (DSM-5, 2013). Consequently, although an 
individual who used marijuana may try other illicit drugs, the individual may not regularly use 
drugs, or have a diagnosis of drug abuse or dependence. 
Little evidence supports the hypothesis that initiation of marijuana use leads to an abuse 
disorder with other illicit substances. For example, one longitudinal study of 708 adolescents 
demonstrated that early onset marijuana use did not lead to problematic drug use (Kandel & 
Chen, 2000). Similarly, Nace et al. (1975) examined Vietnam-era soldiers who extensively 
abused marijuana and heroin while they were in the military, and found a lack of correlation of a 
causal relationship demonstrating marijuana use leading to heroin addiction. Additionally, in 
another longitudinal study of 2,446 adolescents, marijuana dependence was uncommon but when 
it did occur, the common predictors of marijuana dependence were the following: Parental death, 
deprived socio-economic status, and baseline illicit drug use other than marijuana (von Sydow et 
al., 2002). 
When examining the association between marijuana and illicit drugs, focusing on drug 
use versus abuse or dependence, different patterns emerge. For example, a study examining the 
possible causal relationship of the gateway hypothesis found a correlation between marijuana use 
in adolescents and other illicit drug use in early adulthood and, adjusting for age-linked 
experiences, did not effect [sic] this correlation (Van Gundy and Rebellon, 2010). However, 
when examining the association in terms of development of drug abuse; age-linked stressors and 
social roles moderated the correlation between marijuana use in adolescents and other illicit drug 
abuse. Similarly, Degenhardt et al. (2009) examined the development of drug dependence and 
found an association that did not support the gateway hypothesis. Specifically, drug dependence 
was significantly associated with the use of other illicit drugs prior to marijuana use. 
Interestingly, the order of initiation of drug use seems to depend on the prevalence of use 
of each drng, which varies by country. Based on the World Health Organization (WHO) World 
Mental Health Survey that includes data from 17 different countries, the order of drug use 
initiation varies by country and relates to prevalence of drng use in each country (Degenhardt et 
al., 2010). Specifically, in the countries with the lowest prevalence of marijuana use, use of other 
illicit drugs before marijuana was common. This sequence of initiation is less c01mnon in 
countries with higher prevalence of marijuana use. A study of9,282 households in the United 
States found that marijuana use often preceded the use of other illicit drugs; however, prior non-
marijuana drug dependence was also frequently correlated with higher levels of illicit drug abuse 
(Degenhardt et al., 2009). Additionally, in a large 25-year longitudinal study of 1,256 New 
Zealand children, the author concluded that marijuana use correlated to an increased risk of abuse 
of other drugs, including cocaine and heroin (Fergusson et al., 2005).

Dear Sir or Madam: 
On behalf of Boehringer Ingelheim USA Corporation (“BIUSA”), the undersigned 
hereby submits this Citizen Petition pursuant to 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 and section 505 of the Federal 
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (“FFDCA”), 21 U.S.C. § 355, to request the Commissioner of 
Food and Drugs to ensure that any New Drug Application (“NDA”) for a fixed-dose, triple-
combination, inhaled drug product intended for the treatment of patients with chronic obstructive 
pulmonary disease (“COPD”) is not approved as safe and effective unless it meets the 
requirements of the Combination Rule set forth at 21 C.F.R. § 300.50.    
I. 
Actions Requested 
 
For the reasons that follow, BIUSA respectfully requests the Commissioner to refrain 
from approving any NDA for a fixed-dose, triple-combination, inhaled drug product intended for 
the treatment of patients with COPD unless the application is supported by pivotal clinical 
studies that satisfy the requirements of the Combination Rule.  Specifically, the Commissioner 
should refrain from approving any such NDA unless: 
1. It is supported by pivotal, Phase III clinical trials that use active comparators 
containing the same active ingredients as those contained in the proposed triple 
combination therapy, not simply active ingredients in the same therapeutic categories; 
and 
 
 
 
 
Department of Health and Human Services 
June 9, 2017 
Page 2 
 
 
2. It is supported by pivotal, Phase III clinical trials that utilize a factorial design 
adequate to demonstrate that each active ingredient in the proposed triple-
combination makes a contribution to the claimed effects.  The most critical 
comparison in any factorial study of a triple combination of an inhaled corticosteroid 
(“ICS”), long-acting muscarinic agent (“LAMA”) and long-acting β2-agonist 
(“LABA”) should be with the dual combination of the LAMA+LABA components. 
This is the only way to determine whether or not the ICS component, which is not a 
bronchodilator, contributes a meaningful improvement in bronchodilation when that 
is the indication being sought. 
In addition, the Commissioner should convene a meeting of the Pulmonary-Allergy 
Drugs Advisory Committee before approving any NDA for a fixed-dose, triple-combination 
product for the treatment of patients with COPD that does not meet the Combination Rule 
requirements described in this petition. 
II. 
Statement of Grounds 
A. Background Regarding COPD and Available Treatment Options 
COPD is a chronic, progressive disease caused by inflammation and destruction of the 
airways and lung parenchyma.  It is characterized by progressive airflow obstruction and 
typically causes cough, excess sputum production, and dyspnea.  COPD is a leading cause of 
morbidity and mortality worldwide and was the third leading cause of death in the United States 
in 2015. 
The Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) has approved several types of drugs to treat 
patients with COPD, including bronchodilators (both LAMAs and LABAs)1 and anti-
inflammatory agents.2  Drug therapy is typically prescribed for COPD patients to improve 
airflow obstruction, reduce the frequency and severity of exacerbations, and improve exercise 
tolerance and health status.  Treatment, however, is highly individualized. Depending upon a 
patient’s level of symptoms, extent of airway limitations, risk of exacerbations, and existing 
comorbidities, treatment may consist of single-agent (e.g., LAMA or LABA) or double-agent 
                                                
 
1 Bronchodilators, which includes both LABAs and LAMAs, improve airflow obstruction by directly relaxing the 
airway smooth muscles, which results in widening of the airways and concomitant improvements in lung function 
(expiratory flow). 
 
2 Anti-inflammatory agents, such as ICSs, are thought to work by reducing airway inflammation associated with 
COPD. 
 
 
 
 
Department of Health and Human Services 
June 9, 2017 
Page 3 
 
 
combination therapies (LAMA/LABA, LABA/ICS).  In some cases, physicians may even 
prescribe triple-combination therapy consisting of a LABA, a LAMA and an ICS.  Because there 
is no fixed-dose, triple-combination product currently available in the United States, therapy with 
all three agents typically requires the use of two separate inhalers. 
Treatment guidelines for COPD provide advice to physicians on, among other things, 
when to prescribe triple combination therapy.  The GOLD Report, a widely-followed strategy 
document containing evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis, management, and 
prevention of COPD,3 reviewed data regarding the safety and efficacy of triple combination 
therapies and found the results equivocal.  On the one hand, the GOLD Report concludes that 
triple-combination therapy consisting of a LAMA, a LABA, and an ICS improves lung function, 
symptoms and health status and reduces exacerbations compared to ICS/LABA combinations or 
LAMA monotherapy.  GOLD Report, p. 53.  On the other hand, the GOLD Report did not come 
to the same conclusion with respect to the comparison of triple-combination therapy with 
LAMA/LABA combinations.  On the contrary, the GOLD Report highlighted that a randomized 
controlled trial “did not demonstrate any benefit of adding ICS to LABA plus LAMA on 
exacerbations.”  GOLD Report, p. 55.  GOLD thus concluded that “more evidence is needed to 
draw conclusions on the benefits of triple therapy LABA/LAMA/ICS compared to 
LABA/LAMA.”  GOLD Report, p. 55.   
On November 21, 2016, GlaxoSmithKline plc (“GSK”) announced that it had submitted 
an NDA for a once-daily, closed triple-combination therapy containing fluticasone furoate 
(“FF”), umeclidinium (“UMEC”), and vilanterol (“VI”) for the treatment of patient with COPD.4  
If approved, the inhaled product would be the first fixed-dose, LAMA/LABA/ICS combination 
available in the United States.  The primary support for the NDA appears to be a single, pivotal, 
Phase III study called the FULFIL study comparing the proposed triple-combination product 
against Symbicort® Turbohaler® (budesonide/formoterol) (“Symbicort”) in patients with 
advanced COPD.5  Although the FULFIL study reportedly met its two co-primary endpoints,6 its
