design does not allow a comparison of the triple combination to any of the active ingredients in 
the combination (FF, UMEC, VI) or any combinations of those active ingredients (FF/UMEC, 
FF/VI, UMEC/VI).  As noted above, the active comparator used in the FULFIL study is 
Symbicort, which contains budesonide and formoterol, not FF, UMEC or VI. 
GSK reportedly is conducting a second Phase III trial of the triple combination – the 
IMPACT trial – to determine whether the proposed combination reduces exacerbations in COPD 
patients.  Unlike the FULFIL study, the IMPACT trial will compare the triple-combination 
product against two approved once-daily products containing combinations of the active 
ingredients in the triple-combination.7  In particular, the IMPACT study will enroll 
approximately 10,000 patients to assess whether the proposed triple-combination can reduce the 
rate of moderate and severe exacerbations compared to Breo® Ellipta® (FF/VI), a LABA/ICS 
combination, and Anoro® Ellipta® (UMEC/VI), a LAMA/LABA combination. 
B. FDA Should Refrain from Approving any NDA for a Fixed-Dose, Triple-Combination, 
Inhaled Drug Product for the Treatment of Patients with COPD Unless it is Supported 
by Pivotal Clinical Data that Satisfy the Combination Rule 
 
1. The Combination Rule 
 
Under section 505(d) of the FFDCA, FDA cannot approve any drug product if it is not 
shown to be safe or “there is a lack of substantial evidence that the drug will have the effects that 
it purports or is represented to have under the conditions of use prescribed, recommended or 
suggested” in its proposed labeling.  21 U.S.C. § 355(d).8  Fixed-dose combination drug products 
                                                                                                                                                       
 
 
6 “[A]t 24 weeks, there was a clinically meaningful and statistically significant benefit for the triple-combination in 
both lung function, measured as mean change from baseline in trough FEV1 (171 mL, 95% confidence interval 
[148, 194] p < 0.001) and health-related quality of life, measured as mean change from baseline in St. George’s 
Respiratory Questionnaire total score . . ..”  GSK Press Release (Sept. 6, 2016), available at http://us.gsk.com/en-
us/media/press-releases/2016/gsk-presents-positive-results-from-phase-iii-fulfil-study-of-closed-triple-combination-
therapy-ffumecvi-versus-symbicort-turbohaler-in-copd-at-ers-international-congress/. 
 
7 GSK Press Release (July 16, 2014), available at http://us.gsk.com/en-us/media/press-releases/2014/gsk-and-
theravance-announce-initiation-of-phase-iii-programme-with-fixed-dose-triple-combination-treatment-ffumecvi-in-
patients-with-copd/. 
 
8 Substantial evidence is defined as “adequate and well-controlled investigations, including clinical investigations, . . 
. on the basis of which it could fairly and responsibly be concluded by [relevant] experts that the drug will have the 
effect it purports or is represented to have under the conditions of use prescribed, recommended, or suggested in the 
labeling or proposed labeling thereof.”  21 U.S.C. § 355(d)(7). 
 
 
 
Department of Health and Human Services 
June 9, 2017 
Page 5 
 
 
present unique challenges for demonstrating safety and effectiveness because they combine two 
or more active ingredients within a single dosage form.  FDA has explained that “[f]ixed 
combination . . . drugs generally purport to provide greater effectiveness (either in cumulative 
effect, by treating more than one indication, or by facilitating compliance) than either ingredient 
alone, or to enhance the safety or effectiveness of one of the active ingredients.”  80 Fed. Reg. 
79776, 79789 (Dec. 23, 2015).  In addition, “the use of any added active ingredient involves 
some risk, and that risk can only be justified by an added benefit in either safety or 
effectiveness.”  Id. 
To address these special challenges, FDA has adopted the Combination Rule to define the 
types of clinical evidence necessary to support approval of fixed-dose combination drugs.  See 
21 C.F.R. § 300.50.  The Combination Rule is a longstanding FDA requirement that was 
originally codified in regulations in 1971.  See 36 Fed. Reg. 20037 (Oct. 15, 1971) (prior version 
codified at 21 C.F.R. § 3.86).  When the rule was proposed, FDA explained that it was intended 
to ensure that “[n]o drug [is] present in a fixed combination unless its inclusion clearly enhances 
safety or effectiveness ….”  36 Fed. Reg. 3126 (Feb. 18, 1971).  According to FDA, the guiding 
principle of the Combination Rule is that “a fixed dose combination drug must have an 
advantage to the patient over and above that obtained when one of the individual ingredients is 
used in the usual safe and effective dose.”  Id. 
The Combination Rule currently is set forth in FDA’s regulations at 21 C.F.R. § 300.50 
and states in relevant part:  
Two or more drugs may be combined in a single dosage form 
when each component makes a contribution to the claimed effects 
and the dosage of each component (amount, frequency, duration) is 
such that the combination is safe and effective for a significant 
patient population requiring such concurrent therapy as defined in 
the labeling for the drug.   
 
21 C.F.R. § 300.50. 
Accordingly, to satisfy the Combination Rule, an applicant must satisfy several 
requirements.  Most significantly for purposes of this petition, the applicant must demonstrate 
that each active ingredient in the combination “makes a contribution to the claimed effects.”  Id. 
                                                                                                                                                       
 
 
 
 
 
Department of Health and Human Services 
June 9, 2017 
Page 6 
 
 
If the additional active ingredient does not enhance the safety or efficacy of the drug product, 
there is no rational basis to include it, and it thus should be removed from the formulation.9   
2. One or more Pivotal Studies must use Active Comparators With the Same Active 
Ingredients as those Contained in the Proposed Triple-Combination Product 
In order to demonstrate that “each component makes a contribution to the claimed 
effects” of the proposed combination product, a sponsor typically must conduct a factorial study 
comparing the proposed combination to each individual component (or sub-combination of 
components).  The testing should demonstrate that, when used together, the combination 
provides “a benefit greater than each of the active ingredients used alone at its therapeutic dose.”  
80 Fed. Reg. at 79785. 
FDA historically has interpreted the term “component” in the Combination Rule to mean 
“active ingredient.”  80 Fed. Reg. at 79779 (“we have interpreted “component” in § 300.50 to 
mean active ingredient”).  As FDA explained in 1971, the Combination Rule is “intended as 
amplification of the requirement that [an NDA] for a combination drug may be refused unless 
there is substantial evidence that each ingredient designated as active makes a contribution to 
the total effect which the drug combination is represented to have and purports to possess.”  36 
Fed. Reg. 3126 (emphasis added).10  Consequently, it generally is not sufficient to compare the 
combination against active ingredients not contained in the combination, even if those active 
ingredients are within the same drug class.  Such comparisons would not satisfy the Combination 
Rule because they could not support a valid scientific determination that each active ingredient 
in a fixed-dose combination makes a contribution to the total effect. 
FDA also has explained that for drug-device combination products like inhalers, the 
device component used in the active comparators generally should be the same as that used in the 
proposed combination product.11 Because the delivery system of an inhaled drug product “may 
                                                
 
9 Other requirements of the Combination Rule include (1) identifying a significant patient population requiring 
concurrent therapy with the active ingredients in the combination product and (2) demonstrating that the 
combination is safe and effective and has an acceptable benefit-risk profile. 
 
10 See also Summary Review of Regulatory Action for Breo® Ellipta®, p. 18 (May 9, 2013) (emphasis added) (in 
order to demonstrate that each active ingredient makes a contribution to the total effect of the combination, it 
typically is necessary to “compare the combination to each active component to show the contribution of each 
component present in the combination.”), available at 
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2013/204275Orig1s000SumR.pdf. 
 
11 According to FDA, the active comparators in a factorial study typically should be “pharmaceutically the same” as 
the combination product, meaning that the active ingredients and delivery systems should be the same.  Summary 
 
 
 
Department of Health and Human Services 
June 9, 2017 
Page 7 
 
 
affect safety and efficacy,”12 the use of a different delivery system for the active comparators 
could confound any valid comparison between the proposed combination product and the active 
components. 
BIUSA is aware of at least one pending NDA for a fixed-dose, triple-combination COPD 
product supported by a pivotal clinical study in which the active comparators use active 
ingredients and a delivery device that are different than the active ingredients and delivery device 
in the proposed triple-combination drug product.  As noted above, GSK is seeking approval of a 
fixed-dose, LAMA+LABA+ICS combination for the treatment of patients with COPD 
containing the active ingredients UMEC, VI and FF.  However, the pivotal study supporting this 
application, the FULFIL study, used Symbicort® Turbohaler® as the active comparator, a double-
combination product containing budesonide and formoterol fumarate as the active ingredients.  
Although Symbicort® Turbohaler® contains active ingredients within the same general classes 
(LABA and ICS) as two of the active ingredients in GSK’s proposed triple-combination product, 
it does not contain any of the same active ingredients (i.e., UMEC, VI or FF).   
Moreover, Symbicort® Turbohaler® utilizes a delivery device that is different than the 
Ellipta® inhaler device used in GSK’s proposed triple-combination product.  Drugs using the 
Ellipta® inhaler are the appropriate comparators rather than those using a different delivery 
device, like the Turbohaler®.   One reason for this is that the differences in how the Turbohaler® 
and Ellipta® devices operate could affect how the active ingredients are delivered in the lungs, 
thereby affecting safety and effectiveness and further confounding any valid comparison 
between the proposed combination product and the active components.  Equally, there are 
operator factors that may result in different patients using one device more effectively than the 
other.  As a scientific matter, therefore, the FULFIL study is not adequately designed to 
demonstrate that “each component makes a contribution to the claimed effects” of the proposed 
triple-combination product.  As a result, the FULFIL study does not satisfy the Combination 
Rule. 
We note that the requirement to use active comparators containing the same active 
ingredients and delivery device as the proposed combination product is far from insurmountable 
and thus should not be waived or ignored by FDA.  Several double combination inhaled drugs 
with the same active ingredients as the proposed triple combination therapy are available and 
                                                                                                                                                       
 
Review of Regulatory Action for Symbicort Supplement S012, p.3 (Feb. 27, 2009) available at 
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2009/021929Orig1s012.pdf. 
 
12 See Draft Guidance on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: Developing Drugs for Treatment, p. 12 (May 
2016). 
 
 
 
 
Department of Health and Human Services 
June 9, 2017 
Page 8 
 
 
could have been used as active comparators in the FULFIL study, including Breo® Ellipta® (FF, 
VI) and Anoro® Ellipta® (UMEC, VI).  Indeed, GSK reportedly is using both of these approved 
products as active comparators in another study – the IMPACT study – investigating whether 
GSK’s proposed triple-combination is effective in reducing exacerbations in patients with 
COPD.  GSK thus could have used these products in the FULFIL study or in another pivotal trial 
designed to satisfy the Combination Rule.   
In sum, because the FULFIL study uses an active comparator with different active 
ingredients and a different delivery device than GSK’s proposed triple-combination product, it 
does not satisfy the Combination Rule and thus cannot be relied upon by FDA as the primary 
basis for approving the NDA.  In the absence of one or more pivotal studies that satisfy the 
Combination Rule, FDA should refrain from approving the NDA or any similarly situated NDA. 
3. One or more Pivotal Studies Supporting an Unrestricted Indication must use a 
Factorial Design that Satisfies the Combination Rule 
a. The Need for Factorial Studies for a Triple-Combination COPD Product 
In addition to requiring the use of active comparators containing the same active 
ingredients as the proposed combination product, FDA should require NDAs for triple-
combination COPD drug products to be supported by factorial studies that satisfy the 
Combination Rule.   
As noted above, the Combination Rule requires sponsors to demonstrate that “each 
[active ingredient] makes a contribution to the claimed effects.”  21 C.F.R. § 300.50(a).  
Although there is some flexibility regarding data requirements to comply with the Combination 
Rule,13 FDA typically requires factorial studies to support the approval of combination products 
intended to treat patients with COPD, particularly where each active ingredient in the 
combination is directed at the same sign or symptom of the disease or condition (e.g., treatment 
of airflow obstruction).  FDA should follow that policy here and refuse to approve any NDA for 
a triple-combination COPD treatment that is not supported by pivotal trials with a factorial 
design demonstrating that the combination provides a benefit greater than each of the active 
ingredients (or double-combinations) used alone. 
                                                
 
13 See 80 Fed. Reg. at 79785; see also FDA Petition Response, Docket No. FDA-2011-P-0711, p. 12 (July 16, 2012). 
 
 
 
 
Department of Health and Human Services 
June 9, 2017 
Page 9 
 
 
In a recently issued Draft Guidance on developing drugs for the treatment of COPD, 
FDA explicitly supports the use of factorial studies for combination COPD treatments to satisfy 
the requirements of the Combination Rule.  According to FDA:  
A reasonable way to support the efficacy of a combination drug 
product would be to compare the combination drug product to each 
of its constituents in the same clinical study to demonstrate that the 
combination drug product provides clinical benefit that is superior 
to each of its constituents. 
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: Developing Drugs for Treatment [Draft], p. 13 (May 
2016) (“Draft Guidance”).   
FDA appears to have followed this policy uniformly for previously-approved 
combination drugs for the treatment of COPD.  For example, FDA required pivotal factorial 
studies to support the approval of, inter alia, Bevespi Aerosphere® (glycopyrrolate and 
formoterol fumarate) in 2016; Stiolto® Respimat® (olodaterol and tiotropium bromide) and 
Utibron™ (glycopyrrolate and indacaterol) in 2015; Anoro® Ellipta® (UMEC, VI) and Breo® 
Ellipta® (FF, VI) in 2013; Combivent® Respimat® (albuterol and ipratropium bromide) in 2011; 
Symbicort® (budesonide and formoterol fumarate dehydrate) in 2006; and Advair Diskus® 
(fluticasone propionate and salmeterol) in 2000.14  BIUSA is not aware of any prior instance in 
which FDA approved an NDA for a combination COPD product in the absence of factorial 
studies complying with the Combination Rule.  
FDA has indicated that factorial studies are especially appropriate for combination 
products in which the effect of each active ingredient is directed at the same sign or symptom of 
the disease or condition. 80 Fed. Reg. at 79785.  In such cases, factorial studies are used “to 
demonstrate that the combination has a larger treatment effect than one or more of the active 
ingredients alone.” Id.  For a combination of two active ingredients like the COPD products 
identified in the preceding paragraph, the factorial study would be designed to demonstrate that 
the combination is more effective than each individual active ingredient alone.   
For a combination of three active ingredients – the type of combination that is the subject 
of this petition – a factorial study typically would be designed to show that the combination is 
                                                
 
14 E.g., Summary Review of Regulatory Action for Anoro® Ellipta®, p. 17 (Nov. 26, 2013), available at 
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/nda/2013/203975Orig1s000SumR.pdf.  Documentation 
demonstrating that the other combination COPD products were supported by factorial studies is included in their 
respective Action Packages, which are available on FDA’s website at Drugs@FDA.com. 
 
 
 
 
Department of Health and Human Services 
June 9, 2017 
Page 10 
 
 
more effective than all possible two-ingredient combinations. Id.  The factorial study for a triple-
combination thus would have at least four arms comparing the proposed combination (ABC) to 
all possible two-ingredient combinations of the three active ingredients (AB, AC, BC).15 
FDA has never approved a triple-combination drug for the treatment of COPD, but it has 
approved numerous triple-combination therapies for other disease states.  In cases where there 
are no ethical impediments, FDA typically requires factorial studies as described above to 
support approval of triple combinations.  For example, FDA required pivotal factorial studies to 
support the approval of Amturnide™ (aliskirn hemifumarate, amolodipine besylate, 
hydrochlorothiazide) and Tribenzor® (amlodipine besylate, hydrochlorothiazide, olmesartan 
medoxil) in 2010; Exforge HCT® (amlodipine besylate, hydrochlorothiazide, valsartan) in 2009; 
and Tri-Luma® (fluocinolone acetonide, hydroquinone, tretinoin) in 2002.16  FDA should follow 
this requirement here and refuse to approve any fixed-dose, triple-combination COPD product 
with an unrestricted indication that is not supported by pivotal factorial studies demonstrating 
superiority of the triple combination over all double-ingredient combinations. 
b. A Factorial Study Is Especially Necessary to Assess the Contribution of the ICS 
Component of a Triple-Combination Product with respect to Safety and Effectiveness 
 
The comparison against a LAMA/LABA combination in any factorial study is 
particularly critical because of (1) the well-established efficacy of LAMA/LABA combinations 
in improving lung function, and (2) the significant safety risks entailed by ICS active ingredients, 
particularly the increased risks of pneumonia.  Consequently, unless an ICS is shown to make a 
significant additional contribution to the efficacy of a LAMA/LABA combination, COPD 
patients should not be exposed to the increased risks associated with ICS therapy.  As FDA has 
observed, “the use of any added active ingredient involves some risk, and that risk can only be 
justified by an added benefit in either safety or effectiveness.”  80 Fed. Reg. at 79789 (emphasis 
added).   
There is little existing clinical evidence that a LAMA/LABA/ICS combination is more 
effective than a LAMA/LABA combination for treating COPD patients or that the addition of an 
ICS adds any meaningful incremental benefit to a LAMA/LABA combination.  The GOLD 
Report, for example, concluded that “[r]esults from withdrawal studies provide equivocal results

demonstrating that the other combination COPD products were supported by factorial studies is included in their

Petitioner believes that legitimate questions exist concerning the reliability

versus IM naloxone in actual field use.

 There are reasons to believe that intranasal delivery may be contraindicated in

Moreover, nasal insufflation – that is associated with the patient

In the past, as the above list illustrates, the FDA has acted to amend the C.F.R. to codify negative 
monographs that ban or otherwise prohibit the marketing of unapproved OTC products 
containing ingredients determined to be harmful or ineffective in treating the conditions for 
which they were marketed. 
The petitioner asserts that marijuana and THC are drugs as defined by 21 U.S.C § 32l(g)(l)(B & 
C). In addition, both substances are listed as Schedule I controlled substances under the 
Controlled Substances Act, specifically, 21 U .S.C. § 812 (Schedule 1), meaning, in part, that they 
have a high potential for abuse and no currently accepted medical use in treatment in the United 
States. 
Moreover, as recently as June 25, 2015, the Acting Assistant Secretary for Health, Department of 
Health and Human Services, provided the Acting Administrator of the Drug Enforcement 
3 
Administration (DEA) with a comprehensive scientific and medical evaluation of marijuana that, 
among other things, concluded: 
Pursuant to the Controlled Substances Act (CSA, 21 U.S.C. § 811 (b), (c), and (f)), the 
Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is recommending that marijuana 
continue to be maintained in Schedule I of the CSA. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 
has considered the abuse potential and dependence-producing characteristics of marijuana.4 
Petitioner asserts that despite the unlawful status of marijuana and THC and the Acting Assistant 
Secretary's recent scientific and medical findings, numerous products containing marijuana 
and/or THC and claiming to provide therapeutic benefits that are either false, misleading, or 
unsupported by scientific data, continue to be sold OTC and online. 
Marijuana is being sold or distributed as "medical marijuana" in some 29 states and the District 
of Columbia. Unsupported medical claims being made for medical marijuana span a broad range 
of indications, including relieving chronic pain, curing or treating cancer, HIV -AIDS, post-
traumatic stress disorder (PTST), epilepsy, heart disease, etc. 
Many beneficial medicines trace their origin to plants, and marijuana indeed may have beneficial 
molecules whose therapeutic value is yet to be fully determined. Thus far, three cannabinoid 
medicines have been approved for medical use and marketing by the FDA. Each contains a 
version of a molecule found in the plant that sponsors have been able to synthesize and bring to 
market via the FDA's rigorous IND-NDA process for new medicinal drugs.5 
In the June 25, 2015 report by the Assistant Secretary for Health, one of the primary reasons 
given for recommending that marijuana be maintained in Schedule I of the CSA was its lack of 
accepted medical use as this factor is defined for new drugs by the FDCA: 
In conclusion, to date, research on marijuana's medical use has not developed to the point where 
marijuana is considered to have a " currently accepted medical use" or a " currently accepted 
medical use with severe restrictions. " 6 
The petitioner asserts that these conditions, alone or together, establish grounds for the FDA to 
issue a Final Order and a negative monograph stating - as it has in the 22 similar cases codified 
in the C.F.R. and noted briefly above- that marijuana and THC are not ingredients that can be 
generally recognized as safe and effective for use in OTC drugs. It, therefore, is requested that 
the FDA issue a Final Order placing marijuana and THC in a negative monograph to be codified 
at 21 C.F.R. § 310 (Subpart E - Requirements for Specific New Drugs or Devices). 
Moreover, as in the case of daytime sedatives (supra), the Final Order petitioned for herein 
should state that whenever an OTC drug product that contains marihuana, THC, or any other 
constituent molecule of the marijuana plant, is labeled, represented, or promoted for medical 
purposes, it will be considered a new drug within the meaning of section 201 (p) of the FDCA for

In addition, the Final Order should state that clinical investigations undertaken to show that a 
drug product containing marijuana or THC, or any other constituent of the marijuana plant, is 
safe and effective for the purpose intended must comply with the requirements governing the use 
of investigational new drugs (IND) set forth in 21 C.F .R. § 312, as well as the DEA registration 
requirements set forth in 21 C.F.R. § 1301.18 for conducting research with Schedule I controlled 
substances. 
The Final Order being asked for herein should state that any OTC marijuana and/or THC product 
introduced into interstate commerce that is not in compliance with the Final Order and its 
codified negative monograph pertaining to such drugs is subject to regulatory action. 
Recently, the FDA sent warning letters to four online companies selling cannabidiol (CBD), a 
constituent ofthe marijuana plant, advising them to cease making unsupported claims that their 
products can treat or cure cancer and other diseases, including Alzheimer's, arthritis, heart 
disease, and stroke. 7 
While these actions are commendable, a Final Order codifying a negative monograph for drug 
products containing marijuana and/or THC would send an industry-wide warning to the 
estimated 33,000 marijuana businesses in the U.S., many of which are making unsupported 
medical claims for marijuana and THC drug products sold as "medical marijuana." 
The petitioner believes that a Final Order to codify a negative monograph for marijuana and 
THC drugs would have the same effect as orders of a similar nature have had in curtailing the 
unlawful marketing of substances purporting, for example, to be daytime sedatives, deterrents to 
nail biting or thumbsucking, aphrodisiacs, or any of the other 19 or so unapproved drug products 
mentioned above and codified at 21 C.F.R. § 310, Subpart E. 
In requesting a Final Order establishing and codifying a negative monograph for marijuana and 
THC, the undersigned petitioner is aware that these drugs already are subject to federal and state 
statutes as regulated controlled substances. The difference between existing laws and this 
petition is that the latter is intended to address specifically the unsupported medical claims being 
made for drugs containing marijuana and/or THC that are being sold at retail or online. 
As stated, a Final Order and codification of a negative monograph in the C.F.R. - as in the case 
of the 22 negative monographs cited above - would reduce or end the ability of OTC sellers of 
these drugs to assert and advertise unsupported medical claims for their products. It would 
immediately make such claims unlawful and subject the sponsors to regulatory action, including 
injunctive seizure of mislabeled and misbranded drugs, as well as other potential sanctions 
permitted under the FDCA. 
Currently, as in the case involving the recent warning letters sent to four online distributors of 
mislabeled and misbranded drugs containing marijuana, the FDA investigates and takes action 
against individual companies and products, whereas a Final Order establishing and codifying a

serve as a general warning letter to the estimated thousands of current vendors of mislabeled and

21 C.F.R. § 310, Subpart E, requested herein would pertain solely to unapproved marijuana-
based drug products sold OTC. Presumably, a negative monograph as described herein, would 
not apply to products containing marijuana, THC, or any other constituent part of the marijuana 
plant, sold as food, cosmetics, or beverages - unless unsupported medical claims also are made 
for their use. For this reason, petitioner recommends that FDA consider taking similar regulatory 
action against such products that are being manufactured or sold in interstate commerce and for 
which no unsupported medical or therapeutic claims are being made.8

The undersigned submits this petition under sections 505(j) and 505( q) of the 
Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act ("FDC Act") and the related regulations, 21 
C.F.R. §§ 10.30 and 10.35, to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs take the 
actions described below. 
I. 
ACTION REQUESTED 
Jubilant Draxlmage Inc. ("JDI") respectfully requests that the U.S. Food and Drug 
Administration ("FDA") refrain from a~proving any Abbreviated New Drug Application 
("ANDA") referencing JDI's HICON 
(for the preparation of sodium iodide I 131 
solution or sodium iodide I 131 capsules) approved under NDA 021305, unless such 
ANDA includes enhanced stability testing demonstrating that any differences in the 
proposed generic drug formulation do not result in a drug product that is less safe than the 
Reference Listed Drug ("RLD"), HICON, under the applicable conditions of use. 
Specifically, JDI requests that FDA requires a demonstration that differences in the shelf 
life, vial configuration, excipients, and pH stabilizers in the concentrated solution do not 
impact the safety and efficacy of any proposed generic drug product. JDI requests that 
FDA refuses to approve any ANDA that does not demonstrate that the proposed ANDA 
product satisfies these criteria in proposed conditions of use.

A. 
factual Background 
JDI is the N DA holder for NDA 021 305, HICON. The product is approved as a 
radioactive diagnostic agent indicated for the assessment of thyroid function and for 
thyroid imaging. JDI received approval for its capsule on May 19, 2005 and for its oral 
solution on December 5, 2011. 
On February 15, 20 13, International Isotopes Inc. ("Ir) tiled a suitability petition 
requesting permission to submit an ANDA referencing HICON and NDA 02 1305 with a 
change in the strength from that of the RLD from I 000 mCi/mL at the time of calibration 
to 500-3500 mCi/mL at the time of calibration. 
International Isotopes Inc., Citizen 
Petition, Docket No. FDA-20 13-P-02 19 (Feb. 15, 2013). 
FDA granted this Citizen 
Petition on December 8, 20 14 and stated that ''the change in strength of the proposed 
product does not pose questions of safety or effecti veness because the uses, dosage form, 
and route of administration of the proposed drug product are the same as that of the listed 
drug product." f-DA, Response to Citizen Petition, Docket No. FDA-20 13-P-021 9 (Dec. 
8, 20 14). As stated in a press release, 13 submitted its ANDA referencing NDA 02 1305 
in November 20 16. 1 Under the Generic Drug User Fee Amendments, the expected goal 
date for FDA to act on 13's ANDA is September 20 17. See Pub. L. 122-1 44 (2012). 
Though 13 's Suitability Petition discusses only differences in strength between 
HICON and 13's proposed generic version, several other formu lation differences exist. 
13's 1- 13 1 contains up to 3.5 times higher activity concentration than HICON. 
Additionally, after extensive stability testing, JDI's HICON contains an optimized level 
of sodium thiosulfate as a stabilizer while I3 's contains significantly lower levels. Both 
excipients and inactive ingredients differ as well; HICON contains sodium edetate 
('"EDTA") as a metal scavenger and Dibasic Sodium Phosphate to adjust pH while 13's 1-
131 includes neither of these ingredients. 
On February 23, 20 17, JDI sent a letter to Dr. Kathleen Uhl at the Office of 
Generic Drugs at FDA highlighting several concerns with 13 ·s version o fl-131 resulting 
from these formulation differences. This included a discussion of the elements raised in 
this Citizen Petition, including shelf life, vial configuration, concentration of API, 
stabilizers, excipients, and pH of the concentrated solution. All of these differences 
potentially affect the safety and efticacy of13's 1-1 3 1 product.

After 12 years as an approved manufacturer of radioactive iodine, JDI has a 
unique and comprehensive understanding of the product and its preparation in 
radiopharmacies. As such, the public intormation released thus far about 13 's version of 
the product raises significant concerns about product quality, safety, and efficacy. 
B. 
LegaiBackground 
The FDC Act and FDA ·s implementing regulations require that to approve an 
ANDA, bioequivalence to the brand-name RLD must be demonstrated. See FDC Act § 
505(j)(4)(F); 2 1 C.F.R. § 314.127(a)(6)(i). 
An applicant must also show that ·'[t]he 
methods used in, or the facilities and controls used for, the manufacture, processing, and 
packing of the drug product are [not] inadequate to ensure and preserve its identity, 
strength, quality, and purity."

With respect to drug product quality, and, in particular, the attributes that a drug 
product should maintain if it is to be deemed suitable for therapeutic use, FDA requires 
that ANDAs contain a quantum and quality of Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls 
information similar to that included in an NDA. Among other things, manufacturers 
must submit stability data for the drug substance. See generally FDA, Guidance for

III. 
DISCUSSION 
The stability and reliability of l-131 products are paramount. 
With significant 
differences between J D I' s HI CON and 13' s 1- 13 I, J 01 is concerned that safety and 
stabi lity may be compromised by the approval of an ANDA for 1- 13 1 without robust 
stability data. For these reasons, JDI requests that FDA refrains from approving any 
ANDA referencing JDrs HTCON without a demonstration that differences in the shelf 
life, vial configuration, excipients, and pH stabilizers in the concentrated solution do not 
impact the safety and efficacy of the product. 
Upon a report of an adverse event involving a serious radiochemical spill of a 
HICON vial and the subsequent discovery of absent thyroid uptake, JDI undertook an 
internal volatility study comparing several 1-1 31 formulations, including a non-approved 
version of 13 's chemical grade 1-131. The protocol design measured and compared I-131 
release over 14 days. 
As demonstrated in Figure l , the volatility of I3's 1-1 3 1 
(formulation 3 below) was significantly higher than that of HI CON.

Importantly, this increased 1- I 3 I release is sustained throughout the shelf-life of the 13 
iodine formulation. This testing makes clear that the differences in formulations affect 
the stability and therefore the alleged equivalence and safety of 13 ·s proposed 1-1 3 I drug 
product. 
A. 
Shelf Life 
The shelf life of the RLD, HI CON, is 14 days from date of manufacture. HI CON' s 
robust product stability specification was defined by testing the product under conditions 
that mimic proper product preparation and dispensing in a radiopharmacy setting or 
hospital Nuclear Medicine department. 
13 ' s product. as detailed in the suitability 
petition, claims a significantly increased shelf life of 30 days. 
JOI is concerned that this stability and shelf-life determination cannot be 
replicated under actual conditions of use. The vial containing the I- I 3 1 will be punctured 
multiple times through the course of its shelf-life, and oxygen is introduced at every 
puncture. With the introduction of oxygen, product stability necessarily degrades over 
time. 
For this reason, JDI developed its formulation under the specific condition of 
multiple punctures and other applicable conditions of use to ensure that stability 
specifications are maintained. Based on the development for these conditions, a 14-day 
shelf life was established and confirmed for HICON. 
In addition to oxygen concentration, the activity concentration of the product may 
also adversely affect stability over time. 
l3 's I-13 I product has up to 3.5 times the 
activity concentration as HICON, which clearly renders the activity concentration non-
equivalent. Additionally, HI CON has a higher level of sodium thiosulfate than I3 ' s I-
13 1. This activity concentration, coupled with the lower level of sodium thiosulfate and 
other stabilizers in the I3 product, represent a significant challenge to the claim of 30-day 
shelf life under actual radiopharrnacy conditions.

JDI therefore requests that FDA requires testing demonstrating that 13 ·s 1- 13 L 
even with oxygenation, can maintain product stability for a 30-day shelf life under actual 
conditions of use. 
B. 
Vial Configuration and Headspace 
With extensive experience manufacturing HlCON, JDJ has detennined that both 
the volume of product in the vial and the headspacc in the vial are critical manufacturing 
parameters. Volume is directly tied to stability while the headspace directly impacts the 
amount oxygen in the vial; greater headspace is linked to increased oxidation, which 
impacts product stability over time. 
In its suitability petition, 13 proposed variable vial sizes with different amounts of 
headspace. The variation is likely to affect product stability and potentially impact the 
drug·s efficacy. Additionally, JDI has learned from its experience that stability data from 
one vial is not appl icable to a vial of another size, particularly if the vial is larger or has a 
different headspace volume. As such, stability testing should be performed with every 
vial configuration that will be used in order to ensure consistent, reliable shelf-life 
specifications. 
C. 
Excipients 
HJCON's formulation includes EDTA as an excipient. This important excipient is 
a chelate added to act as a metal scavenger, which binds any trace metals that arc present 
in either the raw material or in other cxcipients. EDTA helps mitigate the effect of even 
trace amounts of ubiquitous reduction-oxidation reactive metals, such as iron, copper, or 
manganese, which, in turn, helps prevent the oxidation of iodide ions that could be 
catalyzed by metal impurities in the solution and that would lead to increased volatility. 
13 's 1-131 does not contain a chelate excipient. To support its omission from 13 ·s 
proposed formulation, it is critical to demonstrate that free metals have no impact on the 
finished product. This assessment would need to be perfonned at various concentrations 
for each metal. 
Additionally, a control arm to test for free metals in the product 
specification is also necessary to assure that certain levels were not exceeded. 
JDI 
respectfully requests that FDA requires such a test before approving 13's I-131 product.

D. 
Stabilizers and pH 
As noted. JDI 's I-liCON uses Dibasic Sodium Phosphate to adjust pH while 13·s 1-
131 uses no buffer. As a result, JDI"s I-liCON solution meets the specified pH range of 
USP-grade products, pH 7.5-1 0.0. The buffered Dibasic Sodium Phosphate Solution 
helps counter the known, gradual pH drift that occurs as a function of radio lysis. Without 
this buffer, the product is much more severely impacted by pH driH. While 13"s 1- 131 
uses sodium hydroxide to adjust the starting pH levels, it docs not contain a buffer to 
protect against this drift and maintain the pH value. Further, 13 's version starts at a pH 
of 12.7, which is considerably outside of the USP specifications for pH, and, as noted, 
does not remain consistent. 
Differences in pH increase volatility in an iodide product such as I-1 3 1, as it is 
well-known that volatility of iodide increases dramatically as pH drops be low 7.5. When 
an I- I 3 1 product drifts outside of the USP range, there is increased potential for serious 
patient injury arising from the increased product pH. Without a buffer, it is foreseeable 
that the pH could continue to decrease below 7.5 and result in accelerated rates of 
oxidation because the rate of oxidation is much faster under acidic rather than basic 
conditions. 
Accelerated rates of oxidation could form molecular iodine. 
Molecular 
iodine is a highly volatile radiochemical impurity and potential contaminant that raises 
significant safety concerns. 
Clinical and safety studies should evaluate the risks of 
formation of molecular iodine resulting from pH differences. 
JDI therefore requests that I3 be required to demonstrate that its differences in pH 
levels and buffers do not pose higher safety risks than JDI"s HICON. 
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
HICON has been developed with safety and product stabi lity as key development 
criteria; alternate products that do not meet identical standards when subjected to similar 
scrutiny can pose a risk to patient safety, as well as an increased risk of volatility. 
Furthermore, if stability decreases over shelf life, product efficacy will also be adversely 
affected. 
JDI fully supports generic drug submissions and welcomes and encourages new, 
robust GMP pharmaceutical-grade nuclear medicine products in the United States. 
However, 13 's ANDA displays significant di.tlerences as compared with the RLD, JDI's 
HICON. 
These significant product differences will result in poorer product stability. 
Therefore, JDI requests that FDA refuses to approve 13 ·s ANDA without extensive 
stability data performed under the conditions of use for the product in order to ensure 
product safety and efficacy.

Petition_Text:

CITIZEN PETITION 
Senator Charles E. Schumer and Senator Kirsten Gillibrand hereby submit this citizen petition to 
the Commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) under the federal Food, 
Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA), 21 U.S.C. §§ 301-399, and the Administrative Procedure Act 
(APA), 5 U.S.C. § 553(e). The undersigned ask the agency to take prompt action to prohibit any 
detectable presence of the contaminant 1 ,4-dioxane in cosmetics. 1 
I. 
Introduction 
I ,4-dioxane is a likely human carcinogen that contaminates many cosmetics such as shampoos, 
shower gels, body washes, foaming hand soaps, bubble baths, and lotions. The chemical is not 
identified on labels because companies are not required to disclose contaminants on the 
ingredient lists of cosmetics, making it exceedingly difficult for conswners and their families to 
avoid. Fortunately, technologies exist to minjmize I ,4-dioxane in cosmetics as part of 
responsible manufacturing processes, and many companies already use these technologies. 
Because l ,4-dioxane can cause cancer, serves no purpose in cosmetics, is not identified on 
packaging, and can be minimized during production, FDA should protect the public by requiring 
all companies to utilize the technologies necessary to limit its presence to below detectable 
levels. 
II. 
Agency Action Requested 
1 "Cosmetics" are broadly defined in federal law to include all "articles intended to be rubbed, poured, 
sprinkled, or sprayed on, introduced into, or otherwise applied to the human body or any pa1t thereof for 
cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance," with the exception of true 
soaps. 21 U.S.C. 32 1 (i). T he petition uses the legal term "cosmetic" to refer to this wide variety of 
personal care products subject to FDA oversight under the federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. 
Page I 
The undersigned request that the Commissioner promulgate a rule clarifying that products 
containing detectable concentrations of 1 ,4-dioxane are adulterated and therefore prohibited in 
interstate commerce.2 
III. 
Statement of Grounds 
1. Factual Grounds 
A 1 A-dioxane is a contaminant in cosmetics. Consumers are exposed without their knowledge 
because the presence of 1 ,4-dioxane is not disclosed on product packaging. 
I ,4-dioxane is a byproduct of a method called "ethoxylation" used to process cosmetic 
ingredients.3 Such ingredients are commonly found in a wide variety of cosmetics. According 
to FDA, ingredients that may be contaminated with 1,4-dioxane "include certain detergents, 
foaming agents, emulsifiers and solvents identifiable by the prefix, word, or syllables 'PEG,' 
'Polyethylene,' 'Polyethylene glycol,' 'Polyoxyethylene,' '-eth-,' or '-oxynol-. "'-t The quantities 
of 1 ,4-dioxane in cosmetics vary significantly, and without testing every product on the market, 
which contain 1 ,4-dioxane and in what amounts remains unknown. 5 
The concentration of the contaminant can be limited in the finished ingredients using a method 
refen·ed to as "vacuum stripping."6 FDA has already provided guidance on how to vacuum sttip 
1 ,4-dioxane from cosmetic ingredients and has monitored levels in products for decades. 7 
FDA does not require contaminants like 1 ,4-dioxane to be listed on product labels, so even the 
savviest consumer is left to guess whether it is present in a cosmetic based on knowledge of 
which ingredients may be risky. This is not easy to do~ numerous ingredients are associated 
with 1 ,4-dioxane contamination. Without further agency action, many consumers remain 
unwittingly exposed to this cancer-causing chemicaL 
B. 1,4-dioxane is a cancer-causing chemical that can make its way into exposed individuals' 
bodies, which is especially risky for children.

FDA confirmed in the early 1980s that some amount of 1,4-dioxane is absorbed via exposure to 
the skin from cosmetics. 10 Additionally, the general public may be exposed to 1 ,4-dioxane from 
sources other than cosmetics. Ethoxylated substances that may be contaminated with 1,4-
dioxane are also used in the production of food, agricultural, and household products. 11 The 
chemical is also present in consumer products as a residue from a long list of industrial uses of 
I ,4-dioxane itself, including textile processing, dyes and paints, adhesives, and pesticides. 12 
According to the Consumer Product Safety Commission, "the presence of 1,4-dioxane, even as a 
trace contaminant, is cause for concern." 13 
Children's exposures to 1,4-dioxane are particularly worrisome. Infants and children are 
especially vulnerable to harms from carcinogens; numerous research studies and health agency

with adults, children are exposed to cancer-causing chemicals in greater amounts relative to their

2. Legal Grounds 
Section 301 of the FDCA forbids the introduction and delivery of adulterated cosmetics into 
interstate commerce. 18 The FDCA classifies a cosmetic as "adulterated" if it contains a 
"deleterious substance" rendering the product "injurious to users." 19 1,4-dioxane is just such a 
harmful substance. Therefore FDA should use its authority to issue a rule declaring cosmetics 
contaminated with detectable amounts of 1 ,4-dioxane to be adulterated. 20 
FDA has in the past promulgated mles to ban or restrict the presence of other substances in 
cosmetics shovvn to violate the FDCA.21 For example, the agency prohibited the use of 
methylene chloride as an ingredient because the chemical was found to be carcinogenic to 
animals. 22 1,4-dioxane is also carcinogenic to animals.23 FDA has also banned uses of mercury 
compounds for which the agency found "nojustification."24 Similarly, there is no '"justification" 
for the presence of I ,4-dioxane in cosmetics, as it serves no purpose and can be stripped during 
manufacture. A rule to prohibit detectable levels of I ,4-dioxane contamination in cosmetics 
would be consistent with the goals of the FDCA and with FDA's past rulernakings to protect 
consumers' health. 
IV. 
Conclusion 
The undersigned hereby petition the Commissioner to issue a rule stating that 1 ,4-dioxane is a 
deleterious substance, that detection of its presence in a cosmetic causes the product to be 
adulterated under the FDCA, and that such products are therefore illegal to introduce into 
interstate commerce.

Petition_Text:
May 1, 2017 
 
VIA ELECTRONIC SUBMISSION 
 
Division of Dockets Management 
Food and Drug Administration 
Department of Health and Human Services 
5630 Fishers Lane

Rockville, MD 20852 
CITIZEN PETITION 
 
Dear Sir or Madam: 
 
 
The undersigned hereby submits this Citizen Petition pursuant to 21 CFR 10.30, and in 
accordance with the regulations at 21 CFR 314.161, requesting the Commissioner of Food and 
Drugs to require a new warning concerning the risk of esophageal cancer for all over-the-counter 
(“OTC”) drug products that are labeled to relieve or prevent heartburn associated with reflux 
disease, acid indigestion and sour stomach. 
 
A.  
Action Requested  
 
 
The Petitioner hereby requests that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs immediately   
require a new warning concerning the risk of esophageal cancer for all over-the-counter (“OTC”) 
drug products that are labeled to relieve or prevent heartburn associated with reflux disease, 
acid indigestion and sour stomach   The warnings should note that these OTC drug products do 
not eliminate the risk of esophageal cancer and a person should see their physician if they 
experience persistent heartburn associated with reflux disease, acid indigestion or sour stomach 
due to the risk of esophageal cancer. 
 
 
B.  
Statement of Grounds 
 
 
As many as 15 million Americans experience heartburn every day. Persistent heartburn 
(two or more times per week) can be a symptom of gastroesophageal reflux disease (“GERD”), a 
condition where stomach contents, including acid, splash into the esophagus, producing cellular 
changes that can ultimately result in cancer.  For some patients with esophageal cancer, 
heartburn symptoms are the only warning they are at risk.  Yet most patients are unaware that 
heartburn could be the sign of deadly esophageal cancer. 
 
 
A recent public market research survey of more than 1,000 American adults found that 
only 14% were aware that reflux disease, a condition that causes heartburn, could cause 
esophageal cancer. 
 
 
About three million Americans currently have a condition known as Barrett’s Esophagus, 
a precancerous condition that results in as much as a 125-fold increase in an individual’s chance 
to develop esophageal cancer. More than half of those with Barrett’s Esophagus are unaware

May 1, 2017 
 
Page 2 
 
 
they have the condition because it presents no symptoms.  That is why esophageal cancer is often 
only discovered when it has reached advanced stages when treatment outcomes are very poor. 
 
 
There are a significant number of OTC drug products that are available to relieve or 
prevent heartburn associated with acid indigestion and sour stomach brought on by eating or 
drinking certain food and beverages. 
 
 
Such products include, among others, antacid products such as magnesium hydroxide, 
aluminum hydroxide, and calcium carbonate, ranitidine, famotidine, cimetidine, esomeprazole, 
omeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole and nizatidine.  Many of these products were formerly 
available by prescription and are very effective in relieving the symptoms associated with 
heartburn.  As noted above, persistent heartburn is often the result of stomach acid splashing 
into the esophagus.  This constant exposure to stomach contents can produce cellular changes 
in the esophagus that lead to cancer. 
 
 
Because these products are effective in providing symptomatic relief, many patients 
will not seek medical intervention for persistent heartburn that can lead to Barrett’s Esophagus 
and esophageal cancer. 
 
 
 
The warnings on current products are not sufficient to alert patients to the risk of 
esophageal cancer associated with persistent heartburn resulting from reflux disease, acid 
indigestion or sour stomach. 
 
 
The current warnings instruct patients to: 
 
 
 
Ask a doctor before use if you have 
 
had heartburn over 3 months. This may be a sign of a more serious 
condition 
 
Stop use and ask a doctor if 
 
your heartburn continues or worsens 
 
you need to take this product for more than 14 days 
 
If you need to take more than 1 course of treatment every 4 months. 
 
The Petitioner firmly believes that given the prevalence of Barrett’s Esophagus, a 
stronger warning is warranted on these OTC products that are indicated to relieve or prevent 
heartburn associated with reflux disease, acid indigestion and sour stomach  
 
 
The warnings should include a stronger, bold and prominent statement that persistent 
heartburn can be a sign of increased risk of esophageal cancer and explain that drug products do 
not eliminate that risk.

The warnings should be bold and prominent.  The Petitioner proposes the following 
language for such a warning.  
 
 
PERSISTENT HEARTBURN CAN INDICATE INCREASED RISK OF DEVELOPING 
ESOPHAGEAL CANCER. 
 
THIS MEDICATION WILL NOT ELIMINATE THAT RISK. 
 
 
 
 
ASK A DOCTOR BEFORE USE IF YOU HAVE 
 
HAD HEARTBURN OVER 3 MONTHS.                                             
THIS MAY BE A SIGN OF A MORE SERIOUS CONDITION 
 
STOP USE OF THE PRODUCT AND SEE YOUR PHYSICIAN 
 
 IF YOUR HEARTBURN CONTINUES OR WORSENS; OR 
 IF YOU NEED TO TAKE THIS PRODUCT FOR MORE THAN 14 
DAYS; OR 
 IF YOU NEED TO TAKE MORE THAN 1 COURSE OF 
TREATMENT EVERY 4 MONTHS. 
 
 
 
In our view, the inclusion of a bold, prominent and strong warning will serve to better 
inform patients of the risks associated with persistent heartburn and the need to see their 
physician due to the risk of esophageal cancer that can go undetected if the patient is getting 
symptomatic relief from the OTC drug products. 
 
 
C.  
Environmental Impact 
 
The Petitioner claims a categorical exclusion under 21 CFR 25.31. 
 
 
D.  
Economic Impact Statement 
 
The Petitioner will, upon request by the Commissioner, submit economic impact 
information in accordance with 21 CFR 10.30(b).

May 1, 2017

Certification

Citizen Petition 
 
William Bonificio 
 
Date: 7/11/2017 
 
 
The undersigned submits this petition under 21 U.S. Code § 321 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic 
Act to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to amend the classification of glutaraldehyde-based 
tooth desensitizers from devices to drugs, or revoke their current classifications as devices. 
A. Action Requested 
Currently, glutaraldehyde-based tooth desensitizers are classified as devices. There are many examples 
on the market, but one popular example is Gluma Desensitizer Power Gel by Haraeus (I believe others 
may be being sold illegally without any FDA authorization).  Based on the FDA’s definition of drugs and 
devices, these are clearly drugs and not devices. The classification should be changed to a drug, though 
since formal trials are lacking I am not sure if this is possible. At the least, the device label should be 
removed. 
B. Statement of Grounds 
1) Background of hypersensitivity: 
Dentin hypersensitivity is more commonly known as tooth sensitivity, which almost everyone is familiar 
with.  It has been well established in the academic literature that it caused by perturbations to the fluid 
within exposed dentin tubules, which transfer a stimulus from the environment to tooth nerve.  Basically, 
teeth have fluid filled tubes (filled with plasma exudate) that stretch from the nerve of the tooth outward. 
Normally, these tubules are capped by the tooth enamel or the gum.  However, when the gum recedes or 
the tooth is drilled the tubules can become exposed to the environment.  Once this happens, 
environmental stimuli, such as pressure or changes in temperature can perturb the fluid in the tubules 
which signal back to the nerve. Common methods of resolving hypersensitive are to occlude the tubules, 
so that fluid cannot transfer stimuli from the environment back to the nerve, effectively ‘plugging’ the 
tubules. 
2) Glutaraldehyde for hypersensitivity 
Glutaraldehyde is one such agent that is commonly used to prevent sensitivity.  It’s mechanism of action 
is also well established.  Glutaraldehyde is a common protein crosslinker, and when it is rubbed on the 
teeth it cross links proteins from the saliva and the tubule fluid (such as albumin in the plasma exudate). 
These proteins aggregate and plug the tubules. 
Gluma Desensitizer Power Gel’s summary article in the FDA’s database speaks to this exact mechanism 
of action under their ‘description of the device’ – which is reprinted here: 
“ Gluma Desensitizer PowerGel is used for treatment of hypersensitive dentine (sic). The product should 
be applied only on dentin with a sufficient remaining pulpal wall. It achieves its effects by precipitation of 
plasma proteins, which reduces dentinal permeability and occludes the peripheral dentinal tubules. This 
inhibits the flow of fluid through the tubules which is the cause of sensitivity” 
3) Glutaraldehyde is a drug 
The FDA defines a drug as an article intended for the treatment of a disease by affecting the structure or 
function of the body.  The FDA defines a device similarly, however it is differentiated from a drug in that 
a device “does not achieve its primary intended purposes through chemical action within or on the body 
of man or other animals and which is not dependent upon being metabolized for the achievement of its 
primary intended purposes.” The FDA further guides to the definition of a chemical action by stating that 
it involves “formation or breaking of covalent or ionic bonds”. 
Clearly, crosslinking plasma proteins in the dentin tubules fits every criterion for drug, but not a device. 
The glutaraldehyde is treating a disease (hypersensitivity), clearly there is a structure/function relationship 
(folding proteins to occlude tubules) and clearly it is doing so by a chemical action (the crosslinking is 
breaking and forming covalent bonds based on a long understood action of glutaraldehyde - it is one of the 
most common reagents used in biology). 
C. Environmental Impact 
I claim categorical exclusion (under 21 CFR 25.31(e)) from the requirement to submit an environmental 
assessment. To my knowledge, no extraordinary circumstances exist. 
D. Economic impact 
An economic impact statement will be submitted if requested by the Comissioner, pursuant to 21. C.F.R. 
10.30 (b) 
E. Certification 
The undersigned certifies, that, to the best knowledge and belief of the undersigned, this petition includes 
all information and views on which the petition relies, and that it includes representative data and 
information known to the petitioner which are unfavorable to the petition. 
 
 
William Bonificio

1. Legal Framework 
 
a. 
FDA Classification and Regulation of Devices  
 
The Act defines a “device” to be:

vitro reagent, or other similar related article . . .intended for use in the diagnosis

FDA has identified a broad range of products which are “devices” within the meaning 
of the Act, and which it has further determined shall be classified as class I, class II or class III, 
according to the relative predictability of their safety and effectiveness when used for their 
intended purposes.  For example and relevant to this Petition, FDA has identified “daily activity

21 CFR §890.5050 defines “daily activity assist devices” to include  
 
“ . . . a modified adaptor or utensil (e.g., a dressing, grooming, recreational 
activity, transfer, eating, or homemaking aid) that is intended for medical 
purposes to assist a patient to perform a specific function.”3 
 
FDA has further identified two generic types of devices within this category of “daily 
activity assist devices” which are intended to assist a patient with his or her medications:  
 
1). “Solid Medication Dispenser” (Product Code – NXB), which is intended “ .

provide alerts to patients or healthcare providers for pre-determined medication dosing

A review of the devices listed with FDA with reference to these Product Codes 
establishes that the devices classified as “Solid Medication Dispensers” are typically traditional 
pill boxes or other simple containers which may be components of “Medication Reminders” 
providing visible or audible alerts when the patient should take the medications the patient had 
previously loaded into the Dispenser.6

of a simple “assist” device, such as the plastic pill box or pill organizer (pictured below).

This revolution in patient medication management from pill box (with or without an

FDA Classification and Regulation of Remote Medication Management Systems 
 
On September 20, 2006, FDA issued an order automatically classifying a remote

“ . . . because [the INRange Device] was not within the type of device which

On September 25, 2006, INRange petitioned FDA to reclassify the INRange Device,

By order announced October 17, 2007, FDA announced that it was classifying devices 
of the generic type represented by the INRange Device into class II (special Controls).11  At the 
same time, FDA amended 21 CFR Part 880 by the addition of new Section 880.6315 (“Remote 
Medication Management System”), and it announced the availability of a guidance document 
entitled, “Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff; Class II Special 
Controls Guidance Document: Remote Medication Management System” (referred to hereafter 
as the “Medication Management System Guidance”).12   
 
In announcing this regulatory action, FDA identified the following risks to health

Significantly, FDA did not find that the general controls of the Act of the type applicable

The Medication Management System Guidance emphasizes FDA’s concern over the 
ability of the Remote Medication Management System to correctly identify, select and deliver 
the medication prescribed for the patient.  In particular, FDA has observed that  
 
“[o]ne source of medication error is the inability of the patients to properly

These risks were identified because the indications for use include the treatment of

administer their medications are often without immediate access to the pharmacist instructions 
(usually located on the prescription label located on the front of the amber bottle).  Therefore,

scope of 21 CFR 880.6315 and is Misbranded and is an Adulterated Devices

The FDA Ruled that in-home medication management devices that can be remotely 
controlled are class II medication devices subject to 21 CFR Section 880.6315.  If action is not 
taken by FDA to require manufacturers of such devices to conform to the general controls of 
the Act, including the establishment registration and device listing requirements described in

The undersigned submits this petition (under  21 U.S.C. 321-397 and 21 CFR 10.30) to 
request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to consider reconsider or suspend 
/revoke, if appropriate, 510K Pre-Market Notification K151763 
 
 
A. ACTION REQUESTED 
 
In June of 2015, Millennium Dental Technologies submitted Traditional 510K K151763 
 The reason for Submission: Request for New Clinical Outcome. 
It said the following: “The purpose of this 510(k) application is to present histological 
evidence of true periodontal regeneration to support the proposed clinical outcome 
claim. Images of study specimens are provided for the reviewer's assessment. Some of

principles, functional and performance characteristics, and for the intended uses in 
the stated medical specialties. The PerioLase is designed to comply with applicable 
federal and international safety and performance standards. Histologic data support 
the new clinical outcome claim. There are no new safety and effectiveness issues” 
 
It is requested the FDA give a second look at 510K Pre-Market Notification K151763. 
 
Public will be at the disadvantage if FDA does not carefully review the materials which 
were submitted by the device manufacturer. 
 
Public may consider this device superior, as it claimed an indication, not well supported by 
unbiased studies.  
 
 
B. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
   
 
 The histologic data which was submitted by the device manufacturer appears to be 
heavily biased. Data did not include any controls.  The concerns include, that in 
comparison, conventional therapy (Scaling and Root Planning may also result in 
the same benefit). Also, none of the studies actually show bone regeneration.  
 There was only mention of one other study, a systematic review, which also had 
cited a published work from the study supported by the device manufacturer. 
 FDA, is expected to use unbiased data, or be involved in designing a study, so 
indications are clearly evaluated, or evidence is clearly vetted, In this case, it 
appears this is not done.  
 Consequences of Public Health Importance 
 
The device manufacturer, based on this very limited, highly biased data, was able 
to convince FDA that they can market, and claim that device can “regenerate” oral 
tissues. 
 
The device manufacturer is essentially implying that, due to FDA’s clearance for 
them market this solution to conventional approaches, thus  making a claim of 
superiority, not equivalency. 
 
Manufacturer has made the following claim on its website. Source: 
http://trueregeneration.com/ 
  
THIS IS THE WORLD'S FIRST EVER FDA CLEARANCE FOR TRUE 
REGENERATION! 
No other laser company... 
No other laser device... 
No other laser periodontal therapy...  
...CAN CLAIM TRUE REGENERATION INCLUDING NEW BONE FORMATION. 
 
No biologics used! 
No exogenous growth factors! 
No bone grafts! 
No artificial membranes! 
No scaffolds! 
No stitches!  
Source: http://trueregeneration.com/  
 
In the above example, device manufacturer is implying superiority, and also 
exaggerating their claim, that FDA has cleared them as the device which can truly 
regenerate. By naming their protocol of care used by the device as “True 
Regeneration”, they appear to be obfuscating the truth, that this device is no better than 
conventional therapy in terms of regeneration. Data is heavily biased, and the outcome 
can hardly be considered predictable, as there is only very limited data available.

D. ECONOMIC IMPACT: 
FDA’s Responsibility to Protect Public Health  
Public will be at the disadvantage if FDA does not carefully review the materials which 
were submitted by the device manufacturer. 
 
Public may consider this device superior, as it claimed an indication, not well supported by 
unbiased studies. It appears to be misleading. 
 
FDA is requested to seriously reconsider, the data and to re-evaluate its decision as it is 
heavily biased. Otherwise, consumer, healthcare patients all across the country will 
erroneously consider this to a superior device, as is apparently and inherently claimed by 
the device manufacturer. Consumers will be misled, and it can make  
 
FDA vulnerable to litigation as it can be held liable for not properly vetting the data, 
before giving a clearance to include a clinical indication.  
 
 
E. CERTIFICATION

Dear Sir or Madam, 
The undersigned submits this petition under the same provisions of law that the Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA) relied on to issue fish consumption advice on January 18, 2017, and in 
accordance with 21 C.F.R. 10.20 and 10.30. 
A. ACTION REQUESTED 
We request that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs promptly: 
( 1) withdraw the fish consumption advice that FDA issued jointly with the Environmental 
Protection Agency (EPA) on January 18,2017 (entitled "Eating Fish: What Pregnant 
Women and Parents Should Know" (FDA/EPA 2017) ); and 
(2) issue new fish consumption advice that is: 
(a) designed to achieve the core purpose that the Department of Health and Human 
Services (HHS), FDA, and then FDA together with the Department of Justice 
expressed over a span of years: to inform pregnant women how they can obtain the 
most benefits for their children's neurodevelopmentfromjish while minimizing risk 
from methylmercury: and 
(b) tested through experimental studies with consumers (hereinafter "experimental 
studies") to ensure that it is likely to succeed Experimental studies test how 
consumers respond to a number of possible messages and variations to messages. 
They involve a sufficient number of consumers to be statistically capable of 
predicting how pregnant women will typically respond to the message that FDA 
finally issues. 
By "fish consumption advice," we mean the basic message and explanatory materials for 
consumers in the form of questions and answers (Q & A) that accompany the basic message. By 
"fish" we mean species and market types that are commercially available, typically in grocery 
stores and retail fish markets (hereinafter "commercial fish"). Commercial fish represent most of 
the fish eaten in the United States. FDA has Federal regulatory responsibility for their food 
safety and applied nutrition.1 The advice issued on January 18 (hereinafter "the current advice") 
covers both commercial fish and noncommercial fish, i.e., fish that are caught recreationally and 
for subsistence, mainly from rivers, lakes and streams. FDA has no jurisdiction over 
noncommercial fish. 
B. "ROAD MAP" TO THE "STATEMENT OF GROUNDS" IN 
THIS PETITION 
The "Statement of Grounds" contains three Parts and three Appendices as follows: 
Part 1: Overview of the Problem and the Solution 
This part provides an overview of deficiencies in the current fish consumption advice. These 
deficiencies make it unlikely that the current advice will resolve the primary public health 
problem associated with fish consumption during pregnancy, which is sub-optimum 
consumption that cannot provide the most neurodevelopmental benefits that are possible from 
fish while keeping risk from methylmercury low. The problem can be remedied through well-
crafted advice that is robustly tested for effectiveness in advance of issuance through 
experimental-type studies with consumers. 
Part IT: The Specific Remedies that We are Requesting 
This part contains our specific requests for what the new advice should contain to resolve the 
deficiencies in the current advice and achieve the core purpose for fish consumption as stated by 
HHS, FDA, and DOJ. That core purpose is to enable pregnant women to obtain the most 
benefits that fish can provide to their children's neurodevelopment while minimizing risk from 
methylmercury. 
Part m: What New Fish Consumption Advice Could Look Like 
This part contains an example of fish consumption advice containing the features requested and 
explained in Part II and further explained in the Appendices. This example, or any similar 
advice, should be tested in experimental studies and revised as necessary before issuance to 
ensure that it can succeed. 
Appendix A: Scientific and Background Information Regarding Core Purpose 
This appendix describes how and why the core purpose of obtaining the most benefits while 
minimizing risk came into being. 
Appendix B: Scientific and Background Information Regarding 8-12 Ounces ofFish Per 
Week 
This appendix describes how the recommendation to eat 8-12 ounces of fish per week in the 
current advice came into being. Without a clear connection to enhancing neurodevelopment, 
which the current advice does not make, this amount becomes ambiguous at best, misleading at 
worst, and is likely to be counter-productive.
