Appendix C: Scientific and Background Information Regarding the Consumption 
Categories 
This appendix addresses the science behind the three consumption categories in the current 
advice. The categories are ostensibly designed to minimize risk but two of them do not coincide 
with actual risk nor do they take benefits into account. The appendix further addresses how 
consumption categories, if they are to be included at all, could help pregnant women make 
selections that could maximize, or come close to maximizing, benefits to neurodevelopment for 
their children while minimizing risk from methylmercury. 
C. STATE ME NT OF GROUNDS 
PART 1: 
Overview of the Problem and the Solution 
The weight of credible evidence from long-term studies involving pregnant women and their 
children over the past 15 years strongly indicates that pregnant women who eat commercial fish 
can enhance the neurodevelopment of their children. These enhancements appear as better 
performance on tests of neurodevelopment during childhood as compared to children whose 
mothers eat less or no fish during pregnancy. They occur even though most if not all fish contain 
at least some methylmercury, a neurotoxin that can harm neurodevelopment if exposure to it is 
too high. 
A review ofthis evidence by FDA (FDA 2014), the Advisory Committee to the Dietary 
Guidelines for Americans2 (DGAC 2010), the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United 
Nations in conjunction with the Word Health Organization (FAO/WHO) (FAO/WHO 2011), 
and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) (EFSA 2014), plus groundbreaking 
assessments of that evidence by FDA (FDA 2014) and the FAO/WHO (FAO/WHO 2011), 
revealed that when fish are eaten during pregnancy, improvements in fetal neurodevelopment are 
much more likely than deficits from methylmercury. The FDA and FAO/WHO assessments 
further revealed that there are optimum amounts of fish during pregnancy at which these 
improvements are at their greatest while risk from methylmercury is very low. 
Starting in 2011 HHS and FDA informed the Congress and the public that, as a result of FDA's 
then-ongoing assessment, new fish consumption advice was being developed to inform pregnant 
women how to obtain the most benefits to neurodevelopment that fish could provide their 
children while minimizing risk from methylmercury (Sebelius 2011; Taylor 2011 & 2011a, 
Ireland 2011). In 2014 FDA reiterated that purpose jointly with the Department of Justice 
(DOJ) to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia (FDA/DOJ 2014). 
2 The Dietary Guidelines for Americans are Federal recommendations designed to prevent and reduce diet-related 
chronic diseases and promote good health. They are updated every five years by the Departments of Agriculture and 
Health and Human Services. Each update is preceded by an Advisory Committee Report from an independent panel 
of experts that contains the latest information on the state of the science that will be germane to updating the Dietary 
Guidelines for Americans. 
3 
There is a substantial gap between the amounts of fish that pregnant women typically eat and 
amounts needed to obtain the most benefits to fetal neurodevelopment. It has been estimated that 
as many as 175 million IQ points could have been gained in the United States since 2004 from 
optimum fish consumption had it occurred (Perinatal Nutrition Collaborative 2016). A 
shortfall of this magnitude would dwarf any population-wide deficits caused by over -exposure to 
methylmercury from commercial fish during pregnancy. Over-exposure is not a problem for the 
vast majority of pregnant women and their children in the United States. 
On January 18, 2017, FDA together with EPA issued the current advice. It never mentions 
optimum consumption, maximizing benefits while minimizing risk, or the fact that the benefits 
are enhancements to neurodevelopment. It only states that studies involving fish consumption 
have found benefits to children's "growth and development" in general, and further implies that 
fish are no different from other healthful foods in that respect. The scientific basis for such a 
claim is not clear. All the studies that have found benefits from eating fish during pregnancy 
have involved incremental improvements to neurodevelopment. No studies that we are aware of 
have produced similar findings with other foods. The implication that pregnant women need not 
eat fish in order to obtain the same benefits that fish can provide is highly misleading. 
The current advice is misleading in other respects as well. It divides fish into three categories 
based solely on how to avoid an implied (but unstated) risk from methylmercury. Two of the 
categories ("Good Choices" and "Best Choices") are not supported by current science relating to 
actual risk. One of the categories would involve consumption significantly below optimum 
without an adequate basis in risk for doing so. If the advice had ranked fish according to the 
most benefits they could provide to neurodevelopment while still minimizing risk, many of the 
fish identified as "Good" and "Best" would not be in their current categories. 
The entirety of the advice emphasizes caution over encouragement and risk over benefit. 
References to "harm," "avoid," "limit," eat "no more than," and "mercury" and "methylmercury" 
exceed references to "nutritional benefits," "protein, minerals and vitamins," "growth and 
development," and increasing consumption (once, briefly). The statement in the previous 
FDAJEP A advice that "For most people, the risk from mercury by eating fish and shellfish is not 
a health concern" (FDA/EPA 2004) has been dropped although there is no reason to believe that 
it is now inaccurate. EPA included the same sentence in a press release in 2013 (EPA 2013) and 
has not retracted it to the best of our knowledge. On FDA's web site, the new advice is on a 
page entitled "Foodborne Illness and Contaminants," implying that avoiding harm from 
methylmercury is the primary purpose of fish consumption advice and that obtaining nutritional 
benefits from seafood to solve the larger problem caused by sub-optimum consumption is a 
secondary consideration at best. 
It is axiomatic that in a situation involving both risk and benefit, the more that advice emphasizes 
risk avoidance, the less likely it will be to motivate behavior that will increase the benefit. There 
is evidence that fish advice can reduce consumption to well below optimum amounts by having 
the unintended effect of frightening pregnant women about the risks of methylmercury (Oken et 
al., 2003, Bloomingdale et al., 2010, Sbimsback et al., 2010). This effect may have occurred 
with fish advice issued in 2001 and 2004 that were primarily designed to limit consumption 
because the benefits to fetal neurodevelopment were not yet understood. Now that the 
4 
significant benefits, including a three to five point increase in IQ on an individual basis and 
related gains in productivity and lifetime earnings are understood, FDA had an obligation to 
rigorously test the current advice -- in its totality - in experimental studies to determine whether 
it was likely to accomplish the new core purpose that HHS and FDA had established for it. 
No such testing occurred. Had FDA tested its advice, we believe the agency would have 
discovered that the ambiguities, omissions, misleading implications, and overall emphasis on 
avoiding deficits to neurodevelopment from methylmercury but not on obtaining the most 
benefits to neurodevelopment through optimwn fish consumption combine to make informed 
judgement virtually impossible.3 As a consequence, it is highly unlikely that many pregnant 
women will eat optimum amounts of fish, or at least increase their fish consumption significantly 
toward optimum, or in many cases eat fish at all. An important public health opportunity is 
being lost for years to come. 
The advice claims to be "cautious" and "highly protective" for methylmercury but never explains 
why it should not also be equally "cautious" and "highly protective" against sub-optimum 
consumption that cannot provide the fetus with the highest cognitive potential. That failure is 
bad policy and bad government. For those reasons, we have included in this petition questions 
designed for FDA to explain itself, should it disagree with our requests. 
This petition requests that the current advice be retracted promptly rather than tested in place 
because the risk that its misleading aspects will become ingrained into the national consciousness 
is simply too great.4 We request that FDA replace it with advice along the lines we are 
proposing, but only after it is robustly tested through experimental studies and then adjusted as 
necessary based on the results of those studies.

1. Core Purpose 
l(a). We request that FDA conduct experimental studies with new advice that clearly states the 
core purpose as repeatedly expressed to the Congress and the public by HHS and FDA, and to 
the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia by FDA and DOJ. That core purpose is to 
advise pregnant women how they can maximize neurodevelopmental benefits to their children 
from commercial fish while minimizing risk from methylmercury (Sebelius 2011; Taylor 2011 
& 2011a, Ireland 2011; FDA/DOJ 2014).

Pregnant women -- a highly risk averse population-- should clearly understand what they could 
achieve by increasing their fish consumption by as much as four to six-fold. That increase would 
close the gap between what pregnant women often eat (Lando et al., (2012) and what they need 
to eat in order to obtain the most benefits that fish could provide to their children's 
neurodevelopment (FDA 2014, FAO/WHO 2011). A statement of core purpose would 
contribute significantly to this understanding, thus enabling informed judgment in keeping with 
FDA's Strategic Plan for Risk Communication, and provide a clear basis for each 
recommendation in the advice. 
l(b). Conversely, if FDA has abandoned its core purpose, we request that FDA reissue the 
current advice as a draft for public comment in which the agency clearly states what the new 
core purpose is and the basis for it, and acknowledges and explains the agency's decision to 
abandon the original core purpose. A new core purpose would constitute a radical shift in policy 
not currently disclosed or explained. A full review with opportunity to comment by the scientific 
and public health communities would be essential as a matter of sound public policy. 
l(c). We request that FDA conduct experimental studies with new advice that clearly states that 
it represents a "cautious" and "highly protective" approach to sub-optimum fish consumption as 
well as to any risk from methylmercury. In the Q & A portion of the current advice, Question 2 
in Section I claims that the advice represents a "cautious and highly protective approach" to risk 
from methylmercury. There is no suggestion or indication that this approach extends to risk 
from sub-optimum fish consumption even though there is strong evidence that widespread sub-
optimum consumption is the bigger problem of the two on a population-wide basis. It has been 
estimated that as many as 175 million additional IQ points could have been obtained across the 
U.S. population since 2004 had optimum consumption of commercial fish occurred (Perinatal 
Nutrition Collaborative 2016). A lower bound estimate would still be in the vicinity of 100 
million IQ points by our estimation. (Request 2( e) addresses optimum consumption on an 
individual basis.) 
There is also strong evidence that adverse effects from methylmercury are a risk factor for a 
small percentage of the population and typically involve consumption patterns that are unusual 
for most people (as addressed in Appendix A of this petition). For IQ, FDA's "Quantitative 
Assessment of the Net Effects on Fetal Neurodevelopment from Eating Commercial Fish" 
(hereinafter the FDA Assessment of Net Effects) estimated that loss of a fraction of an IQ point5 
is a risk factor for 1-5 percent of the population (FDA 2014). The Joint F AOIWHO Expert 
Consultation on the Risks and Benefits ofFish Consumption (hereinafter the FAO/WHO 
assessment of net effects) estimated that there are only IQ gains and no losses through at least

national consumption advice to be "cautious" and "highly protective" for methylmercury. But 
the equities here are such that it should also be "cautious" and "highly protective" for the

l(d). We request that FDA conduct experimental studies with new advice that clearly Jinks 
developmental benefits from fish consumption to neurodevelopment. The current advice does 
not do this even though all the studies that motivated the development of a replacement for the 
advice issued in 2004 solely involved neurodevelopment in children. The current advice alludes 
to those studies but states only that they involve "growth and development" (Q & A, section IV, 
Q 1 ). There are two problems with this approach. 
First, pregnant women do not know that the benefits are to neurodevelopment in order to make 
truly informed choices about whether and how much fish to eat. There is evidence that pregnant 
women are influenced by statements about the particular health benefits from fish, e.g., "fetal 
brain and eye development" (Connelly et al., 2014). 
All of the "growth and development" in the studies alluded to in the current advice involved 
neurodevelopment. We are not aware of a good reason for keeping this information from 
pregnant women. The F AOIWHO has recommended that nations "Emphasize the net 
neurodevelopmental benefits to offspring of women of childbearing age who consume fish ... and 
the neurodevelopmental risks to offspring of women of childbearing age who do not consume 
fish" [emphasis added] (FAO/WHO 2011, p. x). The Dietary Guidelines for Americans has 
recommended that pregnant women eat more fish for "visual and cognitive development" 
[emphasis added] (USDA/HHS 2010). EFSA has concluded that 3-4 servings per week is 
associated with "better functional neurodevelopmental outcomes" [emphasis added] (EFSA 
2014, p.1). HHS, FDA, and DOJ have advised the Congress, the public, and the courts that new 
fish consumption advice was being designed to maximize neurodeve/opmental benefits 
[emphasis added] (see l(a) above for cites). 
Second, the current advice essentially claims that the benefits to "growth and development" from 
fish can be obtained from other high-protein foods. (Fish are "like other protein-rich foods" in 
this respect (Q & A, section IV, Q 1; see also (Q & A, section VIII, Q 3)). We are not aware, 
however, of studies that link another food or foods to the same or similar incremental benefits to 
neurodevelopment that have been reported in the fish studies and FDA has not identified any. If 
there are such studies, we urge FDA to name them, name the food, and present the data. 
Advice that fails to tell pregnant women about the neurodevelopmental benefits of fish 
consumption is misleading by omission, with significant potential implications for 
neurodevelopment. Why should a pregnant woman increase her fish consumption, or eat fish at 
all, if she thinks she can obtain the same benefits for her child from other foods?

2. Consumption Target for Servings Per Week to Maximize Benefits 
2(a). We request that FDA conduct experimental studies with new advice that recommends a 
specific weekly consumption target (or targets) for the stated purpose of maximizing benefits to 
neurodevelopment while minimizing risk from methylmercury. The current advice recommends 
that pregnant women eat 2-3 servings (8-12 ounces) offish per week (depending on the types of 
fish consumed, as described later in this petition) but does not state that doing so could maximize 
benefits while minimizing risk. This is a significant omission. We are not aware of a reason to 
recommend eating a specific amount (or amounts) of commercial fish during pregnancy unless it 
represents an optimum amount that could provide the most neurodevelopmental benefits while 
keeping risk from methylmercury close to nonexistent. 
Pregnant women should understand that there is an optimum amount per week for obtaining the 
most neurodevelopmental benefits so that they can make truly informed choices about how much 
fish to eat and why. It was the identification of optimum amounts by FDA in its Assessment of 
Net Effects7 that caused the agency to consider a new core purpose for fish consumption advice 
and embark on new the advice that would achieve that core purpose (see Request l(a) above and 
Appendix A). The Assessment of Net Effects calculates optimum weekly amounts for each of 
nearly 50 species of commercial fish. The overall average is about 12 ounces per week. There is 
strong evidence that pregnant women in the United States often eat fewer than two ounces of fish 
per week (Lando et al., 2012).

4. Why did FDA not conduct experimental studies to determine how pregnant women are

providing an optimum amount or amounts, succinctly explains the consequences for 
neurodevelopment of eating more or less than the optimum over time during pregnancy. The Q 
& A portion of the current advice asks what the consequences are of eating less or more than 2-3

4 ). These questions go to the heart of the advice. 
Eating less over time: The answer to that question should be that eating less over time 
can still benefit neurodevelopment, although the benefits are likely to be smaller than 
they would be if consumption were optimum. FDA's Assessment of Net Effects 
estimated that pregnant women can obtain roughly 70 percent of the maximum possible 
benefits by eating only half of an optimum amount needed to obtain the most benefits 
(FDA 2014, Figure D-3).

children even if eating optimally is beyond their reach. It would be unfortunate if a 
significant number of pregnant women were to conclude that since they cannot reach or

I. 
ACTION REQUESTED 
In light of the recent district court's decision in Perring v. Burwell, 1 Gilead requests that 
FDA promptly award five-year NCE exclusivity to Stribild, which was approved on August 27, 
2012, and extend such exclusivity under FDA's "umbrella policy" to later-approved Gilead

II. 
STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
FDA denied Gilead NCE exclusivity for its fixed-combination drug product, Stribild 
(NDA 203100), based on FDA's since-revised policy that a fixed-combination product 
containing both previously approved and new active moieties are not eligible for such 
exclusivity. FDA revised this NCE policy in February 2014 in response to, in part, a Citizen 
Petition filed by Gilead, but nonetheless, refused to apply its new policy to Stribild and other 
similarly-situated fixed combination drug products. 
In Perring v. Burwell, the District Court in D.C. reviewed FDA's pre-February 2014 
NCE policy for fixed-combination products, determined that such policy was arbitrary and

capricious, and remanded the exclusivity determination for the fixed-combination product 
Prepopik® back to FDA for further review. In light of this decision, Gilead requests that FDA 
also review and revise its NCE exclusivity denial for Stribild, a fixed-combination drug product 
that, like Prepopik, contains a combination of approved and new active moieties. Gilead also 
requests that FDA extend, under its umbrella policy, such five-year NCE exclusivity to the 
subsequently-approved products that contain the new active moieties in Stribild: namely, Tybost, 
and Vitekta. Finally, in accordance with these NCE exclusivity determinations, Gilead also 
requests that FDA withdraw the receipt of any ANDAs referencing these products prior to the 
expiration of their NCE exclusivity periods.2 
A. Statutory and Regulatory Background 
i. NCE Exclusivity for Fixed-Combination Drug Products and FDA's Umbrella 
Policy 
Congress enacted the Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act (Hatch-
Waxman Act) in 1984 as a system to both protect the interests of innovative drug manufacturers 
and provide consumers access to more affordable medicines.3 To that end, Hatch-Waxman put 
in place exclusivity provisions as an incentive to innovators to develop new products while 
authorizing an abbreviated approval process to reduce the cost of drugs for consumers. ANDA 
applicants could rely on FDA's findings of safety and efficacy for a previously approved version 
of the drug as long as the applicant could demonstrate that the proposed generic is "the same as" 
the reference listed drug ("RLD"). 4 At the same time, as a reward for undertaking the onerous 
clinical studies needed for full NDA approvals, Hatch-Waxman awarded periods of exclusivity 
to successful NDA applicants. 5 The scheme was designed to strike "a balance between 
expediting generic drug applications and protecting the interests of the original drug 
manufacturers. "6 
Congress and, by extension, FDA have made several forms of exclusivity available to 
NDA sponsors. New drug products that contain active ingredients that have never received 
approval are eligible for NCE exclusivity, which provides five years of protection for the RLD. 7 
Sections 505(c)(3)(E)(ii) and 505G)(5)(F) of the FDCA provide a five-year exclusivity 
period for approved new chemical entities "no active ingredient (including any ester or salt of the 
active ingredient) of which has been approved in any other application under" 505(b). FDA 
interpreted this provision to extend exclusivity based on whether any active moiety in the drug 
product as a whole had been approved; therefore, FDA extended exclusivity for a drug only if it 
contained no active moiety previously approved by FDA. 8 Thus, NCE exclusivity was

approved regardless of whether it also contained one or more new active moieties. 
FDA also adopted an "umbrella policy," which attaches five-year NCE exclusivity to 
both the first approved drug product that was eligible for NCE exclusivity and to any products 
containing the same active moiety.9 The five-year exclusivity travels with the new active moiety 
to any subsequent products to ensure that a sponsor who develops an active moiety has incentive 
to further develop drug products containing that moiety. 10 Thus, under FDA policies, only drug 
products containing no previously approved active moieties were eligible for five-year 
exclusivity, and any later-approved products containing those active moieties would be similarly 
protected for the duration of the original five-year exclusivity period. 11 
In February 2014, FDA changed its NCE exclusivity policy for fixed-combination 
products. 12 In response to a Citizen Petition filed, followed by two others filed by Ferring and 
Bayer, FDA decided that drug products containing any new active moiety now qualify for NCE 
exclusivity. 13 However, FDA refused to apply the new policy to approved products like Stribild, 
irrespective of whether a generic had been filed at the time of the new policy. 14 
As a result of FD A's policy change, fixed-combination products with new active moieties 
that had not been approved as of October 2014 were eligible for NCE exclusivity even if they 
contain previously approved active moieties; whereas products that had been approved before 
that date were not eligible regardless of whether the product had received an exclusivity 
determination. 15 After the announcement of this policy change, Gilead and Perring filed 
Petitions for Reconsideration on the issue of retroactivity. 16 FDA denied these Petitions, 
concluding that the arguments were adequately considered in the original Citizen Petition 
proceeding and that Petitioners did not demonstrate sound public policy grounds supporting 
reconsideration. 17

actions were contrary to the FDCA and the agency's own regulations, as well as arbitrary and

capricious in violation of Section 706(2)(A) of the Administrative Procedures Act. 18 Initially, 
the Court held that FDA's interpretation ofNCE exclusivity for fixed-combination products was 
not arbitrary and capricious, rejecting Ferring's argument that FDA's fixed-combination NCE 
and umbrella policies created circumstances in which a drug's eligibility for five-year exclusivity 
arbitrarily relied on the order in which NDAs were approved. 19 The Court explained that 
Perring failed to show any evidence in support of its assertions; however, the Court also declined 
to determine whether FDA's refusal to retroactively apply exclusivity was arbitrary and 
capricious and asked the parties for supplemental briefing on the issue. 
Perring moved for reconsideration of the Court's determination that FDA's prior 
interpretation of the NCE exclusivity provision was not arbitrary and capricious. In its motion, 
Perring listed examples in which the order of approvals in fact determined whether a product 
would qualify for NCE exclusivity. Notably, Perring cited Stribild as an example for the court to 
show that "if ... the fixed-dose combination drug product had been approved just hours before 
the single-ingredient product, none of the products would have been awarded NCE exclusivity, 
because each would have contained a previously approved active ingredient. "20 While no new 
single agent product in Prepopik has ever been approved, it relied on drugs like Stribild to show 
how the temporal nature of the guidance was arbitrary and capricious. 
Based on Ferring's new examples of the temporal relationship between approval and 
exclusivity, the Court determined that FDA's NCE exclusivity policy in effect prior to the 
February 2014 revision treated similar cases differently. The Court observed that products lost 
out on five-year exclusivity solely because they had been first approved as part of a fixed-
combination drug product. The Court went on to state that under administrative law principles, 
an agency must treat similar cases in a similar manner unless it can provide a legitimate reason 
for failing to do so; here, FDA's policy as applied to fixed-combination products treated similar 
cases differently, and FDA could not provide a legitimate reason. Thus, the Court held that the 
policy was arbitrary and capricious and remanded it back to FDA for further review consistent 
with the Court's ruling.21 
ii. ANDA Considerations 
Under the FDCA, FDA makes available an abbreviated approval process for 
manufacturers of generic drugs. 22 The ANDA relies on the data of a previously approved NDA 
containing full clinical trials.23 The ANDA applicant must certify to any patents listed for the 
NDA in FDA's compendium Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence 
Evaluations, commonly known as the Orange Book.24 If an ANDA applicant seeks FDA 
approval to market a copy of a brand drug before all of the patents listed in the Orange Book 
have expired, it must challenge the unexpired patents by filing a Paragraph IV certification.25 A

Paragraph IV certification requires the ANDA applicant to provide notice of its FDA filing to 
both the NDA holder and the patent owner.26 
When a generic applicant submits an ANDA, FDA reviews the application for 
completeness and notifies the applicant that its application is substantially complete and has 
officially been "received" by the agency.27 Only when the application is received by FDA, and 
no earlier, can the ANDA applicant send its notice to the NDA holder and the patent holder. 28 
Either or both of these parties must file a patent suit based on the notification within 45 days to 
trigger a 30-month stay, which delays FDA approval of the ANDA for 30 months unless a court 
finds the patent invalid or not infringed prior to the expiration of the stay.29 The first ANDA 
applicant to include a Paragraph IV certification for a particular RLD is eligible for 180-day 
marketing exclusivity, in which FDA may not approve any other ANDA referencing the same 
product.30 
Exclusivity can affect the timing of an ANDA submission. If an NDA has received five-
year NCE exclusivity, an ANDA cannot be accepted or received by FDA for the duration of the 
five-year exclusivity period unless it contains a Paragraph IV certification.
31 An ANDA with a 
Paragraph IV certification may be accepted only after four years of exclusivity have elapsed, 
called the NCE-1 period.32 Conversely, if a product has three-year exclusivity, FDA may accept 
an application at any time, including before the expiration of the three-year period. 33 
Because NCE exclusivity prevents the submission or receipt of an ANDA prior to the 
NCE-1 date, it delays any Paragraph IV certifications, the subsequent 45 days for filing a patent 
infringement suit, and the commencement of the 30-month stay. For products with NCE 
exclusivity, FDA extends the 30-month stay for patent infringement suits for an additional 2.5 
years after the expiration of exclusivity. 34 In other words, products with NCE exclusivity receive 
the full five years of exclusivity, and the 30-month stay runs from expiration of the NCE 
exclusivity. 
B. Factual Background 
Stribild is a fixed dose combination drug product indicated for the treatment of human 
immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV) in adults. Stribild is comprised of two distinct drug 
substances that had received prior FDA approval and two distinct drug substances that were new 
active moieties. The two previously approved substances, emtricitabine ("FTC") and tenofovir 
disoproxil fumarate ("TDF"), received NCE five-year exclusivity upon initial approval as single-
ingredient drugs while the two remaining substances, elvitegravir ("EVG") and cobicistat 
("COBI"), were approved for the first time as part of the fixed combination Stribild product.

Stribild was approved under NDA 203100 on August 27, 2012. While Gilead properly 
requested an exclusivity determination for the fixed-combination product, FDA deferred making 
an exclusivity decision. Concurrently, Gilead submitted separate single-ingredient NDAs for 
EVG (as Vitekta) and COBI (as Tybost) on June 27, 2012.35 Consistent with its exclusivity 
request for Stribild, Gilead requested that EVG and COBI be protected under Stribild's five-year 
NCE exclusivity. 
On January 8, 2013, Gilead filed a Citizen Petition requesting five-year NCE exclusivity 
for Stribild and asking the agency to reevaluate its approach to NCE exclusivity determinations 
for fixed-combination products. In February 2014, FDA denied Gilead's Citizen Petition and 
released a draft guidance document explaining changes to the NCE exclusivity policy for fixed-
combination drugs containing previously approved moieties. FDA awarded Stribild three-year 
exclusivity in March of 2014. Gilead filed a Petition for Reconsideration in March 2014, which 
FDA denied in October 2014 while finalizing its new guidance document. FDA approved 
Tybost and Vitekta with three-year exclusivity in September 2014. 
III. 
ARGUMENT 
A. FDA must revise its arbitrary and capricious fixed-combination NCE exclusivity 
policy to comply with Ferring v. Burwell 
As explained, Perring v. Burwell unambiguously held that FDA's temporally-based NCE 
exclusivity policy was arbitrary and capricious. 36 The Court was clear that FDA provided no 
sound explanation as to why the timing of or the order in which drugs were approved should 
alter the assessment of whether the active moiety is sufficiently novel to warrant protection under 
a five-year exclusivity period. This policy inherently treated similar products differently, as new 
active moieties receiving five-year NCE exclusivity would share such exclusivity with later-
approved fixed-combination drug products containing such moieties while the same products 
approved in the reverse order would receive disparate treatment by being denied NCE 
exclusivity altogether. 
The Court remanded the Prepopik exclusivity determination back to FDA to revise its 
policy such that similar products receive similar treatment. To do so, FDA must grant five-year 
NCE exclusivity to Prepopik, as well as to all similarly situated fixed-combination drug products 
for which NCE exclusivity has previously been denied, including Stribild. 
B. In conformity with Ferring v. Burwell, Stribild and its progeny should receive 
N CE exclusivity 
The Court's determination was broadly based on the nature ofFDA's NCE policy rather 
than specific facts relevant to Prepopik. Indeed, the Court explicitly relied on the Stribild fact 
pattern in reaching its decision in Ferring v. Burwell that FDA's NCE exclusivity policy failed to 
treat similar products the same. This is despite the fact that Prepopik had no subsequent single 
agent approval and thus did not fail to treat single agent products the same. However, referring 
to Stribild, the Court stated that "[t]hese newly highlighted examples now show that, even if the

FDA' s prior interpretation is reasonable under Chevron Step Two from a conceptual standpoint, 
that interpretation produces circumstances that fail to treat 'similar cases in a similar manner. '"37 
Clearly then, the Court's findings apply even more directly to Stribild as they do 
Prepopik, entitling Stribild to five-year NCE exclusivity. In addition, under FDA's long-
standing umbrella policy, the exclusivity applied to Stribild should follow and protect the new 
active moieties EVG and COBI. Accordingly, Tybost and Vitekta are entitled to the remaining 
NCE exclusivity protection awarded to Stribild, which is due to expire on August 27, 2017. 
C. FDA must withdraw "receipt" of any filed ANDAs 
As noted above, the FDCA prohibits FDA from "receiving" any ANDA application prior 
to the NCE-1 date; thus, no ANDA application referencing any of these Gilead products should 
have been received prior to August 27, 2016. Nonetheless, because NCE status had been 
initially denied, FDA received an ANDA with a Paragraph IV certification referencing Tybost in 
January 2016- over 8 months prematurely. Gilead was then forced to bring an infringement 
suit within 45 days of receiving notice of the ANDA filing in order to trigger a 30-month stay 
and prevent premature launch of generic product onto the market. 
Because none of these events should have occurred when then they did, FDA must 
withdraw receipt of the ANDA referencing Tybost and, along with it, the Paragraph IV 
certification. The ANDA filer would incur no harm, as it can refile its ANDA at any time now 
that the NCE-1 date has expired; and Gilead is not required to file suit to trigger the 30-month 
stay until the end of the five-year NCE exclusivity period. 
D. In the interest of fairness, FDA should make this determination promptly 
FD A's initial denial of NCE exclusivity, now held to be arbitrary and capricious, has 
caused Gilead to incur significant costs. Gilead is currently involved in what is now a premature 
ParagraRh IV litigation and could be facing generic competition 18 months earlier than it 
should. 8 Additionally, as this NCE debate ensues, potential ANDA applicants face uncertainty 
as to the exclusivity of Gilead drugs, and those involved in premature litigation are incurring 
unnecessary and wasteful expenditures. It is therefore in the best interest of the industry, as well 
as the public for FDA to make a swift determination and award NCE exclusivity nun pro tune for 
Stribild, along with "umbrella exclusivity" for Tybost and Vitekta.

CITIZEN PETITION 
Pfizer, Inc. ("Pfizer") submits this Citizen Petition pursuant to Section 505 of the Federal 
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act ("FDC Act"), among other provisions of law, and the Food 
and Drug Administration's ("FDA's") implementing regulations set forth at 21 CFR § 10.30. 
For the reasons discussed below, Pfizer respectfully requests that the Commissioner of Food 
and Drugs issue a product-specific bioequivalence (BE) guidance document applicable to any 
Abbreviated New Drug Application ("ANDA") for a generic version of Pfizer's Estring®  
(estradiol vaginal ring) in accordance with the conditions specified in this Citizen Petition 
and require any such ANDA applicant to establish BE for its generic product based on the 
conditions set forth in such guidance document. 
Estring®  is a complex controlled-release vaginal ring. It is approved to be inserted into the 
upper third of the vaginal vault and worn continuously for 3 months, and then, if continuation 
therapy is deemed appropriate, replaced by a new Estring®. There are a number of unique 
features of Estring®  which are essential to its safety and efficacy profile. In order to ensure 
that a proposed generic version of Estring®  matches this safety and efficacy profile, Pfizer 
believes that the standards proposed in this Citizen Petition are critically important and 
should be considered by the FDA in evaluating any ANDA that references Estring®  and 
purports to be therapeutically equivalent. 
1. ACTION REQUESTED 
a. Pfizer requests that the FDA issue a product-specific guidance document applicable to 
generic versions of Estring®  which requires the demonstration of BE in accordance with 
the following requirements: 
1. Demonstration of comparable in vitro release using a discriminating rate of 
release dissolution method capable of reliably detecting manufacturing 
differences over the characteristic release profile for this product 
2. Demonstration of BE with an appropriately designed pharmacokinetic (PK) 
endpoints study that assesses (a) the initial burst of plasma estradiol levels 
following insertion of the first ring with low levels of estradiol over the remainder 
of first 12-week treatment period; and (b) the smaller burst and large decrease in 
estradiol systemic exposure that occurs following insertion of the second ring 
3. Demonstration of BE with an appropriately designed clinical endpoints study that 
evaluates the efficacy and safety over 1 dosing cycle of 12 weeks 
4. Demonstration that the geometry, formulation, physical, and mechanical 
properties of the test product are equivalent to those of Estring®,  and if not, 
implementation of an appropriate vaginal safety study that identifies increased 
risk for vaginal safety events (irritation, ulceration, and infection) posed by 
differences 
b. Pfizer further requests that the FDA promulgate a draft guidance describing the BE 
standards for generic versions of Estring®  and allows sufficient time for public review 
and comment. 
c. Given that no product specific BE guidance currently exists for generic versions of 
Estring®, Pfizer also requests that FDA expedite the review of this petition to ensure that 
appropriate BE standards are published as soon as possible. 
2. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
BACKGROUND 
Estring®  (estradiol vaginal ring) was approved under New Drug Application (NDA) 20-472 
and is indicated for the treatment of moderate to severe symptoms of vulvar and vaginal 
atrophy due to menopause. Estring®  is a slightly opaque ring with a whitish core containing 
a drug reservoir of 2 mg of estradiol. Estradiol, silicone polymers, and barium sulfate are 
combined to form the ring. When placed in the vagina, Estring®  releases estradiol with an 
initial burst followed by a small and constant delivery of 7.5 fig per 24 hours over 90 days. 
Since the release rate of estradiol is mitigated by diffusion through a rate-controlling 
membrane, Estring®  can be categorized as a controlled-release product. 
The low and constant dose of estradiol delivered by the ring gives a rate of estradiol 
sufficient to ameliorate selected vaginal symptoms of estrogen deficiency without appearing

to cause systemic effects of proliferation of the endometrium.I  Estring®  has the following 
dimensions: outer diameter 55 mm; cross-sectional diameter 9 mm; core diameter 2 mm. 
One Estring®  should be inserted into the upper third of the vaginal vault, to be worn 
continuously for 3 months. 
Estradiol in Estring°  is absorbed and acts locally via estrogen receptors in the vaginal 
mucosa. Other approved products for local vaginal treatment of vulvar and vaginal atrophy 
include Vagifem, (estradiol vaginal tablets) and Estrace®  (estradiol vaginal cream). FDA 
has categorized locally acting products such as Estring®, Estrace®, and Vagifem,®  as 
"complex drug products," because challenges exist in demonstrating, BE.2  Althoufh the FDA 
has promulgated product-specific draft BE guidances for Vagifem® and Estrace®  , it has not 
done so for Estring®. Product-specific draft guidances for Estrace°  and Vagifem®  require, 
inter alia, a BE study with PK endpoints and a BE study with clinical endpoints.

intrauterine system),5  FDA issued a proposal in February 2015 to fund a dissolution study to 
evaluate physicochemical differences of long-acting levonorgestrel intrauterine systems

Like Mirena®,  Estring® is a complex locally acting controlled-release drug product that is 
formulated as a vaginal ring, and uses a highly specialized core and sheath design. Estradiol 
is evenly dispersed in the core polymer in a manner such that it is not release rate limiting 
and results in an even dissolution of the drug particles. The core serves as the drug reservoir. 
The surrounding polymer, or sheath, is rate-controlling and the release is affected by both 
formulation and process variables. 
Because of the formulation and manufacturing complexity, the development of a generic 
product should be guided by the Quality by Design (QbD) principles outlined in ICH Q8 
(R2). The input variables for the study should include, but not be limited to, estradiol size, 
shape, and surface area; polymer type, grade and purity; and other excipient characteristics. 
The process parameters to study must include those inherent in polymer extrusion, 
environmental variables, and intermediate and product hold times. 
There are multiple Critical Quality Attributes (CQA) for Estring®; however, the most 
important relative to safety and efficacy is the rate at which estradiol is released from the 
product, which is measured by dissolution testing. It is important to use the ongoing release 
rate (µ,g/time) as the in vitro performance metric for this CQA and not cumulative percent 
released commonly used for other dosage forms. Cumulative percent released has the 
disadvantage of decreasing sensitivity over long times. Small changes later in the profile are 
not easily identified against a large cumulative background. 
The release rate of Estring®  is biphasic in nature with an initial burst of estradiol followed by 
a steady-state release phase as shown in Figure 1. The burst phase is inherent in the product 
design. Because this in vitro phenomenon is mirrored in vivo, it is especially important to 
evaluate both the initial burst and the steady-state component (release of 7.5 1.1g/24 hours). 
Each release phase should be considered separately and its design space defined and 
understood. 
The FDA should require a demonstration of similarity in estradiol release compared to 
Estring®  as a component of the ANDA submission. For each of the 2 phases, profiles should 
be compared using at least 3 time points for each phase, to encompass the initial burst and the 
steady-state release phase of the product. Additionally, since comparisons should be made 
using release rates and not cumulative percent released, a conventional f2 similarity statistic 
may not be appropriate. Therefore, either an alternate model-independent method, or a

Appropriately Designed BE Study With PK End Points 
FDA has required that generic versions of Vagifem®  and  Estrace®  implement a BE stud

In the case of Estring®, estrogen released from the ring acts locally in order to cause the 
desired changes to the vaginal epithelium. Much of that estrogen would act and would be 
metabolized locally and would never enter the systemic circulation. However, some estrogen 
will enter vaginal blood vessels and will be detectable as circulating estradiol. The amounts 
of estrogen that enter the general circulation will determine the woman's systemic exposure 
to estrogen, and hence, will have a bearing on the woman's risk for adverse events that are 
associated with systemic exposure to estrogen.

A generic product should be required to demonstrate equivalent estradiol PK profiles to 
Estring®  for both the first ring (over a 12-week treatment period) and for the second ring (for 
at least the first 4 weeks of the second 12-week treatment period) because a) the estradiol PK 
profiles for Estring are significantly different between the first ring and the second ring; and 
(b) the extent to which a woman is systemically exposed to estrogen affects her risk for 
potentially serious adverse events. Comparable PK should include demonstration of the 
same rate of release as Estring®  (0.80 mg during the first 12-week application period and 
0.35 mg during the second 4-week application period) and the same PK characteristics as 
Estring®  (initial burst of estradiol plasma levels followed by a rapid decline over the next 
24 hours and gradual decline thereafter after administration of a first ring; and a large 
decrease in systemic exposure after administration of a second ring). 
Accordingly, to establish comparable safety and efficacy, a repeat dose BE study with PK 
endpoints should be implemented in which test product and RLD are administered twice. 
The first estradiol ring should be used continuously over 12 weeks, followed by the second 
ring for at least the first 4 weeks. Plasma estradiol levels should be measured for 12 weeks 
following Dose 1 and for at least 4 weeks following Dose 2 using an analytical method with 
a lower limit of quantitation of at least 2 pg/mL. The study population should be healthy 
postmenopausal women with no contraindication to estrogen therapy. BE should be based 
upon the achievement of 90% confidence interval of PK endpoints derived from plasma 
estradiol concentration-time profile for both Dose 1 and Dose 2 with and without baseline 
adjustments.

3. Demonstration of Comparable Efficacy and Safety in Treating Local Symptoms 
Through a BE Study With Clinical Endpoints 
Estring®, Vagifem®, and Estrace®  are complex drugs because the mechanism of action of 
these vaginally administered estrogen products are local through the direct interaction of the 
estradiol administered to the target tissues of the lower genitor-urinary tract where receptors 
are located and respond to estrogen therapy. Since their efficacy is not necessarily related to 
the extent to which estradiol is systemically absorbed (i.e., efficacy is not directly related to 
the PK profile), a generic estradiol ring would need to demonstrate equivalent efficacy and 
similar safety to that of Estring®  by means of appropriately designed clinical trials. 
Therefore, to establish comparable safety and efficacy, a 12-week BE study with clinical 
endpoints should be implemented in which the test product and Estring®  are directly 
compared to placebo and to each other. The study should be a randomized, double-blind, 
placebo-controlled trial in healthy postmenopausal women with symptoms of vulvar and 
vaginal atrophy and no contraindication to estrogen therapy as described in the draft 
guidances for Vagifem®  and Estrace®. 
4. Demonstration of Equivalent Geometry, Formulation, Physical and Mechanical 
Properties 
The geometry, formulation, physical and mechanical aspects together help define the overall 
Estring®  infra-vaginal system. Differences may impact the safe and effective use of a 
proposed generic version. In particular, these factors could influence the local vaginal 
safety/tolerability of the ring over time (e.g., ring expulsion, irritation or ulceration of the 
vaginal wall, etc.). The risks for these adverse events were demonstrated for Estring®  in 
Phase 3 clinical studies that provided 48-week clinical data. 
As noted above, Estring®  has the following dimensions: outer diameter 55 mm; 
cross-sectional diameter 9 mm; core diameter 2 mm. The product is intended to be worn 
continuously for 90 days. A generic ring should have identical dimensions; if different 
dimensions were to be used, then an appropriate vaginal safety study should be required. 
The silicon elastomer type and grade, as well as other excipients used in Estring were 
carefully chosen for their bio-compatibility. Differences may influence the local safety of the 
product. As with geometry, deviations from the Estring®  formulation should necessitate a 
safety study to prove the same bio-compatibility. 
Finally, while a ring may have identical geometry and composition (qualitative and 
quantitative), even small differences in the manufacturing process for a polymer product 
(e.g., time and temperature) can significantly alter the physical and mechanical properties of 
the polymer. These aspects can significantly impact how the ring interacts with the vaginal 
tissue over time. Accordingly, in order to insure equivalent vaginal safety and tolerability, 
Pfizer urges the FDA to require equivalent physical and mechanical properties between the 
proposed generic product and Estring®. Properties to consider include surface roughness, 
percent crystallinity, elastic modulus, and hardness.

In addition, the device components should be tested according to FDA's draft guidance "Use 
of International Standard ISO-10993, Biological Evaluation of Medical Devices Part 1 
Evaluation and Testing" (23 April 2013). The results for all components should be 
comparable to those of Estring®. 
b. FDA Should Promulgate a Product-Specific Guidance for Estring®. 
As noted above, Vagifem®, Estrace®, and Estring®  are examples of complex drug products 
because they are locally acting and not dependent on systemic absorption for efficacy. 
However, unlike Vagifem®  and Estrace®, which are complex immediate-release products, 
Estring®  is a complex controlled-release product intended to remain in situ for 90 days. 
While the FDA has issued product-specific BE guidances for Vagifem®  and Estrace , no 
such product-specific BE guidance has been promulgated by the agency for Estring®. 
Pfizer therefore urges the FDA to issue a draft guidance describing the BE standards for 
generic versions of Estring®  incorporating the recommendations as described above, and in 
addition, allow sufficient time for review and comment before approving any ANDA 
referencing Estring®. 
c. Conclusion 
Estring®  (estradiol vaginal ring) is a complex controlled-release vaginal ring administered 
every 90 days and approved for long-term use. Its safety and efficacy depend upon multiple 
factors. As described in this Citizen Petition, FDA should require any ANDA applicants 
seeking approval to market a generic version of Estring®  to conduct both a BE study with PK 
endpoints and a BE study with clinical endpoints. PK endpoint studies and clinical endpoint 
studies are required for approval of generic versions of both Vagifem®  and Estrace®, two 
local vaginal estrogen therapies initiated daily according to dosing directions in the labels, 
rather than once every 90 days as with Estring®.  In addition, demonstration of comparable in 
vitro rate of estradiol release using a dissolution method that can detect manufacturing 
differences and demonstration of vaginal ring component similarity should also be required 
of any ANDA referencing Estring®. 
Pfizer also urges the FDA to promulgate a draft product-specific BE guidance for proposed 
generic versions of Estring®  and allow sufficient time for public review and comment on 
such guidance. Further, any ANDA referencing Estring®  as the RLD should be required to 
demonstrate BE for its product in accordance with such guidance. Pfizer also requests that 
FDA expedite the review of this petition to ensure that appropriate BE standards for generic 
versions of Estring are published as soon as possible.

CITIZEN PETITION  
The undersigned submits this petition under the Federal Food Drug, and Cosmetic Act 
and in accordance with 21 C.F.R. §§ 10.25(a) and 10.30 to request that the Commissioner of 
Food and Drugs deny approval to any abbreviated new drug application (ANDA) for a sucralfate 
oral suspension drug product that relies on patient-based clinical endpoint studies to establish 
bioequivalence (BE) with Carafate (sucralfate) oral suspension, the reference listed drug (RLD).  
For locally-acting sucralfate, such clinical endpoint studies are inadequate to establish BE. 
A. 
Action Requested 
The undersigned requests that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) deny approval to 
any ANDA for a sucralfate oral suspension drug product that relies on patient-based clinical 
endpoint studies to establish BE with the RLD.   
B. 
Statement of Grounds 
ANDAs are required to include evidence or information to allow FDA to determine that 
the drug product in the application is bioequivalent to the RLD.  21 C.F.R. § 320.21.  Section 
320.24(b) lists appropriate methods for determining BE, in descending order of accuracy, 
sensitivity, and reproducibility: 
 In-vivo concentration of active moiety in human biological fluid; 
 In-vitro test that has been correlated with and is predictive of human 
bioavailability data; 
 In-vivo evaluation based on urinary excretion; 
 In-vivo measurement of an acute pharmacological effect; 
 Well-controlled clinical trials that establish the safety and effectiveness of 
the drug product; 
 
 
 
 A currently available in vitro test (e.g., dissolution rate test) acceptable to 
FDA; and  
 Any other approach FDA deems adequate. 
21 C.F.R. § 320.24(b).  BE testing should be done using the most accurate, sensitive, and 
reproducible approach available among those listed, and the method must be capable of 
establishing BE.  21 C.F.R. § 320.24(a).  When the drug product in the application acts locally 
and is not intended to be absorbed systemically, the applicant may demonstrate BE “by 
scientifically valid methods that are expected to detect a significant difference between the drug 
and the listed drug in safety and therapeutic effect.”  21 C.F.R. § 320.23.   
Unlike systemically acting drugs, for which plasma concentrations can be compared to 
establish BE, sucralfate acts locally and has no measurable plasma concentrations.  Thus, FDA 
had previously advised using clinical endpoint studies as a basis to establish BE for sucralfate 
oral suspension drug products in its July 2014 Draft Guidance.1  The clinical endpoint method in 
that guidance involved a comparative efficacy trial, in which the RLD and the proposed generic 
product were each tested against a placebo.2  A little over a year later, however, in December 
2015, FDA withdrew that guidance,3 presumably because that clinical endpoint method was 
inadequate to establish BE for sucralfate oral suspension products.  As FDA has explained 
previously, the clinical endpoint method “is the least accurate, sensitive, and reproducible of the 
general approaches for measuring bioavailability or demonstrating bioequivalence.”  21 C.F.R. § 
320.24(b)(4).  Thus, ANDAs relying on clinical endpoint studies as recommended by the July 
2014 Draft Guidance to establish BE are relying on a withdrawn FDA standard and should be 
denied for that reason alone. 
In October 2017, FDA published a revised Draft Guidance for sucralfate suspension.4  
The revised guidance relies on in vitro testing of the API, formulation and bioassays to 
demonstrate equivalence for sucralfate oral suspension products.5  The combination of 
withdrawing the guidance that relied on clinical endpoints and promulgating a revised guidance 
that relies on in vitro testing points to FDA’s awareness of the inherent variability and 
unreliability of clinical endpoint studies in establishing BE for sucralfate oral suspension 
products.  This recognition by FDA is scientifically sound; clinical efficacy is not accurately 
quantifiable and therefore, determining product equivalence using clinical endpoints is

More specifically, any primary endpoint in clinical testing of sucralfate oral suspension is 
the proportion of patients who experience ulcer healing after a certain period of treatment, which 
is a binary outcome—either healed or not healed.8  But such a binary outcome cannot account for 
variations in ulcer size and severity at the outset of the trial, which are qualitative measures that 
affect the rate of healing. 9  Because ulcers of varying size and severity heal at different rates, BE 
cannot be effectively established by comparing quantities of patients whose ulcers have healed 
following treatment with sucralfate vs. placebo.10  Thus, a generic product attempting to establish 
BE by this method could actually vary significantly in efficacy from the RLD while still 
producing equivalent rates of ulcer healing, so the method cannot be expected to detect a 
significant difference between the generic product and the RLD.11  Clinical endpoint studies to 
establish BE are generally not sufficient to ensure that a generic sucralfate oral suspension 
product is equivalent to the RLD. 
The undersigned hereby requests that FDA deny approval to any ANDA for a sucralfate 
oral suspension drug product that relies on patient-based studies to establish BE with the RLD, 
including the July 2014 Draft Guidance, because such clinical endpoint studies cannot reliably 
detect a significant difference between the ANDA drug product and the RLD.

Petition_Title: Citizen Petition from Petitioner  Redacted
Petition_Text:
DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES 
FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION 
Matter: Docket No. FDA 2015-E-2724  
 
Docket No. FDA 2013-S-0610 
Determination of Regulatory Review Period for Purposes of a Patent Extension  
for Drug CERDEGLA 
THE UNDERSIGNED SUBMITS THIS PETITION UNDER 35 U.S.C. 156 TO REQUEST 
THE COMMISSIONER OF FOOD AND DRUGS ADMINISTRATION CONDUCT A DUE 
DILIGENCE INVESTIGATION INTO GENZYME AND TO RECOMMEND THAT 
GENZYME’S PATENT TERM EXTENSION APPLICATION BE DENIED OR LIMITED.   
PETITION FOR DETERMINATION OF DUE DILIGENCE and REQUEST THAT FDA 
DETERMINE THAT THE PATENT IS NOT ELIGIBLE FOR PATENT TERM 
EXTENSION OR RESTORATION 
 
I. ACTION REQUESTED COMES NOW a concerned citizen, and pursuant to 35 
U.S.C. 156 requests 1) FDA conduct an investigation into the due diligence of applicant 
Genzyme regarding the drug marketed under the name Cerdelga; 2) FDA determine Genzyme 
failed to act with due diligence during all or part of the period between April 2002 and the 
approval date; 3) FDA determine Genzyme is not eligible for the entire period of patent 
extension or restoration as requested by Genzyme; 4) FDA recommend to the Patent and 
Trademark Office that Genzyme’s patent extension request by denied, rejected, and/or limited.    
 
Applicant Genzyme seeks a patent application for a drug it markets under the name 
Cerdelga.  The extension should not be granted for the following reasons: 1) Genzyme failed to 
act with due diligence; 2) an extension would not fulfill the spirit or purpose of the Drug 
Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act of 1984 (hereinafter “Patent Term Restoration 
Act”); 3) the extension would be contrary to the public interest and would unfairly and 
unnecessarily cost taxpayers and private insurers a significant amount. 
!1
 
Granting the requested extension to Genzyme would not actually reward the scientists 
who developed Cerdelga.  It will not encourage more scientific endeavors and will not result in 
any benefit to the people who put in the hardest work to create Cerdelga.  Instead, an extension 
would only encourage and reward rapacious corporate greed and would only reward the 
elevation of profit over the public interest.  An extension would force patients to wait more than 
five more years for a generic version of a drug for which Genzyme charges over $300,000 per 
year.  An extension would allow Genzyme to keep lining its own pockets with the fruits of 
publicly-funded research.  An extension would wealthy shareholders to continue making money 
off of other people’s misfortune.  An extension would grant Genzyme another four years of free 
reign to gouge insurers, patients, and governments to the tune of $300,000 per year, per 
patient.  
 
Cerdelga’s patent, without the requested extension, will expire in 2022.  By that time, 
Genzyme will have had three decades’ worth of access to a market without generic 
competition.  Thirty years of charging patients $300,000 per year is enough.  Genzyme’s 
gravy train simply has to stop somewhere, and it must stop here.  
 
If the USPTO grants Genzyme’s requested extension, patients would not have access to a 
generic version of a $300,000 per-year drug until 2026.  If the USPTO rejects the extension, as it 
should, patients could have access to a generic version of a $300,000 per-year drug as soon as 
2022.  
 
The writer of this Petition is an individual who currently takes Cerdelga.  The writer 
formerly took Cerezyme from 1994 to 2014 and received Ceredase prior to that.  This writer has 
!2
lived nearly their entire life under the shadow of a $300,000 per year price tag and wonders 
every day whether their life is worth it.  
2. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
RELEVANT FACTS 
General Information Regarding Genzyme, Cerdelga, and Gaucher’s Disease 
1.
Cerdelga treats a very rare genetic disorder called Gaucher’s disease. 
2.
Cerdelga is a pill—a capsule taken by mouth once or twice a day. 
3.
Most other treatments for Gaucher’s which are currently on the market are biologics, 
manufactured with recombinant DNA.  These must be injected over the course of a several-
hours infusion. Infusions are typically given once every two weeks. 
4.
There is one other oral treatment for Gaucher’s, called Zavesca, but because of severe side 
effects, it is only prescribed if the patient cannot tolerate all other treatments.  
5.
Current figures estimate the number of Gaucher’s patients at 10,000 worldwide (https://
www.ijpr.in/Data/Archives/2014/february/1712201302.pdf).  
6.
People with the Gaucher disorder lack the ability to produce a particular enzyme called 
glucocerebrosidase.  The lack of this enzyme arises from genetic mutations—the mutations 
prevent the body from producing the enzyme.   
7.
Genzyme manufactures and markets Cerdelga, although it does so under a licensing 
agreement with the University of Michigan (see articles/press releases “FDA approves U-M 
invented drug for Gaucher disease” and “FDA okays Genzyme pill for Gaucher disease” and 
“Drug Cerdelga Treats Gaucher in Lieu of Infusion Treatment,” attached here as Exhibits A, 
B, and C, respectively).  
!3
8.
Cerdelga is a “small molecule” drug, rather than a “biologic” (see article “Cerdelga, 25 years 
in the making” from biotechprimer.com, attached here as Exhibit D). Cerdelga is not 
manufactured through recombinant DNA technology. 
9.
The fact that Cerdelga is a “small molecule” drug, rather than a “biologic,” makes Cerdelga 
ideal for generic production.   
10. Because Gaucher’s disease is a genetic condition, it cannot be “cured.”  Rather, it is a 
chronic illness which requires continued and ongoing treatment. 
11. Gaucher’s patients thus face decades of ongoing treatment. 
Costs and Finances 
12. Genzyme charges $310,250 per year, per patient, for Cerdelga (see article “New Genzyme 
pill to treat rare Gaucher disease will cost US patients $310,250 a year,” Boston Globe, 
September 2, 2014, attached as Exhibit E).  
13. However, a Genzyme representative “acknowledged the manufacturing cost of the Cerdelga 
pill is less than that of biotech drugs such as Cerezyme.”  Id. 
14. Cerezyme is Genzyme’s infusion-based Gaucher’s treatment, and in 2006, the Wall Street 
Journal reported Cerezyme cost 37 cents per unit to manufacture, against a sales price of 
$3.70 per unit. See “Why Genzyme Can Charge So Much for Cerezyme,” by Geeta Anand, 
Wall Street Journal November 16, 2005, attached here as Exhibit F. 
15. Cerezyme typically cost patients/insurers around $300,000 per year. See “When a Drug 
Costs $300,000,” New York Times Editorial, March 23, 2008, attached as Exhibit G.  
!4
16. Using the information above, one can calculate the production-cost-to-sales-price ratio of 
Cerdelga.  Cerezyme had a 1:10 ratio of production costs to sales price.  Thus, Genzyme’s of 
production for Cerdelga is less than 10% of the price Genzyme sells it for. 
17. Lest FDA think that $310,250 is merely the starting point for negotiation, attached as Exhibit 
H are some of this writer’s Explanation of Benefits forms, describing what the writer’s 
insurer paid for Cerdelga.  This writer’s insurer pays $23,647.68 for a 28-day supply of 
Cerdelga, which equates to $307,424 per year.  
18. Furthermore, the drug data produced by the Centers for Medicare Services, available at 
https://www.cms.gov/Research-Statistics-Data-and-Systems/Statistics-Trends-and-Reports/
Information-on-Prescription-Drugs/2015Medicare.html, shows Medicare and Medicaid do, 
indeed, pay the sticker price for Genzyme’s products.  
19. Because Gaucher’s patients must take management drugs for their entire lives,  Genzyme 
stands to make millions of dollars, even tens of millions of dollars, of profit from the lifetime 
treatment of a single patient.  
20. Genzyme is a subsidiary/division of the Sanofi corporation.  
21. Sanofi’s publicly-available 2014 Annual Report indicated that in 2013, Sanofi as a whole 
spent 4.905 billion Euros on research and development compared with 20.989 billion Euros 
in “gross profit.” 
22. The 2014 Annual Report also indicates that Sanofi-Genzyme took in revenue of 715 million 
Euros from sales of Cerezyme, with 186 million Euros coming from Cerezyme sales in just 
the United States. 
!5
23. Sanofi’s publicly-available 2015 Annual Report indicates that in 2014, Sanofi spent 
approximately 5 billion Euros on research and development against 21.769 billion Euros in 
“gross profit.” 
24. The 2015 Annual Report also indicates that Sanofi-Genzyme took in revenue of  757 million 
Euros from Cerezyme and 66 million Euros from Cerdelga, which had just been introduced 
into the market in autumn 2014.  
25. Genzyme claims to have charitable access programs, including in countries which do not 
have developed medical delivery systems.  However, a 2009 Boston Globe article, attached 
here as Exhibit I, reports Genzyme regularly demands countries pay the full sticker price and 
regularly pressures countries to do so.  
Genzyme’s History of FDA-Approved Treatments for Gaucher’s  
26. Prior to Cerdelga, Genzyme received FDA approval for two other drugs to treat Gaucher’s 
disease. 
27. The first was called Ceredase and was approved in 1992.  
28. Ceredase was a biologic drug formulation which was manufactured directly from human 
placenta material; Genzyme gathered literally hundreds of tons of placenta and purified it for 
infusion into patients (see “Imiglucerase in the treatment of Gaucher disease: history and 
perspective,” by Patrick Deegan and Timothy Cox, in Drug Design, Deveopment, and 
Therapy, 17 April 2012).  
29. For Ceredase, Genzyme charged an average of $300,000, with exact figures based on the 
weight of the patient being treated (see “Orphan Drug Bounty Comes at a Steep Price,” by 
!6
Sarah Jane Tribble and Sydney Lupkin, National Public Radio, January 17, 2017, attached 
here as Exhibit J).  
30. However, it is generally accepted in the Gaucher history, Gaucher community, and scientific 
literature that Genzyme did not invent or develop Ceredase (see “Imiglucerase in the 
treatment of Gaucher disease: history and perspective,” by Patrick Deegan and Timothy Cox, 
in Drug Design, Deveopment, and Therapy, 17 April 2012, attached as Exhibit K).  
31. Rather, it is generally accepted in the Gaucher history, Gaucher community, and scientific 
literature that scientists working at the National Institutes of Health, particularly Dr. Roscoe 
Brady, developed and invented Ceredase (see “Imiglucerase in the treatment of Gaucher 
disease: history and perspective,” by Patrick Deegan and Timothy Cox, in Drug Design, 
Deveopment, and Therapy, 17 April 2012, attached as Exhibit K).  
32. Genzyme’s pricing of Ceredase attracted attention from the Congressional Office of 
Technology Assessment.  That study found Genzyme had only invested approximately $29.4 
million in the development of Ceredase, which it quickly recovered (“Orphan Drug Bounty 
Comes at a Steep Price,” by Sarah Jane Tribble and Sydney Lupkin, National Public Radio, 
January 17, 2017, attached here as Exhibit J). 
33. Representative Henry Waxman, who actually sponsored the Patent Term Restoration Act in 
1984 and who also sponsored and developed the Orphan Drug Act, said of Ceredase: “The 
prices charged are beyond anything that Congress imagined when the act was passed in 
1983…It is hard to believe that companies need the advantages of the Orphan Drug Act for 
drugs that cost tens or even hundreds of thousands of dollars a year” (see “The High Cost of 
!7
Rare Diseases: When Patients Can’t Afford to Buy Lifesaving Drugs,” by Larry Thompson, 
Washington Post, June 25, 1991, attached here as Exhibit L).  
34. In 1994, Genzyme received FDA approval for a second-generation drug, called Cerezyme 
(see FDA approval attached here as Exhibit M). 
35. Cerezyme relied on recombinant DNA technology to manufacture Cerezyme. The gene 
which “codes” for the glucocerebrisidase enzyme was isolated and transferred into a host 
organism.  The organism then grew in bioreactor tanks, producing enzyme for collection (see 
generally, “Imiglucerase in the treatment of Gaucher disease: history and perspective,” by 
Patrick Deegan and Timothy Cox, in Drug Design, Deveopment, and Therapy, 17 April 
2012, attached as Exhibit K).  
36. Genzyme charged approximately $300,000 per year, per patient, for Cerezyme (see articles 
attached here, including “When a Drug Costs $300,000,” New York Times Editorial, March 
23, 2008, attached as Exhibit G).   
37. Since 1994, Genzyme has never lowered the price it charges for Cerezyme. 
38. In November 2005, the Wall Street Journal asked why Genzyme could charge so much for 
Cerezyme, and the Wall Street Journal answered “because it can.”  See “Why Genzyme Can 
Charge So Much for Cerezyme,” by Geeta Anand, Wall Street Journal November 16, 2005, 
attached as Exhibit F. 
39. That article also noted Cerezyme cost 37 cents per unit to manufacture, while Genzyme sold 
it for $3.70 per unit. That means Genzyme had a 90% profit margin. 
40. In 2008 and 2009, Genzyme allowed two serious contaminations to occur in the bioreaction 
tanks which produced Cerezyme.  The first was a viral contamination, and then Genzyme 
!8
found “bits of steel, rubber and fiber” in the drugs.  This led to shortages of Cerezyme, 
rationing, and discipline by the FDA (see, e.g. “More Contamination Troubles for 
Genzyme,” by Robert Weisman, Boston Globe, November 4, 2009, attached as Exhibit N).   
41. The patents on Cerezyme expired on May 23, 2014.  
42. Not coincidentally, Petitioner asserts, Genzyme submitted Cerdelga for FDA approval on 
September 20, 2013. 
Development of Cerdelga—UM Discovers It 
43. Various public statements, press releases, and other admissions by Genzyme confirm that 
Cerdelga was developed in part or in whole by James Shayman while Shayman was an 
employee of the University of Michigan.  See “FDA approves U-M invented drug for 
Gaucher disease” and “FDA okays Genzyme pill for Gaucher disease” and “Drug Cerdelga 
Treats Gaucher in Lieu of Infusion Treatment,” attached here as Exhibits A, B, and C, 
respectively). 
44. Specifically, Cerdelga began as a molecule licensed by the University of Michigan to 
Genzyme in 2000.  The article “FDA approves U-M invented drug for Gaucher 
disease” (attached as Exhibit A) states, “Patents covering these compounds and related 
inventions were licensed to Genzyme, a Sanofi company, in 2000 for clinical development.”  
The article “U-Michigan signs royalty agreement for Gaucher disease drug,” attached here as 
Exhibit O, likewise states, “The drug was developed by Dr. James Shayman, also of U-M, 
prior to and after licensing the compound to Genzyme, a Sanofi company, in 2000.” 
45. The majority of research and development for Cerdelga occurred not at Genzyme, and not by

47. Prior to 2000, Shayman’s lab at the University of Michigan had already developed and

48. Shayman described the work performed after Genzyme came on the scene as “dumbing
