Petition_Title: Citizen Petition from RiceBran Technologies
Petition_Text:
CITIZEN PETITION 
Docket No. FDA-2016-N-3389 for “Evaluation of the Beneficial Physiological Effects of Isolated 
or Synthetic Non-Digestible Carbohydrates; Request for Scientific Data, Information, and 
Comments.” 
February 12, 2017 
 
Division of Dockets Management 
Food and Drug Administration 
5630 Fishers Lane 
Room 1061, HFA-305 
Rockville, MD 20852 
 
Re: 
A Citizen Petition Requesting that FDA Amend 21 C.F.R. § 101.9(c)(6)(i) to Recognize Rice 
Bran Derivative Products That Contain Rice Bran Fiber and Other Components of Rice 
Bran as Containing Dietary Fiber for Purposes of Nutrition Labeling Fiber and products 
derived from Rice Bran that contain Rice Bran Fiber and Other Components of Rice Bran 
as containing Dietary Fiber for Purposes of Nutrition Labeling 
 
Dear Commissioner: 
 
 
The undersigned, RiceBran Technologies, respectfully submits this Citizen Petition under 
the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the Food and Drug Administration’s (“FDA’s” or 
“the Agency’s”) implementing regulation at 21 C.F.R. § 10.30 to request that the Commissioner 
of Food and Drugs amend 21 C.F.R. § 101.9(c)(6)(i) to include products derived from rice bran 
that contain rice bran fiber in the definition of dietary fiber set forth in that regulation. 
 
I. 
Action Requested 
 
 
As demonstrated in this Petition, rice bran fiber has a number of physiological health 
benefits, including improved laxation/bowel function, reduced blood cholesterol levels, and 
attenuated postprandial blood glucose levels. FDA has recognized these physiological effects to 
be beneficial to human health. If an isolated or synthetic non-digestible carbohydrate (with 3 or 
more monomeric units) has one or more of these effects, it meets the definition of dietary fiber 
under 21 C.F.R. § 101.9(c)(6)(i). Rice bran fiber meets this definition of dietary fiber. 
 
 
On May 27, 2016, FDA published the final rule revising the Agency’s nutrition labeling 
regulations. For purposes of nutrition labeling, FDA defined dietary fiber as: 
 
(1) Non-digestible soluble and insoluble carbohydrates (with 3 or more monomeric units) 
and lignin that are intrinsic and intact in plants; 
(2) Isolated or synthetic non-digestible carbohydrates (with 3 or more monomeric units) 
determined by FDA to have physiological effects that are beneficial to human health. 
 
81 Fed. Reg. 33,742 (May 27, 2016); 21 C.F.R. § 101.9(c)(6)(i). The regulation further states: 
 
The following isolated or synthetic non-digestible carbohydrate(s) have been 
determined by FDA to have physiological effects that are beneficial to human health 
and, therefore, shall be included in the calculation of the amount of dietary fiber: [beta]-
glucan soluble fiber (as described in § 101.81(c)(2)(ii)(A)), psyllium husk (as described in 
§ 101.81(c)(2)(ii)(A)(6)), cellulose, guar gum, pectin, locust bean gum, and 
hydroxypropylmethylcellulose. 
 
In light of the evidence of the physiological health benefits of rice bran fiber, Rice Bran 
Technologies requests that FDA amend the above-quoted sentence in the regulation by adding 
“rice bran derivatives containing rice bran fiber,” such that the sentence would read as follows: 
 
The following isolated or synthetic non-digestible carbohydrate(s) have been 
determined by FDA to have physiological effects that are beneficial to human health 
and, therefore, shall be included in the calculation of the amount of dietary fiber: [beta]-
glucan soluble fiber (as described in § 101.81(c)(2)(ii)(A)), psyllium husk (as described in 
§ 101.81(c)(2)(ii)(A)(6)), cellulose, guar gum, pectin, locust bean gum, 
hydroxypropylmethylcellulose, and rice bran derivatives containing rice bran fiber. 
 
II.  
Statement of Grounds 
 
 
For more than 10 years RiceBran Technologies has been the expert in processing and 
distribution of stabilized rice bran and products derived from rice bran.  Using ingredients and 
processing aids occurring naturally in food, RiceBran Technologies creates rice bran derivative 
products by removing some of the water-soluble contents, concentrating the water-soluble 
fractions removed and concentrating the remaining fraction to create functional ingredients for 
the food industry.   
 
A.  
Description of Rice Bran Derivatives containing Rice Bran Fiber 
 
 
Rice bran is comprised of the pericarp, seed coat, aleuronic layer, germ and a small 
portion of the starchy endosperm.  Nutrients in rice bran include soluble and insoluble 
carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals and other micronutrients.  Using proprietary 
methods, RiceBran Technologies creates ingredients that contain concentrated proportions of 
the insoluble carbohydrates, proteins, fats and micronutrients naturally occurring in rice bran.  
Insoluble carbohydrates in rice bran include hemicellulose, cellulose, pectin and lignin.   
 
B.  
Scientific Evidence of Physiological Health Benefits of Rice Bran Derivatives Containing 
Rice Bran Fiber 
 
 
This Petition is based on all relevant research on rice bran fiber identified in a search of 
the published scientific literature, supplemented by unpublished information. 
 
 
The studies were reviewed in accordance with generally accepted methods for 
reviewing scientific research in nutrition, and consistent with FDA’s November 22, 2016 Draft 
Guidance “Scientific Evaluation of the Evidence on the Beneficial Physiological Effects of Isolated 
or Synthetic Non-digestible Carbohydrates Submitted as a Citizen Petition (21 CFR 10.30): 
Guidance for Industry, ( and FDA’s Guidance for Industry: Evidence-Based Review System for the 
Scientific Evaluation of Health Claims, Jan. 2009, 
http://www.fda.gov/RegulatoryInformation/Guidances/ucm073332.htm#system. This Petition 
considered studies of high and moderate quality only. For each physiological health benefit, the 
specific inclusion and exclusion criteria used to select appropriate studies are identified. 
 
 
The strength of the totality of pertinent scientific evidence substantiates the conclusion 
that rice bran fiber has a number of physiological effects beneficial to human health, including 
improved laxation/bowel function, reduced blood cholesterol levels, and attenuated 
postprandial glucose levels/glycemic response. As acknowledged by FDA, any one of these 
beneficial physiological effects is sufficient to warrant the conclusion that rice bran derivatives 
containing rice bran fiber (RBD-F) meet the definition of dietary fiber and, therefore, warrant 
inclusion in 21 C.F.R. § 101.9(c)(6)(i) (Memorandum 137 at 2). 
 
1. Improved Laxation/Bowel Function: 
 
 
FDA identified improved laxation/bowel function as a physiological effect beneficial to 
human health (81 Fed. Reg. at 33,856; see also Memorandum 137 at 3). Moreover, FDA has 
identified increased stool frequency and reduced intestinal transit time as biomarkers for 
improved laxation/bowel function (81 Fed. Reg. at 33,858; Memorandum 137 at 3). 
 
 
The totality of the pertinent scientific evidence establishes that rice bran fiber increases 
stool frequency. 
 
a. 
Mechanism of action 
 
 
 
As mentioned above, rice bran fiber consists of non-digestible carbohydrates, fully 
fermentable, composed of hemicellulose, cellulose, pectin and lignin.  Rice bran hemicellulose 
is composed of arabinoxylan. The β(1-4) glycosidic bonds of cellulose and arabinoxylan, rice 
bran fiber resist hydrolysis and absorption in the human small intestine and reach the large 
intestine essentially complete. There they are selectively fermented to short-chain fatty acids, 
lactate and gases by colonic bacteria. This is accompanied by an increase in bacterial cell mass 
and a higher water content of digesta. Consequently, rice bran fiber lead to softer stools and 
facilitate excretion, and also lead to improved gastrointestinal regularity. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
b. 
Summary of evidence 
 
Methodology 
 
 
Human intervention studies on the effect of rice bran fiber on laxation/bowel function 
were identified and evaluated. Appropriate high and medium quality research studies were 
identified using the following criteria: 
 
Inclusion criteria 
 Primary data on Stool Frequency (SF) and/or Transit Time (TT); Oral-cecal transit time 
was not considered appropriate for investigating laxation/bowel function. 
 Appropriate control group 
 Statistical comparison with control 
 Subjects are part of the healthy general population including individuals at risk;  
 Studies of high and medium quality using FDA’s ranking criteria. 
 
Exclusion Criteria 
 Subjects with a disease relevant for the health benefit endpoint 
 No assessment of SF and/or TT 
 Low quality study ranking using FDA’s ranking criteria 
 No adequate placebo/control 
 Acute study with single or two-time intake of study products only 
 No adequate measurement of SF (via questionnaire or visual analogue scale only, no 
documentation of effective bowel movements) 
 No adequate measurement of TT; oro-cecal transit only and not oro-fecal transit  
 No primary data reported 
 Subjects with abnormal gastrointestinal tract function 
 Enema and/or laxation administration 
 
Appendix A contains laboratory reports demonstrating relative analyzed nutrient contents 
of stabilized rice bran and RiceBran Technologies rice bran derivative product. 
 
Appendix B lists the references for studies that were included in the analysis. 
 
Human intervention Studies 
 
 
High and medium quality studies establish that rice bran fiber increase stool frequency 
and reduce transit time.  
 
 
c. 
Conclusion: rice bran fiber improves laxation/bowel functions 
 
 All of the studies point in the same favorable direction 
 No studies show a contradictory effect 
 
 
Thus, the totality of pertinent scientific evidence shows that rice bran fiber significantly 
improve laxation/bowel function in human subjects as measured by an increased stool 
frequency and a reduced transit time. 
 
 
 
 
2. 
Blood Cholesterol: Rice Bran Fiber Reduces Blood Cholesterol Levels 
 
 
FDA identified a reduced total or low density lipoprotein (“LDL”) blood cholesterol level 
as a beneficial physiological effect to human health because reduced total and LDL cholesterol 
levels have been associated with a reduced risk of heart disease. (81 Fed. Reg. 33,856; see also 
Memorandum 137 at 4). 
 
a. 
Mechanism of action 
 
 
 
The effect of rice bran fiber on blood cholesterol production is linked to their colonic 
fermentation, which produced short-chain fatty acids. In particular, propionate generated by 
the fermentation of rice bran fiber may modulate lipid and cholesterol metabolism. 
 
b. 
Summary of evidence 
 
Methodology  
 
 
All studies on the effect of rice bran fiber on blood cholesterol (total and LDL) were 
identified and evaluated. Pertinent high and medium quality research studies were selected 
using the following criteria: 
 
Inclusion criteria 
 Primary data on fasting total cholesterol (“TC”) and/or LDL cholesterol 
 Study duration with a minimum of 3 weeks 
 Appropriate control group 
 Statistical comparison with control 
 Subjects belong to the healthy general population including individuals at risk, i.e., 
individuals with hypercholesterolemia;  
 Studies of high and medium quality using FDA’s ranking criteria. 
 
Exclusion Criteria 
 No assessment of TC and/or LDL cholesterol 
 Low quality study ranking using FDA’s ranking criteria 
 No adequate placebo/control 
 No statistical comparison vs. placebo 
 No primary data reported 
 Study duration <3 weeks 
 Publications in foreign language 
 Use of roasted chicory root extract 
 Patients with a cardiovascular disease and persons on cholesterol-lowering medication 
 
Appendix C lists the references for studies that were included and excluded for the purpose of 
our review. 
Human intervention studies 
 
 
Table 1 summarizes the studies included in the analysis. Five well-designed and well-
analyzed studies found that rice bran fiber reduced blood cholesterol levels regardless of its fat 
content. One did not observe such effect, which may have resulted from factors other than rice 
bran fiber supplementation. 
 
 
c. 
Conclusion: rice bran fiber reduces blood cholesterol levels in 
hypercholesteremic individuals 
 
 
The totality of the pertinent scientific evidence shows that rice bran fiber significantly 
reduce blood cholesterol levels in hypercholesteremic individuals.  The American Society for 
Nutrition (ASN) Scientific Statement of 2013 documented benefits of cereal fiber regardless of 
fiber sources with grains.  Cereal fiber and/or bran may account for much of the risk reduction 
associated with whole grains. 
 
III. 
Environmental Impact 
 
 
A claim for categorical exclusion from the requirements for an Environmental 
Assessment is made under 21 C.F.R. § 25.30(k). 
 
IV.  
Economic Impact 
 
 
An economic impact statement will be submitted at the request of the commissioner. 
See 21 C.F.R. § 10.30(b)(3). 
 
V. 
Certification 
 
 
The undersigned certifies that, to the best knowledge and belief of the undersigned, this 
Petition includes all information and views on which the Petition relies, and that it includes 
representative date and information known to the Petitioners which are unfavorable to the 
petition. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
               Cherie Pollak 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Vice President Compliance, Regulatory 
and External Affairs 
RiceBran Technologies

Stabilized Rice Bran and RiceBran Technologies Rice Bran Derivative Product 
Studies Reviewed on the Non-digestible Carbohydrates in Rice Bran

The undersigned submits this petition pursuant to the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic 
Act (“FDC Act”) and in accordance with 21 C.F.R. §§ 10.25(a) and 10.30 to request that FDA 
amend the Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations (“Orange Book”) 
to designate ANDA 201587 as a Reference Standard (“RS”) for mupirocin calcium cream, EQ 
2% Base (“mupirocin cream” or “the drug”). The absence of a commercially available RS for 
bioequivalence testing blocks entry of additional, therapeutically equivalent, generic competitors.  
 
I. 
ACTION REQUESTED 
 
The undersigned requests that FDA designate a new RS for mupirocin cream so that an 
Abbreviated New Drug Application (“ANDA”) for a therapeutically-equivalent, generic version 
of the drug can be submitted to the FDA for review. In particular, the undersigned requests that 
FDA list ANDA 201587, currently the only commercially available formulation for this product, 
as a RS for mupirocin cream.  
 
II. 
STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
FDC Act § 505(j) allows the marketing of generic versions of previously approved drug 
products when the generic drug product is the subject of an ANDA. To obtain ANDA approval, 
the applicant must show, among other things that the generic drug has the same active 
ingredient(s) in the same strength, dosage form and route of administration, has essentially 
identical labeling, and is bioequivalent to the reference listed drug (i.e., a previously approved 
drug product, designated as the “RLD” in the Orange Book). In addition, the ANDA applicant 
must conduct in vivo bioequivalence testing of its product against an RS (designated by FDA 
and labeled with an “RS” in the Orange Book) to demonstrate bioequivalence to the RLD. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2 
Generally, FDA selects the RLD to serve as the RS, but FDA is not required to do so. 
FDA may select a different RS based on relevant factors, such as whether the RS is no longer 
marketed and whether selecting a new RS would prevent shortages. Draft Guidance for Industry, 
Referencing Approved Drug Products in ANDA Submissions, at 8-9 (Jan. 2017), hereafter FDA’s 
“RS Guidance” at 8-9. The RS Guidance notes that FDA will also “consider selecting a new 
reference standard when the Agency determines that the quantity of the current reference 
standard in distribution is so limited that a potential ANDA applicant is not able to obtain a 
sufficient quantity for in vivo bioequivalence testing (even if the current reference standard is not 
in the Discontinued Section of the Orange Book).” Id. In selecting a new RS, FDA typically 
selects a drug product that is both therapeutically equivalent to the RLD and the market leader. 
Requests for changes to FDA’s selection of the RS on the basis that there are “limited or no 
quantities of the reference standard in distribution” requires the submission of a citizen petition 
requesting that the Agency select a different listed drug as a new RS. See id. at 9.  
 
Mupirocin Calcium Cream, 2% is indicated for the treatment of secondarily infected 
traumatic skin lesions (up to 10 cm in length or 100 cm2 in area) due to susceptible strains of S. 
aureus and S. pyogenes.  Bactroban® (mupirocin calcium) cream, the NDA formulation of 
mupirocin cream (NDA #050746), was approved approximately 20 years ago and is designated 
in the Orange Book as the RLD and RS formulation. In July 2015, FDA conducted an inspection 
of the Bactroban® manufacturing site, finding cross-contamination and serious cGMP violations.  
Following the inspection, the manufacturer shut down further production at the site, issued a 
recall,1 and received an FDA Warning Letter about the violations at the site.2   
 
The undersigned understands that following the July 2016 recall, Bactroban® has been on 
long-term back order.3 As a result, there is no way for a generic manufacturer to obtain RS 
samples to conduct the required bioequivalence testing for FDA approval of a competing generic 
product. The manufacturer of the remaining formulation (ANDA 201857) has a 99.9% market 
share and is able to charge an artificially high price for the drug as a result.4  
 
The manufacturer of Bactroban® reportedly cannot provide an estimate as to when the 
product may be available.5  Therefore, absent any technical reason why the approved ANDA 
formulation could not serve as a RS (allowing additional formulations of mupirocin cream to be 
tested for bioequivalence), the undersigned hereby requests that FDA designate ANDA 201587 
in the FDA Orange Book as the RS for the drug. Designating a new RS will not only facilitate 
market competition for the product, but will also help limit the potential for a drug shortage,

ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT 
 
An environmental assessment report on the action requested in this petition is not

ECONOMIC IMPACT 
In accordance with 21 C.F.R. § 10.30(b), economic impact information is to be submitted

Citizen Petition  
Date:  August 13, 2018 
The undersigned submits this petition under ll (relevant statutory sections, if known) of the ll (Federal 
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or the Public Health Service Act or any other statutory provision for which 
authority has been delegated to the Commissioner of Food and Drugs) to request the Commissioner of 
Food and Drugs to ll (issue, amend, or revoke a regulation or order or take or refrain from taking any 
other form of administrative action).  
A. The action requested of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is to re‐categorize naloxone 4mg 
nasal spray from legend (prescription only) to over‐the‐counter (OTC) status.
B. The United States is in the midst of an overdose death epidemic, which is being fueled by prescription 
opioids, heroin, and fentanyl. The severity of this crisis is measured in the number of drug overdose 
deaths, which claimed the lives of 64,000 people in 2016. Naloxone is a drug that reverses opioid 
overdose and saves lives. This drug has to be readily available for those who are at risk of overdose, for 
without access to this drug people die.   OTC drugs play an increasingly vital role in America's health care 
system. OTC drug products are drugs that are available to consumers without a prescription and have 
these general characteristics:
• Their benefits outweigh their risks
• The potential for misuse and abuse is low
• Consumer can use them for self‐diagnosed conditions
• They can be adequately labeled
• Health practitioners are not needed for the safe and effective use of the product 
Naloxone meets all of the above criteria:  it has an excellent safety profile, is easy to use, and 
has minimal potential for abuse.  Clearly, the life‐saving benefit outweighs any minimal risk from use in 
non‐opioid overdose settings. Training materials on how to recognize and treat opioid overdose are 
readily available and there is a mobile application with additional instructions and labeling beyond the 
drug facts label (DFL) to ensure appropriate safe use and efficacy. [Innovative Approaches 
for Nonprescription Drug Products – Draft Guidance July 2018] 
Access to naloxone remains a challenge. Oregon and other states have expanded pharmacist 
authority to prescribe and/or dispense legend naloxone products.  First responders and law 
enforcement agencies have expanded carry and deployment policies. Local communities have held 
education and dispensing fairs to put naloxone in the hands of those at risk of overdose.  However, 
despite these state and local initiatives, barriers still exist.  The stigma of addiction continues to be a 
challenge to the widespread use of naloxone.  People at risk of overdose are often hesitant to discuss 
opioid use with health‐care providers.  Canada has already taken action to recategorize naloxone as OTC 
product for these very reasons.  
In conclusion, we believe that re‐categorizing naloxone 4mg nasal spray as an over‐the‐counter 
product will increase access for those who need this life‐saving drug.  Please consider the victims of this 
opioid crisis in your determination.  Thank you.  
C. Categorically excluded.
D. Economic Impact will be submitted at request of commission.

petition includes all information and views on which the petition relies, and that it includes

STATEMENT OF GROUNDS
FDC Act § 505Q) allows the marketing of generic versions of previously approved
drug products when the generic drug product is the subject of an ANDA. To obtain
ANDA approval, the applicant must show, among other things, that with respect to a
listed drug (i.e., a previously approved drug product), the generic drug product has the
same active ingredient(s) in the same strength, dosage form and route of administration,
has essentially identical labeling, and is bioequivaient.

A “listed drug” includes a new drug product that has an effective approval under
FDC Act § 505(j), that has not been withdrawn or suspended under FDC Act
§ 505(e)(I) through (5) or (j)(5), and that has not been withdrawn from sale for reasons
of safety or effectiveness. $ç 21 C.F.R. § 314.3. Listed drugs are identified in FDA’s
Orange Book. An RLD is the listed drug identified by FDA as the drug product on which
an ANDA applicant should rely in seeking approval of an application.
A “reference standard,” designated as “RS” in the Orange Book, is the product
that an ANDA applicant must use to conduct in vivo bioequivalence testing required for
approval. Generally, FDA selects a single RS, which is the same as the RLD. FDA may
select a new RS to further the submission and evaluation of generic drug applications. In
determining whether to select a new RS. FDA will consider the marketing status of the
1USD. the impact a new RS could have on preventing shortages, and the quantity of the
current RS in distribution. See FDA, Draft Guidance for Industry. Referencing Approved
Drug Products in ANDA Submissions, at 8-9 (Jan. 2017). FDA will typically select as a
new RS a drug product that is therapeutically equivalent to the RLD and the market
leader. FDA may also consider other factors that may “make the development process
more efficient.” Id. at 9.
A potential ANDA applicant may request that FDA select a new RS when another
may be more appropriate (cix., if the listed drug that is the RS is no longer marketed), or
if there is no RS in the “Active Section” of the Orange Book. Requests for changes to
FDA’s selection of the RS because the applicant believes another RS is more appropriate
requires the submission of a citizen petition to request that FDA select a different listed
drug as a new RS. See id. at 9.
There is a sound basis for selecting Naproxen Oral Suspension, 25 mg/mL,
approved under ANDA 074190 as a new RS. The current RS (and RLD), NAPROSYN
(naproxen) Oral Suspension, 25 mg/mL, approved under NDA 018965, is reportedly not
available for purchase (and may no longer be marketed) in the United States. This
effectively prevents further generic competition. In an effort to introduce further
competition, FDA should designate Naproxen Oral Suspension, 25 mg/mL, approved
under ANDA 074190, as a new RS. Accordingly, the undersigned requests that FDA
designate in the Orange Book the 25 mg/mL strength drug product approved under
ANDA 074190 as a new RS.

DEFINITION: 
Hyperpigmentation is characterized by a darkening of an area of skin caused by the overproduction of a 
pigment in the skin known as melanin. It is relatively common and usually harmless, but for cosmetic reasons, it 
is a nuisance to those who have it.  
 
Hyperpigmentation is the result of either of two occurrences: (1) an abnormally high concentration of 
melanocytes produce melanin or (2) when melanocytes are hyperactive. For instance, sun exposure stimulates 
the production of melanin. Although it can affect anyone, this condition is more prevalent among certain 
ethnicities such as Asian, Mediterranean, African, or Latino. Hyperpigmentation can affect any part of the body 
including the face, hands, and neck. BrillyantSkin™ SR penetrates deep enough in the skin to effectively target 
the melanocytes.

Sodium salicylate that is removed via sedimentation or filtration will degrade relatively rapidly. The half-
life in soil was previously estimated by the EPI software, to be 720 hours and salicylic acid was "readily 
biodegradable" in soils. The estimated concentration of sodium salicylate in /soilsludge is 10,025 mg/kg.

based on data for Lemna minor. The calculated environmental exposure to sodium salicylate discharged to 
water is a maximum of 3.0 mg/L (ppm), including 75% reduction during treatment at the water waste treatment 
plant, as well as with dilution of the receiving water. This level of exposure is below the LC50 of Daphnia, fathead 
minnow, carp, and algae. It is also well below the level of 60 mg/L set by the FDA. It is expected that the majority 
of the sodium salicylate will decompose before release into the environment.

examine the effects on our medical system of commerce-driven, court-ordered, drug access
restrictions.
The hearing should focus on the following issues: 
 - how would commerce-driven court-ordered restrictions on drug access affect the delivery of
medical care?  We are particularly concerned about the impact of such restrictions on drug
development and patient access to new therapies.  
 - is legislation or rulemaking needed to prevent such restrictions?
We note that such a hearing could advance FDA strategic goals.  Dr. Scott Gottleib, FDA
Administrator, has spoken out recently about pharmaceutical firms trying to “game the system”
to prevent competition.  We assert that allowing the court system to over-ride FDA decisions
about drug access is a clear example of ‘gaming the system.’   A public hearing on the
implications of current legal filings to limit drug access would encourage discussion on the
general question of enabling competition in the pharmaceutical market.   
B. Statement of Grounds.
Hemophilia is a condition which disrupts normal blood coagulation in response to trauma.  
Moderately effective therapies for Hemophilia became available in the mid 1960s.  Prior to
that, the disease was always associated with painful and disabling bleeding episodes, and
frequently caused mortality by early adulthood.  Current drugs allow for far better health
outcomes than in the past,  nevertheless most mortality among patients with severe
hemophilia is associated with bleeding episodes, or conditions created by bleeding episodes, or
consequences of treatment for bleeding.  In summary, the Hemophilia community depends on
therapy, welcomes continued advances and in therapy, and looks forward to the goal of a
complete cure**.   
Patients for Access to Advanced Hemophilia Therapy is a group of Hemophilia patients.  We (in
fact, most of the World) rely on the FDA to oversee drug research development and drug
approval.  We expect the FDA to require rigorous human testing of new drugs, and we expect
FDA to base approval on a careful risk/benefit analysis.  The process is not perfect.  But, overall
it is a process that protects patients and enables therapeutic progress. 
This process is now threatened by a new legal approach which would deny access to approved
drugs based on issues unrelated to medical therapy.  Our immediate concern is that access to
the drug Hemlibra, a newly approved, promising Hemophilia therapy, may be affected by this
new legal approach.  We note with concern that Baxalta/Shire, in a commercial suit over
intellectual property, has requested that the court deny some patients access to Hemlibra*. 
We see this kind of legal action as a threat to FDA’s drug evaluation system;  a threat to the
reward system that funds progress;  and a threat to patients who, like ourselves, need better therapies.
We personally are affected by legal filings to limit Hemlibra access.  Our core group includes
one Hemophilia patient who does not have inhibitors but who now uses Hemlibra.  Patients in
this category would be denied Hemlibra if Shire’s request for a Preliminary Injunction were
totally granted.  Also, one of us is the grandfather of a patient with inhibitors.  The tight
definition of ‘inhibitor patient’ in the proposed Preliminary Injunction might exclude this
patient and therefore render him ineligible for Hemlibra.  
Finally, while most  us do not now use Hemlibra, we intend to discuss with our providers the
risk / benefit of switching from intravenous Factor replacement to subcutaneous Hemlibra. 
Hemlibra would not be available for prescription to those of us planning that conversation if
the Shire Preliminary Injunction were granted.  We believe that it is in the public interest to
hold a hearing on this matter because this legal approach could be used in the future on other
new drugs entering the market. 
We have no opinion on the validity of the Shire claim of patent infringement in the marketing
of Hemlibra.  We simply want to assure that the issue of patent ownership does not impact
access to this potentially breakthrough Hemophilia A therapy.

The undersigned requests that FDA designate ANDA 201587 listed in the Orange Book for

undersigned requests that the FDA list ANDA 201587, which is only currently commercially

 II. Statement of Grounds  
 
Section 505(j) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) permits any person to 
submit to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA or the Agency) an ANDA to seek approval to 
market a generic drug. To obtain approval of an ANDA for a generic drug, the ANDA applicant 
must show, among other things, that the generic drug has the same active ingredient(s) in the 
same strengths, dosage form and route of administration, has essentially identical labeling, and is 
bioequivalent to the reference listed drug (i.e., a previously approved drug product, designated as 
the reference listed drug “RLD” in the Orange Book).  
 
In the current Orange Book, FDA list NDA 050746, BACTROBAN (Mupirocin Calcium Cream), 
EQ 2% Base, held by GLAXOSMITHKLINE, selected as RLD and RS in the current Orange 
Book. However, in the undersigned’s opinion and to the best of its knowledge, no multiple

The undersigned submit this petition to request withdrawal of FDA guidance documents and related 
recommendations concerning assessments of drug dissolution characteristics of the pharmaceutical 
products such as tablet and capsule 
A. Action Requested: 
The petition requests the removal of the following items from the regulatory 
recommendations/requirements: 
 
(1) Guidance for Industry (2018) - Dissolution Testing and Acceptance Criteria for Immediate-
Release Solid Oral Dosage Form Drug Products Containing High Solubility Drug Substances 
(https://www.fda.gov/downloads/Drugs/Guidances/UCM456594.pdf) 
(2) Guidance for Industry (2017) - Waiver of In Vivo Bioavailability and Bioequivalence Studies 
for Immediate-Release Solid Oral Dosage Forms Based on a Biopharmaceutics Classification 
System 
https://www.fda.gov/downloads/Drugs/GuidanceComplianceRegulatoryInformation/Guida
nces/UCM070246.pdf). 
(3) Guidance for Industry (1997) - Dissolution Testing of Immediate Release Solid Oral Dosage 
Forms (https://www.fda.gov/downloads/drugs/guidances/ucm070237.pdf) 
(4) Dissolution Methods Database (https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/dissolution/) 
 
B. Statement of Grounds: 
 
A drug dissolution test is an analytical test used to assess the quality of pharmaceutical products such as 
tablet and capsule (both prescription and non-prescription types). These tests are extensively conducted 
during product development stages as well as later as a quality control tool for establishing quality of 
the manufactured products [1]. The tests are conducted using testers commonly known as drug 
dissolution apparatuses such as paddle and basket. The specifications and instructions to follow for the 
use of these apparatuses are provided in the USP General Chapter <711> [2]. 
There are numerous regulations and Guidance documents available from the FDA which dictate the use 
of these apparatuses [e.g. see 3-5]. 
On the other hand, as per cGMP requirements every equipment, including apparatuses/testers, used for 
drug product manufacturing and evaluation must be validated [e.g. see 6-8] to demonstrate that the 
equipment or testers are qualified and validated for the intended use and purpose. However, the drug 
dissolution testers have never been validated for their intended use. Regulatory authorities (including 
US FDA), pharmacopeias (including USP), manufacturers and/or suppliers of the products and the testers

A. Action Requested 
Bonumose LLC requests the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to amend 21 CFR § 101.9, 
Nutrition Labeling of Food. Specifically, we request to exempt D-tagatose from its classification 
as an added sugar on the Nutrition Facts Panel on foods and beverages (21 CFR § 
101.9(c)(6)(iii)) and amend the regulation to include a voluntary labeling of D-tagatose, similar to 
that which is provided for sugar alcohols (21 CFR § 101.9(c)(6)(iv)). Information supporting this 
petition is enclosed and is summarized by the following points: 
 
1. Unlike other more commonly consumed added sugars such as sucrose and high-
fructose corn syrup (HFCS), D-tagatose does not increase risk for chronic disease. 
Instead, it is associated with a number of positive health outcomes including an 
increase in glycemic control, reduction in risk for tooth decay, function as a prebiotic, 
and reduction in risk for cardiovascular disease (CVD). 
2. Inconsistent methodology has been used to define “added sugars” and regulate their 
labeling. 
3. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar conflicts with FDA rationale regarding 
the purpose of mandatory added sugar labeling. 
4. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar is misrepresentative and 
misinterprets evidence supporting a link between sugars and chronic disease. It also 
results in an inaccurate label that could confuse consumers. 
5. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar contradicts the spirit of recognized 
health claims. 
Background 
 
Bonumose LLC is a food ingredient manufacturer specializing in the affordable 
production of natural rare hexoses. These sugars are significantly healthier than sucrose and 
HFCS yet retain the favorable taste and technical attributes of these more commonly consumed 
sugars. Our company is driven by the scientific evidence suggesting that excess consumption of 
sucrose and HFCS is associated with escalating rates of chronic disease. We highly value 
efforts to provide accurate, reliable information to the public via nutrition labeling, as well as 
provide them with healthy sugar alternatives that are both palatable and functional enough to 
improve public health. 
 
D-tagatose is a monosaccharide that provides a sweet taste and can be used to replace 
more commonly used sugars such as sucrose and HFCS for a variety of food applications 
(Muddada 2012). In addition to its use as a sweetener, D-tagatose can also be used in foods as 
a humectant, texturizer or stabilizer (FDA 2001). It is only partially digested in the small intestine 
(Laerke and Jensen 1999; Bertelsen, Jensen, and Buemann 1999; Saunders, Zehner, and 
Levin 1999) and undergoes fermentation in the large intestine to produce short-chain fatty acids 
(Bertelsen, Jensen, and Buemann 1999; Vigh and Andersen 2007). D-tagatose maintains its 
sweetness and nutritive value at all food use levels. 
 
 
 
  
3 
 
Uses of D-tagatose in foods and beverages were recognized as GRAS on October 25, 
2001 (Arla Foods Ingredients 2001; FDA 2001) and on February 1, 2011 (CJ Cheiljedang 2011; 
FDA 2011). Tables 1 and 2 below contain the levels of D-tagatose that have been approved for 
use in various categories of foods and beverages.

A compilation of data from the U.S., European Union, Australia and New Zealand estimates 
that the average consumption of D-tagatose in adults ranges from 3-9 g/day, with those 
consumers at the 95th percentile consuming up to 18 g/day (Food and Agriculture Organization 
& World Health Organization 2006). Reports that are restricted to U.S. data (USDA Continuing 
Survey of Food Intakes by Individuals, 1994-96) estimate the mean consumption to be 8.9 
g/day, excluding use in chewing gum and dietary and meal supplements. The 90th percentile of 
this population consumed 18 g/day (VonApeldoorn and Speijers 2001). This consumption 
occurs as a sweetener ingredient in food preparations, (often replacing sucrose) rather than as 
a stand-alone item.   
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
5 
 
B. Statement of Grounds 
Rationale Summary: 
 
 
The most recent revision of the Nutrition Facts Panel includes a mandatory declaration 
of added sugars that “is necessary to assist consumers to maintain healthy dietary practices, 
and we proposed to require the declaration of the amount of added sugars in a serving of a 
product” (81 FR 33742 at 33799). Also mandatory is a declaration of the % Daily Value (%DV) 
of those added sugars in a serving of food (relative to a Dietary Reference Value (DRV) of 10 
percent of calories) to “assist consumers in constructing a healthy dietary pattern” (81 FR 33742 
at 33800). Evidence supporting these mandatory declarations was in the form of scientific 
studies linking high added sugar intake with increased risk for chronic disease. Both the 
relationship between added sugars and chronic disease, as well as the contribution of these 
sugars to total caloric intake are inherently physiological parameters. For the purposes of 
maintaining an accurate, informative label that will help consumers make sound dietary choices, 
it is only logical that the added sugars referred to on the label are the same ones which share 
those physiological properties that increase risk for chronic disease. 
 
 
D-tagatose is a naturally-occurring, rare monosaccharide that does not increase risk for 
chronic disease, nor does it share similar metabolic and physiologic characteristics with sugars 
such as sucrose and HFCS that are the subject of many studies linking added sugars with 
disease. D-tagatose consumption is associated with numerous health benefits, and, along with 
other naturally-occurring rare monosaccharides, is grossly misrepresented when classified as 
an added sugar. Inclusion in this category not only conflicts with FDA labeling rationale but 
results in an inaccurate label that could confuse consumers and complicate dietary decisions. 
 
 
Our rationale supporting this petition is described in detail below, but can be summarized 
by the following statements: 
 
1. Unlike other more commonly consumed added sugars such as sucrose and 
HFCS, D-tagatose does not increase risk for chronic disease. Instead, it is 
associated with a number of positive health outcomes including an increase in 
glycemic control, reduction in risk for tooth decay, function as a prebiotic and 
reduction in risk for CVD. 
2. Inconsistent methodology has been used to define “added sugars” and 
regulate its labeling. 
3. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar conflicts with FDA rationale 
regarding the purpose of mandatory added sugar labeling. 
4. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar is misrepresentative and 
misinterprets evidence supporting a link between sugars and chronic disease.  
It also results in an inaccurate label that could confuse consumers. 
5. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar contradicts the spirit of 
recognized health claims. 
 
 
  
6 
 
Finally, we propose a revision to 21 CFR § 101.9(c) to enhance the ability of the Nutrition Facts 
Panel to effectively communicate nutrition information and aid consumers in choosing healthy 
dietary practices.

D-tagatose does not increase risk for chronic disease. Instead, it is associated with a 
number of positive health outcomes including an increase in glycemic control, reduction

Petition_Text:
CITIZEN PETITION 
 
October 14, 2018 
 
The undersigned ("petitioner") submits this petition under Sections 510 and 513 of the Federal Food, 
Drug, and Cosmetic Act and 21 C.F.R. §10.30 to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to take 
administrative action to prevent certain categories of new devices from being cleared for marketing 
without sufficient proof of safety and effectiveness. 
 
A. Action Requested 
 
Petitioner respectfully request that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to take the following 
administrative action: 
Require manufacturers of the following categories of devices (“Device”) whose Indication for Use 
includes applications on the lung and the digestive tracts including the stomach, intestines and rectum for 
resection, transection and/or creation of anastomosis: 
Device Category 1 
- Regulation: 21 C.F.R. 878.4750 
- Classification Name: Implantable Staple 
- Product Code: GDW 
- Common Name: Surgical stapler with implantable staple; and 
Any other surgical stapler with a staple cartridge or reload intended to apply line of staples for 
resection, transection and/or creation of anastomosis whose Indication for Use includes 
applications on the lung and the digestive tracts including the stomach, intestines and rectum. 
Device Category 2 
- Regulation: 21 C.F.R. 878.3300 
- Classification Name: Mesh, Surgical, Polymeric and Mesh, Surgical 
- Product Code: FTM, FTL, OXC  
- Common Name: Staple line reinforcement material; and 
Any other material of any configuration intended to reinforce surgical staple line (commonly called 
staple line buttress or buttressing material) whose Indication for Use includes reinforcing staple line 
applied on the lung and the digestive tracts including the stomach, intestines and rectum for 
resection, transection and/or creation of anastomosis.  
(1) to perform a risk analysis associated with the manner with which the Device is used in surgical 
applications to perform resection, transection and/or creation of anastomosis on the lung and the digestive 
tracts often resulting in creation of a staple line (tissue fastening) patterns or configurations of simple to 
very complex geometries with special focus on dependence of physiological load distribution on the 
staple line geometry and on the anatomical disposition of the staple line on the host organ; and  
(2) to provide data from performance tests as part of marketing clearance review submission, 
appropriately designed to assess impact of the risk factors, identified through the risk analysis, on the 
safety and effectiveness of the Device, in addition to what is presently considered acceptable in 
determining substantial equivalence (SE) to a predicate device and to revise the labeling and Instruction 
for Use of the Device to be in line with the additional performance test data, as needed. 
 
B. Statement of Grounds 
 
Staple Line Leaks 
Postoperative air leak in staple line is a prevalent complication following lung surgery with significant 
healthcare cost implication.1  Although not as frequent, postoperative gastrointestinal leak in staple line 
following surgeries in the digestive tracts is a complication that is important cause of morbidity and 
mortality.2  There is little information available to help pinpoint how and why these apparent and often 
delayed mechanical failure of staple line, intraoperatively tested negative for defect and leak, occurs 
resulting in leakage of organ content.  However, one can say with certainty based on the principle of 
mechanics that the root cause of staple line failure can only be the dynamic tensile stress load (referred to 
as physiological load or physiological organ load in the following) acting on the staple line present on the 
wall of the host organ due to physiological organ motion, breathing/cough in the lung and digestion 
motion in the digestive tracts, in the absence of any other force acting on the staple line other than the 
static gravity with presumed harmful effect.  Barring spontaneous breakdown of staple line, for example, 
due to ischemia of stapled tissue, ultimately it has to be the mechanical action of stapled organ that 
disturbs the staple line and triggers leakage of organ content and/or drives degradation of the staple line 
and causes leakage of organ content over time. 
Unrecognized Risk Factor (Hazard): Uneven Distribution of Physiological Load on Staple Line(s) 
Among the anatomical organs, on which surgical staplers are generally indicated for use, the lung and the 
digestive tracts are associated with distinctive risk factor not found in any other organ, being hollow, 
relatively large and capable of physiological motion in addition to their walls being generally highly 
distensible in comparison to other solid (as opposed to hollow) organs as needed for performing their 
physiological functions.  A staple line applied on the lung or one of the organs in the digestive tract, with 
or without staple line buttress, is subjected to dynamic (varying in time) tensile stress load due to 
physiological motion of the organ (may be referred to as physiological load or physiological organ load 
hereinafter).  In the lung there are ever present and cyclic motion during externally driven, normal 
breathing cycles and intermittent motion lasting for a short period of time during cough.  In the digestive 
tracts there is digestion motion that only occurs while self-powered digestion activities (mixing motion in 
the stomach, peristaltic motion in the intestines and evacuation motion in the rectum) are taking place.  
The dynamic nature of physiological load, the geometry of staple line, the anatomy of stapled organ and 
                                                           
1 Bryan M. Burt, Joseph B. Shrager, “Prevention and management of postoperative air leaks”, Ann Cardiothorac. 
Surg. 2014;3(2):216-218. 
2 J. Kim, M.D., et al., “ASMBS position statement on prevention, detection, and treatment of gastrointestinal leak 
after gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy, including the roles of imaging, surgical exploration, and nonoperative 
management”, Surgery for Obesity and Related Diseases 11 (2015) 739-748. 
the mechanics of physiological motion all cooperate to present risk factor unique to the lung and the 
digestive tracts that could in various ways undermine safety and effectiveness of surgical stapler used on 
those organs.  This risk factor is not of relevance or of such significance as to warrant a close scrutiny to 
the use of surgical stapler on any other organ, a solid organ and blood vessel/vasculature, usually covered 
by the Indication for Use of typical surgical stapler, where hemostasis is only or primary performance 
requirement expected of the device.  A staple line applied on a blood vessel for transection or a tissue 
bundle comprising vasculature for resection/transection is also subjected to physiological load in the form 
of ever present and cyclic blood pressure pulses.  But because of relatively small magnitude of the 
physiological load due to limited size of blood vessel compared to the lung and the digestive tracts and 
stiffness of the vessel wall renders insignificant the risk factor arising from the physiological load to 
hemostasis performance of staple line on these organs. 
1. Unproven Performance – Surgical Stapler: To date there is no clear evidence that the geometric 
configuration of a staple line (including a combination of staple lines, collectively referred to as a staple 
line hereinafter) and/or the anatomical disposition of  a staple line on the host organ has been properly 
recognized by manufacturers or regulatory authorities as a risk factor that could potentially cause a failure 
of a staple line leading to a leak of organ content, in perhaps the worst possible case of clinical 
complication, e.g., in case of the surgeries of the digestive tracts.  No documentary evidence, including 
historical patent application records and marketing brochures of the presently marketed surgical staplers, 
could be found indicating a systematic study of the risks presented by the geometric configuration and/or 
relative anatomical disposition of a staple line has been systematically carried out or the results of such 
study has been incorporated in the designs of the presently marketed surgical staplers.  The only 
performance test sometimes found in 510(k) summaries3, 4, 5 of presently marketed surgical stapler that 
appears to be designed to examine sealing performance of staple line is a burst pressure test which, being 
static tensile stress test and performed only on a relatively simplified application conditions, i.e., a simple 
staple line geometry deployed on a unsophisticated model organ anatomy, has no bearing on the 
performance of the staple line under dynamic tensile stress load from physiological organ motion or under 
complicated application conditions involving a staple line geometry comprising multiple staple lines 
and/or a potentially risky anatomical disposition of a staple line on a host organ.  In clinical use of 
surgical stapler integrity of staple line is usually taken for granted upon visual inspection of superficial 
physical condition of formed staples/tissue immediately after staple firing often followed by a static 
pressure test to look for obvious sign of defect and leak, and subsequently assumed to remain sound or at 
an unknown state of soundness until an event such as staple line leak occurs indicating some sort of break 
in staple line integrity.  In fact surgeons have no factual basis to assume otherwise since manufacturers of 
presently marketed surgical stapler have never provided any realistic performance test data for their 
products.  
2. Unsupported Performance Claims – Staple Line Buttress: Claims of positive effects of presently 
marketed staple line buttress on sealing performance of staple line applied on the lung and stomach in the 
                                                           
3 FDA 510(k) Summary, K133938 
4 FDA 510(k) Summary, K163454 
5 FDA 510(k) Summary, K113706 
manufacturer’s marketing brochure6 are based on retrospective outcomes study involving application of 
presently marketed surgical stapler whose sealing performance has not been fully characterized under 
physiological load or various clinical application conditions as explained above.  Therefore these claims 
should be deemed not fully supported by realistic performance test data. 
Dependence of Load Distribution on Staple Line Geometry and Disposition – Risk Factors Analyzed 
1. Analysis of Physiological Load:  A physics analysis for the purpose of risk assessment, associated with 
a staple line deployed on a hollow organ, of tensile stress on the wall of the host organ due to 
physiological motion would be best performed by interpreting or posing it as a boundary value problem.  
Arising across several branches of physics describable as a partial differential equation with a set of 
constraints (boundary conditions) the boundary value problem can provide a wealth of insights into the 
underlying physics it is posed to describe even when a simplified modeling of the underlying physical 
system is not readily available allowing exact analytic solutions to be found.  For a physical system of 
complicated geometry a computer-based numerical analysis method, widely available and often known as 
Finite Element Analysis (FEM), can be effectively used.   
Obviously a hollow organ, the lung and digestive tracts, with a deployed staple line is not a physical 
system that can be easily modeled physically and analyzed mathematically.  But the following few 
physical facts, pertinent to the analysis at hand, deducible from generally known mathematical properties 
of partial differential equation comprising a boundary condition problem can be relied upon to identify a 
major category of risks a deployed staple line faces when acted on by the physiological tensile stress load 
on the wall of the host organ and to devise specific performance tests to physically characterize the risks 
and the magnitude of harm that may result from the risks.  (For an introductory discussion on this topic, 
please see a primer prepared by the Petitioner mainly for surgeon audience attached to this Citizen 
Petition and also viewable at 
https://www.endoscape.com/files/Pedestrian_Physics_of_Staple_Line_Leaks.pdf). 
(a) Discontinuities in Staple Line: The tensile stress load at a point on the organ wall is given by a first 
spatial derivative of a function representing a physical quantity, in this case, a potential energy of 
physiological organ motion.  At a location along a staple line on the organ wall where this first derivative 
becomes very large or even diverge (be infinite or undefined), often referred to as a discontinuity or 
singularity in mathematics, is a “stress point or hot spot” in which the tensile stress gets “focused or 
concentrated”, i.e., disproportionately large compared to the rest of the staple line.  In physical world a 
discontinuity is most often, but not always, associated with visible and abrupt topographical or geometric 
changes.  For example, a stress point is easily identifiable where there is a disruption on a staple line, e.g., 
a meeting point of two non-linear staple lines or a vertex and apex on a staple line made up of two 
intersecting staple lines.  Two terminal ends of a staple line are also a good example.  The more abrupt or 
sharper this change is at a point on a staple line the larger the stress concentration at that location.  
Discontinuities on a staple line deployed on a distensible organ wall can also occur even in the absence of 
topographical or geometric changes as a result of physiological organ motion which can momentarily 
create a “kink” in the middle of otherwise smooth, continuous staple line in the course of physiological 
                                                           
6 Product Brochure for GORE® SEAMGUARD® Bioabsorbable Staple Line Reinforcement, W. L. Gore & 
Associates, Inc., https://www.goremedical.com 
motion.  Stress point could also arise due to changes in mechanical properties of tissue as further 
discussed below. 
(b) Anatomical Disposition of Staple Line: Placement of a staple line on a host organ has significant 
implication on the distribution of the physiological tensile stress load thereon.  For example, in a staple 
line deployed next to an anatomically fixed point on the host organ a portion of the staple line close to the 
fixed point is more likely subject to higher level of tensile stress than the rest since the portion is not able 
to spread out the tensile stress load being constricted on one end while the rest of the staple line is able to 
move more freely to conform to and effectively spreading out the tensile stress load to neighboring the 
organ wall tissue.  Another example is pair of staple lines of simple linear shape but of different lengths, 
e.g., ones deployed across intestinal tracts of different diameters for dissection.  The discontinuities at 
either ends of the shorter staple line of the two are likely subject to higher tensile stress load than the 
longer one even when the two staple lines are subject to the same tensile stress load factoring in the 
difference in the length because there is less of a chance to spread the tensile stress load out due to shorter 
span between the two ends.  Yet another example for dependence of tensile stress load distribution on the 
anatomical disposition of a staple line is the case of anastomosis with a circular stapler.  More detailed 
discussion on this subject is provided in the section 3 below. 
(c) Material Boundary: Less recognizable than a topographical or geometric change described above a 
boundary where materials, organ tissues in our case, of different mechanical properties constitutes stress 
points.  Change in tissue properties, most importantly tensile modulus (elasticity), inevitably accompanies 
a stapling operation since every time a staple line is deployed on a hollow organ the stapled tissue is 
compressed and become stiffer (work hardened, less elastic) than the undisturbed adjacent to the staple 
line.  In this case the material boundary is formed in a single type of tissue and created along a line 
immediately adjacent to the inner most row of the staple line from the cut edge. Unlike the wall tissue of 
blood vessel, constructed to withstand tensile stress load caused by blood pressure, the wall tissue of the 
lung and the digestive tracts is highly distensible to allow the organ to expand and contract in concert with 
breathing action and digestion motion, respectively.  This difference in mechanical properties between 
staple line and highly distensible native wall tissue of the lung and the digestive tracts is one of the factors 
that exacerbate the risks arising from physiological load on these organs causing it to be concentrated on 
the staple line much like the case of a length of inelastic adhesive tape applied to a latex balloon.  
A material boundary can also formed when two dissimilar tissues are joined by a staple line, an example 
of which is anastomosis between the stomach pouch and the jejunum in a sleeve gastrectomy procedure.  
2. Dependence of Load Distribution on Staple Line Geometry 
For the purpose of categorizing risks associated with the staple line geometry as well as disposition, 
described in the next section, physiological tensile stress load on the wall of host organ is modeled as 
schematically shown in FIGURE 1.  In this model a tensile stress load due to the physiological organ 
motion acting on a portion of a staple line at one point in time is divided into two independent 
components, one transverse (perpendicular) and the other axial (parallel) to the staple line.  Based on this 
model the tensile stress loads on a staple line in all known clinical applications of surgical stapling 
products are categorized into a set of simplified load patterns and presented in TABLE 1.  Factors 
considered in the categorization include the organ anatomy, the geometry of staple line(s), the geometric  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
FIGURE 1. Modeling and Component Analysis of Physiological Organ Load on Staple Line 
Red Arrows - Transverse (Splitting) Component, Purple Arrows - Axial (Stretching) Component 
 
location on the organ of the staple line, the characteristics of organ motion, the physical nature of organ 
content - air or viscous liquid, difference in mechanical characteristics in stapled tissues (e.g., stomach  
and jejunum), inversion of staple line (staple line facing inside the organ lumen), types of stapler - linear 
or circular. 
3. Dependence of Load Distribution on Staple Line Disposition 
Distribution of tensile stress load acting on a staple line can be strongly influenced by anatomical 
disposition of the staple line on the host organ.  A striking example is a concentration of tensile stress 
load on the staple line near the Gastroesophageal (GE) Junction deployed in a sleeve gastrectomy 
procedure.  While the rest of the staple line is relatively free to move with respect to the body of the 
remaining portion of the stomach, the portion near the GE Junction is constrained largely stationary on 
one end immediately adjacent to the GE Junction.  As a result any tensile stress acting on this portion of 
the staple line including contribution from the weight of the remaining stomach and its content must be 
supported entirely by the portion of the staple line being fixed on one end and not being fully able to 
spread the tensile load out to neighboring portions of the staple line.  This fact is supported by clinical 
observation that majority of staple line leaks after sleeve gastrectomy procedures occurs primarily in the 
proximal third of staple line near the GE junction. 
Another example is the case of intestinal anastomosis with use of a circular stapler.  In performing 
anastomosis of large and small intestines a circular stapler deploys rows of staples circularly arranged 
around and perpendicularly to the axis (in the direction of intestine lumen) of the intestines being joined 
substantially constraining the diameter of joined portion of the intestine to that of a circle defined by rows 
of staples.  During a digestive process the intestines often need to be able to expand multiple folds in 
diameter under pressure from the digestive content.  This could lead to concentration of tensile stress load 
on portion(s) of the circular staple line being constricted to a fixed diameter and unable to move with the

In end-to-end, end-to-side and side-to-side anastomosis and anastomosis using a circular stapler, an 
inverted staple line, i.e., staple line disposed inside the lumen of host organ can be an end result of 
stapling operation.  Little or no information is available for the sealing performance of an inverted staple 
line.  In anastomosis of the stomach pouch and the jejunum in Roux-en-Y procedure a staple line is used 
to interconnect two different organs with distinctive mechanical characteristics and physiological 
functions.  No information is available for the sealing performance of such a staple line. 
Probing Risks of Risk Factors – New Performance Tests 
Disproportionately large concentration of tensile stress load on a portion of a staple line could raise 
probability of localized mechanical failure of the staple line that contribute to leakage of organ content.  
As noted previously, manufacturers of presently marketed surgical staplers do not appear to neither had 
envisioned that the stress points could be created on a staple line deployed on a hollow organ like the lung 
and the digestive tracts in the normal course of surgical applications of their products nor have tailored 
the product designs at any point in their evolutionary path with specific aim of reducing possibility of 
creation of stress points.  It would be imperative to establish a set of performance tests for probing the 
presence of weak (stress) points in a staple line and providing quantifiable measure of risks the weakness 
poses to the integrity of the staple (or future tissue fastener) line in its sealing performance. 
The following random list of thoughts or suggestions (representative of the widest extent of my 
knowledge base on the subject discussed in this Citizen Petition at the time of this writing), by no means 
comprehensive, may serve as a pointer providing assistance in visualizing how the risk factor may play 
out in actual clinical applications of surgical stapler on the lung and the digestive tracts and designing 
performance tests for (a) exposing, under controlled condition realistically simulating the field use 
condition, mechanical and physical effects that the risk factor could cause; and (b) ascertaining sealing 
performance limitations these effects could impose on staple line that may have direct ramification on 
safety and effectiveness of new surgical stapler (tissue fastener) presented for marketing clearance review 
with indication of use including the lung and the digestive tracts.  
1. Risks Specific to Surgical Techniques (or Staple line Geometry):  
Analytic (including use of FEA method) and laboratory studies of stress distribution on a staple line with 
discontinuities created in the course of: (a) side-to-side, end-to-side and end-to-end anastomosis; (b) the 
wedge resection of the lung; and (c) anastomosis with a circular stapler during an episode of asymmetric

STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
A. Statutory and Regulatory Background 
1. The Hatch-Waxman Act Created an Abbreviated Approval Pathway for 
Generic Drugs 
Congress enacted the Drug Price Competition and Patent Term Restoration Act (Hatch-
Waxman Act) in 1984 as a system to both protect the interests of innovative drug manufacturers 
and provide consumers access to more affordable medicines.4 To that end, Hatch-Waxman put in 
place exclusivity provisions as an incentive to innovators to develop new products while 
authorizing an abbreviated approval process to reduce the cost of drugs for consumers. ANDA 
applicants could rely on FDA's findings of safety and efficacy for a previously approved version 
of the drug as long as the applicant could demonstrate that the proposed generic is "the same as" 
the RLD. 5 At the same time, as a reward for undertaking the onerous clinical studies needed for 
full NDA approvals, Hatch-Waxman awarded periods of exclusivity to successful NDA 
applicants. 6 The scheme was designed to strike "a balance between expediting generic drug 
applications and protecting the interests of the original drug manufacturers. "7 
Under the FDCA, FDA makes available an abbreviated approval process for 
manufacturers of generic drugs. 8 The ANDA relies on the data of a previously approved NDA 
containing full clinical trials.9 The ANDA applicant must certify to any patents listed for the 
NDA in FDA's compendium Approved Drug Products with Therapeutic Equivalence 
Evaluations, commonly known as the Orange Book. 10 If an ANDA applicant seeks FDA 
approval to market a copy of a brand drug before all of the patents listed in the Orange Book 
have expired, it must challenge the unexpired patents by filing a Paragraph IV certification. 11 A 
Paragraph IV certification requires the ANDA applicant to provide notice of its FDA filing to 
both the NDA holder and the patent owner setting forth the legal and factual basis as to why the 
ANDA applicant believes the patents are not infringed, invalid, or otherwise unenforceable. 12 
When a generic applicant submits its ANDA, FDA reviews the application for 
completeness and notifies the applicant when it determines the application to be substantially

A fundamental requirement under the Hatch-Waxman Act is that the active ingredient

important because the ANDA applicant, doctors, and patients are all relying the clinical trials

A. Apotex's ANDA No. 210299 Violates the "Same Active Ingredient" Requirement 
A drug product described in an ANDA cannot be approved unless it is found to be 
therapeutically equivalent to the RLD. 31 This requires a finding by FDA that the generic drug is 
both pharmaceutically equivalent to the RLD and bioequivalent based on certain prescribed 
testing. 32 Although diclofenac free acid and diclofenac sodium have the same active moiety, they 
have different chemical structures, which makes them different active ingredients and not 
pharmaceutical equivalents. 
The Orange Book states that "[d]rug products are considered pharmaceutical alternatives 
if they contain the same therapeutic moiety, but are different salts." 33 Drug products with the 
same therapeutic moiety that contain different salts are pharmaceutical alternatives and, therefore 
cannot be therapeutically equivalent. Similarly, in a 2013 Guidance for Industry on the 
Regulatory Classification of Co-crystals, FDA compared the properties of solid state 
polymorphic forms of active ingredients with those of co-crystals for purposes of determining 
active ingredient sameness. Significantly, in the glossary to this Guidance FDA provided the 
following definition of a "salt": 
Salts: Any of numerous compounds that result from replacement of part or all ofthe acid 
hydrogen of an acid by a metal or a radical acting like a metal: an ionic or electrovalent 
crystalline compound. Per the current regulatory scheme, different salt forms of the same 
active moiety are considered different active ingredi.ents. (See 21 CFR 314.108 and 21 CFR 
320.1(c).) 
Because the same logic would apply to an acid and salt with the same active moiety, diclofenac 
free acid and diclofenac sodium must be viewed as different active ingredients and thus cannot 
be considered therapeutically equivalent for purposes of an ANDA submission.

CITIZEN PETITION 
 
October 18, 2018 
 
The undersigned ("Petitioner") submits this petition under Sections 510 and 513 of the Federal Food, 
Drug, and Cosmetic Act and 21 C.F.R. §10.30 to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to 
implement a retroactive regulatory action to remedy deficiencies found in the 510(k) process for the 
legally marketed surgical stapler devices and generally improve their safety profiles.  
A. Action Requested 
 
Petitioner respectfully request that the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to take the following 
administrative action for the legally marketed devices belonging to the following category (“Stapler 
Devices”): 
- Regulation: 21 C.F.R. 878.4750 
- Classification Name: Implantable Staple 
- Product Code: GDW 
- Common Name: Surgical stapler with implantable staple; and 
Any other surgical stapler with a staple cartridge or reload intended to apply line of staples for 
resection, transection and/or creation of anastomosis whose Indication for Use includes 
applications on the lung and the digestive tracts including the stomach, intestines and rectum. 
1. Develop a set of standardized performance tests for retroactive assessment of the sealing (containment 
of organ content) performance of the Stapler Devices with focus on and in full consideration of the 
hitherto unrecognized risk factors associated with the designs of the Stapler Devices and the manner with 
which the Stapler Devices are used in the surgical field, as identified in the two prior Citizen Petitions 
submitted by the Petitioner; and 
2. Require the manufacturers of the Stapler Devices: (a) to conduct relevant tests from the set of 
standardized performance tests on their Stapler Devices currently in the market; (b) to make the results of 
the performance tests public in the forms including official reports to the FDA, academic articles in peer 
reviewed literatures and other appropriate means accessible by the public; and (c) to revise the labeling 
and Instruction for Use of the Stapler Devices to be in line with the findings of the performance tests 
conducted, as needed. 
B. Statement of Grounds 
 
Staple Line Leaks 
Postoperative air leak in staple line is a prevalent complication following lung surgery with significant 
healthcare cost implication.  Although not as frequent, postoperative gastrointestinal leak in staple line 
following surgeries in the digestive tracts is a complication that is important cause of morbidity and 
mortality.  There is little information available to help pinpoint how and why these apparent and often 
delayed mechanical failure of staple line, intraoperatively tested negative for defect and leak, occurs 
resulting in leakage of organ content.  However, one can say with certainty based on the principle of 
mechanics that the root cause of staple line failure can only be the dynamic tensile stress load (referred to 
as physiological load or physiological organ load in the following) acting on the staple line present on the 
wall of the host organ due to physiological organ motion, breathing/cough in the lung and digestion 
motion in the digestive tracts, in the absence of any other force acting on the staple line other than the 
static gravity with presumed harmful effect.  Barring spontaneous breakdown of staple line, for example, 
due to ischemia of stapled tissue, ultimately it has to be the mechanical action of stapled organ that 
disturbs the staple line and triggers leakage of organ content and/or drives degradation of the staple line 
and causes leakage of organ content over time. 
Unrecognized Risk Factors 
As are discussed in the two prior Citizen Petitions, in the administrative file, submitted by the Petitioner 
(1. https://www.regulations.gov/document?D=FDA-2017-P-4939 and 2. https://www.regulations.gov/ 
document?D=FDA-2018-P-3896) there exists no publically available records showing that the Stapler 
Devices have been designed with proper considerations of the risks presented by the risk factors identified 
in the two Citizen Petitions on the sealing (containment of organ content) performances of the Stapler 
Devices applied on the lung and the digestive tracts capable of physiological motions.   
There exists no publically available records, either, showing that the data from performance tests designed 
with proper considerations of the risks presented by the risk factors identified in the two Citizen Petitions 
on the sealing performances of the Stapler Devices applied on the lung and the digestive tracts have been 
requisite part of the 510(k) regulatory clearance reviews by the FDA for the Stapler Devices. The only 
performance test found in some of the 510(k) summaries for the Stapler Devices may be founded on an 
erroneous scientific premise (please see the Citizen Petitions cited above) and provides no bearing on the 
sealing performance of staple line applied on the lung or the digestive tracts. 
Probing Risks of Risk Factors – Retroactive Performance Tests 
The performance tests retroactively conducted would serve to: (a) expose, under controlled condition 
realistically simulating the field use conditions, problematic mechanical and physical effects that the risk 
factors could cause; and (b) help ascertain the sealing performance limitations the risk factors could 
impose on a staple line that may provide direct insight into the safety and effectiveness of the Stapler 
Devices in use on the lung and the digestive tracts.  A section in each of the Citizen Petitions is dedicated 
to exploring performance tests pertinent to the risk factors identified therein. 
Needs for and Benefits of Retroactive Performance Tests

II. 
Statement of Grounds 
 
A. Levothyroxine Sodium Drug Products are Widely Used to Treat Hypothyroidism 
 
Levothyroxine sodium is “the sodium salt of the levo isomer of the thyroid hormone 
thyroxine (T4).”1  Such hormones “affect protein, lipid, and carbohydrate metabolism; growth; 
and development.  They stimulate the consumption of most cells of the body, resulting in 
increased energy expenditure and heat production, and possess a cardiostimulatory effect that 
may be the result of a direct action on the heart.”2  This class of drugs is used to “treat 
hypothyroidism, as a thyroid replacement therapy, to suppress the growth of benign goiters and 
thyroid cancer, and as an adjunct to surgery and radioiodine therapy designed to manage some 
types of thyroid tumors.”3 
 
Hypothyroidism is a common condition.  According to the FDA 1 in every 4,000 to 5,000 
babies born in the United States is hypothyroid, and in adults, hypothyroidism has a prevalence 
of 0.5 percent to 1.3 percent.4  Moreover, because congenital hypothyroidism “may result in 
irreversible mental retardation, which can be avoided with early diagnosis and treatment, 
newborn screening for this disorder is mandatory in North America, Europe, and Japan.”5  A 
recent study finds that up to 7% of the general population has hypothyroidism.6  
 
Levothyroxine is the recommended form of thyroid hormone for the routine treatment of 
primary hypothyroidism by the American Thyroid Association7 and the American Association of 
Clinical Endocrinologists.8  Given the high prevalence of hypothyroidism in the general 
population, levothyroxine has been one of the most frequently prescribed medications in the 
United States; in 2017, approximately 122 million prescriptions were dispensed.9

B. Because Levothyroxine Is a Narrow Therapeutic Index Drug, Maintenance of 
Optimal Dosages of Levothyroxine for Individual Patients is Critical 
 
Thyroid replacement therapy is “usually a chronic, lifelong endeavor.” 10  A dosage for 
which an optimal response is achieved must be established for each patient individually.11  It is 
particularly important for patients to regularly take the correct dosages of levothyroxine sodium 
as levothyroxine sodium is a narrow therapeutic index (“NTI”) drug.  
 
FDA defines NTI drugs as “drugs where small differences in dose or blood concentration 
may lead to serious therapeutic failures and/or adverse drug reactions that are life-threatening or 
result in persistent or significant disability or incapacity.”12  In determining levothyroxine 
sodium to be a NTI drug, FDA based its conclusion on, amongst other evidence, the following: 
 
• The range between serum levothyroxine therapeutic and toxic concentrations is 
narrow; 
• Some levothyroxine-associated toxicities are serious and/or irreversible; and 
• Sub-therapeutic levothyroxine concentrations result in inadequate treatment and lead 
to poor clinical outcomes.13 
 
Indeed, some of the serious adverse events that have been found to occur from excessive or 
inadequate treatment with levothyroxine sodium include the recurrence of symptoms (e.g., 
severe depression, fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, edema, and difficulty 
concentrating), osteoporosis, cardiac angina, heart palpitations, atrial fibrillation, worsening of 
ischemic heart disease, preterm delivery in pregnancy, and hypercholesterolemia.  Patients found 
to be particularly susceptible include the elderly, pregnant women and their developing fetuses, 
and those with thyroid cancer.14   
 
Accordingly, it is critical for patients to regularly receive and take the correct dosages of 
levothyroxine, as “the active ingredient levothyroxine sodium is effective in treating 
hypothyroidism and is safe when carefully and consistently manufactured and stored, and 
prescribed in the correct amount to replace the deficiency of thyroid hormone in a particular 
patient.”15
