C. Regulatory History of Levothyroxine Sodium Products 
 
Over the past two decades, FDA has spent considerable resources to address historical 
issues related to levothyroxine sodium products marketed.  The actions that FDA took, as 
detailed below, ensured that patients were able to obtain the correct amount of levothyroxine 
sodium, and therefore, ensured the safety and efficacy of levothyroxine sodium products. 
 
Levothyroxine sodium was introduced into the market during the 1950’s without 
approval of new drug applications (“NDAs”).16  Between 1987 and 1994, FDA received 58 
adverse drug experience reports related to stability and potency of levothyroxine sodium 
products then on the market.17  Further, from 1990 to 1997, there were at least 10 recalls, 
involving 150 lots and more than 100 million tablets, of levothyroxine sodium products for 
inadequate content uniformity, subpotency, and/or stability failures.18  Because of these potency 
and stability problems, FDA declared levothyroxine sodium to be a “new drug” requiring NDA 
submission by August 14, 2000 for all currently marketed and any future levothyroxine sodium 
product.19  This compliance deadline was later extended by one year to August 14, 2001.20 
 
Moreover, in response to physician and patients concerns,21 particularly with regard to 
refills that may involve products from different manufacturers, the FDA examined the stability 
profiles of each levothyroxine sodium product then on the market, and in October 2007, 
mandated that levothyroxine sodium drug products tighten their potency specifications to meet a 
95 percent to 105 percent potency specification over their labeled shelf lives.22  Effective 
October 3, 2009, the United States Pharmacopeia (USP) revised the levothyroxine sodium 
monograph to reflect the narrowed potency specification.23

Drug products that FDA considers to be therapeutically equivalent to other 
pharmaceutically equivalent products for which actual or potential bioequivalence problems have 
been resolved with adequate in vivo and/or in vitro evidence supporting bioequivalence are 
designated “AB.”28  Conversely, the code “BX” is assigned to specific drug products for which 
the data that have been reviewed by the FDA are insufficient to determine therapeutic 
equivalence; such drug products are presumed to be therapeutically inequivalent until the FDA 
has determined that there is adequate information to make a full evaluation of therapeutic 
equivalence.29 
 
The Orange Book describes four “general criteria” that FDA uses to assign therapeutic 
equivalence ratings.  Specifically, FDA generally will rate drug products as therapeutically 
equivalent if the drugs are (1) pharmaceutically equivalent, (2) bioequivalent, (3) adequately 
labeled and (4) manufactured in accordance with current good manufacturing practices 
(cGMP).30   
 
Although FDA can often infer that two products “can be expected to have the same 
clinical effect and safety profile when administered to patients under the conditions specified in 
the labeling” because they fulfill the four “general criteria,” FDA has recognized that this 
approach is sometimes inappropriate.  FDA has stated that drug products meeting the four 
“general criteria” may nevertheless not warrant an “A” rating where the proposed product has 
“differences in packaging configurations, inactive ingredients, or other differences that have 
significant therapeutic implications or otherwise require additional clinical studies to establish 
safety and effectiveness.”31  For example, oral contraceptives packaged in 21-day packages 
without placebos and oral contraceptives packaged in 28-day packages with seven placebos are 
not therapeutically equivalent even though they each contain the same amount of the same active 
ingredient and have the same dosage form, strength and route of administration.32 
 
In the case of levothyroxine sodium tablet products, the manner in which Euthyrox 
tablets are supplied stands apart from all other levothyroxine sodium tablet products currently 
marketed and rated AB2 in the Orange Book.  Specifically, while the different strengths of 
Unithroid, Levo-T, Synthroid, and Mylan’s levothyroxine sodium tablets are differentiated and 
coded by color, all eleven dosage strengths of Euthyrox tablets are offered in the same color, as 
summarized in Table 1 below.

The consistency of color across the eleven dosage strengths of Euthyrox has significant 
therapeutic implications.  In particular, the lack of tablet color differentiation amongst dosage

may be confused if they are switched to an off-white product, causing them to miss doses or take 
too many tablets under the misimpression that they have been dispensed a 50 mcg strength.  
Indeed, a patient who is stable on a 200 mcg dosage strength could end up taking four times that 
amount if they mistakenly believe they have been dispensed the 50 mcg strength instead of their 
usual 200 mcg strength based upon the off-white color of all strengths of Euthyrox. 
 
We believe such risk to be significant because of the high likelihood that such errors 
would occur, given the high volume of levothyroxine sodium products being dispensed each 
year.  Further, we believe that such risks of “look-alike” medication errors cannot be adequately 
addressed solely by color-coded packaging alone, given the possibility of drug products 
becoming separated from the packaging (e.g., by patients using pill boxes).  More importantly, 
we believe any such medication error presents a significant risk to patients, given the narrow 
range between serum levothyroxine therapeutic and toxic concentrations, and the serious risks 
associated with overtreatment or undertreatment with levothyroxine sodium, as discussed above.

AB2 rating for Euthyrox contributes to the risk of “look-alike” medication errors as Euthyrox is

based upon the TE ratings listed in the Orange Book.

dosage strength.   
 
Accordingly, FDA should refrain from approving any sNDA for Euthyrox that requests 
addition of bulk or loose packaging configurations of non-color coded drug product where such 
applicant fails to submit data demonstrating that such packaging allows for safe use under the 
conditions set forth in the drug’s proposed labeling.43  Without such data, there would be 
insufficient data upon which FDA could determine whether approval would result in increased 
numbers of patients who received overtreatment or undertreatment of levothyroxine sodium due 
to otherwise preventable “look-alike” medication errors. 
 
F. Conclusion 
 
For the reasons described above, FDA should change all AB2 ratings for Euthyrox in the 
Orange Book to BX ratings.  FDA should further refrain from approving any supplements 
received for Euthyrox that request the addition of bulk or loose packaging configurations of non-
color coded tablets without sufficient data to demonstrate that such packaging allows for safe use 
of the product under the conditions set forth in the drug’s proposed labeling.  We believe such 
actions to be consistent with FDA’s continued efforts to ensure that patients obtain the correct 
amount of levothyroxine sodium, and to therefore, ensure the safety and efficacy of these 
products. 
 
III. 
Environmental Impact 
 
The actions requested herein are subject to categorical exclusion under 21 C.F.R. § 25.31.

Economic Impact 
 
Pursuant to 21 C.F.R. § 10.30(b), petitioner will submit economic information upon the 
request of the Commissioner.

Citizen Petition led by Dental Professionals 
 
 
Dr. Greg Grillo, DDS and the more than 375 dentists, registered dental hygienists, 
dental assistants, and other citizens listed online at 
https://www.gopetition.com/signatures/stop-sales-of-seven-dangerously-acidic-dry-
mouth-products.html hereby submit this Citizen Petition pursuant to the Federal Food, 
Drug and Cosmetic Act (“FDC Act”) in accordance with 21 C.F.R. §§ 10.25(a) and 
10.30. 
 
I. 
ACTION REQUESTED 
The dental professionals and other citizens request that the US FDA regulate oral 
moisturizer products that are marketed for mitigation, treatment or prevention of dry 
mouth and that linger in the mouth.  The FDA should require that these products be 
regulated as either drugs or devices under the provisions of the FDC Act and require 
proper formulation of these products to assure their safety.  This action is necessary to 
prevent the continued marketing of oral moisturizer products for dry mouth that have a 
pH below the critical pH of tooth enamel and root dentin which can lead to serious dental 
health problems including tooth demineralization, tooth erosion, and dental caries. 
Specific oral moisturizer products presently known to be dangerously acidic and 
erosive of teeth include: 
- OraMoist, by Dentek (2.9 pH) 
- Mouth Kote, by Parnell (3.0 pH) 
- Cotton Mouth Lozenges, by Cotton Mouth Candy Co (3.1 pH) 
- MedActive Oral Relief Lozenges (3.2 pH) 
- Hager Pharma Dry Mouth Drops (4.4 pH) 
- Rite Aid Dry Mouth Discs (5.1 pH) 
- CVS Health Dry Mouth Discs (5.3 pH) 
 
2 
 
II. 
STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
 
Dry Mouth, technically known as xerostomia, is a self-perception of insufficient 
saliva that afflicts about 25% of the population as an effect of medications, systemic 
diseases, or cancer therapy.  Oral moisturizers are used to alleviate dry mouth by 
lingering in the mouth, moisturizing or stimulating saliva production, and lubricating.  
Chronic xerostomia significantly increases the risk of dental caries, demineralization, 
tooth sensitivity, dental erosion, candidiasis, and other oral diseases that negatively affect 
quality of life.  Products that linger in the mouth and are marketed to address dry mouth 
must not present a secondary effect that can harm oral health.   
 
In August 2017, university researchers Delgado and Olafsson at the University of 
Florida College and the University of North Carolina published through NIH an article 
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5546593/ reporting that, to be safe, 
depending on formulation, oral moisturizers should have an acidity level of about 6.7 pH 
or higher and that all oral moisturizers with a pH below 5.5 are dangerous, citing one 
with a pH of 3.0. 
 
In March 2018, with additional authors, the university researchers published tests 
of more oral moisturizers including measures of erosion. 
https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0035/3832/files/Delgado_AADR_2018_Acidity_of_dry
_mouth_lozenges.pdf?10451805702918068836  
 
In the August 2017 NIH publication, Delgado and Olafsson succinctly point out 
the illogic of permitting the marketing of products intended to improve oral health that 
have the opposite effect: 
Manufacturers recommend using oral moisturizers as needed through the day, and 
some products are even intended for swishing or being held in the mouth for as 
long as possible for the maximum effect.  This would seem counter-intuitive if the 
products are acidic, considering the vulnerability of the target group to dental 
erosion and root caries.  For this reason, care should be taken to formulate these 
products with safe pH values for both enamel and root dentin which, based on 
specific formulation, should be around 6.7 or higher. 
 
 
The FDC Act regulatory status of products that are currently on the market 
intended to address xerostomia by lingering in the mouth is often obscure, with most, if 
not all, failing to meet the requirements for a legal drug or device.  The undersigned 
request that the FDA address this public health issue by requiring, through the exercise of

the agency’s drug and device approval authority, that these products be formulated to 
assure their safety.

ECONOMIC IMPACT

submitted only when requested by the Commissioner following review of the petition.  
Petitioner hereby commits to promptly provide this information, if so requested.

Konjac flour, made from the Amorphophallus konjac globose tuber native to Southeast Asia, is 
distributed commercially throughout the Far East as a food ingredient.  Part of Japanese and Chinese 
diets for 1500 years, it is currently consumed in the United States in authentic Asian cuisine.  The Food 
Lawyers® request that konjac flour be included in 21 C.F.R. §101.9(c)(6)(i)’s list of dietary fibers 
because it is an isolated nondigestible carbohydrate providing human physiological benefit recognized 
by FDA.  
 
A. Action Requested 
 
The Food Lawyers® petitions under 21 C.F.R. §10.30 of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act 
requesting The Commissioner of Food and Drugs to engage in rulemaking to amend 21 C.F.R. 
§101.9(c)(6)(i) to include konjac flour, also known as konjac glucomannan, in the regulation’s list of 
dietary fibers.

B. Statement of Grounds 
 
i. Regulatory Requirements Regarding Dietary Fiber 
 
21 C.F.R. §101.9(c)(6)(i) in pertinent part defines dietary fiber as:  “… isolated … non-
digestible carbohydrates (with 3 or more monomeric units) determined by FDA to have 
physiological effects that are beneficial to human health.”  
 
ii. Manufacture of Konjac Flour 
The konjac tuber is ground and milled whereafter alcohol precipitation is used to remove 
starches, protein, cellulose, and low molecular weight sugars to isolate the glucomannan 
which is a water-soluble polysaccharide that is a hemicellulose component in the 
Amorphophallus konjac cell walls (Yang, et al (2017))1.  As such, konjac flour is an isolated 
carbohydrate for purposes of 21 C.F.R. §101.9(c)(6)(i). 
 
iii. Chemical Structure And Nondigestibility of Konjac Flour 
 
 
Konjac Flour is approximately 85% glucomannan.  Glucomannan derived from 
Amorphophallus konjac is composed of β-1,4 linked D-glucose and D-mannose residues 
typically in a ratio of 1.6 mannose to glucose.  As β-1, 4 linkages cannot be hydrolyzed by 
human amylases, konjac Glucomannan passes into the colon unchanged.  The average DP is 
6200 and molecular weight ranges from 200-2000 coda (Tester & Al-Ghazzewi, (2016) 
Glucomannans and nutrition, Food Hydrocolloids journal (2016) 1-9).2 
 
For the foregoing reasons, konjac flour is an isolated non-digestible carbohydrate with 3 or more 
monomeric units. 
 
iv. Konjac flour consumption provides physiological effects determined by FDA to be 
beneficial to human health: Reduction of blood lipids in the form of LDL cholesterol and 
Increased daily fecal weight. 
 
a. Konjac flour consumption provides significant lowering of blood lipids. 
The following peer-reviewed scientific journal articles provide clinical evidence that 
konjac flour consumption significantly lowers blood lipids.

Petitioner is aware of only one study which is contraindicative of the cholesterol 
lowering benefits of glucomannan demonstrated above, and that study acknowledges 
a flaw in execution to account for the outlying result.   
 
Vido et al. (1993) did not observe a statistically significant difference in 
normal cholesterol level obese children treated with glucomannan capsules 
consistent with other studies.8  This anomalous result, as Vido et al. (1993)

 
Vido, et al. (1993) was one of 14 studies included in a meta-analysis reported

Conclusion – The reliability of Vido, et al (1993)’s contraindicative result is undercut 
by the authors’ speculation of non-compliance with the study design due to

b. Konjac flour consumption results in significantly improved laxation (elimination of 
fecal waste through increased daily stool bulk) 
The following peer-reviewed scientific journal article provides clinical evidence that 
konjac flour consumption significantly increases defecation frequency. 
 
i.) Chen, et al (2006) Konjac acts as a natural laxative by increasing daily stool bulk 
and improving colonic ecology in healthy adults. Nutrition 22, 1112-111910 
 
 
8 healthy adults (1 man, 7 women) with low dietary fiber intake (<20 g/day) 
participated in a study of konjac glucomannan consumption of 4.5 g/day after

 
The placebo controlled, single-blind, diet controlled study consisted of a 21-

 
The Konjac glucomannan supplement significantly increased the mean 
defecation frequency (number/day), wet stool weight and dry stool weight 
(g/d), ~27.0% (P<0.05), 30.2% (P < 0.05) and 21.7% (P < 0.05), respectively,

Conclusion – The results of this study demonstrate the FDA accepted physiological 
benefits associated with dietary fiber of increased defecation frequency and increased

The foregoing evidence demonstrates that konjac flour, also called konjac glucomannan, is an

A. Action Requested 
Bonumose LLC requests the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to amend 21 CFR § 101.9, 
Nutrition Labeling of Food. Specifically, we request to exempt D-tagatose from its classification 
as an added sugar on the Nutrition Facts Panel on foods and beverages (21 CFR § 
101.9(c)(6)(iii)) and amend the regulation to include a voluntary labeling of D-tagatose, similar to 
that which is provided for sugar alcohols (21 CFR § 101.9(c)(6)(iv)). Information supporting this 
petition is enclosed and is summarized by the following points: 
 
1. D-tagatose does not increase risk for chronic disease. Instead, it is associated with a 
number of positive health outcomes including an increase in glycemic control, 
reduction in risk for tooth decay, function as a prebiotic, and reduction in risk for 
cardiovascular disease (CVD). 
2. Inconsistent methodology has been used to define “added sugars” and regulate their 
labeling. 
3. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar conflicts with FDA rationale regarding 
the purpose of mandatory added sugar labeling. 
4. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar is misrepresentative because there is 
no evidence supporting a link between D-tagatose and chronic disease. It also 
results in an inaccurate label that could confuse consumers. 
5. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar contradicts the spirit of recognized 
health claims. 
Background 
 
Bonumose LLC is a food ingredient manufacturer specializing in the affordable 
production of natural rare hexoses. These sugars have significant beneficial health attributes yet 
retain the favorable taste and technical properties of more commonly consumed sugars. Our 
company’s purpose is to offer affordable ingredients that enable food and beverage 
manufacturers to produce healthy, delicious products without driving up prices. We highly value 
efforts to provide accurate, reliable information to the public via nutrition labeling, including 
information that could help consumers choose healthy rare sugars that are both palatable and 
functional enough to improve public health. 
 
D-tagatose is a monosaccharide that provides a sweet taste and can be used to replace 
more commonly used sugars such as sucrose and HFCS for a variety of food applications 
(Muddada 2012). In addition to its use as a sweetener, D-tagatose can also be used in foods as 
a humectant, texturizer or stabilizer (FDA 2001). It is only partially digested in the small intestine 
(Laerke and Jensen 1999; Bertelsen, Jensen, and Buemann 1999; Saunders, Zehner, and 
Levin 1999) and undergoes fermentation in the large intestine to produce short-chain fatty acids 
(Bertelsen, Jensen, and Buemann 1999; Vigh and Andersen 2007). D-tagatose maintains its 
sweetness and nutritive value at all food use levels. 
 
Uses of D-tagatose in foods and beverages were recognized as GRAS on October 25, 
2001 (Arla Foods Ingredients 2001; FDA 2001) and on February 1, 2011 (CJ Cheiljedang 2011;

A compilation of data from the U.S., European Union, Australia and New Zealand estimates 
that the average consumption of D-tagatose in adults ranges from 3-9 g/day, with those 
consumers at the 95th percentile consuming up to 18 g/day (Food and Agriculture Organization 
& World Health Organization 2006). Reports that are restricted to U.S. data (USDA Continuing 
Survey of Food Intakes by Individuals, 1994-96) estimate the mean consumption to be 8.9

g/day, excluding use in chewing gum and dietary and meal supplements. The 90th percentile of 
this population consumed 18 g/day (VonApeldoorn and Speijers 2001). This consumption 
occurs as a sweetener ingredient in food preparations, (often replacing sucrose) rather than as 
a stand-alone item.   
 
B. Statement of Grounds 
Rationale Summary: 
 
 
The most recent revision of the Nutrition Facts Panel includes a mandatory declaration 
of added sugars that “is necessary to assist consumers to maintain healthy dietary practices, 
and we proposed to require the declaration of the amount of added sugars in a serving of a 
product” (81 FR 33742 at 33799). Also mandatory is a declaration of the % Daily Value (%DV) 
of those added sugars in a serving of food (relative to a Dietary Reference Value (DRV) of 10 
percent of calories) to “assist consumers in constructing a healthy dietary pattern” (81 FR 33742 
at 33800). These mandatory declarations are the result of FDA’s  determination that high added 
sugar intake may be associated with increased risk for chronic disease. The presence of such a 
relationship, as well as the contribution of traditional sugars to total caloric intake, are inherently 
physiological parameters. For the purposes of maintaining an accurate, informative label that 
will help consumers make sound dietary choices, it is only logical that the “added sugars” 
referred to on the label do not include monosaccharides such as D-tagatose that do not have 
physiological properties that increase risk for chronic disease. 
 
 
D-tagatose is a naturally-occurring, rare monosaccharide that does not increase risk for 
chronic disease, nor does it share similar metabolic and physiologic characteristics with 
traditional sugars. D-tagatose consumption is associated with numerous health benefits, and, 
along with other naturally-occurring rare monosaccharides, is grossly misrepresented when 
classified as an added sugar. Inclusion in this category not only conflicts with FDA labeling 
rationale but results in an inaccurate label that could confuse consumers and complicate dietary 
decisions. 
 
 
Our rationale supporting this petition is described in detail below, but can be summarized 
by the following statements: 
 
1. D-tagatose does not increase risk for chronic disease. Instead, it is associated 
with a number of positive health outcomes including an increase in glycemic 
control, reduction in risk for tooth decay, function as a prebiotic and reduction 
in risk for CVD. 
2. Inconsistent methodology has been used to define “added sugars” and 
regulate its labeling. 
3. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar conflicts with FDA rationale 
regarding the purpose of mandatory added sugar labeling.

4. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar is misrepresentative because 
there is no evidence supporting a link between D-tagatose and chronic 
disease.  It also results in an inaccurate label that could confuse consumers. 
5. Classification of D-tagatose as an added sugar contradicts the spirit of 
recognized health claims. 
Finally, we propose a revision to 21 CFR § 101.9(c) to enhance the ability of the Nutrition Facts 
Panel to effectively communicate nutrition information and aid consumers in choosing healthy 
dietary practices.

D-tagatose improves glycemic control through its effects on post-prandial blood 
glucose levels, fasting glucose levels, fasting insulin levels and levels of HbA1c. 
• 
D-tagatose contributes to the maintenance of tooth mineralization and may 
reduce risk for tooth decay. 
• 
D-tagatose functions as a prebiotic. 
• 
D-tagatose may reduce CVD risk in at-risk individuals through its effects on 
dyslipidemia, GLP-1 and weight gain. 
• 
D-tagatose may improve/maintain hematopoiesis and clotting. 
• 
D-tagatose may function as an antioxidant against iron-induced damage. 
 
 
 
  
10 
 
Several of the physiological characteristics of D-tagatose, in comparison to other 
sweeteners, are included in Table 9. As described in detail in Appendix 1 and summarized in 
Table 9, D-tagatose has a similar taste profile as sucrose but has very different metabolic 
actions. Not only does D-tagatose has a lower caloric value and glycemic index compared to 
other monosaccharides in Table 9 such as glucose and fructose, but also functions as a 
noncariogenic prebiotic. A similar comparison can be made to the disaccharides sucrose, 
lactose and maltose. Furthermore, common sweeteners such as honey, agave syrup, maple 
syrup, corn syrup and HFCS consist of glucose, fructose, sucrose, or combinations thereof. 
None of these common sweeteners include rare hexoses. In addition to D-tagatose, Table 9 
includes D-allulose (D-psicose), another rare hexose with an even lower caloric value and 
glycemic index than D-tagatose. There is limited evidence suggesting that D-allulose may also 
function as a prebiotic, although more research is needed to verify this finding. Also included on 
Table 9 are the sugar alcohols xylitol and lactitol, which share many characteristics of D-
tagatose including a low caloric value and glycemic index and are noncariogenic. Similar to D-
allulose, there is limited evidence suggesting that they may also function as prebiotics, but the 
body of evidence supporting this relationship is not as strong as it is for D-tagatose.

Chapter 1 
Overview 
Background 
The Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA) have been updated in 2010 [1] and 
translated into messages and tips for making healthful food choices [2].  The DGA 
2010 formed the basis for revisions to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) 
Food Patterns (FP).  The Food Patterns provide calorie-based dietary guidance on 
how much Americans should eat from each of the FP components such as Fruit, 
Vegetables, Grains, Protein Foods, Dairy, and Oils to have a healthful diet, while 
simultaneously placing limits on the amounts of added sugars, solid fats, and 
alcoholic drinks that can be consumed.  
The Federal Government, as part of its ongoing nutrition monitoring and 
surveillance activities conducts the What We Eat in America (WWEIA) survey, 
which is the dietary intake component of the National Health and Nutrition 
Examination Survey (NHANES) [3].  The WWEIA, NHANES is a continuous 
survey and is conducted by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the 
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).  The survey uses 24-hour 
dietary recall method to collect data on the types and amounts of foods and 
beverages Americans report that they consume.  The Food and Nutrient Database 
for Dietary Studies 4.1 (FNDDS 4. 1) [4] provides nutrient composition of the 
7,000+ foods and beverages in WWEIA, NHANES [3].  In order to monitor 
whether Americans meet the recommendations of the DGA 2010, the foods in 
FNDDS must be first converted to the respective amounts of FP equivalents 
present in them. 
Why Develop the Food Patterns Equivalents Database? 
Single ingredient FNDDS foods such as orange juice, baked potato, cooked rice, 
baked fish, or skim milk can be directly assigned to Fruit, Vegetables, Grains, 
Protein Foods, and Dairy components, respectively. However, many of the 
FNDDS foods such as pizza, sandwich, fruit salad, chocolate milk shake, fried 
eggs, and casserole are multi-ingredient foods consisting of ingredients that are 
from more than one FP component.  Hence, it is necessary to disaggregate multi-
ingredient foods to ingredients that can be assigned to an FP component before 
computing the amount of FP equivalents present in the food.  The Food Patterns 
Equivalents Database (FPED) serves this purpose by converting foods that are in 
the forms reported consumed to appropriate Food Patterns equivalents amounts, 
thereby providing means to assess the adherence of American diets to the DGA 
recommendations. 
 
 
9 
 
What is Food Patterns Equivalents Database? 
Food Patterns Equivalents Database is the new name for the former MyPyramid 
Equivalents Database (MPED) [5] developed by USDA, Agricultural Research 
Service (ARS), Food Surveys Research Group (FSRG).  The FPED converts FNDDS 
foods to the respective number of cup equivalents of Fruit, Vegetables, and Dairy; 
ounce equivalents of Grains and Protein Foods; number of Alcoholic Drinks; 
teaspoon equivalents of Added Sugars; and gram equivalents of Solid Fats and 
Oils.  Foods in FNDDS 5 are disaggregated to ingredients that can be directly 
assigned to one of the FP components.  Additionally, protein foods are further 
disaggregated to lean fraction and fat. Meat and poultry are disaggregated to lean 
meat and solid fat fractions; dairy foods to low fat fraction, similar to skim milk, 
and solid fat fraction; and seafood and nuts to lean and oil fractions.  
 
In addition, the FPED release includes a Food Patterns Equivalents Ingredients 
Database (FPID) that is similar to FPED for the unique ingredients of FNDDS 
foods.  A few applications of FPID are described in this section. 
What is Food Patterns Equivalents Ingredients Database? 
The FNDDS SR-Links file includes data on the ingredients and the amounts 
present in each of the FNDDS foods (includes beverages). A majority of the 
FNDDS 5 foods are multi-ingredient and are composed of various combinations of 
about 2800+ Standard Reference (SR) foods that form the unique ingredients of 
FNDDS 5 foods.  For the first time, a separate database named Food Patterns 
Equivalents Ingredients Database (FPID) has been developed for these unique 
ingredients. The FP equivalent amounts of FPID ingredients are then applied to 
foods in the FNDDS SR-links file to create FPED. Details on FPID and FPED 
development are described in the later sections.  
 
The methodology for the development of FPED and FPID are essentially the same. 
The FPED includes the amounts of the 37 FP components per 100 grams of each of 
the FNDDS foods, and FPID includes the amounts of the 37 FP components per 
100 grams of each of the unique ingredients of FNDDS foods.  
 
Uses of Food Patterns Equivalents Ingredients Database 
 
The FPID has the potential for many research, economic, and policy applications.  
A few of the major applications of FPID are listed below. 
• Because FPID is ingredient-based, it can be used to estimate the amount of 
FP components present in foods in general, where recipes are available.  
FPID serves as a tool to estimate the amounts of FP components consumed 
by participants of dietary studies.  Additionally, because FPID is used to 
create FPED for foods reported in the national dietary surveys, the dietary 
10 
 
status of the study populations is comparable to that of the national 
population.    
• FPID in combination with ARS Food Intakes Converted to Retail 
Commodities Databases (FICRCDs) [6] can be used to estimate the amounts 
of raw, frozen, or canned fruits and vegetables commodities to be 
purchased to meet the DGA recommendations.  To estimate the amounts of 
raw fruits and vegetables to be purchased, it is necessary to convert fruits 
and vegetables from their consumed forms to purchased forms, which 
include peel, seeds and other refuse. FICRCDs include conversion factors 
that convert fruits and vegetable from consumed forms to purchased forms.  
FICRCDs also include conversion factors to convert cooked grains, legumes, 
meat, poultry, and fish to their respective uncooked or raw forms.  
Appendices 8-11 of this document [FPED 2009-10 Methodology and User 
Guide] include the weights of 1 cup equivalents for many fruits, vegetables, 
and dairy foods that are ingredients of FNDDS foods. 
• The FPID can serve as a resource for estimating the cost of meeting DGA 
recommendations for fruits and vegetable and other food commodities. By 
pricing the commodities, the cost (price) of nutritious food choices can be 
estimated.  
 
The following two examples illustrate the use of FPID cup equivalent weights and 
FICRCD conversion factors in combination to estimate: (1) the amount of raw 
broccoli and cantaloupe commodities to be purchased to obtain one cup equivalent 
of each; (2) the cost (price) of one cup equivalent of raw broccoli and cantaloupe;

Citizen Petition 
 
Panera, LLC (“Panera”) submits this petition under sections 401, 403 and 371 of the Federal Food, Drug, 
and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C 401,403,371) to request the Commissioner of Food and Drugs to amend 21 
CFR 160.100 to clearly define the standard of identity for the term “egg” on the grounds that it would 
promote honest and fair labeling and naming of food products for sale within retailers and foodservice.   
 
A. ACTION REQUESTED 
Panera, LLC proposes that the FDA take the following actions:  
• 
Amend 21 CFR 160.100 to clearly define the term “egg” to reflect a food made from a cracked 
shell egg without addition of additives or further processing (other than pasteurization or other 
treatment to destroy all viable Salmonella microorganisms from the shell egg).  
21 CFR 160.100 currently states:  
No regulation shall be promulgated fixing and establishing a reasonable definition and standard 
of identity for the food commonly known as eggs.  
Subsequent subparts list definitions for alternative egg terms such as egg whites, liquid eggs, and 
frozen egg yolks but do not define the term “egg” or “shell egg”.  
• 
Amend 21 CFR 101.4 to prohibit egg products that contain additives to be labeled under the 
term “egg”, “egg whites” or “egg yolks”. 21 CFR 101.4 (b)(10), (11) and (12) permit egg products 
as defined in 21 CFR 160.105, 21 CFR 160.110, 21 CFR 160.115, 21 CFR 160.140, 21 CFR 160.145, 
21 CFR 160.150, 21 CFR 160.180, 21 CFR 160.185, and 21 CFR 160.190   to be declared as “eggs”, 
“egg whites” or “egg yolks”. Within 21 CFR 160.105, 21 CFR 160.110, 21 CFR 160.115, 21 CFR 
160.140, 21 CFR 160.145, 21 CFR 160.150, 21 CFR 160.180, 21 CFR 160.185, and 21 CFR 160.190 
many of these egg products are permitted to contain various additives such as anti-caking 
agents, whipping agents or preservatives.  
 
 Panera, LLC    3630 South Geyer Road, Suite 100    St. Louis, MO 63127 
Page 2 of 4 
 
21 CFR 101.4 (b)(10), (11) and (12) currently states:  
 
(10) Dried whole eggs, frozen whole eggs, and liquid whole eggs may be declared as "eggs". 
(11) Dried egg whites, frozen egg whites, and liquid egg whites may be declared as "egg whites". 
(12) Dried egg yolks, frozen egg yolks, and liquid egg yolks may be declared as "egg yolks". 
 
An example excerpt from 21 CFR 160.110 is as follows, emphasize added:  
 Frozen Eggs  
a) Frozen eggs, frozen whole eggs, frozen mixed eggs is the food prepared by freezing liquid 
eggs that conform to 160.115, with such precautions that the finished food is free of 
viable Salmonella microorganisms. 
(b) Monosodium phosphate or monopotassium phosphate may be added either directly or in a 
water carrier, but the amount added does not exceed 0.5 percent of the weight of the frozen 
eggs. If a water carrier is used, it shall contain not less than 50 percent by weight of such 
monosodium phosphate or monopotassium phosphate. 
 
 
B. STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
Panera is a national restaurant chain with more than 2,060 bakery-cafes in 46 states and Ontario, 
Canada, operating under the Panera Bread® and Saint Louis Bread Co® names.  
 
Within each of our Panera bakery-cafes we operate multiple businesses, including a traditional bakery 
with baked goods on display; breakfast, lunch and dinner eat-in and to-go businesses; catering 
operations; and cafe-based delivery. In addition, Panera operates a retail food business, selling sliced 
breads, salad dressings, coffee and soups in grocers nationwide. We point this out to emphasize the 
variety of ways consumers can access Panera products. For this reason, complying with any mandated 
labeling laws, including standard of identity, impacts both our in-cafe grab-and-go business and our 
consumer packaged goods business. Our brand uses the CFR to create our retail labels and nutrition 
facts panels, but we also use it to inform and guide our selection of product names and menu 
descriptions. 
 
Prior to launching a new line of breakfast sandwiches, we evaluated not only our own ingredient 
statements, product names, product descriptions and the CFR for eggs and egg products but also those 
of competitors within retail food and foodservice. We chose to use “egg” in the name of our breakfast 
sandwiches because we use a whole, shell egg to craft them. But we found that some foodservice and 
retail competitors use the same term, “egg,” within their product names and product descriptions to 
describe menu items that contain egg patties or egg products containing food additives ranging from 
preservatives to colors to emulsifiers.  
 
 
 Panera, LLC    3630 South Geyer Road, Suite 100    St. Louis, MO 63127

We believe these uses of the term “egg” within the product name and product descriptions to be 
potentially confusing to the consumer.  Our interpretation of the term “egg” is a prepared whole, shell 
egg without additives. However, because, the term “egg” has no definition under 21 CFR 160.100, 
neither Panera nor our competitors have a basis for evaluating the use of the term. Further, as many 
place a food order based on product name or description only (without viewing any ingredient 
information), consumers may order an “egg” yet receive an “egg product”. Under 21 CFR 130.5(b), it is 
stated “any petition for a food standard shall show that the proposal, if adopted, would promote 
honesty and fair dealing in the interest of consumers.” With that in mind, we urge the FDA to evaluate 
the term “egg” and amend 21 CFR 160.100 to offer a clear, concise standard of identity. 
 
Panera proposes adoption of the definition that is found within the Egg Inspection Act (9 CFR 590.1) 
definition section where the term egg is defined as:  
 
“Egg means the shell egg of the domesticated chicken, turkey, duck, goose, or guinea.”  
 
And we propose the addition of the following statement: 
 
The egg shall have no additives. The egg shall have no processing beyond any processing taken to ensure 
that the finished food is free of viable Salmonella microorganisms (i.e. in shell pasteurization). 
 
In addition to the proposed definition, we propose that 21 CFR 101.4 (b)(10), (11) and (12) are amended

safety and/or those used for transportation, i.e., freezing whole eggs. We propose those products that

CITIZEN PETITION 
Re: Generic Drug Products Equivalent to Efudex® (fluorouracil cream, 5%) 
The undersigned, Spear Pharmaceuticals, Inc. ("Spear"), submits this Citizen Petition 
under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act ("FDCA" or "the Act") (21 
U.S.C. § 355) and FDA regulations 21 C.F.R. §§ 10.20, 10.30, 320.1, and 320.22-24. 
I. 
ACTION REQUESTED 
Spear respectfully requests that the Food and Drug Administration ("FDA") reaffirm its 
earlier decision to apply bioequivalence requirements consistent with 21 C.F.R. § 320.24(b)(4) 
( comparative clinical efficacy trials appropriate for topical products) to any new abbreviated new 
drug application ("ANDA") seeking regulatory approval of a topical generic drug product that 
references Valeant Pharmaceuticals Intemational's ("Valeant") product Efudex® (fluorouracil 
cream, 5%) ("Efudex®") as its reference listed drug ("RLD"). There are currently three generic 
versions ofEfudex® on the market today. Two of those (including one sold by Spear) are 
ANDA products that were approved by the FDA on the basis of the successful completion of 
clinical efficacy trials in patients with actinic keratosis. The third is what is commonly referred 
to as an "authorized generic" manufactured by Valeant under its NDA and that is sold by Mylan 
Inc. ("Mylan"). 
On October 20, 2017, the FDA held a public workshop to discuss "Topical 
Dermatological Generic Drug Products: Overcoming Barriers to Development and Improving 
Patient Access." The goal of the workshop was to discuss in vitro and in vivo methods of 
characterizing topical products and to compare topical bioavailability without using comparative 
clinical trials in patients. The FD A's concern stems from the general lack of generic equivalents 
for a number of topical drugs- particularly ones that do not have a generic equivalent at all. 
1 
dermidentical "' 
www.SpearPharma.com 
 
 
 
 
 
2 
 
Pharmacokinetic studies cannot easily be done with topical medications that are not systemically 
absorbed, and therefore clinical trials have historically been the gold standard for testing 
bioequivalence of topical drugs.  The FDA has asked for input and feedback from the industry to 
identify which products should be a priority for the FDA to examine and recommend alternative 
bioequivalence pathways. 
Efudex® should not be a priority for alternative bioequivalence pathways for a number of 
important reasons. 
First, there are already three (3) approved generic versions of Efudex® (fluorouracil 
cream, 5%).  Spear and Taro Pharmaceuticals U.S.A., Inc. (“Taro”) each market a generic 
version of Efudex®, and Mylan sells an authorized generic of the same drug.  These three 
products account for 99.8% of all Efudex® sales.1  This 99.8% figure is substantially above the 
national average in 2016 for penetration of all generic drugs at 89%.2   (More broadly, sales of 
generic 5-fluorouracil topical products generally represent approximately 91% of sales in the 
whole actinic keratosis market.)  While Spear agrees that in general there is a need for more and 
faster generic approvals of topical drugs, the FDA’s resources are better served targeting drugs 
with no generic equivalents (or fewer generic equivalents) as candidates for in vitro 
bioequivalence pathways.  With three generic Efudex® products (constituting 99.8% of all 
prescriptions filled) already on the market, there is no need for an alternative approval pathway 
for this product.   
Second, 5-fluorouracil is a cytotoxic drug which can result in severe side effects if a 
patient is over-exposed to the drug.  No in vitro studies have been correlated with or shown to be 
predictive of human in vivo bioavailability.  Therefore, a clinical trial is the only true way to test 
bioequivalence of a generic Efudex® product, and to be sure its side effects and their severity are 
no worse than the RLD.  The side effect profile for Efudex® is lengthy and includes skin 
erosions, ulceration (destruction of epidermis), and permanent scarring.  To allow a generic 
Efudex® product to enter the market without a clinical trial is to risk severe and irreversible side 
effects in patients treated with that generic drug when it enters the market. As pointed out by the 
FDA in the current draft guidance for 5% 5-fluorouracil cream, it is important to compare the 
proposed ANDA product to the RLD with respect to side effects.  The FDA states: “All adverse 
events (AEs) should be reported….This information is needed to determine if the incidence and 
severity of adverse reactions is different between the test product and RLD.”3  
                                                           
1 IMS NPA Data, IQVIA (available at https://www.iqvia.com/) (last accessed Jan. 18, 2018). 
2 Sam Raney, The Journey from Developing the Research Studies to Drafting a New Regulatory 
Standard, FDA Public Workshop, at 5 (Oct. 20, 2017). 
3 U.S. Food and Drug Admin., Draft Guidance on Fluorouracil, at 3 (2011) (emphasis added). 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
Third, Efudex® is a topical chemotherapy treatment that is used to treat actinic 
keratosis, a precursor to squamous cell carcinoma (“SCC”), a non-melanoma skin cancer.  The 
American Academy of Dermatology reports that the risk of transformation of an actinic 
keratosis to SCC within one year is about 8% (with a range of 0.025% to 20%).4  “Patients 
with actinic keratosis, especially [w]hite men and the elderly, have a sixfold increased odds of 
developing non-melanoma or melanoma skin cancer.”5  While SCC is not the most common 
non-melanoma skin cancer, it accounts “for the majority of NMSC [non-melanoma skin cancer]-
related metastatic disease and death, and are reported to be within the top five most costly 
cancers in the United States.”6  As such, it is essential that a validated and reliable 
bioequivalence method is used for the approval of generic Efudex® products, so that only 
products with comparable efficacy to the RLD are used for the treatment of actinic keratosis. 
Fourth, clinical trials of Efudex® generics have been successfully conducted by at 
least two companies.  Specifically, Spear and Taro each successfully completed clinical trials 
that allowed for FDA approval in April 2008 for Spear, and in March 2010 for Taro, for their 
generic Efudex® products.  Spear tested its generic Efudex® product in a double-blind, placebo-
controlled comparative trial enrolling 318 actinic keratosis patients, which showed 
bioequivalence and found no difference between the Spear product and Efudex® for irritation.  
Taro did a similar double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial in patients with actinic keratosis 
to prove bioequivalence, including (presumably) side effect profiles and efficacy as required by 
the draft FDA guidance of 2010. This shows that the requirement of conducting comparative 
clinical trial in subjects with actinic keratosis is not a significant barrier to approval of generic 
Efudex® products.  Since we know that these trials can be done successfully (as is evidenced by 
the Spear and Taro trials), they should therefore continue to be required. Thus, there is no need 
for an alternative pathway for this drug.   
Fifth, the proposed in vitro permeation testing (“IVPT”) (which measures drug absorption 
across excised or cadaver human skin) produces concerning variability.  IVPT does not study 
the absorption of drug over typical actinic keratosis skin.  Skin thickness, which affects drug 
permeation, varies with age, whether it is diseased, and its anatomical location.7  For example, 
with age, the epidermis becomes thinner, and the composition and function of the skin changes 
in terms of, for example, its cellular structure and lipid content.8    Excised and cadaver skin also 
lacks the metabolic and capillary functions of in vivo skin, which also affect the actual amount of

5 Spencer M. Vale et al., Pharmacoeconomic Considerations in Treating Actinic Keratosis: An 
Update, PharmacoEconomics 35:177-190, at 178 (2017). 
6 Valerie R. Yanofsky, Histopathological Variants of Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A 
Review, J. of Skin Cancer, at 1 (2011).

drug delivered to the site of action in living skin.9  When dealing with a cytotoxic drug such as 5-
fluorouracil that can cause severe side effects and is used to treat a precursor to potentially fatal 
cancer, it is particularly important that a comparative clinical trial—which is doable for this 
drug—be required.  A clinical trial, which tests the drug on actual actinic keratosis patients, will 
more accurately estimate the rate and extent of absorption of Efudex® in the target population.  
An in vitro bioequivalence method might under- or over-estimate the amount of drug delivered 
to the skin, and might lead to the approval of a generic version of Efudex® that will put patients 
at risk of serious side effects (if too much drug is delivered) or fatal cancer (if too little drug is 
delivered)—for no good medical or scientific reason. 
Sixth, the FDA codified the various bioequivalence methods in descending order of 
“accuracy, sensitivity, and reproducibility” in 21 C.F.R. § 320.24.  Those methods are: (1) in 
vivo testing in humans in which the active drug is measured in blood or plasma; (2) in vivo 
testing in humans in which the active drug is measured in urine; (3) in vivo testing in humans in 
which a pharmacological effect of the drug is measured over time; (4) well-controlled clinical 
trials that establish the safety and effectiveness of the drug product in patients; and (5) a 
currently available in vitro test acceptable to the FDA.10  For a generic drug like an oral pill that 
is systemically absorbed, bioequivalence can be shown via pharmacokinetics studies in blood, 
plasma or urine.  This is the FDA’s preferred bioequivalence method.  For topical prescription 
drugs which act locally and are not absorbed systemically, pharmacokinetic studies cannot be 
done.  For those drugs, the FDA has historically required clinical trials, as they are the next best 
method in terms of accuracy, sensitivity and reproducibility, by the FDA’s own admission.  In 
the FDA’s recent public workshop on topical generic drugs, the FDA is now supporting 
approvals with in vitro release testing (“IVRT”) and IVPT which are in vitro tests (within 
category (5) in 21 C.F.R. § 320.24 above), the least accurate, reproducible, or sensitive 
bioequivalence method.   When a generic cytotoxic topical drug with a severe and lengthy side 
effect profile is pending before the FDA for approval, the FDA should require the applicant to 
use the most accurate, reproducible, and sensitive bioequivalence method possible—a clinical 
trial testing safety and efficacy.  Particularly, where, like 5% 5-fluorouracil cream, such a clinical 
comparative study has been done previously, the FDA should continue to require clinical trials to 
be done. 
Seventh, the FDA has concluded in the past that with respect to Efudex®, 
comparative clinical trials are required to determine whether “the incidence and severity of 
adverse reactions is different between the test product and RLD.”11  The FDA must act in a 
manner consistent with its earlier decision to require clinical bioequivalence trials for generic 
versions of Efudex®.  Any deviation from its earlier decision will be accorded less deference by

10 21 C.F.R. § 320.24(b). 
11 Draft Guidance on Fluorouracil, at 3.   
 
 
 
 
 
5 
 
a court, and has a high likelihood of being found arbitrary and capricious.  With Efudex®, there 
is no legitimate scientific or medical reason for deviating from the FDA’s earlier decision to 
require such clinical bioequivalence trials.   
For each of these reasons, the suggestion that the FDA should implement new approval 
pathways is both unnecessary and inappropriate with respect to generic equivalents of Efudex®.  
Such alternative approval pathways would provide little, if any, benefit to the public.  In fact, 
such alternative pathways would create a real risk of significant (and permanent) physical harm 
to patients using a generic not approved upon the successful completion of a clinical trial. 
II. 
STATEMENT OF GROUNDS 
A. 
There Is No Need to Permit Alternative Approval Pathways for Generic Equivalents 
of Efudex® 
At the October 20 public workshop, the FDA made clear that its new quest to approve 
IVRT/IVPT protocols is driven by the lack of generics for topical drugs generally.  Sam Raney, 
PhD, the Scientific Lead for Topical and Transdermal Drug Products, observed that 89% of 
prescriptions dispensed for overall drug products were generics.12  Dr. Raney recommends that 
efficient in vitro bioequivalent methods be used to approve new generic topical products to 
combat the problem of topical products that have no generics available.  Similarly, Robert 
Lionberger, PhD, the Director of the Office of Research and Standards, Office of Generic Drugs 
at FDA, in his concluding remarks at the October 20 session, set the FDA’s goal to have three 
generic products approved for every prescription product to stimulate competition. 
Very few topical drugs meet these criteria. 
But Efudex® and its generics do. 
For Efudex®, there are already three available generic versions: an authorized generic 
(distributed and sold in Mylan packaging), and two ANDA generics (Spear and Taro).13  The 
Spear and Taro products are both ANDA products, and were approved after successfully 
completing comparative clinical efficacy trials.  The generics (including the authorized generic) 
comprised an astounding 99.8% of all Efudex® sales in the year ending in December 2017.14    
                                                           
12 Raney at 5. 
13 Orange Book: Approved Drugs with Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations, U.S. Food and 
Drug Admin., https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/ob/search_product.cfm (last accessed 
Mar. 1, 2018); Mylan Completes Acquisition of Two Limited-Competition Dermatological Drugs 
from Valeant, Mylan (Feb. 6, 2012) http://newsroom.mylan.com/press-releases?item=122494. 
14 IMS NPA Data, IQVIA (available at https://www.iqvia.com/ ) (last accessed Jan. 18, 2018).

This finding is further confirmed by an FTC complaint (now resolved) observing that “Efudex 
sales have been almost completely displaced by sales of the three generic versions of the drug.”15 
More generally, there are four active ingredients on the market today that are used alone 
to treat actinic keratosis: Fluorouracil, Imiquimod, Ingenol Mebutate, and Diclofenac Sodium.  
Of those four, only Ingenol Mebutate does not have a generic and it represents only 4.1% of the 
actinic keratosis market.16  
When comparing the actual prescription sales figures in the actinic keratosis market 
overall, and for Efudex® specifically, an overwhelming number of sales in the actinic keratosis 
market are of generic products.  According to IMS Data available as of January 17, 2018, in the 
12 months ending in December 2017, there were 1,969,509 tubes of product sold in the actinic 
keratosis market.  Only 178,168 of those tubes (9.07%) were for brand products.  An 
overwhelming majority, 91%, of tubes sold in the actinic keratosis market in 2017, were for 
generic drugs.  This is higher than the 2016 national average of generic drug sales.17   
For this reason, Efudex® should not be a priority for the FDA to evaluate alternative 
bioequivalence methods for ANDA approval. 
B. 
5-Fluorouracil Is a Cytotoxic Chemotherapy Drug with Potentially Severe Side 
Effects Used to Treat a Precursor to Skin Cancer 
5-fluorouracil was originally synthesized in the 1950’s by Dr. Charles Heidelberger as a 
systemic chemotherapy treatment, and Hoffmann-La Roche, Inc. conducted the original clinical 
trials proving its anti-cancerous properties.  5-fluorouracil (“5-FU”) “inhibits the activity of 
thymidylate synthetase, which affects pyrimidine synthesis and leads to depletion of intracellular 
TTP pools.  5-FU has also been proposed to interfere with activity of ribosomal RNA binding 
protein (RRBP), at the level of pre-ribosomal RNA (pre-RNA) processing.”18  The original 5-FU 
was introduced in 1957 for clinical use against solid tumors.19  On June 4, 1970, the FDA 
approved NDA 16-831 filed by Hoffmann-La Roche, Inc. for the topical application of 5-
Fluorouracil Cream 5% (Efudex®) to treat solar keratosis.20

The goal of any clinical trial involving 5-FU is to test (1) the comparable efficacy of the 
generic product; and (2) all adverse events must be reported “to determine if the incidence and 
severity of adverse reactions is different between the test product and RLD.”21  The side effect 
profile as described in the Efudex® package insert reads as follows: 
The most frequent adverse reactions to Fluorouracil Cream occur locally and are 
often related to an extension of the pharmacological activity of the drug. These 
include burning, crusting, allergic contact dermatitis, erosions, erythema, 
hyperpigmentation, irritation, pain, photosensitivity, pruritus, scarring, rash, 
soreness and ulceration.22 
These potentially severe side effects from overexposure to 5-FU (which occurs 
frequently) include skin erosions and ulceration.23  Skin erosion is an open area of skin that 
results from loss of part or all of the epidermis.24  Patients who experience skin erosion describe 
the experience as painful and at least temporarily disfiguring.25  Severe side effects of erosions 
and ulceration may lead to oozing, crusting, and scabbing.26  Severe consequences/sequelae of 
erosions and ulceration can result in secondary bacterial infection (impetiginization) and end in 
irreversible scarring.27

common and expected side effect as a result of Efudex® treatment:

In fact, fluorouracil is so toxic that it requires special handling pursuant to safety and 
regulatory standards at all stages—from the manufacture of the drug product to treatment using 
the product.  When manufacturing fluorouracil, all personnel who come in contact with the 
fluorouracil must gown in personnel protective equipment (including a pressurized HAZMAT 
suit, double latex gloves, special rubber boots, and a full mask respirator).  The drug is contained 
in what is dubbed the “Slurry Room”.  To go from the Slurry Room to the rest of the facility, 
personnel must pass through a series of two interlocked doors, where only one door may be open 
at a time. Before exiting the Slurry Room, personnel must have the exterior of their suit rinsed in 
a shower, and the room itself is also rinsed down immediately following sampling or weighing of 
fluorouracil. Once personnel remove the single-use HAZMAT suit and gloves, the protective 
gear is disposed by incineration only.  The entire manufacturing facility, including its HVAC 
system and HEPA filters, is in fact specially designed so that the powdered form of fluorouracil 
is absolutely contained and there is no opportunity for cross-contamination. Fluorouracil is 
“[v]ery hazardous in case of skin contact (irritant), of ingestion.  Hazardous in case of inhalation.  
Slightly hazardous in case of skin contact (permeator), or eye contact (irritant).  Severe over-
exposure can result in death.”31   
The FDA tightly controls human exposure to cytotoxic drugs.  Before any human study 
may be performed using a cytotoxic drug, the FDA requires that an Investigational New Drug 
Application (“IND”) be submitted for FDA approval.32  For 5-FU trials specifically, the FDA 
requires that if the test drug is “applied with fingers, the hands should be washed immediately

Efudex® is a topical chemotherapy treatment used to treat actinic keratosis, a precursor 
to SCC, a non-melanoma skin cancer.34  “Actinic keratosis exists on a continuum with squamous 
cell carcinoma, and shared alterations in gene expression confirm this relationship.”35  The 
American Academy of Dermatology reports that the risk of transformation of actinic keratosis to 
SCC within one year is about 8% (with a range of 0.025% to 20%).36  “Patients with actinic 
keratosis, especially [w]hite men and the elderly, have a sixfold increased odds of developing 
non-melanoma or melanoma skin cancer.”37  While SCC is not the most common nonmelanoma 
skin cancer, it accounts “for the majority of NMSC [non-melanoma skin cancer]-related 
metastatic disease and death….”38  Actinic Keratosis is a common, treatable skin disease that is 
caused by UV damage from sun exposure and is characterized by erythematous, rough papules 
or patches on sun exposed skin.39  Many actinic keratosis patients have around 50-100 actinic 
keratosis lesions, and the average actinic keratosis patient has approximately 10-20 lesions.40  
While SCCs arising from actinic keratosis generally remain localized to the skin, they can 
metastasize with fatal result.41  From SCC arising from sun-exposed skin (and, in sun-exposed 
skin, SCC nearly always arise from pre-existing actinic keratosis), the American Academy of 
Dermatology reports that the rate of metastasis to regional lymph nodes is approximately 5%.42  
Treatment of actinic keratosis is crucial to halt its progression to potentially severe, and even 
fatal, forms of skin cancer.43  For this reason, dermatologists aggressively treat actinic keratosis 
before the actinic keratosis can develop into skin cancer.44 
From December 2016 to present, the FDA has drafted guidances to the industry 
permitting the use of a combination of IVPT and IVRT to show bioequivalence to certain topical 
RLD products.  Those four prescription drugs are acyclovir topical cream, silver sulfadiazine 
topical cream, dapsone topical gel, and ivermectin topical cream.   Unlike 5-FU, none of these

and in accordance with 21 C.F.R. §§ 10.25(a) and 10.30 to request that the Commissioner of 
Food and Drugs (1) deny approval to any abbreviated new drug application for a mycophenolate 
mofetil oral suspension product that relies on only metabolite data to establish bioequivalence to 
the reference listed drug and (2) change the therapeutic equivalence rating from AB for any 
previously-approved abbreviated new drug applications for a mycophenolate mofetil oral 
suspension product that relies on only metabolite data to establish bioequivalence to the 
reference listed drug or that does not include a nasogastric study as required by the current draft 
guidance. 
A. 
Action Requested 
The undersigned specifically requests that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA): 
 Withdraw the current Draft Guidance for Mycophenolate Mofetil Oral 
Suspension1 that allows the use of metabolite data only to establish 
bioequivalence (BE) to the reference listed drug (RLD);  
 Issue new guidance for an ANDA for a mycophenolate mofetil oral suspension 
product to require the use of data for both the parent compound and its metabolite 
to establish BE with the RLD; 
 Deny approval to any ANDA for a mycophenolate mofetil oral suspension 
product that relies on only metabolite data to establish BE with the RLD; 
                                                 
1 Exhibit A, FDA Draft Guidance on Mycophenolate Mofetil Oral Suspension, revised October 2017 (“Oral 
Suspension Draft Guidance”) 
 
2 
 
 Change the therapeutic equivalence rating from AB for any previously-approved 
ANDA for a mycophenolate mofetil oral suspension product that does not use 
both the parent compound and metabolite data to establish BE to the RLD; and 
 Change the therapeutic equivalence rating from AB for any previously-approved 
ANDA for a mycophenolate mofetil oral suspension product that does not include 
the In Vitro Comparative Feeding Tube Studies required by the current Oral 
Suspension Draft Guidance. 
B. 
Statement of Grounds 
Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is the 2-morpholinoethyl ester of mycophenolic acid 
(MPA), an immunosuppressive agent.2  MMF was originally marketed by Genentech3 under the 
trade name Cellcept® and first approved on May 3, 1995, as a capsule product for oral 
administration4.  The CellCept® oral suspension product was approved on October 1, 1998.5   
In October 2017, FDA issued a Draft Guidance on Mycophenolate Mofetil Oral 
Suspension.6  The Oral Suspension Draft Guidance was a revision of a guidance first published 
in June 2010, and revised in February 2014.7  The current Oral Suspension Draft Guidance 
recommends analyzing both mycophenolate mofetil and its active metabolite, mycophenolic acid 
(MPA) to establish BE.8  However, the Oral Suspension Draft Guidance also permits analysis of 
the metabolite only, “if you can demonstrate that it is not possible to measure mycophenolate 
mofetil in plasma accurately and reliably.”9 
The Oral Suspension Draft Guidance’s permission to forego measuring MMF is outdated.  
It is now possible, where it might not have been previously, to quantitatively measure small 
concentrations of MMF in human plasma.10  This method allows BE to be evaluated using MMF, 
in addition to MPA.11  Thus, ANDA applicants can no longer “demonstrate that it is not possible 
to measure mycophenolate mofetil in plasma accurately and reliably,” and the Oral Suspension 
Draft Guidance should be revised accordingly.

In addition, analysis of the metabolite only is not sufficient to ensure BE of a generic 
MMF oral suspension product.  Thus, any mycophenolate mofetil oral suspension products with 
previously-approved ANDAs should not be rated AB for therapeutic equivalence until the 
products can demonstrate BE using both MMF and MPA pharmacokinetics. 
Mycophenolate mofetil is a prodrug, which is converted in vivo to its active metabolite, 
MPA.12  After oral administration, MMF is essentially completely hydrolyzed by 
carboxylesterases to MPA.13  However, formulation excipients can affect carboxylase activity, 
thus affecting the conversion of MMF to the active metabolite MPA.14   
MPA undergoes further metabolism, which is affected by individual genetics and can 
additionally lead to pharmacokinetic variability.15  The oral bioavailability of MPA is near 
100%, but can vary from person to person.16  MPA blood level differences can drastically affect 
the outcome for patients, potentially causing acute toxicity (for high levels) or transplant 
rejection (for low levels).17   
ANDAs are required to include evidence or information to allow FDA to determine that 
the drug product in the application is bioequivalent to the RLD.18  Analysis of MPA 
pharmacokinetics to establish BE, as required by the Oral Suspension Draft Guidance, ensures 
that differences in MPA metabolism are accounted for in any potential generic MMF oral 
suspension product.  However, without demonstrating BE for MMF as well, a potential generic 
MMF oral suspension product may vary significantly from the RLD in its MMF 
pharmacokinetics, which can then lead to unpredictable outcomes for patients.   
Although systemic concentrations of MMF are very low following administration, 
requiring analysis of the pharmacokinetics of MMF in the BE analysis would protect patients.  
Any generic MMF oral suspension product should be required to demonstrate that both MMF 
and MPA have equivalent pharmacokinetics to the RLD.  Patients may have variability in 
metabolism in converting MMF to MPA, which would not be accounted for if only 
pharmacokinetics of MPA are considered.  This could lead to variations in dosing and efficacy 
for patients given generic MMF oral suspension products if BE is not established with both 
MMF and MPA.

Requiring analysis of prodrug pharmacokinetics to prove BE is not unreasonable.  For 
example, FDA has recommended measuring concentrations of parent compounds to establish BE 
for other prodrugs, including midodrine hydrochloride19 and temozolomide20, both of which are 
converted in vivo to active metabolites21.  The same should be required for mycophenolate 
mofetil, particularly since technology exists that can accurately and reliably measure the parent 
compound in human plasma. 
Finally, the Oral Suspension Draft Guidance requires in vitro comparative feeding tube 
studies, which ensure that nasogastric administration of the generic MMF oral suspension 
product actually delivers the same amount of MMF to a patient as the RLD.  These studies are 
essential to demonstrate that the generic MMF oral suspension product is the same as the RLD.  
Without confirmation that an equivalent dose is administered by a generic MMF oral suspension 
product, a patient receiving that generic product could actually be receiving too much or too little 
active ingredient, which affects whether that product is safe and effective for the patient.  Thus, 
any mycophenolate mofetil oral suspension products with previously-approved ANDAs should 
not be rated AB for therapeutic equivalence until the products can demonstrate equivalence by 
the in vitro comparative feeding tube studies. 
The undersigned hereby requests that FDA deny approval to any ANDA for a MMF oral 
suspension product that relies on only metabolite data to establish BE to the RLD.  In addition, 
the undersigned requests that FDA change the therapeutic equivalence rating from AB for any 
previously-approved ANDA for a MMF oral suspension product that (1) relies on only 
metabolite data to establish BE to the RLD or (2) does not include a nasogastric study as 
required by the current draft guidance.  These actions are appropriate and necessary because 
MPA pharmacokinetics alone are insufficient to establish BE with the RLD. 
C. 
Environmental Impact 
Petitioner believes that under 21 C.F.R. § 25.31, this petition does not require an 
environmental impact analysis report. 
D. 
Economic Impact 
Under 21 C.F.R. § 10.30(b), economic impact information is to be submitted only when 
requested by the Commissioner following review of the petition.  Petitioner hereby commits to 
promptly provide this information, if so requested.

Petition_Title: Citizen Petition from the Alliance for Natural Hea
Petition_Text:
Citizen Petition 
March 15, 2018 
On behalf of our more than 610,000 consumer members, the Alliance for Natural 
Health USA submits this petition under 21 C.F.R. Section 10.20 and 10.30 and under 
sections 503A and 503B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to request the 
Commissioner of Food and Drugs revise its Investigational New Drug Applications 
Guidance to clarify that an investigational new drug application is not required for 
dietary supplements to conduct a study when there is no intent to seek drug approval for 
the product or the clinical investigations are being used to substantiate a legal dietary 
supplement claim. 
A. Action Requested 
This petition requests that the Commissioner revise Section VI.D.1. of the Guidance for 
Clinical Investigators, Sponsors, and IRBs: Investigational New Drug Applications 
(INDs) – Determining Whether Human Research Studies Can be Conducted Without an 
IND to clarify that an investigational new drug application is not required for dietary 
supplements to conduct a study when the sponsor or manufacturer or distributor has no 
intent to seek drug approval for the product or the clinical investigations are being used 
to substantiate a legal dietary supplement claim, e.g., structure/function claim or health 
claim. 
Although portions of this Guidance have been stayed (see the Notice of Stay published in 
the Federal Register of October 30, 2015 (80 FR 66907)), the Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA) still maintains that the investigation of conventional foods or 
dietary supplements to diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, or prevent a disease, continues to 
require an IND. 
The Commissioner should remove the final paragraph of Section VI.D.1: 
However, if the clinical investigation is intended to evaluate the dietary 
supplement’s ability to diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, or prevent a disease, an 
IND is required under part 312. For example, a clinical investigation designed 
to study the relationship between a dietary supplement’s effect on normal 
structure or function in humans (e.g., guarana and maximal oxygen uptake) or 
to characterize the mechanism by which a dietary supplement acts to maintain 
 
2 
such structure or function (e.g., fiber and bowel regularity) would not need to 
be conducted under an IND. However, a clinical investigation designed to 
evaluate a dietary supplement’s ability to prevent osteoporosis or to treat 
chronic diarrhea or constipation would need to be conducted under an IND. 
B. Statement of Grounds 
The FDA requires an IND for clinical trials to evaluate a dietary supplement’s ability to 
diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, or prevent a disease. However, supplements are not 
drugs and are not intended to diagnose, cure, mitigate, or prevent disease. A supplement 
company may need to conduct a study that investigates a supplement’s ability to 
diagnose, cure, mitigate, treat, or prevent a disease in order to substantiate a legal 
dietary supplement claim. Section 201(ff)(3)(B)(ii) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. 
321(ff)(3)(B)(ii)) excludes from the definition of a dietary supplement any “article 
authorized for investigation as a new drug, antibiotic, or biological for which 
substantial clinical investigations have been instituted and for which the existence of 
such investigations has been made public, which was not before such approval, 
certification, licensing, or authorization marketed as a dietary supplement or as a 
food.” 
Requiring an IND naturally creates published studies, and turns a dietary ingredient 
into a drug if it has not been previously marketed as a dietary supplement or as a food. 
Thus, Section VI.D.1. of the IND Guidance means that complying with the law to 
substantiate a claim to legally market a dietary ingredient will turn it into a drug and 
threaten its very status as a marketable dietary ingredient. 
The FDA promulgated Title 21 C.F.R. Part 312 to provide procedures and requirements 
governing the use of investigational new drugs as part of the drug approval process, and 
not as a way of regulating the clinical study of foods and dietary supplements. The 
agency made this purpose clear in the preamble to its final rule establishing Part 312, 
called the IND Rewrite: 
This action is one part of a larger effort by FDA to improve the agency’s drug 
approval process . . . The objectives of the IND Rewrite final rule are to establish 
an efficient investigational drug process in order both: (a) To focus FDA’s 
attention during the early phase of clinical research on protecting the safety of 
human test subjects . . . and (b) to facilitate consultation between FDA and drug 
sponsors . . . to help ensure that the design of major clinical trials is acceptable 
and will support marketing approval if the test results are favorable. These 
changes are also intended to encourage innovation and drug development while 
continuing to assure the safety of test subjects. 
It is therefore clear that at the time that FDA promulgated its IND regulations, the 
agency intended them to apply solely to articles being researched as therapeutic drugs 
for which new drug applications were contemplated.  
In the IND Guidance, the FDA explains that an IND is needed if three conditions exist – 
one condition being that the research involves a drug. Drugs are defined under Part 321 
 
3 
as, among other things, “articles intended for use in the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, 
treatment, or prevention of disease in man or other animals.” Further, Part 312 says that 
IND’s are required for all products that are subject to section 505 of the FD&C Act, 
which pertains to new drugs. 
Supplements are not covered under these regulations because supplements are not 
drugs intended to cure or mitigate disease. The Dietary Supplement Health and 
Education Act of 1994 excludes from the definition of dietary supplement “an article 
authorized for investigation as a new drug…for which substantial clinical investigations 
have been instituted and for which the existence of such investigation has been made 
public,” unless the article was marketed before the IND became effective. 
If an IND is required for clinical investigations on a new dietary ingredient to 
substantiate a structure/function or health claim it could eliminate the ability to market 
the product as a dietary supplement. Furthermore, a supplement claiming to diagnose, 
cure, mitigate, treat, or prevent disease is, by definition, a misbranded drug. Thus, 
supplement research should not trigger IND regulations. 
Furthermore, the FDA has historically regulated products based on intended use, which 
is determined by the manufacturer’s marketing representations and labeling of a 
product. Courts have consistently upheld this approach, which is also supported by past 
agency statements. The FDA should do the same in this case – consider the end use of 
the product rather than the intention of the clinical investigation to determine whether 
an IND is required. The FDA offers no rationale or legal basis for the IND Guidance’s 
departure from past agency practice to now focus on the intent of the clinical 
investigation to evaluate a product’s intended use. 
For assurance that a study should not require an IND, signed affidavits can attest to a 
company or researcher’s intention to not market the supplement or food as a drug 
following a clinical trial assessing the therapeutic benefits of a supplement or food. 
Conclusion 
Dietary supplements should not be subject to IND regulations intended for drugs that 
could eliminate the ability to market a product as a dietary supplement. 
The FDA should clarify that, if the supplement under investigation is fully compliant 
with IRB procedures and not represented as a drug through marketing statements, and 
any claims made for the supplement are lawful dietary supplement claims, then FDA 
should not regulate the product as a drug by applying its Part 312 procedures.  
Signed affidavits can attest to a company or researcher’s intention to not market the 
supplement or food as a drug following a clinical trial assessing the therapeutic benefits 
of a supplement or food. 
C. Environmental Impact 
Petitioner claims a categorical exclusion under 21 C.F.R. §25.30(h). 
 
4 
D. Economic Impact 
Pursuant to 21 C.F.R. §10.30(b), economic impact information will be submitted by the 
Petitioner upon the request of the Commissioner.  
E. Certification 
The undersigned certifies, that, to the best knowledge and belief of the undersigned, this 
petition includes all information and views on which the petition relies, and that it 
includes representative data and information known to the petitioner which are 
unfavorable to the petition. 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
Gretchen DuBeau, Esq. 
Executive and Legal Director  
Alliance for Natural Health USA  
 
Cc: Mr. Steven Tave, Director, Office of Dietary Supplement Programs

NDA, Tyvaso also includes the Tyvaso Inhalation System Refill Kit, which contains a

A. 
Statutory And Regulatory Background 
 
1. Approval of new drugs under section 505(b) and 505(j) of the FDCA 
 
To obtain approval to market an innovative drug, a manufacturer must submit an 
NDA under section 505(b) of the FDCA.  The NDA must contain scientific data and 
other information demonstrating that the drug is safe and effective.8  Specifically, the 
NDA must show that the “drug is safe for use,” and “will have the effect it purports or is
